More than three centuries and a half ago, in the mid spring of 1492, the angel of the dawn travelled, as he travels still, with broad slow wing from the Levant to the Pillars of Hercules, and from the Caucasus over the snowy Alpine ridges to the dark nakedness of the western isles. He saw nearly the same firm outlines and unstable waters; the same mountain shadows lying long in the same valleys; olive-mounts whose leaves turned pale as fish-bellies when the light struck them sideways; pine-forests breathing out resin and coldness; broad plains green with young corn that smelled, even from the height of the sky, of damp earth newly broken, and of the sweet sourness of grass after rain. He saw domes and spires lifting themselves by river-sides, and masts along the many-curved sea-coast like reeds at the edge of a marsh, all in the same places where they rise to-day.

And as that faint travelling light slipped into the dwellings of men, it fell, then as now, on nestling children warm as loaves drawn from an oven; on the haggard waking of sorrow and sickness, when the mouth tastes bitter as if one had chewed wormwood; on the hasty rising of the hard-handed labourer whose palms smelled of iron tools and wet rope; and on the late sleep of the night-student, who had been questioning stars, sages, and his own soul for a hidden knowledge that might break through the barrier of brief life. River-courses that have shaped men have hardly changed; and the other streams—the life-currents in human hearts—ebb and flow still with the same great needs, the same great loves and terrors. Hunger and labour, seed-time and harvest, love and death: these are headings that return like the tolling of an old bell over new roofs.

If, instead of following the dim daybreak, our imagination pauses on a certain spot and waits for fuller morning, we may see a world-famous city whose outline has scarcely altered since the days when Columbus was still waiting and arguing for three poor vessels. The very standing of it there—by water, under hills—seems like an unviolated symbol amidst the flux of human things, reminding us that we resemble the men of the past more than we differ. And if the spirit of a Florentine citizen—one whose eyes were closed for the last time while Columbus’s petition was still in the air—could return and pause where our thought is pausing, he might believe there would be fellowship and understanding for him among the inheritors of his birthplace.

Let us suppose such a Shade is permitted to revisit the glimpses of golden morning, and stands once more on the hill of San Miniato, looking down on Florence from the south. He is clothed as he lived: the folds of his well-lined black silk lucco hang in grave unbroken lines from neck to ankle; his plain cloth cap with its becchetto—long strip of drapery to serve as scarf in case of need—sits above a penetrating face. Not handsome, perhaps, but with a firm mouth; the lip and chin close-shaven, as if he had always wanted to keep himself distinctly human, and not let beard and indulgence make a mask of him. That face is charged with memories: of keen bargaining in cool loggie; of councils where men’s voices rose and fell like a tide; of dinners in which the meat was carved with ceremony and the jokes were sliced as sharply.

As he looks, familiarity is stronger than any perception of change. He thinks he might descend among the streets and take up the busy life where he left it. For it is not only the mountains and the westward-bending river he recognises; not only Mount Morello’s dark side opposite, and the long valley of the Arno stretching its grey low-tufted luxuriance toward Carrara; and the steep height of Fiesole with its crown of monastic walls and cypresses; and the green and grey slopes sprinkled with villas he can name as he looks at them. He recognises things closer to daily walks. Though he misses the ring of towers—seventy or more once surmounting the walls like a diadem—his eyes do not dwell on the blank; they are drawn to the unique tower springing like a tall flower-stem from the square turreted mass of the old palace in the heart of the city, none the worse for four centuries. The great dome too—greatest in the world—once only a daring thought in the mind of a small quick-eyed man: there it rises still, its curves eclipsing the hills.

And the bell-towers—Giotto’s with its distant hint of colour, the graceful-spired Badia, and the rest—he remembers looking at them from the shoulder of his nurse, before he could even pronounce the names that later would sit in his mouth like well-known foods. “Surely,” he thinks, “Florence can still ring her bells with the solemn hammer-sound that used to beat on the hearts of her citizens and strike out the fire there.” In his memory, the bells were not mere ornament; they were a whole city’s breathing made audible—metal lungs that gave measure to fasting and feasting, to work and worship, to the hush before trouble and the roaring after a victory. He listens for them now as one listens for the first crackle from a hearth on a cold morning.

On the right stands the long dark mass of Santa Croce, where they buried famous dead—laying laurel on cold brows and fanning them with the breath of praise and banners. But Santa Croce had no spire then. Florentines were too full of great building projects to carry them all out in stone and marble: there were frescoes and shrines to pay for; there were rapacious condottieri to bribe, royalty to flatter, territories to purchase; façades and spires must wait. Now his eye catches the spire. “What architect can the Frati Minori have employed to build that?” he wonders, and the wonder has an edge, as if he had expected to taste a familiar broth and found an unknown herb in it. “If it had been built in my day, Filippo Brunelleschi or Michelozzo would have devised something of another fashion—something worthy to crown Arnolfo’s church.”

With a sigh, he lets his eyes travel to the city walls, and there the change draws wonder in earnest. Why are five of the eleven convenient gates closed? And why—above all—are the towers levelled that were once glory and defence? Has the world become so peaceful, then? Do Florentines dwell in such harmony that there are no conspiracies to bring ambitious exiles home again with armed bands at their back? These are difficult questions; it is easier, and pleasanter, to recognise the old than to account for the new.

There flows Arno, with its bridges just where they used to be: the Ponte Vecchio, least like other bridges in the world, laden with the same quaint shops where our Spirit remembers lingering on his way—perhaps to look at the progress of Messer Luca Pitti’s great palace, built with huge stones quarried from the hill of Bogoli behind; perhaps to transact business with the cloth-dressers in Oltrarno. The Pitti roof is hidden from San Miniato; but the yearning of the old Florentine is not for Messer Luca’s ambitious house. It is for the narrow streets and the humming piazze where life was thick as steam above a pot and every man’s voice seemed to carry flavor—salt of sarcasm, pepper of envy, honey of flattery—according to the company.

Is not the anxious voting with black and white beans still going on down there? Who are the Priori now, eating their soberly regulated official dinners in the Palazzo Vecchio—removes of tripe and boiled partridges, dishes whose smell clung to official robes as surely as incense clung to church hangings—seasoned by practical jokes against the ill-fated butt among those potent signors? Are not the significant banners still hung from windows, still distributed with decent pomp under Orcagna’s loggia every two months? He remembers the weight of civic ritual as something like the weight of a well-made loaf: dense, sustaining, and shared. Life had zest when he trod those marble steps and shared the dignities. His politics had an area as wide as his trade, stretching from Syria to Britain; but they had also the passionate intensity that belongs only to a narrow scene of corporate action, where men meet every day, measure each other with the eye, and cannot escape the echo of their own words. There, public life had its own acoustic law: the murmur under a loggia, the chant of a procession, the sudden shout in a piazza—each sound a thread binding the citizen to the common good, or tightening into a noose when factions pulled.

He loved his honours and his gains, the business of counting-house and guild, of council-chamber and committee. He loved his enmities too, and fingered the white bean meant to keep a hated name out of the borsa with more complacency than if it had been a golden florin. He loved to strengthen his family by a good alliance, and went home with triumphant light in his eyes after concluding a satisfactory marriage for son or daughter under his favourite loggia in the evening cool. He loved his game at chess there, and his biting jest, and even his coarse joke, as not beneath the dignity of a man eligible for the highest magistracy. In the way of office he had learned much: he had been of the Ten who managed war, of the Eight who attended to home discipline, of the Priori—Signori—heads of the executive; he had risen even to Gonfaloniere; he had gone on embassies to Pope and Venetians; he had been commissary to the hired army, directing inglorious bloodless battles where no man died of brave breast wounds, virtuosi colpi, but only of falls and tramplings. So he had learned to distrust without bitterness, to look on life mainly as a game of skill—yet not dead to traditions of heroism and clean-handed honour.

And it was part of his pride that he was tinctured with the learning of his age, judging not altogether with the vulgar but in harmony with the ancients. In his prime he had been eager for the most correct manuscripts; he had paid many florins for antique vases and disinterred busts—some truncis naribus, their noses missing like crusts broken off by time, but not the less “authentic.” In his old age he had made haste to see the first sheets of that fine Homer which was among the early glories of the Florentine press. Yet for all that he had not neglected to hang up a waxen image of himself under the Madonna Annunziata, nor to do penance in large gifts to shrines of saints whose lives had not been modelled on the study of classics; he had not even neglected liberal bequests toward buildings for the Frati, against whom he had levelled many a jest. The unseen Powers were mighty. Who knew—who was sure—that there was any name given behind which there was no angry force to appease, no intercessory pity to win? Were not gems medicinal, though they only pressed the finger? Were not all things charged with occult virtues? Lucretius might be right—he was ancient and a great poet. Luigi Pulci, too, suspected of believing nothing from the roof upward, had often sounded right over supper when wine and jokes circulated fast, though he was only a poet in the vulgar tongue. There were learned personages who maintained that Aristotle—wisest of men unless Plato were wiser—was thoroughly irreligious; and a liberal scholar must entertain all speculations.

But negatives might, after all, prove false; nay, seemed manifestly false, as circling hours swept past and turned round with graver faces. For had not the world become Christian? Had he not been baptised in San Giovanni, where the dome is awful with symbols of coming judgment, where the altar bears a crucified Image that disturbs perfect complacency like a sudden silence at the end of a song? He was not a pagan philosopher, nor a philosophising pagan poet, but a man of the fifteenth century, inheriting its strange web: belief and unbelief; Epicurean levity and fetichistic dread; pedantic ethics mouthed by rote and crude passions acted out with childish impulsiveness; a leaning toward self-indulgent paganism and yet inevitable subjection to conscience, which in the unrest of new growth filled the air with prophecies and presentiments.

He had smiled, perhaps, and shaken his head dubiously when simple folk spoke of a Pope Angelico who was to come and bring in a new order—purify Church from simony, clergy from scandal—too different from what existed under Innocent the Eighth for a shrewd merchant to calculate upon. But he felt the evils of the time nevertheless; for he had public spirit, and public spirit can never be wholly immoral, since its essence is care for a common good.

That very Quaresima—Lent—of 1492 in which he died, still erect in his old age, he had listened in San Lorenzo, not without a mixture of satisfaction, to the preaching of a Dominican friar, Girolamo Savonarola. The Frate denounced with rare boldness the worldliness and vicious habits of the clergy; he insisted that Christian men must not live for their own ease while wrong triumphed in high places, must not spend wealth in outward pomp even in the churches while fellow-citizens suffered want and sickness. The words had moved his audience to such a pitch that women even took off their ornaments and delivered them up to be sold for the needy—metal and gem transformed into bread, broth, and linen. It was an alchemy more persuasive than any scholar’s disputation, and it had its own sound: the soft clink of chains and rings dropped into a wooden chest, the little gasp when a clasp was undone, the hush afterward as if the very air had been chastened.

“He was a noteworthy man, that Prior of San Marco,” thinks our Spirit. “Somewhat arrogant and extreme—especially in his denunciations of speedy vengeance. Ah, Iddio non paga il Sabato! God does not pay on a Saturday. The wages of men’s sins often linger in their payment, and I myself saw much established wickedness of long-standing prosperity. But a Frate Predicatore who wanted to move the people—how could he be moderate? He might have been less defiant and curt to Lorenzo de’ Medici, whose family were the makers of San Marco. Was that quarrel ever made up? And our Lorenzo himself, with dim outward eyes and subtle inward vision—did he get over that illness at Careggi? It was a sad uneasy face he would carry out of a world that had given him so much; and there were strong suspicions his handsome son would play Rehoboam. How has it all turned out? Which party is likely to be banished and have its houses sacked just now? Is there any successor of the incomparable Lorenzo, to whom the Great Turk sends presents—rare animals, rare relics, rare manuscripts, or fugitive enemies—suited to the tastes of a Christian Magnifico who is lettered and devout, and also slightly vindictive? And what scholar dictates the Latin letters of the Republic—what fiery philosopher lectures on Dante in the Duomo and goes home to write bitter invectives against the father and mother of the bad critic who faults his spelling? Are wiser heads leaning toward alliance with Pope and the Regno, or inclining ears to orators of France and Milan?”

“There is knowledge of these things to be had in the streets below,” he says to himself, “on the beloved marmi in front of the churches, and under the sheltering loggie, where surely citizens still have gossip and debates, bitter and merry jests as of old. The buildings are there. The changes cannot be so great in uncounted years. I will go down and hear—I will tread the familiar pavement, and hear once again the speech of Florentines.”

Go not down, good Spirit; for the changes are great, and the speech of Florentines would sound as a riddle in your ears. The very cadence you trusted—the old civic music of voices and bells—has shifted; meanings have slipped as fish slip in the hand, and words once warm with shared use have cooled, hardened, or vanished. If you must go, mingle with no politicians on the marmi, or elsewhere; ask no questions of trade in the Calimala; confuse yourself with no inquiries into scholarship, official or monastic. Only look at sunlight and shadow on the grand walls built solidly and enduring in their grandeur. Look at the faces of little children, making another sunlight amid the shadows of age. Look, if you will, into the churches, and hear the same chants, see the same images as of old—the images of willing anguish for a great end, of beneficent love and ascending glory. See upturned living faces, lips moving to the old prayers for help. These things have not changed.

Sunlight and shadow bring their old beauty and wake the old heart-strains at morning, noon, and eventide; the children are still the symbol of the eternal marriage between love and duty; and men still yearn for the reign of peace and righteousness—still own that life to be the highest which is conscious voluntary sacrifice. For the Pope Angelico is not come yet.

The Loggia de’ Cerchi lay folded into the very ribs of old Florence, where streets ran narrow as knife-cuts behind the Badia, and the stranger seldom threaded them unless he hunted—half in shame, half in reverence—for a certain severely simple doorway bearing the boastful sentence: Qui Nacque Il Divino Poeta. Once, in Dante’s hearing, those stones had answered back with iron and fury—family against family, the clash of steel as familiar as prayer. Now, in the fifteenth century, the same alleys gave out a different music: the hoarse teasing of woolcarders, the slap of hands on wet cloth, the unhistorical quarrels and fat jokes that rose from San Martino and Garbo like steam from a boiling pot.

Under the loggia, in the early morning of the ninth of April, 1492, two men held one another with their eyes as if a thread were drawn tight between them. One stood over the other, stooping, looking downward with the patient scrutiny of a man who had learned to appraise life by touch and bargain; the other lay on the pavement and stared up as if he had been woken from a dream by a sudden trumpet.

The standing man spoke first. Grey-haired, broad-shouldered, built in the Tuscan manner that seems hewn with the fist and polished with the pickaxe, he had a gravity cut deep about brow and mouth—as if he meant to refute, in advance, any contempt a passer-by might take from his rough workmanship. On the stones beside him he had set down a great bag of skins, swollen with its contents, and from his front hung a pedlar’s basket where small women’s-wares—thread, pins—lay cheek by jowl with jagged bits of glass, likely taken in trade.

“Young man,” he said, pointing with a thick finger, “when your chin has got a stiffer crop on it, you’ll know better than to take your nap in street-corners with a ring like that on your forefinger. By the holy ’vangels! if it had been anybody but me standing over you two minutes ago—but Bratti Ferravecchi is not the man to steal. The cat couldn’t eat her mouse if she didn’t catch it alive, and Bratti couldn’t relish gain if it had no taste of a bargain. Why, one San Giovanni, three years ago, the Saint sent a dead body in my way—a blind beggar, with his cap well-lined with pieces—but, if you’ll believe me, my stomach turned against the money I’d never bargained for, till it came into my head that San Giovanni owed me the pieces for what I spend yearly at the Festa; besides, I buried the body and paid for a mass—and so I saw it was a fair bargain. But how comes a young man like you, with the face of Messer San Michele, to be sleeping on a stone bed with the wind for a curtain?”

To the newly roused listener the man’s deep gutturals came as through water; yet the warning needed no translation. He looked down, saw the ring, and—obedient as a body trained by peril rather than politeness—slipped it off and thrust it under his doublet. As he rose he stretched himself, as if to coax blood back into limbs chilled by dawn-stone.

“Your tunic and hose match ill with that jewel, young man,” Bratti said, weighing him as he would a garment held up to the light. “Anybody might say the saints had sent you a dead body; but if you took the jewels, I hope you buried him—and you can afford a mass or two for him into the bargain.”

At those words a quick pain—like a needle under the nail—ran through the young man’s frame, arresting the careless lift of his chest. For one instant he turned on Bratti with a sharp frown that was more than sleep-shaken irritation. Then his face smoothed itself as a cook smooths flour over a board to hide last night’s knife-marks. He took off the red Levantine cap that hung like a great purse over his left ear, pushed back long dark-brown curls, and glanced down at his own weathered dress.

“You speak truth, friend,” he said, smiling as if the world were a jest worth hearing twice. “My garments are as weather-stained as an old sail, and they are not old either—only, like an old sail, they have had a sprinkling of the sea as well as the rain. The fact is, I’m a stranger in Florence; and when I came in footsore last night I preferred flinging myself in a corner of this hospitable porch to hunting any longer for a chance hostelry, which might turn out to be a nest of blood-suckers of more sorts than one.”

“A stranger, in good sooth,” Bratti answered, narrowing his eyes as if the young man’s vowels were coins whose stamp he did not trust. “For the words come all melting out of your throat, so that a Christian and a Florentine can’t tell a hook from a hanger. But you’re not from Genoa? More likely from Venice, by the cut of your clothes?”

“At this present moment,” the stranger said, still with that easy smile, “it is of less importance where I come from than where I can go to for a mouthful of breakfast. This city of yours turns a grim look on me just here. Can you show me the way to a more lively quarter, where I can get a meal and a lodging?”

“That I can,” said Bratti; and he looked pleased with the power of being needed. “And it is your good fortune, young man, that I have happened to be walking in from Rovezzano this morning, and turned out of my way to Mercato Vecchio to say an Ave at the Badia. That, I say, is your good fortune. But it remains to be seen what is my profit in the matter. Nothing for nothing. If I show you the way to Mercato Vecchio, you’ll swear by your patron saint to let me have the bidding for that stained suit of yours, when you set up a better—as doubtless you will.”

“Agreed, by San Niccolò,” the other laughed. “But now let us set off to this said Mercato, for I feel the want of a better lining to this doublet of mine which you are coveting.”

“Coveting? Nay,” said Bratti, and swung his skin-bag up onto his back with the practiced jerk that settles weight into muscle. He set off, and as he walked his voice broke open into the marketplace cry—harsh, creaking, like a cart-wheel complaining on dry axles, yet pitched to travel through stone corridors and morning air.

“Chi abbaratta—baratta—b’ratta—chi abbaratta cenci e vetri—b’ratta ferri vecchi?”

The street answered him with other sounds: a shutter lifted and thumped, a donkey’s hoof beat a hollow note, a woman called a child by some endearing name that held its own local flavor—one of those words that lose their savor when carried beyond their native quarter. Bratti’s cry kept its rhythm, the way a kitchen keeps its rhythm even under grief: the knife still falls, the pot still sings, the hands still know what they are doing.

“It’s worth but little,” he said presently, letting his voice drop back into talk. “Hose and altogether, your clothes are worth but little. Still, if you’ve a mind to set yourself up with a lute worth more than any new one, or with a sword that’s been worn by a Ridolfi, or with a paternoster of the best mode, I could let you have a great bargain, by making an allowance for the clothes. For, simple as I stand here, I’ve got the best-furnished shop in the Ferravecchi, and it’s close by the Mercato. The Virgin be praised! it’s not a pumpkin I carry on my shoulders. But I don’t stay caged in my shop all day: I’ve got a wife and a raven to stay at home and mind the stock. Chi abbaratta—baratta—b’ratta? ... And now, young man, where do you come from, and what’s your business in Florence?”

“I thought you liked nothing that came to you without a bargain,” said the stranger. “You’ve offered me nothing yet in exchange for that information.”

“Well, well; a Florentine doesn’t mind bidding a fair price for news: it stays the stomach a little though he may win no hose by it. If I take you to the prettiest damsel in the Mercato to get a cup of milk—that will be a fair bargain.”

“Nay; I can find her myself, if she be really in the Mercato; for pretty heads are apt to look forth of doors and windows. No, no. Besides, a sharp trader like you ought to know that he who bids for nuts and news, may chance to find them hollow.”

“Ah! young man,” Bratti said, giving him a side glance—half suspicion, half admiration—“you were not born of a Sunday—the salt-shops were open when you came into the world. You’re not a Hebrew, eh?—come from Spain or Naples, eh? Let me tell you the Frati Minori are trying to make Florence as hot as Spain for those dogs of hell that want to get all the profit of usury to themselves and leave none for Christians; and when you walk the Calimara with a piece of yellow cloth in your cap, it will spoil your beauty more than a sword-cut across that smooth olive cheek of yours. Abbaratta, baratta—chi abbaratta?—I tell you, young man, grey cloth is against yellow cloth; and there’s as much grey cloth in Florence as would make a gown and cowl for the Duomo, and there’s not so much yellow cloth as would make hose for Saint Christopher—blessed be his name, and send me a sight of him this day!—Abbaratta, baratta, b’ratta—chi abbaratta?”

“All that is very amusing information you are parting with for nothing,” the stranger returned, with a little edge of scorn. “But it happens not to concern me. I am no Hebrew.”

“See, now!” Bratti cried, delighted as if he had made a clean trade without putting hand to purse. “I’ve made a good bargain with mere words. I’ve made you tell me something, young man, though you’re as hard to hold as a lamprey. San Giovanni be praised! a blind Florentine is a match for two one-eyed men. But here we are in the Mercato.”

They came out of the close alleys into the broad piazza men called the Mercato Vecchio, the Old Market. It had been the belly of Florence for longer than anyone could count: provision-traffic from time immemorial, so that fond minds said the very ancestors from Fiesole once descended here from their high fastness to trade with the valley’s rustics. Wealth had not fled it in those earlier decades of the century: the Medici and other powerful houses of the popolani grassi had lived there, their ears perhaps not much offended by the loud roar of mingled dialects, their eyes not much shocked by the butchers’ stalls that old Antonio Pucci praised as a chief dignity of any market worth the name.

Yet that particular glory of mutton and veal was absent now: Lent still lay over Florence like a thin veil over bright food. The butchers’ “Art” stood in abeyance, and it was the harvest-time of those who trafficked in what the season allowed—market-gardeners with their heaps of greens, cheesemongers, sellers of macaroni, corn, eggs, milk, dried fruits. The change pulled women’s voices to the fore, so that the piazza rang with a sharper treble, the calls rising and falling like birds over a field.

Even so, the market had its perennial chorus: the experimental ringing of pots and pans; the chink and slap of money at the changers’ boards; the tempting cries from old-clothes stalls; the dice-players’ challenges; the vaunting of new linens and woollens, of wooden-ware, kettles, frying-pans. Narrow inlets choked with mules and carts, and the air thickened with remonstrance—those uncomplimentary phrases that seem to remain unchanged from age to age when bodies are crowded and tempers warmed.

And beneath the uglier sights—rags, beggary, the open-air drama of gaming where eagerness trembled and despair went blank, where sobs and blasphemy and blows came in their bitter sequence—there were still gentler offerings. Brood-rabbits with wide astonished eyes; doves and singing-birds for children’s gifts; kittens for sale; and here and there a handsome gattuccio, a Tom-cat with the highest character for mousing, his whiskers twitching at every scent. There were young cheeks, softly rounded and freshened by the start from far-off castelli at daybreak; and older faces, too, with the unfading charm of honest goodwill—like the steady fragrance of bread that persists even when the oven is cold.

High on a pillar in the center—an old pillar fetched from San Giovanni—stood Donatello’s stone Plenty, with a fountain near it where, as Pucci said, the good wives freshened their utensils and their throats also; not because wine was beyond them, but because they preferred to save the money for their husbands. The water’s trickle made its own mild music under the louder human din, a small clean sound that could steady the mind if one listened for it.

But on this particular morning the market’s face looked altered, as if some gust had turned every head at once. The deschi were only partly dressed with their goods, and purchasers had indeed assembled, alert for the finest greens, the most unexceptionable butter; yet when Bratti and the stranger entered, attention had slid away from bargaining into talk. Traders had turned their backs on their wares and joined knots of speakers that clustered at different points. An old-clothes vendor, caught mid-action in hanging out a pair of long hose, had in his distraction slung them round his own neck and hurried after the nearest group. A cheesemonger, oratorical by trade, stood with a piece of marzolino in one hand and a knife in the other, scoring his emphatic pauses straight into the cheese as if it were paper. Elderly market-women, their egg-baskets at dangerous angles, contributed a wailing fugue of invocation that rose and broke like wind over reeds.

In the general distraction, the Florentine boys—sour crabs, and proud of it—saw opportunity as quickly as a rat scents an unguarded pantry. Some darted at nuts and dried figs; others chose the farinaceous Lenten delicacies at cooked provision-stalls. Dogs, too, who had learned to take kindly to meatless fare, nosed with discriminating hunger and then vanished under the nearest shelter. Mules, kicking and plunging among impeding baskets, stretched their muzzles toward aromatic green-meat, snatching at parsley and fennel; the torn stems released their sharp scent in little bursts, as if the air itself were bruised.

“Diavolo!” Bratti muttered as he and his companion came, quite unnoticed, upon the noisy scene. “The Mercato is gone as mad as if the most Holy Father had excommunicated us again. I must know what this is. But never fear: it seems a thousand years to you till you see the pretty Tessa and get your cup of milk; but keep hold of me, and I’ll hold to my bargain. Remember, I’m to have the first bid for your suit—specially for the hose, which, with all their stains, are the best panno di garbo—as good as ruined, though, with mud and weather stains.”

He turned toward an old woman on the outside of the nearest group and shouted close to her ear, as if he meant to drive his words in like a nail.

“Ola, Monna Trecca! Here are the mules upsetting all your bunches of parsley: is the world coming to an end, then?”

Monna Trecca wheeled round, half fierce, half bewildered—eyes darting from Bratti to her disarranged goods and back again. Then she rushed toward her stall, flinging her first volley of rage at him as if he had personally loosened the mule’s halter.

“A bad Easter and a bad year to you, and may you die by the sword!”

Bratti, untroubled, slipped into the place she had left, within hearing of the narrative that had been holding her. He made a sign to the stranger to keep close.

“I tell you I saw it myself,” said a fat man, gripping a bunch of newly bought leeks as if the green shafts were proof in his hand. “I was in Santa Maria Novella and saw it myself. The woman started up and threw out her arms, and cried out and said she saw a big bull with fiery horns coming down on the church to crush it. I saw it myself.”

“Saw what, Goro?” asked a slim man with a roguish twinkle, dressed in a close jerkin, a skull-cap lodged carelessly over his left ear as if it had fallen there by chance. A delicate linen apron was tucked up on one side, and a razor sat in his belt. “Saw the bull, or only the woman?”

“Why, the woman, to be sure; but it’s all one, mi pare,” the fat man answered, contemptuous of such distinctions. “It doesn’t alter the meaning—va!”

“Meaning? no, no; that’s clear enough,” several voices broke in at once—and then the market’s speech became a hailstorm of phrases: “Lights shooting over San Lorenzo for three nights together”—“Thunder in the clear starlight”—“Lantern of the Duomo struck with the sword of Saint Michael”—“Palle”—“All smashed”—“Lions tearing each other to pieces”—“Ah! and they might well”—“Boto caduto in Santissima Nunziata!”—“Died like the best of Christians”—“God will have pardoned him”—words crossing and striking, each speaker needing utterance more than reply.

Perhaps only three were silent: Bratti, piecing scraps into sense; the barber with the razor; and a thin-lipped, eager-looking man in spectacles with a pen-and-ink case at his belt—the sort who carried words like tools and made his living by their exactness.

“Ebbene, Nello,” Bratti said, edging near enough to speak to the barber. “It appears the Magnifico is dead—rest his soul!—and the price of wax will rise?”

“Even as you say,” Nello answered; and then, with a sudden grave speed that made the words tumble like beans on a table, he added, “and his waxen image in the Nunziata fell at the same moment, they say—or at some other time, whenever it pleases the Frati Serviti, who know best. And several cows and women have had still-born calves this Quaresima; and for the bad eggs that have been broken since the Carnival, nobody has counted them. Ah! a great man—a great politician—a greater poet than Dante. And yet the cupola didn’t fall, only the lantern. Che miracolo!”

A sharp lengthened “Pst!” cut across the guttural pelting. It came from the pale man in spectacles. The effect was immediate: the noise dropped, and all eyes fixed on him, waiting—as mouths wait for salt.

“’Tis well said you Florentines are blind,” he began, in an incisive high voice. “It appears to me, you need nothing but a diet of hay to make cattle of you. What! do you think the death of Lorenzo is the scourge God has prepared for Florence? Go! you are sparrows chattering praise over the dead hawk. What! a man who was trying to slip a noose over every neck in the Republic that he might tighten it at his pleasure! You like that; you like to have the election of your magistrates turned into closet-work, and no man to use the rights of a citizen unless he is a Medicean. That is what is meant by qualification now: netto di specchio no longer means that a man pays his dues to the Republic: it means that he’ll wink at robbery of the people’s money—at robbery of their daughters’ dowries; that he’ll play the chamberer and the philosopher by turns—listen to bawdy songs at the Carnival and cry ‘Bellissimi!’—and listen to sacred lauds and cry again ‘Bellissimi!’ But this is what you love: you grumble and raise a riot over your quattrini bianchi; but you take no notice when the public treasury has got a hole in the bottom for the gold to run into Lorenzo’s drains. You like to pay for footmen to walk before and behind one of your citizens, that he may be affable and condescending to you. ‘See, what a tall Pisan we keep,’ say you, ‘to march before him with the drawn sword flashing in our eyes!—and yet Lorenzo smiles at us. What goodness!’ And you think the death of a man, who would soon have saddled and bridled you as the Sforza has saddled and bridled Milan—you think his death is the scourge God is warning you of by portents. I tell you there is another sort of scourge in the air.”

“Nay, nay, Ser Cioni,” Nello put in, light as a hand that flicks flour from a sleeve, “keep astride your politics, and never mount your prophecy; politics is the better horse. But if you talk of portents, what portent can be greater than a pious notary? Balaam’s ass was nothing to it.”

“Ay, but a notary out of work, with his inkbottle dry,” said another bystander, ragged at the elbows. “Better don a cowl at once, Ser Cioni: everybody will believe in your fasting.”

Ser Cioni turned away and left the group, his indignation stiff as dried paste. As he moved, he uncovered the sallow yet mild face of a short man who had been standing behind him, shoulders bent by some sedentary labor, as if his back had learned to bow over parchment.

“By San Giovanni, though,” the fat man with leeks said, as if his beliefs had been jostled out of their accustomed basket, “I am not sure there isn’t some truth in what Ser Cioni says. For I know I have good reason to find fault with the quattrini bianchi myself. Grumble, did he say? Suffocation! I should think we do grumble; and let anybody say the word, I’ll turn out into the piazza with the readiest, sooner than have our money altered in our hands as if the magistracy were so many necromancers. And it’s true Lorenzo might have hindered such work if he would—and for the bull with the flaming horns, why, as Ser Cioni says, there may be many meanings to it. It may have more to do with the taxes than we think. For when God above sends a sign, it’s not to be supposed he’d have only one meaning.”

“Spoken like an oracle, Goro!” Nello said. “Why, when we poor mortals can pack two or three meanings into one sentence, it were mere blasphemy not to believe that your miraculous bull means everything that any man in Florence likes it to mean.”

“Thou art pleased to scoff, Nello,” said the sallow, round-shouldered man, now visible, “but it is not the less true that every revelation, whether by visions, dreams, portents, or the written word, has many meanings, which it is given to the illuminated only to unfold.”

“Assuredly,” Nello answered. “Haven’t I been to hear the Frate in San Lorenzo? But then, I’ve been to hear Fra Menico in the Duomo too; and according to him, your Fra Girolamo, with his visions and interpretations, is running after the wind of Mongibello, and those who follow him are like to have the fate of certain swine that ran headlong into the sea—or some hotter place. With San Domenico roaring è vero in one ear, and San Francisco screaming è falso in the other, what is a poor barber to do—unless he were illuminated? But it’s plain our Goro here is beginning to be illuminated, for he already sees that the bull with the flaming horns means first himself, and secondly all the other aggrieved taxpayers of Florence, who are determined to gore the magistracy on the first opportunity.”

“Goro is a fool!” said a bass voice, dropping into the chatter like a great bell among little tinklings. “Let him carry home his leeks and shake his flanks over his wool-beating. He’ll mend matters more that way than by showing his tun-shaped body in the piazza, as if everybody might measure his grievances by the size of his paunch. The burdens that harm him most are his heavy carcass and his idleness.”

After Bratti had melted back into the knot of men whose words clacked together like dice in a cup, the young stranger stood a while in the broken shade of the Loggia, listening to a Florentine morning he could not quite translate.

The piazza was never silent; it breathed. Hooves struck the stones with a hollow patience; a cartwheel complained in its wooden throat; vendors called their wares in clipped Tuscan that rose and fell like a song everyone knew by heart. But through it all ran another sound—the quick, excited undertone of rumor, the crowd’s shared appetite. He was outside that hunger. Whatever stirred their city-pride and city-fears was a dish cooked for native tongues.

He waited for Bratti’s promised escort until waiting began to taste of dust. The air itself teased him: a drift of warm bread from some unseen oven-mouth; the green bite of crushed fennel underfoot; and, sharper than all, the clean animal sweetness of milk carried on a faint current, as if morning were ladling itself into cups.

At the suggestion of that scent, he thrust his hand beneath his torn mantle into the purse at his waist and searched it with fingers grown suddenly meticulous. He turned the little pouch inside-out, as though a coin might be hiding in a fold the way a bay-leaf hides in stew.

Nothing.

“Not an obolus, by Jupiter,” he muttered—not in Tuscan, not in any Italian a Florentine ear would claim as kin. The words fell soft, almost amused, but his mouth had the dry pull of hunger. “I thought I had one poor piece left. Then I must get my breakfast for love.”

He drifted along the edge of the market, looking, not for the noisiest stall but for the quietest mercy. The farther he went from the storm of talkers, the more the piazza’s other music came clear: the slow snort of beasts, the rope creak, the occasional dull splash of water from a bucket. Near a corner where the gossip thinned, two mules stood as if anchored there by habit, their collars bright with red tassels that bobbed when they shifted weight. One mule bore wooden milk-vessels, their staves darkened by countless mornings; the other carried panniers heaped with herbs and salads—mint, chicory, tender lettuces, fronds of something feathery that smelled of anise when the breeze lifted it.

Leaning with her elbow on the milk-mule’s neck was a young girl, scarcely more than sixteen, her face framed in a red hood that made her cheeks look rounder, her prettiness almost infant-like because her hair was hidden. Sleep had taken her where she stood; she dozed in that half-leaning, half-standing posture of someone who had risen in the dim before dawn, strained milk by lamplight, tied down lids, and walked miles from a castello with the steady, resigned endurance of country feet.

The stranger had no compunction about waking her—but he did it as gently as one might lift a crust from a cooling loaf to see if it had browned. He touched her cheek lightly, and the girl’s dream must have been full of the herb-mule’s perfume, for when her lips parted with a faint breath it was as if a sprig of thyme had brushed them.

She started awake, blue eyes opening wide, and the confusion that followed sleep in a public place flushed her skin. She heard him speaking, but the voice was strange—soft, and not belonging to the vowels she knew. For a heartbeat she assumed it must be nonsense, and she turned her face a little aside, lifting the corner of her green serge mantle as a screen, the way one hides a bowl from flies.

He tried again, shaping his words toward the few phrases he knew would be familiar, letting his tone play at beggary. “Forgive me, pretty one, for awaking you. I’m dying with hunger, and the scent of milk makes breakfast seem more desirable than ever.”

“Muoio di fame,” he said, as if the common cry could buy him pardon.

This time she understood. The mantle dropped. Without answering, she reached up to the mule’s load, unfastened a lid with practiced fingers, and in moments held out a large cup of milk. It was still warm—not hot, but the living warmth that clings when milk has been handled quickly, carried close, kept from the morning chill. Its scent was clean and thick, and when he lifted it he felt the rim damp with the mule’s patient nearness and the girl’s early labor.

He made no more compliments before drinking. He drank as if he meant to remember it: the first swallow sweet and grassy, the next richer, a faint animal salt at the end. The piazza’s noise receded behind that taste. While he drank, the little maiden gathered courage to study him. His long dark curls fell in disordered abundance; his clothes, though damaged, were not those of any beggar she had ever been warned against—too fine in their ruin, as if they had been made for a body that knew music and pride.

While she looked, her hand moved of its own accord toward a bag hanging by the mule’s side. When he lowered the cup, she was holding out bread: a thick piece, torn from a loaf with a dense, honest crumb, the crust browned hard enough to sing under teeth. The smell of it—wheat and smoke—made his stomach clench.

“But perhaps that is your own breakfast,” he said, eyeing her with an instinctive gentleness. Hunger did not wholly drown courtesy in him.

“No,” she answered quickly, and then, as if words were too much, she only pushed it nearer. The glance she gave him—blue, shy, encouraging—was like the quiet offer a hearth gives to cold hands.

“No,” he said again, smiling, “I have had enough without payment. A thousand thanks, my gentle one.”

Still she pushed the bread nearer, almost impatient at his refusal, and as his long dark eyes rested on her baby-face, she found herself meeting them for longer than was safe. The piazza, with its hawkers and carts, seemed suddenly as private as a kitchen if one keeps one’s back to the door.

“Ah then, if I must take the bread,” he said, laying his hand on it, “I shall get bolder still, and beg for another kiss to make the bread sweeter.”

His speech had grown wonderfully intelligible despite that foreign softness. For an instant she blushed so deeply it seemed the red hood had overflowed into her cheeks. She lifted her mantle again to her mouth, half laughing, half afraid, a gesture that said no without the firmness of no.

He leaned forward—too confidently—and his fingers touched the arm that held the shielding mantle.

A harsh voice snapped close to his ear, cutting through the market’s hum like iron on stone.

“Who are you—with a murrain to you? No honest buyer, I’ll warrant, but a hanger-on of the dicers—or something worse. Go! Dance off, and find fitter company, or I’ll give you a tune to a little quicker time than you’ll like.”

He drew back and looked at the speaker with a glance provokingly free of alarm. Saucy amusement broke across his face into a broad, beaming smile as he took in the woman who had appeared like a kitchen-spoon raised against a thief.

She was stout but brawny, the strength of a working body wrapped in a man’s jerkin slipped over her green serge gamurra. A peaked hood—perhaps once part of a better mantle—was fastened around her sunburnt face. Coarse and prematurely wrinkled as it was, it carried a half-sad, half-ludicrous maternal resemblance to the tender baby-face of the little maiden—a resemblance like a prophecy one doesn’t want to read, the same features spoken in a harsher dialect.

There was something almost disarming in that bright young smile, but Monna Ghita was not a woman to betray weakness. Her anger only grew louder, as if volume could guard her daughter.

“Yes, yes, you can grin as well as other monkeys in cap and jerkin. You’re a minstrel or a mountebank, I’ll be sworn. You look for all the world as silly as a tumbler when he’s been upside down and has got on his heels again.” Then she wheeled on the girl, whose frightened face invited scolding more safely than a stranger’s eyes. “And what fool’s tricks hast thou been after, Tessa? Giving away the milk and victuals, it seems—ay, ay, thou’dst carry water in thy ears for any idle vagabond that didn’t like to stoop for it, thou silly staring rabbit! Turn thy back, and lift the herbs out of the panniers, else I’ll make thee say a few Aves without counting.”

Tessa obeyed at once, fingers trembling as she began to fuss with the herb-panniers, pretending busyness as a shield. The stranger, still holding the bread he had not yet bitten, turned his smile into something pleading.

“Nay, Madonna,” he said, voice soft as steam rising from a pot, “don’t be angry with your pretty Tessa for taking pity on a hungry traveller, who found himself unexpectedly without a quattrino. Your handsome face looks so well when it frowns, that I long to see it illuminated by a smile.”

“Va via! I know what paste you are made of.” Monna Ghita’s eyes narrowed; she had kneaded enough dough in her life to distrust anything too airy. “You may tickle me with that straw a good long while before I shall laugh, I can tell you. Get along, with a bad Easter! else I’ll make a beauty-spot or two on that face of yours that shall spoil your kissing on this side Advent.”

As she lifted her formidable hands—those talons ready to mark his skin like the imprint of a bread-slicer—two men had come near enough to hear, drawn by the promise of sport the way boys are drawn by the smell of roasting chestnuts.

Bratti had arrived a minute or two before and was murmuring to his companion, “What think you of this pretty parrot, Nello? Doesn’t his tongue smack of Venice?”

“Nay, Bratti,” said the barber under his breath, with the quiet vanity of a man whose trade was intimacy, “thy wisdom has much of the ass in it, as I told thee just now—especially about the ears. This stranger is a Greek, else I’m not the barber who has had the sole and exclusive shaving of the excellent Demetrio, and drawn more than one sorry tooth from his learned jaw. And this youth might be taken to have come straight from Olympus—at least when he has had a touch of my razor.”

Then Nello raised his voice, not sorry to stir the pot. “Orsù! Monna Ghita! What has happened to cause such a thunderstorm? Has this young stranger been misbehaving himself?”

“By San Giovanni!” Bratti put in, cautious still, his earlier suspicions about the stranger’s shabby finery and glinting jewels not entirely cooled. “He did right to run away from me, if he meant to get into mischief. I can swear I found him under the Loggia de’ Cerchi, with a ring on his finger such as I’ve seen worn by Bernardo Rucellai himself. Not another rusty nail’s worth do I know about him.”

“The fact is,” said Nello, eyeing the stranger good-humouredly, “this bello giovane has been a little too presumptuous in admiring the charms of Monna Ghita, and has attempted to kiss her while her daughter’s back is turned—for I observe that the pretty Tessa is too busy to look this way at present. Was it not so, Messer?” he finished, with a courtesy that made mockery taste like honey.

“You have divined the offence like a soothsayer,” the stranger said, laughing. “Only that I had not the good fortune to find Monna Ghita here at first. I begged a cup of milk from her daughter, and had accepted this gift of bread—for which I was making a humble offering of gratitude—before I had the higher pleasure of being face to face with these riper charms which I was perhaps too bold in admiring.”

“Va, va! Be off, every one of you, and stay in purgatory till I pay to get you out, will you?” Monna Ghita barked, elbowing Nello aside. She seized her mule’s lead and shoved forward, forcing the stranger to jump away as an approaching market-cart ground toward them, its axle groaning and its load rattling like bones in a basket. “Tessa, thou simpleton, bring forward thy mule a bit: the cart will be upon us.”

As Tessa turned to take the bridle, she stole one timid glance at the stranger. It lasted no longer than it takes to taste whether soup needs salt, but in it she caught his hand lifting in a small beckoning motion—a private farewell smuggled through the public clamor. He had been watching for that single opening, that moment when her mother’s body and the cart’s bulk made a wall between them.

Across the cart, Bratti raised his voice. “Ebbene! I leave you with Nello, young man—for there’s no pushing my bag and basket any farther, and I have business at home. But you’ll remember our bargain, because if you found Tessa without me, it was not my fault. Nello will show you my shop in the Ferravecchi, and I’ll not turn my back on you.”

“A thousand thanks, friend!” the stranger called, laughter still in him, as if the milk had warmed not only his belly but his courage.

Then he turned away with Nello up the narrow street that led most directly toward the Piazza del Duomo, leaving behind him the scent of herbs and the warm memory of bread taken for love, while the market’s voices closed again like a door—Tuscan words, Tuscan quarrels, Tuscan laughter—each sound a kind of belonging he could hear, but not wholly speak.

“To tell you the truth,” the young stranger said, once the press of carts and sweating mules had loosened a little and the air was less thick with hoof-clatter, “I’m not sorry your patron has handed me over to someone with a less barbarous accent—and a less riddling errand. Is it common among Florentines for a hawker of cracked glass and old rags to speak of a shop where he sells lutes and swords?”

“Common? No. Our Bratti isn’t common,” Nello answered, and his words came out the way steam pours from a pot the moment you lift the lid. “He has a theory and lives up to it—which is more than I can say for any philosopher I’ve had the honor to shave. Bratti means to squeeze the utmost relish out of life—meaning, hard bargaining—then wind it up with a bargain for the easiest passage through purgatory by leaving Holy Church his winnings when the game is done. He’s had his will drawn for it at the cheapest terms a notary could be coaxed to. I’ve told him often, ‘Bratti, your bargain limps, and you’re the lame side of it. Doesn’t it make you a little melancholy to stare at the pictures of Paradise? You’ll never be able to chaffer there for rags and rusty nails. Saints and angels want neither pins nor tinder. And except with San Bartolommeo—who carries his skin in an inconvenient fashion—I see no chance of your striking a deal for second-hand clothing.’”

He checked himself, crossed his fingers to his brow, and made the sign of the cross as if to rinse his mouth of the irreverence. Even his voice changed, as though a bell had been struck in the morning air.

“But God pardon me—light talk ill suits a morning when Lorenzo lies dead and the Muses are tearing their hair—always a painful thought to a barber. And you yourself, Messere—when a man with your speech and presence takes up with so sorry a night’s lodging, it argues misfortune.”

“What Lorenzo is it whose death you speak of?” The stranger’s attention fastened there with a hungry quickness; the sidelong question about his own condition slipped past him as if unheard.

“What Lorenzo?” Nello’s eyes widened at the ignorance. “There’s but one Lorenzo whose death can throw the Mercato into an uproar, set the Duomo’s lantern leaping as if in despair, and make the lions of the Republic feel they must devour one another at once. I mean Lorenzo de’ Medici—our Pericles—if I may dare the comparison in the ear of a Greek.”

“Why not?” the other said, and laughed as lightly as if laughter were a habit of breathing. “I doubt Athens, even in Pericles’ day, could have produced so learned a barber.”

“Yes—yes,” Nello cried, gratified, as if he’d been served a cup of spiced wine exactly to his taste. “I thought I could not be mistaken—else I have shaved the venerable Demetrio Calcondila to little purpose. But pardon me: I’m lost in wonder. Your Italian is better than his, though he has been forty years in Italy—better even than accomplished Marullo’s, and he’s married the Italic Muse more ways than one, since he has married our learned and lovely Alessandra Scala.”

“It will ease your wonder,” said the stranger, “to know I come of Greek stock planted in Italian soil longer than your mulberry trees. I was born at Bari, and my—” he stopped, as if a word in his throat had edges, “—I was brought up by an Italian. In fact I’m a Greek much as your peaches are Persian: the dye subdued till I was dipped again by long abode and much travel in the land of gods and heroes. And to confess something private—this same Greek dye, and a few ancient gems I carry, are all shipwreck has left me. But when towers fall, it’s ill for the small nest-builders. The death of your Pericles makes me wish I had turned toward Rome, as I should have done but for a fallacious Minerva in the shape of an Augustinian monk. ‘At Rome,’ he said, ‘you will be lost in a crowd of hungry scholars; but at Florence every corner is penetrated by the sunshine of Lorenzo’s patronage. Florence is the best market in Italy for such commodities as yours.’”

“Gnaffè—and so it will remain, I hope,” Nello said, with the stubborn cheer of a man who refuses to let grief sour his morning. “Lorenzo wasn’t the only patron and judge of learning in our city—heaven forbid! Because he was a large melon, every Florentine besides isn’t a pumpkin. Have we not Bernardo Rucellai? Alamanno Rinuccini? Plenty more. And if you want to be informed on such matters, I, Nello, am your man. It seems to me a thousand years till I can be of service to a bel erudito like yourself. And first of all—in the matter of your hair.”

He tipped his chin toward the stranger’s beard as if it were a dish set on the table in need of trimming.

“That beard, my fine young man, must be parted with, were it as dear to you as the nymph of your dreams. Here at Florence we love not to see a man with his nose projecting over a cascade of hair. Remember—you will have passed the Rubicon when once you have been shaven. If you repent and let your beard grow after it has acquired stoutness by struggle with the razor, your mouth will by-and-by show no longer what Messer Angelo calls the divine prerogative of lips, but will look like a dark cavern fringed with horrent brambles.”

“That is a terrible prophecy,” the Greek said. “Especially if your Florentine maidens are many of them as pretty as the little Tessa I stole a kiss from this morning.”

“Tessa? She is a rough-handed contadina,” Nello returned, with the sniffing precision of a man who can sort scents in a crowded market. “You will rise into the favour of dames who bring no savour of mule-stables with them. But to that end you must not have the air of a sgherro—of an ill-reputed fellow. You must look like a courtier and a scholar of the polished sort, such as our Pietro Crinito—like one who sins among well-bred, well-fed people, not one who sucks down vile vino di sotto in a chance tavern.”

“With all my heart,” said the stranger. “If the Florentine Graces demand it, I’m willing to give up this small matter of my beard, but—”

“Yes, yes,” Nello broke in. “I know. It is the bella zazzera—the hyacinthine locks—you do not choose to part with. And there is no need. Just a little pruning—ecco!—and you will look not unlike the illustrious Pico di Mirandola in his prime. And here we are, in good time, in the Piazza San Giovanni, at the door of my shop. But you pause—you want to look at our wonder, our Duomo, our Santa Maria del Fiore. Well—well—one glance; but I beseech you to leave a closer survey till you have been shaved. I am quivering with the inspiration of my art even to the edge of my razor. Come round this way.”

He took the stranger’s arm, warm-blooded and proprietorial, and guided him to the south side of the piazza. There the whole great triad stood at once before them: the immense dark shell of the cupola rising like a stored thundercloud made stone; Giotto’s campanile, slender and sure as a reed that has learned to sing; and the quaint octagon of San Giovanni in front, its bronze gates still bearing, though dimmed, the gilded glory of their first blaze.

The inlaid marbles were fresher then—pink, white, and purple like salt and rose and crushed berry under a clean knife—before four centuries of winter would mellow the white toward ochre. The cathedral façade had not yet been smeared into stuccoed shame, but wore the magnificent promise of half-completed marble inlay and statued niches devised long ago by Giotto. And up the campanile the eye climbed, through harmonies of color and form, into the clear April air; the city’s morning noises—the clipped call of vendors, the wooden knock of carts, the metallic laughter of bridles—seemed for an instant to thin, as if the very soundscape had been rinsed by that upward beauty.

But the young Greek, though his eyes were drawn upward as by a string, stood with his arms folded and his curls falling back, and there was a slight scorn on his lip. When his gaze came down again it moved coolly, scanning, measuring—piquing, like a knife that tests bread with no intent to eat.

“Well, my fine young man,” Nello said, impatience pricking through his civic devotion, “you make as little of our cathedral as if you were the Angel Gabriel come straight from Paradise. Have you ever seen finer work than our Giotto’s tower? Any cupola that would not look a mere mushroom beside Brunelleschi’s? Any marbles finer, or more cunningly wrought than these our Signoria got from far-off quarries at a price that would buy a dukedom? Come now—have you ever seen anything to equal them?”

“If you asked me with a scimitar at my throat, after the Turkish fashion—or even with your own razor,” the Greek said, smiling, “you might wring a confession of the true faith from me. But with my throat free, I venture to tell you your buildings smack too much of Christian barbarism for my taste. I have a shuddering sense of what is inside—smoked Madonnas; fleshless saints in mosaic, staring down idiotic astonishment and rebuke; skin-clad skeletons on crosses, or stuck all over with arrows, or stretched on gridirons; women and monks with heads aside in perpetual lamentation. I have seen enough of those wry-necked favorites of heaven at Constantinople.”

He had wandered toward the Baptistery gates as he spoke, as if drawn by metal rather than by stone.

“But what is this bronze door rough with imagery? These women’s figures seem moulded in another spirit from the starved saints. These heads in high relief speak of a human mind within them, instead of being mere indexes to spasms and colic.”

“Yes—yes,” Nello said, triumph returning. “I think we shall show you by-and-by our Florentine art is not barbarous. These gates were moulded half a century ago by Lorenzo Ghiberti, when he counted hardly so many years as you do.”

“Ah—I remember,” the stranger said, turning away, his appetite for contemplation already sated like one who has tasted and moved on. “I have heard your Tuscan sculptors and painters have studied the antique a little. But with monks for models and legends of mad hermits and martyrs for subjects, the vision of Olympus itself would be small use to them.”

Nello gave a shrug that meant he understood too well.

“You are of the same mind as Michele Marullo—ay, and as Angelo Poliziano himself, in spite of his canonicate, when he relaxes a little in my shop after lectures and talks of the gods waking from their long sleep, making woods and streams vital once more. But he rails against the Roman scholars who would have us all talk Latin again. ‘My ears,’ he says, ‘are sufficiently flayed by the barbarisms of the learned; and if the vulgar are to talk Latin I would as soon have been in Florence the day they took to beating all the kettles in the city because the bells were not enough to stay the wrath of the saints.’”

As Nello spoke, the piazza’s sounds pressed and retreated—the long groan of a cart-axle, the splash of water from a bucket, the sudden shrill quarrel of a bird in the eaves—each noise taking its turn like instruments in a street ensemble. The barber seemed to savor it as other men savor broth: not merely hearing, but tasting the city through the ear.

“If you want the flavor of our scholarship,” he went on, “you must frequent my shop. It is the focus of Florentine intellect, and in that sense the navel of the earth—as my great predecessor Burchiello said of his shop, on the frivolous pretension that his street of the Calimara was the centre of the city. And here we are: the sign of ‘Apollo and the Razor.’ Apollo bestows the razor on the Triptolemus of our craft—the first reaper of beards—the sublime Anonimo, whose mysterious identity is indicated by a shadowy hand.”

At the threshold a solemn, dark-eyed youth moved aside.

“I see thou hast had custom already, Sandro,” Nello said. “Now make all clear for this signor. Prepare the finest-scented lather, for he has a learned and handsome chin.”

The stranger’s eyes travelled past the shop into a room divided by a latticed screen, and beyond that into a smaller walled enclosure where a few bays and laurels circled a stone Hermes. The air inside had its own composed odor—soap, warmed metal, the faint sourness of old oil in a lamp, and the greener breath of leaves from the little court—as distinct from the piazza’s mingled sweat and dust.

“You have a pleasant little adytum there,” he said. “I suppose your conclave of eruditi meets there?”

“There, and no less in my shop,” Nello answered, leading him inward. The inner room held benches, a table with one manuscript and one printed book lying open in solemn capitals, a lute, a few oil sketches, and a model or two of hands and ancient masks. “My shop is a fitting haunt of the Muses—as you will acknowledge when you feel the sudden illumination and serene vigour that come with a clear chin. Ah—you can make that lute discourse, I perceive. I too have skill that way, though a serenata is useless when daylight discloses a visage like mine—no fresher than an apple that has stood the winter.”

He pointed to a sketch.

“Look at that: a fancy of Piero di Cosimo’s—strange, freakish painter—who says he saw it by long looking at a mouldy wall.”

Three masks were drawn: a drunken laughing satyr; a sorrowing Magdalen; and between them a rigid, cold Stoic face. They rested obliquely on the lap of a child whose cherub features rose above them with a gaze that promised something beyond all masks.

“A symbol,” said the Greek, and as he spoke he touched the lute strings so they murmured like distant water. “The child perhaps is the Golden Age—wanting neither worship nor philosophy. And the Golden Age can always come back so long as men are born as babies, and not into the world in cassock or furred mantle. Or the child may mean the wise philosophy of Epicurus, removed alike from the gross, the sad, and the severe.”

“Ah—everybody has his own interpretation,” Nello said. “Ask Piero himself and he will tell you his pictures are an appendix Messer Domeneddio has been pleased to make to the universe, and if a man doubts the meaning he had better inquire of Holy Church. He has been asked to paint the picture after the sketch; he puts his fingers in his ears and shakes his head—the fancy is past, he says. A strange animal, our Piero. But now all is ready for your initiation into the mysteries of the razor.”

“Mysteries they may well be called,” he continued, his spirits rising as he wrapped the stranger in the shaving cloth like a shroud. “Mysteries of Minerva and the Graces. I get the flower of men’s thoughts because I seize them in the first moment after shaving. Ah—you wince at the lather. It tickles the outlying limits of the nose, I admit.”

Sandro had brought the bowl; the brush moved in circles, whipping soap to a foam that held air like whipped egg whites, and the scent rose—clean fat and herb, sharp as rosemary bruised between fingers. The razor, when Nello laid it open, gave off a thin metallic note, a dry whisper of iron against air.

“That is why a barber’s shop is fit for wit and learning,” Nello went on. “Look at a druggist’s shop—there is a dull conclave at the sign of ‘The Moor’ that pretends to rival mine. What inspiration comes from nauseous decoctions? And you no sooner enter than you see a doctor of physic like a gigantic spider disguised in fur and scarlet waiting for prey—or blocking the doorway on a bony hack, inspecting saliva. Your chin a little elevated, if it please you: contemplate that angel blowing the trumpet from the ceiling. I had it painted expressly for the regulation of clients’ chins.”

He set the blade to work. The sound was intimate and precise—soft rasp, soft rasp—as if a dry leaf were being pared into obedience. Each stroke left behind a strip of bare skin cooling under air, and the young man’s face, freed, began to seem younger, clearer, as if a fog had been wiped from a window.

“Besides,” Nello said, “a druggist who decocts is a man of prejudices: he has poisoned people according to a system and must defend his system. A barber can be dispassionate; the only thing he stands by is the razor—unless he is an author. That was the flaw in Burchiello: he was a poet and had a prejudice about his own poetry. I escaped that. I saw early authorship is narrowing, in conflict with the liberal art of the razor which demands impartial affection for all men’s chins. Ecco, Messer—the outline of your chin and lip is as clear as a maiden’s. Now fix your mind on a knotty question—whether you are bound to spell Virgil with an i or an e—and say if you do not feel unwonted clearness on the point. Only, if you decide for the i, keep it to yourself till your fortune is made: the e has the stronger following in Florence.”

The Greek’s eyes glittered with amusement beneath the lather’s edge.

“I have it on the authority of our young Niccolò Machiavelli,” Nello added, “keen enough to discern il pelo nell’ uovo, and a great lover of delicate shaving though his beard is hardly of two years’ date—that no sooner do the hairs begin to push themselves than he perceives a certain grossness of apprehension creeping over him.”

“Suppose you let me look at myself,” the stranger said, laughing. “The happy effect on my intellect is perhaps obstructed by doubt as to the effect on my appearance.”

“Behold yourself,” said Nello, and held up a Venetian mirror from Murano, gleaming like still water. “The true nosce teipsum—as I have named it—compared with which steel or silver is mere darkness. See now how diligent shaving preserves the human outline, instead of making no distinction between your physiognomy and that of a bearded owl or Barbary ape. I have seen men whose beards invaded their cheeks so that one might pity them as victims of a brutalising chastisement out of Dante’s Inferno—if they had not strutted with strange triumph in their extravagant hairiness.”

The Greek watched his own newly bared face. It did indeed seem as if time had been pared away with the stubble; the cheekbones were more evident, the mouth more mobile—made for speech, and, perhaps, for persuasion.

“It seems to me,” he said, “you have taken away some of my capital with your razor—I mean a year or two of age, which might win me readier credit for my learning. Under the inspection of a patron whose vision has grown dim, I shall have a perilous resemblance to a maiden of eighteen in the disguise of hose and jerkin.”

“Not at all,” Nello said, now clipping the too extravagant curls with shears that made a crisp, satisfying bite. “Your proportions are not those of a maiden. And for your age—I remember seeing Angelo Poliziano begin his lectures when he had a younger beard than yours; and between ourselves his juvenile ugliness was not less signal than his precocious scholarship. Whereas you—no, no—your age is not against you.”

Then, as if turning a spit to show the other side, he lowered his voice.

“But between ourselves—let me hint that your being a Greek, though only an Apulian Greek, is not in your favour. Certain scholars hold your Greek learning is but a wayside degenerate plant until transplanted into Italian brains; and now there is such a plentiful crop of superior quality, your native teachers are mere propagators of degeneracy.”

He stepped back, satisfied.

“Ecco! Your curls are now the right proportion to neck and shoulders. Rise, Messer, and I will free you from the encumbrance of this cloth. Gnaffè! I almost advise you to retain the faded jerkin and hose a little longer—they give you the air of a fallen prince.”

“But the question is,” the young Greek said, leaning against the high back of a chair, meeting Nello’s admiring scrutiny with an anxious, practical look, “in what quarter I am to carry my princely air so as to rise from the fallen condition. If your Florentine patrons share this scholarly hostility to Greeks, I see not how your city can be a hospitable refuge for me, as you seemed to say.”

“Pian piano—not so fast,” said Nello, planting his thumbs in his belt and nodding to Sandro to set things in order. “I will not hide there is prejudice among us. And though, as a barber unsnared by authorship, I share no prejudices, I must admit Greeks are not always such pretty youngsters as yourself. Their erudition is often uncombed and unmannerly, encrusted with a barbarous Italian that makes their converse hardly more euphonious than a Tedesco in vinous loquacity.”

He went on, warming to the city’s own self-knowledge.

“And again—excuse me—we Florentines have liberal ideas about speech. We consider the tongue, which can flatter and promise so cleverly, must have been partly made for those purposes; and truth is a riddle for eyes and wit to discover, which it were mere spoiling of sport for the tongue to betray. Still, we have our limits: beyond them we call dissimulation treachery. But it is said of Greeks that their honesty begins at what is the hanging point with us—and that since the old Furies went to sleep, your Christian Greek has so easy a conscience he would make a stepping-stone of his father’s corpse.”

The stranger’s face flushed—anger rising as naturally as blood rises to a cut—so that for a moment the barber saw not a supple client but a young man with pride like salt on a raw tongue.

“Be not offended, bel giovane,” Nello hastened, good-nature recovering his footing. “I repeat only what I hear; my eloquence is the cream I skim off clients’ talk. Heaven forbid I should fetter my impartiality by entertaining an opinion. And as for the scholarly objection—” he twisted his mouth into a grimace that mocked the mockers, “—the fact is, you are heretics, Messer. Jealousy has nothing to do with it. If you would just change your opinion about leaven and alter your Doxology a little, our Italian scholars would think it a thousand years till they could give up their chairs to you. Yes, yes—chiefly religious scruple; and partly the authority of a great classic—Juvenal, is it not? He, I gather, had his bile stirred by the swarm of Greeks, as our Messer Angelo is fond of quoting about your incorrigible impudence—audacia perdita.”

“Pooh!” said the Greek, and his lightness returned like a musician finding his key again. “The passage is a compliment.

‘Ingenium velox, audacia perdita, sermo
Promptus, et Isaeo torrentior.’

A rapid intellect and ready eloquence may carry off a little impudence.”

“Assuredly,” Nello said. “And since you know Latin literature as well as Greek, you will not fall into Giovanni Argiropulo’s mistake, who ran full tilt against Cicero and pronounced him all but a pumpkin-head. Let me give you one bit of advice—trust a barber who has shaved the best chins and kept eyes and ears open for twenty years—oil your tongue well when you talk of the ancient Latin writers, and give it an extra dip when you talk of the modern. A wise Greek may win favour among us—witness our excellent Demetrio, loved by many and not hated immoderately even by the most renowned scholars.”

“I discern the wisdom of your advice so clearly,” the Greek said, his bright smile lighting his face as if the razor had not only cleared his chin but polished his expression, “that I’ll ask for a little more. Who, for example, would be the most likely patron for me? Is there a son of Lorenzo who inherits his tastes? Or any other wealthy Florentine specially addicted to purchasing antique gems? I have a fine Cleopatra cut in sardonyx, and one or two other intaglios and cameos—curious and beautiful—worthy to be added to the cabinet of a prince. Happily I fastened them within the lining of my doublet before I set out on my voyage. Moreover, I should like to raise a small sum for my present need on this ring of mine”—he drew the ring out and slipped it back on his finger—“if you can recommend me to any honest trafficker.”

“Good-day, Messer Domenico,” Nello called out, his voice skimming over the shop like a quick trill over a bowl’s rim. Two men had entered together: the first, grave and thickset with years; the second, tall and spare, wrapped in a mantle that had known better winters. Nello nodded to the latter as one nods to a regular whose silence is part of his trade.

“You come as opportunely as cheese on macaroni,” Nello went on, already drawing his razor with the brisk economy of a cook reaching for a knife he trusts. “Ah! you are in haste—wish to be shaved without delay—ecco! And this is a morning when every one has grave matter on his mind. Florence orphaned—the very pivot of Italy snatched away—heaven itself at a loss what to do next. Oimè! Well, well; the sun is nevertheless travelling on towards dinner-time again; and, as I was saying, you come like cheese ready grated.”

He spoke as if he were seasoning the air—too much perhaps, but with instinct, making even calamity part of the day’s broth. Outside, bells worried the morning with their metal insistence; inside, the little domestic orchestra held its own: the click of the strop, the whisper of bristles under soap, the faint simmering murmur of the street beyond the threshold.

“For this young stranger,” Nello continued, with the satisfaction of a man laying out a dish he has arranged himself, “was wishing for an honourable trader who would advance him a sum on a certain ring of value, and if I had counted every goldsmith and money-lender in Florence on my fingers, I couldn’t have found a better name than Menico Cennini. Besides, he hath other ware in which you deal—Greek learning, and young eyes—a double implement which you printers are always in need of.”

The elderly man—Domenico Cennini, son of that Bernardo who had once, hearing of German marvels, cast his own types in Florence—could do nothing but sit in lathered patience while Nello’s tongue ran on. His hands lay still, resigned as dough beneath a cloth; only his eyes moved, slow and weighing, to the stranger who stood near the door.

“This fine young man has unlimited Greek, Latin, or Italian at your service,” said Nello, as if offering a pantry with its jars unsealed. “He is as great a wonder of juvenile learning as Francesco Filelfo or our own incomparable Poliziano. A second Guarino, too, for he has had the misfortune to be shipwrecked, and has doubtless lost a store of precious manuscripts that might have contributed some correctness even to your correct editions, Domenico. Fortunately, he has rescued a few gems of rare value. His name is—you said your name, Messer, was—?”

“Tito Melema,” the young man answered.

He slipped the ring from his finger as one might set down a last crust saved from hunger, and presented it to Cennini. The barber, not less swift with his razor than with his speech, had already freed Domenico from the shaving-cloth; the man rose, rubbing his chin with the careful touch of someone who knows the value of a clean edge.

Meanwhile the companion who had entered with the goldsmith—tall, about fifty, with a short-trimmed beard, an old felt hat pressed down on his brow, and a mantle frayed to the colour of road-dust—had watched Tito as if measuring him for a frame. Now he spoke abruptly, the words clipped like herbs under a knife.

“Young man, I am painting a picture of Sinon deceiving old Priam, and I should be glad of your face for my Sinon, if you’d give me a sitting.”
