Tito started. The blood withdrew a little, as if the accusation had been laid on his skin like cold metal. He turned, those long dark eyes fixing on the speaker with the astonishment of a man who hears his name called in a dialect he has not spoken since childhood.

But Nello would not let the moment curdle.

“Piero,” he cried, “thou art the most extraordinary compound of humours and fancies ever packed into a human skin. What trick wilt thou play with the fine visage of this young scholar to make it suit thy traitor? Ask him rather to turn his eyes upward, and thou mayst make a Saint Sebastian of him that will draw troops of devout women; or, if thou art in a classical vein, put myrtle about his curls and make him a young Bacchus, or say rather a Phoebus Apollo, for his face is as warm and bright as a summer morning; it made me his friend in the space of a ‘credo.’”

“Ay, Nello,” said the painter, pausing between phrases as if he were listening to something inside his own skull and mistrusting the outer world’s racket, “and if thy tongue can leave off its everlasting chirping long enough for thy understanding to consider the matter, thou mayst see that thou hast just shown the reason why the face of Messere will suit my traitor. A perfect traitor should have a face which vice can write no marks on—lips that will lie with a dimpled smile—eyes of such agate-like brightness and depth that no infamy can dull them—cheeks that will rise from a murder and not look haggard.”

He spoke without heat, almost like a man describing the proper cut of meat for a given stew—matter-of-fact, cruel in its precision.

“I say not this young man is a traitor,” he went on. “I mean, he has a face that would make him the more perfect traitor if he had the heart of one, which is saying neither more nor less than that he has a beautiful face, informed with rich young blood, that will be nourished enough by food, and keep its colour without much help of virtue. He may have the heart of a hero along with it; I aver nothing to the contrary. Ask Domenico there if the lapidaries can always tell a gem by the sight alone.”

The bells outside flung themselves again upon the air—brazen, insistent, as if each stroke were a hand striking a table to demand attention. The painter’s eyelids twitched.

“And now I’m going to put the tow in my ears,” he said, “for thy chatter and the bells together are more than I can endure: so say no more to me, but trim my beard.”

With that he drew out two bits of tow, stuffed them into his ears, and dropped into the chair before Nello. It was an odd, domestic remedy against the city’s unceasing clangour, like placing a cloth over a pot to keep it from boiling over—an act of self-preservation in a Florence whose soundscape could bruise the mind as surely as hunger bruises the body.

Nello shrugged, his mouth twisting into a look he threw at Tito—a silent aside that meant: A whimsical fellow; take it as jest.

Tito had stood a moment as if pinned, his gaze still on the painter, trying to translate the man’s meaning and finding that no language—Greek, Latin, Italian—could carry the exact taste of that ambiguous insult. But Piero’s turning away, tow in ears, helped Tito recover his composure; he shifted his attention to Cennini, as a man returns to the business of bread when talk turns sour.

Cennini held the ring between finger and thumb with reverent steadiness, as though it were not merely pledge but text—an object to be read. The shop’s smells—soap, damp wool, faint metal—seemed to sharpen around that small circle of gold.

“This is a curious and valuable ring, young man,” he said. “This intaglio of the fish with the crested serpent above it, in the black stratum of the onyx, or rather nicolo, is well shown by the surrounding blue of the upper stratum. The ring has, doubtless, a history?” He looked up keenly, as if the stone’s layers invited the same scrutiny into a man’s past.

“Yes, indeed,” Tito answered, meeting the gaze frankly, letting his voice carry warmth where his face had cooled. “The ring was found in Sicily, and I have understood from those who busy themselves with gems and sigils, that both the stone and intaglio are of virtue to make the wearer fortunate, especially at sea, and also to restore to him whatever he may have lost.”

He smiled, the expression quick as a knife’s flash, bright and disarming.

“But,” he continued, “though I have worn it constantly since I quitted Greece, it has not made me altogether fortunate at sea, you perceive—unless I am to count escape from drowning as a sufficient proof of its virtue. It remains to be seen whether my lost chests will come to light; but to lose no chance of such a result, Messer, I will pray you only to hold the ring for a short space as pledge for a small sum far beneath its value, and I will redeem it as soon as I can dispose of certain other gems which are secured within my doublet, or indeed as soon as I can earn something by any scholarly employment, if I may be so fortunate as to meet with such.”

“That may be seen, young man, if you will come with me,” said Cennini, decision settling in his tone like clear stock after the scum is skimmed. “My brother Pietro, who is a better judge of scholarship than I, will perhaps be able to supply you with a task that may test your capabilities. Meanwhile, take back your ring until I can hand you the necessary florins, and, if it please you, come along with me.”

“Yes, yes,” cried Nello, delighted at an arrangement he could call his own handiwork. “Go with Messer Domenico, you cannot go in better company; he was born under the constellation that gives a man skill, riches, and integrity, whatever that constellation may be—which is of the less consequence because babies can’t choose their own horoscopes, and, indeed, if they could, there might be an inconvenient rush of babies at particular epochs. Besides, our Phoenix, the incomparable Pico, has shown that your horoscopes are all a nonsensical dream—which is the less troublesome opinion. Addio! bel giovane! don’t forget to come back to me.”

“No fear of that,” Tito said. He beckoned farewell as he turned at the door, his bright face catching what little morning light filtered past the shopfront, like wine poured thin but still glowing. “You are to do me a great service:—that is the most positive security for your seeing me again.”

When the door shut behind him, the bells outside pressed their harsh sweetness into the air again, but muffled now by distance and the painter’s tow.

“Say what thou wilt, Piero,” Nello said, as he set his razor to work on the beard before him, “I shall never look at such an outside as that without taking it as a sign of a lovable nature. Why, thou wilt say next that Leonardo, whom thou art always raving about, ought to have made his Judas as beautiful as Saint John! But thou art as deaf as the top of Mount Morello with that accursed tow in thy ears.”

He shook his head, amused and stubborn, as if insisting that sweetness must mean honey and cannot ever mean poison.

“Well, well,” he added, lowering his voice as the blade made its soft, sure scrape, “I’ll get a little more of this young man’s history from him before I take him to Bardo Bardi.”

The Via de’ Bardi lay on the Oltrarno side, a long, river-breathed artery between the Ponte Vecchio and the open space by the Ponte alle Grazie. In the later hours the Arno softened everything: it took the harsh teeth of old stone and returned them as a wavering tenderness—window after window broken into the water’s slow, darkened gold. Yet the street had a memory that refused to be drowned in reflection. Even as carts creaked and sandals scuffed and the river murmured under the bridges, the place seemed to listen for older noises: the clang of iron on iron, the thud of stones hurled from a hill, the roar of an armed people pressing into narrow inlets between walls.

Once, those walls had been the Bardi’s—proud hands that had known, with equal appetite, the sword-hilt and the glittering edge of coined metal. Their eyes had been Florentine in the keenest way: able to measure power not only in blood but in contracts, in warehouses, in wool bales and galleys. They rose, purchased lands and feudal dignities, and stood, for a time, like a great banking engine driving Europe’s wars. Then came the splendid debtor’s splendid default; the sudden fear of creditors; the crash that ran along Mediterranean coasts like a storm through rigging. Even that did not bend their necks as much as the people’s rage did in 1343, when the street between the bridges became a trap and a fortress together. They held it like panthers at bay until the assault came from the hill behind. Twenty-two great houses by the river were sacked and burned, and many who bore the name were driven out.

But Florentine families were rooted like old vines: cut them back, scorch them, and still they sent up shoots. The Bardi rose again and again in altered shapes—now honorable, now disgraced, now rich, now shamed into hiding. Yet the old street by the water passed into other hands; and by 1492 it had long been thick with other names, especially the Neri, who owned a stretch of the hillward side.

In one of the Neri houses there lived, however, a Bardi still—a descendant from the branch that had been Counts of Vernio. The pride remained; the hunger to leave a track on the fast-whirling earth remained. But the instrument had changed. This Bardi did not stalk the streets with armed men, did not hang vassals from feudal rights, did not plot voyages of credit and cargo. His hand, deep-veined and cramped, had been shaped by years of copying manuscripts; his dinners had grown spare, first by choice, then by necessity; his clothes had worn into threadbare honesty. He sat among books and marble fragments—among the dead—seeing them now only by the light of remembered sight. He was blind, moneyless, and famous in a small, fierce way: Bardo de’ Bardi, to whom Nello the barber had promised to introduce a young Greek named Tito Melema.

Bardo’s house stood on the hillward side of the street, one of those sombre, massed stone buildings with narrow windows and a roofed terrace above, as if the structure itself mistrusted the world and chose to watch it through slits. The main door—grim, with scrolled hinges—opened on a groined entrance-court, empty but for a massive lamp-iron hanging in the center like a black fruit. A smaller door admitted to a stone stair and to ground-floor rooms used as warehouse by the proprietor. The first floor too was stacked with precious stores meant for roads and seas: perhaps to the Scheldt, perhaps down the African coast, perhaps to islands in the Aegean or the shores of the Euxine. Even in the morning quiet, those lower stories had their own hushed music: the faint shift of packed goods, the smell of hemp rope and dried skins and spice dust that had settled into the mortar. When Maso, the old serving-man, returned from the Mercato with his small load of cheap vegetables, the damp green scent of them—cabbage leaves, onions with their papery bite, herbs bruised by handling—rose with him as he climbed slowly, step after step, until at last he reached the second storey and the door of his master.

We follow him across the ante-chamber to the door on the left. He opened it and merely looked in and nodded, as if words were another weight to carry.

“Ah, you are come back, Maso. It is well. We have wanted nothing,” said a clear young voice from the far end of the room.

The room was long and spacious, its order so scrupulous that it seemed an act of devotion, the kind that makes a household ritual out of dusting and placing. Shelves ran around the walls, packed with books and antiquities arranged as if each had its appointed seat in a choir. Here and there, set on stands before the shelves, the past displayed itself in fragments: a beautiful feminine torso; a headless statue with a muscular arm uplifted, gripping a sword that had lost its blade; rounded infant limbs severed from their trunk, the marble dimples inviting a tenderness the stone could never return; well-preserved Roman busts; two or three vases from Magna Graecia. A large table in the center bore antique bronze lamps and small vessels in dark pottery. The colors were mostly pale or sombre: vellum bindings with deep-ridged backs; marble livid from long burial; bronze waiting for sun to coax out its greenish tinge; a once-splendid patch of carpet worn down to a dim, tired pattern. The narrow windows looked on the Via de’ Bardi, and the sun was not yet high enough to send any cheer into the room.

The brightest color was a girl’s hair.

She stood before a carved leggio, a churchlike reading-desk, and her hair—reddish gold—lay in an unbroken ripple, like sunset clouds on a clear autumn evening. A black fillet held it above small ears; it flowed forward again, a natural veil for her neck above a square-cut gown of black rascia. Her eyes were bent on a large volume. One long white hand rested on the desk; the other clasped the back of her father’s chair, not with languor but with a steadiness that looked like habit trained into duty.

The blind father sat with his head uplifted and turned a little toward her, as if sight had become a posture rather than a faculty. His delicate paleness under a black velvet cap made the likeness between them more evident: both had the same refined brow and nostril, and both lacked any rose in the cheek. Yet in both, too, the full firm mouth and powerful chin gave a proud tenacity, a latent impetuousness. In her it showed in the backward poise of the head and the grand line of neck and shoulders. One could not tell whether such a face would win love or only admiration edged with dread; everything depended on the eyes—the direct messengers. The father’s eyes had long been silent. The daughter’s hazel eyes were fixed on the Latin pages of Politian’s Miscellanea, and her voice, clear and distinct, carried the words across the room like a controlled, steady chant.

“There was a certain nymph of Thebes named Chariclo, especially dear to Pallas; and this nymph was the mother of Teiresias. But once when in the heat of summer, Pallas, in company with Chariclo, was bathing her disrobed limbs in the Heliconian Hippocrene, it happened that Teiresias coming as a hunter to quench his thirst at the same fountain, inadvertently beheld Minerva unveiled, and immediately became blind. For it is declared in the Saturnian laws, that he who beholds the gods against their will, shall atone for it by a heavy penalty... When Teiresias had fallen into this calamity, Pallas, moved by the tears of Chariclo, endowed him with prophecy and length of days, and even caused his prudence and wisdom to continue after he had entered among the shades, so that an oracle spake from his tomb: and she gave him a staff, wherewith, as by a guide, he might walk without stumbling... And hence, Nonnus, in the fifth book of the Dionysiaca, introduces Actreon exclaiming that he calls Teiresias happy, since, without dying, and with the loss of his eyesight merely, he had beheld Minerva unveiled, and thus, though blind, could for evermore carry her image in his soul.”

As she reached the end of the passage, her hand slipped from the back of the chair and met her father’s, which had risen at that moment as if in answer to the story’s touch. She did not look around; she began to shape the Greek quotation with a voice subtly altered, tightened by something she refused to let rise. But the old man spoke, and his words cut in with quick, nervous authority.

“Stay, Romola; reach me my own copy of Nonnus. It is a more correct copy than any in Poliziano’s hands, for I made emendations in it which have not yet been communicated to any man. I finished it in 1477, when my sight was fast failing me.”

Romola crossed the room with the queenly step that belonged to her tall, finely-wrought frame—a simple motion, as if she had never learned to think of grace because she had always possessed it.

“Is it in the right place, Romola?” Bardo asked. He was perpetually seeking that assurance, like a man touching the edge of a table in the dark to prove it still stood where memory had built it.

“Yes, father; at the west end of the room, on the third shelf from the bottom, behind the bust of Hadrian, above Apollonius Rhodius and Callimachus, and below Lucan and Silius Italicus.”

In the clearness of her diction, a fine ear might have caught a faint weariness pushing against habitual patience—like a low note under a melody. But when she turned with the volume and saw his arms lifted a little, stretched out with eager, tremulous need to seize it, pity brimmed in her eyes. She hastened to lay the book on his lap, then knelt close by him, looking up as if love itself were a light strong enough to press through the barrier of blindness. Pride and passion, which often seemed to tremble in her features as if ready to harden, were softened now into womanliness by that mingled pity and affection. Something deeper than her proud mouth and firm chin found its outlet chiefly through her eyes.

Bardo, unaware of her radiance, looked flushed and agitated as his hand explored the edges and back of the large book.

“The vellum is yellowed in these thirteen years, Romola.”

“Yes, father,” she said gently. “But your letters at the back are dark and plain still—fine Roman letters; and the Greek character”—she opened the book on his knee—“is more beautiful than that of any of your bought manuscripts.”

“Assuredly, child,” Bardo said, moving his finger across the page as if he could still feel line and margin. “What hired amanuensis can be equal to the scribe who loves the words that grow under his hand, and to whom an error or indistinctness in the text is more painful than a sudden darkness or obstacle across his path? And even these mechanical printers who threaten to make learning a base and vulgar thing—even they must depend on the manuscript over which we scholars have bent with that insight into the poet’s meaning which is closely akin to the mens divinior of the poet himself; unless they would flood the world with grammatical falsities and inexplicable anomalies that would turn the very fountain of Parnassus into a deluge of poisonous mud. But find the passage in the fifth book, to which Poliziano refers—I know it very well.”

Romola drew a low stool close to his knee, laid the book on her lap, and read the four verses that held Actreon’s exclamation.

“It is true, Romola,” Bardo said when she had finished. “It is a true conception of the poet; for what is that grosser, narrower light by which men behold merely the petty scene around them, compared with that far-stretching, lasting light which spreads over centuries of thought, and over the life of nations, and makes clear to us the minds of the immortals who have reaped the great harvest and left us to glean in their furrows? For me, Romola, even when I could see, it was with the great dead that I lived; while the living often seemed to me mere spectres—shadows dispossessed of true feeling and intelligence; and unlike those Lamiae, to whom Poliziano, with that superficial ingenuity which I do not deny to him, compares our inquisitive Florentines, because they put on their eyes when they went abroad, and took them off when they got home again, I have returned from the converse of the streets as from a forgotten dream, and have sat down among my books, saying with Petrarca, the modern who is least unworthy to be named after the ancients, ‘Libri medullitus delectant, colloquuntur, consulunt, et viva quadam nobis atque arguta familiaritate junguntur.’”

“And in one thing you are happier than your favourite Petrarca, father,” Romola said, with the affectionate tact of one who knows how to humor without mocking. “For he used to look at his copy of Homer and think sadly that the Greek was a dead letter to him: so far, he had the inward blindness that you feel is worse than your outward blindness.”

“True, child; for I carry within me the fruits of that fervid study which I gave to the Greek tongue under the teaching of the younger Crisolora, and Filelfo, and Argiropulo; though that great work in which I had desired to gather, as into a firm web, all the threads that my research had laboriously disentangled, and which would have been the vintage of my life, was cut off by the failure of my sight and my want of a fitting coadjutor. For the sustained zeal and unconquerable patience demanded from those who would tread the unbeaten paths of knowledge are still less reconcilable with the wandering, vagrant propensity of the feminine mind than with the feeble powers of the feminine body.”

“Father,” Romola said, flushing suddenly, her tone wounded, “I read anything you wish me to read; and I will look out any passages for you, and make whatever notes you want.”

Bardo shook his head and smiled with a bitter sort of pity. “As well try to be a pentathlos and perform all the five feats of the palaestra with the limbs of a nymph. Have I forgotten thy fainting in the mere search for the references I needed to explain a single passage of Callimachus?”

“But, father, it was the weight of the books, and Maso can help me; it was not want of attention and patience.”

Bardo shook his head again. “It is not mere bodily organs that I want: it is the sharp edge of a young mind to pierce the way for my somewhat blunted faculties. For blindness acts like a dam, sending the streams of thought backward along the already-travelled channels and hindering the course onward. If my son had not forsaken me, deluded by debasing fanatical dreams, worthy only of an energumen whose dwelling is among tombs, I might have gone on and seen my path broadening to the end of my life; for he was a youth of great promise. But it has closed in now,” he continued after a pause; “it has closed in now;—all but the narrow track he has left me to tread—alone in my blindness.”

Romola rose abruptly, stung beyond stillness. She carried the large volume back to its place and set it with exactness, as though order could be an answer to pain. Then she stood at some distance, arms stretched down, fingers tightly clasped. Her gaze moved over the lifeless company around her—the parchment backs ranked like silent jurists, the unchanging mutilated marble, the obsolete bronze and clay. The room had its own quiet sound: the faint creak of the leggio settling, the far murmur of the street filtered through stone, the river’s low, persistent breath. In that quiet, her father’s words rang with a sharper edge than any noise outside. If Florence was full of cries and bells and bargaining calls, here the silence itself pressed like a hand; it held memory in place and made every reproach echo longer.

Bardo, usually quick to notice her movements, was now too full of rankling remembrance to attend to her.

“Yes,” he went on, “with my son to aid me, I might have had my due share in the triumphs of this century: the names of the Bardi, father and son, might have been held reverently on the lips of scholars in the ages to come; not on account of frivolous verses or philosophical treatises, which are superfluous and presumptuous attempts to imitate the inimitable, such as allure vain men like Panhormita, and from which even the admirable Poggio did not keep himself sufficiently free; but because we should have given a lamp whereby men might have studied the supreme productions of the past. For why is a young man like Poliziano (who was not yet born when I was already held worthy to maintain a discussion with Thomas of Sarzana) to have a glorious memory as a commentator on the Pandects—why is Ficino, whose Latin is an offence to me, and who wanders purblind among the superstitious fancies that marked the decline at once of art, literature, and philosophy, to descend to posterity as the very high priest of Platonism, while I, who am more than their equal, have not effected anything but scattered work, which will be appropriated by other men? Why? but because my son, whom I had brought up to replenish my ripe learning with young enterprise, left me and all liberal pursuits that he might lash himself and howl at midnight with besotted friars—that he might go wandering on pilgrimages befitting men who know of no past older than the missal and the crucifix?—left me when the night was already beginning to fall on me.”

His voice had risen in protest, then sank into a tremulous, plaintive reproach. Romola turned back, and her heart swelled with forgiving pity. Whatever pride stood erect in her, love knelt down easily. She returned to his side, seated herself near, and placed her hand on his knee—too proud to offer consolations that might sound like pleading for her own worth, yet eager that he should feel she was there.

“Yes, Romola,” Bardo said, and his left-hand—heavy with massive prophylactic rings—fell a little too heavily on the delicate blue-veined back of her right. She bit her lip to keep from starting. “If even Florence only is to remember me, it can but be on the same ground that it will remember Niccolò Niccoli—because I forsook the vulgar pursuit of wealth in commerce that I might devote myself to collecting the precious remains of ancient art and wisdom, and leave them, after the example of the munificent Romans, for an everlasting possession to my fellow-citizens. But why do I say Florence only? If Florence remembers me, will not the world remember me? ... Yet,” he added after a pause, his voice dropping into sadness, “Lorenzo’s untimely death has raised a new difficulty. I had his promise—I should have had his bond—that my collection should always bear my name and should never be sold, though the harpies might clutch everything else; but there is enough for them—there is more than enough—and for thee, too, Romola, there will be enough. Besides, thou wilt marry; Bernardo reproaches me that I do not seek a fitting parentado for thee, and we will delay no longer, we will think about it.”

“No, no, father; what could you do? besides, it is useless: wait till some one seeks me,” Romola said quickly, as if the words had the taste of iron and she wished them done and swallowed.

“Nay, my child, that is not the paternal duty. It was not so held by the ancients, and in this respect Florentines have not degenerated from their ancestral customs.”

“But I will study diligently,” Romola said, and her eyes widened with anxiety, as if she were trying to make her resolve visible. “I will become as learned as Cassandra Fedele: I will try and be as useful to you as if I had been a boy, and then perhaps some great scholar will want to marry me, and will not mind about a dowry; and he will like to come and live with you, and he will be to you in place of my brother... and you will not be sorry that I was a daughter.”

The last words rose into a sob she could not wholly master. Something in them touched the fatherly fibre in Bardo. He lifted his hand upward, searching, and when she bent her head beneath it, he stroked her golden hair gently, leaning toward her as if some glimmer could still be found there.

When Maso opened the door again, the cool hush of the house was broken by the small, familiar noises of welcome: the scrape of a shoe on brick, the soft clap of a cloak shaken straight, and Nello’s voice—always ready to fill an empty space as readily as steam fills a kitchen.

He entered first, bowing low to Romola with the flourish of a man who had bowed to women all his life and meant every bow to be a compliment to himself. Yet he did not come alone. With a hand laid lightly, almost coaxingly, upon the stranger’s sleeve, he guided him forward as if ushering a prized dish from the fire to the table.

“Messer Bardo,” said Nello, and in this room, before blindness and learning, even Nello’s tone grew measured, “I have the honour of presenting to you a Greek scholar, eager to have speech of you—not less from what I have told him of your learning and your priceless collections, than because your patronage may further him in the transient need to which he has been reduced by shipwreck. His name is Tito Melema, at your service.”

Romola’s astonishment sprang up so quick it was almost a physical thing—like the sudden scent of crushed mint where one expected only dust. Nello had said nothing of the Greek’s youth. Those who came to her father were mostly men with brows scored by years of dispute and parchment-light; this new face, fresh as a spring fig split open, belonged rather to the world of sunlight and sea-winds than to the shadowed mines of books.

Only once before had a youthful masculine beauty been stamped upon her memory with that deep, unreasoning fidelity which clings to the smell of a mother’s bread: the face of her brother, long lost—fair, with sunny hair like her own. That recollection rose now like a ghost at the edge of her sight. But the habit of her soul toward strangers—proud self-dependence, the refusal to ask for anything, even by a smile—stood firm as a white embankment. Tito bowed; she answered with her usual pallor and composure, though her heart made a quick, rebellious movement behind it.

His black sajo fell plain and unadorned to the knee; the austerity of the garment only threw into stronger relief the rich-tinted life of his face. When he lifted his eyes, there was in them a gentle, beseeching admiration—an appeal without demand. If he had been too handsome, that look was his atonement: it asked to be allowed near, not to conquer. Romola felt the heat rise in her cheeks, a brief flush like embers coaxed into colour; then it vanished as quickly, as if her will had set a lid upon it.

“Messere, I give you welcome,” said Bardo, with the grave condescension of a man who had long been accustomed to be asked and not to ask. “Misfortune wedded to learning, and especially to Greek learning, is a letter of credit that should win the ear of every instructed Florentine; for since the period when your countryman, Manuelo Crisolora, diffused the light of his teaching in the chief cities of Italy, no man is held worthy of the name of scholar who has acquired merely the transplanted and derivative literature of the Latins. Such inert students are stigmatised as opici—barbarians—according to the phrase of the Romans themselves, who frankly replenished their urns at the fountain-head.

“I am, as you perceive, and as Nello has doubtless forewarned you, totally blind: a calamity to which we Florentines are held especially liable—whether owing to the cold winds rushing upon us in spring from the passes of the Apennines, or to that sudden transition from the cool gloom of our houses to the dazzling brightness of our summer sun, by which the lippi are said to have been made so numerous among the ancient Romans; or to some occult cause that eludes our surmises. But I pray you be seated. Nello, my friend, be seated.”

He paused, as always, until his fine ear had taken the measure of the room—the settling of bodies, the soft creak of a chair leg, the slight brush of Romola’s gown as she took her usual place at his right hand. Blindness had trained him to live by sound as others lived by sight; the air of the house itself seemed tuned to his hearing, keeping away the clatter of the street as a cook keeps away flies from cooling milk.

“From what part of Greece do you come, Messere?” he continued. “I had thought your unhappy country almost exhausted of sons who could cherish any image of her original glory, though indeed the barbarous Sultans have shown themselves not indisposed to engraft on their wild stock the precious vine their own fierce bands have hewn down. From what part of Greece do you come?”

“I sailed last from Nauplia,” said Tito; “but I have resided both at Constantinople and Thessalonica, and travelled in various parts little visited by Western Christians since the triumph of the Turkish arms. I should tell you, however, Messere, that I was not born in Greece, but at Bari. I spent the first sixteen years of my life in Southern Italy and Sicily.”

At the name and the cadence of these places, something passed over Bardo’s delicate features like a shadow over still water. He leaned forward, stretched his right hand a little toward Romola, and turned his head as if to speak to her; then, as though remembering himself, he drew back, and his voice fell.

“Excuse me—is it not true—you are young?”

“I am three-and-twenty,” said Tito.

“Ah,” said Bardo, and there was a subdued excitement in the single syllable. “And you had, doubtless, a father who cared for your early instruction—who, perhaps, was himself a scholar?”

A pause—small, but it quivered in the room like a sudden silence in a marketplace. Tito’s lip trembled for an instant, as if the remembrance he touched were tender and raw.

“Yes,” he said at last, “at least a father by adoption. He was a Neapolitan, and of accomplished scholarship, both Latin and Greek. But”—another pause, like a hand briefly tightening—“he is lost to me—was lost on a voyage he too rashly undertook to Delos.”

Bardo sank backward, too finely wrought to press upon pain that sounded so near. Romola, who knew the secret fibres in her father that such words had struck, felt with an odd, startled certainty that this stranger had slipped at once within the boundary that lay between their shut-in lives and the rest of men.

Nello, smelling a pause as a cook smells a pot in danger of boiling over, took it upon himself to stir.

“In truth,” he said, “it is as clear as Venetian glass that this fine young man has had the best training; for the two Cennini have set him to work at their Greek sheets already, and it seems to me they are not men to begin cutting before they have felt the edge of their tools. They tested him well, we may be sure. And if there are two things not to be hidden—love and a cough—I say there is a third, and that is ignorance, when once a man is obliged to do something besides wagging his head. The tonsor inequalis is inevitably betrayed when he takes the shears in his hand; is it not true, Messer Bardo? I speak after the fashion of a barber, but, as Luigi Pulci says—

“‘Perdonimi s’io fallo: chi m’ascolta
Intenda il mio volgar col suo latino.’”

“Nay, my good Nello,” said Bardo, with friendly severity, “you are not altogether illiterate, and might doubtless have made a more respectable progress in learning if you had abstained somewhat from the cicalata and gossip of the street-corner, to which our Florentines are excessively addicted. But still more if you had not clogged your memory with those frivolous productions of which Luigi Pulci has furnished the most peccant exemplar—a compendium of extravagances and incongruities, removed farthest from the models of a pure age, resembling rather the grylli—the conceits—of a period when mystic meaning was held a warrant for monstrosity of form; with this difference, that while the monstrosity is retained, the mystic meaning is absent. In contemptible contrast stands the great poem of Virgil, who—so I long held with Filelfo before Landino had taken upon him to expound the same—embodied the deepest lessons of philosophy in a graceful and well-knit fable.

“I cannot but regard the multiplication of these babbling, lawless productions, albeit countenanced by patronage and in some degree by the example of Lorenzo himself, otherwise a friend to true learning, as a sign that the glorious hopes of this century are to be quenched in gloom—nay, that they have been the delusive prologue to an age worse than that of iron: an age of tinsel and gossamer, in which no thought has substance enough to be moulded into consistent and lasting form.”

Nello spread his palms and shrugged, as if the rebuke had slipped from him like oil from a ladle.

“Once more, pardon. I find myself knowing so many things in good Tuscan before I have time to think of the Latin for them; and Messer Luigi’s rhymes are always slipping off the lips of my customers—that is what corrupts me. And, indeed, talking of customers, I have left my shop and my reputation too long in the custody of my slow Sandro, who does not deserve even to be called a tonsor inequalis, but rather to be pronounced simply a bungler in the vulgar tongue. So, with your permission, Messer Bardo, I will take my leave—well understood that I am at your service whenever Maso calls upon me. It seems a thousand years till I dress and perfume the damigella’s hair, which deserves to shine in the heavens as a constellation—though indeed it were a pity for it ever to go so far out of reach.”

Three voices answered him in a small fugue of farewell as he retreated, bowing to Romola, beckoning Tito with a flick of his fingers, and taking with him the scent of street-air and shop-sachet. He went satisfied: the pretty youngster whom he had brought like a gift had been received with favour, and Nello knew well when a dish had taken its seasoning.

When the door closed and the house settled again into its quieter breath, the little flare of wrath that Nello’s quotation had kindled in Bardo seemed already burned down to a steady ember. He addressed Tito anew with his customary calm, as if the mind, once diverted into the channel of scholarship, flowed there willingly.

“Ah, young man, you are happy in having been able to unite the advantages of travel with those of study. You will be welcome among us as a bringer of fresh tidings from a land that has become sadly strange to us except through the agents of a now restricted commerce and the reports of hasty pilgrims. Those days are far distant that I myself witnessed, when men like Aurispa and Guarino went out to Greece as to a storehouse and came back laden with manuscripts which every scholar was eager to borrow—and be it owned with shame, not always willing to restore. Nay, even the days when erudite Greeks flocked to our shores for refuge seem far-off now—farther off than the on-coming of my blindness.

“But doubtless, young man, research after the treasures of antiquity was not alien to the purpose of your travels?”

“Assuredly not,” said Tito. “On the contrary, my companion—my father—was willing to risk his life in his zeal for the discovery of inscriptions and other traces of ancient civilisation.”

“And I trust there is a record of his researches and their results,” said Bardo, and his eagerness sharpened the words, “since they must be even more precious than those of Ciriaco, which I have diligently availed myself of, though they are not always illuminated by adequate learning.”

“There was such a record,” said Tito; “but it was lost, like everything else, in the shipwreck I suffered below Ancona. The only record left is such as remains in our—in my memory.”

“You must lose no time in committing it to paper,” said Bardo, interest growing as yeast grows when it finds warmth. “Doubtless you remember much, if you aided in transcription; for when I was your age, words wrought themselves into my mind as if fixed by the tool of the graver. Wherefore I constantly marvel at the capriciousness of my daughter’s memory, which grasps certain objects with tenacity, and lets fall all those minutiae whereon depends accuracy—the very soul of scholarship. But I apprehend no such danger with you, young man, if your will has seconded your training.”

At the mention of Romola, Tito ventured to look toward her; and when he smiled at the charge against her memory, his face opened into its brightest light. The effect upon her was as immediate as a draught of warm broth taken in the chill of fasting. She had been made to feel a culprit so often for that very deficiency that the simple human sweetness of amusement instead of rebuke was like the dawning of a new sense—the sense of comradeship.

They did not look away at once, as if they had stolen something. Their eyes met and held, and the smile passed between them frankly.

“She is not really so cold and proud,” thought Tito.

“Does he forget too, I wonder?” thought Romola; “yet I hope not, else he will vex my father.”

But he turned back, compelled by Bardo’s waiting attention.

“I have had much practice in transcription,” he said; “but in the case of inscriptions copied in memorable scenes, rendered doubly impressive by the sense of risk and adventure, it may have happened that my retention of written characters has been weakened. On the plain of the Eurotas, or among the gigantic stones of Mycenae and Tyrins—especially when the fear of the Turk hovers over one like a vulture—the mind wanders, even though the hand writes faithfully what the eye dictates. But something doubtless I have retained,” he added, with modesty that was not false—only lightly seasoned with policy—“something that might be of service if illustrated and corrected by a wider learning than my own.”

“That is well spoken,” said Bardo, delighted. “And I will not withhold from you such aid as I can give, if you like to communicate with me concerning your recollections. I foresee a work that will be a useful supplement to the Isolario of Christoforo Buondelmonte, and may take rank with the Itineraria of Ciriaco and the admirable Ambrogio Traversari.

“But we must prepare ourselves for calumny, young man,” Bardo went on, energy rising as if the book were already bound and handed about. “If your writing contains novelties you will be charged with forgery; if my elucidations should clash with any principles of interpretation adopted by another scholar, our personal characters will be attacked. We shall be impeached with foul actions. You must prepare yourself to be told that your mother was a fish-woman, and that your father was a renegade priest or a hanged malefactor. I myself, for having shown error in a single preposition, had an invective written against me wherein I was taxed with treachery, fraud, indecency, and even hideous crimes. Such—such are the flowers with which the glorious path of scholarship is strewed!

“But tell me: I learned much concerning Byzantium and Thessalonica long ago from Demetrio Calcondila, who has but lately departed from Florence; but you, it seems, have visited less familiar scenes?”

“Yes,” said Tito, readily, “we made what I may call a pilgrimage full of danger, for the sake of visiting places which have almost died out of the memory of the West, for they lie away from the track of pilgrims; and my father used to say that scholars themselves hardly imagine them to have any existence out of books. He held that a new and more glorious era would open for learning when men should begin to look for their commentaries on the ancient writers in the remains of cities and temples—nay, in the paths of rivers, and on the face of valleys and mountains.”

“Ah!” said Bardo, fervidly. “Your father, then, was not a common man. Was he fortunate—may I ask? Had he many friends?” The last words were weighted; in them Romola heard other names unspoken, other memories kept like old spices in a jar and opened only with trembling.

“No,” said Tito. “He made enemies—chiefly, I believe, by a certain impetuous candour; and they hindered his advancement, so that he lived in obscurity. And he would never stoop to conciliate: he could never forget an injury.”

“Ah!” Bardo’s voice drew the syllable out, long and deep.

Tito, wishing to turn aside from that too-personal road, continued quickly.

“Among our hazardous expeditions I remember with particular vividness a hastily snatched visit to Athens. Our hurry, and the double danger of being seized as prisoners by the Turks, and of our galley raising anchor before we could return, made it seem like a fevered vision of the night—the wide plain, the girdling mountains, the ruined porticos and columns, either standing far aloof as if receding from our hurried footsteps, or else jammed confusedly among the dwellings of Christians degraded into servitude, or among the forts and turrets of their Moslem conquerors, who have their stronghold on the Acropolis.”

“You fill me with surprise,” said Bardo. “Athens, then, is not utterly destroyed and swept away, as I had imagined?”

“No wonder you should be under that mistake,” said Tito, “for few even of the Greeks themselves, who live beyond the mountain boundary of Attica, know anything about the present condition of Athens—or Setine, as the sailors call it. I remember, as we were rounding the promontory of Sunium, the Greek pilot on board our Venetian galley pointed to the mighty columns standing on the summit of the rock—the remains, as you know well, of the great temple erected to the goddess Athena, who looked down from that high shrine with triumph at her conquered rival Poseidon. And our pilot, pointing to those columns, said, ‘That was the school of the great philosopher Aristotle.’ And at Athens itself, the monk who acted as our guide in the hasty view we snatched, insisted most on showing us the spot where Saint Philip baptised the Ethiopian eunuch, or some such legend.”

“Talk not of monks and their legends!” said Bardo, breaking in with sudden heat. “It is enough to overlay human hope and enterprise with an eternal frost to think that the ground trodden by philosophers and poets is crawled over by insect-swarms of besotted fanatics or howling hypocrites.”

“Perdio, I have no affection for them,” said Tito, with a shrug. “Servitude agrees well with a religion like theirs, which lies in renunciation of all that makes life precious to other men. And they carry the yoke that befits them: their matin chant is drowned by the voice of the muezzin, who from the gallery of the high tower on the Acropolis calls every Mussulman to prayers. That tower springs from the Parthenon itself; and every time we paused and directed our eyes towards it, our guide set up a wail that a temple once won from the diabolical uses of the pagans to become the temple of another virgin than Pallas—the Virgin Mother of God—was now again perverted to the accursed ends of the Moslem.

“It was the sight of those walls of the Acropolis, disclosed in the distance as we leaned over the side of our galley when it was forced by contrary winds to anchor in the Piraeus, that fired my father’s mind with the determination to see Athens at all risks, in spite of the sailors’ warnings that if we lingered till a change of wind they would depart without us. But after all it was impossible for us to venture near the Acropolis; the sight of men eager in examining old stones raised suspicion that we were Venetian spies, and we had to hurry back to the harbour.”

“We will talk more of these things,” said Bardo, eagerness returning like a tide. “You must recall everything, to the minutest trace left in your memory. You will win the gratitude of after-times by leaving a record of the aspect Greece bore while yet the barbarians had not swept away every trace of the structures Pausanias and Pliny described. You will take those great writers as your models; and such contribution of criticism and suggestion as my riper mind can supply shall not be wanting.

“There will be much to tell; for you have travelled—you said—in the Peloponnesus?”

“Yes; and in Boeotia also,” said Tito. “I have rested in the groves of Helicon, and tasted of the fountain Hippocrene. But on every memorable spot in Greece, conquest after conquest has set its seal, till there is a confusion of ownership even in ruins, that only close study and comparison could unravel. High over every fastness, from the plains of Lacedaemon to the straits of Thermopylae, there towers some huge Frankish fortress, once inhabited by a French or Italian marquis, now either abandoned or held by Turkish bands.”

“Stay!” cried Bardo, whose mind was now too fully possessed by the shape of the future book to follow the thread of Tito’s landscape. “Do you think of writing in Latin or Greek? Doubtless Greek is the readier clothing for your thoughts, and it is the nobler language. But, on the other hand, Latin is the tongue in which we shall measure ourselves with the larger and more famous number of modern rivals. And if you are less at ease in it, I will aid you—yes, I will spend on you that long-accumulated study which was to have been thrown into the channel of another work—a work in which I myself was to have had a helpmate.”

He paused, as if the word helpmate had rung like a struck bell in some hidden chamber.

“But who knows whether that work may not be executed yet? For you, too, young man, have been brought up by a father who poured into your mind the long-gathered stream of his knowledge and experience. Our aid might be mutual.”

Romola watched her father’s growing excitement and felt, beneath it, the deeper currents she had lived beside all her life: hope rising with pain braided through it, the yearning for what had been broken. The room itself seemed to listen, held by the fine web of Bardo’s expectation. She kept turning her eyes toward Tito, anxious lest he should, by any sign of reluctance, scatter the vision of co-operation that made her father’s face look strangely younger. If he knew about her brother—if he understood why certain questions trembled—he would be gentler still. An eighteen-year-old heart readily weaves belief from the youth and sweetness that has moved it: it imagines depths behind a sympathetic face as easily as a child imagines gods in weather.

And Tito, in truth, was far from impatience. He liked sitting there, liked the sense that Romola’s attention returned to him again and again like a hand feeling for something warm. He was pleased that Bardo took interest in him. The prospect of a learned labour to be shared did not press on his imagination with weight enough to trouble his ease; it lay before him like a path bordered by olive trees—something to be walked when the day came.

“I shall be proud and happy,” he said, answering Bardo’s last words, “if my services can be held a meet offering to the matured scholarship of Messere. But doubtless”—and here he glanced toward Romola—“the lovely damigella, your daughter, makes all other aid superfluous; for I have learned from Nello that she has been nourished on the highest studies from her earliest years.”

“You are mistaken,” said Romola. “I am by no means sufficient to my father: I have not the gifts that are necessary for scholarship.”

She spoke not with anxious humility, but with a proud gravity—as if even in self-distrust she would not beg to be contradicted.

Bartolommeo Scala, Secretary of the Florentine Republic—the man to whom Tito Melema had fastened his hopes as one ties a boat to a stout ring in a shifting current—lived near the Porta Pinti in a handsome palace whose very threshold preached its owner’s story. Over the entrance were the arms: an azure ladder laid across a golden field, and above it the motto, Gradatim. Step by step. It was a boast made visible, and he meant it to be read without anyone’s indulgence.

He was vain and ceremonious; but there was a blunt honesty in him too, for he truly believed himself deserving and felt no need to counterfeit humility. The top rung of his ladder had long been reached. For twenty years he had held the secretaryship; he had declaimed on the ringhiera of the Palazzo, while Marzocco the lion wore his gold crown for princely occasions and the crowd shouted “Viva Messer Bartolommeo!” He had gone ambassador to Rome and come back jeweled with titles—titular Senator, Apostolic Secretary, Knight of the Golden Spur; and eight years earlier he had worn, for his turn, the gonfalonier’s dignity, last summit of a Florentine citizen’s appetite. Meanwhile, like so many men whom the world feeds, he had grown richer and heavier, and, like so many whom the world flatters, more tender of his own importance; and like successful mortality in general, he had also grown more gouty.

That afternoon in May, when he granted Tito the interview Tito had so carefully sought, the secretary sat under the loggia he had built at the back of his palace, where the garden opened in a breadth of lawn and flowers. The sun warmed the borders beyond the shade; bees made their small diligent music above rosemary and thyme, and from somewhere deeper among the citrus there came the wet trickle of water into stone—sound that soothed even those whose tempers were otherwise inflamed. Scala’s too stately silk lucco had been cast aside; he wore a looser mantle over his tunic, and his swollen foot lay propped and cushioned with the helpless dignity of a man obliged to rule from a chair.

On one side of him sat his beautiful daughter Alessandra, with her husband Marullo—the Greek soldier-poet—whose foreign consonants, even in Italian, carried a different weight, like a song learned in another valley. On the other were two friends, not oppressively illustrious and therefore easier to please. Yet even in this agreeable shade, with the garden scents rising and the soft city-noise muffled by walls, Messer Bartolommeo’s content was soured.

For on the table before him lay certain papers—letters—whose very ink seemed to have dried with a sting in it. They were chiefly a correspondence between himself and Politian; and, in that age when scholars could turn their quarrels into entertainment as readily as cooks turn yesterday’s bread into a new dish, Scala had again brought them out to be tasted, savored, and judged.

The quarrel was pretty enough in its origin: one of those learned squabbles that begin like play with a pin and end like war with a spear. Politian, having once sought Alessandra’s hand and been refused, kept a sharp tooth ready for the too-prosperous secretary who had declined to call the greatest scholar of the time son-in-law. Scala, for his part, was an able public servant, and—worse in the eyes of offended genius—a lucky one. But the world, which seldom gives a man one weakness, had bestowed on him another that made him vulnerable: he had an itch for authorship, and he wrote badly.

He was one of those excellent men who, sitting in their slippers with an aching foot, will “pen poetical trifles” to amuse their own hours, and then, under pretense of privacy, send them out to friends in letters—the fifteenth-century’s way of printing without confessing to it. Scala had friends ready to praise: Ficino and Landino, amiable wanderers in the Medicean park, called his Latin prose elegant and masculine. The terrible Joseph Scaliger, who would in another century name him totally ignorant of Latinity, was comfortably unborn. Yet the fatal coquetry of writing is rarely satisfied with praise from those already disposed to be kind. That supercilious Politian—so acute, so disliked, so necessary in a circle that wished to think itself refined—must be made to know that the solid secretary, even amid affairs, could throw off verses that showed what he might do if he chose.

So Scala had sent Politian a Latin epigram, and—ineffable moment—there was in it a false gender. The culex, the gnat—too well known along the Arno, where summer evenings are sweet until that needle-hum begins at the ear—had been treated as of the inferior, feminine kind. To a man whose mind pricked at errors as a gnat pricks at skin, it was an invitation.

Politian replied with the freedom of a friend, and pleasantly, in the same form: a Latin epigram correcting the mistake. Scala answered with a bad joke in Latin verse, referring to Politian’s unsuccessful suit for Alessandra—salt thrown into the wound and calling itself wit. Politian found Scala’s verses very pretty, very facetious; the more pity, he said, that they were incorrect. And since Scala had alleged imitation of a Greek epigram, Politian—instructive, generous—enclosed a Greek epigram of his own on the same insect. There was a lively conceit about Venus, Cupid, and the culex, much relished at the time, founded partly on the zoological fancy that the gnat, like Venus, was born from the waters.

Scala’s reply had been full of perfumed contempt. His verses, he said, had never been intended for a scholar with such delicate olfactories as Politian, nearest of living men to the perfection of the ancients; a taste so fastidious that sturgeon itself must seem insipid to him. Scala defended his own lines nevertheless—they were hasty, uncorrected, meant as a cooling distraction in summer heat for himself and friends satisfied with mediocrity, he not being one of those who courted publicity through the booksellers. As for Greek, he had barely enough to make out the sense of Politian’s gracious epigram, to say nothing of tasting its elegances; but—Politian had written it. What more could be required?

Then, in a postscript—like a cook who cannot resist putting his finger into another’s sauce and declaring what spice is wrong—Scala ventured criticism. The comparison of the gnat to Venus, on account of watery origin, was ticklish, he feared. Venus might be offended; and unless the poet meant Thales’s doctrine, that cold damp origin was doubtful for a creature so fond of warmth. A fish were a better comparison; or, for flight, an eagle; or, for darkness, a bat or owl—so on, so on, with the heavy assurance of a man who will not admit he has missed the very flavor of the dish he is judging.

Here Politian had found his true feast. He wrote that he had not been aware, when Scala’s verses were placed before him, that there was any question of sturgeon: rather of frogs and gudgeons. He made short work of Scala’s defense of his Latin, and mangled him terribly for the stupid cavils against the Greek epigram. For the damp origin of the gnat there was Virgil’s authority—alumnus of the waters. And the fish, eagle, bat, owl? Nihil ad rem. An eagle might fly higher; it did not follow the gnat could not fly at all. He was ashamed, he said, to dwell on such trivialities and swell a gnat into an elephant; yet he added, with that elegant sting of his, that he was not to be caught by false blandishments in the presence of those who slandered him in his absence—capping his point with a Greek quotation like powder packed into a bullet.

It did not end there. The logic could scarcely get worse, but the secretary grew more pompously self-assertive, and the poet’s temper more venomous. Politian posed as one willing to hold up a mirror to an inflated man, that he might cease defending bad Latin against authorities sanctified by centuries—unless, indeed, he designed to sink in literature as he rose in honors, so that men of letters might at least feel themselves his equals. Scala retorted that nowhere would Politian find a more devout admirer of antiquity than in Scala’s writings. Scala blushed for the age. Some, indeed, wanted their own works exalted beside the divine monuments of the ancients; he could not oblige them. And as to honors—if envious men found them offensive—let them look at his life, from the day he came in penury to Florence.

Politian’s reply was savage enough to make even paper smell rank. He was not surprised Scala found the age distasteful, since Scala was so distasteful to the age. It was perfectly accurate, he said, that he had called Scala a branny monster: formed from the off-scourings of monsters, born amid the refuse of a mill, eminently worthy the long-eared office of turning the paternal millstones—in pistrini sordibus natus et quidem pistrino dignissimus.

These letters, the secretary had brought out today not merely for old relish. Here was a new Greek scholar—Tito—whose palate for language could be tried. And on nothing did Scala more crave an opinion from someone who might claim superior knowledge than on Politian’s Greek epigram about the culex.

So, after introductions and polite talk of Tito’s travels—overseas, under other skies, where the sea has its own constant breath and the evening air tastes of resin and salt—they fell to examining Tito’s gems. The stones went from hand to hand like small preserved fragments of an older world: the light caught their veins and inclusions; they were discussed with the same minute affection a careful cook gives to rare spices brought in from afar, pinched and smelled before they are trusted to the pot. From the gems it was an easy slide—like a knife slipping from fruit to meat—into mention of the lamented Lorenzo’s eagerness in collecting such relics, and from that into classical tastes and their present condition in Florence.

Politian, inevitably, had to be named: a man of eminent ability, no doubt, but arrogant—setting himself up as a Hercules appointed to destroy the literary monstrosities of the age; writing letters to elders without signing them, as if the words were revelations that could have only one source. And after all, were not his criticisms often questionable, his tastes perverse? He was fond of mocking men who thought they wrote like Cicero because they ended every sentence with esse videtur; yet, boasting freedom from servile imitation, did he not run after strange words and affected phrases? Even in the much-praised Miscellanea—was every point tenable?

Tito, who had lately been looking into the Miscellanea, had much to say that pleased the secretary—he would have found it easy to please, from disposition alone, and not from calculation, though calculation sat quietly in him like yeast waiting to work. He spoke with the right assurance, seasoning his praise and censure so that Scala could taste himself justified. Thus he showed himself, in Scala’s eyes, quite worthy to sit in judgment on the notable correspondence concerning the culex.

The Greek epigram was produced—as carefully as a choice morsel set before a guest whose approval is desired—and Tito read it with a composed face. The garden’s sounds went on: the water’s trickle; a distant vendor’s call softened by distance; a blackbird fluting from the greenery; and, at intervals, the thin whine of the very creature they were disputing about, threading through the afternoon like a mocking accompaniment. Scala’s gouty foot throbbed in time with his irritation, and he leaned forward, eager.

Tito was ready. He scarified the epigram to Scala’s content—finding fault where fault was wished for, touching the places that could be made tender, and doing it with the deftness of a man who knows how to carve at table so the best slices fall where he intends. Yes: the comparison was strained. Yes: there were affectations. Yes: the transmarini—the Greeks themselves—might well make light of such elegance. Tito’s Greek, which had seemed to promise impartial authority, became the very knife Scala needed to cut Politian down again in his imagination.

“O wise young judge!” Scala’s look said plainly, and his voice soon followed. Here, at last, was a person whose ear could catch the fine errors, who could appreciate satire even in the vulgar tongue. And Scala—who, excellent man, never seeking publicity through booksellers, was never without some “hasty uncorrected trifles” ready like sherbet for a visitor on a hot day, or in cold weather a cordial—produced a few little matters: sonnets turning on well-known foibles of Politian’s. They were not to go farther, of course; merely to amuse the company. They were passed round, relished with that furtive pleasure which always accompanies forbidden sweetness.

Enough: Tito took his leave under urgent invitation to come again. His gems were interesting—especially the agate with a lusus naturae, a most wonderful semblance of Cupid riding on a lion; and the “Jew’s stone,” with a lion-headed serpent enchased in it. The secretary agreed to buy both—the latter as reinforcement of his preventives against the gout, which gave him twinges severe enough to make plain how intolerable life would be without rings of rare virtue and an amulet worn close under the right breast. Remedies, like words, were half their power in the belief that named them; and Scala loved names, mottoes, titles, talismans—things that could be displayed or touched as proofs.

But Tito was assured, as he was escorted through the palace and out toward the Porta Pinti, that he himself was more interesting than his stones. He had come by recommendation of Bardo de’ Bardi—an old acquaintance of Scala’s, a worthy scholar, though, like many of the secretary’s friends, perhaps inclined to overvalue himself. Yet Tito must return not on Bardo’s account, but on his own manifest accomplishments.

The interview could hardly have ended more auspiciously. As Tito walked out near the gate, where the street’s noise rose a little harsher—iron on stone, wheels on paving, voices crossing like competing birds—he let himself enjoy, in the shelter of his own thoughts, a quiet laugh over the affair of the culex. Fortune, he felt, could scarcely mean to turn her back on him again just now, since she had taken him by the hand so decidedly within that cool loggia, among herbs and water-sound and the sweet, sharp pleasure of a learned spite.

Midsummer could coax the North to its feet on a pale edge of dawn—the dew still clinging like sifted salt to grass beside a dusty path, the young shoots in the coppice lifting their sharper green through the older oak and fir—without any need to remember whose feast it was.

But a Florentine, and most of all a Florentine of the fifteenth century, woke as if the very light had been named. The eastern sun struck the Arno with a particular gaiety, as though the river itself had been rinsed and set out like a bright platter; and the bells did not merely ring: they spoke, in a language every street knew, saying, San Giovanni. Their peal went through plaster and stone, through the sleeping crumbs of last night’s bread on a board, through the thin films of wine left in cups—an acoustic tide that made the city’s nerves lift and settle in time, until even the busiest mind moved to the festival’s cadence.

San Giovanni had worn Florence’s devotion for centuries—since Lombard queens commanded honour, since chroniclers like Villani could reach back to Constantino and Pope Sylvester, to that older, shrewder compromise with the past when the idol Mars was not shattered but set respectfully on a tower by the Arno, lest the city suffer “mutation” if the old tutelar force were affronted. Yet the fifteenth century had lost that cautious politeness toward the Man-destroyer. The spear and shield no longer kept watch beside the water. Florence now trusted in craft and coffers; and if arms were needed, arms could be hired with florins—and on the florins, always, San Giovanni looked out, stamped into gold as if sanctity were a guarantee of weight and purity.

Much had happened between the old patron and the new: Guelf and Ghibelline had made their arguments in blood, Blacks and Whites had split families, famine and flood and pestilence had emptied bowls and beds alike. And still the city had grown fat with glory—taking towns that once overawed it, pressing down especially on Pisa, whose marble had risen too proudly and whose masts had been too much admired on coasts where Florence meant to be known. In courts across Europe, even as far as Africa, the Florentine name circulated like coin: pure gold, dyes that held their colour like stubborn fruit skins, textures finished with such cunning that other cities’ cloth seemed raw beside them, scholarship and poetry and the kind of wit that could keep a bank’s books honest while it bent princes to its terms. A Pope, with a taste for pointed sayings, had called Florentines “the fifth element.” And, the people told themselves, for so high a destiny the thanks were due, in no small part, to San Giovanni, whose image rode every florin as it passed from palm to palm.

So his day must be kept with a devotion that did not separate the sacred from the street. The vigil came first—old Florentine fashion: dancing and jesting, and the likelihood of stones thrown and shutters broken; but above all, sights that only a city with a clever Cecca in its service could manage. Saints, with almond-shaped glory and their ring of winged cherubs, seemed to float down from painted domes into the narrow lanes, moving slowly through the press as if heaven had folded itself to street width. More wonderful still, there were saints made gigantic, attended by angels, not seated in fresco stillness but advancing in a mysterious glide like colossal figures escaped from high tribunes.

The clouds were woven cloth; the saints and cherubs were unglorified men propped by firm bars; the giants were steady-headed fellows on stilts, broadened like Greek tragedians by masks and stuffed shoulders. Yet only a miserably unimaginative Florentine thought of the carpentry first—and not merely unimaginative, but edging on impiety; for if sacred things were imaged, was not some virtue of the sacred carried in the image? And when a troupe of merry black demons followed—armed with claws and thongs and other instruments of sport, ready for impromptu farces of bastinado and clothes-tearing—why, that was simply the demons’ manner of keeping vigil. Tuscany slipped from devout to burlesque as water slips around an angle; the saints had had their passage, had made their pause before the gates of San Giovanni, and now the city made room for laughter that tasted of pepper after honey.

On the morrow—the great day thus opened—Florence must see her dependent places render their symbols: standards and offerings from conquered towns, protected districts, villages held since memory’s beginning. All were to be carried in solemn pomp to the old octagonal church—once cathedral, now baptistery—where every Florentine brow had felt the chrism traced into the sign of the Cross. The whole city, from white-haired men to striplings, matrons to lisping children, must be dressed in its best to honour the day and watch the great sight. And later, when the sun sloped and the streets cooled, there would be the Corso: unsaddled horses clothed in rich trappings, running right across the city from the Porta al Prato through the Mercato Vecchio to the Porta Santa Croce, where velvet and brocade banners—_palii_ with silk linings and gold fringe—waited on a triumphal car, fit trophies for the city that half-clothed the well-dressed world.

Afterward: more dancing; and the chroniclers of the century’s opening could swear that through the whole day there were weddings, and gatherings grand as any court’s, with so much piping and song, so many balls and feasts and ornaments, that earth might have been mistaken for Paradise.

In 1492 it was harder to make that mistake and keep a straight face. Lorenzo—magnificent, subtle—was dead; in his place sat Piero, arrogant and incautious, a change that did not bode well unless, as some wryly said, a wise horse might prefer a bad rider because he is easier to throw. Already grief for Lorenzo began to thin into murmurs: talk of a broader basis of government, of arresting corruption, of giving every man his share in jealousy and ambition—the old ideal liberty of quarrelsome days when Florence raised great buildings, reared her own soldiers, drove out would-be tyrants at sword-point, and boasted of keeping faith even to her own loss. Lorenzo was dead; Pope Innocent lay dying; the Neapolitan succession threatened trouble; Milan intrigued; Italy might soon be set by the ears. Difficult times—so much the more reason, many thought, to keep the festivals. When a city’s breath grows tight, it listens harder for the bells that tell it its own name.

Midsummer morning, that year, was bright enough to sting the eyes. Early—betimes—offerings for the grand procession assembled in the Piazza della Signoria: that famous space watched by the massive turreted Palazzo Vecchio and the spacious Loggia of Orcagna, scene of state ceremony. The sky spread a fair blue tent; beneath it the bells swung so vigorously that any evil spirit with sense enough to be formidable must have fled long ago. Faces swarmed at windows and terrace edges; sombre stone houses were brightened with hanging draperies; the palace tower, the older square tower of the Bargello, and the spire of the Badia nearby stood like stern cooks tasting the air, keeping watch over the simmer of the crowd below. On the broad polygonal flags of the piazza, banners unfurled; horses shifted under rich trappings; and the gigantic _ceri_—tapers fitly called towers—rose like strange, aggrandised descendants of those torches that once lit the Church in catacombs. In Florence’s midsummer glare, procession must move early; narrow streets offered shade, but the wide spaces flung back heat like a stone oven.

And where the pomp was to pause—the Piazza del Duomo—Florence had contrived another tent than the sky. From the octagonal baptistery in the centre to the cathedral façade and the surrounding walls, blue drapery was stretched forty feet high or more, embroidered with yellow lilies and familiar coats of arms; beneath it, sheaves of banners drooped at careful angles, a rainbow-lit shelter for the waiting spectators who leaned from windows, lined the pavement’s edge, and strained their necks toward the coming show.

One of those spectators was Tito Melema.

Bright among brightness, he sat at the window of the room above Nello’s shop. His right elbow rested on the red drapery at the sill; his head leaned back into his right hand, which pressed his curls against his ear as if he were listening not only to voices in the room but to the city’s festival-speech below. The months since his first appearance in Florence—weather-stained tunic and hose then—had changed him less than one might expect, except for that added radiance good fortune gives, like the barely perceptible finishing of a flower after it has drunk morning sun. His face held a bland liveliness, far from excitability and far from gloom: the expression of a companion who is welcome with men and women alike, never noisy from uneasy vanity, never contracted by resentment.

Close behind him, snug in the narrow angle between chair and frame, stood Nello in holiday suit, slender and alert. At Tito’s left was the younger Cennini—Pietro, the erudite corrector of proof-sheets, not Domenico the practical—his mind as neat as a compositor’s case. Tito’s gaze moved between the pageant below and the knot of talkers around him, several of whom had come in after seeing the procession begin in the Signoria.

Piero di Cosimo was among them, raising laughter with grimaces and anathemas against the bells. No ear-stuffing was barricade enough, he declared; the more he stopped his ears the more he felt the vibration in his skull, as if the sound were kneading his very brain. He swore he would bury himself in the most solitary spot of the Valdarno on a _festa_, if he were not condemned, as a painter, to lie in wait for secrets of colour—those sudden recipes of banner-light and human grouping that could be caught only when the city boiled over.

Tito turned from the whimsical painter, smiling, and looked down at the little drama playing along the chequered border of spectators under the blue canopy. It was then that he saw, near the marble steps before the Duomo—almost opposite Nello’s shop—a face upturned toward him, fixing on him a gaze too intent to be the common glance of a stranger.

A tonsured head rose above the black mantle and white tunic of a Dominican—common enough in Florence. But the look was not common. It carried a faint suggestion—certainly not unpleasant—and for that very reason it startled Tito. What pleasant association had he ever had with monks? None. Yet the flash of recognition, or something like it, struck and was gone almost before he could grasp it.

“Nello!” Tito said hastily, then, as the figure turned away, added with a note of disappointment, “Ah—he has turned round. That tall, thin friar going up the steps. I wanted you to tell me if you knew aught of him.”

“One of the Frati Predicatori,” Nello answered carelessly. “You don’t expect me to know the private history of the crows.”

“I seem to remember something about his face,” Tito said, frowning a little as if trying to recover a taste that had vanished from the tongue. “It is an uncommon face.”

“What? you thought it might be our Fra Girolamo? Too tall; and he never shows himself in that chance way.”

“Besides,” put in Francesco Cei, the popular poet, “that loud-barking ‘hound of the Lord’ is not in Florence just now. He has taken Piero de’ Medici’s hint—to carry his railing prophecies on a journey for a while.”

“The Frate neither rails nor prophesies against any man,” said a middle-aged personage at the other corner of the window, with the tone of one who had heard too much careless phrasing. “He only prophesies against vice. If you think that an attack on your poems, Francesco, it is not the Frate’s fault.”

“Ah—he’s gone into the Duomo now,” Tito murmured; his eyes had followed the Dominican eagerly. “No, I was not under that mistake, Nello. Your Fra Girolamo has a high nose and a large under-lip. I saw him once—he is not handsome; but this man…”

“Truce to your descriptions!” Cennini broke in, leaning forward with the impatience of scholarship confronted by spectacle. “Hark—see! Here come the horsemen and the banners. That standard—carried on the horse with white trappings—that with the red eagle holding the green dragon between his talons, and the red lily over the eagle—is the Gonfalon of the Guelf party; and those cavaliers close round it are the chief officers of the Guelfs. One of our proudest banners, grumble as we may. It means triumph of the Guelfs—which means triumph of Florentine will—which means triumph of the _popolani_.”

“Nay, go on, Cennini,” said the middle-aged man, dryly. “Which means triumph of the fat _popolani_ over the lean, which again means triumph of the fattest _popolano_ over those who are less fat.”

“Cronaca, you are becoming sententious,” said the printer, chuckling. “Fra Girolamo’s preaching will spoil you and make you take life by the wrong handle. Trust me, your cornices will lose half their beauty if you begin to mingle bitterness with them; that is the _maniera Tedesca_ you used to declaim against when you came from Rome. The next palace you build we shall see you trying to put the Frate’s doctrine into stone.”

“That is a goodly show of cavaliers,” Tito said—he had learned, already, the surest way to please Florentines was to admire what they admired, and to ask for the names. “But are there not strangers among them? I see foreign costumes.”

“Assuredly,” Cennini said. “There are the Orators from France, Milan, and Venice. Behind them English and German nobles; it is customary that all foreign visitors of distinction pay their tribute to San Giovanni in the train of that gonfalon. For my part, I think our Florentine cavaliers sit their horses as well as any of those cut-and-thrust northerners, whose wits lie in their heels and saddles; and yon Venetian—he would feel himself more at ease on the back of a dolphin. We ought to know something of horsemanship: we excel all Italy in the sports of the Giostra, and in the money we spend on them. But you will see a finer show of our chief men by-and-by, Melema; my brother himself will be among the officers of the Zecca.”

“The banners are the better sight,” Piero di Cosimo broke in, for once forgetting his quarrel with noise as the winding stream of colour poured forward. “The Florentine men are so-so; they make but a sorry show at this distance with their patch of sallow flesh-tint above black garments. But those banners—with velvet and satin and minever and brocade, with their endless play of delicate light and shadow! _Va!_ Your human talk and doings are a tame jest; the only passionate life is in form and colour.”
