“Ay, Piero, if Satanasso could paint, thou wouldst sell thy soul to learn his secrets,” Nello retorted. “But there is little likelihood of it, seeing the blessed angels themselves are such poor hands at chiaroscuro—if one may judge from their _capo-d’opera_, the Madonna Nunziata.”

“There go the banners of Pisa and Arezzo,” Cennini said. “Ay, Messer Pisano, it is no use for you to look sullen; you may as well carry your banner to our San Giovanni with a good grace. ‘Pisans false, Florentines blind’—the second half will hold no longer. There come the ensigns of our subject towns and signories, Melema; they will all be suspended in San Giovanni until this day next year, when they will give place to new ones.”

“They are a fair sight,” Tito said. “San Giovanni will surely be as well satisfied with that produce of Italian looms as Minerva with her peplos—especially as he contents himself with so little drapery. But my eyes are less delighted with those whirling towers, which would soon make me fall from the window in sympathetic vertigo.”

The “towers” were indeed a Florentine glory: the gigantic _ceri_, tapers so tall that the name was half-hyperbole and half devotion to wax as if wax could purchase grace. Yet hyperbole must be engineered to stand upright. These _ceri_, some so large they had to be carried on wheels, were hollow—wood and pasteboard under their waxen show, gilded and carved and painted in successive rings: warriors on horseback, foot-soldiers with lance and shield, dancing maidens, animals, trees, fruits—everything, the old chronicler said, that could delight eye and heart. Their hollowness had a further virtue: men could stand within them and whirl them continually, making the painted circles spin into phantasms. Numerous together, they were calculated to breed dizziness on a scale truly magnificent—like looking too long into boiling sugar as it turns from clear to gold, the eye drawn and drawn until it aches.

“_Pestilenza!_” Piero di Cosimo muttered, backing from the window as the rotating colours made his stomach revolt. “Those whirling circles one above another are worse than the jangling of all the bells. Let me know when the last taper has passed.”

“Nay, you will surely like to be called when the _contadini_ come carrying their torches,” Nello said, teasing. “You would not miss the country-folk of the Mugello and the Casentino, of whom your favourite Leonardo would make a hundred grotesque sketches.”

“No,” Piero said stubbornly. “I will see nothing till the car of the Zecca comes. I have seen clowns enough holding tapers aslant—with and without cowls—to last me for my life.”

“Here it comes, then, Piero—the car of the Zecca,” Nello called after an interval in which towers and tapers, descending in size, had made their slow transit under the blue canopy.

“_Fediddio!_” Francesco Cei exclaimed as the next spectacle rolled into view. “That is a well-tanned San Giovanni—some sturdy Romagnole beggar-man, I’ll warrant. Our Signoria plays host to all the Jewish and Christian scum that every other city shuts its gates against, and lets them fatten on us like Saint Anthony’s swine.”

The car of the Zecca—the Mint—had once been simply an immense wooden tower adorned like the other tributary _ceri_, mounted on a splendid car and drawn by two mouse-coloured oxen whose mild heads looked out from rich trappings bearing the arms of the Zecca. But the latter half of the century had begun to be ashamed of the painted spirals and rings that had delighted the earlier half; the “tower-puppets” had become a proverb—any ill-painted figure that looked, as figures sometimes will even in great ages, as if it had been boned for a pie, was called a _fantoccio da cero_. Improved taste, with Cecca to serve it, had devised for the magnificent Zecca a triumphal car like a pyramidal catafalque, with ingenious wheels warranted to turn all corners easily.

Round the base stood living figures of saints and angels arrayed with a sculptor’s care, stiffly graceful as if carved. And on the summit, thirty feet above the flags, well bound to an iron rod and holding an iron cross firmly fixed, stood the living representative of Saint John the Baptist: arms and legs bare, a garment of tiger-skins about his body, a golden nimbus fastened upon his head—Precursor as cloister and church had long imagined him, not yet revealed to painters as the brown, sturdy boy who might play among the Holy Family. Where could the patron saint be more fitly set than on the symbol of the Mint? Was not coining money the surest token that a city had won independence? By San Giovanni’s blessing, this “beautiful sheepfold” of his had shown that token earliest among Italian cities.

Yet the annual honour of representing the saint was not one of the high prizes of public life. It was paid with something like ten shillings, a cake weighing fourteen pounds, two bottles of wine, and a handsome supply of light eatables. The money came from the Zecca; the payment in kind arrived by peculiar “privilege” in a basket suspended on a pole from an upper window of a private house. Thereupon the austere saint’s eidolon did not disdain to refresh himself: he ate a reasonable share of sweets, drank wine, flung the remnants to the crowd, and then—embracing the mighty cake securely with his right arm—kept that comical, bountiful posture through the rest of his passage as the tall car jerked and vibrated on its slow way around the piazza toward the northern gate of the Baptistery.

“There go the Masters of the Zecca, and there is my brother—you see him, Melema?” Cennini cried, pride stirring as pleasantly as a well-fed fire. “Behind come the members of the Corporation of Calimara, the dealers in foreign cloth which we have given our Florentine finish—men of ripe years, matriculated before you were born. And then comes the famous Art of Money-changers.”

Tito slipped down again among the dispersing throng, letting the press of bodies close behind him as if he had never been there at all. Nello’s question—carelessly met with a shrug and an indifferent phrase—still hung in the air, but Tito had already folded the truth away inside himself with the same unstudied deftness with which a practised hand tucks a corner of linen beneath a basket-lid. He knew perfectly well whose face had glanced up at him from under that square, stiff-edged veil of white—Tessa’s, with those clear blue eyes that made even cheap daylight seem cleaner. And for a heartbeat, as he went round the piazza towards the Corso degli Adimari, he let himself wish he might meet that gaze again, just once, as one might wish for the taste of a cherry before dinner.

But the wish was swallowed up almost at once by the sourer after-flavour of a different sight: the friar—gaunt with fasting, skin drawn tight over bone, eyes burning as if their fire were fed on hunger. The man had looked at him, at Tito, not vaguely into the crowd but straight, with a recognition that made the air feel thinner. Somewhere in the long strings of his travel, in the inns that reeked of lamp-oil and garlic, on ship-decks where tar and salt stung the nostrils, in sun-bleached courts where Greek and Latin had been tossed back and forth like bread between hands—somewhere, that face had been. The memory clung like a cobweb to the mouth: thin, persistent, tickling with an importunity that was not pain but was not nothing. Folly, he told himself; sweep it away. He turned into a side-street, letting Florence take him in with her warm stone and her familiar music.

The city had its own orchestration at midday: the clatter of hooves on hard paving, the thin, bright cry of a vendor, a woman scolding from an open shutter, the steady rasp of a broom against a threshold. Sound here was not merely noise; it was the pulse by which you knew whether the streets were well or fevered. Tito had come from seas where the wind was loud and mindless and from ports where iron chains sang their horrible songs; Florence, by contrast, kept time with bells and human voices. Even the procession’s last echoes were already being eaten up by the ordinary daily murmurs—the domestic, breathable hum that made life seem possible.

Yet he quickened his steps, for the sun was higher than he liked. The procession had detained him from the visit he meant to pay in the Via de’ Bardi, in that room where his coming was awaited with a hunger more poignant than any appetite for food. He could see beforehand the scene of his entrance as vividly as if it were a picture already hung: Bardo’s blind face brightening all over, joy diffusing itself through that darkened countenance like lamplight through thin parchment; and Romola—Romola with the faint swift flush creeping up her neck and cheeks, no diminution of her majesty, only an added tremor of living womanhood, like the soft bloom on a marble fruit. Her look had that boy-like frankness which seemed a paradox in a woman so noble; it drew you toward her as the clean, plain smell of new bread draws one from the street.

They were comrades—better comrades than lovers, for lovers may dissemble, but comrades must share the day. Around the blind man’s chair, hours passed with the rhythm of study and talk: she always appealing, he answering, explaining, bringing a text to life, turning a phrase as one turns a morsel in the pan so that it takes colour evenly. Tito could feed knowledge to Bardo, and Romola, precise and eager, tasted every word with a seriousness that made it impossible for him to be idle. Yet he felt himself oddly in subjection to her simplicity. It was the first time he had known that reverent awe before noble womanhood—an old worship, almost pagan, as if she were some great earth-goddess whose power ran deeper than learned argument, older than books, rooted in something untranslatable.

They had never been alone together. He could not even build a plausible love-scene in his fancy; his mind, so quick at improvising, balked at the task. He could only long—wildly and privately—for what he knew was impossible: that Romola would some day say, simply and without ornament, that she loved him.

He had known love in easier forms. In Greece, under a white sun, leaning over a wall where a little peasant girl had set down her water-pot, he had felt the shy warmth of her body edging nearer and nearer until she had asked him, innocent as a child asking for a fig, to kiss her, offering her round olive cheek. Such love came like fruit brought to your hand. Romola’s would never come so. Would it come at all? That was the apple he had set his mind on—the one highest on the bough.

He was young, fresh with youth—not a man of fierce passions, but one whom impressions entered readily, as scent enters cloth. It was inevitable that he should feel tenderly toward Romola; as inevitable as that the white irises should mirror themselves in clear water. And yet he had no coxcombry. He knew—without needing to say it aloud—that she stood above him. Many men had felt the same before a great-eyed child: the instinct to protect mixing with the sense of being judged by a purity you cannot counterfeit.

Still, fortune had come quickly to him in Florence, and fortune is a persuasive cook: it seasons hope until it seems nourishing. His first interview with Bartolommeo Scala had been auspicious; Scala’s favour had grown, warm and steady, and it had led to a prospect that would have fixed Tito in Florence even if Romola had never existed.

Politian held the chair of Greek as well as Latin, for Florence maintained professorial seats though the university had been removed to Pisa. But for long there had been Demetrio Calcondila too—an eminent Greek among the emigrants—who balanced the Italian’s predominance. Calcondila had gone to Milan, and now those who wished Politian taught a little humility—men not all of them fools, though some would swallow mediocre verses with their summer wine—were ready to support another Greek chair as a counterweight. Lorenzo himself had once supported Calcondila while still patronizing Politian, so precedent made the measure seem not envious but zealous for true learning. Tito, with his lucid Greek and pleasant manner, was to be hoisted into that place.

He sailed, in truth, under a fair wind. He convinced fair judges that his ability matched his luck; and he wore success with such easy good-humour that as yet no one had been pricked by it. The best society was likely to open to him—the society with more plate than the little circle of enamelled silver in the middle of a brass dish; where brocade was not forbidden by the Signory. In such rooms, where talk and music were part of the air one breathed, what handsome young scholar who could touch the lute and send a gay song down the table would not be welcome? His liquid voice, his bright face, his ready smile lent life a holiday air, as colours hoisted on a mast make even a weary man ashamed to show his weariness.

And there was more: he had sold all his jewels—except the ring he would not part with—and he was now master of five hundred gold florins. The sum lay like a warm loaf on the table before him, solid, fragrant with promise. But the moment he first held it all—coin upon coin, the dull gold catching sunlight—was the first crisis that had ever forced his facile nature into a true struggle.

It happened in the room above Nello’s shop, which Tito had hired for his lodging. The elder Cennini—printer, goldsmith, and a Florentine with the firm-sounding conscience of a man who deals in weights and measures—had brought the last portion of the money from Bernardo Rucellai, purchaser of the two most valuable gems.

“Ecco, giovane mio!” Cennini said, setting the purse down with the careful thud of something that has consequence. “Now you have a pretty little fortune; and if you will take my advice, you will let me place your florins in a safe quarter, where they may increase and multiply instead of slipping through your fingers for banquets and other follies—follies rife among our Florentine youth. It has been too much the fashion of scholars—especially when, like our Pietro Crinito, they think their scholarship needs scent and embroidery—to squander with one hand till they must beg with the other. I have brought you the money; you are free to make a wise choice or an unwise. We Florentines hold no man a member of an Art till he has shown his skill and been matriculated; and no man is matriculated to the art of life till he has been well tempted. If you make up your mind to put your florins out to usury, let me know to-morrow. A scholar may marry, and should have something ready for the morgen-cap. Addio.”

When the door had closed behind Cennini, Tito stood still. His smile faded as if a shadow had passed over it. He did not touch the money. He stood with his thumbs in his belt, staring down at the scattered gold, arrested in that peculiar stillness that comes when the mind’s eye has fixed on an inward picture so vivid it makes the outer world dim.

A man’s ransom.

Who was it that had said five hundred florins was more than a man’s ransom? The words struck him with the blunt force of a smell remembered suddenly—like burnt resin catching in the throat.

If, now, under this midday sun—on some far coast where heat lay on the skin like a hand—a man somewhat stricken in years were toiling as a slave: hewing wood, drawing water, stumbling under loads, perhaps struck because he was slow, because age made his joints stiff and his breath short. A man not without high thoughts, with a heart passionate even in its weariness. A man who long years ago had rescued a little boy from filth, blows, and cruel wrong; had brought him sweet food and tender care; had made a home open like paradise. If that man were alive—if he were saying to himself, with the stubborn confidence of love, “Tito will find me: he had only to carry our manuscripts and gems to Venice; he will raise money and never rest”—could Tito look at the gold and say, I will stay in Florence, fanned by soft airs of promised love and prosperity; I will not risk myself for his sake?

No—surely no, if it were certain.

But certainty was exactly what he did not have. The galley had been taken by a Turkish vessel on its way to Delos; that was known, brought by report of the companion galley that escaped. There had been resistance; bloodshed, likely enough. A man had been seen falling overboard. Who survived? What happened to them in the net of possibilities—sale, escape, death, the slow sinking into anonymity? Tito knew too well the omnipresence of chance: he himself had been shipwrecked and had only narrowly escaped drowning, his lungs still remembering the taste of salt water, his ears still remembering the roar that swallows all human cries. The rumour of pirates settled in Delos might be truth, or might be tavern talk, useless as froth.

What would probably happen if he went to Venice now? He could get authoritative letters—yes, he knew how such things might be arranged. Then he would set out for the Archipelago, and—what? He might be seized himself; he might spend all his florins on preliminaries, bribes, voyages, the endless grease that makes wheels turn—and end again a destitute wanderer, with no gems left to sell, no footing anywhere. He could see that outcome with a clarity sharper than any imagined moment of finding his father and carrying him deliverance.

Was it fair that he, in ripe youth, whose life until lately had had the restraint of a school, should turn his back on love and distinction—on a future that now seemed within reach—and perhaps never be offered such a promise again?

“And yet,” he told himself, trying to keep his inward voice steady, “if I were certain that Baldassarre Calvo was alive, and that I could free him—by whatever exertions or perils—I would go now. Now, when I have the money. It was useless to debate before. I would go to Bardo and to Bartolommeo Scala, and tell them the whole truth.”

But he did not say—could not bear to say—how much that truth mattered. He did not dwell on the fact that if those men knew everything, there would be no decent alternative but to seek the benefactor who, if alive, was the rightful owner of the gems. He did not insist to himself—though he was not ignorant of it—that Greeks of distinction had crossed seas again and again, had pleaded with crowned heads and mitred heads, had spent fortunes and risked capture, all for the sake of freeing relatives from Turkish slavery; and that the world did not call it exceptional virtue. It was simply what one did. The great heart of mankind had made that law long before any statute.

This was his first real colloquy with himself. Until now, he had moved by the impulse of the moment; and one impulse—swift, smooth, almost unconscious—had been to conceal half the fact. He had spoken of Baldassarre as “lost,” with an equivocation that had seemed slight as a seasoning, hardly worth noting. He had never stood still long enough to smell his own motives.

What was the use of telling the whole? The thought had crossed him more than once since leaving Nauplia—like a guilty desire rising unbidden with the morning—that it was, after all, a relief to be quit of Baldassarre; and he had found himself wanting to know who it was that had fallen overboard. Such thoughts, he told himself, spring naturally from an irksome relation. Baldassarre had grown exacting; older, stranger; always scrutinising Tito’s mind to see whether it matched his own enormous expectations. Age, in a thickset man beyond sixty, heavy-browed and bald, whose intensity has become monotony and repetition, can be looked at from many angles and seldom from an attractive one. Such a man, cast among new acquaintances, would hardly find rank, youth, and beauty laid at his feet. The feelings that gather fervour from novelty do little for the dimmed and faded; if love remains to them, it must be the love rooted in memory—fidelity that goes on distilling sweetness when all other sweetness dries up.

And memory was not absent. Far back, when Tito had been seven, Baldassarre had snatched him from blows; had taken him to a home where food was not fought for but given; where the smell of warm bread and olives was not a rare luxury but daily comfort; where there were caresses, and the safe weight of a man’s arm around a child. From that time until their parting, Tito had been the centre of Baldassarre’s fatherly care. Tito had been docile, quick, pliant, eager to acquire: a lovely boy with a grace that seemed like a promise. He had seemed without vice, as if his beauty were the outward sign of an inward balance that knew no unrest. Even when he was silent where Baldassarre expected response, he did not look sullen; even when he shirked labour, he could melt refusal into a charming half-smile, half-plea, so that the pleasure of looking at him compensated the disappointment. There was ineffable good-humour in the curves of his mouth. And his talent—so quick that everything came readily, from philosophical systems to the rhymes of a street ballad caught at one hearing—had been a continual delight. Would any one have said he had not made a rich return? Would any one have foreseen that gratitude and affection might fail at a great demand?

He did not admit to himself that gratitude had failed. He held tight to the phrase like a man holding tight to a crust when the stew is thin. But it was not certain. Not certain Baldassarre was in slavery; not certain he lived.

“Do I not owe something to myself?” Tito asked inwardly, his shoulders making a faint motion—the first movement since he had fixed his gaze on the florins. “Before I quit everything, before I incur again risks of which I am already weary, I must have at least a reasonable hope. Am I to spend my life in a wandering search? I believe he is dead. Cennini is right about my florins: I will place them in his hands to-morrow.”

And when, the next morning, he carried that resolve into action, he had chosen his colour in the game. He had given his wishes a direction from which it would be hard to turn. From that point, it became impossible that he should not desire it to be true that his father was dead; impossible that he should not be tempted toward baseness rather than let the exact facts of his conduct come to light.

For beneath every guilty secret there breeds a brood of guilty wishes, blind and hungry, living on darkness. The stain of a deed often lies less in the doing than in what comes after—in the subtle adjustment of desire, the enlistment of self-interest on the side of falsity. Confession purifies not by magic but because it sweeps away the hope lodged in lies, and restores the soul to the noble plainness of simplicity.

In that first distinct inward debate, the scattered notions that had hitherto drifted and broken apart had gathered into one channel. The little rills of selfishness had met and deepened; the current would not again meet the same resistance. He had left vague the question whether he might return and ascertain Baldassarre’s fate; now he had forged for himself a definite excuse. He had avowed—only to himself—a choice he would have been ashamed to avow to others, and that would have made him ashamed in the sudden, living presence of his father.

And shame was there, even so: the inward blush, the reflex of that outer law written by the great heart of mankind, a law that exists even when sympathy is faint. It rose against his determination, colouring it with unease. That was why he kept asserting to himself, with a stubbornness that needed repetition, that Baldassarre was dead—or that, at the least, search would be hopeless.

Three weeks had slipped away since Tito, with the easy confidence of a man who dislikes rough edges more than he loves any distant good, had poured his bright florins into Cennini’s palm. And on this day of San Giovanni, when Florence steamed in holiday heat and every narrow lane held a draught of warm dust and laughter, he carried himself as if the city were made expressly to agree with him. He turned out of the blaze into a shaded street, lifted off his black cloth berretta, and let the air touch his curls. His brow told no story—neither innocence nor guile—only youth, smooth and well-shaped; his eyes, wide and clear, moved with that untroubled glance which makes a face seem honest to those who want honesty, and harmless to those who want harmlessness. If admiration followed him, it did so as it follows a bright day: willingly, without asking why.

The festa had unknotted from the solemn lines of procession and was now streaming everywhere, seeking its next diversion. Such loosened moments were when a crowd’s appetite for sport turned peevish, when it wanted something living to poke and laugh at. Near San Martino, by the hostelry of the Bertucce, a clump had formed—bodies pressed shoulder to shoulder, heads craning, voices flinging their mirth like stones.

Tito would have slipped away; the Via de’ Bardi drew him, and time, like a creditor, was already tapping his shoulder. But under the laughter he caught a thin, shaken cry, a child’s voice cracked with fear: “Loose me! Holy Virgin, help me!”

That sound tugged at the gentler seam in him. He pushed forward.

In the middle of the knot a man in parti-coloured cerretano dress held fast the wrists of a young contadina, laughing and coaxing as if her terror were only another trick. The onlookers sided with him in the quick, local cruelty of dialect—Florentine words for fool and simpleton spilling out with a nimble pride, as though the language itself were a cudgel they enjoyed swinging. The girl’s hood had fallen back; light-brown hair lay neatly plaited and pinned with a long silver clasp. Then the struggle turned her face toward Tito, and he saw, as suddenly as if the crowd had parted like water, Tessa—blue eyes flooded, lower lip trembling, baby features distorted by fright.

She saw him too. Hope flared through tears with the immediacy of a child recognizing a hand that has fed it.

Tito broke the circle. He caught her about the waist, drew her to him, and his voice cut through the merriment.

“Loose this child! By what right do you hold her against her will?”

The cerretano’s sharp-featured face—every angle tilted upward into impishness—showed small teeth in a grin that wanted to pass for good humour. He released her wrists, flung his hands behind him, shoulders rising in half apology, half protest.

“I mean the ragazza no evil in the world, Messere—ask this respectable company. I was only going to show a few samples of my skill, and she would have helped me well with that kitten face of hers—people trust what looks innocent. I promised her a lapful of confetti. But Messer has doubtless better confetti at hand, and she knows it.”

Laughter burst, greased by the sight of Tessa clinging to Tito’s arm as if it were a beam in floodwater. The laughs were not words to her; they were only the roar of beasts she had escaped. Tito, with irritation already pricking him—this delay, these eyes, these tongues—hastened to move.

The conjuror tossed the fallen hood back over Tessa’s head with a jaunty flourish. “Orsù, bear me no malice; come back when Messere can spare you.”

“Ay, Maestro Vaiano—she’ll come back presently, as the toad said to the harrow!” someone called, and the boys’ voices caracoled after the phrase, pleased with their own cruelty.

Tito thrust through toward a side-street, meaning to drop this troublesome incident as he would shake off dust. Yet the next street, too, greeted them with holiday remarks—some blunt, some leering, all carried on the loud common air like birds that had learned to sing only one coarse tune. He bent his head toward Tessa and spoke kindly but fast, as one speaks to a child who must be quieted on the way.

“Now, little one—where were you going? Are you come alone to the festa?”

Her fear surged back as soon as the cerretano was behind them. “Ah, no! I have lost my mother in the crowd—and my father-in-law. They will be angry—he will beat me. It was in San Pulinari—somebody pushed me and I couldn’t stop, and I got away from them. Oh, I don’t know where they’re gone! Please, don’t leave me!”

The sob at the end shook her like wind in a small tree.

Tito hurried on. The Badia was near; in a church one could speak quietly, and perhaps he could leave her with some orderly protection. But at that hour the doors were shut. They paused under the cloister’s shelter, where the sound of the festa dimmed into a distant murmur—like surf heard from behind a wall. The quieter acoustics soothed her only a little. Tito tried to shape the problem into a simple errand.

“Have you no cousin in Florence, my little Tessa? No friend whose house you can find? Or are you afraid to walk by yourself now that conjuror has frightened you? I am in haste to Oltrarno, but if I could take you near—”

“Oh, I am frightened—he was the devil, I know he was. And I don’t know where to go. I have nobody. My mother meant to have her dinner somewhere, and I don’t know where. Holy Madonna! I shall be beaten.”

Her mouth drooped. The beads above her green serge bodice rose and fell with her breath; tears began again, large and hot, falling as if they had been held back and now hurried to make up for lost time. She lifted her holiday apron to catch them, trying to be small, to be unseen.

It would have been brutal to leave her; and if Tito had a vice, it was not brutality but an almost childish need to keep the world smooth. He wished—briefly—that he had not been expected in the Via de’ Bardi, because duty, like harsh bread, is hardest when one is already warmed by something sweet.

He laid his hand on her apron, then, as one calms a frightened creature, rubbed her cheek and kissed its soft roundness.

“My poor little Tessa. Leave off crying. Let us see what can be done. Where is your home—where do you live?”

No answer at first; only the sobbing subsided into little catches of breath.

“Come. I’ll take you a little way, if you will tell me where you want to go.”

The apron fell. Her face cleared with the swift, unreasoning gratitude of a child: fear receded as if distance alone could undo it.

“I think I’ll go home, if you’ll take me,” she whispered, looking up at him with wide blue eyes that held something sweeter than a smile—an entire trust.

“Come then, little one,” Tito said, his tone softening as he offered his arm. “Which way is it?”

“Beyond Peretola—where the large pear-tree is.”

“Peretola? Out at which gate, pazzarella? I am a stranger—you must remember.”

“Out at the Por del Prato,” she said, clinging fast.

Tito did not know every turning well enough to choose quietness with certainty. Besides, where there were most people, there might be most chance of finding Monna Ghita, and so ending this accidental chivalry. He went straight toward Porta Rossa and Ognissanti, showing his bright, placating face to all observers who flung their jokes at the handsome young signor and his heavy-shod little maiden. The streets were full of mixed lives: decent holiday folk; apprentices with frolic that turned sour at envy; bold-eyed women under the yellow veil; beggars thrusting caps forward in a mockery of his haste; dicers and loungers whose voices carried a too-easy cruelty; boys whose tongues moved together like a flock trained to mob. Florence’s soundscape was not all bells and sacred singing; under the festa ran a coarse, persistent racket, a kind of public appetite that made a lost girl’s terror reasonable.

At Piazza d’Ognissanti Tito slackened. Heat pressed on both of them; the space opened wide, with stone benches against old walls. They sat.

“Holy Virgin,” Tessa breathed, “I am glad we have got away from those women and boys; but I was not frightened, because you could take care of me.”

“Pretty little Tessa,” Tito said, amused. “What makes you feel so safe with me?”

“Because you are so beautiful—like the people going into Paradise: they are all good.”

He saw nearby stalls with fruit and sweetmeats—their scent rising even above the human smell of sun and bodies: ripe apricots giving off that faint winey perfume; fresh-baked cakes smelling of warm flour and anise; comfits bright as beads. The thought of feeding her was easy kindness, and easier still than finding her mother.

“It is a long while since breakfast,” he said. “Are you hungry?”

“Yes, I think I am—if you will have some too.”

He bought apricots, little cakes, comfits—hands passing coins, paper and cloth rustling, the vendor’s singsong cry cutting through the air. He tipped the fruit into Tessa’s apron, which she gathered up like a pouch; the apricots lay there like small suns, downy and fragrant, their skins blushing where they had ripened most.

“Come,” he said. “Let us walk on to the Prato, and then perhaps you will not be afraid to go the rest of the way alone.”

“But you will have some,” she insisted, lifting the apron slightly as if offering a sacrament. “And we could eat together.”

“We will see,” he said aloud. And in his mind, warmed by the girl’s simple devotion and by the sight of her cradling food as if it were treasure, the fancy rose that she could have been the rustic heroine of some new pastoral—if only he had time to idle in the sun like poets and shepherds. The mischief, he told himself, was done: he was late already; another half-hour would hardly matter. And this—this was pleasant.

As they walked, she began to talk, words tumbling like grain from a loosened sack.

“We have a garden and plenty of pears, and two cows, besides the mules; and I’m very fond of them. But my father-in-law is a cross man. I wish my mother had not married him. I think he is wicked—he is very ugly.”

“And does your mother let him beat you, poverina? You said you feared it.”

“Ah, my mother herself scolds me. She loves my young sister better, and thinks I don’t do work enough. Nobody speaks kindly to me—only the Pievano when I go to confession. And the men in the Mercato laugh at me. Nobody ever kissed me and spoke to me as you do—only I talk so to my little black-faced kid, because I’m very fond of it.”

She did not seem to notice that Tito, in his fine dress and easy bearing, was no longer the same figure who had begged milk from her. To her he was still chiefly a face and a voice—something dropped out of brightness into her harsh day. In her world, language had always come weighted: commands, scoldings, coarse jests. Her own simple country speech, with its unguarded tenderness, did not stand in Florentine mouths. Here, in these streets, she heard words weaponized; she could not have said it so, but she felt it: the city’s dialect made sport of her, as if the very sounds told her she belonged beneath them.

They reached the Prato, a broad open space within the walls where young men played calcio and practised their strength. At midday it lay quiet, grass shimmering, the air thick and still, the distant preparation at the gate for the coming race like a muted promise. For a moment the noise of Florence seemed held back, as if the city inhaled here.

Tito stopped at the border of the open meadow.

“Now, Tessa, you will not be frightened if I leave you to walk the rest of the way by yourself. Addio! Shall I come and buy a cup of milk from you in the Mercato to-morrow morning—to see you are quite safe?”

He spoke soothingly, but he saw the instant sorrow in her widening eyes, the mouth corners sinking. She said nothing. She only opened her apron and looked down at the apricots and sweetmeats as if they had suddenly become too much—too heavy with the meaning of being given and not shared. Then she looked up, complaint trembling out of her.

“I thought you would have some, and we could sit down under a tree outside the gate, and eat them together.”

“Tessa, Tessa—you little siren,” he said, laughing as he kissed both her cheeks. “You would ruin me. I ought to have been in the Via de’ Bardi long ago. No—I must go back now. You are in no danger. There—I’ll take an apricot. Addio!”

He stepped away as he spoke. Tessa went pale; a sob rose like a wave. She turned, as if there were no use pleading, and began to walk on. She held her apron so forgetfully that the fruit rolled out onto the grass—soft thuds, the faintest bruising sound, as if even sweetness could be wasted.

Tito looked after her. He saw her shoulders lift with the sob she tried to swallow, saw the apricots tumble. He could not help himself; gentleness pulled him back as surely as vanity had pulled him forward into the crowd.

He went after her and stooped, gathering up the fallen fruit one by one, their skins warm from her body and the sun.

“See, my silly one,” he said. “Come—leave off crying. I will go with you, and we’ll sit down under the tree. Only remember, I must go back sometime.”

So it happened that not far beyond the gate they found a great plane-tree, its broad leaves making a net of shade. The air there was different: cooler, threaded with the whisper of leaves, the faint insect drone, the distant muffled rumble of the city like a sea held at bay. They sat under it, and the feast was spread on Tessa’s lap. She leaned against the trunk; Tito stretched opposite, elbows resting on the rough green growth that clung in the shade. Sunlight slipped through the boughs and played over them, moving and pausing like a living thing.

Tessa ate slowly, tasting with the reverence of someone for whom fruit was not a mere snack but a season’s gift. The apricots split under her small fingers, juice shining on the torn flesh; the smell rose richer as the pit was freed. The cakes crumbled, sweet with spice; the comfits clicked between teeth. Her contentment returned so completely it was as if fear had been only a bad dream.

“You pretty bird,” Tito said, watching her weigh in her mind whether to save the remains because he had said he would have no more. “To think of anyone scolding you! What sins do you tell at confession, Tessa?”

“Oh—a great many. I am often naughty. I don’t like work, and I can’t help being idle though I know I shall be beaten and scolded. And I give the mules the best fodder when nobody sees, and then when the Madre is angry I say I didn’t do it, and that makes me frightened at the devil. I think the conjuror was the devil. I am not so frightened after confession. And see—I’ve got a Breve here, that a good father who came to Prato preaching this Easter blessed and gave us all.”

She drew from her bosom a tiny bag, carefully tied, holding it up as solemnly as a relic. In that small gesture lay generations: poor folk binding comfort into scraps of parchment, faith made portable, language reduced to scrawls that promised protection even when read by none. It was a charm that belonged to her world, where the sacred had to be worn close because the day itself was hard.

“And I think the holy Madonna will take care of me,” she added, “she looks as if she would. And perhaps if I wasn’t idle, she wouldn’t let me be beaten.”

Tito, amused and moved by turns, leaned into the softness of the hour.

“If they are so cruel, Tessa—shouldn’t you like to leave them, and go live with a beautiful lady who would be kind to you, if she would have you to wait on her?”

She held her breath. Her eyes fixed on him, then wavered.

“I don’t know,” she said at last, doubtful because happiness offered too easily feels like a trick.

“Then should you like to be my little servant, and live with me?” Tito asked, smiling, meaning only to watch the pretty spark his words would make.

Joy flushed over her face at once. “Will you take me with you now? Ah—I shouldn’t go home and be beaten then.” She paused, then added with sudden practical sorrow, “But I should like to fetch my black-faced kid.”

“Yes, you must go back to your kid, my Tessa,” Tito said, rising, as if that settled it neatly. “And I must go the other way.”

Then, stepping from the shade into sun, he muttered with a half-laugh, “By Jupiter, it is not a pleasant time of day to walk from here to the Via de’ Bardi. I am more inclined to lie down and sleep in this shade.”

And that inclination—so often the true pilot of his life—won. He had risen early; had waited; had watched sights; had walked in sun; and the cool hush under the plane-tree, with Tessa near like an added softness in the air, tempted him past resistance. He lay down again, put his cap beneath his head on a tuft of grass by her side. It was not comfortable; he shifted, and then asked, as easily as if it were the most natural thing in the world, to rest his head against her lap. In that posture, cradled by her small warmth and by the leaf-dappled shade, he fell asleep.

Tessa sat still as a dove on its nest. The city’s sound was far away; here the world was leaf-whisper, breath, the occasional faint call from beyond the gate. When he slept deeply, she dared to touch the dark curls falling back from his ear, as if they were something sacred. She was too happy to sleep, too happy even to imagine waking would bring departure. In childhood—and in childish hearts that remain so—the new sweetness feels like a spell that will remake everything forever, leaving no path back to the old scolding voices.

Time slipped. The sun moved. Shade shifted in slow patterns along the grass.

At last Tito’s sleep broke into a doze in which he was again in the Via de’ Bardi, explaining why he had not appeared when expected. The image jolted him awake like a hand on the shoulder. He started up, sat straight, stretched his arms, shook out his cap.

“Tessa, little one—you have let me sleep too long. My hunger and the shadows together tell me the sun has travelled since I fell asleep. I must lose no more time. Addio.” He patted her cheek with one hand, settled his cap with the other.

She said nothing, but her face shifted toward misery; the tears gathered, ready to spill.

He spoke again, forcing into his voice a seriousness it did not naturally carry, the nearest he could come to sternness.

“Now, Tessa—you must not cry. I shall be angry; I shall not love you if you cry. You must go home to your black-faced kid; or if you like, go back to the gate and see the horses start. But I can stay with you no longer. If you cry, I shall think you are troublesome to me.”

The tears stopped as if struck down. Terror at the change in him turned her pale; she trembled, eyes widened with the grief she dared not let fall. The power of a word—love withdrawn, anger promised—was stronger than any charm she wore.

Tito’s gentleness required sorrow to be kept out of sight. He softened again at once, searching for a neat ending, a sweet plug to stop the ache.

“Look now,” he said, opening the wallet at his belt. “Here is a pretty charm I have had a long while—ever since I was in Sicily, a country far away.”

He fumbled among the small disorder of coins and trifles, unhooked the wallet, and tipped its contents onto Tessa’s lap. There, among odds and tokens, lay his onyx ring.

“Ah, my ring!” he exclaimed, slipping it onto his right forefinger. “I forgot to put it on again this morning. Strange—I never missed it!”

Then he found what he wanted: a small pointed bit of red coral, polished and vivid as a drop of sealed wax.

“See, Tessa,” he said, holding it up. “This little coral horn—like your goat’s horn, is it not? There is a hole, so you can put it on the cord round your neck with your Breve. Then the evil spirits cannot hurt you. If you ever see them coming in the shadow round a corner, point this at them—and they will run away. It is a buona fortuna, and will keep you from harm when I am not with you. Come—undo the cord.”

She obeyed, her fingers clumsy with haste, comfort flooding back as if the world were indeed being rearranged into safety. The coral hung beside the tiny bag of parchment; red against her skin, like a bright promise.

“And now you will give me a kiss,” Tito said, already sweeping the wallet’s contents back and hanging it at his waist, speaking as he worked to save time, “and look happy, like a good girl, and then—”

But she had already leaned forward and kissed his cheek, quick and obedient, mouth soft as a child’s blessing.

“Oh, you pretty pigeon!” Tito cried, laughing. He pressed her cheeks between his hands, crushing her features together and covering them with a general, impartial kiss, more playful than tender.

Then he sprang up and walked away. He did not look back until he was ten yards off; then he turned and gave a parting beck. Tessa watched him, still, not crying—her distress held down by fear and by the new weight of the coral charm at her throat. That was enough for him. His own ease depended on not seeing pain.

As he went, the distance to the Via de’ Bardi seemed longer than before, the sun heavier. The calm shade and the scent of fruit clung to him like a sweetness he had borrowed and must now pay for in hot steps.

“I wonder when Romola will kiss my cheek in that way?” he thought—half idly, half with the inward impatience of a man who wants the finest things without the rough labour of earning them.

No other excuse would be needed, he told himself. To Bardo and Romola he would say simply he had been unexpectedly hindered; their proud delicacy would ask no more. He hastened to Ognissanti, swallowed food quickly—bread and whatever the host could set before him—more to quiet hunger than to taste it, then crossed the Arno by the Ponte alla Carraja and made his way as directly as possible toward the Via de’ Bardi, leaving behind him, under a plane-tree, a girl with apricot-stained fingers and a charm against devils, listening to the fading of his footsteps as if the sound itself were the measure of her safety.

When Fra Luca’s voice fell into silence, Tito did not at once move away. He stood as if his feet had forgotten their errand, while the last crush of passengers thinned and the friar, gathering his robe about him with a slow, pained care, passed under the shadowed arch and into Santa Felicita. Only then did Tito turn and take the Via de’ Bardi, letting the daylight strike his face into its customary composure.

“If this monk is Florentine—if he means to stay in Florence—then all must come out.”

The thought went with him like a pebble in the shoe: small, but altering every step. Yet he was not so shaken that he could not do what was due in the ordinary order of things. He must go to Bardo, he must excuse himself for having stayed away, he must appear the same bright guest who could make an evening seem warmer by his mere entrance. It was still possible—perhaps in the end unavoidable—that he should accept the changed conditions and speak Baldassarre’s name aloud; but that candour would throw an ugly light backward, showing his first silence not as modest confusion but as a studied evasion, a choice to enjoy safety and settle his florins while his benefactor’s fate was only a rumour in the sea-wind. For the moment it was wiser to behave as if nothing had happened. The night was long. No one could know the exact hour at which a letter had reached his hand. He might postpone the instant when his life must change its taste.

So he climbed to the second storey room where Romola and her father sat apart from the street’s holiday noise as they sat apart from its weekday noise—among parchments that smelt of old glue and dust, among marble that kept the cool breath of the quarry. Outside, Florence rang with bells and shouts and the passing laughter that was like a stream over stones; within, the air had its own hush, broken by the thin rasp of a page turned, the tick of a tool, the murmured Latin that clung to Bardo’s lips as naturally as Tuscan clung to others.

Tito entered with a brightness only a little dimmed—dimmed just enough to be taken for regret at his lateness. He made that regret credible by naming what he had sacrificed: the Corso, the press of faces, the colour and swagger of it. And then he threw more animation than usual into the evening, as if gaiety could be kneaded and set to rise by sheer will. He spoke quickly, lightly; he made his voice a pleasant instrument against the room’s scholastic dryness. Yet all the while his mind worked beneath the talk like a mill whose stones grind on unseen: each word he uttered fell into place above, while below a different labour went on, leaving its own separate deposits—hard conclusions settling out of soft feeling.

By the time he went down the stone stairs and stepped from the grim doorway into starlight, his thoughts had reached a new stage. A purpose, like a sauce long simmered down, had thickened into something that would cling.

The next day, when he had finished the duties of his professorial work and the air began to soften towards afternoon, he turned up the Via del Cocomero toward San Marco. Florence had its usual music: the slap of sandals, the creak of carts, the calls of sellers; and in that weave of sound there were quieter threads—the drip of a fountain somewhere behind a wall, the flutter of pigeons, a far hammer on metal. Tito noticed all as one notices the scent of bread while passing a bakehouse: not as a thing to stop for, but as a thing that sweetens motion. He was going to learn from Fra Luca precisely how much the monk conjectured, on what grounds he had ventured his conjecture, and how long he meant to remain under San Marco’s roof. On that fuller knowledge Tito would mould a statement that should, in any event, save him from the necessity of leaving Florence.

He had never before needed to invent a lie carefully shaped to another man’s mind; yet the occasion had come now—the occasion which circumstance never fails to beget when a man has already consented to a tacit falsity. His ingenuity, trained in pleasing, in adapting, in finding the right phrase for the right ear, was ready. It seemed to him, with a growing ease, that he was not bound to go in search of Baldassarre.

He had once said—had meant, perhaps, as far as a young man means anything in a moment—that on fair assurance of his father’s existence and whereabout he would unhesitatingly go after him. But why was he bound? When he looked steadily, stripping the question of all the fine wrappings that society tied about it, what was the end of life but to draw from it the utmost sum of pleasure? His own life was in bloom. It promised more delight—rich, varied, quick to respond—not for himself alone but for others too, than the wintry remainder of a man past keen enjoyment, a man whose thoughts had stiffened into that rigid bareness which made companionship a demand and not a gift.

And had not Baldassarre already done his work? Those old ideas—rules, histories, habits of mind—were already sown in Tito’s fresh soil; they lived there as germ and sap. That, Tito told himself, was the true order of nature: maturity as a nest for youth. Baldassarre had had his draught. It was Tito’s turn now.

Besides, even the prospect offered no clear path: “I think they are going to take me to Antioch.” A phrase like that opened not a road but a vista of fog. A long voyage; then months, perhaps years, of search with no guarantee it would not end in emptiness. To leave behind at starting a life of distinction and of love, a life seasoned with praise like salt in food, and with tenderness like oil. And if he found anything, what would he find? The old companionship again, exacting, familiar, its claims known by rote in advance—like a dish whose bitterness you can taste before it reaches your mouth.

Certainly the gems and therefore the florins were, in the narrow sense of possession by which ordinary business was settled, Baldassarre’s. But in that larger view—so Tito was teaching his conscience to say—by which the world belonged to youth and strength, they were rather his who could turn them into the richest portion of lived sweetness. He knew that this was not the language of men. Florentines—those loud judges who could turn a man’s name into a proverb in a week—would expect him to snatch at the first chance of rescue, to fling money and self after the lost benefactor as one flings bread to a starving mouth. But what was the sentiment of society? A tangle of traditions and opinions, full of inherited words whose meanings had shifted like dialects under conquest: a dominant lexicon calling one thing “duty” and another “shame,” binding men with syllables that tasted noble on the tongue while they served common envy. No wise man, Tito thought, would let such a web guide him except so far as his own comfort required.

It was not the florins he cared for—perhaps not at all, except for Romola’s sake. He could part with money readily enough. It was the joy, due to him and close to his lips, that he refused to thrust away and so travel on, thirsty. Those maxims that demanded a man fling away the good that made existence sweet—were they not often only the lining of selfishness turned outward? They had been coined by men who desired others to sacrifice themselves for their benefit. Tito would rather Baldassarre did not suffer; he disliked suffering as he disliked a sour smell in a room. But could any philosophy prove he was bound to care for another’s suffering more than for his own? To do that he must have loved Baldassarre devotedly—and he did not. Was that his fault? Gratitude? Looked at closely, it made no valid claim. Baldassarre’s life would have been dreary without him; are we indebted to men for pleasures they have given themselves?

Once he began to dissolve Baldassarre’s claim, his thought acted like a strong acid, eating rapidly through every tissue of sentiment that had once seemed tough. He lacked that dread which, though some called it mere fear for one’s own skin, was in truth something rarer: the awe of a Nemesis, the sense that wrong-doing carried with it an unseen echo in the world’s soundscape, a threat that lived not in any priest’s tale but in the trembling of the soul. Religious pagans had felt it; Christians gave it names and faces; and even the crowd, without theology, carried a shadowy fear at anything called wrong. It was a fear that could crush ordinary cowardice, because it was the first recognition of a law restraining desire—a check upon the bold, cold analysis that can never prove obligation sacred once feeling has been banished.

“It is good,” sang the old Eumenides, “that fear should sit as the guardian of the soul, forcing it into wisdom—good that men should carry a threatening shadow in their hearts under the full sunshine; else, how should they learn to revere the right?”

That guardianship might become needless—but only when outward law was needless too, when duty and love ran together like two streams made one. Tito, as he entered the outer cloister of San Marco and asked for Fra Luca, felt no such shadow. He thought himself too cultivated, too sceptical for it. He had been nurtured in contempt for priests’ tales, made the more contemptible by priests’ impudent lives; he had been fed on learned disputes about the Chief Good until it seemed a matter of taste, like preferring one herb to another.

Yet fear lived strongly in him—the fear of whatever might rob him of pleasure. And he feared, distinctly, that Fra Luca might be the instrument that drove him out of Florence.

A lay brother—the kind called a _fra converso_—answered him. The man’s accent was plainly that of a raw contadino; his slow eyes held no prying curiosity, only the dulled patience of those who have listened all their lives to wind in vines and the creak of carts in rutted roads.

“Fra Luca? Ah, he is gone to Fiesole—to the Dominican monastery there. They took him on a litter in the cool of the morning. The poor Brother is very ill. Could you leave a message for him?”

“Thanks,” Tito said, letting his tone carry polite regret and no urgency. “My business can wait.”

He turned away with a relief that loosened something tight in his chest, as if a cord had been cut. The cloister sounds returned to him—the small footfalls on stone, the faint voice somewhere reading, the distant bell that measured the day like a ladle measuring broth. All seemed to say: wait.

“This friar is not likely to live,” he thought. “I saw he was worn to a shadow. And at Fiesole there will be nothing to recall me to his mind. Besides, if he should come back, my explanation will serve as well then as now. But I wish I knew what it was that his face recalled to me.”

Tito’s footfall on the worn Florentine stones had the buoyancy of a man who has slipped the noose for another day. The clutch of immediate fear was gone; his spirits sprang back, light and glittering as oil spread on water. He was going to Romola.

And yet—threaded beneath that easy gladness—Romola’s life rose before him like a fresco of patient hands: the steady ordering of her father’s hours, the gentle endurance of his demands, the long fidelity to tasks that yielded no applause. It was the sort of goodness Tito admired as one admires a well-built hearth—warm, necessary, and not meant, in his imagination, to burn him. He was not in love with wickedness; he still had the clean appetite of youth for ordinary joys, for the taste of comfort and the scent of praise. The poison he had taken into his life would work slowly, drop by drop, like bitter herbs steeping in sweet wine until the sweetness itself became suspect.

He meant, with an almost childlike obstinacy, that everything should go on as before: his smile should win him friends, his learning should win him “golden opinions,” his pliancy should keep him in harmony with the people he cared for. Above all, he cared for Romola. There might be richer alliances in Florence for a young Greek with a ready mind and an insinuating grace, but there was no woman like her—no other gaze so clear and honest, no other presence that could quiet him as surely as a lute-string, once touched, imposes its rhythm on the air. When he neared her home, anticipation itself began to play on him like those vibrations one feels in the bones before one hears the full chord.

He mounted the stone stairs; Maso was behind him; the door was still between him and the room where Romola sat. And already Bardo’s blind, vigilant voice met him.

“Welcome, Tito mio,” it said, with a new vigor, as if some inner spring had been wound tighter since their first labors together. “Thou hast brought fresh manuscript, doubtless; but since we were talking last night I have had new ideas. We must take a wider scope—we must go back upon our footsteps.”

Tito entered, offered his reverence to Romola with that careful courtesy which never forgot itself, and went—by habit and by policy—straight to the old man’s chair. He placed his hand within the palm that was held out to receive it and took the low cross-legged leather seat close to Bardo’s elbow, as if he belonged there.

“Yes,” he said in his gentle tone, “I have brought the new manuscript; but that can wait your pleasure. I have young limbs, you know, and can walk back up the hill without difficulty.”

He did not look at Romola while he spoke, yet he felt her eyes on him—warm, delighted, as if the very words “young limbs” were a promise that life would be generous.

“That is well said, my son.” Bardo had begun of late to call him so, and the word had weight—patronage, affection, possession. “And I perceive with gladness that thou dost not shrink from labor, without which, the poet has wisely said, life has given nothing to mortals. It is too often the palma sine pulvere—the prize without the dust—that attracts young ambition. But what says the Greek? ‘In the morning of life, work; in the mid-day, give counsel; in the evening, pray.’ I might be thought to have reached that helpless evening; yet not so, while I have counsel within me which is yet unspoken. For my mind, as I have often said, was shut up as by a dam; the waters lay dark and motionless; but thou, my Tito, hast opened a duct for them, and they rush forward with a force that surprises myself.”

As he spoke he stooped toward the manuscript that had rolled; his ear, jealous and keen, caught Tito’s slight movement.

“And now,” Bardo continued, “what I want is this: that we should go over our preliminary ground again, with a wider scheme of comment and illustration. Else I may lose opportunities which I now see retrospectively, and which may never occur again. Thou markest what I am saying, Tito?”

Tito might have been forgiven a hidden sigh. To turn back was to unweave and reweave, to knead again dough already shaped, to labor for hours in that minute erudition the age prized—laborious as picking bones from a fish for a delicate palate. But impatience was not his nature, and Romola’s nearness was like a steady perfume—quieting, pleasant, making even the stale dust of parchment seem part of a rich domestic air.

“Assuredly,” he said. “You wish to enlarge your comments on certain passages we have cited.”

“Not only so. I wish to introduce an occasional excursus,” said Bardo, warming, his hands alive in the air as if he still saw the lines. “Where we have noticed an author to whom I have given special study; for I may die too soon to achieve any separate work. And this is not a time for scholarly integrity and well-sifted learning to lie idle, when it is not only rash ignorance that we have to fear, but when there are men like Calderino who have recourse to impudent falsities of citation to serve the ends of their vanity and secure a triumph to their own mistakes.”

His voice bit sharply on the names, as if the syllables themselves were bitter. The room around them, lined with orderly ranks of volumes—leather, vellum, wood—had its own hush, broken only by the faint crackle of the city beyond, and the soft, dry sound of pages handled. In that silence, the old man’s passion sounded the more vehement.

“Wherefore,” he said, “I think it not well that we should let slip the occasion that lies under our hands. And now we will turn back to the point where we have cited the passage from Thucydides, and I wish thee, by way of preliminary, to go with me through all my notes on the Latin translation made by Lorenzo Valla—for which the incomparable Pope Nicholas the Fifth, with whose personal notice I was honored while I was yet young, paid him five hundred gold scudi.”

The coins seemed to clink in Bardo’s memory; Tito could almost hear them against a table, bright and heavy.

“But inasmuch as Valla, though otherwise of dubious fame, is held in high honor for severe scholarship,” Bardo pursued, “it is the more needful that his name should not be as a stamp warranting false wares. Therefore I would introduce an excursus on Thucydides, wherein my castigations of Valla’s text may find a fitting place. My Romola, thou wilt reach the needful volumes—thou knowest them—on the fifth shelf of the cabinet.”

Romola rose at once; and Tito, rising with her, said, “I will reach them, if you will point them out,” and followed her quickly into the adjoining small room.

It was a narrower chamber, but the same severe abundance: shelves close-ranked with books in perfect order, each spine a familiar ridge beneath Romola’s hands, as if the room itself were an extension of her father’s mind—stored, classified, immovable. The air carried the mingled scents of old glue, rubbed leather, and the faint mineral dryness of paper that has drunk years of Florentine sunlight.

“There they are,” Romola said, pointing upward. “Every book is just where it was when my father ceased to see them.”

Tito did not climb at once. He stood beside her, and because they had never stood together in this smaller room before, the place seemed suddenly intimate—like a pantry entered after the household has gone to sleep, where even the jars and hanging herbs seem to listen.

“I hope,” Romola went on, turning to him with grave trust, “I hope he will not weary you; this work makes him so happy.”

“And me too, Romola,” Tito murmured, letting the softness of his voice do what a bolder approach would have risked. “If you will only let me say—I love you—if you will only think me worth loving a little.”

His face, dark and beautiful, came nearer than it had ever been; his tenderness looked up at her like a plea. Romola’s calm, earnest eyes held his without coquetry, as if love, once recognized, must be spoken plainly.

“I do love you,” she whispered.

The words were simple, but her voice—never before in her life had it sunk to that low, intimate murmur—made them feel like something newly minted, warm from the press of the soul. It seemed to them both that they looked at each other a long while before her lips moved again; and yet it was only a breath before she added, “I know now what it is to be happy.”

Their faces met; the dark curls touched, and for an instant mingled with the rippling gold of her hair. Then, quick as lightning—because the world outside this moment still existed, because Bardo’s ear was jealous and time was theirs only by stealth—Tito set his foot on a projecting ledge of the shelves and reached down the needed volumes.

When they went back, they were content to be silent and separate. That first mutual certainty—like waters once joined—had its own sweetness, the more exquisite because it was not immediately disturbed by craving.

Bardo, eager, had not yet become impatient.

“You have the volumes, my Romola?” he said as they returned. “And now thou wilt get thy pen ready; for, as Tito marks off the scholia we determine on extracting, it will be well for thee to copy them without delay—numbering them carefully, mind, to correspond with the numbers in the text which he will write.”

So the household rite resumed itself: the old blind scholar enthroned in his chair, Tito at the leggio where he read and wrote, Romola at the table just before him, ready to pass what her father needed, to lift a volume from his knee, to lay it aside, to keep the labor moving as a cook keeps a sauce from catching—stirring, watching, measuring, always attentive. Ink smelled sharp and metallic; the quill whispered; parchment gave its dry resistance; and beyond, Florence murmured—cart-wheels on stone, a distant call, a sudden laugh that died away.

They had always sat so since the work began, but today everything was altered by what had passed in the narrow room. To be opposite each other now—Tito taking a book from Romola’s hand, her fingers close to his—was like tasting bread one has eaten every day and discovering suddenly the sweetness of the grain. Yet neither sought to steal more than their task allowed: Romola’s love was too deep and calm to require petty tokens. It encompassed him like a rich evening light that makes even labor beautiful.

Two hours passed. The daylight thinned, as if someone were slowly turning down a lamp; the words on the page began to drown in grey. They were just desisting because the light failed when the door opened.

A figure entered that jarred against the sober room as a street-drum jars against a cloister chant.

It was a short, stout woman of about fifty, black-eyed, brisk, and richly dressed. A black velvet berretta, embroidered with pearls, hugged her head; beneath it, massive black braids were arranged with elaborate care, surmounting a small bulging forehead and falling in heavy plaited curves over her ears. Her cheeks bore an astonishing carmine tint high on the fat flesh, the rest of her face sallow by contrast. Three rows of pearls lay upon the cushion of her neck, and beneath them a gold necklace. Her trailing black velvet gown and long drooping sleeves of rose-colored damask were slightly faded, but they spoke to any practised eye of costly work patiently done—six months of a craftsman’s labor. A rose-colored petticoat showed itself with deliberate propriety, its fringe dimmed white, its seed-pearl arabesques still catching the failing light. A handsome coral rosary hung from one side of a belt that emerged into certainty at a silver clasp wrought in niello; from the other side depended a crimson velvet scarsella stitched with pearls. In her little fat right hand—soft as if made of paste—she carried a small book of devotions glittering with velvet, pearls, and silver.

Tito recognized Monna Brigida at once; she was too frequent here to startle him. She was a cousin of Bardo’s dead wife and had helped nurse and mind Romola in her girlhood. For that service she was pardoned, though Bardo had banished “feminine triviality” from his house as one banishes smoke from a library.

Romola turned with an affectionate smile and rose to draw a leather seat a little farther from her father’s chair, to spare his ear the coming torrent.

“La cugina?” Bardo asked, hearing the short steps and the sweep of drapery.

“Yes, yes, it is your cousin,” Monna Brigida said in her alert voice, raising her fingers smilingly at Tito and lifting her face for Romola’s kiss. “Always the troublesome cousin breaking in on your wisdom.” She sat and began to fan herself with the white veil hanging over her arm. “Well, well! If I didn’t bring you some news of the world now and then, I do believe you’d forget there was anything in life but these mouldy ancients—who want sprinkling with holy water if all I hear about them is true.”

Her voice filled the room as a strong spice fills a stew, overpowering the delicate scent of parchment and ink.

“Not but what the world is bad enough nowadays,” she rattled on, “for the scandals that turn up under one’s nose at every corner. I don’t want to hear and see such things, but one can’t go about with one’s head in a bag. And it was only yesterday—well, well, you needn’t burst out at me, Bardo, I’m not going to tell anything. If I’m not as wise as the three kings, I know how many legs go into one boot.”

She drew breath and plunged on again, as if breath itself were a mere pause between waves.

“But Florence is a wicked city—is it not true, Messer Tito? for you go into the world. Not but what one must sin a little—Messer Domeneddio expects that of us, else what are the blessed sacraments for? And what I say is, we’ve got to reverence the saints and not to set ourselves up as if we could be like them, else life would be unbearable—especially if things go on after this new fashion.”

Her fan fluttered; pearls shifted softly against velvet with each movement.

“For what do you think? I’ve been at the wedding to-day—Dianora Acciajoli’s with the young Albizzi that there has been so much talk of—and everybody wondered at its being to-day instead of yesterday; but, cieli! such a wedding as it was might have been put off till next Quaresima for a penance. There was the bride looking like a white nun—not so much as a pearl about her—and the bridegroom as solemn as San Giuseppe. It’s true. And half the people invited were Piagnoni—funeral mourners they call them now—these new saints of Fra Girolamo’s making.”

She sniffed, as if the memory had a smell—wax, damp cloth, and moral severity.

“And to think of two families like the Albizzi and the Acciajoli taking up such notions, when they could afford to wear the best! Well, well, they invited me—but they could do no other, seeing my husband was Luca Antonio’s uncle by the mother’s side—and a pretty time I had of it while we waited under the canopy in front of the house before they let us in. I couldn’t stand in my clothes without giving offence. There was Monna Berta—who has had worse secrets in her time than any I could tell of myself—looking askance at me from under her hood like a pinzochera, and telling me to read the Frate’s book about widows, from which she had found great guidance.”

Monna Brigida’s voice rose on the word “widows” with the indignation of one whose very wardrobe had been put on trial.

“Holy Madonna! it seems as if widows had nothing to do now but to buy their coffins and think it a thousand years till they get into them, instead of enjoying themselves a little when they’ve got their hands free for the first time. And what do you think was the music we had, to make our dinner lively? A long discourse from Fra Domenico of San Marco about the doctrines of their blessed Fra Girolamo—the three doctrines we are all to get by heart. He kept marking them off on his fingers till he made my flesh creep.”

She lifted her own fingers as if the gesture itself had pursued her home.

“The first is, Florence, or the Church—I don’t know which, for first he said one and then the other—shall be scourged. If he means the pestilence, the Signory ought to put a stop to such preaching, for it’s enough to raise the swelling under one’s arms with fright. Then he says Florence is to be regenerated; but what will be the good of that when we’re all dead of the plague, or something else? And the third thing—and what he said oftenest—is that it’s all to be in our days. He marked that off on his thumb till he made me tremble like the very jelly before me.”

At the word “jelly” her mouth softened, remembering, despite herself.

“They had jellies, to be sure, with the arms of the Albizzi and the Acciajoli raised on them in all colours—they’ve not turned the world quite upside down yet. But all their talk is, we are to go back to the old ways. Up starts Francesco Valori—whom I’ve danced with in the Via Larga when he was a bachelor and as fond of the Medici as anybody—and he makes a speech about the old times, before the Florentines had left off crying ‘Popolo’ and begun to cry ‘Palle’—as if that had anything to do with a wedding!—and how we ought to keep to the rules the Signory laid down heaven knows when, that we were not to wear this and that, and not to eat this and that—”

At “not to eat,” her fan stopped for a moment, as if even her body protested at the thought of regulations on the table—Florentine tables with their sugared almonds, their spiced wines, their sauces warmed over coals and scented with rosemary, their meats glazed and their fruits piled like painted offerings. The austerity she described was not merely moral; it was an assault on taste, on the remembered sweetness of feast-days.

“—and how our manners were corrupted,” she went on, “and we read bad books; though he can’t say that of me—”

“Stop, cousin!” Bardo cut in, his imperious voice snapping like a shut volume. He had a remark to make, and only a sharp command could dam that stream.

Monna Brigida started, pursed her mouth, and stared at him with round eyes, wounded and ready.

“Francesco Valori is not altogether wrong,” Bardo said, his tone changing to that stern didactic measure Romola knew so well. “Bernardo rates him not highly, and is rather of opinion that he christens private grudges by the name of public zeal; though I must admit that my good Bernardo is too slow of belief in that unalloyed patriotism which was found in all its lustre amongst the ancients. But it is true, Tito, that our manners have degenerated somewhat from that noble frugality which is the parent of true magnificence.”

He spoke of frugality not as starvation but as discipline—the measured hand that can be grand when grandeur is worthy.

“For men, as I hear, will now spend on the transient show of a giostra sums which would suffice to found a library and confer a lasting possession on mankind. Still, I conceive it remains true of us Florentines that we have more of that magnanimous sobriety which abhors a trivial lavishness that it may be grandly open-handed on grand occasions than can be found in any other city of Italy. The Neapolitan and Milanese courtiers laugh at the scarcity of our plate, and think scorn of our great families for borrowing from each other that furniture of the table at their entertainments. But in the vain laughter of folly, wisdom hears half its applause.”

“Laughter, indeed!” Monna Brigida burst out the instant he paused, the word springing from her as if she had been forced to hold it in her throat. “If anybody wanted laughter at the wedding to-day they were disappointed. When young Niccolò Macchiavelli tried to make a joke and told stories out of Franco Sacchetti’s book—how it was no use for the Signoria to make rules for us women because we were cleverer than all the painters and architects and doctors of logic in the world, for we could make black look white and yellow look pink and crooked look straight, and if anything was forbidden we could find a new name for it—Holy Virgin! the Piagnoni looked more dismal than before, and somebody said Sacchetti’s book was wicked.”

Her voice carried contempt for the new piety that could not bear a joke, as if laughter itself were a sin.

“Well, I don’t read it—they can’t accuse me of reading anything. Save me from going to a wedding again if that’s to be the fashion, for all of us who were not Piagnoni were as comfortable as wet chickens.”

She fanned harder, making a small hiss in the air.

“I was never caught in a worse trap but once before, and that was when I went to hear their precious Frate last Quaresima in San Lorenzo. Perhaps I never told you about it, Messer Tito? It almost freezes my blood when I think of it. How he rated us poor women! and the men too, to tell the truth, but I didn’t mind that so much. He called us cows, and lumps of flesh, and wantons, and mischief-makers—and I could just bear that, for there were plenty others more fleshy and spiteful than I was—though every now and then his voice shook the very bench under me like a trumpet.”

As she spoke, the room seemed to tremble again, as if that trumpet had followed her through the streets to Bardo’s calm study.

“But then he came to the false hair, and—O misericordia!—he made a picture—I see it now—of a young woman lying a pale corpse, and us light-minded widows—of course he meant me as well as the rest, for I had my plaits on, for if one is getting old, one doesn’t want to look as ugly as the Befana—us widows rushing up to the corpse, like bare-pated vultures, and cutting off its young dead hair to deck our old heads with.”

She shuddered and pressed her lips tight, as if the taste of that image were bitter on her tongue.

“Oh, the dreams I had after that! And then he cried, and wrung his hands at us, and I cried too. And to go home, and to take off my jewels—this very clasp—and everything, and to make them into a packet—fù tutt’uno; and I was within a hair of sending them to the Good Men of Saint Martin to give to the poor, but, by heaven’s mercy, I bethought me of going first to my confessor, Fra Cristoforo, at Santa Croce. He told me it was all the work of the devil, this preaching and prophesying of their Fra Girolamo, and the Dominicans were trying to turn the world upside down, and I was never to go and hear him again, else I must do penance for it. For the great preachers Fra Mariano and Fra Menico had shown how Fra Girolamo preached lies—and that was true, for I heard them both in the Duomo—and how the Pope’s dream of San Francesco propping up the Church with his arms was being fulfilled still, and the Dominicans were beginning to pull it down.”

Her pearls lifted with her breath, then settled again.

“Well and good: I went away con Dio, and made myself easy. I am not going to be frightened by a Frate Predicatore again. And all I say is, I wish it hadn’t been the Dominicans that poor Dino joined years ago, for then I should have been glad when I heard them say he was come back—”

“Silenzio!” Bardo’s voice rang out loud and shaken, as if someone had struck a brass plate in the quiet room.

Romola half started from her chair; her hands clasped; her eyes flew to Tito, and in that look there was a child’s sudden appeal and a woman’s restrained anguish. Monna Brigida gave a little scream and bit her lip.
