“Donna!” Bardo cried again. “Hear once more my will. Bring no reports about that name to this house; and thou, Romola, I forbid thee to ask. My son is dead.”

His whole frame seemed to vibrate with passion, the blind body making visible what the blind eyes could not. In that moment the room’s former peace was gone; even the books, standing in their ranks, seemed to share the shock, as if a secret had been struck like a hidden string.

No one spoke. Monna Brigida lifted shoulders and hands in mute dismay; then, as quietly as possible, she rose. She nodded many times at Tito and Romola, motioning them not to move, and stole out with the guilty haste of a fat spaniel who has barked at the wrong time.

In the deepening silence, Tito’s mind worked with the speed of a knife flashing in skilled hands.

Bardo’s son was not truly dead, then—not dead as Tito had supposed. A monk. “Come back.” Fra Luca—yes: it was the likeness, the shared bone and line, that had made that face seem half-known to him when he saw it. The thought struck cold and hard.

If only he were dead at Fiesole at that moment.

The selfish wish rose irresistibly, thrusting itself before every other thought like a hand snatching the choicest morsel. Bardo’s rigid will would keep Romola from seeking her brother—but it could not prevent the brother, if living and returned, from speaking what he knew to others. And worse: the very coupling of Romola’s name with Tito Melema’s might be enough to awaken Fra Luca’s suspicions, especially since he had carried Tito’s description as an index at his neck.

No. Nothing but Fra Luca’s death could remove all danger.

Yet Fra Luca’s death was highly probable. Tito let his mind settle back, after the first shock, into that confident hope as into a warm bed: probability could be made into certainty if one waited—if one was careful.

They sat in silence for many minutes, the twilight growing thicker, as if the city outside had exhaled a darker breath. At last Romola ventured, gently, as if to restore the broken order with the simplest domestic act—

“Shall I light the lamp, father, and shall we go on?”

“No, my Romola,” Bardo said, his voice quieter but still strained. “We will work no more to-night. Tito, come and sit by me here.”

Tito left the reading-desk and seated himself on Bardo’s other side, close to his left elbow.

“Come nearer to me, figliuola mia,” Bardo said after a pause.

Romola came and sat on a low stool, resting her arm on her father’s right knee so that he might lay his hand on her hair, as he loved to do—an old habit, tender and possessive, like a blessing spoken by touch. The room was dim; the unsaid words made it heavier than darkness.

“Tito,” Bardo began, and there was a trembling in him that pride could not wholly hide, “I never told thee that I had once a son.”

He had forgotten—forgotten, in the storm of their first interview, what he had let slip then; now emotion forced confession out of him as a wound forces blood.

“But he left me—he is dead to me. I have disowned him for ever. He was a ready scholar as thou art, but more fervid and impatient, and yet sometimes rapt and self-absorbed, like a flame fed by some fitful source. From the very first he showed a disposition to turn away his eyes from the clear lights of reason and philosophy and to prostrate himself under the influences of a dim mysticism which eludes all rules of human duty as it eludes all argument.”

His hand on Romola’s hair pressed, then trembled, as if memory itself were something he wanted to hold down and could not.

“And so it ended,” he said. “We will speak no more of him. He is dead to me. I wish his face could be blotted from that world of memory in which the distant seems to grow clearer and the near to fade.”

He paused. Neither Romola nor Tito dared to speak. Bardo’s voice was too tremulous, his poise too uncertain, like a vessel that might spill if touched.

After a moment he raised his hand, found Tito’s shoulder, and let it rest there, as if seeking steadiness from the living warmth beside him. Then he went on, with an effort to be calmer, pouring out what pride would have hidden, because the heart, once shaken, will have its utterance.

The afternoon of the seventh of September had that languor Florence knows so well: heat stored in stone, light thickened to honey, the air almost edible with dust and late-summer fig. Two months had gone since Romola and Tito had let their voices—shy at first, then certain—name what their hearts had already rehearsed. And now Tito, stepping down from the street into Nello’s shop, brought with him the outer city: the faint clatter of hooves on paving, a distant vendor’s cry, the muffled chorus of a place that never wholly falls silent.

Inside, the barber’s room smelled as it always did—citrus oils, warm skin, wetted linen—layered today with the drowsy paper-scent of a book left open like a loaf gone stale. Nello lay stretched on the bench with his cap over his eyes, one leg drawn up, the other slipping toward the ground as if it had tired of holding its own weight. A manuscript volume had fallen with him and lay crushed, its leaves dog-eared and flattened under the dull tyranny of sleep.

In the corner, Sandro sat solemn as an altar boy, playing _mora_ against himself: right hand demanding numbers, left hand answering slowly, as though the fingers were old peasants reluctant to leave the furrow. The boy watched his own hands as if they were a small, private miracle.

Tito moved as softly as one who steals a pinch of salt from the jar so the cook won’t hear. He snatched up the lute, bent over the sleeping barber, and touched the strings with a lightness that was almost a breath. Then, as if the notes themselves had drawn him into their current, he sang under his voice:

“Quant’ è bella giovinezza,
Che si fugge tuttavia!
Chi vuol esser lieto sia,
Di doman non c’è certezza.”

Nello woke as a bird wakes—no heavy hauling of consciousness, only a sudden flutter into wakefulness. The cap flew off; he sprang upright, blinking once, and the next moment his whole face was alive with jest.

“Ah, my Apollino! Late with my siesta, it seems. That comes of not falling asleep in a natural way, but swallowing a potion of potent poesy. Listen how I begin to match words by the first letter, like some trovatore—bad symptom, that. I fear the good wine of my understanding is running away at the spigot of authorship. I shall be left an empty cask with only the smell of dregs, like many another incomparable genius I could name.”

He stretched both arms long as a man measuring cloth, then brought them round to seize Tito’s curls and tug them playfully, as if the boy’s bright head were a fruit he meant to test for ripeness.

“What is it, my Orpheus? There’s coaxing in that soft strain. Show me the very needle’s eye of your desire, as the sublime poet says, and I’ll thread it.”

“That is a tailor’s image for your sublime poet,” Tito answered, still letting his fingers fall in a gentle, dropping way on the strings, like water from a thin spout. “But you have divined the reason of my affectionate impatience. I want you to give me an extra touch of your art—not on my chin; no—but on the _zazzera_, which is as tangled as Florentine politics. You slip your comb in so adroitly it flatters the skin and stirs the animal spirits in that region; and a little of your most delicate orange-scent will not lie amiss. I am bound to the Scala palace. I must present myself in radiant company. The young cardinal Giovanni de’ Medici is to be there, and he brings with him a certain Bernardo Dovizi of Bibbiena, whose wit runs so fast I see no way to out-rival it save by smelling of orange-blossoms.”

Nello had already seized his comb and flourished it like a conductor’s baton. He pushed Tito backward into the chair with the easy authority of a man who has guided a hundred necks into linen, wrapped the cloth around him, and began that practiced work: the teeth of the comb finding their path through the thick hair, tugging just enough to make the scalp quicken, then easing off, smoothing, parting, taming. His fingers were nimble, scented faintly of soap and bitter peel.

“Never talk of rivalry, bel giovane,” he said. “Bernardo Dovizi is sharp, yes, but he won’t cast a net to catch the wind. And he has the same weasel look as his brother Ser Piero—the creature Piero de’ Medici keeps to slip through small holes for him. No. You distance all rivals. Soon you’ll touch the sky with your forefinger. They say you have carried enough honey to sweeten sour Messer Angelo himself. He has pronounced you less of an ass than might have been expected, considering there is such a good understanding between you and the Secretary.”

Tito smiled—one of those smiles that made even self-interest look like charm—and let his head incline under the comb. “Between ourselves, Nello mio, Messer Angelo has more genius and erudition than I find in all the other Florentine scholars together. It answers well enough for them to cry me up now, when Poliziano is beaten down with grief, or illness, or something else. I can try a flight with such a sparrow-hawk as Pietro Crinito; but Poliziano—he is a large-beaked eagle. He would swallow me, feathers and all, and not feel the difference.”

Nello clicked his tongue and worked in a little oil, rubbing it between his palms before pressing it into Tito’s hair. The scent rose immediately—orange with a thread of something resinous—bright as the first cut into rind.

“I won’t contradict your modesty if you insist on it,” he said. “But we clever Florentines can’t keep saying the same things every day of our lives, as we must if we always told the truth. We cry down Dante and cry up Francesco Cei, just for variety. And if we cry you up as a new Poliziano, heaven has taken care the lie shall not be so big as it might. And are you not a pattern of virtue in this wicked city? Ears double-waxed against every siren invitation that would lure you from the Via de’ Bardi—and from the great work that is to astonish posterity?”

“Posterity,” Tito said, letting the word slide out as if it were a coin of doubtful stamp, “whom it will probably astonish as the universe does, by the impossibility of seeing what the plan of it was.”

“Yes—something of that sort was prophesied here the other day,” Nello replied. “Cristoforo Landino said the excellent Bardo is one of those scholars who lie overthrown in their learning, like cavaliers in heavy armour, and then get angry because they are over-ridden. A pithy remark, and not, I think, a herb from his own garden; for of all men to feed one with an empty spoon and gag one with vain expectation by long discourse, Messer Cristoforo is the pearl.”

He stepped back, surveyed his handiwork with the satisfaction of a cook who has coaxed a sauce to the right sheen, and whisked away the cloth.

“Ecco! Perfect. Impossible to add a grace more! But love is not always fed on learning, eh? I shall have to dress the _zazzera_ for the betrothal before long—is it not true?”

“Perhaps,” Tito said, smiling, “unless Messer Bernardo should next recommend Bardo to require that I yoke a lion and a wild boar to the car of the Zecca before I can win my Alcestis. But I confess he is right to hold me unworthy of Romola. She is a Pleiad—she may grow dim by marrying any mortal.”

“_Gnaffè_, your modesty is in the right place there,” Nello said, and his hands—still smelling of orange—made a quick, dismissive wave, as if batting away flies. “Yet fate seems to have measured and chiselled you for the niche left empty by the old man’s son—who, by the way, Cronaca was telling me, is now at San Marco. Did you know?”

Something went through Tito like a thin wire struck by lightning: no cry, no visible start, only a sudden inward jolt that made his breath change. He hid it as he had learned to hide so many things—by bending at once to a practical action. He stooped, picked up the fallen manuscript, and began smoothing the crushed leaves with careful fingers, pressing them flat as though neatness could keep danger at bay.

“No,” he said, and his voice sounded natural enough. “He was at Fiesole, I thought. Are you sure he has come back to San Marco?”

“Cronaca is my authority.” Nello shrugged. “I don’t frequent that sanctuary, but he does. Ah!” He took the book from Tito, peered at its abused pages, and sighed in mock tenderness. “My poor _Nencia da Barberino_! It jars your scholarly feelings to see pages dog’s-eared. I was lulled to sleep by that rustic maiden—‘prettier than the turnip-flower,’ ‘with a cheek more savoury than cheese.’ But to get such a well-scented notion of the _contadina_, one must lie on velvet cushions in the Via Larga—not go to look at the Fierucoloni stumping in to the Piazza della Nunziata this evening after sundown.”

“And who are the Fierucoloni?” Tito asked, as if it were nothing to him—settling his cap, touching the edge as though testing its fit.

“The _contadine_,” Nello replied, “come down from the mountains of Pistoia, the Casentino, heaven knows where, to keep their vigil at the Nunziata, and sell their yarn and dried mushrooms at the _Fierucola_—the little Fair. They make a queer show with paper lanterns, howling their hymns to the Virgin on this eve of her nativity. Wild work in the piazza. One may get a stone or two about one’s ears or shins without asking. I was never fond of that pressing attention. Addio.”

Tito left with the orange-blossom scent clinging to him like a promise meant for an evening that might never arrive. The Scala palace received him with its usual murmur of fine voices and rustle of garments; the air inside was cooler, scented faintly with wax and the stored sweetness of old wood. Yet the visit ended earlier than he had expected. The boy-cardinal Giovanni de’ Medici—youngest of red-hatted fathers, already practiced in all the indulgences that make a man’s face broad and memorable—was detained at his favourite pastime of the chase and failed to appear.

Half an hour before sunset Tito came out again, intending to go straight to the Via de’ Bardi. The city, however, had begun to change its note, as it always did toward evening: footsteps quickened, voices rose, the soundscape thickened with the anticipation of crowds. He had gone only a little way when, to his astonishment, he saw Romola advancing toward him along the Borgo Pinti.

She was wrapped in a thick black veil and mantle, a darkness moving through the amber of late light; but her figure and her walk were unmistakable. By her side was a short, stout form—Monna Brigida—whom he recognized despite the unusual plainness of her dress. Romola had not been bred to devotional observances; her going out beyond the familiar roof-loggia was rare and always arranged in advance because of Bardo’s jealousy of being left alone. Tito felt at once that something urgent had driven her into the street without warning him.

She saw him through the veil and hurried.

“Romola—has anything happened?” Tito asked, turning to walk beside her.

Romola did not answer immediately, and Monna Brigida’s voice burst in, practical and breathless, as if she were scolding a kettle for boiling too slowly.

“Ah, Messer Tito, you do well to turn round, for we are in haste. And is it not a misfortune? We must go round by the walls and turn up the Via del Maglio because of the Fair. The _contadine_ coming in block up the way by the Nunziata, which would have taken us to San Marco in half the time.”

Tito’s heart leapt hard—so hard it seemed to strike his ribs and rebound. “Romola,” he said, lowering his voice, “are you going to San Marco?”

They had passed out of Borgo Pinti and now walked under the city walls. On their left lay wide gardens, green and hushful, their leaves holding the day’s heat like cupped hands. Here the noise of Florence fell away. The city’s clamour became a distant wash; nearer were the small, living sounds—the whisper of wind in vines, a bird’s brief call, the faint scrape of a hoe far off. Romola lifted her veil a little to breathe, and Tito saw the subdued agitation in her face.

“Yes, Tito mio,” she said, looking at him with sad, steady eyes. “For the first time I am doing something unknown to my father. It comforts me that I have met you, for at least I can tell you. But if you are going to him, it will be well for you not to say you met me. He thinks I am only gone to my cousin, because she sent for me. I left my godfather with him: he knows where I am going, and why.”

Tito’s mind, which usually ran like a smooth mill-wheel, began to race and grind all at once. He tried to keep his face composed while his thoughts flew forward, striking sparks from fear: what would be asked, what would be said, what would be revealed.

“You remember that evening,” Romola went on, “when my brother’s name was mentioned, and my father spoke of him to you?”

“Yes,” Tito answered. His own voice sounded as if it came from farther away.

“The _cugina_ had heard he was come back. The evening before—the evening of San Giovanni—as I afterwards found, he had been seen by our good Maso near the door of our house. But when Maso went to inquire at San Marco, Dino—my brother—he was christened Bernardino, after our godfather, but now he calls himself Fra Luca—had been taken to the monastery at Fiesole because he was ill.

“But this morning a message came to Maso, saying he was come back to San Marco; and Maso went to him there. He is very ill, and he has adjured me to go and see him. I cannot refuse, though I hold him guilty. I still remember how I loved him when I was a little girl, before I knew he would forsake my father. And perhaps he has some word of penitence to send by me.”

Her words moved as quietly as water, yet each one seemed to press on Tito’s chest. She spoke again, and her voice trembled—not with fear, but with the strain of acting against years of obedience.

“It cost me a struggle to act in opposition to my father’s feeling, which I have always held to be just. I am almost sure you will think I have chosen rightly, Tito, because I have noticed your nature is less rigid than mine, and nothing makes you angry. It would cost you less to be forgiving; though, if you had seen your father forsaken by one to whom he had given his chief love—by one in whom he had planted his labour and his hopes—forsaken when his need was becoming greatest—even you, Tito, would find it hard to forgive.”

What could he say? The truth—his own truth—was a twisted thing, full of hidden bones. He could not tell Romola that such offences ought never to be pardoned; he could not find the courage to dissuade her from going. He felt as if the air under the walls had thinned; even the birds and leaves seemed to listen, and the city beyond, with its coming fair and its hymns, was only a distant, indifferent roar.

“You are right, my Romola,” he said at last. “You are always right—except in thinking too well of me.”

There was something genuine in it, and the words made him momentarily pale, his lip quivering as though he had tasted something too sharp. In the orange-scent on his hair there was suddenly a bitter edge, as if the blossom had been bruised.

Romola, who interpreted all things largely—her mind prepossessed with high beliefs—looked at him with tearful brightness, touched with keen joy that he felt so strongly whatever she felt. Without pausing in her walk, she said:

“And now, Tito, I wish you to leave me, for the _cugina_ and I shall be less noticed if we enter the piazza alone.”

“Yes, it were better you should leave us,” Monna Brigida said, blunt as always. “For to say the truth, Messer Tito, all eyes follow you; and let Romola muffle herself as she will, every one wants to see what is under her veil, for she has that way of walking like a procession. Not that I find fault with her, only it doesn’t suit my steps. And indeed I would rather not have us seen going to San Marco, and that’s why I am dressed as if I were one of the Piagnoni themselves, and as old as Sant’ Anna; for if it had been anybody but poor Dino—who ought to be forgiven if he’s dying, for what use is a grudge against dead people? Make them feel while they live, say I—”

No one made any scruple of interrupting Monna Brigida. Tito raised Romola’s hand to his lips—warm through the thin glove, real as bread in a man’s palm—and murmured, “I understand. I obey you.” Then he turned away, lifting his cap in a sign of reverence that native Florentines rarely made. Bernardo del Nero would have sneered at it as the fawning of a Greek; Romola, loving homage, had always found in it an added grace.

He was half glad to be dismissed, half aching to cling to her for the last moments of her unquestioning love. For in his mind the future had already begun to unroll like a scroll whose ink he dreaded: this brother—Fra Luca—would, before all things, want to know; and Romola, before all things, would confide. She would tell her father’s position, her own; she would speak of the coming betrothal, of the young scholar chosen to fill the place left vacant long ago by a wandering son. And then the name. Tito could hear it spoken in his imagination with Romola’s sincere softness—Tito—and he could hear what would answer it from a man who had renounced the world and yet carried the world’s knowledge like a wound.

Fra Luca would tell all he knew and all he guessed. Tito saw no net of lies that could now catch this wind. The worst consequences of his earlier dissimulation would walk straight into daylight.

It was all over with his prospects in Florence. He pictured Messer Bernardo del Nero, satisfied as a farmer whose warning about late frosts has come true; the talk under every loggia—the young Greek professor, his benefactor in slavery. The words would pass mouth to mouth like a bitter herb, each person crushing it to taste its sharpness.

For the first time in his life, Tito felt too fevered and agitated to trust his usual self-command. The city’s sounds struck him differently: each call, each laugh, each footfall seemed too loud, too near, like the beginning of a storm. He gave up his intended visit to Bardo and walked up and down under the walls until the yellow light in the west had quite faded.

Then, without any distinct purpose, he took the first turning—Via San Sebastiano—which led him directly toward the Piazza dell’Annunziata.

He was in one of those lawless moments that come when we have no guide but desire, and the path desire had promised seems suddenly closed. He was ready to follow any beckoning that offered an immediate purpose—any sound in the darkening city that would drown, for a little while, the beating of his own heart.

The first surge of bodies at the mouth of the piazza struck Tito like a gust of hot breath from an oven-door—so thick with smoke, sweat, and trampled dust that it seemed you could taste it on the tongue. Nello’s talk of the Fierucoloni came back to him at once, and he let himself be drawn in with a perverse relish. The jostling, the hoots, the rough laughter—each shove was a kind of relief, as if the crowd’s elbows could knead out that new, dreary awareness of the future which had begun to lie in him like cold dough that would not rise. For a moment, the thought that had lately flashed on him—of going after Baldassarre after all—was beaten down under the sheer press of the living.

From every inlet men and women strained into the square, and above the writhing heads paper lanterns on poles bobbed like wavering will-o’-the-wisps. A monotonous chant ran through the din as a steady thread, but across it snapped and crackled other noises: shrill boys’ taunts, whistles, a drum’s blunt thump, little bells that rang as if in mock devotion. Now and again a floating light vanished with a smash—some stone thrown for the pure luxury of mischief—followed by a scream and a fresh outbreak of shouts.

Yet, around the outskirts where the crush was less murderous, the fair went on with its steady trades, as methodical as any household routine. Ragged men with quick eyes and tongues like castanets tempted countryfolk to “fair” gaming. Two masqueraders on stilts waded above the crowd, stealing lanterns and swinging them so their light skimmed faces and vanished again. A cautious trader did a brisk business at a covered stall, selling hot berlingozzi—round, farinaceous cakes that sent up a warm, faintly aniseed steam when they were split. In another nook a fellow stood on a barrel, his back braced to a pillar of the loggia by the Spedale degl’ Innocenti, vending pills “invented by a doctor of Salerno” that would ward off toothache and drowning with equal certainty. Not far off a tumbler flipped and folded himself on a platform; and at the narrow throat of the Via de’ Febbrai a knot of apprentices, scorning the slack sport of stone-throwing, waged a concentrated private battle that had its own sharp chorus of clacks and yells.

Tito, carried along by whatever gap opened, found himself for a moment close to a trotting file of barefoot contadine. Their heels struck the stones with a hard, patient rhythm, and their bundles—yarn, eggs, a little cheese wrapped in leaves—rode on their backs as if grown there. Their faces were bronzed and sun-dried, the clothing a patchwork of obsolete stuffs, dim with hereditary dirt, so that to the townsfolk they looked like a way-worn ancestry returning from some pilgrimage begun a century ago. These were the mountain women of Pistoia, scant-feeding and hardy, bringing a year’s labour in modest skeins; carrying in their hearts, along with their merchandise, that thin hope of good and the wide, dim fear of harm that must somehow be bargained away with the Blessed Virgin. Tonight the miraculous image—painted, so they believed, by angels—would be unveiled, and its power would stream out as surely as scent from a broken herb.

Another shift of the crowd pushed Tito toward the piazza’s boundary, where the stationary seekers of small coin had planted themselves with prudence, keeping their backs safe. There he saw Bratti, his acquaintance—Bratti, the pedlar—set against a pillar with an air not of anxious selling but of offended greatness. His mouth was pursed in disdainful silence; his glance measured anyone who approached with cold superiority. One hand gripped a serge covering over the basket slung before him, as if it were a reliquary.

Two women came up, curious, their noses twitching like dogs at a closed kitchen door. Bratti tightened the cover and turned his head away.

It was too provoking. One asked at last what he had.

“Before I answer that, Monna, I must know whether you mean to buy,” Bratti said, as if he were a physician refusing to show a remedy to idle onlookers. “I can’t show such wares as mine in this fair for every fly to settle on and pay nothing. My goods are a little too choice for that. Besides, I’ve only two left, and I’ve no mind to soil them; for with the chances of the pestilence that wise men talk of, there is likelihood of their being worth their weight in gold. No, no: andate con Dio.”

The women looked at each other.

“And what may be the price?” said the second.

“Not within what you are likely to have in your purse, buona donna,” Bratti returned, in compassionate contempt. “I recommend you to trust in Messer Domeneddio and the saints: poor people can do no better for themselves.”

“Not so poor!” the woman snapped, and hauled out her money-bag with a show meant to sting him. “Come, now! what do you say to a grosso?”

“I say you may get twenty-one quattrini for it,” Bratti replied coolly, “but not of me, for I haven’t got that small change.”

“Come; two, then?” She flushed with impatience, while her companion’s eyes sharpened with envy. “It will hardly be above two, I think.”

There was the usual dance of bidding and refusal, a mercantile coquetry as old as the markets. At last Bratti let his disdain soften into reluctant virtue.

“Since you’ve set your mind on it,” he said, slowly lifting the serge as if unveiling a sacred dish, “I should be loth to do you a mischief; for Maestro Gabbadeo used to say, when a woman sets her mind on a thing and doesn’t get it, she’s in worse danger of the pestilence than before. Ecco! I have but two left; and let me tell you, the fellow to them is on the finger of Maestro Gabbadeo, who is gone to Bologna—as wise a doctor as sits at any door.”

The “precious” objects lay there like the meanest kitchen iron: two clumsy rings, beaten into the fashion of old Roman rings such as were sometimes dug from the ground. Their rust was a fine recommendation; their power, entirely hidden, could not be tested and so could not be denied. The grossi were paid without grumbling. The first woman, lacking such handsome coins, finally bartered some of her yarn after much show of reluctance on Bratti’s part, and carried off the second ring as if it were a loaf that would keep death from the threshold. Bratti covered his basket again—now stuffed with miscellaneous wares, likely gained through bargains of that same sort—and as he shifted from the pillar he came suddenly upon Tito.

Tito would have avoided recognition if he had had the time.

“By the head of San Giovanni, now,” Bratti cried, catching Tito as if fortune had dropped him into his hand, “this is a piece of luck. For I was talking of you this morning, Messer Greco; but, I said, he is mounted up among the signori now—and I’m glad of it, for I was at the bottom of his fortune—but I can rarely get speech of him, for he’s not to be caught lying on the stones now—not he! But it’s your luck, not mine, Messer Greco, save and except some small trifle to satisfy me for my trouble in the transaction.”

“You speak in riddles, Bratti,” Tito said. “Remember, I don’t sharpen my wits, as you do, by driving hard bargains for iron rings: you must be plain.”

“By the Holy ’Vangels! it was an easy bargain I gave them. If a Hebrew gets thirty-two per cent, I hope a Christian may get a little more. If I had not borne a conscience, I should have got twice the money and twice the yarn.” Bratti’s glance flicked to Tito’s hand. “But, talking of rings, it is your ring—that very ring you’ve got on your finger—that I could get you a purchaser for; ay, and a purchaser with a deep money-bag.”

“Truly?” Tito said, looking down at it, the metal catching a stray wink of lantern-light.

“A Genoese who is going straight away into Hungary, as I understand. He came and looked all over my shop to see if I had any old things I didn’t know the price of; I warrant you, he thought I had a pumpkin on my shoulders. He had been rummaging all the shops in Florence. And he had a ring on—not like yours, but something of the same fashion; and as he was talking of rings, I said I knew a fine young man, a particular acquaintance of mine, who had a ring of that sort. And he said, ‘Who is he, pray? Tell him I’ll give him his price for it.’ And I thought of going after you to Nello’s to-morrow; for it’s my opinion of you, Messer Greco, that you’re not one who’d see the Arno run broth, and stand by without dipping your finger.”

Tito missed not a syllable, but his mind worked all the while, quick and noiseless. Why keep the ring? Sentiment—mere fancy—had kept it on his finger when the other gems had gone. If he had sold it too, might he have escaped Fra Luca’s identification? The ring had been taken from Baldassarre and set on Tito’s hand when it had grown to fit; but what good was there in those superstitious scruples about dead metal? It had helped toward recognition. And recognition—once a triumph, a ladder—had become a claim from the past, and claims were dangerous.

Here was a way to be rid of it without seeking out a buyer, without lingering over the thing.

“You speak with your usual wisdom, Bratti,” he said smoothly. “I have no objection to hear what your Genoese will offer. But when and where shall I have speech of him?”

“To-morrow, at three hours after sunrise, he will be at my shop,” Bratti answered, smelling profit as a cook smells a roast before it is brought in. “And if your wits are of that sharpness I have always taken them to be, Messer Greco, you will ask him a heavy price; for he minds not money. It’s my belief he’s buying for somebody else, and not for himself—perhaps for some great signor.”

“It is well,” Tito said. “I will be at your shop, if nothing hinders.”

“And you will doubtless deal nobly by me for old acquaintance’ sake, Messer Greco,” Bratti added, already tasting his “small trifle,” “so I will not stay to fix the small sum you will give me in token of my service in the matter. It seems to me a thousand years now till I get out of the piazza, for a fair is a dull, not to say a wicked thing, when one has no more goods to sell.”

Tito gave a hasty sign of assent and adieu, and moved away; but the crowd took him again, shoving him first toward the middle, then back, in a zigzag drift that made choice seem a childish boast. In this helpless current he was carried to the end of the piazza opposite the church, where a deep recess—formed by an irregular line of houses—held an entertainment that drew laughter like flies to syrup.

Bursts of mirth broke a monologue that turned now slow and oratorical, now rattling and buffoonish. A girl was pushed forward into the inner ring with pretended reluctance; elsewhere a bold minx elbowed her way in with cheerful purpose. The square’s light was strange—stars pricking out above, lanterns wavering below—so that faces and gestures blurred unless the light happened to swing close. But in this recess there was a stronger glow that cut the spectators’ heads into dark profiles; and above them rose the head of a man wearing a white mitre marked with yellow cabalistic signs.

“Behold, my children!” he cried, voice sharp as a cleaver’s ring on stone. “Behold your opportunity! neglect not the holy sacrament of matrimony when it can be had for the small sum of a white quattrino—the cheapest matrimony ever offered, and dissolved by special bull beforehand at every man’s own will and pleasure. Behold the bull!” He flourished a parchment with huge seals. “Behold the indulgence granted by his Holiness Alexander the Sixth, who, being newly elected Pope for his peculiar piety, intends to reform and purify the Church, and wisely begins by abolishing that priestly abuse which keeps too large a share of this privileged matrimony to the clergy and stints the laity. Spit once, my sons, and pay a white quattrino! This is the whole and sole price of the indulgence. The quattrino is the only difference the Holy Father allows to be put any longer between us and the clergy—who spit and pay nothing.”

Tito thought he knew that voice; it had a particular upward sting. The face was shadowed by the light behind, but as he edged closer he saw the set of it—angles that seemed to cut the air. Within the ring, behind the speaker, stood an altar-like table on a little platform, draped in red cloth stitched all over with yellow signs. Thin tapers burned at the back. On the table lay conjuring litter: a large open book in the centre, odd implements scattered about, and at one front corner a monkey tethered by a cord, clutching a small taper which, with his constant fidgeting, slanted and dipped like a reed in wind. An impish boy in a white surplice kept cuffing the monkey and resetting the taper, as if managing a troublesome kitchen-fire that refused to stay lit.

The man in the mitre wore a surplice too, and over it a chasuble with the signs of the zodiac roughly marked in black on yellow. Tito’s recognition settled: Maestro Vaiano, the mountebank—the same he had once thwarted when he rescued Tessa. Tessa: the thought of her came with a sudden tenderness, as the smell of warm bread comes back to a man in exile.

“Come, my maidens!” Vaiano called, feeding the crowd’s appetite like a vendor with a pan of fritters. “This is the time for the pretty who can have many chances, and for the ill-favoured who have few. Matrimony to be had—hot, eaten, and done with as easily as berlingozzi! And see!” He held up a cluster of tiny bags. “To every bride I give a Breve with a secret in it—the secret alone worth the money you pay for the matrimony. The secret how to—no, no, I will not tell you what the secret is about, and that makes it a double secret. Hang it round your neck if you like, and never look at it; I don’t say that will not be the best, for then you will see many things you don’t expect: though if you open it you may break your leg, è vero, but you will know a secret! Something nobody knows but me! And mark—I give you the Breve, I don’t sell it, as many another holy man would: the quattrino is for the matrimony, and the Breve you get for nothing. Orsù, giovanetti, come like dutiful sons of the Church and buy the Indulgence of his Holiness Alexander the Sixth.”

It suited the audience exactly—this blend of mock ritual and cheap license. The fierucola was a small feast-day; the townsmen could be content with jokes less indecent than carnival’s, and the women, laughing and nudging, began to itch for the little bags with their promised secrets. Couples had already gone through the ceremony: the conjuror’s solemn gibberish over the open book, the grotesque grimaces, the required spitting, the monkey’s antics—all punctuated by peals of laughter.

Now a well-looking, merry-eyed youth of seventeen shoved forward with a plump brunette on his arm, her ragged dress displaying her round limbs with a rough, peasant picturesqueness.

“Fetter us without delay, Maestro!” the youth cried, “for I have got to take my bride home and paint her under the light of a lantern.”

“Ha! Mariotto, my son, I commend your pious observance—” Vaiano began, when a sudden chattering behind him warned that another kind of ceremony had broken loose.

The monkey, that imperfect acolyth, had reached the end of his patience. A cuff administered just as his taper drooped to a horizontal line sent him springing back with a violence that proved too much for the slackened knot on his cord. In an instant he had leaped to the far end of the table, his chatter sharp and furious. The boy in the surplice snatched up a wand to threaten him; the monkey answered by leaping onto the head of a tall woman in the front, dropping the taper as he flew, and perching there like a malicious crown. Screams erupted. People reeled back, and not a few—half believing in hidden powers—looked on the beast as capable of some mischief beyond teeth and claws. Even Vaiano’s face tightened with alarm for his familiar.

In the scramble to seize the string, Tito was shoved out of the circle. He did not care to fight his way back for more of that laughter. He let the crowd carry him instead toward the Nunziata, where the church doors stood open and the sound spilled out—one long chant, steady as a mill-wheel’s song, promising rest to the ear.

Inside, the brilliance pressed on his eyes after the piazza’s scattered lanterns and broad shadows. For the first moments he could see nothing clearly—only yellow splendour, thickened by incense into a haze that seemed almost edible, as if one might chew the air and find resin and smoke on the teeth. To many of the peasant-women, used to mountain valleys where twilight comes early and the sky is half hidden by rock, that light itself was a miracle; and the choir’s uninterrupted chant lay over the senses like cool cloth after fever, undoing the harsh knots of the outer noise.

Gradually the scene resolved. In a chapel on the left of the nave, wreathed with silver lamps, the miraculous fresco of the Annunciation stood unveiled; from Tito’s oblique view on the right it looked almost dark, drowned by the glare around it. The great church was filled with peasant-women, kneeling or standing—coarse bronzed skins and dingy mountain clothes beside softer faces and whiter draperies of valley folk. And above them, spreading high along walls and ceiling, pressed another crowd as close as bodies could: votive waxen images, effigies of men and women clothed as in life—Florentines of high name in black silk lucco as when they sat in council; popes, emperors, kings, cardinals; famous condottieri with plumed morions mounted on their chargers; strangers too, Mohammedans among Christian cavaliers, tolerated here in wax if not always in word. Some were blackened, their robes tattered by centuries of breath and smoke; others were fresh and bright, new-made doubles of the living in red mantle or steel corselet. Between them were wedged detached waxen limbs—arms, legs, and other members—tokens of pain and cure, with here and there a gap where an image had been removed in public disgrace or had fallen ominously, as Lorenzo’s had done half a year before. It was a resurrection-swarm, the dead and the living mingled in a mute pageant, as if the city’s memory—its ranks and names—had been pressed into one crowded ceiling, while below the nameless prayed.

Tito’s eyes wandered over the multitude in search of something that was not painted or waxen. He had already thought of Tessa; the white hoods among the women made him half expect to glimpse her face. It was a thought to court—anything rather than the inward image of Romola looking at him with changed eyes. But he searched in vain. Wearied by the sameness of the scene, he turned toward the door—and there, just against the doorway, he caught sight of Tessa, hardly two yards away.

She knelt with her back against the wall, behind a group of peasant-women who stood craning for a nearer place. Her head drooped a little aside with a look of weariness, and her blue eyes were directed not toward the unveiled Virgin but absently toward an altar-piece where the Archangel Michael stood armored, young-faced, hair floating among bearded and tonsured saints. In her right hand she held a bunch of cocoons, hanging at her side as if she had forgotten them; her cheek looked paler—whether from the light or from fatigue—and her lips were pressed together in a pout. Her eyelids half fell now and again. She was like a sweet child fallen asleep in the middle of a vigil.

An almost physical longing seized Tito—to step into that small, unjudging world and feel again the touch of her trust. Here was a creature without the moral measuring that could condemn him, a refuge from suspicion and exacting demands; and in his new fear of disgrace and solitude, her ignorance shone like a safe hearth.

He glanced cautiously around to make sure Monna Ghita was not near. Then he slipped to Tessa’s side, knelt on one knee, and breathed, as softly as one might speak to a skittish bird, “Tessa!”

She scarcely started—no more than if a gentle wind had fanned her. She turned, and Tito’s face was close to hers. To her it was more beautiful than the Archangel’s, though Michael was so mighty and good, living with the Madonna and the saints and prayed to along with them. She smiled in happy silence, as if his nearness filled her mind and left no room for words.

“My little Tessa,” he whispered. “You look very tired. How long have you been kneeling here?”

She gathered her thoughts slowly, as if waking. At last she said, simply, “I’m very hungry.”

“Come, then; come with me.”

He lifted her from her knees and led her out beneath the cloisters around the atrium—open now, not yet painted with Andrea del Sarto’s later splendors. The air here was cooler, carrying faint traces of wax and incense from within, and beyond, from the piazza, the smell of fried dough and hot cake.

“How is it you are all by yourself, and so hungry, Tessa?”

“The Madre is ill,” she said, words tumbling out once they began. “She has very bad pains in her legs, and sent me to bring these cocoons to the Santissima Nunziata, because they’re so wonderful; see!” She lifted the bunch—pale cocoons arranged with a fortuitous regularity on their stem, like a rustic offering that had its own quiet geometry. “And she had kept them to bring them herself, but she couldn’t, and so she sent me because she thinks the Holy Madonna may take away her pains; and somebody took my bag with the bread and chestnuts in it, and the people pushed me back, and I was so frightened coming in the crowd, and I couldn’t get anywhere near the Holy Madonna, to give the cocoons to the Padre, but I must—oh, I must.”

“Yes, my little Tessa, you shall take them,” Tito said, the promise coming readily, as if it cost him nothing. “But first come and let me give you some berlingozzi. There are some to be had not far off.”

“Where did you come from?” Tessa asked, bewilderment and reproach mixed like milk and water. “I thought you would never come to me again, because you never came to the Mercato for milk any more. I set myself Aves to say, to see if they would bring you back, but I left off, because they didn’t.”

“You see I come when you want some one to take care of you, Tessa,” he said. “Perhaps the Aves fetched me, only it took them a long while. But what shall you do if you are here all alone? Where shall you go?”

“Oh, I shall stay and sleep in the church—a great many of them do—in the church and all about here—I did once when I came with my mother; and the patrigno is coming with the mules in the morning.”

When Romola reached the doorway of San Marco, a friar was already waiting, as if her coming had been counted like the strokes of a bell. Monna Brigida slipped away into the adjoining church, and Romola was led through the outer cloister to the chapter-house door—the farthest place a woman might be taken. Beyond this threshold the convent kept its rules as strictly as it kept its silence.

The door opened. A dim, sifted light lay over the stone, mingling with the small living flame of two tapers set behind a low truckle-bed. The air was stale with wax and damp wool, with that faint medicinal sourness of a sickroom where the body has grown too light for its own bones. Propped almost upright, a monk lay with a little crucifix lifted before his eyes, his fingers clinging to it as a starving man clings to bread. His face was sharpened to the look of something carved and then left too long in wind: the cheek hollow, the lips drawn, the hazel eyes sunk deep as wells gone dry. Above that suffering face, the tonsured crown still held a ring of golden hair.

Romola, throwing back her veil, was aware in one blurred instant of another monk standing near the bed with his black cowl pulled low, and of a pale crucified figure painted high on the wall, sorrowful faces beneath it watching from their frescoed dusk. But all those impressions were swallowed up as the dying man’s eyes lifted from the crucifix and met hers.

“Dino!” she said—low, like a cry caught in the throat.

She did not bend to him. She held herself straight, two paces away, as if that distance were a last defense. The monk’s habit on her brother’s body struck her like a brand: the visible sign of undutiful flight that had left her father desolate; the sign of a superstition that dared to call desertion holiness. In her father’s house, truth had been a daily bread, sliced clean by reason, without the Church’s blessing. The Church belonged, in Romola’s mind, to the crowded life of the many from which they had stood apart; she had never learned to see in it anything but a power that fed on fear and asked for obedience in place of understanding. And yet her heart—so apt to cling—searched that wasted face for the boy she had loved, for some warmth that might soften the years.

The monk looked at her as if he were looking through her, like one who revisits earth only in memory. There was no bright leap of recognition, no tremor of a brother’s joy. Only a remote steadiness, as if his soul had already stepped beyond the body and spoke back through it with effort.

“My sister,” he said, the words coming distinctly but with breaks, as though each syllable cost breath. “It is well thou hast not longer delayed to come; for I have a message to deliver to thee, and my time is short.”

At “message” her heart moved, half-opening in spite of itself. She thought of her blind father sitting among his books and marbles, fingers feeling for what eyes could no longer find; she thought of the hunger in that proud, lonely life for one more voice from the son who had left. Now, at the last, there might be repentance; there might be the plain human questions—How did blindness come? Was he in pain? Did he still remember?—and some tender word, imperfect but precious, to lay like oil on old wounds.

“Romola,” the monk began again, “I have had a vision concerning thee. Thrice I have had it in the last two months: each time it has been clearer. Therefore I came from Fiesole, deeming it a message from heaven that I was bound to deliver. And I gather a promise of mercy to thee in this, that my breath is preserved in order to—”

His chest labored; breath broke him off. The word “vision” cooled her as if a wet cloth had been laid on her heart. Her father’s bitter contempt for such things rose in her like an instinct. She could not keep silence.

“Dino, I thought you had some words to send to my father. You forsook him when his sight was failing; you made his life very desolate. Have you never cared about that—never repented? What is this religion of yours, that places visions before natural duties?”

The hazel eyes turned slowly and rested on her. He seemed to weigh whether answer was worth his failing strength. At last he spoke, and his voice had the same low, passionless remoteness, as if death had drained him of the human heat that makes words plead.

“No,” he said. “No; I have never repented fleeing from the stifling poison-breath of sin that was hot and thick around me, and threatened to steal over my senses like besotting wine. My father could not hear the voice that called me night and day; he knew nothing of the demon-tempters that tried to drag me back from following it. My father has lived amidst human sin and misery without believing in them: he has been like one busy picking shining stones in a mine, while there was a world dying of plague above him. I spoke, but he listened with scorn. I told him the studies he wished me to live for were either childish trifling—dead toys—or else they must be made warm and living by pulses that beat to worldly ambitions and fleshly lusts; for worldly ambitions and fleshly lusts made all the substance of the poetry and history he wanted me to bend my eyes on continually.”

Romola’s blood rose. She could not let that touch her father.

“Has not my father led a pure and noble life, then?” she burst out, the words springing with the quick heat of belief. “He has sought no worldly honours; he has been truthful; he has denied himself luxuries; he has lived like one of the ancient sages. He never wished you to live for worldly ambitions and fleshly lusts; he wished you to live as he himself has done—according to the purest maxims of philosophy in which he brought you up.”

The flush came into her face, and her whole frame quivered. It was a defense spoken partly from the deep habit of reverencing her father’s life, partly from that youthful certainty which repeats what it has been taught as one repeats a recipe known by heart: measured, established, beyond dispute.

Fra Luca looked at her long, and the strangeness of his passionless gaze made her own passion seem solitary, unheard.

“What were the maxims of philosophy to me?” he said at last. “They told me to be strong, when I felt myself weak; when I was ready, like the blessed Saint Benedict, to roll myself among thorns and court smarting wounds as a deliverance from temptation. For the Divine love had sought me, and penetrated me, and created a great need in me—like a seed that wants room to grow. I had been brought up in carelessness of the true faith; I had not studied the doctrines of our religion; but it seemed to take possession of me like a rising flood. I felt that there was a life of perfect love and purity for the soul; in which there would be no uneasy hunger after pleasure, no tormenting questions, no fear of suffering.

“Before I knew the history of the saints, I had a foreshadowing of their ecstasy. For the same truth had penetrated even into pagan philosophy: that it is a bliss within the reach of man to die to mortal needs, and live in the life of God as the Unseen Perfectness. But to attain that I must forsake the world: I must have no affection, no hope, wedding me to that which passeth away; I must live with my fellow-beings only as human souls related to the eternal unseen life. That need was urging me continually: it came over me in visions when my mind fell away weary from the vain words which record the passions of dead men: it came over me after I had been tempted into sin and had turned away with loathing from the scent of the emptied cup. And in visions I saw the meaning of the Crucifix.”

He paused, fighting for breath. The sound of his breathing filled the little chamber; it was like an uneven rasp against stone, a harsh reminder that life itself is a kind of labor. Romola felt the futility of argument as one feels the futility of offering food to a man who has chosen fasting for salvation. Her mind could not reach his mind; it was as if she stretched her hand and met only shadow.

When he spoke again, his chest had quieted a little.

“I felt whom I must follow,” he said; “but I saw that even among the servants of the Cross who professed to have renounced the world, my soul would be stifled with the fumes of hypocrisy, and lust, and pride. God had not chosen me, as he chose Saint Dominic and Saint Francis, to wrestle with evil in the Church and in the world. He called upon me to flee. I took the sacred vows and I fled—fled to lands where danger and scorn and want bore me continually, like angels, to repose on the bosom of God. I have lived the life of a hermit; I have ministered to pilgrims; but my task has been short: the veil has worn very thin that divides me from my everlasting rest. I came back to Florence that—”

“Dino,” Romola interrupted, a sudden ache cutting through her anger, “you did want to know if my father was alive?”

It was as if she offered him, at last, a mouthful of the plain bread of home—something real, something human, something that could be shared.

“—That before I died I might urge others of our brethren to study the Eastern tongues, as I had not done, and go out to greater ends than I did; and I find them already bent on the work,” he went on, untouched by her yearning. “And since I came, Romola, I have felt that I was sent partly to thee—not to renew the bonds of earthly affection, but to deliver the heavenly warning conveyed in a vision. For I have had that vision thrice. And through all the years since first the Divine voice called me, while I was yet in the world, I have been taught and guided by visions. For in the painful linking together of our waking thoughts we can never be sure that we have not mingled our own error with the light we have prayed for; but in visions and dreams we are passive, and our souls are as an instrument in the Divine hand. Therefore listen, and speak not again—for the time is short.”

Her mind recoiled. Yet as he spoke, another presence moved into the room. The cowled figure that had shifted away at her entrance returned and took his place on the far side of the bed, the cowl still shadowing his face.

“Kneel, my daughter,” said a strong, rich voice, startling after the dying whisper. “For the Angel of Death is present, and waits while the message of heaven is delivered: bend thy pride before it is bent for thee by a yoke of iron.”

It was not the harsh bark of command; it was calm certainty, a voice that seemed to sit in the air as naturally as a bell note sits in a piazza at evening—claiming space, ordering attention. The very sound made Romola’s nerves vibrate. She turned toward the speaker. His face was hidden, but her eyes fell on his hands where they lay folded against the black mantle: hands of an almost transparent delicacy, beautiful as if fashioned for fine work—turning pages, lifting a chalice, laying a wet cloth on fevered lips. There was something in them that pleaded against hardness.

He leaned forward. The right hand took the crucifix gently from Fra Luca’s tiring grasp; the left lifted a wet sponge and touched it to the dying man’s lips with practiced tenderness. In bending, the cowl fell back, and the taperlight struck his features full.

The face was one made for the crowd’s description and the crowd’s memory: high arched nose, a prominent under-lip, thick dark hair like a coronet above the brow—signs of energy and passion; and blue-grey eyes that shone mildly beneath auburn lashes—eyes that suggested acute sensibility, like the fine hands. Romola knew him then. It was Fra Girolamo Savonarola, Prior of San Marco—he whom she had chiefly disliked among monks because he was more noisy than the rest, his voice sounding in Florence like a trumpet that would not be silenced.

Her rebellion gathered itself. Yet the look of his eyes, the quiet possession of his tone, worked against her resistance.

“Kneel, my daughter,” he repeated, “the pride of the body is a barrier against the gifts that purify the soul.”

He looked at her with mild fixity, as if his will made a still place in her. She felt the strange pressure of a personality that moves others without touch. Slowly, unwillingly, she sank to her knees. And in the very act of yielding—like lowering one’s head to pass beneath a lintel—something in her inner posture changed. Her proud erectness was gone, and with it a portion of her defiance; she found herself passive, as if the air in that room had thickened into a medium in which her own will could not strike out so sharply.

Fra Luca began again.

“Romola, in the deep night, as I lay awake, I saw my father’s room—the library—with all the books and the marbles and the leggio where I used to stand and read; and I saw you—you were revealed to me as I see you now, with fair long hair, sitting before my father’s chair. And at the leggio stood a man whose face I could not see. I looked, and looked, and it was a blank to me, even as a painting effaced. And I saw him move and take thee, Romola, by the hand; and then I saw thee take my father by the hand; and you all three went down the stone steps into the streets, the man whose face was a blank to me leading the way.

“And you stood at the altar in Santa Croce, and the priest who married you had the face of death; and the graves opened, and the dead in their shrouds rose and followed you like a bridal train. And you passed on through the streets and the gates into the valley, and it seemed to me that he who led you hurried you more than you could bear, and the dead were weary of following you, and turned back to their graves.

“And at last you came to a stony place where there was no water, and no trees or herbage; but instead of water, I saw written parchment unrolling itself everywhere, and instead of trees and herbage I saw men of bronze and marble springing up and crowding round you. And my father was faint for want of water and fell to the ground; and the man whose face was a blank loosed thy hand and departed: and as he went I could see his face; and it was the face of the Great Tempter.

“And thou, Romola, didst wring thy hands and seek for water, and there was none. And the bronze and marble figures seemed to mock thee and hold out cups of water, and when thou didst grasp them and put them to my father’s lips, they turned to parchment. And the bronze and marble figures seemed to turn into demons and snatch my father’s body from thee, and the parchments shrivelled up, and blood ran everywhere instead of them, and fire upon the blood, till they all vanished, and the plain was bare and stony again, and thou wast alone in the midst of it. And then it seemed that the night fell and I saw no more...

“Thrice I have had that vision, Romola. I believe it is a revelation meant for thee: to warn thee against marriage as a temptation of the enemy; it calls upon thee to dedicate thyself—”

The pauses grew longer, the breaks more cruel. A fit of gasping seized him; his eyes clung to the crucifix as if it were the last light in a narrowing tunnel. When the spasm eased, he forced out more words, thin and barely audible.

“To renounce the vain philosophy and corrupt thoughts of the heathens: for in the hour of sorrow and death their pride will turn to mockery, and the unclean gods will—”

The phrase died, unfinished, like a candle snuffed by a sudden draught.

Romola’s reason told her it was no more than a dream—youthful memory and ascetic certainty baked together in the hot oven of fever. Yet the vision’s images struck her nerves like painful cries heard in the night: not to be answered, not to be forgotten. And she had never before sat so close to death. Her life had been sombre, but it had not been torn by the extremity of pain; she had not watched breath grow scant and precious, each draw a struggle. The frescoed sorrow-faces on the wall seemed to press nearer, and to join the pale face on the bed in one company. The air itself felt hushed, as if the room listened for the last syllable.

“Frate,” said the dying voice at last.

Fra Girolamo bent down. There was silence. The soundscape of that small chamber narrowed to the slight crackle of the tapers and the irregular rasp of breath.

“Romola,” the voice came again.

She leaned forward, her heart tightening. Again silence—words fighting and failing behind lips that could no longer carry them.

“Fra Girolamo, give her—” the dying man tried.

“The crucifix,” said Fra Girolamo, and his voice, steady, seemed to lay a plank across the gulf that was opening.

No other sound came from Fra Luca. The gaze that had been fastened on the crucified figure loosened, went vacant, and ceased.

“Dino!” Romola cried—low, but piercing—as the certainty fell on her that the silence of misunderstanding could never be broken, that all the human words she had wanted were now locked away where no pleading could reach them.

After a few minutes—minutes that were like a long, slow toll—Fra Girolamo said, “Take the crucifix, my daughter. His eyes behold it no more.”

Romola stretched out her hand. The touch of the small carved wood seemed to ease the strained cord within her. A great sob broke from her, the first full yielding of her pride to grief. She bent her head beside her dead brother and wept aloud. It seemed to her that daylight itself must be altered forever by this first close vision of death—that even the familiar sounds of home, the scrape of a chair on stone, the turning of a page, the pouring of water into a cup, would never again be free of what she had heard here: breath failing, silence final.

Fra Girolamo moved to the door and called in a lay Brother waiting outside. Then he came back and spoke to Romola with gentle command.

“Rise, my daughter, and be comforted. Our brother is with the blessed. He has left you the crucifix, in remembrance of the heavenly warning—that it may be a beacon to you in the darkness.”

She rose trembling. She drew her veil over her head as if to wrap herself back into the world she knew, and hid the crucifix under her mantle, close against her breast.

Fra Girolamo led her out into the cloistered court. Now the sky was a deep bowl of night, the stars cold and innumerable; a lantern burned near the entrance, and its small light made a bright island on the stones. Several figures in the dress of dignified laymen were grouped there—frequenters of San Marco who had come to visit the Prior and, hearing he kept vigil in the chapter-house, had waited.

Romola passed them as if through water. She was dimly aware of footsteps shifting, of rustle and murmur, of the Prior’s voice saying low, “Our brother is departed,” and of a hand laid on her arm as though to guide her. The great quiet of the convent held even these men’s movements in check, the way a countryside at night compels softness in speech. Then the door opened, and she was out in the wide piazza of San Marco with only Monna Brigida beside her and the servant bearing the lantern.

The open space, the freer air, revived her—as if the lungs, tight in that room of dying breath, could now fill again. What she had seen remained vivid, painfully distinct, but it began to draw in upon itself as the ordinary impressions of life returned: the uneven stone underfoot, the faint night smells of Florence—dust, old walls, a trace of smoke—and the far, living city-sounds that made a world beyond convent silence. She quickened her steps with nervous longing to be again with her father—and with Tito; for were they not together while she had been away? The grotesque images of the vision clung like a bad dream not shaken off, and yet they drove her all the more toward the beloved faces and familiar voices that would tell her she was awake.

Tito, we know, was not with Bardo. His destiny, in that same hour, was being shaped by guilty consciousness and the despairing belief that Romola already held a knowledge which must part them at last. And the lips that could have carried that knowledge to her—the simplest human words, asked and answered in the warmth of kinship—were closed forever.

So the prevision Fra Luca had given Romola was one drawn from that shadowy region where souls seek wisdom apart from the human sympathies that are the very substance of wisdom; while the revelation that might have come through plain filial and brotherly affection had been carried into irrevocable silence.

Early the next morning Tito came out of Bratti’s shop in the cramped lane of the Ferravecchi with fifty florins hidden close, as if coin, like a spice, kept its virtue best when it was kept from the air. The Genoese stranger had gone off with the onyx ring.

For an instant Tito’s mind—quick in such reckonings as a steward’s—touched the thought that if Fortune, by one of her turnings, should yet save him from quitting Florence, it would have been better not to have parted with the ring, since it had been noticed on his hand and had passed in men’s talk for a relic of tender memory. But the thought slipped away. His first fever of alarm had sunk into a dull, regretful heaviness, like a stomach that has been over-stimulated and now revolts from the very smell of its own indulgence. He had cared too keenly for pleasures that came to him only through other men’s good opinion; and now he almost wished he had never tempted ignominy by shrinking from what other men named obligation.

Yet deeds, once done, are not like dishes left half-tasted that can be pushed aside. They go on, having their own appetite and their own motion; and the dreadful vitality of his last deed pressed on Tito now for the first time, not as a thought but as a weight.

He meant to go back to his lodging in the Piazza di San Giovanni, but he would not take the shortest way through the Mercato Vecchio. He would not see Tessa. Not yet. He was in no humour to seek anything; he could only wait for the first sign of his altered lot, as one waits for the first crack of thunder when the air has turned sultry and the swallows fly low.

The piazza lay washed in that warm morning sunlight under which the autumn dew still lingers on shadowed stone, and the very marble seems to give back heat like a hearth-stone. It was a festival morning—the Nativity of the Virgin—when idleness itself feels almost pious, and men are tempted to lounge as if lounging were a mode of thanksgiving. Round the octagonal baptistery stalls were being spread with fruit and flowers: figs whose skins were breaking with sweetness, bunches of grapes still powdered with bloom, late peaches smelling of sun, and marigolds and basil that gave out a sharp, clean scent when the vendors’ fingers bruised the leaves. Laden mules stood with the solemn patience of beasts that know their hour; their jaws worked steadily in their nose-bags with a sound like soft grinding of grain, while the drivers, perhaps, had gone through the hospitable sacred doors to kneel and let the chant and organ-wind wash the dust of the road out of their ears.

On the wide marble steps of the Duomo lay scattered groups of beggars and talkers. Here an old crone with white hair and a hard, sunburnt face encouraged a round-capped baby to try its bare feet on the warmed stone; a dog sat near and snuffed at the little ceremony with suspicious gravity. There two shaggy-headed boys leaned to watch a pale cripple cutting a face on a cherry-stone, his knife-tip making tiny crisp clicks. Above them men were knotting and unknotting themselves into laughing clusters, or standing in close couples, words and hands moving together, as if speech in Florence were never complete without gesture.

But the busiest knot of all was the one Tito could not avoid: Nello the barber’s awning, red and white, pitched like a little pavilion of respectability. It was the hour when yesterday’s gossip still tasted fresh, like bread scarcely cooled, and Nello’s tongue had its keenest edge when his razor was busiest; the deft glide of steel seemed to set the words going, and the words to keep the steel bright. Men preferred to be shaved out in the air, where neighbours could see that they were men who kept their chins in order. There is nothing sublime in sitting with the chin lathered and thrown back while one’s nose is made a handle of; and yet, when everyone is in the fashion, the fashion itself gives gravity, and the lathered chins look at one another as if on matters of state.

Tito foresaw that he must be drawn in. He must smile, retort, be perfectly at ease—as if the ordeal were no more than swallowing bitter pills wrapped in cheese and bread. A man who let anticipation choke him was only a man with weak nerves.

But at that moment a hand fell on his shoulder.

The sudden touch jarred him like an unexpected sound in a quiet room—like a door flung open when one is listening for footsteps. For an instant, despite all his self-command, his face betrayed the inward shock as he turned.

The owner of the hand laughed lightly. He was about Tito’s age, with keen features, a small close-clipped head, and a lip and chin shaven so closely that the whole face suggested a mind trimmed of every superfluity, ready to cut and turn quickly. His eyes were bright with hope and friendliness—the kind of young brightness that has not yet learned bitterness; for at that time Florence had only pleasant prophecies for Niccolò Macchiavelli, expected to mend the broken fortunes of his ancient family.

“Why, Melema,” he said, “what evil dream did you have last night, that you took my light grasp for that of a sbirro—or something worse?”

“Ah, Messer Niccolò!” Tito answered, recovering in an instant, as if his very fear taught him dexterity. “It must have been an extra amount of dulness in my veins this morning that shuddered at the approach of your wit. But I have had a bad night.”

“That is unlucky,” said Macchiavelli, “because you will be expected to shine without any obstructing fog to-day in the Rucellai Gardens. I take it for granted you are to be there.”

“Messer Bernardo did me the honour to invite me,” said Tito; “but I shall be engaged elsewhere.”

“Ah! I remember—you are in love,” Macchiavelli returned, with a shrug. “Else you would never have such inconvenient engagements. Why, we are to eat a peacock and ortolans under the loggia among Bernardo Rucellai’s rare trees. There are to be the choicest spirits in Florence and the choicest wines. Only, as Piero de’ Medici is to be there, the choice spirits may happen to be swamped in the capping of impromptu verses. I hate that game; it is a device for the triumph of small wits, who are always inspired the most by the smallest occasions.”

“What is that you are saying about Piero de’ Medici and small wits, Messer Niccolò?” cried Nello, whose light figure at that moment predominated over the Herculean frame of Niccolò Caparra.

Caparra, the famous worker in iron—seen last in the Mercato Vecchio with bared muscular arms and leathern apron—was now in holiday suit, and sat submissively while Nello skipped round him, snapped the cloth beneath his chin, lathered him with quick circles, seized him by the nose as if it were indeed a handle, and scraped with magical speed. Caparra looked like a lion that had donned linen and tunic to go into society and had agreed, for once, to let someone else rule the edge of steel.

“A private secretary will never rise in the world if he couples great and small in that way,” said Nello. “When great men are not allowed to marry their sons and daughters as they like, small men must not expect to marry their words as they like. Have you heard the news Domenico Cennini here has been telling us?—that Pagolantonio Soderini has given Ser Piero da Bibbiena a box on the ear for setting on Piero de’ Medici to interfere with the marriage between young Tommaso Soderini and Fiammetta Strozzi, and is to be sent ambassador to Venice as a punishment?”

“I don’t know which I envy him most,” said Macchiavelli, “the offence or the punishment. The offence will make him the most popular man in all Florence; and the punishment will take him among the only people in Italy who have known how to manage their own affairs.”

“Yes, if Soderini stays long enough at Venice,” Cennini answered, “he may chance to learn the Venetian fashion and bring it home with him. The Soderini have been fast friends of the Medici; but what has happened is likely to open Pagolantonio’s eyes to the good of our old Florentine trick of choosing a new harness when the old one galls us—if we have not quite lost the trick in these last fifty years.”

“Not we,” said Niccolò Caparra, rejoicing in the free use of his lips again. “Eat eggs in Lent and the snow will melt. That’s what I say to our people when they get noisy over their cups at San Gallo and talk of raising a romor. I say, never do you plan a romor; you may as well try to fill Arno with buckets. When there’s water enough, Arno will be full—and that will not be till the torrent is ready.”

“Caparra,” said Nello, “that oracular speech is due to my excellent shaving. You could never have made it with that dark rust on your chin. Ecco, Messer Domenico, I am ready for you now. By the way, my bel erudito,” he added, seeing Tito move towards the door, “old Maso has been seeking for you, but your nest was empty. He will come again presently. The old man looked mournful and in haste. I hope there is nothing wrong in the Via de’ Bardi.”

“Doubtless Messer Tito knows that Bardo’s son is dead,” said Cronaca, who had just come up.

Tito’s heart gave a leap—so sharp it seemed to strike his ribs like a hand. Had the death happened before Romola saw him?

“No,” he said, steadying his voice by a habitual art, and turning to lean against the doorpost as if he had abandoned his purpose of going away. “I had not heard it. I knew that his sister had gone to see him. Did he die before she arrived?”

“No,” Cronaca said. “I was in San Marco at the time, and saw her come out from the chapter-house with Fra Girolamo, who told us that the dying man’s breath had been preserved as by a miracle, that he might make a disclosure to his sister.”

In that moment Tito felt his fate fall into place with a click, as when a latch shuts. His mind flew back over all the circumstances of his leaving Florence; and with the swiftness of fear it seized a plan—get back his money from Cennini before the disclosure had grown public. If he once held his money, he need not stay to endure scorching looks and biting words; he could be gone, like smoke driven out by a sudden gust. He would wait, go away with Cennini, and get it at once.

With that project in him he stood motionless, hands in his belt, eyes fixed absently on the ground. Nello, glancing at him, felt sure the Greek was troubled only for Romola, and, thinking him a pretty image of self-forgetful sadness, just perceptibly pointed his razor at him with a challenging look at Piero di Cosimo, who had never forgiven his refusal to see any prognostic of character in Tito’s handsome face. Piero, leaning against the other doorpost close by, shrugged; repeated challenges had shifted him from neutrality into a positive inclination to believe ill of the much-praised stranger.

“So you have got your Fra Girolamo back again, Cronaca?” said Nello. “I suppose we shall have him preaching again this next Advent.”

“And not before there is need,” said Cronaca gravely. “We have had the best testimony to his words since the last Quaresima; for even to the wicked wickedness has become a plague, and the ripeness of vice is turning to rottenness in the nostrils even of the vicious. There has not been a change since the Quaresima, either in Rome or at Florence, but has put a new seal on the Frate’s words—that the harvest of sin is ripe, and that God will reap it with a sword.”

“I hope he has had a new vision, however,” said Francesco Cei, sneering. “The old ones are somewhat stale. Can’t your Frate get a poet to help out his imagination for him?”

“He has no lack of poets about him,” Cronaca returned, with quiet contempt, “but they are great poets and not little ones; so they are contented to be taught by him, and no more think the truth stale which God has given him to utter than they think the light of the moon is stale. But perhaps certain high prelates and princes who dislike the Frate’s denunciations might be pleased to hear that, though Giovanni Pico, and Poliziano, and Marsilio Ficino, and most other men of mark in Florence reverence Fra Girolamo, Messer Francesco Cei despises him.”

“Poliziano?” Cei laughed scornfully. “Yes—doubtless he believes in your new Jonah; witness the fine orations he wrote for the envoys of Sienna, to tell Alexander the Sixth that the world and the Church were never so well off as since he became Pope.”

“Nay, Francesco,” said Macchiavelli, smiling, “a various scholar must have various opinions. And as for the Frate—whatever we may think of his saintliness—you judge his preaching too narrowly. The secret of oratory lies, not in saying new things, but in saying things with a certain power that moves the hearers—without which, as old Filelfo has said, your speaker deserves to be called, ‘non oratorem, sed aratorem.’ And, according to that test, Fra Girolamo is a great orator.”

“That is true, Niccolò,” said Cennini from the shaving-chair; “but part of the secret lies in the prophetic visions. Our people—no offence to you, Cronaca—will run after anything in the shape of a prophet, especially if he prophesies terrors and tribulations.”

“Rather say, Cennini,” Cronaca answered, “that the chief secret lies in the Frate’s pure life and strong faith, which stamp him as a messenger of God.”

“I admit it—I admit it,” said Cennini, opening his palms as he rose. “His life is spotless: no man has impeached it.”

“He is satisfied with the pleasant lust of arrogance,” Cei burst out bitterly. “I can see it in that proud lip and satisfied eye of his. He hears the air filled with his own name—Fra Girolamo Savonarola, of Ferrara—the prophet, the saint, the mighty preacher, who frightens the very babies of Florence into laying down their wicked baubles.”

“Come, come, Francesco, you are out of humour with waiting,” said Nello, conciliatory. “Let me stop your mouth with a little lather. I must not have my friend Cronaca made angry: I have a regard for his chin; and his chin is in no respect altered since he became a Piagnone.
