And for my own part, I confess, when the Frate was preaching in the Duomo last Advent, I got into such a trick of slipping in to listen to him that I might have turned Piagnone too, if I had not been hindered by the liberal nature of my art—and also by the length of the sermons, which are sometimes a good while before they get to the moving point. But as Messer Niccolò says, the Frate lays hold of the people by some power over and above his prophetic visions. Monks and nuns who prophesy are not of that rareness. For what says Luigi Pulci? ‘Dombruno’s sharp-cutting scimitar had the fame of being enchanted; but I am rather of opinion it cut sharp because it was of strongly-tempered steel.’ Yes, yes; Paternosters may shave clean, but they must be said over a good razor.”

“See, Nello!” said Macchiavelli. “What doctor is this advancing on his Bucephalus? I thought your piazza was free from those furred and scarlet-robed lackeys of death. This man looks as if he had had some such night adventure as Boccaccio’s Maestro Simone, and had his bonnet and mantle pickled a little in the gutter—though he himself is as sleek as a miller’s rat.”

Nello lifted his eyes and drew out a low, long sound, half amusement, half disgust. A round-headed, round-bodied man was approaching on a raw young horse that held its nose out with threatening obstinacy and backed whenever the reins asked it for straightness, as if it had free notions about authority far in advance of the age. The rider’s saddle-bags bulged, swaying with each reluctant step, and the leather looked greasy with use.

“And I have a few more adventures in pickle for him,” Nello murmured, so that only those nearest could hear. “Which I hope will drive his inquiring nostrils to another quarter of the city. He’s a doctor from Padua; they say he has been at Prato for three months, and now he’s come to Florence to see what he can net. But his great trick is making rounds among the contadini. Do you note those great saddle-bags? They are to hold the fat capons and eggs and meal he levies on silly clowns with whom coin is scarce. He vends his own secret medicines, so he keeps away from the doors of the druggists; and for this last week he has taken to sitting in my piazza for two or three hours every day and making it a resort for asthmas and squalling bambini. It stirs my gall to see the toad-faced quack fingering greasy quattrini, or bagging a pigeon in exchange for his pills and powders. But I’ll put a few thorns in his saddle, else I’m no Florentine. Laudamus!—he is coming to be shaved; that’s what I’ve waited for. Messer Domenico, go not away: wait; you shall see a rare bit of fooling, which I devised two days ago. Here, Sandro!”

He whispered in Sandro’s ear. Sandro rolled his solemn eyes, nodded, and, after a slow smile that came like dawn over a hillside, took to his heels with surprising rapidity.

“How is it with you, Maestro Tacco?” said Nello aloud as the doctor, with difficulty, brought the horse’s head round towards the shop. “That is a fine young horse of yours, but something raw in the mouth—eh, Maestro?”

“He is an accursed beast, the vermocane seize him!” Maestro Tacco burst out, descending and fastening an old bridle, mended with string, to the iron staple in the wall. Then, recollecting himself with a merchant’s caution, he added, “Nevertheless—a sound beast and valuable, for one who wanted to purchase and get a profit by training him. I had him cheap.”

“Rather too hard riding for a man who carries your weight of learning, eh, Maestro?” said Nello. “You seem hot.”

“Truly, I am likely to be hot,” said the doctor, taking off his bonnet and showing a bald low head and a flat broad face: high ears, a wide lipless mouth, round eyes, and deep arched lines above projecting brows. If the epithet “toad-faced” suited him, it did so with an injustice to the harmless creature of ponds. “Riding from Peretola when the sun is high is not the same thing as kicking your heels on a bench in the shade like your Florence doctors. Moreover, I have had not a little pulling to get through the carts and mules into the Mercato, to find out the husband of a certain Monna Ghita, who had had a fatal seizure before I was called in; and if it had not been that I had to demand my fees—”

“Monna Ghita!” said Nello. “Peace be with her angry soul! The Mercato will want a whip the more if her tongue is laid to rest.”

At the name, Tito—roused from the rigid stillness of his plan—felt the old vague, half-formed thought about Tessa press forward again, like the scent of a remembered kitchen suddenly rising from a covered pot. If Monna Ghita were taken out of the way, it would be easier for him to see Tessa again—whenever he wanted to see her.

“Gnaffè, Maestro,” Nello went on in a tone of sympathy sweetened with mockery, “you are the slave of rude mortals who, but for you, would die like brutes without help of pill or powder. It is pitiful to see your learned lymph oozing from your pores as if it were mere vulgar moisture. You think my shaving will cool and disencumber you? One moment, and I have done with Messer Francesco here. It seems to me a thousand years till I wait upon a man who carries all the science of Arabia in his head and saddle-bags. Ecco!”

He held up the shaving-cloth with a flourish. Maestro Tacco advanced and seated himself, preoccupied with his heat and self-importance, so deaf to the irony that the words slid off him like water off oiled leather.

“It is but fitting,” said Nello, snapping the cloth in place, “that a great medicus like you should be shaved by the same razor that has shaved the illustrious Antonio Benevieni, the greatest master of the chirurgic art.”

“The chirurgic art!” The doctor’s contempt broke out as if a bitter herb had touched his tongue. “Is it your Florentine fashion to put masters of the science of medicine on a level with men who do carpentry on broken limbs and sew up wounds like tailors, and carve away excrescences as a butcher trims meat? Via! A manual art such as any artificer might learn—and which has been practised by simple barbers like yourself—on a level with the noble science of Hippocrates, Galen, and Avicenna, which penetrates into the occult influences of the stars and plants and gems!—a science locked up from the vulgar!”

“No, in truth, Maestro,” said Nello, working his brush slowly, as if he loved to make the lather rise and swell, white and heavy, and to keep the other man’s mouth busy while his own plot ripened, “I never thought of placing them on a level. I know your science comes next to the miracles of Holy Church for mystery. But there—you see—is the pity of it,”—and here he slid into a tone of regretful concern—“your high science is sealed from the profane and the vulgar, and so you become an object of envy and slander. I grieve to say it, but there are low fellows in this city—mere sgherri—who go about in nightcaps and long beards and make it their business to sprinkle gall in every man’s broth who is prospering. Let me tell you—for you are a stranger—this is a city where every man had need carry a large nail ready to fasten on the wheel of Fortune when his side happens to be uppermost. Already there are stories—mere fables, doubtless—beginning to be buzzed about concerning you, that make me wish I could hear of your being well on your way to Arezzo. I would not have a man of your metal stoned; for though San Stefano was stoned, he was not great in medicine like San Cosmo and San Damiano…”

“What stories? what fables?” stammered Maestro Tacco. Alarm made his breath quick and his voice thick, and the lather under his nostrils gave him the look of a man half-muzzled.

“Lasso! I fear me you are come into the trap for your cheese, Maestro. The fact is, there is a company of evil youths who go prowling about the houses of our citizens carrying sharp tools in their pockets;—no sort of door, or window, or shutter, but they will pierce it. They are possessed with a diabolical patience to watch the doings of people who fancy themselves private. It must be they who have done it—it must be they who have spread the stories about you and your medicines. Have you by chance detected any small aperture in your door, or window-shutter? No? Well, I advise you to look; for it is now commonly talked of that you have been seen in your dwelling at the Canto di Paglia, making your secret specifics by night: pounding dried toads in a mortar, compounding a salve out of mashed worms, and making your pills from the dried livers of rats which you mix with saliva emitted during the utterance of a blasphemous incantation—which indeed these witnesses profess to repeat.”

“It is a pack of lies!” the doctor cried, struggling for utterance, and then stopping in terror as the razor approached his throat.

“It is not to me, or any of this respectable company, that you need to say that, doctor. We are not the heads to plant such carrots as those in. But what of that? What are a handful of reasonable men against a crowd with stones in their hands? There are those among us who think Cecco d’Ascoli was an innocent sage—and we all know how he was burnt alive for being wiser than his fellows. Ah, doctor, it is not by living at Padua that you can learn to know Florentines. My belief is, they would stone the Holy Father himself, if they could find a good excuse for it; and they are persuaded that you are a necromancer, trying to raise the pestilence by selling secret medicines—and I am told your specifics have in truth an evil smell.”

“It is false!” burst out the doctor, as Nello drew the razor away for an instant. “It is false! I will show the pills and the powders to these honourable signori—and the salve—it has an excellent odour—an odour of—of salve.”

He started up with the lather still clinging to his chin and the cloth still knotted round his neck, and began fumbling in his saddle-bag with feverish hands, as if he would drag his own reputation out by force. In the same instant Nello, quick as the flick of flame, shifted the shaving-chair so that it stood close by the horse’s head; and Sandro, returned and waiting as if he had only been part of the air till summoned, placed himself at a sign near the bridle.

“Behold, Messeri!” cried Maestro Tacco, bringing out a small box and flinging it open before them.

The loggia on the roof of Bardo’s house rose above the neighbouring tiles and chimneys, a square gallery wrapped round by four walls as if the building wore a crown. On the side that looked toward the street, the roof rested on columns; on the other three sides it was guarded by a wall pierced with arched openings, so that at the back—where one looked over a tangle of mean little dwellings towards the hill of Bogoli—Romola could pace in sunlight and shadow without the eyes of the street finding her.

Near one of those arches, close to the door by which he had come up, Tito waited.

The light fell slantwise across the stones, warming them, drawing out a faint mineral smell from mortar and old rain, and yet it seemed to him a mocking brightness, as if day itself had taken sides against him and made his fears stand out sharply on the pavement. He had never built his hopes on Romola’s passion being strong enough to overbear the revulsion that must follow her discovery of his secret: he was too keen-sighted—too practised in reading the limits of other hearts—for that sort of vanity. Her love, he knew, had grown from her belief in him; and if belief were plucked out by the roots, the flower would wither at once.

And yet, as he pictured her coming towards him—radiant, dignified, made deliciously mortal by the softness of those hazel eyes—there rose in him an ignoble wish that she had been something less than she was, if only that she might have let him clasp and kiss her without judgment, before they parted. He had had no full caress from her—no unmeasured intimacy; only, now and then, a long look that was like a touch, a kiss that was quickly given and quickly withdrawn, a pressure of the hand whose warmth lingered on his palm like spice on a cup. He had so often longed for them to be alone. They were going to be alone now; and he saw her already, in his imagination, standing apart from him with that inexorable purity which was harder to beguile than any anger.

His heart leapt as the door moved. Romola was there.

It was like lightning—too swift for separate seeing. He felt rather than beheld the glory that seemed to hang about her head, the tender, tear-laden appeal of her eyes; he heard rather than understood the cry with which she said, “Tito!” And in that same instant she was in his arms, sobbing with her face hidden against him, as if her grief had found at last the one breast where it might break without shame.

How she had yearned through the night-watches to see that bright face again! The new image of death; the bewildering doubt poured into her by a story of a life so unlike her own that it stood outside her sympathy like a foreign tongue; above all, the haunting vision which she seemed not only to hear in that low, gasping voice, but to live through—as if it had been her own dream—had made her more conscious than ever that it was Tito who had first brought warmth into her days, who had first loosened the iron pain of her brother’s remembrance and let hope run, like a stream unblocked, through her heart.

She would tell Tito everything: there was no other being to whom she could pour it out. She had held herself rigid all the morning before her father, biting back tears as one bites back an outcry; but here the long-pent sob might come forth. Proud and self-contained to the world, she was, in her love, as unguarded as a child.

“My Romola! my goddess!” Tito murmured, and his voice had that rich caressing quality which made words seem like touch. He clasped her gently, and kissed the thick golden ripples where her hair lay warm against her neck. A breath of her came to him—something like violets crushed in the palm with the salt of tears—and he felt himself, for the moment, in paradise. Disgrace, shame, parting—there was no fear of them any longer. This happiness was too strong to be marred even by the knowledge that she was deceived in him; rather, he rejoiced in her delusion, as men rejoice in a well-spiced dish whose ingredients are not questioned. Concealment had been wisdom. If he regretted anything, it was his needless dread—unless, indeed, dread were worth all suffering for the sake of this sudden rapture.

Her sobs spent themselves; she lifted her head. They stood silent, looking at each other with that sweet wonder which belongs to young love when it has, for the first time, no witnesses. Her long white hands rested on his dark-brown curls; his dark fingers were lost in the streaming gold of her hair, as if his touch could not bear to leave it. Each face was to the other a new world of meaning. A cold sadness pressed on Romola’s heart, making her linger the more in that silent nearness, as one lingers in the scent of bread when the mind has been sickened with other odours; and Tito did not even seek her lips, because to change their stillness seemed to risk breaking the spell.

“Tito,” she said at last, “it has been altogether painful, but I must tell you everything. Your strength will help me to resist the impressions that will not be shaken off by reason.”

“I know, Romola—I know he is dead,” said Tito. His long lustrous eyes told nothing of the many wishes that would have welcomed that death long ago, if wishing had been a knife with an edge. Romola read only her own pure thoughts in those dark depths, as in happy dreams we read letters clearly where, waking, we should see only blots.

“So changed, Tito! It pierced me to think it was Dino. And so strangely hard: not a word to my father; nothing but a vision he wanted to tell me. And yet it was so piteous—the struggling breath, and the eyes that seemed to look toward the crucifix, and yet not to see it. I shall never forget it; it seems as if it would come between me and everything I shall look at.”

Her voice faltered; the heart swelled in her again until it forced her to break off. But the need to disburden her mind to Tito urged her to master herself, as one steadies a trembling hand to keep it from spilling something precious.

“It was strange, Tito. The vision was about our marriage, and yet he knew nothing of you.”

“What was it, my Romola? Sit down and tell me,” said Tito, leading her to the bench near by.

A quick fear had shot through him that this “vision” might touch Baldassarre—as if some long-buried taste could suddenly rise again on the tongue. The fear made him crave a change of place, as if moving his body could move the thought away.

Romola told him all that had passed from her entrance into San Marco, leaving out hardly one of Dino’s words, so burned were they into her memory. She spoke with the fidelity of one repeating a chant heard once, where the cadence and the very pauses are remembered; and behind her speech there seemed to linger the hush of that place—the muffled footfalls, the distant murmur of prayer, the oppressive stillness broken now and then by a sound like a drawn breath. Even here under the open arches, the loggia’s air felt to her as if it carried an echo of cloistered walls.

But when she reached the end of the vision she paused. The rest—the dying look, the last gasps—came too vividly to be uttered, and she sat staring outward through the arch as if the hill and the roofs were far away and she saw only the chapter-house again. Tito’s mind, meanwhile, was at ease. That vague monkish warning had swept over him like a white mist and left no stain. He waited in silence, expecting her to speak again.

“I took it,” she said at last, as if he had been following the unspoken thread of her thoughts. “I took the crucifix; it is down below in my bedroom.”

“And now, my Romola,” Tito answered, leaning towards her with entreaty, “you will banish these ghastly thoughts. The vision was an ordinary monkish vision, bred of fasting and fanatic ideas. It surely has no weight with you.”

“No, Tito; no. But poor Dino—he believed it was a divine message. It is strange,” she went on, meditatively, “this life of men possessed with fervid beliefs that seem like madness to their fellow-beings. Dino was not a vulgar fanatic; and that Fra Girolamo—his very voice seems to have penetrated me with a sense that there is some truth in what moves them: some truth of which I know nothing.”

“It was only because your feelings were highly wrought,” said Tito, in the tone he used when he wanted to lay a cool hand over a feverish mind. “Your brother’s state of mind was no more than a form of that theosophy which is the common disease of excitable, dreamy natures in all ages; the same ideas your father’s old antagonist, Marsilio Ficino, pores over in the New Platonists—only your brother’s passionate temper drove him to act out what other men write and talk about. And for Fra Girolamo, he is simply a narrow-minded monk with a gift of preaching, and of infusing terror into the multitude. Any words, any voice, would have shaken you then. When your mind has had a little repose, you will judge of such things as you have always done before.”

“Not about poor Dino,” said Romola. “I was angry with him; my heart seemed to close against him while he was speaking. But since then I have thought less of what was in my own mind and more of what was in his. Oh, Tito! it was very piteous to see his young life coming to an end in that way. That yearning look at the crucifix when he was gasping for breath—I can never forget it. Last night I looked at the crucifix a long while, and tried to see that it would help him, until at last it seemed to me by the lamplight as if the suffering face shed pity.”

“My Romola,” Tito said, and his tenderness took on an edge of impatience, “promise me you will resist such thoughts. They are fit for sickly nuns, not for my golden-tressed Aurora, who looks made to scatter all such twilight fancies.” He added, in a lower tone, as if reminding her of the world beyond their solitude, “Try not to think of them now; we shall not long be alone together.”

He turned her face towards him with a gentle touch. Romola’s eyes had been fixed absently on the arched opening, but she had not seen the distant hill; she had been in San Marco still, among pale images of sorrow and death. His hand and voice recalled her to the warm present. In the sunlight she saw again the rich dark beauty of Tito’s face, which seemed to gather about it all images of joy—vine tendrils and purple grapes in her imagination, the strong corn swelling under the vibrating heat, bright-winged creatures darting and settling among flowers, and, mingled with it all, the remembered rhythm of festival sounds: the beat of feet on hard earth, the ring of cymbals lifted high, the quick sting of laughter, the throbbing of strings as if a heart had been made audible. Even the city’s air came to her as a kind of music—pigeon wings, distant voices, the far-off hammering that Florence never let die, a shrillness in merriment as if joy itself had a keen edge.

What thought could reconcile the worn anguish of Dino’s face—his straining after something invisible—with this satisfied strength and beauty that shone on her like a sun that had never known dusk? Were these indeed in one world, or were there only clashing deities to be worshipped blindfold—first in mad gladness, then in wailing? For an instant Romola felt a dizziness, a sudden need of something to grasp, as if she stood between two languages and could not translate her experience from one into the other. But no answer rose to meet that need; and it vanished before the returning rush of young sympathy with the glad, loving presence before her.

“Your mind lingers apart from our love, my Romola,” Tito murmured, softly reproachful. “It seems a forgotten thing to you.”

She looked at him in silence until the sadness melted from her own face, as frost melts when the sun returns.

“My joy!” she said, and the fullness of her voice sounded like a promise.

“Do you really care for me enough, then, to banish those chill fancies,” said Tito with his bright smile, “or shall you always be suspecting me as the Great Tempter?”

“How should I not care for you more than for everything else?” Romola answered. “Everything I had felt before in all my life—about my father, and about my loneliness—was a preparation to love you. You would laugh at me, Tito, if you knew what sort of man I used to think I should marry—some scholar with deep lines in his face, like Alamanno Rinuccini, and with rather grey hair, who would agree with my father in taking the side of the Aristotelians, and be willing to live with him. I used to think about the love I read of in the poets, but I never dreamed that anything like it could happen to me here in Florence, in our old library. And then you came, Tito, and were so much to my father, and I began to believe that life could be happy for me too.”

“My goddess! is there any woman like you?” Tito said, and there was real wonder in his fondness at the majesty and simplicity mingled in her.

“But, dearest,” he went on, more timidly, as if he feared to touch what might be a sore place, “if you minded more about our marriage, you would persuade your father and Messer Bernardo not to think of any more delays. But you seem not to mind about it.”

“Yes, Tito, I will. I do mind. But I am sure my godfather will urge more delay now, because of Dino’s death. He has never agreed with my father about disowning Dino, and you know he has always said that we ought to wait until you have been at least a year in Florence. Do not think hardly of my godfather. I know he is prejudiced and narrow, but yet he is very noble. He has often said it is folly in my father to want to keep his library apart, that it may bear his name; yet he would try to get my father’s wish carried out. That seems to me very great and noble—that power of respecting a feeling which he does not share or understand.”

“I have no rancour against Messer Bernardo for thinking you too precious for me,” Tito said; and it was true. Messer Bernardo’s caution could not sting him, since it was grounded in Romola’s worth.

“But your father, then, knows of his son’s death?” Tito asked.

“Yes. I told him—I could not help it. I told him where I had been, and that I had seen Dino die; but nothing else; and he has commanded me not to speak of it again. But he has been very silent this morning, and has had those restless movements which always go to my heart; they look as if he were trying to get outside the prison of his blindness. Let us go to him now. I persuaded him to try to sleep, because he slept little in the night. Your voice will soothe him, Tito: it always does.”

“And not one kiss? I have not had one,” said Tito, in the gentle, dependent tone that made his reproach sound like a plea.

A sweet pink blush spread over Romola’s face and neck with the quickness of light. She bent towards him, and their lips met with a reverence as if such a thing could never become common. It seemed to her impossible that kisses could ever be like the daily bread one eats without thinking—yet even bread, she knew, is made of innumerable small acts, patient and repeated, which are forgotten only because they are faithful.

“Let us walk once round the loggia,” Romola said, “before we go down.”

They moved slowly along the front of the house where the city opened itself to sight. Roofs lay piled like broken waves; beyond them the river’s line was guessed rather than seen; on the further side the buildings rose again, and the air carried up a mixture of sounds—voices that struck sharply and died, a cry from a distant vendor, a burst of laughter with a thin metallic ring, the ceaseless undertone of tools and traffic. Even here, in sunlight, Florence seemed to Tito to make its music with hard instruments.

“There is something grim and grave to me always about Florence,” he said, pausing. “And even in its merriment there is something shrill and hard—biting rather than gay. I wish we lived in Southern Italy, where thought is broken, not by weariness, but by delicious languors such as never seem to come over the ingenia acerrima Florentina. I should like to see you under that southern sun, lying among the flowers, subdued into mere enjoyment, while I bent over you and touched the lute and sang to you some little unconscious strain that seemed all one with the light and the warmth. You have never known that happiness of the nymphs, my Romola.”

“No,” she said, and her eyes softened with the confession as with a taste long imagined and never tried. “But I have dreamed of it often since you came. I am very thirsty for a deep draught of joy—for a life all bright like you. But we will not think of it now, Tito; it seems to me as if there would always be pale sad faces among the flowers, and eyes that look in vain. Let us go.”

When Tito turned away from the Via de’ Bardi that day, he walked as men do when a noose has been loosened from the throat—not with gratitude so much as with a quickened appetite for air. The street sounds came back to him as if they had been muffled during his late suspense: the clop of a mule’s hoof on uneven paving; a distant hammer on bronze; a woman’s voice, sharp as a knife over a market-board, bargaining in the Florentine tongue that bit and clacked in Tito’s ear with its rough, homely certainties. The city had its own breath—smoke from kitchen chimneys, sour wine lees tipped into gutters, warm bread carried under a cloth—and his mind, released from the immediate presence of Romola and her father, began to turn and worry at the little abrasions left by the danger he had escaped.

He had been thoroughly freed, as he told himself, from the peril that had threatened him; and because fortune had done this for him, it seemed only fair that she should. He had not been brought to account; he had not been forced to look too long at the face of his own first deception. Who was hurt? The results to Baldassarre were too doubtful, too entangled in all the “ifs” that make an easy pillow for a man who wishes to sleep. The load was lifted; he could breathe; and it was precisely that lightness—this delight in immunity—that was silently dulling the very sensibility which might have saved him from future snares.

Yet there remained one thing that tugged like a thread caught on a nail: the ring.

In those hours of dread he had not only felt, but acted as he would not have done had he truly foreseen. He would not have parted with that familiar gem. Romola would notice its absence; so would others who had seen it on his hand, that glittering token he had professed to prize. If he could not produce it, he must explain—must feign some noble purpose, some special gift bought with the money. And Tito, for the moment, felt a nausea at the very taste of simulation, as though he had been chewing too long on sweetmeats that had turned cloying.

After all, the ring was a slight matter.

But then—Tessa.

The thought came with an odd domestic vividness, as if he saw again the little round face and the pouting lips, and felt on his palm the warmth of a small hand that trusted. Should he seek her out and undeceive her at once? Or let daylight and the stir of life end happy dreams without his intervention? A dream, after all, is like a dish of milk and honey given to a child: pleasant while it lasts, and when it is done there is no need to scold the tongue for having been sweetened.

The sweet, innocent, pouting little thing—impossible not to think of her. And with the thought came the homelier question that had pricked him even then: did her step-father use her more cruelly now her mother was dead? Tito imagined carrying her some small present—something that would make her eyes widen with that quick gratitude of the poor, who are accustomed to being refused. A scarf? A ribbon? A little gilt image? And then a counter-thought came, cold as water: if he saw her again, if he undeceived her, what then? Tell Romola? Let Romola find some happier lot for her?

No. That unlucky little incident of the _cerretano_ and the marriage—his allowing Tessa to part from him wrapped in delusion—must never come under Romola’s gaze. Not because Romola would fail to pity; rather because Romola’s pity, once awakened, had a force that would tear away coverings Tito meant to keep in place. And besides, no enlightenment could wholly expel what had already planted itself in Tessa’s mind; there would always be a risk—some childish betrayal, some babbled phrase in the wrong dialect to the wrong ear. Even a child’s love, when disappointed, may have a sharpness in it, a little gall. Yes—she must be a little in love with him; and for that very reason it might be wisest that he should not see her again.

It was a trifling adventure, he argued—just such a thing as a country girl might brood over until some ruddy contadino, smelling of sun-warmed fields and crushed fennel, made his acceptable love; then she would loosen her tongue and learn—by chance, by laughter, by some neighbor’s coarse wisdom—that she was free.

_Dunque_—good-bye, Tessa. Kindest wishes.

People are apt to think that resolutions taken for their own ease will hold like iron. Tito made up his mind that the affair should have no further consequence for him; and with that mind made up, he turned to what could be managed, shaped, seasoned—what could be turned into a pleasing dish for another’s eyes.

The fifty-five florins that had come from the ring were not to lie idle. He had already conceived a pretty ingenious thought—one that would help him account for the absence of the gem, and would also serve as a gentle barrier against the recurrence in Romola of those monkish fancies that jarred upon him. He would replace a thing with a thing: trade the personal token for an object that looked like art, like taste, like devotion to the antique—something that could sit in the household as naturally as a carved chest or a painted panel, and silently teach Romola’s mind to play where he wished it to play.

So he went to the Via Gualfonda, to find Piero di Cosimo—the painter then most esteemed for fantastic mythological invention, precisely the sort Tito’s purpose required.

Entering the court on which Piero’s dwelling opened, he saw at once the heavy iron knocker thickly wrapped with wool and cunningly lashed with cords. The absurdity of it had its own rationale; Tito remembered how Piero defended his ears against obtrusive noise, as if the city’s clamour were an invasion of the soul. It struck Tito—who was always quick to profit by another man’s peculiarity—that this painter’s very oddness was a kind of acoustic piety: he would not have his inward images battered by common thunderings and cries.

Tito tapped modestly with his knuckles; then, growing more importunate, shook the door. No answer. He was already moving away—half vexed with himself for wasting time, thinking he might better have waited to encounter Piero again at Nello’s—when a little girl entered the court with a basket of eggs on her arm. She went straight to the door as if it were an everyday altar. Standing on tiptoe, she pushed up a small iron plate that slid in grooves, put her mouth to the opening, and piped, “Messer Piero!”

In a moment came the metallic music of bolts drawn back; the door opened; and Piero stood there in a red night-cap and a loose brown serge tunic, the sleeves rolled up to the shoulder as if he were about to knead bread or butcher game rather than paint gods. He darted one surprised glance at Tito—no more than a brushstroke—then held out his hand for the basket, re-entered, and presently returned with the empty basket.

“How much to pay?”

“Two grossoni, Messer Piero,” said the child. “They are all ready boiled, my mother says.”

Piero drew the coin from the leathern scarsella at his belt. The little maiden trotted away, not without a few upward glances of awed admiration at the handsome young signor who did not belong to her world of eggs and ash and hearthstone.

Piero’s look at Tito was much less admiring.

“What do you want at my door, Messer Greco?” he said. “I saw you this morning at Nello’s. If you had asked me then, I could have told you that I see no man in this house without knowing his business and agreeing with him beforehand.”

“Pardon, Messer Piero,” Tito answered, with a good-humour smooth as well-pressed oil. “I acted without enough reflection. I remembered nothing but your admirable skill in inventing pretty caprices, when a sudden desire for something of that sort prompted me to come to you.”

Piero’s odd manners were too notorious for Tito to take this as a personal affront; and even had there been insult intended, Tito’s instinct was not to resent but to win. He watched Piero’s face—how it distorted itself, as if flattery were a sour fruit in his mouth. The painter grinned, stretching the corners of his lips and pressing down his brows in a way that hid his feelings like a mask.

“And what may that need be?” he asked, after a pause; for the hint of invention called to him like a trumpet muffled by cloth.

“I want a very delicate miniature device, taken from certain fables of the poets, which you will know how to combine for me,” Tito said. “It must be painted on a wooden case—I will show you the size—in the form of a triptych. The inside may be simple gilding: it is on the outside I want the device. It is a favourite subject with you Florentines—the triumph of Bacchus and Ariadne; but I want it treated in a new way. A story in Ovid will give you the necessary hints. The young Bacchus must be seated in a ship, his head bound with clusters of grapes, and a spear entwined with vine-leaves in his hand: dark-berried ivy must wind about the masts and sails, the oars must be thyrsi, and flowers must wreathe themselves about the poop; leopards and tigers must be crouching before him, and dolphins must be sporting round. But I want to have the fair-haired Ariadne with him, made immortal with her golden crown—that is not in Ovid’s story, but no matter, you will conceive it all—and above there must be young Loves, such as you know how to paint, shooting with roses at the points of their arrows—”

“Say no more!” Piero broke in, the words snapping like a twig underfoot. “I have Ovid in the vulgar tongue. Find me the passage. I love not to be choked with other men’s thoughts. You may come in.”

He led the way through the first room. The air within struck Tito with the mixed scent of ashes and old wood, faintly sweetened by the stale, sulphury breath of boiled eggs. The basket the child had brought stood on the open hearth near a heap of broken shells, white and jagged as little skulls, and a bank of ashes that had the soft grey of sifted flour. It was as if the painter’s household fed itself on the simplest country fare—eggs boiled in their own skins, eaten with salt, the shells tossed down where they fell—while his mind feasted on monsters and gods.

In strange keeping with this sordid litter, there stood a low bedstead of carved ebony, covered carelessly with a piece of rich oriental carpet, the kind that might have lain on the steps to a Madonna’s throne. There was a carved _cassone_, its sides and lid painted with devices; and little else in that large room but casts, wooden steps, easels, rough boxes—all webbed over with cobwebs like old bread left too long in a pantry.

The next room was larger and more crowded, and its very disorder seemed alive. The double door beneath the high window was thrown open, and beyond it lay a garden—no, rather a thicket—where fig-trees and vines trailed in tangled wildness among nettles and hemlock. A tall cypress lifted its dark head from a stifling mass of yellowish mulberry-leaves. The outdoor dampness seemed to have crept indoors; in one corner, among carved marble fragments and rusty armour, tufts of long grass and dark feathery fennel had thrust their way up, and a large stone vase, tilted on its side, looked as if it were pouring ivy in a frozen stream across the floor.

All about the walls hung pen and oil sketches: fantastic sea-monsters; dances of satyrs and maenads; Saint Margaret rising out of the devouring dragon; Madonnas with supernal light upon them; studies of plants; grotesque heads. On rough, irregular shelves lay a few books scattered among drooping bunches of corn, bullocks’ horns, pieces of dried honeycomb, stones with rare-coloured lichen, skulls and bones, peacocks’ feathers, and great birds’ wings. It was a storeroom of the world’s fragments, as if Piero collected not things but the very textures of existence—hard horn, brittle comb, papery feathers—so that his painted marvels might taste, as it were, of truth.

Rising from the dirty litter of the floor were lay figures: one in the frock of a Vallombrosan monk, grotesquely crowned with a helmet and barred visor; another smothered with brocade and skins tossed over it in haste.

And among all this heterogeneous still life, living creatures moved with homely unconcern: speckled and white pigeons perched and strutted, too tame to fly at the entrance of men; three corpulent toads crawled near the door-stone with the slow intimacy of accustomed tenants; and a white rabbit—apparently the model for one that frightened Cupid in a picture of Mars and Venus set on the central easel—twitched its nose contentedly over a box of bran. Their small sounds—the soft scrape of claws, the pigeons’ low coo, the rabbit’s faint rustle—made a gentle counterpoint to the city outside, as if here, in this ear-stuffed sanctuary, the world’s louder discourse had been negotiated down to the domestic.

“And now, Messer Greco,” said Piero, signing to Tito to sit on a low stool near the door, while he stood over him with folded arms, “don’t be trying to see everything at once, like Messer Domeneddio, but let me know how large you would have this same triptych.”

Tito indicated the dimensions, and Piero marked them on a piece of paper.

“And now for the book,” Piero said, reaching down a manuscript volume.

Tito found the passage and gave it him. “There’s nothing about Ariadne there,” he said; “but you will remember I want the crowned Ariadne by the side of the young Bacchus: she must have golden hair.”

“Ha!” Piero pursed his lips abruptly, as if tasting a new spice. Then, looking down into Tito’s face, he added, “And you want them to be likenesses, eh?”

Tito laughed, and a blush rose—quick, like wine rising in a glass when it is poured too fast. “I know you are great at portraits, Messer Piero; but I could not ask Ariadne to sit for you, because the painting is a secret.”

“There it is!” said Piero. “I want her to sit to me. Giovanni Vespucci wants me to paint him a picture of Oedipus and Antigone at Colonos, as he has expounded it to me: I have a fancy for the subject, and I want Bardo and his daughter to sit for it. Now, you ask them; and then I’ll put the likeness into Ariadne.”

Tito’s mind ran swiftly over the request—over Bardo’s proud, thorny scholarship, and Romola’s grave reluctances; over how certain words, uttered in the right dialect and tone, could open a door that force would only bar more firmly. “Agreed,” he said, “if I can prevail with them. And your price for the Bacchus and Ariadne?”

“_Baie_! If you get them to let me paint them, that will pay me. I’d rather not have your money: you may pay for the case.”

“And when shall I sit for you?” Tito asked lightly; “for if we have one likeness, we must have two.”

“I don’t want your likeness; I’ve got it already,” Piero answered, with the blunt relish of a man who enjoys having surprised another. “Only I’ve made you look frightened. I must take the fright out of it for Bacchus.”

As he spoke, he laid down the book and went to look among some paintings propped face to the wall. He returned with an oil sketch in his hand.

“I call this as good a bit of portrait as I ever did,” he said, gazing at it as he advanced. “Yours is a face that expresses fear well, because it’s naturally a bright one. I noticed it the first time I saw you. The rest of the picture is hardly sketched; but I’ve painted you in thoroughly.”

He turned the sketch and held it toward Tito.

There Tito was—right hand uplifted with a wine-cup, the attitude of triumphant joy; and yet the face was turned away from the cup with eyes dilated and lips pallid in an expression of such intense fear that Tito felt, absurdly, a cold stream slide through his veins, as if his body had taken instruction from the painted terror. For a moment, the room’s quiet creatures and the rustle of the thicket outside seemed to fall away, and only that silent scream of a face remained—fear pinned in colour.

“You are beginning to look like it already,” Piero said, with a short laugh, moving the picture away again. “He’s seeing a ghost—that fine young man. I shall finish it some day, when I’ve settled what sort of ghost is the most terrible—whether it should look solid, like a dead man come to life, or half transparent, like a mist.”

Tito was ashamed of his sudden sensitiveness—it ran strangely counter to his habitual command of himself. He forced a careless tone, as if swallowing down an unexpected bitterness.

“That is a subject after your own heart, Messer Piero—a revel interrupted by a ghost. You seem to love the blending of the terrible with the gay. I suppose that is the reason your shelves are so well furnished with death’s-heads, while you are painting those roguish Loves who are running away with the armour of Mars. I begin to think you are a Cynic philosopher in the pleasant disguise of a cunning painter.”

“Not I, Messer Greco,” Piero said promptly. “A philosopher is the last sort of animal I should choose to resemble. I find it enough to live, without spinning lies to account for life. Fowls cackle, asses bray, women chatter, and philosophers spin false reasons—that’s the effect the sight of the world brings out of them. Well, I am an animal that paints instead of cackling, or braying, or spinning lies.”

His words fell with a kind of rough honesty, like coarse salt thrown on the tongue—no elegance, but a sting of flavour that stayed.

“And now,” he added, “I think, our business is done; you’ll keep to your side of the bargain about the Oedipus and Antigone?”

“I will do my best,” Tito said, taking the strong hint and rising at once.

“And you’ll let me know at Nello’s. No need to come here again.”

“I understand,” Tito answered, laughingly, and lifted his hand in a friendly sign of parting.

When he passed back into the court, the city’s louder pulse met him—voices bouncing from stone, the clang of a shutter, the call of a hawker. For an instant, those sounds felt like a coarse net flung over finer things. Yet Tito, whose nature was to take each atmosphere as it served him, let the noise bear him along. In his mind the little triptych began already to exist: grapes swelling in painted clusters, ivy curling round a mast, Ariadne’s gold hair catching a light that was not the sun’s—and behind that, like a stain on the palate that sweet wine cannot wash away, the image of himself with the lifted cup and frightened eyes, as if some uninvited ghost had found a way, not into Piero’s picture only, but into the very feast Tito meant to set before Romola.

Messer Bernardo del Nero held to his counsel as one holds to a well-seasoned rule at the hearth: the marriage must wait till Easter. He said it with the same quiet firmness with which an old housekeeper will bid a young cook let the broth stand, and not stir it into haste. Bardo, who could be obstinate on points that lived in books and syllables, yielded at once on a matter that smelt to him of accounts and contracts, for here Bernardo’s practical judgment had long been the hand that guided his.

Yet even Bernardo—who had never warmed to Tito with the easy liking others felt, and who watched the young Greek’s pliancy as a man watches oil on water—found himself answering, in spite of his distrust, to that worldly argument which is like a strong spice: success makes the most doubtful dish seem savoury. Tito was rising swiftly among those whose favour in Florence was as necessary as salt. He had grown especially welcome to the young Cardinal Giovanni de’ Medici, who had spoken of taking him into his learned retinue on an approaching journey to Rome. And at the gay suppers in the Via Larga, amid the clink of cups and the soft chorus of laughter that ran like a ripple over the talk, the bright Greek—always ready of tongue, never quarrelsome—was more and more desired. He could admire the incomparable skill of Piero de’ Medici at those Florentine games where he himself made no pretence to excel; his praise fell with the exact lightness of grated cheese, neither too much nor too little, and somehow made every host feel his own entertainment the more delectable for having called it forth.

So it came about, by an unfailing sequence, that Tito’s reputation as an agreeable companion in “magnificent” society cast a richer glaze on his learning and talent. He was accomplished enough that the estimate which grew around him did not crack when tested. And Bernardo’s old attachments—those strong Florentine fibres that bind a man to names and houses as vines bind to a trellis—began to argue down his newer, feebler prejudice against this supple stranger. To an old Florentine it was impossible to despise the recommendation of standing well with the best families; and as Tito became thoroughly received into that circle whose views were the unquestioned standard of social value, it seemed irrational to keep a check upon satisfaction in him as Bardo’s son-in-law and Romola’s husband.

It was undeniable that Tito’s coming had been like the lighting of a lamp in a room long shut from the sun. For Bardo and his daughter, the first promise of it had even been surpassed. The blind old scholar—whose proud truthfulness would never enter into that trade of feigned, preposterous admiration, and then the answering measurelessness of vituperation, which made the warp and woof of learned intercourse—had fallen into neglect among his fellow-citizens. When his name was spoken at all, men said, with the easy cruelty of those who do not hear their own harshness, that though his blindness and the loss of his son were pitiable, he was tiresome in contending for the value of his labours; and that his discontent sat oddly on one who had been openly regardless of religious rites, and who in past days had refused offers made on the slight condition that he would take orders—without which patrons could not readily provide for every scholar.

But since Tito’s coming, Bardo’s name no longer suggested only that stale monotony of complaint. It was understood that the old man had left off his plaints, and that the fair daughter was not to be shut up in dowerless pride, waiting for a _parentado_. The winning manners and growing favour of the handsome Greek, who was expected to enter into the double relation of son and husband, made the new interest thoroughly friendly; and it was no longer rare for a visitor to enliven the quiet library.

Then the house began to have its own sound again: not the empty hush that presses on the ears and makes the heart listen too much to itself, but the wholesome acoustic life of footsteps on stone, of a cloak brushed back, of voices lowered instinctively under a roof of books. Elderly men came from that half-conscious prompting to renew former intercourse which arises when an old acquaintance begins to be newly talked about. Young men, whom Tito had once asked leave to bring, found it easy to go again when they overtook him on his way to the Via de’ Bardi; and resting their hands on his shoulder, fell into easy chat, their speech mingling with the faint crackle of parchment turned and the far-off call from the street that rose and fell like wind in a narrow lane.

For it was pleasant to look at Romola’s beauty; to see her, like old Firenzuola’s type of womanly majesty, “sitting with a certain grandeur, speaking with gravity, smiling with modesty, and casting around, as it were, an odour of queenliness.” She seemed to unfold like a strong white lily under this genial breath of admiration and homage. In those days the house itself had a gentler atmosphere, as if some careful hand had set fresh herbs to sweeten it; and the change was all one to her with the new bright life in Tito’s love. She took in the sounds and looks of friendliness as one takes in the scent of warm bread—without analysing, only feeling that it nourished.

Tito had even strengthened, in Bardo’s mind, the old hope he hugged like a last jar of precious honey: that before he died he might see his library secured—never merged in another collection, never transferred to a body of monks and called by the name of a monastery, but remaining for ever the Bardi Library, for the use of Florentines. The old habit of trusting in the Medici could not die out while their influence was still the strongest lever in the State; and Tito, once he had the ear of Cardinal Giovanni de’ Medici, might do more even than Messer Bernardo toward winning the desired result, for he could speak to a learned audience of the peculiar value of Bardo’s collection with that quick, persuasive exactness which made knowledge seem like a dish brought steaming to the table rather than a thing stored cold on shelves.

Tito himself talked sanguinely of it, willing to cheer the old man. And he was conscious—though he did not say so—that Romola repaid those gentle words to her father with a kind of adoration which no direct tribute to herself could have won. Here was her deepest appetite: not for praise, but for the comfort that fed her father’s spirit. When Tito touched that, he touched her.

As Christmas went by and the prospect of the marriage drew nearer, the question of the library came up more than once between Bernardo del Nero and Romola—always out of Bardo’s hearing. For Bardo nursed a vague belief, which they dared not disturb, that his property, apart from the library, was adequate to meet all demands. He would not even—except under some momentary pressure of angry despondency—admit to himself that the will by which he had disinherited Dino would leave Romola the heir of nothing but debts; or that he needed anything from patronage beyond the security of a separate locality assigned to his books, in return for a deed of gift by which he made them over to the Florentine Republic.

“My opinion is,” said Bernardo to Romola, in a consultation they had under the loggia, where the air carried every word with a clear, measured resonance, “that since you are to be married, and Messer Tito will have a competent income, we should begin to wind up the affairs, and ascertain exactly the sum that would be necessary to save the library from being touched, instead of letting the debts accumulate any longer. Your father needs nothing but his shred of mutton and his macaroni every day, and I think Messer Tito may engage to supply that for the years that remain; he can let it be in place of the _morgen-cap_.”

“Tito has always known that my life is bound up with my father’s,” Romola answered. “And he is better to my father than I am: he delights in making him happy.”

“Ah, he’s not made of the same clay as other men, is he?” said Bernardo, smiling.

Romola’s eyes had that happy brightness which made even grave speech seem like music. “Thy father has thought of shutting woman’s folly out of thee by cramming thee with Greek and Latin; but thou hast been as ready to believe in the first pair of bright eyes and the first soft words that have come within reach of thee, as if thou couldst say nothing by heart but Paternosters, like other Christian men’s daughters.”

“Now, godfather,” said Romola, shaking her head with playful protest, “as if it were only bright eyes and soft words that made me love Tito! You know better. You know I love my father and you because you are both good, and I love Tito too because he is so good. I see it, I feel it, in everything he says and does. And if he is handsome, too, why should I not love him the better for that? It seems to me beauty is part of the finished language by which goodness speaks.” She looked up with one of her loving smiles at the stately old man. “You know you must have been a very handsome youth, godfather—you were about as tall as Tito, and you had very fine eyes; only you looked a little sterner and prouder, and—”

“And Romola likes to have all the pride to herself?” said Bernardo, not inaccessible to such coaxing.

Then, with the same return to what was solid and measurable that always marked him, he added, “However, it is well that in one way Tito’s demands are more modest than those of any Florentine husband of fitting rank that we should have been likely to find for you; he wants no dowry.”

So the matter was settled in that way between Messer Bernardo del Nero, Romola, and Tito. Bardo assented with a wave of the hand when Bernardo told him it would be well now to begin to sell property and clear off debts. He had long been accustomed to think of debts and property as a sort of thick wood his imagination never penetrated, still less got beyond; he could hear the talk of it as one hears distant chopping, without seeing the tree that falls.

And Tito set himself to win Messer Bernardo’s respect by inquiring, with his ready faculty, into Florentine money-matters: the secrets of the _Monti_ or public funds, the values of real property, the profits of banking. He made figures sound friendly, turning them over with the same deftness with which a practised hand turns thin slices on a hot pan—quick, sure, never letting anything burn.

“You will soon forget that Tito is not a Florentine, godfather,” said Romola. “See how he is learning everything about Florence.”

“It seems to me he is one of the _demoni_, who are of no particular country, child,” said Bernardo, smiling. “His mind is a little too nimble to be weighted with all the stuff we men carry about in our hearts.”

Romola smiled too, in happy confidence, hearing in Bernardo’s tone no warning that could pierce her. The house, with its renewed voices and softened silences, seemed to her a place where every sound promised continuance—where even the oldest hopes might yet be kept warm, like a pot set at the side of the fire until Easter.

The last week of Carnival had come round again, like a feast-day whose very merriment was grown habitual—salted into the life of Florence as surely as the city’s bread was salted with no salt at all. By daylight the streets already rang as if night had never ended: maskers in file, singing what Lorenzo’s taste had once made indispensable; the rigoletto footed in the piazzas under a sky of hard blue cold; and, mixed with the jests, the old brutality that Florence called its privilege—poles thrust crosswise to bar a passage until a tribute was paid for suppers and bonfires, and then, when the appetites were fed, the sport of stones, as if the very hands of boys were taught to fling pain for pastime.

Yet there was, too, a common picturesqueness that belonged to quick blood and quick senses—the smell of crushed orange-peel underfoot, hot chestnuts smoked at corners, and the far-off fat hiss from frying-pans where poor households made a little holiday out of oil and flour. Over all lay the city’s loudness—pipes and chanting, laughter and quarrel, the clack of wooden pattens on stone, the incessant cry of sellers—so that the air itself seemed braided of noise.

It was in the high morning, when Carnival spirits were still willing to lounge and recount last night’s pranks, that Tito Melema pressed forward briskly toward the Via de’ Bardi, and with him walked young Bernardo Dovizi—keen-eyed already, as if his glance were learning to pierce the future as well as the present. They talked eagerly, their words and gestures belonging to some thread of purpose that had little to do with the masquerade around them; and yet, now and then, each cast a rapid look aside, as if the crowd itself might contain a face that could alter their plans.

At the turning toward the Lung’ Arno, Tito’s quick survey caught precisely what he dreaded to meet at such a moment. A small figure in a white hood moved along with a timid, forlorn air—unmistakably Tessa. The very sight of her was like feeling a buried seed stir in the earth just when one had laid a garden-bed smooth and thought it orderly. Tito’s thoughts were full, and full of one unique sweetness: this evening was to be his betrothal to Romola.

The ceremony had been fixed sooner than had first been intended. The fitting-up of rooms in Bardo’s dwelling—scantily furnished always, save for the great library that had been a realm in itself—had been going on for some time, Tito’s florins turning into chairs and hangings, into the visible promise of a shared life. But though the marriage and betrothal had meant to wait until after Easter, when Tito’s year of probation, pressed on him by Bernardo del Nero, should be complete, a sudden proposition had come: he must go with Cardinal Giovanni to Rome, to aid Bernardo Dovizi—who was to gather books as other men gathered offices—in arranging a library, using that superior Greek which made Tito valuable. There was no refusing what lay so plainly on the road of advancement. Tito, therefore, had pleaded that the betrothal should be before his departure. If he and Romola were outwardly pledged as well as inwardly, parting would hurt less; and, more, he would have a claim that Messer Bernardo, and any other cautious elder, could not lightly nullify. The betrothal—rings exchanged, contracts signed—was more than half a marriage already, to be completed later by the nuptial blessing. Romola’s feeling had met his in this desire; the elders had been won.

And now, with departure to Rome looming the next day, he was hurrying to snatch a morning visit to Romola—to speak and to hear those last words that lovers, like cooks tasting the final seasoning, cannot omit before the dish is sent out to the table. It was not a moment when any recognition that could detain him was pleasant; least of all the recognition of Tessa.

As he continued to talk with Dovizi, there ran under his words an uncomfortable certainty: Tessa had seen him; she would follow. The direct way by the Arno and over the Ponte Rubaconte offered no easy escape. She would not dare to speak while he was not alone; so he meant to keep Dovizi at his side until he reached Bardo’s door. He quickened his pace, taking up new strands of talk; yet the sense of those blue eyes behind him grew stronger, as if he heard her small footsteps in the vast city’s roar. It irritated him—more, perhaps, because pity made evasion feel faintly cowardly, and yet he persevered.

He managed the parting at the doorway with Dovizi cleverly, saying his addio without turning his face in the one direction that would let him see a white hood hovering too near. As he went up the stone steps, he tried to persuade himself that perhaps Tessa had not seen him at all; or if she had, perhaps she would not follow. But that hope was thin as Carnival sugar.

When the visit was over, he came out again with a quick step and an air that pretended to notice nothing on either side. Yet the eye takes in more than the will permits, and before any touch came, he knew—knew too well—that she stood near, close to the doorway, small and waiting.

A hand caught his arm—not the light timid touch he might have expected, but a grasp tightened by desperation, for she had started forward when she saw his haste. When Tito stopped and turned, her face was frightened, as if she already feared the consequence of her boldness.

“Tessa!” The sharpness in his voice was new to her.

“Why are you here? You must not follow me—you must not stand about door-places waiting for me.”

Her eyes widened, the tears springing as quickly as a well that has been unstoppered; she could find no words. Tito’s fear leaped at once—not mere ridicule, but the risk of being seen in the Via de’ Bardi with a girlish contadina looking up at him with that unmistakable claim of sorrow. The street was of high, silent dwellings, not of traffic; but Messer Bernardo del Nero, or some other dangerous acquaintance, might appear at any instant. Even on any other day it would have been awkward. On this day it was intolerable.

And yet it was impossible—brutal—to drive her away with harshness. That folly with the cerretano, that bargain with his own ease, had lain quiet for months, and now rose up like an unseasonable weed in the very path of his triumph. He spoke hurriedly, because haste was the nearest thing he could offer in place of cruelty.

“Tessa, I cannot—must not—talk to you here. I will go on to the bridge and wait for you there. Follow me slowly.”

He turned at once and walked fast toward the Ponte Rubaconte. On the bridge he leaned against the wall of one of the quaint little houses that stood there at even distances, and watched for her coming.

It would have softened a harder man than Tito to see her approach. The round face that had once been all sun and childish laughter under the “Nunziata” door was paler now; and the air of her was like a creature accustomed to the crack of a stick and the harshness of hunger—like a little kid that has learned to flinch from the hand that ought to feed it. The bridge at that hour was the least frequented; only a few passed by, their footsteps and voices swallowed by the river’s broader sound.

Tito began at once, losing no time.

“Now, Tessa, I have very little time. You must not cry. Why did you follow me this morning? You must not do so again.”

“I thought—” Her voice was a whisper, and the sob rose in her throat as if it had been waiting there all these months for the mere sound of him. “I thought you wouldn’t be so long before you came to take care of me again. And the patrigno beats me, and I can’t bear it any longer. And always when I come for a holiday I walk about to find you, and I can’t. Oh, please don’t send me away from you again! It has been so long, and I cry so now, because you never come to me. I can’t help it, for the days are so long, and I don’t mind about the goats and kids, or anything—and I can’t—”

The sobs came fast then, and the tears—great drops that clung on her lashes and fell as if each were heavy with all the unspoken time. Tito felt the necessity like a knot: he must send her away at once; but he could not—could not—leave her in hopeless grief. He saw, dimly, a farther trouble beyond this moment; but the present difficulty pressed too hard to weigh distant consequences.

“Tessa, my little one,” he said, letting his voice soften into the old caressing tone which was for her like warm broth to a chilled stomach, “you must not cry. Bear with the cross patrigno a little longer. I will come back to you. But I’m going now to Rome—a long, long way off. I shall come back in a few weeks, and then I promise you to come and see you. Promise me to be good and wait for me.”

The remembered voice soothed her as surely as the scent of baked bread calms a child in a strange house. She lifted her eyes to him—trusting, still glittering with tears—trying, and failing, not to sob.

Again he urged, gently, “Promise me, my Tessa.”

“Yes,” she whispered. “But you won’t be long?”

“No, not long. But I must go now. And remember what I told you, Tessa. Nobody must know that you ever see me, else you will lose me for ever. And now, when I have left you, go straight home, and never follow me again. Wait till I come to you. Good-bye, my little Tessa: I will come.”

There was no help for it. He turned away and did not look back. He had no time to spare for seeing how she bore it; and he would not have been strong enough to bear the sight without making some promise that would entangle him further. When he did look round, he was already in the Via de’ Benci, where the bridge lay out of view. Tessa, obedient in her misery, would do what he had told her.

So the immediate difficulty ended; but it left in Tito’s mind a vexation, like a sour note lingering under music—this return of Tessa at the very instant when it was impossible to end all difficulty by undeceiving her. Yet his spirit was penetrated now by the hope of a first love and by all the prospects that flattered ambition. The future necessity of grieving Tessa was to him scarcely more than a faint cry of some small suffering creature in a thicket, heard by a merry cavalcade riding in sun on the open plain.

When, for the second time that day, he hastened over the Ponte Rubaconte, the thought of her did not perceptibly dull his happiness. He was muffled in his mantle—less against the cold than against the notice his dainty apparel might invite. He went up the stone steps by twos, and said to Maso, who met him,

“Where is the damigella?”

“In the library; she is quite ready, and Monna Brigida and Messer Bernardo are already there with Ser Braccio, but none of the rest of the company.”

“Ask her to give me a few minutes alone; I will await her in the salotto.”

He entered a room newly fitted up in the utmost contrast with the half-pallid, half-sombre tints of the library. The walls were bright with caprices—nymphs and loves sporting under blue sky among flowers and birds. There were red leather seats, a central table, two tall white vases; and a young faun, flute at his lips, modelled by a promising youth named Michelangelo Buonarotti, stood as if he had drawn a breath of outdoor air into the chamber. Even within doors, one had the sensation of sunlight and open space—the promise of pleasure as immediate as the scent of crushed violets.

Tito kept his mantle about him and looked toward the door.

Romola entered—white and gold—more than ever like a tall lily. Her white silk was bound by a golden girdle that fell with large tassels; above it the rippling gold of her hair, and above that again the white mist of her long veil, fastened on her brow by a band of pearls—Bernardo del Nero’s gift—and now parted off her face so that it floated backward. In the torchless daylight of the room, she seemed to carry her own light, like something refined out of purity and pride.

“Regina mia!” Tito took her hand and kissed it, still keeping his mantle round him. He stepped back, as lovers will, to look again at what they can hardly believe is theirs; and she stood, calm in delight, with that exquisite self-consciousness which rises under an admiring gaze.

“Romola, will you show me the next room now?” he said, checking himself, remembering that time might be short. “You said I should see it when you had arranged everything.”

Without speaking she led the way into a long narrow room, brightly painted also, but here only with birds and flowers—no frolic of naked deities, only leaves and wings and blossoms, as if the walls meant to breathe softly around more intimate things. The furniture was old. In an open cabinet between the two narrow windows were faded objects for a woman’s use or ornament, placed with careful reverence; above the cabinet hung the portrait of Romola’s mother. And below it, on the cabinet’s top, stood the crucifix Romola had brought from San Marco—dark, severe, a memory of sorrow set where daily eyes must meet it.

“I have brought something under my mantle,” Tito said, smiling. He threw off the large loose garment and showed the little tabernacle painted by Piero di Cosimo. The painter, in his strange, fantastic way, had carried out Tito’s intention charmingly, and so atoned for long delay.

“Do you know what this is for, my Romola?” Tito took her hand and led her toward the cabinet. “It is a little shrine, which is to hide away from you for ever that remembrancer of sadness. You have done with sadness now; and we will bury all images of it—bury them in a tomb of joy. See!”

As he took hold of the crucifix, a slight quiver passed over Romola’s face. But she did not resist; indeed she herself wished to still certain importunate memories and questionings that flitted like unexplained shadows across her happier thought. Tito opened the triptych and placed the crucifix within the central space; then closed it, turned the key, and set the little tabernacle where the crucifix had stood.

“Now, Romola, look and see if you are satisfied with the portraits old Piero has made of us. Is it not a dainty device? and the credit of choosing it is mine.”

Romola looked, and her eyes grew moist with joy. “Ah! it is you—it is perfect!” she said, gazing at the miniature Bacchus with his purple clusters. “And I am Ariadne, and you are crowning me! Yes, it is true, Tito; you have crowned my poor life.”

They stood hand in hand, looking at their imaged selves; and yet the living presence was more beautiful—she, lily-white and golden; he, dark and glowing above his purple tunic bordered with red.

“And it was our good strange Piero who painted it?” Romola said. “Did you put it into his head to paint me as Antigone, that he might have my likeness for this?”

“No,” Tito answered; “it was he who made my getting leave for him to paint you and your father, a condition of his doing this for me.”

“Ah! I see now what it was you gave up your precious ring for. I perceived you had some cunning plan to give me pleasure.”

Tito did not blench. Romola’s illusions about him, and the tenderness that made them, had long ceased to trouble him; they pleased him like the taste of honey that costs no labour.

“I might have spared my ring,” he said lightly; “Piero will accept no money from me; he thinks himself paid by painting you. And now, while I am away, you will look every day at those pretty symbols of our life together—the ship on the calm sea, and the ivy that never withers, and those Loves that have left off wounding us and shower soft petals that are like our kisses; and the leopards and tigers—they are the troubles of your life that are all quelled now; and the strange sea-monsters, with their merry eyes—let us see—they are the dull passages in the heavy books, which have begun to be amusing since we have sat by each other.”

“Tito mio!” Romola’s voice half laughed with love; then, with a sudden practical longing as if she could not bear even a small barrier between her and what was now theirs, she held out her hand. “But you will give me the key?”

“Not at all!” Tito said, with playful decision; and opening his scarsella he dropped the little key into it. “I shall drown it in the Arno.”

“But if I ever wanted to look at the crucifix again?”

“Ah! for that very reason it is hidden—hidden by these images of youth and joy.”

He pressed a light kiss on her brow, and she said no more. Strong souls submit when they feel no valid reason to resist, and her desire at that moment was for harmony, not debate.

They went then to join the waiting company; and presently a dignified little procession moved over the Ponte Rubaconte toward Santa Croce. Bardo, unaccustomed for years to leave his house, walked with a more timid step than usual; and the slow pace suited well the gouty dignity of Messer Bartolommeo Scala, who honoured the occasion with his presence, bringing his daughter Alessandra. It was customary, at a sposalizio, to have a long troop of kindred and friends—so long that laws had once been needed to limit the number to four hundred, two hundred on each side, because the guests must be feasted after this first ceremony as well as after the nozze itself, and the very beginning of matrimony could ruin a man as surely as a bad harvest. But Bardo, poor and proud, had kept himself free from appearing to trade on his family name; he would have no invitations given on the mere strength of friendship. The modest train of twenty behind the sposi were, with a few exceptions, friends chosen on personal grounds.

Bernardo del Nero walked as a vanguard before Bardo, who was led on the right by Tito, while Romola held her father’s other hand. Bardo had himself been married at Santa Croce, and insisted that Romola should be betrothed and married there, rather than in the little church of Santa Lucia near their house; for in his mind the great church stood always complete, with that final hope within it—that burial might one day be granted him among the Florentines who had deserved well. The way was short and direct and lay somewhat aloof from the loudest riot, if only they could return before the dances or shows began in the great piazza.

The west was red as they passed the bridge, laying a mellow light on the little procession and giving it a touch of solemnity, deepened by the blind father in their midst. After the ceremony, when Tito and Romola came out upon the broad steps with the golden links of destiny on their fingers, evening had deepened into a struggling starlight, and the servants had lit their torches. The flames hissed faintly in the cold air; and in the pause after church-words the city’s soundscape changed—less laughter near at hand, more distant chanting borne in one long drift, as if the very stones were listening.

A strange, dreary chant met their ears—a wail like a Miserere. At the far end of the piazza a stream of people seemed driven backward by something approaching from the Borgo de’ Greci.

“It is one of their masqued processions, I suppose,” Tito said. He was now alone with Romola, while Bernardo took charge of Bardo.

As he spoke, there rose into view, high above heads, a huge ghastly image of Winged Time with scythe and hour-glass, ringed by his winged children, the Hours. He stood upon a tall car covered wholly in black; the bullocks that drew it were black as well, their horns alone showing white above the gloom. In the sombre shadow of the houses, to those who saw from a distance, it was as if Time and his brood floated through the air—apparitions rather than pageant. Behind came what looked like a troop of the sheeted dead, gliding above the blackness; and as they glided slowly they chanted in that wailing strain, a sound that seemed to drain warmth out of the skin.

Cold horror seized Romola. In the first instant it was as if her brother’s vision—never effaced from her mind—were half fulfilled. She clung to Tito. He divined what rose within her and spoke quickly, as if his voice could shut a door against dread.

“What dismal fooling sometimes pleases your Florentines! Doubtless this is an invention of Piero di Cosimo, who loves such grim merriment.”

“Tito, I wish it had not happened,” she said. “It will deepen the images of that vision which I would fain be rid of.”

“Nay, Romola, you will look only at the images of our happiness now. I have locked all sadness away from you.”

“But it is still there—it is only hidden,” Romola murmured, scarcely aware she spoke, as if some part of her listened past his words to that chant fading down the piazza.

“See, they are all gone now!” Tito said, eager, drawing her attention to the open space where the black car had passed. “You will forget this ghastly mummery when we are in the light, and can see each other’s eyes. My Ariadne must never look backward now—only forward to Easter, when she will triumph with her Care-dispeller.”

It was the seventeenth day of November in the year 1494—more than eighteen months since Tito and Romola had been bound to one another in that Easter brightness when, after the old Greek fashion, sugared comfits had rained upon them like a small, crackling hail of promised sweetness. Many a Florentine hearth since then had known the familiar rites of kneading and simmering—oil warmed, onions softened, bread revived with broth—yet the city’s larger life had altered as wholly as a loaf changes when the leaven takes it. For private fortunes in Florence were not unlike the smallest figs on a laden branch: each swelling fruit drew its sap from the same unseen circulation; and Tito’s and Romola’s married lot, with all its domestic duties and vanities, depended now on the grand public currents that were turning Italy.

Only a week earlier the old centuries seemed to have stepped back into Florentine blood. The great bell in the palace tower had sent out its hard, hammering alarm—sound not so much heard as felt, as when a cleaver strikes the butcher’s block—and at that vibration men had poured into the streets with rusty weapons, with axes from workshops, with cudgels snatched up as readily as a baker snatches the peel when he smells scorching. The Medici had been driven out. San Gallo had shut its gate upon Piero—arrogant, exasperating Piero—fleeing toward Bologna with hired horsemen stumbling after him in their panic; and it had shut upon his younger brother too, the cardinal slipping away in a Franciscan’s disguise. A price had been set on both their heads. There had been sackings after the old precedent, as if the city, having long fasted from its own will, made a rough feast of vengeance; the ignominious painted images on public walls—those reminders of past conspiracies—had been effaced; exiled enemies were called home again, names and families coming back like spices long kept in a chest, pungent the moment the lid is lifted. The half-fledged tyrants were out of their splendid nest in the Via Larga, and the Republic could taste its own tongue again.

And now, scarcely a week later, that same palace in the Via Larga had been swept and dressed for a new tenant.
