If bright drapery roofing the streets with unwonted colour, if banners and hangings poured from windows like streamed ribbons of saffron and crimson, if carpets and tapestry were laid over every step and stone where exceptional feet might tread—if these things were proof of joy, then Florence was joyful in expectation of its guest. Colour ran like a rich sauce from the palace in the Via Larga round by the Cathedral, on to the great Piazza della Signoria, and across the Ponte Vecchio to Porta San Frediano, the gate that looks toward Pisa. There, close to the gate, a platform and canopy had been erected for the Signoria; Messer Luca Corsini, doctor of law, could feel his heart fluttering at the thought of the Latin oration he must read, as a man’s stomach flutters when he is pledged to carve before a crowded table and fears his hand may shake. Chief elders prepared themselves—smooth chin, well-lined silk lucco—ready to walk in procession; well-born youths examined their rich tunics cut after the French mode, trusting that on Florentine bodies the new fashion would seem not foreign but graceful. And the clergy, from the archbishop in his effulgence down to the long file of monks—black, white, and grey—had been early at counsel on how to marshal themselves, how to bear relics and sacred banners and jeweled vessels so that every pace would agree with the expected arrival of the illustrious visitor at three o’clock.

An unexampled visitor. He had crossed the Alps with an army Italy had not seen: Swiss in thousands, grim as winter, well used to fight for love and hatred as well as for hire; cavaliers proud of lineage; an infantry such as astonished the eye, where one man in a hundred carried an arquebus; and cannon of bronze that did not throw stones but iron balls, drawn not by bullocks slow as oxen at a press but by horses, and able to fire again before a city could patch the breach made by the first shot. Men compared him to Charlemagne, welcome conqueror and rebuilder, regulator and benefactor of the Church; others spoke rather of Cyrus, liberator of a chosen people, restorer of the Temple. For he came with projects that sounded like a sung legend: he would march through Italy amid jubilees; he would satisfy all complaints at Rome; he would take Naples by hereditary right and a little fighting; and from Naples, that convenient threshold, he would go on to the Turks, cutting some down and converting the rest to Christ.

It befitted, they said, the Most Christian King, head of a nation strengthened by the devices of subtle Louis the Eleventh—dead these ten years in much fear for his soul. This antitype of Cyrus and Charlemagne was Louis’s son: young Charles the Eighth of France. And because the tale had such breadth, because the tread of so great a host seemed to shake the ordinary pattern of days, there spread through Florence a conviction that the French king’s advent belonged to those events at which marble statues might sweat, fiery warriors might fight in the air, and beasts might bring forth monstrous births—that this was not mere human policy, but in a peculiar sense the work of God. So myth made itself at home beside the baker’s hearth and the dyer’s vat: a woman might set her beans to soak overnight and speak, in the same breath, of omens in the sky; a man might sharpen his knife for cutting meat and whisper of statues perspiring.

That conviction rested not only on the sheer weight of a foreign invasion, but on moral emotions that the times had shaped into presentiments—emotions that had found a remarkable utterance in one voice. Fra Girolamo Savonarola, Prior of San Marco, had spoken in such a way that men felt his words as they felt the city’s bells, entering not only the ear but the marrow.

On a September morning, when news rang through Italy that the French army had entered, Savonarola preached in the Cathedral from the text, “Behold I, even I, do bring a flood of waters upon the earth.” He believed—by a guidance beyond his own—he had reached that place in Genesis at just the hour when the world’s fact would fit the ancient figure; and he declared the “flood,” at once avenging wrath and purifying mercy, to be the French host. Many in his audience—men counted among the choicest spirits of the age, the cultivated minds of the most cultivated city—believed him too, and listened with a shuddering awe. For in Savonarola there was a power rarely paralleled: he pressed his belief into other men’s minds as a strong hand presses the stamp into warm wax.

As long as four years earlier he had proclaimed from Florence’s chief pulpit that a scourge was coming upon Italy and that by it the Church would be purified. He spoke as if he bore a mission like the Hebrew prophets, and as if the Florentines, to whom his warning was sent, were in some way a second chosen people. Prophetic talk was no rarity in that age—visions and heraldings were common enough in street and cloister. Yet precisely because so many candles flickered with petty gossip about fate, Savonarola stood out like a beacon whose flame shows the sea-banks and the rocks. His prophecy did not peer into corners; it cast light far out for warning and guidance.

To some sober minds, even, the supernatural character of his insight seemed attested by the very state of the world. At the close of 1492—the year Lorenzo de’ Medici died and Tito Melema came to Florence a wanderer—Italy was enjoying peace and prosperity with no near and definite danger. There was no fear of famine: corn, wine, and oil had been plenteous; new palaces rose in fair cities, new villas on pleasant slopes and summits; and those who had more were not much troubled by those who had less. Citizens’ armour was rusting; populations had grown tame, licking the hands of masters who bought ready-made armies as they bought goods from Smyrna. Even the fear of the Turk had dulled, and the Pope found it more immediately profitable to take bribes from him for a little prospective poisoning than to plan crusade or conversion.

It was a handsome establishment for the few—partitioned empire, roomy universal Church—in which lust and obscenity, lying and treachery, oppression and murder could be pleasant and useful and, if managed with dexterity, not dangerous. And as a fringe to the solid delights of tyranny and avarice, there was patronage of learning and art: flattery in the choicest Latin, painters who could set saint and harlot on the same wall with impartial skill. The Church, it was said, had never been more disgraced at its head, never shown fewer signs of renewing vital belief below; and yet it prospered. The heavens smiled; the earth did not tremble. And still there was a man in Florence who for two years and more had been declaring that a scourge was at hand—that the world was not framed for the lasting convenience of hypocrites, libertines, and oppressors. He saw, he said, a sword hanging from those smiling heavens: the sword of God’s justice, soon to fall in purifying punishment on Church and world.

In Ferrara, seventeen years before, the contradiction between men’s professed beliefs and their lives had struck him with force enough to destroy his appetite for the world, and at twenty-three he fled into the cloister. He believed God had entrusted the Church with the sacred lamp of truth for the guidance and salvation of men; and he saw the Church’s corruption turning it into a sepulchre that hid the lamp. As years passed, scandal multiplied; hypocrisy gave way to impudence. Had the world then ceased to have a righteous Ruler? Was the Church forsaken? No: in the Sacred Book, he held, there was a record of the past that showed the future in a glass; and when the wickedness of the chosen people—type of the Christian Church—had grown crying, God’s judgments had descended. Reason itself, he argued, declared vengeance imminent: what else could turn men from obstinate evil? And unless the Church were reclaimed, how could the promises be fulfilled that the heathen should be converted and the whole world subject to one true law?

He had seen his belief reflected in visions, as he had since youth. Yet the force of his demonstration lay less in those inward pictures than in his burning indignation at wrong; in his fervent faith in an unseen Justice that would end wrong, and an unseen Purity to which lies and uncleanness were abomination. To his ardent, power-loving soul—believing in great ends and longing to achieve them by a strong will—faith in a supreme righteous Ruler became one with faith in speedy divine interposition that would punish and reclaim.

Meanwhile, under the splendid masquerade of sacred and secular dignities which made the lives of fortunate churchmen and princely families so luxurious, conditions were at work that slowly disturbed the general festivity. Ludovico Sforza of Milan—gallant, splendid patron of Leonardo da Vinci—held the ducal crown in his grasp and wanted to set it on his own head rather than let it rest on the brow of a feeble nephew, who might, with little trouble, be poisoned out of the way. But Ludovico feared the Spanish-born old King Ferdinand and Crown Prince Alfonso of Naples, who, not disliking cruelty and treachery when they served themselves, objected to poisoning a near relative for the advantage of a Lombard usurper. Naples, in turn, feared its suzerain Pope Alexander Borgia. All three watched Florence anxiously, for its midway territory might, by underhand backing, determine the game; and all four, with every small state, feared Venice—cautious, stable, strong—stretching arms along the Adriatic and dreaming of ports on the western coast.

Lorenzo de’ Medici, they said, had long kept such jealousies from outbreak, maintaining Florence’s alliance with Naples and the Pope while persuading Milan it was for general advantage. But young Piero’s rash vanity soon nullified his father’s wary policy, and Ludovico, roused to suspicion of a league against him, sought a move that would checkmate his adversaries: he would invite the French king into Italy to take Naples as heir of Anjou. Ambassadors—“orators,” in that haranguing time—went and came; a recusant cardinal, refusing to acknowledge a Pope elected by bribery and being Alexander’s enemy, went and came too and seconded the invitation with hot rhetoric; the young king listened willingly. Through 1493 the rumour grew louder: Charles the Eighth would cross the Alps with a mighty army. Italian populations, long accustomed since Italy ceased to be the heart of empire to look for an arbitrator from afar, began to regard his coming as a means of redressing wrongs and avenging grievances.

In that rumour Savonarola heard the proof of his prophecy. What filled the ears of the prophets of old, if not the distant tread of foreign armies coming to do justice? He no longer stared vaguely at the horizon: he pointed to the rising cloud. The French host was the new deluge to cleanse the earth of iniquity; Charles was God’s chosen instrument, as Cyrus had been. All who desired good rather than evil should rejoice. The scourge, he promised, would fall destructively on the impenitent alone. Let any city—Florence above all, Florence beloved of God, since to its ear the warning had been sent—repent and turn as Nineveh had done, and the storm-cloud would roll past, leaving only refreshing drops.

Fra Girolamo’s word had been mighty; yet now, with the new Cyrus three months already in Italy and not far from Florence’s gates, expectation was mixed, and fear and distrust predominated. It was not clear he had redressed anything. The Florentines had little to thank him for. He held their strong frontier fortresses, surrendered to him by Piero without honourable terms; he had not quelled the alarming revolt of Pisa, encouraged by his presence to throw off the Florentine yoke; and the orators—even with a prophet among them—could win no assurance beyond this: he would settle everything when he was within Florence’s walls.

Still, there was one satisfaction: Piero had been fairly pelted out for that ignominious surrender, and in the act the Republic’s spirit had tasted its old heat. Therefore the preparations for this guest were not merely those of a city resigned to submission. Behind the bright hangings and banners that proclaimed joy, another kind of readiness lay hidden, agreed upon by government and people as naturally as a household keeps flour and salt against hard weather. Within walls, well out of sight, hired soldiers had been hastily called in from the surrounding districts. Old arms were furbished; sharp tools and heavy cudgels were laid carefully at hand to be snatched up on a moment’s notice. Excellent boards and stakes waited to become barricades; stones were stored for an unexpected hail from upper windows. Above all, there was a temper in Florence—newly relishing the pleasure of resistance—that was eager to fight any personage who might try to hector over them.

That humour was not softened by the sight of occasional parties of Frenchmen arriving beforehand to choose their quarters—perhaps with a hawk on the left wrist, and, in the figure that ran through men’s talk, a piece of chalk in the right to mark Italian doors; and creditable historians imply that many sons of France carried, at that time, something approaching swagger, a seasoning sure to whet Florentine appetite for stone-throwing. Such was Florence on the morning of the seventeenth of November, while the city’s ears lived between two sounds—the festive murmur under drapery and the remembered iron bell—and while even in kitchens, where oil hissed quietly and bread was cut, men spoke in their own dialect of fate and foreigners, and found that no dominant, polished Latin could translate the taste of fear that lay, sharp as raw garlic, on the tongue.

The sky lay low and pewter-grey over Florence; yet in the Piazza del Duomo that sober weather was almost an afterthought, pushed back by man-made brightness. Blue draperies stretched like a second firmament between the stone fronts, and against that borrowed heaven the lilies blazed in yellow bunches, the coats of arms repeating themselves like stamped wafers on a feast-day loaf. At the angles of the Baptistery the sheaves of banners had already been loosened and let fall, their edges lifting and settling with each little gust as if breathing; but the Duomo steps were still bare—no carpet yet—only the chill, pale marble, dulled by the tread of many ordinary soles.

It was the hour of the Advent sermons. Those very reasons which had dressed the piazza in holiday color were reasons why the preaching within could least be spared; and still, not every foot turned toward the great doors. The piazza swelled and ebbed with men moving briskly as if errands had sprouted from the stones; and there were knots of idlers who did not idle—faces angled with vigilance, heads bent close in quick talk, ears pricked for the next scrap of report. Above it all, bells and voices made a restless canopy of sound: the distant call of a vendor under an archway, the clack of shoes on paving, the scrape of a cartwheel somewhere in a side street—each noise like a pebble tossed into the same troubled pool.

At the corner that looked toward the Via de’ Cerretani—where the piazza’s painted rainbow of festoons ended and the grey morning resumed its reign among the sombre houses—stood a dense cluster of working people. Their clothing wore the signatures of their trades: wool-dust ingrained in sleeves, grease-dark smears on aprons, the stiffened patches where dye had splashed and dried. Many carried weapons; others held tools that could become weapons with a mere change of intention. The feel of their bodies in that colder, unadorned street was like a different season intruding—bare brawny arms, soiled cloth, the metallic scent of iron and sweat.

They were listening to Ser Cioni, a thin notary whose voice had the bite of vinegar. Two years and a half ago the Mercato had answered him with laughter and contempt; now he spoke with the complacent edge of a man who finds his words landing where he meant them to.

“Never talk to me,” he was saying, “never talk to me of bloodthirsty Swiss or fierce French infantry. They might as well be in the narrow mountain passes as in our streets. Peasants have destroyed the finest armies of our condottieri, once they were caught between precipices. I tell you, Florentines need fear no army in their own streets.”

“That’s true, Ser Cioni,” answered a man whose arms and hands were stained crimson with dye so that, from a distance, they looked dipped in blood. A small hatchet sat in his belt like a promise. “Those French cavaliers came squaring themselves in their smart doublets the other day, and saw a sample of the dinner we could serve up for them. I was carrying my cloth in Ognissanti when I saw my fine Messeri go by, turning their noses as if the Vespucci and the Agli were poor lodgings, and eyeing us like top-knotted cocks that pity a hen for not strutting. ‘Yes, my fine Galli,’ says I, ‘stick out your stomachs—I’ve got a meat-axe that will go inside you all the easier.’ And presently the old cow lowed, and I knew something had happened—no matter what. I threw my cloth into the first doorway, took hold of my meat-axe, and ran after my cavaliers toward the Vigna Nuova. ‘What is it, Guccio?’ says I, when he came up. ‘I think it’s the Medici coming back,’ says he. Bembè! I expected so! We reared a barricade, and the Frenchmen looked behind and saw themselves in a trap; and up came a swarm of our Ciompi, and one with a great scythe mowed off a fine cavalier’s feather—it’s true! And the lasses peppered a few stones down to frighten them. But Piero de’ Medici wasn’t come after all. Pity, for we’d have left him neither legs nor wings to go away with.”

“Well spoken, Oddo,” said a young butcher, his knife at his belt and his voice smelling of slaughterhouse boldness. “My belief is Piero will be a good while before he wants to come back; he looked as frightened as a hunted chicken when we hustled and pelted him in the piazza. He’s a coward. We’ll swallow no Medici any more, whatever else the French king wants to make us swallow.”

“But I like not those French cannon they talk of,” put in Goro, none the less fat for two years’ added grievances. “San Giovanni defend us! If Messer Domeneddio means so well by us as your Frate says he does, Ser Cioni, why shouldn’t he have sent the French another way to Naples?”

“Ay, Goro,” said the dyer, with a laugh that was not quite merry, “that’s a question worth putting. Thou’rt not such a pumpkin-head as I took thee for. Why, they might have gone by Bologna, eh, Ser Cioni? Or if they’d gone to Arezzo—we’d not have minded their going to Arezzo.”

“Fools! It will be for the good and glory of Florence—” Ser Cioni began, but his sentence snapped short. Several voices broke out at once with, “Look there!” and faces swung toward a party advancing along the Via de’ Cerretani.

“It’s Lorenzo Tornabuoni,” someone said, “and one of the French noblemen who lodge in his house.”

Ser Cioni’s mouth tightened. “He pretends to look well satisfied—that deep Tornabuoni—but he’s a Medicean in his heart: mind that.”

The approaching group was brilliant, as if a strip of courtly tapestry had been unrolled into the street. Lorenzo Tornabuoni’s presence carried its own distinction; beside him the Frenchman glittered with displayed white linen and embroidery so lavish it seemed stitched from the spoils of altars. Two other Florentine gentlemen wore handsome dresses meant for the coming procession. And on the left hand of the Frenchman walked a figure who, for all his plainness, drew the eye as a dark wine draws it among pale watered drinks.

Tito Melema wore only black. Mourning made his elegance severer, like a well-forged blade left unadorned; presently the black would be covered with a red mantle, for he was to walk in procession as Latin Secretary to the Ten. He had grown conspicuously serviceable to the city’s new guests—his familiarity with Southern Italy, his readiness in French learned in boyhood, his visits to the camp at Signa. Good fortune gave him a lustre that was not merely in his clothes: it sat on his lips in a smile, in his voice as he listened and explained with that easy grace which seemed to promise agreement before it was asked for.

Yet if one watched him closely—closer than a casual glance that takes the surface polish—there was a change not to be measured by eighteen months. Something had withdrawn from him, something like the dew that vanishes as morning grows conscious of itself: the final departure of moral youthfulness, the distinct self-conscious adoption of a part. His eyes were still clear; the lines of his face still soft; but the light within had a different angle, as if it now shone through a chosen mask.

The Frenchman, eager to carry ceremonial knowledge back to Signa, wanted a final survey of the piazza where the royal procession would pause for religious observance. As they entered, gazes gathered like birds to scattered grain—yet not all were admiring. There were remarks, not especially hushed, about the Frenchman’s hoof-shaped shoes, those royal excesses of toe. There were snarls about “Mediceans,” and no one cared to tuck the sound away safely out of foreign hearing.

But Lorenzo Tornabuoni had the practiced art of swallowing annoyance without showing the throat move; and Tito, besides a natural knack for softening ill-will with good humor, carried the unimpassioned detachment of the alien. Florentine names and inherited hatreds did not strike him in the blood as they struck those born to them; their weight sat in his mind rather than his marrow.

They halted where the Duomo could be seen obliquely, the great dome looming like a patient animal under its grey sky. The festoons and devices over the central doorway drew a little demur from the Frenchman, and Tornabuoni beckoned to Piero di Cosimo, who, as usual at that hour, lounged before Nello’s shop with the air of a man who let the world happen for his amusement.

Piero came, and soon their talk grew animated. The Frenchman’s astonishment at Piero’s odd, pungent statements turned it into a comedy; and Tito, translating literally, became the hinge on which the laughter swung. Even those who had been snarling found their curiosity stronger than their sourness. Faces wore that half-smiling, half-humiliated look of people excluded from a joke that is plainly delicious. The piazza’s blue draperies and yellow lilies, the rainbow light they created, fell around the laughing group; and the grave church-goers had disappeared within the Duomo walls. For an instant it seemed the city had remembered how to keep a holiday.

But beyond the piazza’s bright cloth and contrived cheer, the unadorned streets remained in their grey temper; and from that greyness came on-comers whose purpose had nothing to do with brocade and processions. Here too the French dress and hoofed shoes were visible—yet now they were pressed upon by a swelling number of Florentines whose looks were not friendly.

In the van of the advancing tumult were three men in scanty clothing. Each had his hands bound together with cord; each had a rope fastened about his neck and body so that the French soldier holding the loose end could check rebellion with a jerking threat of throttling. The soldiers, by broken Italian and occasional strokes of the knotted cord, drove their prisoners to beg.

Two obeyed. At every passer-by they held out their bound hands and pleaded in thin, piteous tones, “For the love of God and the Holy Madonna, give us something toward our ransom! We are Tuscans: we were made prisoners in Lunigiana.”

But the third man remained silent beneath all blows. He did not look like the others. Those were young and hardy and, in the clothing their captors’ avarice had left them, resembled stout vulgar mendicants. This man had crossed into old age and could hardly be less than four or five and sixty. A beard had grown long and neglected; hair fell thick and straight around the bald crown, nearly white like ash left after a fire. His thick-set figure was still upright though emaciated, holding a stubborn dignity as if bone remembered strength even when flesh had thinned. In the midst of his yellow, bloodless, deeply wrinkled face, his dark eyes and strong dark eyebrows kept a strange isolated intensity—as if two embers had refused to go out. Yet the eyes were fitful: after a quick fierce sweep over windows and faces, they dropped into a lost wandering look. Still his lips did not move. He held his hands down. He would not beg.

Florentines who had first witnessed this had given money readily: some in half-automatic obedience to an appeal that used God’s name like a key to old locks; others through the unquestioning awe created by tales of French cruelty—the very awe the French counted on as insurance for their insolence. But the farther the group pushed toward the city’s heart, the less that compliance held. The soldiers found themselves escorted by a growing troop of men and boys whose chorus needed little translation.

“French dogs!” “Bullock-feet!” “Snatch their pikes!” “Cut the cords and make them run for their prisoners! They’ll run as fast as geese—don’t you see they’re web-footed?”

The soldiers understood enough: the tone, the laughter, the forward pressure. They began to dislike their position. Their hands wanted weapons, but their grip had to stay on the ropes. They hurried, seeking the shelter of an inn.

“Santiddio! here’s a sight!” cried the dyer, as soon as the meaning of the tumult struck him like a fist. “And the fools do nothing but hoot. Come along!” He snatched the axe from his belt and ran, the butcher and the others streaming after him—save only Goro, who slipped away up a narrow passage as if swallowed by stone.

The dyer did not strike anyone; he merely pushed forward beyond the soldiers and planted himself among his fellows, flourishing his axe. But in that act he became a symbol, like the lifting of a familiar gonfalon. The crowd’s noise tightened; bodies pressed nearer; the air grew sharp with human breath and anger.

Then the first flame of action leapt—quick as the flick of a kitchen fire catching on a shred of dry rosemary. It was Lollo, the conjuror’s impish lad, dancing and jeering at the front, a knife always ready at his side like a secret he loved. Compassion for the prisoners was not his motive; he simply felt the mischief in his fingers: to jump forward, cut a rope, and spring back before the soldier could strike—an amusing piece of dexterity.

Now, with the hooting and jostling rising, Lollo took his moment. He was close to the oldest prisoner. In an instant his knife flashed, the cord parted like a snapped string.

“Run, old one!” he piped into the prisoner’s ear, and he himself darted away as if winged, like a frightened fowl.

The old man did not hesitate. Escape had sat in his mind like hunger; and the crowd’s temper had fed it into hope. He ran at once. His speed alone would not have saved him, but the Florentines surged between him and his captor, a living wall of elbows and shoulders. He ran into the piazza, hearing behind him the tramp and scramble as the other two prisoners were freed too. The soldiers fought their way after them, slow-footed in their hoof-shaped shoes, impeded by bodies and blows—more hindered than truly attacked, for many preferred shouting invitations to courage rather than paying its cost.

One of the younger prisoners turned up the Borgo di San Lorenzo and drew off part of the hubbub like a diverted stream. But the main struggle rolled toward the piazza, and eyes swung round in alarmed curiosity. From the outside one could not guess the cause precisely; the French dress was screened by the mass of Florentines.

“An escape of prisoners,” said Lorenzo Tornabuoni as he and his party turned, standing just against the Duomo steps, and saw a prisoner rush past. “The people are not content with having emptied the Bargello the other day. If no other authority is in sight they will fall on the sbirri and secure freedom to thieves. Ah—there is a French soldier. That is more serious.”

He had glimpsed a soldier struggling along the north side of the piazza; but the object of pursuit had chosen another direction. The eldest prisoner, wheeling round the Baptistery, ran toward the Duomo. Whatever bitterness he held against men, he still trusted stones that had heard prayers for centuries. Sanctuary was surer than his legs.

He reached the steps and began to mount; but his foot struck a shock against the marble edge, and he pitched forward toward the group of signori, their backs turned. He recovered balance only by clutching at an arm.

It was Tito Melema who felt that clutch: soiled, worn fingers closing on velvet, a grasp that was not a petition but a claim.

Tito turned his head.

He saw the face of his adoptive father, Baldassarre Calvo, close to his own.

They looked at each other, silent as death. Baldassarre’s dark eyes burned with fierce recognition; his grip tightened on Tito’s sleeve as if he would haul out truth by force. Tito’s cheeks and lips went bloodless; terror held him in a fascination so complete it was like a spell. For them the piazza’s sounds fell away—the shouts, the bell-notes, the scrape of shoes—until there was only the roaring within the skull.

It seemed long. It was no more than a moment.

The first sound Tito truly heard was Piero di Cosimo’s short laugh, close at hand; Piero was the only one placed to see Tito’s face.

“Ha, ha! I know what a ghost should be now.”

“This is another escaped prisoner,” said Lorenzo Tornabuoni, leaning to look. “Who is he, I wonder?”

Tito’s mouth moved before his mind had finished deciding. In such instants passion speaks and chooses, and afterward one can only stand by and watch the deed as if it belonged to someone else.

“Some madman, surely,” Tito said.

The words, once out, seemed to carry their own poison. Tito felt, as he kept his eyes on Baldassarre, that something like a dart shot from those eyes into his veins. But the next instant Baldassarre’s grasp loosened. He did not cry out. He did not plead. He slipped away like a shadow drawn back into a doorway, and disappeared within the Duomo.

“You start at shadows easily,” Piero said again, and his laugh had the hard ring of steel struck against stone. “My portrait was poor—poor as a cook who can name every herb and yet cannot coax their breath into the pot. But the original—ah, the old fellow had the tiger in him. I must go into the Duomo and look at him again.”

“It is no pleasant thing,” Lorenzo Tornabuoni answered, smoothing his courtesy over Tito’s shaken look as one lays oil upon troubled water, “to be gripped by a madman—if madman he be. Yet perhaps he is only a ruffian. We shall hear. But we must see whether we have authority enough to stop this brawling between our people and your countrymen.” He turned that last to the Frenchman.

They went forward with their swords out; not in haste, but with that deliberate advance which makes a way through a crowd as a paddle cleaves a canal. The quiet onlookers, drawn by the scent of trouble as by the smell of roasting chestnuts at a corner brazier, closed in behind them, forming an escort. Tito went also. He could not do otherwise. Whatever Florence should know of this Baldassarre must be measured and tasted by him first, as a careful steward tastes wine before he lets it be poured for guests. And already the first palsy of terror—cold as wet linen clapped upon the skin—was giving place to quick devices, as timidity will run when danger snaps at its heels.

The rabble of men and boys, not so much bent on striking as on hooting and worrying the soldier—like sparrows tormenting a hawk they dare not face alone—fell back when the signori approached with naked swords. The French soldier was questioned. His story came out plain enough, though his tongue and theirs did not fit well together: he and his fellows had brought prisoners inside the walls to beg money for their ransom. Two were Tuscan soldiers taken in Lunigiana; the third was an elderly man caught with a party of Genoese, after French foragers had clashed with them near Fivizzano. The old one might be mad; he was harmless. The soldier knew nothing more, for he could not understand a word the elder said—those strange sounds, flung out with the urgency of hunger, were to him mere harsh wind in a foreign street.

Tito heard thus far; then all other speech became muffled, as if a hand had been pressed over his ears. He caught only the city’s common noises—the clack of a sandal, the thin crying of a boy selling figs, the harsh chorus of jeers—and through that, an inward sound louder than all: the beating of his own blood. He was roused only when one voice, distinct and near, addressed him.

It was Tornabuoni. “Will you come back with us, Melema? Or, since Messere is going off to Signa now, will you wisely follow the fashion of the times and go hear the Frate? He will be like the torrent at its height this morning—muddy, deafening, carrying everything with it. It’s what we must all do, you know, if we would save our Medicean skins. I should go myself if I had the leisure.”

Colour had returned to Tito’s cheeks—like warmth coaxed back into chilled fingers held near a kitchen fire—and he made an effort to answer lightly. “Of course I am among the admirers of the inspired orator,” he said, smiling; “but unfortunately I shall be occupied with the Segretario until the time of the procession.”

“I am going into the Duomo,” Piero said, with a boy’s persistence, “to look at that savage old man again.”

“Then have charity enough,” Tornabuoni replied, “to show him to one of the hospitals for travellers, Piero mio. The monks may find out whether he belongs in a cage.”

So they parted—words breaking apart like bread shared at a table, each man taking his portion and turning away. Tito went toward the Palazzo Vecchio, where Bartolommeo Scala awaited him.

The walk was short, yet for Tito it stretched and lengthened like the minutes in a morning dream, when a man thinks he moves and still the door will not be reached. Each patch of street and piazza held something that pricked him: memory of what he had done, foresight of what might be done to him, fear gnawing with small sharp teeth. It was as if a serpent had begun to coil around his limbs—not in a sudden strike, but in patient tightening, the kind that leaves no space to breathe.

Baldassarre living, and in Florence, was not merely an old man risen from a grave: he was revenge made flesh—a living thing that would not lie down and sleep, any more than a winding serpent rests until it has crushed its prey. Tito knew the temper of that man: love and hatred in him were not passing tastes, but burning appetites that subdued all else, like a fever that takes over the body and makes even water taste bitter. Such passion can turn a man into his own sacrificer, laying himself on the altar of the thing he worships—self-destruction offered up as devotion.

Baldassarre had slackened his grasp and vanished. Tito read that as clearly as a cook reads from the colour of an onion just how long it has sweated in oil: the vengeance was not abandoned; it was being studied so it might be sure. If he had not flung out those decisive words—“He is a madman”—if he had had the courage to acknowledge Baldassarre, would the risk have been less? He might have said he had received what he believed to be certain proof of Baldassarre’s death. And who could contradict him with certainty? Fra Luca was dead. The crew of the companion galley—those who had brought the news of the fight with pirates—were scattered shadows on the sea’s memory. What were the chances that Baldassarre had ever met again any man among them? Tito tasted bitterness at the thought that a timely, well-seasoned falsehood, devised in the right instant, might have saved him from fatal consequences.

Yet that falsehood would have demanded perfect self-command at the moment of shock. And he had not had it. The words had leaped from him without premeditation, like something born suddenly into the light after being begotten and nourished in darkness. Tito was meeting that inexorable law of souls: we school ourselves for sudden deeds by the repeated choice of good or evil, until character is formed as surely as dough is formed by kneading—each push and fold adding to the final texture.

There was now, as he saw it, only one chance: the chance that Baldassarre might fail. And then Tito’s mind, driven into cruelty by fear, clutched at a thought more active and more hateful than any he had allowed himself before. Might not his own unguarded words have some truth in them? Enough truth, at least, to shelter him—to let him deny whatever Baldassarre might say about him, and have others believe the denial? The old man had looked strange and wild. A heart and brain as eager as Baldassarre’s, long gnawed by suffering, might well have been pushed into madness. If so, then the vengeance that aimed at disgrace might be baffled by the world’s shrug and laughter.

But there was another vengeance—one that could not be baffled by wit, by phrasing, by any clever turning of a story as a spit is turned over the fire. Baldassarre belonged to a race to whom the dagger’s thrust seems as natural as a tiger’s outleap. Tito shuddered at disgrace—yes; but he carried also that physical dread which clings to a soft, pleasure-loving nature, and makes wounds and death not a release but an abomination. His mind flew at once, with a practical swiftness, to hidden defensive armour—something under his silk that might turn steel aside.

He wondered at the mastery of this fear, how it had seized him. It was like a blighting disease fallen in a night, turning the young joy of life into pain, so that even the air tasted different, as if the bread of existence had been baked with ash. And still, there remained one open resource: he might turn back, seek Baldassarre, confess all—confess to him, to Romola, to all the world.

But that thought did not truly enter him; it hovered and passed like the sound of a distant bell lost under nearer clamor. Repentance that breaks every mooring to evil asks for more than selfish fear. Tito had no sense that truth could be strength and safety; the only strength he trusted was the strength of his own ingenuity and dissimulation. Now that the first shock—which had betrayed him by the telltale signs of fear—had ebbed, he believed he could be ready for all emergencies with cool deceit, and with armour.

And it marked Tito’s nature at this crisis that no direct measure for ridding himself of Baldassarre occurred to him. Possibilities passed before him—lying, denial, flight even—yet never the thought of removing his enemy. His dread bred no active malignity; he would still have been glad to spare pain to any mortal. His life had been shaped by one continual choice: to make existence easy to himself, to carry his lot so it should pinch him nowhere—seeking always the softest cushion, the sweetest morsel, the quietest corner where harsh sounds could be kept at bay. That habitual choice had set him, more than once, in places he had never meant to enter.

Now the question was not whether he would share the common pressure of destiny with his suffering fellow-men. It was whether all the resources of lying—those words that slip between tongues and meanings, those convenient translations of the self into whatever dialect power requires—could save him from being crushed at last by the consequences of his own making.

When Baldassarre, his wrists knotted together so that the cords bit the old flesh, the rope looped about his neck and girding his body like a rough harness, shouldered his way behind the hanging curtain, the cool breath of the Duomo struck him—stone-chill, faintly damp, and steeped in that mingled scent of beeswax, tallow, and old incense which clings to a church as smoke clings to rafters. He had expected emptiness: a cavern of marble where the silence was dead and the images—pale saints, rigid limbs, dim panels—stood like lifeless tokens. He had expected, at most, a thin trickle of worshippers somewhere in the choir, their chant a monotonous humming as indifferent as a mill-wheel heard far off.

Instead, the nave was alive.

It was a sea of faces—warm with breath, shadowed with lashes, mouths held still as if the whole multitude had been commanded to keep the very air unmoving. The ranks were mixed as grain and chaff are mixed on a threshing-floor: magistrates with grave brows; women in rich hoods; artisans with hands that bore the stain of metal and dye; country folk whose coarse cloaks carried the honest smell of wet wool and field-earth. All were turned toward the same angle where nave and choir met, toward a pulpit that seemed, in that instant, the hearthstone of the whole city.

In it stood a Dominican, dark-haired, strong-featured, a crucifix caught in his hand as a cook catches up a knife—no ornament, but an instrument. His voice had been shaping words before Baldassarre saw him, but for the first minutes the old man heard only the blood in his own ears, the rush and crash of remembered things. His entrance, though he had tried to make it as noiseless as an animal slipping into a stall, drew a brief pricking of eyes. Near the doorway, a few heads turned; suspicion flared and then faltered. The rope told its own tale—escaped prisoner. Yet the church was sanctuary; and the grey hair, the hollow cheeks, the wild misery stamped on his face, took the edge from fear and left pity behind, like the softened scrape after a blunt blade is removed.

He stood pressed against the stone by the doorway, motionless, his gaze wandering down to the pavement as if the pattern of worn flags might give him counsel. Soon, as when a new sound in a forest is judged harmless and the birds go back to feeding, attention flowed away from him and returned to the stronger current—the sermon.

Among the eyes that had marked him were Romola’s. She had entered late by a side door and stood where the main entrance lay full in her view. Grey hairs drew her as surely as the smell of bread draws the hungry. There was something in her that answered to age’s sorrows—an instinct trained by a life of tending and being tended, by the daily knowledge that the old carry their pains as quietly as they carry their years. The rope round the stranger’s neck, the look of suffering that seemed not of today only but of a long yesteryear, moved her with a swift, domestic compassion, as if she had seen an elder at her own table sit down with an unspoken wound.

She fancied, when his eyes roved outward for a moment, that they met hers. But Baldassarre saw nothing distinctly—not her, not any single face. The cathedral, the multitude, the lifted pulpit were only a flash of scene, like a sudden opening in cloud, and then the fiercer inner storm closed again. Tito’s image—his smile, his very movements—kept thrusting itself upon him with the heat of fever, as though memory were a brand pressed against his mind. The future could not shape itself; he had only the bitter sense of his failing strength and a hardening resolve—no trust, nowhere.

Then the sound found him.

It was as if the great domed space had been a brazen vessel struck with a hammer, and the blow sent a vibration through his marrow. A voice, loud and full, rang out like thunder returned from stone to stone—so sure, so exultant in its own truth, that Baldassarre’s heart leaped to it as a parched mouth leaps at the thought of water.

“The day of vengeance is at hand!”

He quivered and lifted his head. He was too far to see more than the preacher’s general shape—arm outstretched, crucifix lifted; but he strained for the voice again, panting for it as one pants for the next draught.

A pause came. The friar’s arm lowered. He set the crucifix on the pulpit’s edge and crossed his arms upon his breast, looking over the multitude as if he would meet each gaze, as if his eyes would name every soul.

“All ye in Florence are my witnesses,” he said, and his words, though they carried, had a steadiness like a knife laid flat. “For I spoke not in a corner. Ye are my witnesses that four years ago, when there were yet no signs of war and tribulation, I preached the coming of the scourge. I lifted up my voice as a trumpet to the prelates and princes and people of Italy and said, The cup of your iniquity is full.”

The phrases came with the force of things flung down—vivid, weighty. He spoke of pleasant wine turned to molten lead; of priests who said there was no Presence in the sanctuary, and who thought they might sin behind the veil; of sacred garments becoming winding-sheets of flame. He painted music changed to shrieks and hissing, couches to thorns, the breath of wantons to pestilence. Even the air seemed to change with it, as if the cathedral’s hush became a listening skin. Sound here was not mere sound: it was atmosphere, the city’s shared breath held in a single chest.

“Trust not in your gold and silver,” he cried, “trust not in your high fortresses… though the walls were of iron… the Most High shall put terror into your hearts and weakness into your councils… He shall break in pieces mighty men without number, and put others in their stead.”

And then, with the same certainty that a man has when he names his own hands, he spoke of his mission—chosen, unworthy servant; the Scriptures alive in him; visions; angels. Not as one selling an art in the market, but as one possessed by something too urgent for barter.

“For four years I have preached,” he said, “three things… that in these times God will regenerate his Church, and that before the regeneration must come the scourge over all Italy, and that these things will come quickly.”

He turned on those who wanted morality without prophecy—virtue as a thin, tidy dish served without fire. He would not have it. God, he said, was not far off; judgment was not a dead parchment. Storm, fire, pestilence—armies—were ministers, driven by angels’ breath. And Italy, chosen land with sanctuary within her, had polluted it.

“Behold,” his voice rose, and the stones seemed to throw it back doubled, “the ministers of his wrath are upon thee—they are at thy very doors!”

At the height of passion he fell suddenly silent. His hands dropped and then clasped before him. Yet the silence did not loosen the crowd; it bound it. Through the vastness of the Duomo, faces stayed lifted, eyes fixed, bodies still—breathing statues, held by a spell made not of incense but of sound withheld.

Then, in low clear tones, he began again.

“Yet there is a pause… a stillness before the storm… the winds are stayed, that the voice of God’s warning may be heard. Hear it now, O Florence… Repent and forsake evil: do justice: love mercy… that the spirit of truth and holiness may fill your souls and breathe through all your streets and habitations…”

The word “breathe” seemed to pass through the building like a soft draught, and Romola, listening, felt it as one feels the difference between a courtyard where water trickles and birds answer, and a street where iron wheels grind and men shout for gain—one nourishes, one wears away. Here, the voice made a kind of acoustic shelter: no clatter of commerce, no huckster’s cry, no polished flatteries of art sold for applause—only the grave music of warning, and the answering hush.

“For the sword is hanging from the sky,” he cried now, and the hush itself seemed to sharpen. “It is quivering… The sword of God upon the earth, swift and sudden!”

He spoke of the French king at the gates; of horses, cannon wheels, the earth shaking; of a multitude that could shave the land bare. The foreign army, he said, was God’s sickle; the wicked would melt and be mown like stubble. He named tyrants and unbelieving priests who trafficked in souls, who made a throne out of the multitude’s vices, who brought fornication into the sanctuary. The punishment he promised was not a distant metaphor: it was heat, stench, burning—so tangible that one could almost taste bitter smoke at the back of the throat.

But then he turned, and the hardness became command and promise.

“Thou, O Florence, take the offered mercy. See! the Cross is held out to you: come and be healed. The tyrant is driven out… and no blood has been spilled. And now put away every other abomination… wash yourselves from the black pitch of your vices… put away the envy and hatred that have made your city as a nest of wolves.”

His words had the bite of lye on stained cloth, as if he would scrub the city clean down to its weave. He promised that armies might pass like a flight of birds, Pisa might be restored, famine and pestilence kept far from the gates—if Florence would not keep the accursed thing lying in the camp.

Then, in the next breath, his tone altered. Authority melted into entreaty; the harsh edge softened like a simmering broth turning mellow after long fire. His voice took on the yearning cadence of a mother calling children in from danger.

“Listen, O people, over whom my heart yearns… For you I toil, for you I languish… Take me, stretch me on thy cross… let the thorns press upon my brow… I desire to be made like thee in thy great love. But let me see the fruit of my travail—let this people be saved!”

He lifted his arms, his eyes to heaven. The great voice trembled, swelled, broke, rose again. He spoke of concord as of angelic song—voices rising together, not in the jangling contest of the streets but in one harmony, a sound-world where the spirit could live. He spoke of a witness remembered among men, of iniquity not prospering forever.

At last the passion overcame speech. He ended in a sob and fell on his knees, burying his face in his mantle.

The change rippled outward like a struck chord in a vast instrument. The audience, carried not only by belief but by deeper sympathies than theory, answered at once: a loud sob rose from the multitude, rolling under the dome as if the whole city had exhaled grief and longing in one breath.

In that great sob Baldassarre’s voice mingled.

No one there vibrated more strongly to the tones than he did; but it was as if all the strings of his inner harp had been wrenched away except one. Threat—vengeance—pursuit beyond death, an avenger holding the hated sinner in an eternal grapple: that alone rang clear to him. The wisdom he had once prized, the old contempt for priestly things, slipped from his soul like a tongue he had forgotten how to speak—lost words, dead sounds. Even had he remembered them, what could they answer to the thirst in him? The denunciation fell on his nerves with the force of self-evidence. He did not ask; he was seized, as a war-horse is seized by the clangor that promises battle.

No word that was not a threat reached him. The mercy, the cleansing, the call to love—these passed like wind over stone. But the fierce delight that vengeance might be endless rose higher when the preacher offered himself as victim. To Baldassarre, that offering meant only a dark triumph: that he too was giving himself—signing with his own blood—into an unending fire that would be coolness compared with his hatred’s burning.

“I rescued him—I cherished him,” the old thought surged in him with the bitter taste of betrayal, as if he were chewing ash. “If I might clutch his heart-strings for ever! Come, O blessed promise! Let my blood flow; let the fire consume me!”

He clenched his bound hands, driving his long nails into his palms until pain made its own sharp, clean note within the roar; and with the rest—under the same vast dome, in the same shared hush broken by one great human sound—he burst into a sob.

Outside the Duomo, while Baldassarre still trembled under Savonarola’s voice—as if that sound had entered him like strong wine—he had not marked the quiet opening of a door behind, nor the tread that made no haste. Another man had slipped in and stood a little aside, not to pray, not to be converted, but to look, as a painter looks, for a face that cannot be invented.

It was Piero di Cosimo.

The sermon had sunk into one of those pauses when a multitude ceases to be many bodies and becomes one breathing creature—here a stifled sob, there a throat clearing itself as if it could cough out terror; a soft rustle of sleeves, like dry leaves worrying each other. In that break of utterance, Piero moved forward, and with the sure touch of one who handled knives for pigments and canvases as easily as for bread, laid his hand on the escaped prisoner’s arm.

Baldassarre turned. Tears were still travelling down the furrows of his cheeks, slowly, as if the flesh were too worn to carry them faster; but his chest rose with a long, vigorous sigh, the sort that ends a storm and leaves a bitter stillness. Piero spoke low, so the sound of his words would not be stolen by listening piety.

“Shall I cut your cords for you? I have heard how you were made prisoner.”

Baldassarre did not answer at once. Suspicion sharpened his wet eyes. His gaze went over Piero’s face as if reading it in a dialect he had once known and half forgotten, looking for the trick of a familiar enemy in a stranger’s mouth.

At last he said, “If you will.”

“Better come outside,” Piero murmured.

Again the old man looked at him sidelong. Piero, guessing that this was a man to whom help always came with a hook in it, smiled a little, drew out a knife, and with a swift, clean motion severed the cords. The sound was small—just a faint creak of strained fibre giving way—but to Baldassarre it was like the first crack of ice under spring sun, the promise of movement.

Piero watched him fold his arms and flex his hands, taking a slow pleasure in the return of muscular sensation, as a starved man tastes bread crumb by crumb to be sure the mouth is still his. There was something in the old face—its fierce inward listening, its abrupt changes, as if some other voice were always speaking behind the visible one—that made Piero think, not without a shrug of pity, that talk of madness might not be mere excuse.

“Well,” he thought, “if he does mischief, they’ll tie him again. But the poor devil shall have a chance—at least.”

“You are afraid of me,” Baldassarre said, in the same undertone, not accusing so much as naming what he felt. “You don’t want to tell me anything about yourself.”

“No,” Baldassarre answered, and his tone had a quiet decision in it, like a door shutting without a slam. “I have nothing to tell.”

“As you please,” said Piero. “But perhaps you want shelter, and may not know how hospitable we Florentines are to visitors with torn doublets and empty stomachs. There’s an hospital for poor travellers outside all our gates; and if you liked, I could put you in the way to one. There’s no danger from your French soldier. He has been sent off.”

Baldassarre nodded—no thanks in the movement, but assent—and turned as if the offer were not kindness but information. Together they left the church.

Outside, Florence received them with her Sunday noises: the clustered murmurs under archways, the uneven beat of sandals on stone, a distant hammer where someone, impatient of salvation, had gone back to work; from a stall near the way, the sharp, friendly call of a vendor; and always, above and around, the great piazza’s reverberation—sound that did not die where it was born, but wandered, crossed itself, came back altered, as voices do in memory. Piero had the habit of hearing these things as part of a picture: a city’s sound was its underpainting, the ground on which colour must sit.

They went along the Via dell’ Oriuolo, toward the gate of Santa Croce. Piero walked at Baldassarre’s side, studying him with the same appetite with which he studied fish in a market—knowing that every surface held some truth about its hidden life.

“You wouldn’t like to sit to me for your portrait, should you?” he said suddenly, as if proposing a supper. “I am a painter. I would give you money to get your portrait.”

At that, Baldassarre’s suspicion returned with a sudden contraction of the brow, like a muscle remembering pain. He looked at Piero sharply.

“No,” he said, and the word was a blade.

“Ah!” Piero answered curtly, the sound clipping short. The refusal did not offend him as rudeness; it struck him as the refusal of a rare thing to be possessed. “Well, go straight on, and you’ll find the Porta Santa Croce, and outside it there’s an hospital for travellers. So—you’ll not accept any service from me?”

“I give you thanks for what you have done already,” Baldassarre said, and there was a stiff propriety in the phrase, as if he spoke it in a language learned for occasions of debt. “I need no more.”

“It is well,” said Piero, with a shrug that dismissed the business without dismissing the image. They parted—Baldassarre moving forward with the hard directness of a man led by something inward; Piero turning back, already tasting the thought of him.

“A mysterious old tiger!” the painter said to himself, as he went toward the Piazza del Duomo again. “Well worth painting. Ugly—with deep lines—looking as if the plough and the harrow had gone over his heart. A fine contrast to my bland and smiling Messer Greco—my Bacco trionfante—who has married the fair Antigone in contradiction to all history and fitness. Aha! his scholar’s blood curdled uncomfortably at the old fellow’s clutch!”

When Piero re-entered the piazza, the multitude who had listened to Fra Girolamo were pouring out from all the doors. Their haste to go each upon his own way showed how important they held the preaching that had detained them from the day’s other duties: the market to be visited, the cook to be scolded for stale oil, the oxen to be watered, the ledger to be balanced, the dough to be kneaded before it cooled and turned stubborn under the hands.

Piero leaned against an angle of the Baptistery and watched. The crowd unreeled like a long woven cloth, pattern after pattern passing the eye: the cut of a sleeve, the shine of a fur edging, the sober black lucco that made authority visible even when the voice was silent. Faces came by—keen, various, stamped with Florentine daylight—faces such as Masaccio had painted more than fifty years before, such as Domenico Ghirlandajo had not yet quite ceased to paint: the same city breeding the same bone and gaze, handing down its expressions like recipes, altered a little by each generation’s salt.

This morning was a peculiar occasion, and the Frate’s audience, always mixed, had represented even more completely than usual the classes and parties of Florence.

There were men of high birth, used to public charges at home and abroad, newly conspicuous as enemies of the Medici and friends of popular government, but also thorough Piagnoni, embracing to the utmost the Frate’s doctrines and practical teaching, frequenting San Marco as if another Samuel lived there. Some had an authoritative, handsome presence—Francesco Valori among them—hot in temper, made hotter by the comfort of thinking Heaven had signed their policies. Others—like Soderini—carried less of the ardent Piagnone and more of the prudent statesman, whose wisdom is not a flame but a slow fire that cooks without scorching.

There were men, too, of family like Piero Capponi, brave lovers of sober republican liberty, who preferred fighting to arguing, and had no special need to call any idea false if it kept out the Medici and made room for public spirit. At their elbows went doctors of law, their heads full of Accursius and the brethren, yet not so consumed by commentary that ardour had been boiled away: Messer Luca Corsini himself, who on a memorable day to come would lift his learned arms in street stone-throwing for religion, freedom, and the Frate.

And among the dignities carrying their black lucco or furred mantle with habitual authority, there was abundant sprinkling of faces more contemplative and sensitive—scholars inheriting names like Strozzi and Acciajoli, already minded to take the cowl and join San Marco; artists, too, wrought to a new and higher ambition by Savonarola’s teaching. One young painter, lately surpassing himself in a fresco of the divine child on the wall of the Frate’s bare cell, passed by with eyes still stained, as it were, with his own colours—unaware that one day he would wear the tonsure and cowl and be called Fra Bartolommeo.

There was the mystic poet Girolamo Benevieni, hurrying perhaps to carry tidings of the beloved Frate’s speedy coming to Pico della Mirandola, who was never to see the light of another morning. There were well-born women dressed with scrupulous plainness, whose finer grace remained the chief distinction between them and less aristocratic sisters. There were many of the genuine popolani—men of the Major and Minor Arts—conscious of purses threatened by war-taxes, their faces set as if they could already hear the coins clink away. And more striking and various than any other portion of the Frate’s disciples, there was the long stream of poorer tradesmen and artisans, whose faith and hope in his divine message ranged from the rough, undiscriminating trust in him as friend of the poor and enemy of luxurious oppressors, to that eager tasting of biblical subtlety which takes hold of the sedentary artisan: a pale flame lighting the long dim spaces beyond the board where he stitched, as if those far-off texts were broth for the mind, warming him through the cold of daily labour.

Yet among all these disciples were scattered many who were not disciples at all. Some were Mediceans who, out of fear and policy, had begun to show the presiding spirit of the popular party a feigned deference, like men who bow to a new master while counting the silver still hidden under the floor. Others were sincere advocates of free government, but regarded Savonarola simply as an ambitious monk—half sagacious, half fanatical—who had made himself a powerful instrument with the people, and must be taken as one takes weather: disliked, discussed, but endured.

There were even bitter enemies: members of the old aristocratic anti-Medicean party, determined to get the reins once more tight in the hands of certain chief families; and licentious young men who hated him as the killjoy of Florence, the man who would snuff out song and feast as if joy were a theft. The sermons in the Duomo had already become political incidents, drawing ears of curiosity and malice as well as faith. Men of ideas—young Niccolò Macchiavelli among them—came to observe and report to friends away in country villas; men of appetites, like Dolfo Spini, came to feed hatred and lie in wait for accusations, angry as hunters whose game is driven away by bells.

Perhaps no preacher ever had a more massive influence than Savonarola; perhaps no preacher ever had more heterogeneous material to work upon. One secret of that massive influence lay in the mixed character of his preaching itself. Baldassarre, wrought into an ecstasy of self-martyring revenge, was only an extreme case among the partial, narrow sympathies of the audience. In Savonarola’s preaching there were strains that appealed to the finest susceptibilities, and elements that gratified low egoism, tickled gossiping curiosity, and fascinated timorous superstition. His need of personal predominance, his labyrinth of allegorical interpretations, his enigmatic visions, his false certainty about divine intentions—these never ceased, within his large soul, to be ennobled by fervid piety, passionate sense of the infinite, active sympathy, and clear-sighted demand that selfish interests submit to the general good.

But for the mass, all the pregnancy of his words lay in the strong assertion of supernatural claims, in denunciatory visions, in the false certainty that made sermons like political bulletins; and once that audience had been mastered, it was necessary to his nature—and, as he believed, to their welfare—that he should keep the mastery. The effect was inevitable. No man struggles to retain power over a mixed multitude without suffering vitiation; his standard must be their lower needs rather than his own best insight.

As Piero stood listening now to the piazza’s ebbing roar—the cries thinning, footsteps scattering into side streets, the Duomo’s great doors swallowing the last reverberations—he watched not only faces but the way voices changed as people left the sacred vaulting and entered open air. In the church, sound had gathered, been held, made solemn by stone; outside, it broke apart, each man reclaiming his own tone, his own dialect, his own habitual inflection—some clipped and dominant, some soft with country vowels, some thick with the shop’s jargon. It was in these differences, untranslatable one into another, that Florence kept her memory; and it was also here that power worked, for the loudest lexicon always tried to rename what it did not own.

The mysteries of human character have seldom been presented in a way more fit to check the easy judgments of those who think they know, than in Girolamo Savonarola. Yet one may reverence him without closing eyes to fact, if one regards his life as a drama with great inward modifications answering to outward change. Up to this period, when his more direct action on political affairs had only just begun, it is likely that his imperious need of ascendancy had burned undiscernibly within the strong flame of his zeal for God and man.

It was the fashion of old, when an ox was led out for sacrifice to Jupiter, to chalk the dark spots and give the offering a false show of unblemished whiteness. Let the chalk be flung away. Boldly say: the victim is spotted; yet it is not therefore in vain that his mighty heart is laid on the altar of men’s highest hopes.

By six of the evening Florence had begun to breathe again, as a cook breathes when the oven-door is shut at last and the long roast is safely in the dark heat. The entry of the new Charlemagne—so the flatterers named him—was fairly over; and those who had been stationed high on turreted roofs, where the city’s stone ribs rose into air, had had their fill of magnificence. From that height the procession had uncoiled along the Pisan road like a bright, dangerous river laid upon the valley’s green; drums had rolled as steadily as pestles in a mortar, trumpets had blared, and the tramp of horses had beaten the earth in thick, impatient measures. The bells, caught in the same fervour, flung their excited peals across the roofs until every narrow street seemed to ring like metal struck too often.

There was no obliging sunlight to turn banners into flame or plumes into spun gold. Yet the very lack of glitter made the thing more distinct—no veil of dust rose to soften edges—and when the picked troops came close they showed their several nations as plainly as different grains in one sack. Tall, tough Scotch archers; Swiss halberdiers, heavy and grim as if carved from mountain stone; nimble Gascons ready to wheel, to climb, to spring; cavalry wherein each rider looked like an errant knight with spear set and charger champing. It was a comfort—comfort being the word the prudent always seek—to repeat to oneself that such strength would injure nobody but the enemies of God.

With that assurance the eye could take its pleasure in the rest: nobles and knights and pages of chosen lineage; sword-hilts bossed and jewelled; satin scarfs embroidered with devices that pretended at once to piety and love; gold chains lying on brocade as fat as poured honey; jewelled aigrettes trembling above brows; horse-trappings stiff with gold thread; mantles that seemed to have drunk whole vats of dye. And over the head of the Most Christian King a canopy, borne by select youths, rose and swayed—its embroidery and pearls catching the lamplight of the day as a glazed tart catches firelight. To sum it with an old diarist whose spelling lagged behind his wonder: it was great magnificence.

For the Signoria, standing on their platform against the gates, grandeur had come mixed with the taste of bitterness. Their orator, Messer Luca Corsini, had had his Latin welcome marshalled and rehearsed like a recipe memorised to the syllable; but when rain began—cold, sour rain that slicked plumes and set horses stamping—his well-studied periods broke off and ran together like ink in wet parchment. Men and beasts grew impatient; the press of bodies jostled dignities out of their places; and the learned city, shamed out of its own language, was forced into a makeshift welcome in hurried French.

In that sudden confusion Tito Melema found the sort of moment he could use. As one of the secretaries he stood behind the Signoria among officials, those lesser personages who are flung together like trimmings when a great dish is served and all hands crowd the table. “Somebody step forward and say a few words in French,” Soderini said, his temper clipped short by the rain.

No one of high importance wished to risk a second stumble.

“You, Francesco Gaddi—you can speak.” But Gaddi, mistrusting his own readiness, shrank back. He thrust Tito forward instead, as one pushes a nimble boy toward a task when the older man fears his own hands. “You, Melema.”

Tito stepped forward in an instant, with that air of profound deference which came as naturally to him as walking. He spoke the few needful words in the name of the Signoria—no more, no less, as neatly portioned as a careful cook’s pinch of salt—and then, with the grace of one who never seems to hurry though the world hurries him, he gave way and let the king pass on.

His presence of mind, which had failed him in the terrible crisis of the morning, served him this time like a well-trained livery servant—faithful enough when danger was not visible. When men complimented him afterwards on the service, he laughed it off as nothing; and to those who had not witnessed it he let Gaddi have the credit. Tito was popular for the same reason sweetmeats are popular: they flatter the palate. The touchstone by which men try us is most often their own vanity.

Other things, too, had turned out worse than the ingenious preconceptions. The Florentine procession of clergy and laity, that had been meant to meet the king in orderly splendour, found its way choked and was driven to a makeshift course through back streets, so that the encounter could happen only at the Cathedral. And if the young monarch under the canopy, seated on his charger with his lance along his thigh, had looked more like a Charlemagne and less like a hastily modelled grotesque, the imagination of his admirers would have been better served. One might have wished that the scourge of Italian wickedness and “Champion of the honour of women” had had a less miserable leg, and only the common sum of toes; that his mouth had been less reptilian in its width of slit; his nose and head less exorbitant in outline. But the thin leg rested on cloth of gold and pearls; the face was only a brief interruption—some inches of flesh—amid black velvet and gold and the blaze of rubies and the brilliant tints of the embroidered, bepearled canopy. Great magnificence still.

The people had cried Francia, Francia, with an enthusiasm measured by the canopy’s splendour; and, according to immemorial custom, they tore that same canopy to pieces for spoil as greedily as children tear sugared bread, each eager for his own sweet fragment. Royal lips had kissed the altar as due. At last, after mishaps, the royal person and retinue were lodged in the palace of the Via Larga; the rest of the nobles and gentry were dispersed among Florence’s great houses; and the terrible soldiery were encamped in the Prato and other open quarters. The business of the day was ended.

But the streets, under the November stars, had an aspect Florentines scarcely knew. Instead of the usual gloom—broken only by a feeble lamp here and there before a saint’s image at a corner, or a redder stream of light from an open doorway—lamps hung in the windows of all houses. Light lay along the stones so that men walked as securely as by day. Yet light did not quiet the city’s ear. Under that illumination every sound declared itself: footfalls were crisp; distant laughter rose and sank; the murmur of talk drifted out of doorways; and, threaded through it all, the persistent after-ringing of bells seemed to live in the bones of the houses. There are nights when a city’s noises nourish the spirit, like hearth-crackles and a spoon against a bowl; and there are nights when the same noises, multiplied by excitement, become a kind of coarse grinding that leaves the mind raw. Florence had the second sort of music now: splendour lay on the surface, but the soundscape was bruised by power.

Along those illuminated streets, at about eight, Tito Melema walked homeward. He had been exerting himself throughout the day under the pressure of anxieties kept hidden like a knife in one’s sleeve; and at last he had slipped away unnoticed from after-supper gaiety. Now, with leisure to face his circumstances, he hoped to adjust himself to them and to probabilities until he could rid himself of what he called childish fear.

If only he had not been wanting in the presence of mind necessary to recognise Baldassarre in that morning’s surprise—if only he had been able to meet the apparition with a steadier face—it would have been happier for him on all accounts. For he still winced under the thought that he was deliberately inflicting suffering on his father; in his easier, more pleasant imaginings he would have preferred Baldassarre prosperous and content, like an old vine that has done its bearing and is allowed to rest. But he had left himself no second path now. There could be no longer any conflict. The one thing to do was to take care of himself.

He was advancing from the Piazza di Santa Croce along the Via dei Benci, his mind half full of calculations that had no taste or scent—mere dry measures—when, nearing the angle that turned into the Borgo Santa Croce, his ear was struck by music that was not evening revelry but vigorous labour: the music of an anvil.

The hammer’s rhythm cut cleanly through the city’s other sounds, as if it insisted on an older law than bells and trumpets. Tito gave a slight start and quickened his pace. The sounds had suggested a welcome thought. He knew them. They came from the workshop of Niccolò Caparra, famous resort of Florentines who cared for curious and beautiful iron-work. What made the giant at work so late? But so much the better; Tito could do that small bit of business tonight instead of tomorrow morning.

Preoccupied though he was, he could not help pausing a moment as he came before the shop. The wide doorway stood at the truncated angle of a great block of houses, surmounted by a little loggia roofed with fluted tiles and supported by stone columns with roughly carved capitals. Within, the red light—thick, hot, like the glow seen through the slit of a bread-oven—framed the black relief of Niccolò himself. The smith’s grand figure rose and fell in rhythmic labour; his huge arms lifted, descended; and each time the hammer fell it seemed to drive not only the metal but the night’s very din into order. Two slighter ebony figures—one at the anvil, one at the bellows—set off Niccolò’s massiveness as thin herbs set off a joint of meat.

Tito darkened the doorway with a very different outline, standing silent, for it was useless to speak until Niccolò should deign to pause. That was not until the smith had beaten the head of an axe to its due sharpness and dismissed it from the anvil. In the meantime Tito, with a glance round, satisfied himself that the object he sought had not disappeared.

Niccolò turned, rested his hammer on his hip, and gave an unceremonious but good-humoured nod. “What is it, Messer Tito? Business?”

“Assuredly, Niccolò; else I should not have ventured to interrupt you when you are working out of hours, since I take that as a sign that your work is pressing.”

“I’ve been at the same work all day—making axes and spear-heads,” Niccolò said, and the words came out with the bluntness of struck iron. “And every fool that has passed my shop has put his pumpkin-head in to say, ‘Niccolò, wilt thou not come and see the King of France and his soldiers?’ and I’ve answered, ‘No: I don’t want to see their faces—I want to see their backs.’”

“Are you making arms for the citizens, then, Niccolò, that they may have something better than rusty scythes and spits in case of an uproar?”

“We shall see. Arms are good, and Florence is likely to want them. The Frate tells us we shall get Pisa again, and I hold with the Frate; but I should be glad to know how the promise is to be fulfilled if we don’t get plenty of good weapons forged? The Frate sees a long way before him; that I believe. But he doesn’t see birds caught with winking at them, as some of our people try to make out. He sees sense, and not nonsense.” Niccolò’s bellows-man worked the handle with a steady creak between phrases, like an accompaniment. “But you’re a bit of a Medicean, Messer Tito Melema. Ebbene! so I’ve been myself in my time, before the cask began to run sour. What’s your business?”

“Simply to know the price of that fine coat of mail I saw hanging up here the other day. I want to buy it for a certain personage who needs a protection of that sort under his doublet.”

“Let him come and buy it himself, then,” Niccolò said, blunt as ever. “I’m rather nice about what I sell, and whom I sell to. I like to know who’s my customer.”

“I know your scruples, Niccolò. But that is only defensive armour: it can hurt nobody.”

“True: but it may make the man who wears it feel himself all the safer if he should want to hurt somebody. No, no; it’s not my own work; but it’s fine work of Maso of Brescia. I should be loth for it to cover the heart of a scoundrel. I must know who is to wear it.”

Tito saw there was no kneading this man into a softer shape. “Well, then, to be plain with you, Niccolò mio, I want it myself,” he said. “The fact is, I am likely to have a journey to take—and you know what journeying is in these times. You don’t suspect me of treason against the Republic?”

“No, I know no harm of you,” Niccolò answered, with the same blunt fairness. “But have you the money to pay for the coat? For you’ve passed my shop often enough to know my sign: you’ve seen the burning account-books. I trust nobody. The price is twenty florins, and that’s because it’s second-hand. You’re not likely to have so much money with you. Let it be till to-morrow.”

“I happen to have the money,” Tito said. He had been winning at play the day before, and his purse was still heavy. “I’ll carry the armour home with me.”

Niccolò reached down the finely wrought coat. It fell together into little more than two handfuls, supple as a net drawn up from water, each ring catching a brief spark from the forge-light. Tito felt, even through his gloves, the faint chill of metal that had been hanging away from the fire: a coldness like night caught in iron.

“There, then,” Niccolò said, when the florins had been told down on his palm. “Take the coat. It’s made to cheat sword, or poniard, or arrow. But, for my part, I would never put such a thing on. It’s like carrying fear about with one.”

The words struck Tito with an unpleasant exactness. Fear—named aloud—seemed suddenly louder than the anvil’s beat, as if the city’s whole clamour had condensed into that one syllable.
