But he smiled, and his smile had the practiced ease of one who seasons bitterness with a little sweetness so others will swallow it.

“Ah, Niccolò, we scholars are all cowards. Handling the pen doesn’t thicken the arm as your hammer-wielding does. Addio!”

He folded the armour under his mantle and went quickly out again, crossing the Ponte Rubaconte while the lamps burned above the street and the night’s noises—bells remembered, feet, distant cries, the far-off clink of weapons being made—followed him like a second garment.

Tito had crossed the Ponte Rubaconte with his newest purchase hidden beneath his mantle, the metal hugging his ribs like a second, colder flesh. The Arno below ran thick and whispering, carrying the day’s uproar away in broken ripples; but the bridge stones still held the trampling echoes of hoof and boot, and the air tasted of wet leather, trodden rose-leaves, and the faint sourness that follows a crowd.

At home, Romola paced the old library with the unwearied step of one who has learned to move in a narrow world and yet keep it from stifling her. The shelves, the tables, the ink-horns and pens—all those familiar instruments of her father’s life—stood about her like silent witnesses. She had refused the day’s spectacle. Almost every window in Florence had flowered with faces to watch the French king and his nobles, but Romola’s face had not been among them. Since her father’s death, the very notion of festivity felt like a dish set before an empty chair.

He had died three months ago—swiftly, in the way sudden endings sometimes come to those who have long imagined their own slow decline. Even now she could taste the hour again as one tastes something bitter that will not be washed away by sweetness.

The bell had sounded long past the accustomed evening, and Bardo’s head, bent in his chair, had lifted with a listening impatience that Romola knew too well.

“Is not Tito coming to write?” he had said, as if he were naming a necessity of nature, like bread at table.

“No, father; he had to go to a supper at the cardinal’s,” Romola answered, turning excuse into gentleness as women will, as if softness could make up for absence. “You know he is wanted so much by every one.”

“Ah! then perhaps he will bring some positive word about the library,” Bardo said, catching at hope the way an old man catches at warmth. “The cardinal promised last week.”

She had watched his face settle—pacified, for a moment, by that thin promise. Then, after silence, a sudden flush had risen, the blood protesting against resignation.

“I must go on without him, Romola. Get the pen. He has brought me no new text to comment on; but I must say what I want to say about the New Platonists. I shall die and nothing will have been done. Make haste, my Romola.”

She had risen at once—docile, trained by years to spring at the sound of that need—and in the next minute stood ready, pen poised, the ink smelling sharp and alive.

“I am ready, father.”

But the room had fallen into a stillness that was not one of his pauses for thought. She had waited, accustomed to those long gaps where his mind wandered and returned with a phrase that had been ripened in silence. She had not looked up at once.

When she did, the posture had not changed; only life had gone out of it. She had spoken again—too late—“I am quite ready, father!” and that second readiness had been answered by the unanswering.

In the first violence of grief there had come, like a stealthy sweetness in a draught one meant to drink only for medicine, a thought that shamed her: Perhaps my life with Tito will be more perfect now. She had remembered it afterwards with a sting of indignation against herself, as if she had found in her own heart a foreign coin, bright and false.

For the dream she had carried—of three lives fitted together without friction, father and husband and herself as one happiness—had never come to full fruition. The shower of bridal sweets had dropped thorns among the sugared almonds. The crowned Ariadne under the snowing roses had felt more and more the hidden pricks in the garland.

And still, she told herself, it was not Tito’s fault. He had been gentle; he had never ceased to be gentle. Even to her father he had been all smiles and soft answers, laying phrases as deftly as a cook lays herbs over bitterness so that a man may swallow what he would otherwise reject. Yet the daily weight of Bardo’s demands—monotonous, exacting, unrelenting as hunger—could not be borne by any one but herself, month after month, year after year. She could see that now with the clear sight that comes when a burden is finally set down. She alone had the patience that sprang from blood and reverence and long habit; even she had sometimes been inwardly rebellious, her spirit cramped like a limb held too long in one posture.

Before their marriage, and even for some time after, Tito had seemed unwearying, more ready than she; but novelty is a sauce that sharpens appetite, and we lift loads readily when we believe ourselves strong. Pressure grows irksome by degrees, until the desire for relief becomes like thirst.

Romola told herself she had been foolish in girlhood, ignorant in the way of marriage. She would not make unfair demands on the man to whom she had given her deepest love and worship. If sadness had breathed on their lot while she watched her father sink, month after month, from elation into disappointment as Tito gave him less time and more excuses—if she had felt a lonely heartache when Tito’s share in the joint work dwindled to bland refusals—that sadness, she insisted, was destiny’s doing, not Tito’s. If he stayed away, it was because they were never alone; if he went to other engagements when her timid pleading might have kept him, he excused himself with such charming gaiety, and lingered with such fond playfulness that her complaint dissolved even while it rose. The heartache remained, but it was swallowed as women swallow the bitter edge of reality for love’s sake.

Her imagination worked incessantly to reconcile what she felt with what she believed. How could Tito be as good as she had thought him, and yet find it impossible to sacrifice those pleasures that society offers—pleasures more vivid to a bright creature like him than to graver natures? She herself, had she been free, would have liked more gaiety, more admiration; but she had given that up for her father, and she would have given up much more at Tito’s lightest wish. Perhaps their difference was only the old difference between man and woman: her affection absorbed her wholly, while his overflowed into the world. If there were inferiority, she insisted it must be hers. Tito was kinder than she, better-tempered, less proud; he had no angry retorts. He met complaints with sweetness and evaded unpleasantness as quietly as a cat slips from a noisy courtyard.

And Romola—large-natured enough to distrust herself—doubted her own impressions the more because love and pride both demanded a story she could live with. Disappointment—there was no softer word that told the truth—might be the common portion of wives; she did not know their hearts. Yet her case had its own sharpness: her father’s claims had asked unusual sacrifice from her husband, and Tito’s love had not been great enough to make it easy. She would not resent a self-delusion. Better any endurance than the admission, even to herself, that Tito acted unworthily. To cease to love would be to stand on the edge of a world that breaks away beneath one’s feet.

And now her father was gone. Even in the first moments when his chair stood empty, hope had crept in: there would be no more importunate claim dividing her from Tito. Their young lives would flow in one current; the true marriage would begin.

But guilt shadowed that hope. It made her clutch with the more fervour at the one thing she could still do for her father: fulfil his supreme wish. Piety to his memory would be her atonement for the joy that had dared to rise from his death.

Bardo’s life had been like a long seed-time without harvest: laborious, simple, untainted by vulgar ambitions, embittered by frustrated hopes, ending in darkness. What remained of it—besides the tablet in Santa Croce and an unfinished commentary begun on Tito’s text—was the collection he had scraped together with half a century’s frugality: manuscripts, coins, antique fragments, the very bones and organs of dead thought. To Romola, the fulfilment of his ambition about the library was no mere duty; it was sacramental, like keeping a lamp burning by a grave.

The collection was safe from creditors. When the deficit had been ascertained, Bernardo del Nero—no rich man by Florentine standards, yet generous in his old-fashioned way—had advanced the sum, accepting the lien as security.

“The State will repay me,” he had said, making light of a service that cost him inconvenience. “If the cardinal finds a building, as he seems to say he will, our Signoria may consent to do the rest. I have no children; I can afford the risk.”

But in the last ten days hope in the Medici had gone out like a candle in a draught. Even the famed Medicean treasures in the Via Larga were in danger of being scattered. French agents, sniffing through Florence as men sniff through a pantry, had begun to say—boldly, with that smooth greed that calls itself right—that Lorenzo’s antique gems belonged by nature to the first nation in Europe. And the Florentine State, with war for Pisa hanging like a hungry mouth and subsidies to the French king sure as taxes, might well prefer coin to manuscripts. Money was the only language some councils listened to, and it was a loud one.

Romola had been reared in learned seclusion, where the past was more vivid than the present. She could weigh the Pnyx and the Forum in her mind, and find them nobler than the councils of living Florentines. Public affairs had been, for her, faint and distant like drums heard across fields. Yet now the expulsion of the Medici meant, above all else, the extinction of her best hope for Bardo’s library. The uneasy times, the suspicion among shopkeepers and rabble, the danger for Medicean friends like her godfather and Tito—these she noted, but like a woman hearing of storms at sea while she is thinking of bread in the oven. Her new sharp attention to wars, visits, changes, was kindled solely by love and duty to her father’s memory.

Her ardour had always poured itself into affection. The learned pursuits she shared with Bardo had been toil borne for his sake, not nourishment sought for her own hunger. Tito’s brilliance delighted her only because it was his, because it flashed out of the face she loved. The larger possibilities of her nature lay folded like wings that had never been tried; sometimes they made a vague ache, nothing more.

But this personal stake in public events made her want at last to understand Fra Girolamo’s influence—this preaching that was drawing Florence as a fisherman draws with a strong line. Tito, as secretary and useful talent, moved in the heart of business, yet what he told her only made her long to hear the voice that commanded the city’s attention, to learn for herself what promise or threat the monk offered concerning the French.

That morning, for the first time, she had gone to an Advent sermon in the Duomo.

When Tito left her, she had resolved suddenly; she went first to Santa Croce and stood where her father lay, as one stands before a hearth where the fire has gone out and yet the smell of smoke lingers in the stones. Then she walked on to the Duomo. The earlier memory of Dino—of his words and his presence—was still there in her as a half-healed mark, but it had been covered by the daily wear of marriage, quieted by the subjection that comes to a wife who loves with full reliance. She expected Savonarola’s voice might move her in spite of his narrow monkishness, because she remembered the power it had had before.

The sermon deepened rather than altered her impression: this preacher of tribulations, fanatical though he seemed, was still a man she might revere. His denunciations and exhortations held her attention; they did not pierce her with terror or remorse. It was like distant thunder—grand, rolling, shaking the air but not the earth beneath her feet.

Yet when he invoked martyrdom, she sobbed with the rest. A new sensation passed through her—a strange sympathy with something that lay outside the definable interests of her life. It was like the thrill stirred by rare heroic touches in history and poetry; and yet the difference was like that between recalling music and being seized by living harmonies vibrating through bone and breath. Still, that emotion seemed to fall outside the inner sanctuary of her existence. It did not rearrange her loyalties; it only left a lingering echo, as a great bell leaves the ear full after the sound has ceased.

Now, in the library, she was not thinking of Fra Girolamo. She listened for Tito’s step with the anxious patience of one who has counted too many hours by absence.

Through these three months of double solitude she had thought of each day as an epoch in which their union might at last become more complete. She knew she had sometimes been too sad, too urgent about her father’s memory—too critical, or too coldly silent, when Tito narrated the talk and bustle of his world—too hasty in suggesting they should live as simply as Bardo had done, to scrape together enough to repay Bernardo and ease the difficulties about the library. She saw that she asked much: Tito could not feel as she felt; it was hard to ask him to relinquish the luxuries he laboured to obtain.

Next time he came home, she would suppress every prompting that isolated her from him. She laboured, as loving women do, to shape herself to the beloved. She strangled each rising impulse of suspicion, pride, resentment, with a desperate resolution; she felt equal to any self-infliction that would save her from ceasing to love. The thought of not loving was like a nightmare in which the world breaks away all round, leaving one’s feet over darkness.

She waited long. Tito had not come straight home after leaving Niccolò Caparra. The hours thickened; the city’s noises altered—shouts fading into scattered calls, then into the steady domestic sounds of doors barred, pots set down, water poured, the distant bark of a dog. Florence had its own acoustic climate, shifting with the day like wind over grain. When at last, more than two hours after the time she had imagined him crossing the bridge, she heard the great door of the court turn on its hinges, the sound went through her like a hand on the heart.

She hurried to the head of the stone steps. A lamp hung there, and its steady flame made the stairwell smell of oil and warmed dust. They saw each other clearly as he ascended.

Eighteen months had written more change on Romola’s face than on Tito’s. Her expression was subdued now, less cold, more beseeching; and as a pink flush spread over her cheeks with the sudden joy of his return, she looked lovelier than on the first day he had seen her. Then, any on-looker would have said Romola was born to command and Tito to bend; now her mouth trembled slightly and there was timidity in her gaze.

He made an effort to smile when she spoke.

“My Tito, you are tired; it has been a fatiguing day: is it not true?”

Maso was near; nothing more was said until they had crossed the antechamber and closed the library door behind them. The wood burned bright on the great dogs, giving out a scent of resin and smoke that should have promised comfort. Romola’s gentle voice was another welcome. She took off his mantle; he turned and kissed her—briefly—and then went to the high-backed chair set near the fire, flung himself down, tossed away his cap, and said, not peevishly but with a weary remonstrance, and a slight shudder as if cold had reached him beneath his clothes—

“Romola, I wish you would give up sitting in this library. Surely our own rooms are pleasanter in this chill weather.”

The words hurt her with their indifference. She had never seen him so unlike himself; he was usually all lively attention. She had built up his return in her mind through the long waiting, as one builds up a dish in hope—measuring, imagining the savour—and now the first taste was flat.

He must be very weary, she told herself quickly, hunting for excuses in his face as if bodily fatigue could translate moral chill into mere weakness.

“I wonder you have forgotten, Tito,” she said, gently, yet with anxiety. “You know I am making the catalogue on the new plan that my father wished for; you have not time to help me, so I must work at it closely.”

Instead of meeting her glance, Tito closed his eyes and rubbed his hands over his face and hair, as if he would wipe off something clinging. He knew he was behaving unlike himself; he promised himself amends to-morrow. But the day had raised again, like something long buried and suddenly breaking the crust, his secret fears—fears which, if Romola knew them, would estrange her for ever. Feeling already in danger from her mind, he felt an alienation already begun between them, and with it a repulsion he had not chosen. He was vexed with himself, yet could not summon warmth on command; he could only offer an excuse.

“I am not well, Romola; you must not be surprised if I am peevish.”

“Ah, you have had so much to tire you to-day,” Romola said, and knelt close beside him. She laid her arm across his chest and pushed his hair back with a caress, as she might smooth down a child’s hair after fright. The fire made the metal dogs glow red at the edges; the crackle of resinous wood rose and fell like breathing.

Then, under her forearm, she felt something hard, unyielding—no bone, no belt buckle—something that gave no warmth back. She started, drew her arm away, and looked at him with alarm.

“What have you got under your tunic, Tito? Something as hard as iron.”

“It is iron—it is chain-armour,” he said at once. He had been prepared for the discovery and spoke quietly, as of a thing not to be hurriedly explained.

“There was some unexpected danger to-day, then?” Romola said, seeking a reasonable cause. “You had it lent to you for the procession?”

“No; it is my own. I shall be obliged to wear it constantly, for some time.”

“What is it that threatens you, my Tito?” Her voice rose with terror, and she clung to him again, as if her arms could ward off knives.

“Every one is threatened in these times, who is not a rabid enemy of the Medici. Don’t look distressed, my Romola—this armour will make me safe against covert attacks.” He put his hand on her neck and smiled, and for a moment the habit of kindness flowed back, as warm broth returns to the lips after a draught of cold water.

“But my godfather, then,” Romola said, fear rushing outward to all she loved, “is not he, too, in danger? And he takes no precautions—ought he not? since he must surely be in more danger than you, who have so little influence compared with him.”

“It is just because I am less important that I am in more danger,” Tito answered readily. “I am suspected constantly of being an envoy. Men like Messer Bernardo are protected by their position and extensive family connections, which spread among all parties; while I am a Greek that nobody would avenge.”

“But, Tito—is it a fear of some particular person, or only a vague sense of danger, that has made you think of wearing this?” She could not keep down the thought that this might be something meaner than prudence; her anxiety had an undertaste of shame, as if she feared to find cowardice in the man she worshipped.

“I have had special threats,” Tito said. “But I must beg you to be silent on the subject, my Romola. I shall consider that you have broken my confidence, if you mention it to your godfather.”

“Assuredly I will not mention it,” she said quickly, blushing at having seemed to question him. Then, after a pause, her love found words that were almost a lament. “But, dearest Tito—it will make you very wretched.”

“What will make me wretched?” His face changed almost imperceptibly, as if a small dart had touched him.

“This fear—this heavy armour.” She shuddered, feeling the chill of it under her palm. “I can’t help shuddering as I feel it under my arm. I could fancy it a story of enchantment—that some malignant fiend had changed your sensitive human skin into a hard shell. It seems so unlike my bright, light-hearted Tito.”

“Then you would rather have your husband exposed to danger, when he leaves you?” Tito said, smiling, turning her tenderness into a playful challenge. “If you don’t mind my being poniarded or shot, why need I mind? I will give up the armour—shall I?”

“No, Tito, no. I am fanciful. Do not heed what I have said.” She shook her head, ashamed of her imagination. “But such crimes are surely not common in Florence? I have always heard my father and godfather say so. Have they become frequent lately?”

“It is not unlikely they will become frequent,” Tito said, “with the bitter hatreds that are being bred continually.”

She fell silent. The chain under his tunic seemed to have made a sound in her mind, like a muffled clink that would not cease. She shrank from insisting further, as if pressing the subject might press also on some hidden sore in him. She tried to shake it off, to pour warmth back into the moment.

“Tell me what has happened to-day,” she said, forcing cheerfulness as one stirs honey into a draught. “Has all gone off well?”

“Excellently well,” Tito answered. “First of all, the rain came and put an end to Luca Corsini’s oration, which nobody wanted to hear; and a ready-tongued personage—some say it was Gaddi, some say it was Melema, but really it was done so quickly no one knows who it was—had the honour of giving the Cristianissimo the briefest possible welcome in bad French.”

“Tito, it was you, I know,” Romola said, brightening at once, and kissed him. “How is it you never care about claiming anything? And after that?”

“Oh! after that, there was a shower of armour and jewels and trappings, such as you saw at the last Florentine giostra, only a great deal more of them. There was strutting, and prancing, and confusion, and scrambling; and the people shouted, and the Cristianissimo smiled from ear to ear. After that there was a great deal of flattery, and eating, and play. I was at Tornabuoni’s. I will tell you about it to-morrow.”

The mention of eating and play brought with it, for Romola, not a lively curiosity but a faint sense of distance. She thought of tables spread, spices crushed under knife, capons turning, wine poured into bright cups—rich smells rising, laughter mingling with music—while in this house the fire was more often for warmth than for feasting, and her own days had been filled with ink and lists and the dry dust of parchment. Yet she checked the thought at once; she would not let it sour her voice.

“Yes, dearest, never mind now.” She leaned closer, searching his face. “But is there any more hope that things will end peaceably for Florence—that the Republic will not get into fresh troubles?”

Tito shrugged. “Florence will have no peace but what it pays well for; that is clear.”

Her face clouded, and she felt again how all these great matters touched her chiefly through one narrow point: the library, the debt, the chance of keeping her father’s treasure from dispersal. She forced herself back into lightness.

“You would not guess where I went to-day, Tito. I went to the Duomo, to hear Fra Girolamo.”

Tito looked startled. For an instant his mind leapt—like a rat darting in a wall—to that earlier terror of his own, the thought of a face in the crowd, of a man he feared; and the sound of the Duomo’s vast interior seemed to strike him again—the roar of voices, the hollow swell of chanting, the echoing footfalls under the dome.

Romola read his look differently.

“You are surprised, are you not? It was a sudden thought. I want to know all about the public affairs now, and I determined to hear for myself what the Frate promised the people about this French invasion.”

“Well,” Tito said, recovering himself, and taking up playfulness like a shield, “and what did you think of the prophet?”

“He certainly has a very mysterious power, that man,” Romola answered. “A great deal of his sermon was what I expected; but once I was strangely moved—I sobbed with the rest.”

“Take care, Romola,” Tito said lightly, relieved that her words had not gone where his fear had darted. “You have a touch of fanaticism in you. I shall have you seeing visions, like your brother.”

“No; it was the same with every one else,” she said. “He carried them all with him—unless it were that gross Dolfo Spini, whom I saw there making grimaces.” She paused, then added, the picture coming back with the vividness of something odd in the midst of solemnity. “There was even a wretched-looking man, with a rope round his neck—an escaped prisoner, I should think, who had run in for shelter—a very wild-eyed old man: I saw him with great tears rolling down his cheeks, as he looked and listened quite eagerly.”

A slight silence fell, as if the fire had suddenly sunk. Tito’s face altered again—so small a change that a stranger might not have noticed, but Romola felt it in the air between them, as one feels a draft in a room.

“I saw the man,” Tito said at last. “The prisoner. I was outside the Duomo with Lorenzo Tornabuoni when he ran in. He had escaped from a French soldier. Did you see him when you came out?”

“No,” Romola answered. “He went out with our good old Piero di Cosimo. I saw Piero come in and cut off his rope, and take him out of the church.” Her eyes returned anxiously to Tito. “But you want rest, Tito? You feel ill?”

“Yes,” Tito said, rising.

And as he rose, the chain-armour moved beneath his tunic with the faintest rustle, like dry leaves underfoot—a sound Romola scarcely heard, but he did. To him it was the perpetual reminder that he must live in continual dread: not only of knives in the street, but of what that wild-eyed old man might have said or done, somewhere in Florence, where every whisper found an echo.

Four days later Romola went along the Via Gualfonda toward the dwelling of Piero di Cosimo. The way thither lay through streets that had begun to feel like a narrow throat in which two breaths struggled for mastery. Here were French soldiers, planted in knots, staring as if Florence were a curious dish set before them—tasting it with their eyes, judging its temper; and here were Florentines, pausing with folded arms, letting their own glances answer back like the rasp of a file. The air had that strained, metallic clearness that comes before a storm; and underneath it ran the city’s sound—footfalls on broad flags, the clink of a spur against stone, the blunt thud of a staff, the burr of many voices gathered into a continual murmur that made the ear tired. Even the bells, when they spoke, seemed to do it with a kind of wary reserve, as if the old bronze throats knew there were foreign ears listening.

At first Florence had played the host with all the lavish cunning of a great house that understands ceremony as it understands bread—something that must be kneaded and offered at the right moment, fragrant, warm, flattering to appetite. There had been compliments, and feasts, and those Mysteries in the churches where clouds and angels were hoisted and made to float as if Heaven had been hired by the day. There had been balls, and suppers, and the Most Christian guest had scattered his attention among Florentine dames with a practised gaze, as though desire itself were a coin to be spent. But when the sweetmeats of festivity were cleared away and the talk became a talk of business and power, it appeared the new Charlemagne meant to eat Florence as one eats a conquered city—entering with lance in rest, speaking of leaving a viceroy behind, letting fall that he might bring back the Medici.

To Florentine minds, this tasted like sour wine poured into a cup that had been offered in good faith. Piero de’ Medici’s policy, disowned by the people, had been the only offence Florence had committed against France; yet the remedy proposed was the return of that very house. The logic of an “elect instrument of God” was singular. And Florence, whose pride was as sensitive as a palate trained on fine oil and clean wheat, was resolved not to submit. The resolve was being beaten out in consultations within the Old Palace; and outside, on the piazzas and in the streets, it began to show itself whenever a chance offered for some small flouting of a Frenchman too insolent in his air of conscious pre-eminence.

In such a temper of the city, the streets were no pleasant promenade for well-born women; but Romola, shrouded in black veil and mantle, with old Maso at her side, moved with a guarded security. If the world’s looks slid over her, the world’s sounds did not: she heard the sharpened accents, the quick laughs that were half a challenge, the sudden hush when a knot of men saw her pass. Yet her impatience drew her onward. She was going to Piero di Cosimo.

The copy of her father’s portrait as Oedipus—her father blind, yet still a presence, still a face that must not fade—was not finished. Piero was capricious in his work: now pushing forward with a feverish zeal, now leaving a painting for months as if it were a loaf forgotten in the oven’s mouth until it hardened past comfort. He might thrust a panel into a corner or coffer where it could lie like a buried bone, utterly unremembered. Romola was a favourite with him; he would bend to her wishes when they were before his eyes. But a general good-will was no safeguard against the sudden whim that made him turn away and let the world drift.

He had said a week before that perhaps the picture would be finished by now. Romola clung to that “perhaps” with nervous hunger. It seemed to her that if she did not get the image into her keeping, the lines of her father’s face—those lines the darkness had deepened, that listening look she remembered—might grow dim in her mind. And with this desire there was a sharpness of compunction: a sense of defect in her devotedness, a craving to be loyal not merely in deeds but in memory. Love, she felt, asks for completeness; it cannot bear a gap, even if the gap be only in the heart’s picture.

By special favour, Romola might intrude on the painter without warning. She lifted the iron slide and called “Piero!” in a flute-like tone—the tone of that little maiden who had brought eggs when Tito was present. The answer came quickly, and when the door opened, Piero’s quickness explained itself in a way that made Romola laugh.

“Ah, Madonna Romola—is it you? I thought my eggs were come; I wanted them.”

“I have brought you something better than hard eggs, Piero. Maso has got a little basket full of cakes and confetti for you,” she said, smiling as she drew back her veil. She took the basket from Maso, uncovered it, and stepped within. “I know you like these things when they come to you without trouble. Confess you do.”

“Yes—when they come to me as easily as the light does,” said Piero, folding his arms and looking down at the white and amber sweets, the crisp little cakes dusted like flour, the sugared seeds that crack between the teeth and send up a faint breath of fennel and anise. He lifted his eyes to her face and hair with the painter’s frank delight; her hood, dragged backward by the weight of her veil, had fallen so that the light touched her as it touched fresh bread—revealing.

“And they are come along with the light now,” he added. Then, with a suspicious narrowing of the eyelids, “But I know what the sweetmeats are for. They are to stop my mouth while you scold me.”

“Well—go on into the next room,” he continued, already turning, “and you will see I have done something to the picture since you saw it, though it’s not finished yet. But I didn’t promise, you know. I take care not to promise:—

“‘Chi promette e non mantiene
L’anima sua non va mai bene.’”

The door that opened on the wild garden was closed now, shutting out the rough green and the freer air. Within, the painter had been at work. Yet not at Romola’s portrait. That stood on the floor propped against the wall. Piero stooped to lift it, peering at some detail as he took it in his hands to carry it to better light.

And in lifting it away he disclosed another picture behind it—an oil-sketch of Tito, smaller, set far within the larger panel like a secret within a secret. Piero, careless of where he left things and now intent only on placing Romola’s portrait on the easel, did not at first know what he had shown.

But Romola, catching the face in a flash, stopped as if a hand had seized her.

“That is Tito!”

Piero looked round and gave a silent shrug—the shrug of a man vexed with his own forgetfulness. Romola’s astonishment held her silent for an instant; then, as her eyes took in the whole—Tito’s handsome head, and with it the grim figure beside him, the noose-like rope, the crouched misery of the other face—she felt a puzzled alarm rise like bitterness at the back of the tongue.

“What a strange picture!” she said. “When did you paint it? What does it mean?”

“A mere fancy of mine,” Piero answered, lifting off his skull-cap, scratching his head, and making the familiar grimace with which he pushed away any chance of betraying feeling. “I wanted a handsome young face for it, and your husband’s was just the thing.”

He stepped forward, stooped, and lifted the sketch with its back toward her, pretending to glance at it as if it were a thing not worth attention before putting it aside. But Romola had already fixed on what pierced her—the rope, the old savage face—and behind it surged the remembrance of chain-armour, that cold, secret protection Tito had taken on the very morning in question. The painter’s image joined itself to her own fear, and the joining made a sharp, unmistakable sound in her mind, like two stones struck together.

“Don’t put it away,” she said quickly, going to his elbow. “Let me look again. That man with the rope round his neck—I saw him. I saw you come to him in the Duomo. What was it that made you put him into a picture with Tito?”

Piero’s eyes shifted; he saw no better shelter than a portion of truth.

“It was a mere accident,” he said. “The man was running away—running up the steps, and caught hold of your husband. I suppose he had stumbled. I happened to be there and saw it, and I thought the savage-looking old fellow was a good subject. But it’s worth nothing—it’s only a freakish daub of mine.”

He ended with an affected contempt, moving the sketch away decisively and setting it on a high shelf, as if to thrust it out of sight and mind alike. “Come and look at the Oedipus.”

Yet the very haste with which he hid the picture gave it weight. Romola felt it as one feels a coarse grain under fine cloth: the effort to smooth it only makes the roughness more certain. It seemed to say there was something unpleasant—something that told against Tito—in the circumstances out of which the sketch had grown.

But her pride and delicacy drew back. To press questions might seem to confess that she could harbour suspicion against her husband. Her voice, when it came, was quiet, held in as if she feared its own tremor might betray her.

“He was a strange, piteous-looking man, that prisoner. Do you know anything more of him?”

“No more,” said Piero. “I showed him the way to the hospital—that’s all. See now—the face of Oedipus is pretty nearly finished. Tell me what you think of it.”

Romola turned and gave her whole attention to her father’s portrait. The room smelt of oil and pigments, of damp wood, of the stale edge of eggs that had been broken and beaten for tempera in hard times; but the basket of cakes and confetti had begun to shed its own delicate fragrance—almond and sugar, a faint hint of citrus peel—softening the harsher odours, as kindness softens harsh speech. She stood long before the painted face, letting her eyes travel slowly over the brow, the lids, the mouth that had learned to hold itself in patience. The world’s noises seemed to sink away, and she heard instead the remembered sound of her father’s voice, the particular cadence of his Greek, the old words that had made a home within her even when his sight was gone. The portrait did not give her the language—no painting could restore that untranslatable music—but it gave her the listening look: the head inclined as if toward some inward utterance the eyes could never read.

“Ah,” she said at last, softly, “you have done what I wanted. You have given it more of the listening look.” She turned to Piero with bright moist eyes. “My good Piero, I am very grateful to you.”

“Now that’s what I can’t bear in you women,” Piero burst out, turning impatiently and kicking aside the litter on the floor—broken sticks, rags stiff with colour, a brush that had dried to a blunt tail. “You are always pouring out feelings where there’s no call for them. Why should you be grateful to me for a picture you pay me for, especially when I make you wait for it? And if I paint a picture, I suppose it’s for my own pleasure and credit to paint it well, eh? Are you to thank a man for not being a rogue or a noodle? It’s enough if he himself thanks Messer Domeneddio, who has made him neither the one nor the other. But women think walls are held together with honey.”

“You crusty Piero! I forgot how snappish you are,” Romola said, smiling through her tears. She reached into the basket and took out a crisp sweet—one that would crack cleanly and melt into syrup on the tongue. “Here—put this nice sweetmeat in your mouth.”

Piero accepted it with the surly gratefulness of a creature that prefers its pleasures hidden. His mouth worked, and the sugar softened him in spite of himself; his fingers went back into the basket for another with the inevitableness of appetite after long restraint. He had eaten nothing but hard eggs for a fortnight, and these cakes, light as if the flour had been sifted through air itself, seemed to him a festival.

“It’s good, Madonna Antigone,” he said, with his mouth full, letting the old playful name fall as naturally as a crumb.

Romola stood opposite him, and for a little while the new anxiety in her breast was suspended by the sight of this naïve enjoyment—by the simple truth that hunger, answered honestly, makes a brief peace. The city’s harsh murmur and the hidden sketch, the foreign gaze and the rope about the prisoner’s neck, all receded before the homely fact of a man eating.

“Good-bye, Piero,” she said at last, setting down the basket. “I promise not to thank you if you finish the portrait soon and well. I will tell you you were bound to do it for your own credit.”

“Good,” Piero answered curtly. He helped her with deft hands to fold the mantle and veil about her, as if dressing a figure for a picture. When he had closed the door behind her, he stood a moment with the sweetness still on his tongue, and thought, not without relief: “I’m glad she asked no more questions about that sketch. I should be sorry for her to guess that I thought her fine husband a good model for a coward. But I made light of it; she’ll not think of it again.”

He was too sanguine, as open-hearted men are apt to be when they attempt a little simulation. For the thought of the picture pressed more and more on Romola as she walked homeward. Outside, the street’s sounds met her again—the tramp of boots, the scrape of a chair dragged in some tavern, the sharp call of a vendor threading between groups, the French speech striking her ear with its alien consonants like stones in a loaf. The city’s acoustic life, once a familiar net that held her, felt torn and knotted; even the echo beneath an archway seemed to have changed, as if the very stone were learning a new language against its will.

She could not help putting together two facts: the chain-armour, and the encounter Piero had described between Tito and the prisoner—an encounter on the morning when the armour was adopted. The painter had given Tito a look of terror. Had he seen it—seen something true and caught it, as painters sometimes catch what words cannot hold? What could it all mean?

“It means nothing,” she tried to assure herself. “It was a mere coincidence.” Yet the assurance tasted thin, like watered wine. “Shall I ask Tito about it?”

Her mind answered at last, sternly: No. She would not question him about anything he had not told her spontaneously. It would be an offence against the trust she owed him.

Her heart answered, more faintly, as if speaking in a dialect she dared not let anyone else hear: I dare not ask him.

There was a terrible flaw in the trust. She felt herself afraid of any hasty movement, as men are who hold something precious and want to believe it is not broken—lest a single touch should make the crack widen, and the thing fall into irreparable fragments with a sound that all the city could hear.

“The old fellow has vanished,” Piero di Cosimo was saying, his voice rasping like a knife drawn over a palette. “Went on towards Arezzo the next morning. Not liking the smell of the French, I suppose, after being their prisoner. I went to the hospital to ask after him—I wanted to know if those broth-making monks had found out whether he was in his right mind. They said he showed no signs of madness—only took no notice of questions, and seemed to be planting a vine twenty miles off. A mysterious old tiger. I should have liked to know more of him.”

It was the twenty-fourth of November, a week since the French had come in, and they were gathered in Nello’s bottega at the odd hour when honest hunger begins to argue with the clock. The shop held its usual mingling of scents: warm soap and strop-leather; pomade with a faint note of crushed rosemary; the close human smell of woollen cloaks damped by fog; and, from some alley vendor outside, the teasing drift of roasted chestnuts whose split skins gave off a sweet smoke that made even politics feel like something one could chew and swallow.

Nello himself, half perched on the board against the shop-window, had been thrumming his lute with two fingers, letting the notes fall into the room as if to keep the air from turning too sharp with talk. Now and then he glanced out toward the piazza, reading the city by its sounds—the scrape of sandals pausing, the impatient clack of a cartwheel that could not get through, the sudden hush that runs like a ripple when men stop speaking to listen for news.

At last he laid the lute down with a thump. “Ah,” he said, and his relish for spectacle made his moustaches lift, “I would not for a gold florin have missed that sight of French soldiers waddling in their broad shoes after their runaway prisoners. And it happened when I’d gone to shave magnificent chins. Always so. If ever I quit this navel of the earth, the piazza takes the opportunity of birthing a marvel.”

“Yes,” Piero said, with the sour pleasure of a man who enjoys pricking a bubble, “you ought to have been there—just to see your favourite Greek look as frightened as if Satanasso had laid hold of him. I like to see your ready-smiling messeri caught in a sudden wind and made to show their lining. What colour do you think a man’s liver is, who looks like a bleached deer the moment a chance stranger grips him?”

“Nay, Piero—keep that vinegar for thine own eggs,” Nello flung back. “What is it against my bel erudito that he started when he felt claws on him and saw an unchained madman at his elbow? Your scholar is not like those beastly Swiss and Germans whose heads are fit for battering-rams, and whose appetites are so large they’d swallow a cannon-ball before breakfast. We Florentines count other qualities in a man besides that vulgar stuff called bravery, which you can buy by the dozen in the market.”

In the inner room a voice called out, half laughing, half warning. “Treason, Nello! That is not the doctrine of the State. Florence is grinding its weapons; and the last well-authenticated vision announced by the Frate was Mars standing on the Palazzo Vecchio with his arm on San Giovanni Battista’s shoulder, and San Giovanni offering him a piece of honeycomb.”

“It is well, Francesco,” Nello answered, as if he were setting a capon to roast and had no fear it would burn. “Florence has a few thicker skulls to bombard Pisa with. There will still be finer spirits left at home to do the thinking and the shaving. And as for our Piero here—if he makes such a point of valour, let him carry his biggest brush for a weapon and his palette for a shield, and challenge the widest-mouthed Swiss in the Prato to single combat.”

“Va,” growled Piero. His face, cut into strange lines by old scars, made an expression that never quite confessed what lay behind it. He drew tow from his scarsella and stuffed his ears, as if to cork out nonsense. “Thy tongue runs on like a mill when the Arno’s full—whether there’s grist or not.”

“Excellent grist,” Nello insisted, enjoying his own seasoning. “For it would be as reasonable to expect a grizzled painter like thee to be fond of getting a javelin inside thee as to expect a man whose wits have been sharpened on the classics to like having his handsome face clawed by a wild beast.”

“There you go,” Piero said, and even with his ears stopped he found words enough, “supposing you’ll get people to put their legs into a sack because you call it a pair of hosen. Who said anything about a wild beast? Fighting is a trade, and it’s not my trade. I should be a fool to run after danger—but I could face it if it came to me.”

“How is it you’re so afraid of thunder, then?” Nello pursued, like a cook who will not leave a pot untasted. “You hide with the rats as soon as the storm comes on.”

“That is because I have a particular sensibility to loud sounds,” Piero snapped. “It has nothing to do with courage or conscience.”

“Well then,” said Nello, throwing out his hands as if scattering flour, “Tito Melema may have a particular sensibility to being seized unexpectedly by prisoners escaped from French soldiers. Men are born with antipathies. I myself can’t abide the smell of mint. Tito was born with an antipathy to old prisoners who stumble and clutch. Ecco!”

The laugh went round the little company as naturally as bread passed at table. Plainly Piero’s bitterness toward Tito was not the taste of the room. Piero, muttering, pressed the tow deeper and glowered as if the air itself had offended him; and Nello, triumphant, went on:

“No, my Piero, I can’t afford to have my bel erudito decried; and Florence can’t afford it either, with her scholars moulting off at forty. Our Phoenix Pico gone straight to Paradise, as the Frate has told us; and incomparable Poliziano, not two months since, gone to—well, well. Let us hope he is not gone to eminent scholars in the Malebolge.”

“By the way,” said Francesco Cei, who liked a jest even when the city was on edge, “have you heard that Camilla Rucellai has outdone the Frate in prophecy? She prophesied two years ago that Pico would die in the time of lilies. He has died in November. ‘Not at all the time of lilies,’ said the scorners. ‘Go to!’ says Camilla; ‘it is the lilies of France I meant, and they seem close enough under your nostrils.’ Euge, Camilla! If the Frate can prove any one of his visions as well fulfilled, I’ll be a Piagnone to-morrow.”

“You are too flippant about the Frate, Francesco,” said Pietro Cennini, who spoke as carefully as if weighing spices, mindful that too much ruins the dish. “We are all indebted to him in these weeks for preaching peace and quietness, the laying aside of party quarrels. Men of small discernment would be glad to see the people slip the Frate’s leash now. And if the Most Christian King is obstinate to-day, and will not sign what is fair and honourable to Florence, Fra Girolamo is the man we must trust to bring him to reason.”

“You speak truth, Messer Pietro,” said Nello. “The Frate is one of the firmest nails Florence has to hang on—at least so say the most respectable chins I have the honour of shaving. But young Messer Niccolò was saying here the other morning—and doubtless Francesco means the same—there is a wonderful power of stretching the meaning of visions, like Dido’s bull’s hide. A dream may mean whatever comes after it. Franco Sacchetti tells how a woman dreams of a serpent biting her, breaks a cup next day, and cries, ‘Look you, I knew something would happen—it’s plain what the serpent meant.’”

“But the Frate’s visions are not of that sort,” said Cronaca, with the obstinacy of a man who has listened until the very sound of certain words has become his refuge. “He not only says what will happen—the Church scourged and renovated, the heathens converted—he says it shall happen quickly. He is no slippery pretender—he is—”

“What is this? what is this?” Nello broke in, springing off the board as if the piazza had plucked him by the sleeve. He thrust his head out at the door. “People are streaming in and shouting. Something’s happened in the Via Larga. Aha!”

He was out on the threshold, cap waving, laughter bursting from him; and the others crowded behind, drawn by that great Florentine appetite for news, which is like appetite for food—the more a man has had, the sharper his hunger becomes.

The piazza had been full of that lazy sprinkling of artisans who pause and drift like bits of wood on a river, ready to whirl into a current. Now it thickened, and the sound thickened with it: voices layering, feet scuffing, the distant clatter of a shutter flung open, and, above all, a kind of jubilant roar that rolled and recoiled from stone to stone. Yet the thing that came into the piazza was not a herald with a trumpet, nor a mounted messenger, but a man carried aloft on a bench snatched from somewhere, as if the crowd had seized the nearest furniture to make a throne.

Tito Melema sat there, borne above shoulders, smiling in amused surrender to the compulsion. His cap had slipped and now hung by the becchetto loosely wound about his neck. Seeing the group at Nello’s door, he lifted his fingers in a beckoning recognition. The next moment he had leaped from the bench onto a cart piled with bales, standing in the broad space between the Baptistery and the Duomo steps, while the people swarmed about him with the noisy eagerness of poultry waiting for grain.

But when he began to speak, his clear mellow voice cut through the tumult; and the piazza, trained by sermons and proclamations, fell into a silence that had its own music—only a far-off hammer tap, only the faint hiss of breath between teeth, only the city’s great stone listening.

“Citizens of Florence!” Tito said. “I have no warrant to tell the news except your will. But the news is good, and will harm no man in the telling. The Most Christian King is signing a treaty honourable to Florence. But you owe it to one of your citizens—one who spoke a word worthy of the ancient Romans—you owe it to Piero Capponi!”

At once the silence broke into a roar, as if a wine-skin had burst.

“Capponi! Capponi! What said our Piero?”
“Ah! he wouldn’t stand being sent from Herod to Pilate!”
“We knew Piero!”
“Orsù! Tell us—what did he say?”

When the cries abated enough to let sense through, Tito lifted his hand, and began again.

“The Most Christian King demanded a little too much—was obstinate—said at last, ‘I shall order my trumpets to sound.’ Then, Florentine citizens, your Piero Capponi, speaking with the voice of a free city, said, ‘If you sound your trumpets, we will ring our bells!’ He snatched the copy of the dishonouring conditions from the secretary’s hands, tore it in pieces, and turned to leave the royal presence.”

Shouts surged up again, and impatience, that other Florentine condiment, demanded more.

“Then, Florentines,” Tito continued, “the high majesty of France felt, perhaps for the first time, all the majesty of a free city. The Most Christian King himself hastened from his place to call Piero Capponi back. The great spirit of your city did its work by a great word, without need of the great actions that lay ready behind it. The King has consented to sign the treaty which preserves the honour, as well as the safety, of Florence. The banner of France will float over every Florentine galley in sign of amity and common privilege—but above that banner will be written the word Liberty!

“That is all the news I have to tell; is it not enough?—since it is for the glory of every one of you, citizens of Florence, that you have a fellow-citizen who knows how to speak your will.”

The sound that answered him was like the sea driven into a narrow bay. Tito looked round, inwardly amused, at faces flushed with the thought that Capponi had spoken for each of them, that the mouth had somehow been the mouthpiece of their own unshaped desires. He enjoyed the irony that had, in an instant, made him—an alien, and known friend to the Medici—into an orator pleasing ears that cried for a good they could not have defined except in that one treasured word: liberty. He was glad, in his light way, that he had been laid hold of and hurried along when he came out of the palace in the Via Larga with a commission to the Signoria. It was easy—pleasant—this art of speaking to general satisfaction. A man who knew how to persuade need not fear any party; he could convince each that he was only feigning with the others. From above, the gestures of weavers and dyers looked comical, like birds pecking in a yard, each certain he would get the first grain.

He was beginning to feel at ease in his armour, and did not know it. One hand held his recovered cap; the other rested at his belt. His long lustrous eyes held the light of complacency as he made a parting reverence before springing down from the bales.

Then, suddenly, his glance struck and caught on a face that did not share the crowd’s harvest-look. A man stood there clean-shaven, hair close-clipped, wearing a decent felt hat like any poor citizen who has kept a shred of order in his dress. Another eye might have passed him by; a single glance could hardly have sworn him to be the escaped prisoner who had clutched Tito on the steps. But to Tito it was not merely that—this face was one he had known long years before.

In a second, everything was compressed: the sight of Baldassarre looking at him; the sensation shooting through him like a fiery arrow; the act of leaping from the cart. He would have sprung down at that instant whether he had seen Baldassarre or not—he was in haste to reach the Palazzo Vecchio—but now haste had another taste, metallic and bitter on the tongue. Yet he did not betray himself by look or movement; inwardly he told himself he would not be surprised again. He must be prepared to see this face rising up continually, like that intermittent blotch that comes in diseased vision and spoils whatever else you look at.

But Baldassarre’s reappearance—so much closer to his own old likeness now that beard and rags were gone—tightened dread as a cord tightens when the knot is pulled. Madness seemed less likely when the man was shaven and decently clad. Certainly the face had changed—how could it be otherwise?—and yet if he were perfectly sane, with his powers and learning, why linger thus instead of crying his name? Unless it was to make vengeance more complete. He did linger; and that, at least, offered the one cheap mercy of time. Flight began to seem Tito’s only resource.

As he turned his back on the Piazza del Duomo, the new part he had been playing slipped from him like a cloak thrown off in heat. He was no longer thinking of the many things his ready brain and tongue made easy, but of the few things destiny had made hard.

Behind him, the enthusiasm he had fed with contempt created a scene grander than his private fear. The crowd, after his disappearance, began to turn toward the outlets leading to the Via Larga, when the sight of the mazzieri entering from the Via de’ Martelli announced the approach of dignitaries. The treaty must already be signed; these were the syndics, commissioners charged with its effecting, come away from the royal presence. Piero Capponi was coming—the firm heart that had spoken for Florence.

The crowd’s change was as striking as a kitchen gone suddenly quiet when the master steps in. Voices dropped and softened; men shuffled back; the press parted. Silence gathered, and became so complete that the tread of the syndics on the broad pavement, and the rustle of their black silk garments, could be heard distinctly, like rain heard at night when all else sleeps. There were four of them: Guidantonio Vespucci and Domenico Bonsi, learned doctors of law; Francesco Valori, grown popular in these late days; but it was not on them the piazza fixed its hunger.

The moment belonged to another man—firm in presence, loving order like one whom fortune had made a merchant and nature had made a soldier, as little inclined to humour the people as to humour any other unreasonable claimant. When he appeared at the entrance, one loud shout broke the silence cleanly, like a bell struck true:

“Capponi! Capponi! Well done, Capponi!”

The simple resolute man looked round with grave joy, letting the sound of gratitude enter him while it was living breath, not carved praise. Two years later they would give him a great funeral when he had died in fight—torches borne by all the magistracy, and torches again, and trains of banners. It is not known that the oration over his bier gave him any joy. Let us be glad he had thanks and praise while he lived.

It was the first time Baldassarre had set foot again in the Piazza del Duomo since the day of his escape—since the day he had stood there half naked, his hair a matted offense, a rope biting his throat like a leash. The very stones remembered. The air itself seemed to retain the crowd’s old hiss and ripple—those quick little laughs, the sharp intake when someone points, the cruel, light music of strangers enjoying a spectacle that cost them nothing.

He had wanted to hear the monk preach again. He had hungered for that voice as a man hungers for bread when his mouth is dry and empty—hungered for the cadence that gathered up a city’s scattered minds and made them tremble together. Yet he had shrunk from returning, because the words that had struck him there were not only a wound but a verdict.

“Some madman, surely.”

Tito’s voice—polished, easy, the kind of voice that could glide over any truth and make it seem an ornament—had dropped those words as if they were nothing. But they had clung like burrs. Not because they were base—though they were; not because they were cruel—though they were; but because in the instant they were spoken Baldassarre had felt a colder thing than anger: the fear that he might not be able to prove them false.

He was not mad. He carried within him the piteous stamp of sanity: the clear knowledge that parts of his mind were broken, that the old chambers of memory had collapsed and left him wandering among rubble. He could measure his own feebleness. He could feel the gaps, like missing teeth that the tongue cannot help but seek.

And with the first hot surge of vengeance there had wakened, too, a wary caution—the caution of a wild creature that knows it is fierce but not whole; the caution of an insect whose foothold has crumbled, leaving it clinging and still. That distrust—of himself, of his tongue, of the treacherous slipping away of thought—had made him turn from Piero di Cosimo’s friendly hand. It had made him cautious in the hospital, answering the brethren in phrases that could not betray him: he had been made prisoner by the French on his way from Genoa. Nothing more.

Yet even there, among the smells of boiled herbs, stale straw, and the sour breath of many bodies lying too close, the monks had looked at him and seen what he could not entirely hide—age, yes, and misery, but also the remnant of another station. They gave him more than the ordinary alms: a coarse woollen tunic that scratched his skin like nettles but kept the damp from his bones; peasant shoes that creaked with fresh stitching; and a few danari, the smallest Florentine coins, light as contempt in the palm and yet heavy with possibility.

He had set out on the road to Arezzo at dawn. The countryside was washed in a thin November light; vines stood stripped and black against pale sky, and the wind moved through bare branches with a dry, whispering hush. But after the first little town he stopped, and with two danari bought the one thing he needed more than food: he bought a face he might dare to show.

The barber’s shop smelled of lather and iron—warm water, stale pomade, the metallic tang of scissors and razors wiped on cloth. A pot of soap simmered near the brazier, sending up steam that carried a fatty sweetness. The barber had a little hand-mirror of bright steel. Baldassarre had not looked at himself in years, not truly. Now, when his eyes caught that small shining circle, a thought shot through him so sharply it made his breath catch.

Was he so changed that Tito had not known him?

The thought stopped his inner currents as a stone stops water. He trembled, pushing away the barber’s arm with a hand that shook like a leaf.

“Give me the mirror,” he said. He wanted to see himself before the razor scraped away what time had grown.

The barber, noticing his tremulousness, held it up. In the dull steel, Baldassarre saw his own face as if it were an image dredged from silt.

No. He was not so changed as that. The wrinkles were the same ones he had known three years ago—only deeper now, ploughed and hardened. The skin on his brow rose in little superficial bosses like cipher-marks—meaningless signs of long use. It was yellower, more like rind than flesh. The shaggy white beard—no disguise to eyes that had looked closely at him for sixteen years; no disguise to eyes that, if they had searched for him at all, should have expected him to be altered, as men search for the beloved among drowned bodies cast up by the sea.

Something in his glance was different, yes; but it was a difference that should have made recognition more—not less—terrible, as a familiar voice heard in a cry.

The doubt was folly. He had felt it in the Piazza: Tito had known.

He pushed the mirror away. The momentary arrest broke. Hatred rushed on again like a river released.

He turned back toward Florence, but he would not enter until dusk. He left the highroad and sat by a little pool that lay like a dark coin sunk in earth, shadowed on one side by alder-bushes still freckled with yellow leaves. The air was calm; the pool’s surface held the sky without a tremor. And because it was still, it tempted him.

A mirror again.

He bent over it and stared, slow now, without the barber’s eyes watching. Was there something wandering in his face—something imbecile, like what he felt in his mind?

Not in this moment. Now his look was eager, intent, full of purpose. But at other times—yes. In the long hours when he felt the vague ache of an unremembered past—when he seemed to sit in a dark loneliness, visited by whispers that died the instant he strained his ear, and by forms that approached and floated away as he thrust out his hand—then, doubtless, there was continual frustration in his gaze. And worse still, when the thick cloud parted for an instant and hope sprang up—only for the cloud to roll together again and leave him helpless—then there must be a blank confusion on his face, like sudden blindness.

Could he prove anything? Could he even begin to allege anything and trust that the links of thought would not snap and fall? Would any man believe that he had once had a mind full of rare knowledge, busy with close thoughts, ready with various speech? It had slipped away from him, that store he had gathered laboriously year by year, like grain laid up against famine—spilled and scattered as if some careless hand had overturned the bin.

Was it gone forever, like water poured from an urn into the wide ocean? Or was it still within him, dammed up by some obstruction that might break?

He clung to that hope, because without it the future narrowed to a single coarse action. And his mind, since he had first risen from his straw and walked feebly into sunlight only to discover a new darkness inside himself, had indeed changed in uneven ways—partly gradual, partly sudden. His body had strengthened; his will had hardened; the memories most entwined with feeling had returned—his tenderness, his joy, his pain—and alongside them had grown the steady, burning sense of lost knowledge.

Once or twice, when excitement had seized him, there had come a flash—an instant when he seemed wholly himself again, as old men doze and wake for a heartbeat into the youth they thought gone: he had seemed to see Greek pages and understand them, to feel his mind move unbenumbed among familiar ideas. The darkness had returned at once, more horrible for the light that had mocked him.

But what if it came again—and stayed long enough?

Long enough to achieve revenge. Not the blunt, brief revenge of a quick death. Something slower, under the same sky that had watched him forsaken; on the same earth where he had fainted in despair. Something that would make Tito’s fair, smiling hardness cry out and moan, not once, but again and again.

He straightened from the pool, folded his arms, and tried to force his mind into planning. Knowledge and opportunity: he must wait for both. And while he waited he must live without begging. For what he dreaded most now—more than hunger, more than cold—was to have any man think him a foolish, helpless old creature. No one must suspect that half his memory was gone. The lost strength might return; and if it returned only for a little while, that might be enough.

He knew how to begin.

Bratti Ferravecchi.

He had repeated the words so often since he first heard them that they were like a refrain beating in his head, hard to dislodge. In Genoa, a man with Tito’s ring on his finger had told him the ring was bought in Florence, from a young Greek—well dressed, handsome dark face—in the shop of a rigattiere named Bratti Ferravecchi, in the street also called Ferravecchi.

That information had shaken him with a violence almost like joy. Until then, his fervent nature had clung to faith in Tito; he had not believed himself wilfully forsaken. At first he had said, My parchment has never reached him. That is why I still toil at Antioch. But he is searching. He knows where I was lost. He will trace me out and find me.

Then, when he was taken to Corinth, he had persuaded his owners—by the assurance that he would be sought out and ransomed—to make sure inquiries at Antioch would not fail. And in Corinth he had thought, Here at last he must find me. Here he cannot miss me, whichever way he comes.

But before another year had passed, illness had come—the fever that left him shattered in body and mind, worse than worthless to his owners except for a ransom that did not arrive. He remembered himself then, sitting helpless in morning light, head between his hands, eyes blank, lips moving uncertainly. He had looked so like a hopeless imbecile that his owners were content to rid themselves of him. A Genoese merchant, compassionate to him as an Italian, took him aboard his galley.

In long months among islands and along the seaboard, he had regained strength of limb, but on landing at Genoa he had felt so weary and desolate that he had almost wished the illness at Corinth had killed him. Only one possibility held him back from that wish: perhaps Tito was not dead, but imprisoned or destitute; perhaps Tito still lived, and if he lived there was still hope—faint, long deferred—that Baldassarre might find his child again, clasp hands, meet eyes that remembered him as he had been before his mind broke.

Then he had chanced upon the stranger with Tito’s onyx ring. Though Baldassarre could never have described the ring beforehand, the sight of it stirred dormant fibres; he knew it. The fact that Tito, nearly a year after his father’s loss, had been living in prosperity in Florence and had sold a gem he ought not to have sold but in extremity—Baldassarre shrank from accounting for it. Better to be stunned than to think. He tried to feel only joy: I shall see him again. Perhaps he thought I was dead. The mystery will be explained. At least I shall meet eyes that remember me. I am not alone.

And now he told himself again: I am not alone in the world; I shall never be alone, for my revenge is with me.

It was as the instrument of that revenge—as something external, subservient—that he bent down once more to examine himself with hard curiosity. He told himself he did not care for this withered old man, unloved, forsaken—his soul like a deserted home where the ashes were cold and the walls bare except for marks of what had been. Yet passion, even when it is low, has a point where it ceases to be properly egoistic; it becomes like a fire kindled inside us, and everything else—body, memory, pride—is mere fuel.

He stared at the pale, black-browed image in the water until it seemed a separate creature listening to his thought.

“I was a loving fool,” his mind said to it. “I worshipped a woman once and believed she could care for me. Then I took a helpless child and fostered him. I watched him as he grew to see if he would care for me—care for me over and above the good I gave. I would have torn open my breast to warm him with my life-blood if I could only have seen him care a little for the pain of my wound. I laboured, I strained to crush out of this hard life one drop of unselfish love.

“Fool! Men love their own delights; there is no delight to be had in me. And yet I watched until I believed I saw what I watched for. When he was a child he lifted soft eyes to me and held my hand willingly. I thought, This boy will surely love me a little. Because I give my life to him and strive that he shall know no sorrow, he will care a little when I am thirsty—the drop he lays on my parched lips will be a joy to him.

“Curses on him! I wish I may see him lie with those red lips white and dry as ashes; and when he looks for pity, I wish he may see my face rejoicing in his pain. It is all a lie—this world is a lie—there is no goodness but in hate. Not one drop of love came with all my striving. Life has not given me one drop. But there are deep draughts in this world for hatred and revenge. I have memory left for that. There is strength in my arm—there is strength in my will—and if I can do nothing but kill him—”

But his mind recoiled from the thought of that swift punishment. His whole soul had been thrilled into a fierce belief in an eternity of vengeance: he, an undying hate, clutching forever an undying traitor, hearing that fair, smiling hardness cry out through endless anguish. Yet he wanted, first, a slow revenge here, under this mortal sky.

And as soon as he tried again to fix on means, the sense of his weakness pressed on him like frost in the joints. This despised body—the instrument of a sublime vengeance—must be nourished and clothed. If he must wait, he must work. But what work? He had no craft, no skill. He wondered whether the sight of written characters might kindle his lost power, whether he might dare to seek work as a copyist, win credence for his past scholarship. But he dared trust neither hand nor brain.

He must take the labor of a beast of burden. Florence was mercantile; it needed porters. He could carry weights. Thanks to the strange justice that struggled in this confused world on behalf of vengeance, his limbs had recovered something of their old sturdiness. He had nothing else men would pay for.

Then an urgency in his thought brought a suggestion, like the smell of food suddenly remembered when one is starving.

Something hung by a cord around his bare neck: something so paltry that the piety of Turks and Frenchmen had spared it—a tiny parchment bag blackened with age. It had hung there when he was a boy, a charm his mother had put upon him. He had kept it not because he believed in its magic, but because it was a relic of her love. Such brevi were not meant to be opened; piety demanded they remain sealed.

At any earlier moment of his life he would have said no hunger could tempt him to tear it open for the chance of an amulet worth coin. But now a thirst had come like the thirst that makes men open their own veins. The possibility flashed—what if, inside, there was not parchment but a stone?

His fingers snatched at it. He felt in an instant the long years he had worn it, and the far-off sunny balcony at Naples where he had leaned against his mother’s knee and looked toward blue water. For a heartbeat the past was so near that he could almost hear it—the low sea-sound, the soft Neapolitan lilt that had once named him. And then that sound was swallowed by the harsher Florentine air, by the city’s dominant tongue—sharp-edged, public, careless with private lives. The old words were unreachable, untranslatable now, even to himself; his own history had become a dialect he could no longer speak.

It brought no hesitation. All piety had been melted and poured into one shape: revenge.

He bit and tore at the doubles of parchment until they split. And then—the sight made him pant—there was an amulet.

Very small. But as blue as those remembered waters: an engraved sapphire. Worth gold ducats.

The moment he saw the ducats in his mind, he saw some of them turned into a poniard. Not to use at once—no, not yet—but to possess. To feel a handle in his fist, to try an edge with his thumb—so that when memory failed and thought broke, he would not feel so helpless. Steel did not ask for talents; steel did not slip away like recollection. It could be the unfailing friend of feeble justice.

A hard, sparkling triumph lit under his black eyebrows as he wrapped the little sapphire again in parchment and wound the string tight.

Dusk was falling. He rose and walked toward Florence. With his danari he bought bread—coarse, dark, smelling of sour grain and the heat of the oven that had baked it. He ate slowly, feeling the crust abrade his gums, feeling the simple act of chewing anchor him in his body. All around, the world had its evening noises: distant carts, a dog’s bark answered by another, the soft clop of hooves on stone—sounds that settled on the mind like weather. He listened as if listening could keep him whole.

He could sleep in the open air if he must; plenty did, tucked into corners where the city’s stone held a little warmth. In the next few days he sold the sapphire, bought more clothing, bought a bright dagger, and still had two gold florins left. He hoarded them like seeds in winter. His lodging was an outhouse with a heap of straw in it, in a thinly inhabited part of Oltrarno. The straw smelled of old harvest—dry, dusty sweetness mixed with the musk of damp—and it pricked through his tunic when he lay down. He meant to look for work as a porter.

He had bought his dagger at Bratti’s.

When he paid his meditated visit one evening at dusk, he found the singular rag-merchant just returned from his rounds, emptying his basketful of broken glass and old iron among a handsome display of second-hand goods—smart pieces of apparel, musical instruments, weapons—lit broad in the window as if poverty itself could be arranged to look inviting.

As Baldassarre entered and looked toward the window, his eye fastened at once on a dagger hanging high against a red scarf. The scarf made a field of color behind the steel, like meat behind a blade. By buying the dagger he could satisfy his longing and open his errand indirectly, without naming the onyx ring too soon.

He bargained with a caution that masked urgency. The shop smelled of old leather, dust, tarnish, and the faint sweetness of cloth that has been folded too long. Bratti’s voice was nasal and lively; his words came in flourishes, as if he were selling not objects but the story of himself.

In the course of haggling, Baldassarre let fall, with careful carelessness, that he came from Genoa and had been directed to Bratti’s by an acquaintance who had bought a very valuable ring there. Had the respectable trader any more such rings? Was that sort of treasure often within reach?

Bratti launched at once into a boastful stream: rings like that were not for common hands. But Bratti Ferravecchi had rare connections—owing to his known wisdom and honesty. Yes, yes, it might be true that he was a pedlar; he chose to be a pedlar. Rich enough, he was, to kick his heels in his shop all day if he pleased. But those who thought they had said all there was to say about Bratti when they called him a pedlar were further from truth than the other side of Pisa.

How had such a ring come his way? Because he—Bratti—had particular knowledge of a handsome young signor who had not looked quite so fine a feathered bird when Bratti first laid eyes on him as he did now. That young man had been found sleeping under the Loggia de’ Cerchi, and see what had come of it! Bratti’s discerning eye, Bratti’s connections, Bratti’s—Bratti’s everything.

By a question or two, repeated as if from deafness—for Baldassarre seemed rather deaf, asking Bratti to say many things twice—he drew out, without trouble, as rough and rambling an account of Tito’s life as the pedlar could supply: the early sale of jewels; the immediate, quiet settlement in Florence; the marriage; the great prosperity.

Bratti never suspected the decent customer cared about Tito. The curiosity, of course, must be about Bratti—about the remarkable rigattiere who stood at the center of so many fortunate turns.

Baldassarre left the shop with the dagger at his side and a general knowledge of Tito’s conduct and position. But the question that burned most—What story had he told about his previous life, about his father?—that would be harder to answer.

Meanwhile, Baldassarre wanted to learn all he could about Florence. Yet to his acute distress, the new details he gathered would not stay. They slid away as if his mind were a sieve. He could retain only a few, and only by constant repetition. He began to fear listening to new discourse, lest it wash away what he had already forced himself to remember. The city was full of talk—markets bursting with cries, church steps buzzing with gossip, workshops clanging and singing with labor—but all that sound could become torment: too much noise was not music, only erosion, wearing down what little structure remained inside him.

On the day Tito had seen him in the Piazza del Duomo, this anguish was fresh; and Tito’s ready speech had fallen on him like the mockery of a glib, defying demon.

That evening, as he went back to his straw and passed the booksellers’ shops in the Via del Garbo, he paused. Volumes lay open, their pages spread like cut loaves showing crumb—inviting, promising nourishment. Could he, by long gazing, seize again the slippery threads of memory? Could he plant his fingers somewhere firm and pull himself up from these waters that flowed over him?

Temptation won. He bought the cheapest Greek book he saw.

He carried it home and sat on his heap of straw, holding the book where the light from the small window fell. The paper had its own smell—dry, slightly sour, like old linen; the ink lay black and matte, strokes that had once been living speech caught and pinned. He stared at the characters, waiting for the inward light—the familiar quickening, the sense of meaning rising like yeast.
