Nothing rose.

Soon evening thickened. The window’s light faded, the lines blurred, and still he stared. Darkness made little difference. His strained eyes seemed still to see the white pages with unintelligible black marks upon them, as if the very language he had lived in had died inside him, leaving only shapes—silent, dominant, refusing him entrance.

“My Romola,” Tito said on the second morning after his speech in the Piazza, while the house was still cool and the courtyard sounds had not yet risen to their full day’s clatter, “I am to receive grand visitors to-day. The Milanese Count comes again, and the Seneschal de Beaucaire—the great favourite of the Cristianissimo. They will want to be shown the antiquities and the library, and there will be nothing but smiling ceremony with those rustling magnates whom we are not likely to see again. I know you do not care for it. Perhaps you had better give up your work to-day, and go to see your cousin Brigida.”

Romola heard, beneath the lightness, the particular wish he was careful not to shape into a command. She assented at once, because yielding in such small things had become one of her ways of loving: like setting a crust to soak for soup because he liked it that way, or seeing that the oil in the lamp was strained clear of bitterness. Yet when she came back in her hood and mantle, the buckle newly fastened at her throat, her glance went out beyond the threshold as if it could already see the city’s lungs expand.

“Oh, what a long breath Florence will take,” she said, “when the gates are flung open and the last Frenchman is walking out of them. Even you are getting tired, with all your patience, my Tito; confess it. Ah—your head is hot.”

He was bent over the desk, writing, the quick scratch of the pen a dry insect-sound in the hush. She laid her hand on his head as she had done many times, intending it for a parting caress—the touch that had been as homely between them as laying a cloth straight or tasting broth for salt. Often, at that touch, he would lift his face, lean back a little, and meet her eyes with that ready smile which made the house feel inhabited. But now her hand lay there, and he did not raise his head. It seemed to him as if he could no more lift it than if her palm had turned to lead.

He spoke lightly, his pen running on. “The French are as ready to go from Florence as the wasps to leave a ripe pear when they have just fastened on it.”

Romola’s senses, trained by love to mark the smallest changes—as one marks at table when a familiar loaf has been baked too long, or a jar has taken an alien taint—felt the absence of the accustomed movement and look. She drew away her hand.

“I am going, Tito.”

“Farewell, my sweet one. I must wait at home. Take Maso with you.”

Still he did not look up. She went out without adding more, her footfall swallowed by the stone passage, and the morning outside meeting her with its mingled voices: the splash of water flung from a pail, a vendor’s call rising and falling like a chant, the iron ring of a distant hammer. Very slight things make epochs in married life; and for the first time Romola admitted to herself—not in anger, but in a sudden, cold clearness—that Tito had changed, and that the change had turned towards her.

Was the reason in herself? She might have believed it, as wives so readily do, searching their own hearts as if a fault there must be the hidden worm. But there were those strange facts—the armour, the picture—standing in her memory like objects found out of place in a well-ordered pantry, suggesting hands at work when she had thought the room secure. The meaning of them was a sealed jar she could not open.

No sooner did Tito feel assured she was beyond sight than he laid down his pen and lifted his head with a relieved breath, as if he had been holding it under water. He looked about him with a kind of delighted safety—only parchment, only broken marble, harmless fragments that could not judge. Then came a sharp disgust with himself. He would have chosen, if he could, to be even more than usually kind. His whole nature leaned toward keeping Romola’s tenderness as a man keeps warmth in a house by shutting out draughts. Yet he could not master, in an instant, that involuntary shrinking from her which had risen by subtle links out of the very qualities in him that made him dread her pain.

He was about to take a step which he knew would rouse her deep indignation. He would have to endure displeasure, perhaps anger, before he could win forgiveness; and Tito could never find it easy to face anger. He was far from defiance: his instincts were those of the creature that smooths and slips away from blows. Scruples, sentimental and unprofitable, did not torment him; he had argued them down with swift skill whenever they threatened to swell. But freedom from scruple is not freedom from the dread of what is disagreeable. Unscrupulousness may rid you of much, but not of toothache, nor wounded vanity, nor the hollow sound of loneliness in the room when love has withdrawn; and Tito, tasting beforehand the bitterness of the coming collision, felt as if he were being driven to a desperate leap by something close behind—teeth and claw—while his own nature was that of a timid animal that would rather creep softly and never startle any one.

Long before, he had come to think—quietly, as one convinces oneself that stale bread must be used and not wasted—that this tenacious obedience to Bardo’s wishes about the library had become, under present difficulties, a piece of sentimental folly: it deprived himself and Romola of substantial advantages. That thought might have lain inert, like yeast kept too cool to rise, if the events of the last week had not pressed on him with a new motive and opened a rare opportunity. Not until his dread had been aggravated by seeing Baldassarre look more like his sane self—more like a man whose eyes might suddenly recognise and accuse—not until Tito had begun to feel that he might be compelled to flee from Florence, did he bring himself to resolve on using his legal right to sell the library before the great chance offered by French and Milanese bidders slipped away.

If he had to leave Florence, he did not mean to leave it as a destitute wanderer. He had grown used to agreeable conditions—the ease of well-served meals, the soft assurance of being greeted with regard, the comfort of money ready to quiet a difficulty as oil quiets the squeal of a hinge. He wanted to carry with him all means at hand for keeping life pleasant. Among the things he wished to carry was Romola; and not, if possible, any infamy. Success had sharpened his appetite for all pleasures that depend on an advantageous place among men, and it could look to him only like a hideous alternative to decamp under dishonour, even with diamonds hidden in a bag, and accept the life of an adventurer.

He could not make himself independent of the Florentines who courted him; still less could he make himself independent of Romola. She was the wife of his first love—he loved her still; she belonged to that furniture of life he shrank from losing, as one shrinks from coming home to a room stripped bare. He winced under her judgment. He could not measure how far revulsion might carry her. And that husband’s sense of power which tempts betrayals that a lover would never dare was not enough to counteract Tito’s uneasiness. This was the weight that had held his neck stiff beneath her hand: the light of her eyes would have brought too near the prospect of struggle.

But it was not to be helped. If they had to leave Florence, they must have money. Indeed, Tito could not arrange life at all to his mind without a considerable sum. And the very habit of arranging life to his mind had been the source of all his misdoing. He could have made any sacrifice that was not unpleasant.

The day went on. The rustling magnates came and went: the smell of damp woollen cloaks and perfumed leather drifted through passages; boots rang on stone; foreign voices rose and fell with the clink of metal as cases were opened and shut. The bargains were concluded. When Romola returned, nothing grave was spoken that night. Tito was even gayer than usual, chatty and sparkling, pouring out tales of what he had seen and heard during the French visit—the bright surfaces of it, the pageant and the phrases—like a man ladling sweet wine to cover the taste of a bitter herb in the cup.

Romola thought she discerned effort in his liveliness, and because she loved him she chose the kind interpretation: that he knew he had wounded her in the morning and was making amends. Yet inwardly she ached at that sign of growing distance—that there was an offence about which neither dared speak, as if their speech itself had begun to lose words for what was passing between them.

The next day Tito remained away from home until late at night. It became a marked day to Romola for another reason. Piero di Cosimo, stimulated to greater industry on her behalf by the fear that he might have been the cause of pain to her in the past week, sent home her father’s portrait.

The picture had the faint, pungent odour of oil and varnish newly laid—an odour that always seemed to Romola like something half nourishment, half wound, as if the very act of making likeness were both a keeping and a hurting. She propped it against the back of Bardo’s old chair, as one sets bread beside the place of the dead at a remembered feast, and sat looking at it until the afternoon light began to thicken towards dusk. Outside, Florence sounded as it had sounded for generations: a rhythm of voices and footsteps, an occasional burst of quarrel, the far-off peal of a bell, the living city’s pulse beating through stone. Yet through all ran that harsher undertone—the tramp of foreign soldiery, the rough laughter that did not belong to Florentine streets, the iron language of occupation. It was as if a familiar song were being drowned by a louder, coarser refrain.

She had been gazing for some time when the door opened behind her and Bernardo del Nero came in.

“It is you, godfather! How I wish you had come sooner—it is getting a little dusk,” Romola said, going towards him. She took him as if she could steady herself by his presence, as by a sturdy old table that had stood in the house through many rearrangements.

“I have just looked in to tell you good news, for I know Tito has not come yet,” Bernardo said. “The French king moves off to-morrow—not before it is high time. There has been another tussle between our people and his soldiers this morning. But there’s a chance now of the city getting into order once more and trade going on.”

“That is joyful,” Romola said, and in her voice there was the thirst of one who has heard too long the wrong sounds in her own streets. “But it is sudden, is it not? Tito seemed to think yesterday there was little prospect of the king’s going soon.”

“He has been well barked at—that’s the reason,” Bernardo said, smiling, with the ease of a man whose humour has survived many storms. “His own generals opened their throats pretty well, and at last our Signoria sent the mastiff of the city—Fra Girolamo. The Cristianissimo was frightened at that thunder, and has given the order to move. I’m afraid there’ll be small agreement among us when he’s gone; but at any rate all parties are agreed in being glad not to have Florence stifled with soldiery any longer. The Frate has barked this time to some purpose.”

As he spoke, the room seemed to Romola to listen with them—the old walls that had heard Latin disputes, Greek quotations, the rustle of pages turned by Bardo’s eager fingers. Florence too was a listener: a city that knew how much the nature of the sounds in its streets could soothe or scourge the mind.

Bernardo’s eyes fell on the picture. “Ah—what is this?” he said, as Romola clasped his arm and led him in front of it. “Let us see.”

He began to unwind his long scarf while she placed a seat for him, careful, as always, with these domestic ministries which were her silent language.

“Do you not want your spectacles, godfather?” she asked, anxious that he should see precisely what she saw, not merely some dim substitute.

“No, child, no,” Bernardo said, uncovering his grey head as he seated himself with firm erectness. “For seeing at this distance, my old eyes are perhaps better than your young ones. Old men’s eyes are like old men’s memories; they are strongest for things a long way off.”

He sat silent a while, and Romola watched his face as she watched the painting—seeking in him, too, the true likeness of her dead. At last she said, apologetically, as if defending a plain dish set before a guest when one had wished to offer something finer, “It is better than having no portrait. It is less like him now than the image I have in my mind; but then that might fade with the years.”

She rested her arm on the old man’s shoulder as she spoke, drawn towards him strongly by their common interest in the dead—the need to preserve what time and noise and new tongues wear away.

“I don’t know,” Bernardo said at last. “I almost think I see Bardo as he was when he was young better than that picture shows him to me as he was when he was old. Your father had a great deal of fire in his eyes when he was young. It was what I could never understand, that he, with his fiery spirit, which seemed much more impatient than mine, could hang over the books and live with shadows all his life. However—he had put his heart into that.”

He gave a slight shrug at the last words; and Romola heard in his voice something that met her own feeling. Her father’s hunger had been for a world held fast in words—words already slipping into silence as fewer mouths shaped them, as if the very dialects and learned tongues he loved were seeds drying out for want of earth.

“And he was disappointed to the last,” she said involuntarily.

Then, fearing her words might seem an accusation against Tito, she hurried on, as if to cover the sound: “If we could only see his longest, dearest wish fulfilled just to his mind!”

“Well, so we may,” Bernardo said kindly, rising and putting on his cap. “The times are cloudy now, but fish are caught by waiting. Who knows? When the wheel has turned often enough, I may be Gonfaloniere yet before I die; and no creditor can touch these things.”

He looked round as he spoke, taking in the room with the practised eye of one who knows how quickly a house can be emptied when power shifts. Then, turning to her, he patted her cheek. “And you need not be afraid of my dying; my ghost will claim nothing. I’ve taken care of that in my will.”

Romola seized the hand that rested against her cheek and pressed it to her lips in silence, as if she could draw courage from the salt of old friendship.

“Haven’t you been scolding your husband for keeping away from home so much lately?” Bernardo said, ready to turn from the grave subject as men do who know a woman’s heart is tender. “I see him everywhere but here.”

The flush spread over Romola’s neck and face. “He has been very much wanted; you know he speaks so well. I am glad to know that his value is understood.”

“You are contented then, Madonna Orgogliosa?” Bernardo said, smiling as he moved to the door.

“Assuredly.”

Poor Romola. There was one thing that would have made the pang of disappointment in her husband harder to bear: that any one should know he gave her cause for disappointment. If it was weakness, it was close to nobleness. The woman who willingly lifts the veil of her married life has profaned it—from a sanctuary into a vulgar place.

The next day, Romola—like every Florentine who had listened for eleven days to the foreign tramp of boots and the scrape of alien harness—lived in a fever of expectancy. The French were going at last. The thought ran through her like warm wine after a chill fast: not merely relief for the city, but a dim, half-superstitious hope that the dread which had thickened round Tito since their coming might loosen and fall away with the last file of soldiers.

All day the streets had been full of sound—the high metallic clatter where lance-shafts struck stone, the hoarse calls of men driving carts, the restless stir of hooves, and above it the impatient undertone of the Arno, muffled under bridges. Romola, wrapped close in her mantle, went up beneath the loggia at the top of the house and waited where she could command the bridges and the road towards the Porta San Piero. She watched for the passing gleam of steel and the ripple of banners, and as each division moved on, the noise altered like a change of wind in a pinewood: nearer, harsher; then thinning, breaking, and at last leaving behind that peculiar hollow after-silence which makes one aware of every domestic sound—the far clink of a pail, a child’s cry, the soft scuffle of sandals on stair.

When the gates were shut she went back again, as if she must take the final vibration into her body. Then the bells burst out—great peals that rolled through dusk like waves of bronze. She let them buffet her head and heart; she wanted to be shaken, deafened, made other than herself for a moment. In those strokes she fancied deliverance, as if the city were being rung clean.

It was almost dark when she went down to the library. The room had that wide, solemn gloom which seemed to drink in light rather than reflect it; her single oil-lamp made a little yellow island at the far end of the table, and the fire, neglected, had sunk to a dull red, smelling faintly of cold ash. She had forced herself to come there with a resolution—she would not waste another day in trembling fancies; she would copy the catalogue as she had promised, line after line, name after name, each title like a grain stored against future hunger.

Tito had gone out early; she did not look for him yet. Before he came she meant to leave this chill room and take her place in the pretty saloon with the dancing nymphs and birds—she had made that change every evening since Tito had spoken of the library as gloomy, as if she could warm his temper by warm walls.

She had scarcely dipped her pen twice when she heard the step she knew, quick and light upon the stones. Tito came in.

Her first impulse was tenderness at once: how lonely he must feel entering this cavern of shadow with only one thin lamp and the fire dying. She rose and almost ran to him.

“Tito, dearest—I did not know you would come so soon,” she said, nervously, lifting her white arms to unwind his becchetto.

He smiled—one of those bright, well-practised smiles that had often been like sunshine for her—and clasped her, but with a playful backward motion of the head.

“I am not welcome then?”

“Tito!” The reproach in her voice was the old one—loving, half-laughing—and he answered it with a fond kiss, stroking her hair as he used to do, lingering as if he had no concern to rid himself of cloak or mantle. It was so like the manner she had missed that her heart leaped.

It will come back, she said to herself, the old happiness will perhaps come back. He is like himself again.

And indeed he was taking pains to be like himself, while beneath the smoothness his heart beat hard with a fear that no armour could wholly keep off.

“If I had expected you,” Romola said, helping at last to loosen his wrappings, “I would have had a little festival prepared for this joyful ringing of the bells. I did not mean to be here in the library when you came home.”

“Never mind, sweet,” he answered carelessly. “Do not think about the fire. Come—come and sit down.”

There was a low stool against his chair, and she took it by habit, as once she had sat at her father’s knee. She rested her arm upon Tito’s knee and looked up, waiting for him to speak, noticing—because she could never help noticing—that he still had not once looked towards the portrait propped near Bardo’s chair.

“I have been enjoying the clang of the bells for the first time, Tito,” she began, trying to keep her voice light. “I liked being shaken and deafened by them: I fancied I was something like a Bacchante, possessed by a divine rage. Are not the people looking very joyful to-night?”

“Joyful after a sour and pious fashion,” Tito said, shrugging. “But in truth, those who are left behind have little cause for joy. The most reasonable ground of gladness would be to have got out of Florence.”

His tone had been careless, almost conversational, and yet he made his face grave enough to draw her into anxious question.

“Why, Tito? Are there fresh troubles?”

“No need of fresh ones, my Romola. There are three strong parties in the city, all ready to fly at each other’s throats. If the Frate’s party is strong enough to frighten the other two into silence—as seems most likely—life will be as pleasant as a funeral. They have their plan of a Great Council simmering already; and if they get it, the man who sings sacred lauds the loudest will be the most eligible for office. Besides, the city will be drained—first by this great subsidy to the French king, and then by the war to get back Pisa. The prospect would be dismal enough without the rule of fanatics. Florence will be delightful for worthies who amuse themselves by going into crypts and lashing their own backs; but for everything else, the exiles have the best of it.”

He paused only long enough to let his conclusion seem the natural end of his list.

“For my own part, I have been thinking seriously that we should be wise to quit Florence, my Romola.”

She started as if the bells had struck her in a new place. Cold ran up her arms; the pressure in her throat made speech difficult. Of course he knew what such words touched.

“Tito—how could we leave Florence? Surely you do not think I could leave it—not yet—not for a long while.”

“That,” he said, with the same easy gentleness, “is all a fabric of your own imagination, my sweet one. Your secluded life has made you lay false stress on a few things. You remember I used to tell you, before we were married, that I wished we were somewhere else. If you had seen more places and more people you would know what I mean. There is something in the Florentines that reminds me of their cutting spring winds—always keen, always prying. I like people who take life less eagerly. It would be good for my Romola to see a new life. I should like to dip her a little in the soft waters of forgetfulness.”

He kissed her brow, laid his hand on her hair with that caress which had once been enough to dissolve every resistance in her. But now she felt it no more than if a cool mouth had touched plaster. Her mind was filling with the sick sense of distance—of some widening gulf between their meanings.

“Tito,” she said, gathering her breath, “it is not because I suppose Florence is the pleasantest place in the world that I desire not to quit it. It is because I—because we have to see my father’s wish fulfilled. My godfather is old—seventy-one. We could not leave it to him.”

“It is precisely those superstitions,” Tito said, still gently, “that hang about your mind like bedimming clouds, that make one reason the more why I would have us two hundred leagues from Florence. I am obliged to take care of you in opposition to your own will sometimes. If those dear eyes—so tender—see falsely, I must see for them, and save my wife from wasting her life in disappointing herself by impracticable dreams.”

Romola sat still. She heard in his words, as one hears a knife on a whetstone, the direction they must go: he wanted to be rid of the task, the tie, the vow made at a death-bed; and he expected her to let his cleverness decide the shape of duty. Inside her, something set itself hard as a kneaded dough that has taken its salt: she would resist—she would bear pain rather than yield on this trust. But the first pain was the confession that they were divided, that his will moved where hers could not follow.

Her silence pleased him. Like many men who have learnt to talk fluently, he overvalued the power of his arguments and did not imagine how they looked when they touched another’s deepest tenderness. He continued in a remonstrating tone, as if soothing a child from needless fear.

“You know, dearest—your own clear judgment always showed you—that the notion of isolating a collection of books and antiquities, and attaching a single name to them for ever, has no valid good for its object; and, more, it may be defeated in a thousand ways. See what has become of the Medici collections! For my part, I consider it blameworthy to entertain petty views of appropriation. Why should Florence possess the benefits of learned research and taste more than any other city? I understand your feeling about the wishes of the dead; but wisdom must put limits to such sentiments, else lives may be wasted in futile devotion—like praising deaf gods for ever. You gave your life to your father while he lived; why demand more of yourself?”

“Because it was a trust,” Romola said, low but distinct. “He trusted me. He trusted you, Tito. I did not expect you to feel as I do—but I did expect you to feel that.”

“Yes, dearest—of course,” he replied with smooth patience. “If your father’s real welfare or happiness were concerned. But there is no question of that now. If we believed in purgatory, I should be as anxious as you to have masses said; and if I believed it could now pain your father to see his library preserved and used in a rather different way from what he had set his mind on, I should share your strictness. But a little philosophy should teach us to rid ourselves of those air-woven fetters mortals hang round themselves—spending their lives miserable under mere imagination of weight. Your mind, which seizes ideas so readily, can discriminate between substantial good and these brain-wrought fantasies. Ask yourself—what possible good can these books and antiquities do, stowed under your father’s name in Florence, more than if they were divided, or carried elsewhere? Is not dispersion into hands that know how to value them one means of extending usefulness? This rivalry of Italian cities is petty. The loss of Constantinople was the gain of the whole civilised world.”

As he spoke, Romola felt a contempt rising within her like bile—contempt that did not quench love, but made love bruised and despairing. His large phrases had no warmth for what lay nearest; his wide sympathies seemed like painted fruit—fair to look at, without scent, without juice. She drew her arm from his knee and clasped her hands before her, sitting cold and motionless as water that has locked itself under frost.

“You talk of substantial good, Tito,” she said, and her voice began to rise in spite of her restraint. “Are faithfulness and love and sweet grateful memories no good? Is it no good that we should keep our silent promises—promises on which others build because they believe in our truth? Is it no good that a just life should be justly honoured? Or is it good that we should harden our hearts against the wants and hopes of those who have depended on us? What good can belong to men who have such souls? To talk cleverly, perhaps, and find soft couches for themselves, and live and die with their base selves as their best companions.”

There was a ring of scorn in the last words, a sharpness as of metal struck. She paused, but other words trembled at her lips, and he let them come, watching.

“I know of no good for cities or the world if they are to be made up of such beings. But I am not thinking of other Italian cities and the whole civilised world—I am thinking of my father, and my love and sorrow for him, and his just claims on us. I would give up anything else, Tito—I would leave Florence—what else did I live for but for him and you? But I will not give up that duty. What have I to do with your arguments? It was a yearning of his heart, and therefore it is a yearning of mine.”

Her voice had steadied into firmness; she believed she had met the hardest part—she had spoken the truth and would stand by it.

But Tito had seen, with a quick inward calculation, that persuasion would not bend her. He must end the struggle by making resistance useless. If he did not speak now, the disclosure would come in another form to-morrow. Necessity braced him. He kept his tone quiet.

“I am sorry to hear you speak in that spirit of blind persistence, my Romola,” he said. “Because it obliges me to give you pain. But I partly foresaw your opposition; and as a prompt decision was necessary, I avoided that obstacle, and decided without consulting you. The care of a husband for his wife’s interest compels him to separate action sometimes—even when he has such a wife as you, my Romola.”

She turned her eyes on him, breathless.

“I mean,” he said, answering the look, “that I have arranged for the transfer—both of the books and of the antiquities—where they will find the highest use and value. The books have been bought for the Duke of Milan. The marbles and bronzes and the rest are going to France. Both will be protected by the stability of a great Power instead of remaining in a city exposed to ruin.”

Before the last words were out, Romola had sprung up. She stood over him, hands tightened and hanging rigid, and in her face there was, for the first time in her life, a fierceness that made her beauty terrible.

“You have sold them?” she said, as if her ears were betraying her.

“I have,” Tito answered, and his boldness shrank a little before her look.

“You are a treacherous man!” The words grated as they left her throat.

For a moment she was silent. Tito sat still; he knew that now no ingenuity could sweeten what had been done. Then she turned away abruptly, her breath coming fast.

“It may be hindered—I am going to my godfather.”

In an instant Tito started up, went to the door, locked it, and put the key in his scarsella. Something hard—an authority that had lain latent in him—came to the surface. He was not angry; he only felt the scene as something exceedingly unpleasant, something after which he would wish to be away. But he must first reduce her to passiveness.

“Try to calm yourself a little, Romola,” he said, taking up the easiest attitude he could manage, leaning against a pedestal under the bust of a grim old Roman. His face had paled; his heart beat with a moral dread that made his cleverness feverishly alert. He had shut her scorn in—but had shut himself in with it.

Romola had halted as she saw the key vanish into his pouch. Her eyes flashed; her whole frame seemed possessed by a force that sought outlet in action. The pain of disappointed love, which a little before had been crushing her, was annihilated now in pure indignation. She could not care, in this moment, that the man she despised was her husband. The pride and fierceness of her father’s blood woke fully at last.

“Try at least to understand the fact,” Tito went on. “Do not seek to take futile steps that may be fatal. It is of no use for you to go to your godfather. Messer Bernardo cannot reverse what I have done. Only sit down. You would hardly wish—if you were quite yourself—to make known to any third person what passes between us in private.”

He saw that he had touched the fibre of her delicacy. But she did not sit; she was scarcely conscious of her body.

“Why can it not be reversed?” she said after a pause. “Nothing is moved yet.”

“Simply because the sale has been concluded by written agreement. The purchasers have left Florence, and I hold the bonds for the purchase-money.”

“If my father had suspected you of being a faithless man,” Romola said, and her scorn seemed to insist on darting out before any other thought, “he would have placed the library safely out of your power. But death overtook him too soon; and when you were sure his ear was deaf and his hand stiff, you robbed him.”

She drew breath, and the next words came with gathered passion.

“Have you robbed somebody else—who is not dead? Is that the reason you wear armour?”

It was as if she had struck him. At first Tito felt horribly cowed; the disgrace he dreaded seemed to loom larger. Then resistance rose in him—such dislike as he had, such instinct to master what threatened him. Her, at least, his quick mind told him, he could master.

“It is useless,” he said coolly, “to answer the words of madness. Your peculiar feeling about your father has made you mad at this moment. Any rational person—looking at the case from due distance—will see I have taken the wisest course. Apart from the influence of your exaggerated feelings on him, I am convinced Messer Bernardo would be of that opinion.”

“He would not!” Romola cried. “He lives in the hope of seeing my father’s wish exactly fulfilled. We spoke of it together only yesterday. He will help me yet. Who are these men to whom you have sold my father’s property?”

“There is no reason why you should not be told, except that it signifies little. The Count di San Severino and the Seneschal de Beaucaire are now on their way with the king to Siena.”

“They may be overtaken,” Romola said eagerly, the first blind fury giving way to anxious thought, “and persuaded to give up their purchase.”

“No, they may not,” Tito answered with cool decision.

“Why?”

“Because I do not choose that they should.”

“But if you were paid the money?—we will pay you the money,” Romola said. The words showed more nakedly than reproach how far he had become to her a stranger—an adversary to be bought off. Yet she spoke them with less bitterness than pleading. Tito felt stronger; her first storm had spent itself.

“No, my Romola. Understand that such thoughts are impracticable. You would not, in a reasonable moment, ask your godfather to bury three thousand florins in addition to what he has already paid on the library. I think your pride and delicacy would shrink from that.”

Her courage chilled; she trembled and, as if her limbs had suddenly remembered their weight, sank down on a carved chest near her.

Tito’s voice continued, clear and narrow, and it made her shudder as if cold water were being poured over a heated cheek.

“Moreover, it is not my will that Messer Bernardo should advance the money, even if the project were not utterly wild. And I beg you to consider, before you take any step or utter any word, what will be the consequences of placing yourself in opposition to me—of trying to exhibit your husband in the odious light which your own distempered feelings cast over him. What object will you serve by injuring me with Messer Bernardo? The event is irrevocable. The library is sold. And you are my wife.”

He spoke for effect, measuring each phrase. He waited and watched.

Romola kept her eyes on the ground. Several minutes passed. When she answered, her voice was changed—quiet, cold, as if something in her had drawn back and shut a door.

“I have one thing to ask.”

“Ask anything I can do without injuring us both, Romola.”

“That you will give me that portion of the money which belongs to my godfather, and let me pay him.”

“I must have some assurance from you first,” Tito said, “of the attitude you intend to take towards me.”

“Do you believe in assurances, Tito?” The bitterness came back like a taste on the tongue.

“From you, I do.”

“I will do you no harm. I shall disclose nothing. I will say nothing to pain him or you. You say truly—the event is irrevocable.”

“Then I will do what you desire to-morrow morning.”

“To-night, if possible,” Romola said, “that we may not speak of it again.”

“It is possible,” he answered, moving towards the lamp. She sat still, looking away with absent eyes, as if she no longer inhabited the room but only waited in it.

Presently he returned and bent over her, putting a paper into her hand.

“You will receive something in return—you are aware, my Romola?” he said gently; now that he felt secure, his manner sought to be propitiating, as if the matter were already passing into a thing to be forgiven.

“Yes,” she answered, taking the paper without looking at him. “I understand.”

“And you will forgive me, my Romola, when you have had time to reflect.”

He touched her brow with his lips; she made no sign—seemed unaware, as if her skin were numb. She heard him unlock the door and go out. She listened. The great door of the court opened and shut again, and the sound had in it a finality like the drop of a bar.

At that, she sprang up—as if some sudden liberty, terrible and empty, had been flung upon her. She went straight to her father’s chair, where his picture was propped, and fell on her knees before it. The strong control that had held her voice so cold broke utterly; sobs burst from her as if her very breath had been dammed and was rushing out at last.

Baldassarre had drifted through Florence as a leaf drifts between walls, seeking not charity—he had long since ceased to believe in that word—but the cheapest corner of shelter where a man might lie down and not be driven off with curses. The city pressed on him with its stony passages and its thin, trapped strip of sky; every turn seemed to repeat itself, and the very sameness made his broken memory ache, as if it were being forced to name streets it could not recall.

His feet, without clear bidding, carried him toward the one uneven rise within the walls, where a man could climb above tiled roofs and see, beyond them, the ring of hills and the wide valley that the Arno alone opened to view. He had been told—by Bratti, whose words came back in scraps like stones in a pocket—that Tito’s dwelling lay in the Via de’ Bardi. Baldassarre had looked along that street, then turned up behind it to the slope commonly called San Giorgio, glad of any ground that was not flat and hemming, glad of air that did not sound so boxed-in.

The hill was mostly gardens, thinly peopled; the soil smelled different there—less of damp stone, more of turned earth and leaf-mould—and the soundscape shifted too. The city’s clatter thinned, and in its place came small domestic noises: a bucket chain creaking, a goat’s impatient bleat, the soft crack of someone snapping kindling. Even in his misery, the change steadied him, as if the hill kept a memory of older Florence when life had been measured by water carried, beans shelled, bread baked, and not by the metallic shouts of crowded streets.

There was one scarred patch of ground, jagged with great stones, that seemed to remember an old hurt: a landslip, long ago, had broken houses there and left the place uncultivated ever since. Just above the edge of that roughness stood a queer little square building like a tower cut short and capped with fluted tiles. Close by, an outhouse leaned against a piece of ruined wall. Under a large mulberry-tree—half-dead now, shaking its last leaves into the open doorways—a small, dried, hard old woman was untying a goat with two kids.

Baldassarre saw at once that one part of the outbuilding was for beasts, but the other—its door hanging open—held nothing but straw and a few tools. It was the sort of shelter a man who wanted no questions would choose.

He spoke to the old woman. She did not look up. He came closer and raised his voice until it seemed to hurt his own throat. Then she stared, blinking, and answered only with a slow shake of the head and the muffled monotony of the deaf.

“No—no lodging.”

He persisted, shaping the matter with his hands and his few serviceable Italian words: poor stranger, far over seas; no money for hostels; only straw; a quattrino or two each week. She watched him as one watches a dog that might bite, muttering to herself in a thick undertone. Then, as if a calculation had ripened, she disappeared into the little house and returned with a hatchet. Pointing with it to a heavy chump of wood half-buried under litter, she asked if he would chop it up. If he would, he might lie in the outhouse for one night.

He took the hatchet and set to work. The blows fell clean; his arms still knew what his mind had lost. The old woman—Monna Lisa—stood with her arms akimbo, pleased in a narrow, thrifty way, talking low to herself as if her thoughts were another room she could lock.

It had lain there since her old man died, she muttered; might as well have been a stone on the fire. This stranger chopped well, though he spoke with a foreign tongue and looked odd. Cheaper than hiring a lad. And if he only wanted straw, he could earn it with errands up and down the hill. Who would know? A sin kept hidden was half forgiven.

The “her” she named without naming had eyes pressed, at that moment, to a round hole cut in the shutter of an upper window. The shutter was not closed for punishment; it was closed because glass was a luxury and draughts were free. A hole four inches wide served for looking out, and it required a low stool—rickety, but faithful—to reach it. On that stool stood Tessa.

She had darted to the opening at the first loud foreign voice, hungry for any change in her days. She watched the old man’s bent back, the lift and fall of his arms, the pale chips flying, the mulberry leaves shivering down like tired birds. When dusk gathered and she saw him go into the outhouse and sit on the straw, an irresistible thought took hold of her like the smell of supper taking hold of a hungry child.

She would bring him part of her food. She would talk to him.

He was not deaf like Monna Lisa. And there were things a girl could say that were wasted if you had to shout them at someone who already knew your whole small history. Besides, he was a stranger; strangers came from far away and went away again, belonging nowhere in particular. It was naughty—obedience was the largest part of Tessa’s notion of duty—but naughtiness could be confessed at Easter. What else did she have to confess? That she sometimes fell asleep over her beads? that she had been a little cross because Monna Lisa’s deafness made life feel like talking into wool?

Her pretty, pouting face brightened with the pleasure of the transgression. She still wore the simple dress of a contadina, but one made ready for a festa: dark-green serge, clean and neatly set; a red girdle; red glass beads at her throat; her brown hair, rough with its own curl, knotted and pinned with silver. On her hand was a new ornament she could not stop admiring: a fine gold ring that caught light like a secret.

She sat for a minute on her stool, hugging her knees, hovering on the edge of disobedience as if it were the edge of a warm hearth. She had been commanded to make no acquaintances. She had been warned—half in jest, half in threat—that if she did, her new happiness would vanish like treasure turned to lead when brought into daylight. And she had been so obedient that even when she went to church she shaded her face with her hood and pursed her lips tight, as if keeping her very breath from escaping to the world.

Her obedience, too, had been sharpened by fear: the memory of Nofri, the stepfather who beat and drove her, lurked like a shadow behind any unfamiliar footstep. But this old man—this old man was not Nofri. And he likely knew nothing of Nofri. If she fed him, he would be kind; he would not betray her. Monna Lisa would say no. Therefore Monna Lisa must not be asked.

Supper was being prepared downstairs—she knew it by the smell rising through the boards: macaroni piled like a small mountain, steamed until it went soft at the heart, then tossed so the strands shone; cheese grated over it until the scent was sharp and nutty, melting in the heat and clinging in little threads. The fragrance could have gentled a thief.

Tessa tripped down with solemn purpose, put on an innocent face, asked what the noise of talking had been, and before Monna Lisa could gather an answer, knitted her brow with a tiny peremptory air—like a kitten trying to look dangerous—and declared she chose to eat her supper below. Then she sent the old woman upstairs.

Three minutes later she had a lantern in one hand and a wooden bowl of macaroni in the other. She went out to the outhouse and kicked softly at the door.

Baldassarre, roused from a heavy reverie, opened to the lantern-light and saw—impossibly—this small, bright creature in clean festival dress, her eyes wide with delight as if she had found a song in a ruined place. For a moment he doubted whether he was awake.

“I’ve brought you some supper,” she said, lifting her mouth to his ear and shouting, as if he too were deaf like Monna Lisa. “Sit down and eat it, while I stay with you.”

Surprise and distrust rose first in him. Yet he had no impulse to push her away; the kindness struck him like a blow that had no place to land. He sank back on the straw. Tessa came close, set the bowl on his lap, placed the lantern before them so the light fell warm on the steam, crossed her hands, and nodded at the food with a smile that said, You may—yes, truly—you may eat.

In the hurry of doing her daring deed, she had forgotten that a stranger might hear. She fell into her old habit of gesture and loudness, the way one does when the house you live in has swallowed speech into deafness.

The macaroni was rich with cheese, and there was something in its plain warmth that reached past thought. Baldassarre had been gnawing dry bread. He ate.

Tessa watched two or three mouthfuls vanish before she dared to speak again; his eyes had seemed fierce at first. Then she leaned close and cried, “I like my supper, don’t you?”

The look he turned on her was not a smile—his face seemed carved to forget how—but it softened, like a dog’s eyes softening when a hand that might strike instead strokes.

“Yes,” he said. “But I can hear well. I’m not deaf.”

“It is true; I forgot,” Tessa said, clasping her hands. “But Monna Lisa is deaf, and I live with her. She’s kind, and I’m not frightened at her. We live very well—we have plenty of nice things. I can have nuts if I like. And I’m not obliged to work now.”

She spoke quickly, as if pouring out what had been dammed up. “I used to have to work, and I didn’t like it; but I liked feeding the mules. I should like to see poor Giannetta again—the little mule. We’ve only got a goat and two kids, and I used to talk to the goat a good deal, because there was nobody else but Monna Lisa. But now I’ve got something else—can you guess what it is?”

She drew back and looked at him with a challenging smile, as if she had offered a riddle with a prize inside it.

“No,” Baldassarre said, putting aside the bowl, staring at her as one stares at a half-remembered face from one’s own youth.

“You like me to talk to you, don’t you?” Tessa said. “But you must not tell anybody. Shall I fetch you a bit of cold sausage?”

He shook his head. He did not stop her with words, but his refusal was gentle. His gentleness made her bolder.

“Well, then—I’ve got a little baby,” she said, her voice dropping into awe, as if the word itself were holy. “Such a pretty bambinetto, with little fingers and nails! Not old yet; it was born at the Natività, Monna Lisa says. I was married one Natività—a long, long while ago—and nobody knew. O Santa Madonna! I didn’t mean to tell you that!”

She hunched her shoulders and bit her lip, staring at him as if expecting thunder for the secret spilled. But the stranger’s face did not change much; perhaps strangers did not understand what was grave and what was play in a girl’s life.

“Yes,” she went on, half to herself, “you are a stranger. You don’t live anywhere or know anybody, do you?”

“No,” Baldassarre said, speaking as if he were answering his own thought more than hers. “I only know one man.”

“His name is not Nofri, is it?” Tessa asked, sudden fear tightening her.

“No,” Baldassarre said, noticing it. “Is that your husband’s name?”

Tessa laughed, clapping her hands—pure relief turned into amusement. “No, indeed! But I must not tell you anything about my husband. You would never think what he is—not at all like Nofri!”

She laughed again at the very idea, as if the name Nofri could only belong to heaviness and blows, while the thought of her husband belonged to brightness.

“But I don’t see him very often,” she added, more gravely. “Sometimes I pray to the Holy Madonna to send him oftener, and once she did. But I must go back to my bimbo now. I’ll bring it to show you to-morrow. You would like to see it. Sometimes it cries and makes a face, but only when it’s hungry, Monna Lisa says. You wouldn’t think it, but Monna Lisa had babies once, and they are all dead old men. My husband says she will never die now, because she’s so well dried. I’m glad of that, for I’m fond of her.”

She paused, listening to something beyond the door—the hill’s nighttime hush, the goat’s soft shifting, the far city noise like a sea inside a shell. Then she asked, “You would like to stay here to-morrow, shouldn’t you?”

“I should like to have this place to come and rest in—that’s all,” Baldassarre said. “I would pay for it, and harm nobody.”

“No, indeed; I think you are not a bad old man,” Tessa said with earnest judgment. “But you look sorry about something. Tell me, is there anything you shall cry about when I leave you by yourself? I used to cry once.”

“No, child,” he answered. “I think I shall cry no more.”

“That’s right,” she said, pleased, as if he had promised her a gift. “And I’ll bring you some breakfast, and show you the bimbo. Good-night.”

She took up her bowl and lantern and shut the door behind her.

To Baldassarre the visit had been only a pale, brief rainbow against a blackness: a gleam that did not change the deep water he struggled in. When his waking drifted into the harsher images of sleep, he scarcely held her in mind.

But Tessa held him.

No sooner had she gone inside than she told Monna Lisa what she had done and insisted that the stranger must be allowed to come and rest in the outhouse when he liked. Monna Lisa, whose thrift had already begun to imagine him carrying burdens and fetching water, made a show of reluctance, shook her head, and said Messer Naldo would be angry if any man were allowed about the house.

Tessa refused to believe it. Naldo had said nothing against strangers who lived nowhere. This one knew nobody except one person—and that person was not Nofri.

At last Monna Lisa gave way with the air of yielding to sin rather than choosing profit. “Well, if I let him stay for a while and carry things up the hill for me,” she said in her thick undertone, “thou must keep thy counsel and tell nobody.”

“No,” said Tessa. “I’ll only tell the bimbo.”

“And then,” Monna Lisa went on, leaning closer as if even the walls had ears, “God may love us well enough not to let Messer Naldo find out anything about it. For he never comes here but at dark; and since he was here two days ago, it’s likely he’ll never come at all till the old man’s gone away again.”

“Oh me, Monna,” Tessa said, clasping her hands, longing and complaint knotted together, “I wish Naldo had not to go such a long, long way sometimes before he comes back again.”

“Ah, child,” Monna Lisa answered, with the solemnity of the old who keep the world’s distances like proverbs, “the world’s big, they say. There are places behind the mountains; and if people go night and day, night and day, they get to Rome and see the Holy Father.”

Tessa fell silent before that mystery, rocking her baby and singing syllables with no clear words, yet full of meaning the way a lullaby is—sound shaping comfort where language cannot. Her voice tried to imitate the sweet certainty of a triple chime, as if bells could keep absence from growing.

The next morning she was unusually industrious, driven by the promise of more talk and the pleasure of making the poor old stranger glad with breakfast and the sight of her baby. But when she was ready to carry the food, she found Monna Lisa had already put him to work drawing water. The chain and bucket made their slow, familiar complaint; the water answered with its cool slap, and that little domestic rhythm—pull, creak, splash—filled the air more kindly than the city’s shout.

Tessa postponed her paternosters and hurried down, indignant on his behalf, insisting he must sit on his straw so she could sit by him while he ate. That posture delighted her all the more because it was an old posture from her other life—straw shared with goats and mules, warmth made where there was none.

“I will not let Monna Lisa give you too much work,” she said, bringing him steaming broth and soft bread. The broth carried the scent of simmered bones and herbs, simple and honest; the bread yielded under the fingers, not like yesterday’s stone. “I don’t like much work, and I daresay you don’t. I like sitting in the sunshine and feeding things. Monna Lisa says work is good, but she does it all herself, so I don’t mind. She’s not cross; you needn’t be afraid of her being cross. And now—eat that, and I’ll go and fetch my baby and show it you.”

She returned with the small mummy-case bundled close in her arms. Yet the little thing inside seemed lively enough, with unusually large dark eyes that looked out solemnly, and only the faintest promise of a nose.

“This is my baby,” Tessa said, sitting close to Baldassarre so the lantern-light touched the child’s face. “You didn’t think it was so pretty, did you? It is like the little Gesù, and I should think the Santa Madonna would be kinder to me now—is it not true? But I have not much to ask for, because I have everything now—only that I should see my husband oftener.”

She hesitated, then offered the bundle with careful pride. “You may hold the bambino a little if you like—but I think you must not kiss him, because you might hurt him.”

Her prohibition came with a soothing excuse, as if she feared he would feel slighted. Baldassarre took the child, the weight of it scarcely more than a loaf, and yet it changed the air between them.

“Poor thing! poor thing!” he said, and the depth of his voice made the pity sound like a threat. To him it did not seem that this guileless, loving young creature reconciled him to the world; rather it seemed she stood beside him against it—something tender that the world would injure, something that would need avenging.

“Oh, don’t you be sorry for me,” Tessa said quickly. “Though I don’t see him often, he is more beautiful and good than anybody in the world. I say prayers to him when he’s away. You couldn’t think what he is!”

She took the baby back with a wide, mysterious glance, almost wishing he would question her, almost craving the weight of being asked to speak more.

“Yes, I could,” Baldassarre said, and there was bitterness in him like old wine turned sour.

“No, I’m sure you never could,” Tessa said, earnest as a vow. “You thought he might be Nofri,” she added, with triumph, as if that settled everything forever. “But never mind—you couldn’t know. What is your name?”

At the question, Baldassarre’s hand went over his knitted brow. He looked at her blankly, and the blankness was not a trick. It was as if a door in his mind had been slammed and bolted, and he stood outside it.

“Ah, child—what is it?” he said.

Sometimes he remembered his name well enough; sometimes, had he been able to summon it now, he would have chosen not to give it. But a sudden demand on his broken memory struck him into helplessness. In that moment he felt nothing but the emptiness where certainty ought to have been.

Tessa, ignorant as she was, learned pity by the look on his face. “Never mind,” she said softly. “You are a stranger; it is no matter about your having a name. Good-bye now, because I want my breakfast. You will come here and rest when you like—Monna Lisa says you may. And don’t you be unhappy, for we’ll be good to you.”

“Poor thing!” Baldassarre said again—whether of the baby, of Tessa, or of something in himself that could not be named in any tongue that still lived whole on his lips.

Messer Naldo came again sooner than anyone in the Via de’ Bardi would have guessed. It was the evening of the twenty-eighth of November—only eleven days since his last ascent—and the haste of his return, like a man drawn back by a string he pretends not to feel, belonged to an impulse that had begun to tug him towards the hill of San Giorgio.

When Tito first found this lodging for Tessa—more than a year and a half ago, after his coming back from Rome—he had flattered himself that he acted merely out of kindness. The unlucky mummery of words and garlands had made the foolish little creature believe him her husband; and then, because she was a thing so pretty, so trustful, so ready to cling like a child to any hand that would not strike it, he had not had the heart to tear away her illusion. Or so he argued when he needed to stand well with his own conscience.

Yet he was not in love with Tessa. His first ideal passion had been stirred by another woman altogether—Romola—whose very presence seemed to take hold of him as the scent of warm bread takes hold of one passing a baker’s door: not a mere sweetness to be tasted and forgotten, but a nourishment that lodges itself in the blood. With Romola there was a reverence in his desire; with Tessa there was a softness, an ease, a yielding indulgence that asked nothing of him beyond smiles and caresses. His nature was too fine, his intellect too alive, to be tempted into coarseness; but he had spun a web about himself and Tessa, and once the first sticky threads were laid, the rest seemed to weave itself in spite of him—like that creeping vine that covers a wall not because the wall invites it, but because it can.

He had taken pains to keep the secret safe. Monna Lisa, who seldom stirred beyond her threshold save for two shops and a yearly confession, knew nothing of his true name or dwelling. She knew only that he paid well—well enough to make her old age comfortable—and she troubled herself little further. There was mystery, certainly: a contadina girl and a signor who came rarely and with caution. But to Monna Lisa, deaf as a post unless one shouted straight into her ear, it might well be a lawful marriage. Tessa, too, had been frightened into silence: Tito had made her believe that if she spoke of the manner of their wedding she would lose him forever. The old woman’s deafness—ironically—had served as a second lock on the door of the secret; it had saved Tessa from letting her words run away, as they had with Baldassarre.

At first Tito’s visits were rare enough to suggest he was forever travelling. They were prompted chiefly by a wish to see that Tessa was housed, fed, and harmlessly happy. And if he found his coming pleasanter than the anticipation of it—if he felt again, each time, the charm of her loving ignorance and her bright animal trust—still he had not needed her. He wanted to preserve the simplicity that made her so soothing: to keep her a true contadina, not dress her up into something she was not, not widen her world until her very talk lost its fresh piquancy and became like watered wine. He would have been shocked to see her aping another rank; he would have mourned the flower plucked and stuck into a vase among wilting exotics. So he provided little luxuries that suited her childish appetite: nuts enough to crack with squirrel joy, a bit of better bread, a small store of oil that shone green-gold in the flask, and cheese that smelt of the goats and the hillside—honest, pungent, domestic. It kept her pleased; it kept her unchanged; and, by a coincidence convenient to his own purse, it kept his expenses within bounds that left him money for his public life.

For a while, too, his conscience had been quieted by the belief that his “kindness” had simply overmastered him. On the day of his betrothal to Romola, when Tessa had pursued him with her innocent claim, he had felt real annoyance; when he set out to see her again, he had meant sincerely to tell her the truth. The intention served later as proof in his own mind that he had not planned this double life out of mere self-indulgence. In the first fervour of his devotion to Romola, he needed such proofs. Strong feeling makes its own piety. Even a man sinking in self-deceit will still shrink from offending the thing he most reveres. Tito could not yet commit, without some inward wince, a secret offence against his wedded love.

But he was careful—more careful, perhaps, because the offence was secret. And if once or twice, before Bardo’s death, the knowledge that Tessa was up the hill had tempted him to escape a little weariness of the old scholar, it had still been only an easy turning aside, like stepping out of a draughty passage into a warm kitchen where one can hear the fire crack and smell garlic rubbed on toast. The true hunger for Tessa—hunger not for her body only, but for her credulous adoration—had come much later, and it had a mark upon it as definite as an illness that alters the senses.

It was the day he first saw Baldassarre, and bought the armour.

Crossing the bridge that night with the coat of mail in his hands, he had felt a shrinking from going straight to Romola. Romola trusted him; she too knew little of the actual world’s brutal cunning. But behind her frank eyes lay a judging nature, and her trust was not the trust of a pretty creature unable to think; it sprang from nobleness—an alarming touchstone. After the shock of that day, after the living grasp of the Past on the steps of the Duomo, Tito had wanted ease—repose from self-control—somewhere he could let his mind settle itself for the morrow without caring what he looked like in the present hour. And there was Tessa: safe as a pen of kids, unconstraining as a hearth where no one asks questions. So while Romola waited and listened for him, he turned his steps up the hill.

And no wonder those steps took the same course again, eleven days later, on this November evening, when he had just recoiled from Romola’s first outburst of scorn. He could not wish Tessa in Romola’s place. Romola belonged to the world of his ambition, the world where a man with faculty and purpose seeks to plant his name. But he wanted refuge from a standard that stung him; he wanted to lie down, for an hour, where no voice of moral censure could reach him. Tessa’s little soul—so easily comforted, so quickly pleased—offered that refuge.

It was scarcely more than eight o’clock when he climbed the stone steps to Tessa’s door. Usually she heard his entrance and ran to meet him, her bare feet light, her chatter beginning before she crossed the threshold. Not tonight. When he opened the door, he saw why.

A single dim light burned above the dying fire, making the room smell of old smoke, warm straw, and the faint sweet-sour of goat’s milk spilled and dried on the earthen floor. By the bed where the baby lay, Tessa knelt, her body fallen forward, her cheek sunk on the pillow’s edge. Her brown rosary, usually hung above the picture of the Madonna with its little golden palm-branches, lay in the loose grasp of her right hand. She had gone asleep over her beads.

Tito stepped lightly across the little room and sat down close to her. Perhaps the creak of the door had slid into her dream; for within two moments she opened her eyes without any start, and remained motionless, looking at him as if the mere sight of him filled all her senses and made movement needless. When he slipped his hand under her chin and stooped to kiss her, she said, in that soft breathy wonder of hers—

“I dreamed it, and then I said it was dreaming—and then I awoke, and it was true.”

“Little sinner,” Tito said, pinching her chin, “you have not said half your prayers. I will punish you by not looking at your baby; it is ugly.”

The words, though smiling, hurt her. A child’s pride lives fiercely in a mother’s heart; and Tessa bent anxiously over the baby, pouting with distress.

“Ah, it is not true! He is prettier than anything. You do not think he is ugly. You will look at him. He is even prettier than when you saw him before—only he’s asleep, and you can’t see his eyes or his tongue, and I can’t show you his hair—and it grows—isn’t that wonderful? Look at him! It’s true his face is very much all alike when he’s asleep, there is not so much to see as when he’s awake. If you kiss him very gently, he won’t wake: you want to kiss him, is it not true?”

He satisfied her with a butterfly kiss on the warm little cheek of the bundled infant—a small mummy swaddled tight, breathing with a faint milky sweetness in the air—and then he set his hand on her shoulder, turned her face to his, and said, as if to draw her back to himself,

“You like looking at the baby better than looking at your husband, you false one!”

She was still kneeling. Now she rested her hands on his knee and looked up at him like one of Fra Lippo Lippi’s round-cheeked angels, adoring and unquestioning.

“No,” she said, shaking her head. “I love you always best, only I want you to look at the bambino and love him; I used only to want you to love me.”

“And did you expect me to come again so soon?” Tito asked, letting her prattle on because her simple sounds, like the clink of plates and the hush of a kitchen at night, soothed him. The jar of Romola’s scorn still throbbed in his nerves; he wanted noise that asked nothing—words that did not judge.

“Ah, no,” Tessa said. “I have counted the days—to-day I began at my right thumb again—since you put on the beautiful chain-coat, that Messer San Michele gave you to take care of you on your journey. And you have got it on now.” She peeped through the opening in the breast of his tunic, as if the hidden links were a charm. “Perhaps it made you come back sooner.”

“Perhaps it did, Tessa,” he said. “But don’t mind the coat now. Tell me what has happened since I was here. Did you see the tents in the Prato, and the soldiers and horsemen when they passed the bridges—did you hear the drums and trumpets?”

“Yes,” she said, and her voice took a small tremble, as if the noise had lodged itself unpleasantly in her. “And I was rather frightened, because I thought the soldiers might come up here. And Monna Lisa was a little afraid too, for she said they might carry our kids off; she said it was their business to do mischief. But the Holy Madonna took care of us, for we never saw one of them up here.” Then she drew nearer and lowered her voice, as if even walls might listen. “But something has happened—only I hardly dare tell you, and that is what I was saying more Aves for.”

“What do you mean, Tessa?” Tito said, anxiety pricking through the softness. “Make haste and tell me.”

“Yes—but will you let me sit on your knee? because then I think I shall not be so frightened.”

He lifted her onto his knee and put his arm around her; yet his face grew grave. It seemed that even here, where the fire was low and the baby slept, something unpleasant would pursue him.

“At first I didn’t mean to tell you,” she whispered, as if softness of sound could soften the deed. “Because we thought the old man would be gone away before you came again, and it would be as if it had not been. But now he is there, and you are come, and I never did anything you told me not to do before. And I want to tell you, and then you will perhaps forgive me, for it is a long while before I go to confession.”

“Yes,” Tito said, forcing gentleness. “Tell me everything, my Tessa.” He began to hope it was some little folly—some small mischief that could be laughed away.

“Oh, you will be sorry for him. I’m afraid he cries about something when I don’t see him. But that was not the reason I went to him first; it was because I wanted to talk to him and show him my baby, and he was a stranger that lived nowhere, and I thought you wouldn’t care so much about my talking to him. And I think he is not a bad old man, and he wanted to come and sleep on the straw next to the goats, and I made Monna Lisa say, ‘Yes, he might,’ and he’s away all the day almost, but when he comes back I talk to him, and take him something to eat.”

“Some beggar, I suppose.” Tito’s throat tightened. “It was naughty of you, Tessa, and I am angry with Monna Lisa. I must have him sent away.”

“No,” Tessa said quickly, eager to defend. “I think he is not a beggar, for he wanted to pay Monna Lisa, only she asked him to do work for her instead. And he gets himself shaved, and his clothes are tidy: Monna Lisa says he is a decent man.” She hesitated, her fingers picking at Tito’s sleeve as if she kneaded a little fear into crumbs. “But sometimes I think he is not in his right mind. Lupo, at Peretola, was not in his right mind, and he looks a little like Lupo sometimes, as if he didn’t know where he was.”

“What sort of face has he?” Tito asked, and his heart began a strange beating, as if it heard footsteps in the dark. Baldassarre had haunted him until the very air seemed full of his father’s breath and curses. Already, before Tessa finished, the image had leapt up in his mind—Baldassarre on straw not many yards away. “Fetch your stool, my Tessa, and sit on it.”

“Shall you not forgive me?” she said timidly, sliding from his knee.

“Yes. I will not be angry—only sit down, and tell me what sort of old man this is.”

“I can’t think how to tell you,” she said, troubled, searching for words as if they were herbs she had never gathered before. “He is not like my stepfather Nofri, or anybody. His face is yellow, and he has deep marks in it; and his hair is white, but there is none on the top of his head: and his eyebrows are black, and he looks from under them at me, and says, ‘Poor thing!’ to me, as if he thought I was beaten as I used to be; and that seems as if he couldn’t be in his right mind, doesn’t it? And I asked him his name once, but he couldn’t tell it me: yet everybody has a name—is it not true? And he has a book now, and keeps looking at it ever so long, as if he were a Padre. But I think he is not saying prayers, for his lips never move.” Her voice broke into a small frightened plaint. “Ah, you are angry with me, or is it because you are sorry for the old man?”

Tito’s eyes were fixed on Tessa, but he had ceased to see her. He saw only what her words conjured: the yellow face, the black brows, the bald crown, the book, the lost name—like a man whose native tongue has been rubbed away until his own past cannot answer when it is called. That absence in his gaze frightened Tessa more than anger would have done. She slipped down to kneel at his side again. She dared not touch him. She dared not speak.

Her fear made her fingers find the familiar comfort of the rosary as hands find bread in darkness. She lifted the beads from the floor and began telling them again, her lips moving silently, her wide blue eyes shining with anxious tears.

Tito was unconscious of her, unconscious of his own stillness. He was in that wrapt state in which the mind grips pain and presses it closer, not to soothe it but to master it. A new possibility rose before him—so sudden, so tempting, it seemed like a providence that had walked in unannounced.

Here—within a few steps—might be the Past itself, not in the public glare of the Duomo steps with witnesses and danger, but hidden behind a rough outhouse door. Here might be a chance to retrieve that moment when living hands had clutched him and he had denied them. He might be face to face with his father without any eyes to watch; he might ask forgiveness and reconciliation. He had money now from the sale of the library—money enough to carry Baldassarre away quietly, out of Florence, down to Southern Italy where, under the likely French rule, Tito had already laid foundations for patronage. Romola need never know the whole truth: she had no sure means of tying that prisoner in the Duomo to Baldassarre, nor of learning what had passed on the steps, except from Baldassarre himself. And if Baldassarre forgave, he might consent to bury the offence.

With that easy spring into relief from present misery, there rose the darker possibility: Baldassarre might refuse to be appeased, fierce-hearted as ever. Yet if he refused, things would be as before—only now there would be no witness. Tito was not preparing repentance with a white sheet and taper, for men to gape at; he was preparing a repentance that would make life pleasant again and keep all the ugliness hidden. His soft-heartedness—his craving never to stand in harsh relations with any living creature—stirred strongly now that his father was brought near. He longed to have the world cushioned again with goodwill, and he longed for it more fiercely because Romola’s scorn had left him bruised. He could smile pleadingly on those he had injured and offer kindness; his quick mind could not taste, truly, the honey of such offers on the lips of the wronged.

The opportunity hemmed in calculation. He started up and stepped toward the door.

Tessa gave a little cry as her beads slipped and dropped. The sound—small as it was—snapped Tito out of his trance. He turned quickly.

“My Tessa, get me a lantern,” he said. Then, as she rose in frightened obedience, he added, “and don’t cry, little pigeon. I am not angry.”

They went down the stairs. Tessa was about to shout the need of a lantern into Monna Lisa’s ear, as one must do with the deaf, when Tito—having opened the outer door—stopped her.

“Stay, Tessa—no. I want no lantern. Go upstairs again, and keep quiet, and say nothing to Monna Lisa.”

Before the half-minute was spent he stood alone before the closed door of the outhouse, moonlight whitening the old, paintless wood and throwing every crack into sharp relief. The night was quiet enough that he could hear, faintly, the goats’ shifting and a small scuffle of straw; the hill held the city’s distant murmurs as a shell holds sea-sound, dulled and far away.

In this last decisive moment, a tremor ran over him—a sudden shrinking from the possible tiger-glance, the possible tiger-leap. Yet why should he, young, armoured, fear an old man without a weapon? It was only a moment’s hesitation. He laid his hand on the door. Was his father asleep? Was there nothing but this plank and latch between him and the voice that could bless him—or curse him beyond bearing?

Baldassarre was not asleep.

High in the wall of the hovel was a square opening where the moonbeams fell in a pale stream. If Tito could have looked through it, he would have seen his father seated on straw, holding something that glimmered like a small white star. Baldassarre was feeling the edge of his poniard, taking refuge in sensation from a hopeless blank of thought—a gulf between his passion and its aim.

He was in one of those wretched moments when consciousness returns only to show helplessness. While there had been light he had pored over the book that lay open beside him, trying to force memory awake. He had tried to recall the names of his jewels, the symbols engraved on them—signs once vivid as dialect words in one’s mouth, now slipping away into a darkness that made him rage. At other times a name or symbol had come back, as if startled from hiding; but tonight all were gone. The effort at inward seeing ended in paralysis. He was reduced to a mad sense that he was a solitary pulse of just rage in a world full of defiant baseness. He had unsheathed his dagger, and for a long while his mind narrowed to one image and one dreamed sensation: the sensation of plunging steel into a base heart—of making the body confess what the tongue would not.

Tito pulled at the door. It dragged against the ground, as old doors do, scraping with a harsh complaint. Baldassarre started up from his dreamlike state in vague amazement, not knowing where he was. He had not yet risen fully; he was still on one knee when the door swung wide and he saw, dark against the moonlight, with the rays striking one bright mass of curls and one rounded olive cheek, the living image of his reverie—no longer shadow, but real, close, as water at the lips after thirst.

No thought crossed that thirst. In one instant, before Tito could spring back, the old man—given preternatural strength by rage—leapt forward and the dagger flashed.

In the next instant the blade snapped in two. Under the parrying force of Tito’s arm, Baldassarre fell backward onto the straw, clutching the hilt with its broken bit. The pointed end lay shining on the ground at Tito’s feet.

Tito had felt a great heart-leap of terror, a staggering under the weight of the thrust. Now he felt triumph—deliverance and safety. The armour had proved itself; vengeance lay helpless. But the triumph did not breed a devil’s impulse. Rather, seeing his father close and unable to harm him made reconciliation seem easier. Fear was gone; what remained was a naked need—stronger now for being unmixed—to be free from the knowledge that he was hated.

They looked at each other a little while: Baldassarre motionless in despairing rage, Tito bending slightly forward, listening with his whole body for some sign that the past might be turned into ease. Then Tito spoke in soft tones, as they had sounded long ago before the last parting on the shores of Greece.

“Padre mio!”

He paused. No movement. No sound but the faint restless stir of straw settling, and the far-off murmur of Florence like a city breathing in its sleep.

“I came to ask your forgiveness!”

Again he paused, letting the words hang as if they might be balm in the air. But there was no sign of change. Baldassarre lay as he had fallen, leaning on one arm, trembling—not with gentleness, but with shock and thwarted fury.

“I was taken by surprise that morning,” Tito went on, choosing what seemed to him the clearest, strongest words. “I wish now to be a son to you again. I wish to make the rest of your life happy, that you may forget what you have suffered.”

He stopped. It was useless to say more until he knew Baldassarre understood—until he saw, at least, that the mind behind those dark brows had caught the sense. Perhaps the mind was too distempered. Perhaps rage and the fall had stunned it.

Presently Baldassarre moved. He threw away the broken dagger and slowly, trembling still, began to raise himself. Tito put out his hand to help him. And so quick are men’s souls, that in the very instant when Tito felt his atonement might be accepted, a darting thought shot through him of the irksome efforts acceptance would require.

Baldassarre clutched the offered hand, raised himself, and still clutched it as he stepped close—so close that their faces were scarcely a foot apart. Then he spoke in a deep, shaking voice, each clause like a blow struck with remembered strength.

“I saved you—I nurtured you—I loved you. You forsook me—you robbed me—you denied me. What can you give me? You have made the world bitterness to me; but there is one draught of sweetness left—that you shall know agony.”

He let Tito’s hand fall. Going backward a little, he rested an arm on a projecting stone in the wall, then sank again to a sitting posture on the straw. The outleap of fury that had driven the dagger-thrust had exhausted him; but the words remained, sharp as iron on the tongue, and Tito stood in the moonlit doorway with the snapped blade at his feet as if the night itself had spoken judgment.

For several days Tito saw little of Romola, though he made it appear—by the very economy of his visits—that he was sparing her.

The morning after, he came to her with a softened voice, as one speaks in a house where someone lies feverish. He told her it would be better if she removed any small things that were peculiarly her own from the library, since agents would soon be coming to pack the antiquities. He did not name the sale again; he let it stand like a dish already carried from the table, leaving only its scent to accuse the appetite that had been mocked.
