Romola sat in her own room, near the little painted tabernacle that had always seemed to watch with fixed, tender eyes over human wavering. Tito, leaning to kiss her brow, suggested she remain there—away from the noise of strange footsteps. She assented quietly, without resistance and without consent that felt like consent. The night had been one long waking to her; and though her frame was sound and accustomed to endurance, sensation had become a dull, continuous pain—as if something within her had been struck, not once, but again and again, until the place could no longer cry out and could only ache.

Tito saw she was ill—saw it in the way her lips kept their line as if speech would tear them, in the way her gaze had withdrawn, leaving the eyes open but not receiving him. Yet he dared say no more. He only dared, perceiving her hand and brow were stone-cold, to fetch a furred mantle and lay it lightly about her shoulders, as one wraps a child who has forgotten to shiver.

And every brief interval that he returned to her the scene was nearly the same. He offered a small service, a mild word, the measured touch of tenderness that asks no questions. She seemed to have lost the power of speaking to him, or of looking at him. If she answered at all, it was with that obedience that is not submission but absence.

“Patience!” he said to himself, in the corridor where the house-sounds—the creak of boards, the faint clink of a distant vessel, the stir of servants—came and went like indifferent breaths. “She will recover it, and forgive at last. The tie to me must still remain the strongest.”

When a stricken person is slow to lift her eyes and behave as if nothing had happened, the striker glides easily into the posture of the aggrieved; he feels no bruise himself, and the sweetness of his own recent conduct is ever present to him, like a draught he has just tasted and can still savour. Tito, indeed, was not made for resentment. The constant bent of his mind was toward propitiation. He would have borne much for the sake of feeling Romola’s hand rest on his head again as it had rested on that morning when he first shrank from looking at her—when he had felt, like a man who has dropped a precious cup, the instant before the crash.

Yet waiting was not hard, because his life out of doors was growing more and more engaging to him. Often what is in strictness the slow outgrowth of the whole character may still be traced back to one impression, a single taste that lingers and begins to govern the appetite. Since that moment in the Piazza del Duomo, when he, mounted on the bales, had felt a keen pleasure in the consciousness that he could tickle the ears of men with any phrase that pleased them, his imagination had kept glancing toward political activity—toward that kind of public life which troubled Florence, like a pot forever set to boil, was always ready to demand.

Only the fresh dread of Baldassarre—waked in the same moment—had lain across that path like a huge rock in a narrow street, forcing him into the sale of the library as a preparation for possible flight, at the very instant when Florence had begun to taste new to him. That dread was nearly removed now. He must still wear his armour; he must keep ready the coolness and ingenuity by which a man turns danger into a game. But he no longer felt compelled to leave Florence and seek fortune elsewhere. His father had refused the offered atonement—had forced him into defiance; and an old man in a strange place, with his memory gone, was weak enough to be defied.

Tito’s implicit desires were shaping themselves into explicit thought. As the freshness of young passion faded, life took on for him more and more the look of play—an agreeable mingling of skill and chance, where the winnings are sweeter because one pretends they are not one’s very life. And the game in Florence promised to be rapid and exciting: revolutionary shifts, party struggle, the restless sound of crowds and councils. It was a game sure to include much of that unavowed action in which brilliant ingenuity—able to rid itself of inconvenient beliefs while keeping the one certainty that “ginger is hot in the mouth”—sees the path of superior wisdom.

No sooner were the French guests gone than Florence was agitated like a colony of ants when a sudden shadow has passed and the whole shaken order must be repaired. In the streets, in shops, at doorways where women bargained for bread and greens, in the little wine-shops where men leaned close over their cups, the same questions rose and fell, threaded through daily need: How were they to raise the money for the French king? How were they to manage war with those obstinate Pisan rebels? Above all, how were they to mend their plan of government, so as to find the best way of choosing magistrates and voting laws?

Until those questions were answered, trade would falter—flour would not grind into bread without fear, silk would not pass from loom to market without hesitation. And that large body of working men, not counted as citizens, with not so much as a vote to serve as an anodyne to their stomachs, were likely to grow impatient. Hunger hears and remembers; it is more acute than any clerk of records. Something must be done.

First, the great bell was sounded to call the citizens to a parliament in the Piazza de’ Signori. Its voice rolled across the stone like a command the city could not refuse. The sound gathered men as scent gathers bees—drawing them out of workshops and counting-houses, out of arcades, out of doorways where the day’s simple food had been set down unfinished. Voices multiplied beneath it; boots struck the pavement; the air filled with that particular Florentine mixture of argument and mirth that can, in an instant, harden into menace.

When the crowd was wedged close, and hemmed in by armed men at all the outlets, the Signoria—the Gonfaloniere and the eight Priors for the time being—came out and stood by the stone lion on the platform in front of the Old Palace. They proposed that twenty chief men of the city should be given dictatorial authority, by which for one year they might choose all magistrates and set the frame of government in order. And the people shouted assent, feeling themselves, for that moment, the electors of the Twenty.

It was a very old Florentine fashion, this “parliament,” by which the will of the few was made to seem the choice of the many. The shouting in the Piazza soon ended; but not the debating inside the palace. There the talk went on day after day and far into the night, when lamps made wavering islands of light and the air grew thick with human breath and irritation.

Was Florence to have a Great Council after the Venetian mode—where officers might be elected and laws voted by a wide number of citizens of a certain age and ascertained qualifications, without question of rank or party? Or was it to be governed on a narrower, less popular scheme, where the hereditary influence of good families would be less diluted by the votes of shopkeepers?

Doctors of law disputed, each argument served with care, like dishes set forth in splendid order: each had its own seasoning of precedent, its garnish of Latin, its aroma of public virtue. Messer Pagolantonio Soderini alleged excellent reasons for the popular scheme; Messer Guidantonio Vespucci alleged reasons equally excellent for a more aristocratic form. It was a question of boiled or roast—prejudged by the palates of the disputants—and the excellent arguing might have been prolonged a long while with no other result than deferring the cooking.

The majority inside the palace, power already in their hands, agreed with Vespucci and thought change should be moderate. The majority outside, conscious of little power and many grievances, feared change less. And outside the palace another force was steadily giving the vague desires of that majority the shape of a determinate will.

That force was the preaching of Savonarola.

Impulsed partly by the spiritual necessity laid upon him to guide the people, and partly by the prompting of public men who could get no measures carried without his aid, he was passing rapidly in his daily sermons from the general to the special—from telling his hearers they must postpone private passions and interests to the public good, to telling them precisely what sort of government they must have in order to promote that good—from “Choose whatever is best for all” to “Choose the Great Council,” and “the Great Council is the will of God.”

To Savonarola these were as good as identical propositions. The Great Council was, for him, the only practicable plan for giving expression to a public will broad enough to counteract the vitiating influence of party interest. It was a plan that would make honest, impartial public action at least possible. And the purer the government of Florence could become—the more secure from the designs of men who saw their own advantage in the moral debasement of their fellows—the nearer would the Florentine people approach the character of a pure community, worthy to lead the way in the renovation of the Church and the world.

Fra Girolamo’s mind never stopped short of that sublime end. The objects toward which he felt himself working always kept the same moral magnificence; he had no petty malice, no private grudges to gratify. Even in the last terrible days, when ignominy and torture—and the fear of torture—laid bare every hidden weakness, he could say to his importunate judges: “Do not wonder if it seems to you that I have told but few things; for my purposes were few and great.”

It was more than three weeks before every last volume, stand, bust, and casket in the Bardi library had been swaddled in straw, corded into cases, and borne away as if the very air of that room were being emptied. Romola did not close her eyes to it. Each evening, when the men’s boots and gruff calls had ceased on the stair, she took her hand-lamp and went among the littered straw and the fresh-splintered wood, pausing where a pedestal stood naked, where a familiar object lay on its side like a body flung down. At first she went with a bitter hunger for proof—proof that there was reason enough why love had fallen dead in her, why the world had turned barren. Later she went because that pain, kept warm by sight and touch, was the only strong life left to her affections. It was as if grief, by being walked through and handled, could be made to answer like a living thing.

On the twenty-third of December she knew the last packages were to go. She ran to the loggia at the top of the house, not from hope but from the need of one more pang: she could not bear that the final moment should pass without her eyes, as if by not seeing she could be accused of consenting.

The day was clouded and already edging toward dusk. The Arno ran dark, shivering under its own skin; the hills looked bruised with shadow; and Florence, with her ring of stone towers, had the hush of a city seen from above when light is too weak to pick out movement—tomb-like, as if the living had withdrawn and left only architecture to remember them. Santa Croce, where her father lay, was a deeper blot within the general dimness. Across the bridge, slow as deliberate cruelty, crawled the white load—white canvas over timber and straw—moving with the steadiness of Fate that does not hasten because haste would be mercy. It went inch by inch over the arch, and then slid into the narrow street and was swallowed. Romola felt less that she witnessed it than that her father, imprisoned beneath stones, was compelled to be conscious of it without the solace of her hand reaching his. In her imagination he lay there listening, helpless, while his hope was carried away to be buried where no name would call it back.

She remained after it had vanished, unheeding the chill that crept under her garments. The gloom soothed her, covering her like mourning cloth and keeping out the bright, discordant life of others. Then, abruptly, the great bell in the palace-tower burst out—not the iron hammer of alarm, but a restless, triumphant peal, as if someone shook victory into the air. Before its vibration had died, other bells answered from other towers, one after another, until the whole city seemed a single instrument. The sound swelled and spread; it filled the space between walls and across the river so completely that the air appeared made of ringing. And with the growing clang came little flames—signal-lights kindling between the palace turrets and along the girdling towers—quivering as if the sound itself had struck fire.

That sudden noise and leaping light wounded Romola like sharp blows. In her bitterness they were not civic rejoicing but demons’ triumph—Florence exulting at the very hour her life was being stripped bare by her husband’s treachery. Little more than three weeks ago she had been intoxicated by these same bells, hearing in the city’s gladness a prophecy of her own. Now the general joy was cruelty. It was Florence flinging out loud exultation to stun sorrow and loneliness, and she stood apart from it as from a crowd that has no ear for the one person weeping.

She told herself she would never join hands with gladness again, only with those whom gladness, by its hard nature, forgets. Rejoicing seemed mockery—men shouting paeans with heaviness in their souls and then searching their neighbours’ faces to discover whether joy truly existed. She had lost faith in the happiness she once thirsted for. It looked to her now like a soft-handed smiling thing with a narrow selfish heart—always fed, always eager to be amused, always turning away from endurance as from a bad smell.

She ran down from the loggia, pressing her hands against her ears as if she could push the sound back out of her skull. She was hurrying across the antechamber when she was startled into stillness by meeting Tito, who was coming to seek her.

His step was elastic; a radiance of satisfaction—not quite his usual easy brightness, but something more confident—shone about him. The bells had set their glitter on his face as firelight does.

“What! the noise was a little too much for you?” he said lightly, for her hands clapped tighter over her ears at the sight of him, as if the city’s clang and his presence were one assault. He took her gently by the wrist and drew her arm within his, leading her into the saloon with its painted nymphs and fauns that danced perpetually above human misery. Then he went on, speaking with the airy ease that made words seem like ornaments rather than pledges.

“Florence is gone quite mad at getting its Great Council, which is to put an end to all the evils under the sun; especially to the vice of merriment. You may well look stunned, my Romola—and you are cold. You must not stay so late under that windy loggia without wrappings. I was coming to tell you that I am suddenly called to Rome about some learned business for Bernardo Rucellai. I am going away immediately, for I am to join my party at San Gaggio to-night, that we may start early in the morning. I need give you no trouble; I have had my packages made already. It will not be very long before I am back again.”

His hand, as he spoke, held hers with an accustomed right, like one who expects no resistance, only submission under a smooth voice. He knew he had nothing to look for from her except quiet endurance. He could not even dare to kiss her brow that evening; but he pressed her hand to his lips and left her.

As the door closed, Tito felt what he had been obliged to feel for days: Romola was more unforgiving than he had imagined. Her love was not that sweet clinging instinct stronger than all judgments—the charm, as he began to see now, that makes a wife’s anger melt into need. Yet this petrified coldness was, for him, more convenient than passionate opposition. Her pride, her capacity of seeing where resistance would be useless, saved him trouble.

But the moment he was gone, the cold immobility that came over her like inevitable frost in his presence broke. She was far indeed from quiet endurance. The days since the scene that had severed her from Tito had been filled with active planning: she had been measuring out hours like portions of bread, storing up resolve as if it were provisions for a journey.

She called old Maso.

“Maso,” she said, her voice suddenly firm with decision, “we take our journey to-morrow morning. We shall be able now to overtake that first convoy of cloth, while they are waiting at San Piero. See about the two mules to-night, and be ready to set off with them at break of day, and wait for me at Trespiano.”

She meant to take Maso as far as Bologna, and then send him back with letters—one to her godfather, one to Tito—telling them she was gone and never meant to return. She had arranged everything so that secrecy might be perfect: her broken love, her broken life were not to be made a spectacle for curious eyes. Bernardo del Nero was absent at his villa, slipping away from political suspicions into his chosen refuge—land and labour—and she had paid him without seeking an interview. He did not even know the library had been sold; he would naturally conjecture that Tito had found some sudden good fortune to raise the sum. Maso, with his wintry withered age, cared for one thing—to do what she told him—and had been admitted into her confidence only so far as to understand that the journey must be hidden.

Romola did not mean to go to bed that night. When she had fastened her door, she took her taper to the carved and painted chest that held her wedding-clothes. The white silk and gold lay there, the long white veil, the circlet of pearls. A sob rose against her will; the garments looked like a shroud for dead happiness. In a tiny gold loop of the circlet a sugar-plum had lodged—a pink hailstone left from the shower of sweets. Tito had detected it first and had said it should always remain there.

And now, as she stared, memory rose in a wave so sudden that it seemed to carry her bodily backward into the time of perfect trust. She felt again the presence of the husband whose love had made the world fresh and wonderful to her, as to a child sitting still among sunny flowers—heard the gentle tones, saw the soft eyes before any lie had looked out of them, breathed again that large freedom of the soul that comes from believing the nearest being to us is also the greater. In those brief moments the tears always came: the tenderness in her, so long trained to give itself, felt akin to the bereaved mother’s pang when she imagines the tiny fingers still warm on her breast and then finds them marble to her lips as she bends above the silent bed.

But besides the white and gold there was something else in the chest: a dark coarse bundle rolled and corded. Romola turned her eyes from the bridal brightness to the roughness, and as her hands touched the serge the tears were checked. The harshness recalled her to the present as cold water recalls a fevered patient. She unfastened the thick white cord and spread the bundle on the table. It was the grey serge dress of a sister of the third order of Saint Francis—living in the world, yet set apart for pious works—one of those whom Florentines called a Pinzochera.

Romola was going to wear it as disguise. She determined to put it on at once, so that if she must snatch any sleep before dawn she would wake ready to depart. She put off her black garment. As she thrust her soft white arms into the harsh sleeves and felt the hard rope-girdle bite her fingers while she tied it, she welcomed the rude sensations. They suited the contempt she had conceived for pleasure—that dexterous contrivance for selfish ease, that shrinking from endurance when others were bending under burdens too heavy for them—which now, in her mind, had Tito’s face. Then she gathered her long hair, drew it tight back from her face, bound it in a hard knot, and took a square of black silk, tying it as a kerchief across her head and under her chin; over that she drew the cowl.

She lifted the taper to the mirror. The disguise would be complete to any one who had not lived close to her. To herself she looked strangely like Dino—only let the cheeks waste, let the eyes sink a little more, and the resemblance would be almost a sorrowful mockery. Was she becoming like him in anything else? Only in this: she understood now how men could be driven to rush away forever from earthly delight, how they could choose images of sorrow rather than of joy, as if the world’s beauty were an insult.

She did not linger at her own reflection. She began to gather and pack the relics of her father and mother—those too large for her small travelling-wallet—into the chest with the wedding-clothes, to be committed to her godfather when she was safely gone. First the portraits; then, one by one, the small objects that had sacred memory clinging to them, each going either into the wallet or into the chest with a sense of laying away pieces of herself.

She paused. There was still something to strip away, something that belonged to the past she meant to turn her back on forever. She put thumb and forefinger to her betrothal ring—but for a moment they rested there without drawing it off.

Her mind had been running like a strong current toward the act of quitting Tito, breaking an outward tie that no longer matched the inward bond. Yet the mere motion toward removing the ring brought an arresting sense, as if she were violently rending her life in two. Outward symbols have a stubborn power; they knit our active life into an external identity that does not yield easily to the wavering changes of consciousness. The ring, that small circle of gold, seemed suddenly to hold the weight of a whole history.

If the beloved Tito who had put it on her finger were not in any valid sense the same Tito she had ceased to love, why return him this sign? Why not keep it as memorial of what had been? The ring, by asserting their identity in palpable metal, shook her in a way she could not explain. Half-truths are like that: they haunt us as dull pulses never fully born into sound.

But another voice in her rose and drowned those muffled murmurs, fierce with wounded pride.

“It cannot be! I cannot be subject to him. He is false. I shrink from him. I despise him!”

She snatched the ring from her finger and laid it on the table beside the pen she meant to use. Again she clung to the one law she recognized—the law of her affections. Tenderness and keen fellow-feeling for those near and loved had been the religion of her life: it had made her patient where she was naturally impetuous; it could have made her heroic. Now that strength was gone—or rather it had become the strength of repulsion. She recoiled from Tito in proportion to the energy of the love he had disappointed, and to her lifelong devotion to her father which he had violated past forgiveness. It seemed as if every motive had slipped away except indignation and scorn, which now served her as oars to drive herself out of the harbour.

She was not following precedent, nor obeying adopted maxims. The grand severity of the stoic philosophy her father had made familiar was ready on her lips; its lofty spirit had stirred echoes in her. But she had never used it as rule. She had endured and forborne because she loved; and maxims that told her to feel less, to hold her heart loose lest Nature’s onward course should jar it, had been powerless against her tenderness—just as they had been powerless against her father’s yearning for fame. She had appropriated no theories. She had simply lived strong in affection; and life without that energy came to her as a new problem.

She meant to solve it in what seemed a simple way: to cut herself loose from the man she loved no longer. Her mind had never bowed to obligation except where personal love and reverence were concerned; other human relations had never pressed upon her with equal reality. Now, she felt, she had only one thing to obey—the instinct to sever herself.

Yet that firm resolution did not save her from shifting anguish. When the preparations were nearly complete, she lingered. She put off writing the irrevocable words that would part her from her little world. The past weeks rushed in again with cruel speed and seized even her limbs: she sat to write, and her hand fell. Tears came—not the sob of remembered happiness at the pearls and pink hailstone, but bitter tears for the delusion that had blighted her youth. And with them came tingling shame at the ignominious words she had flung at Tito—“Have you robbed some one else who is not dead?” To have had such speech wrung from her, to have spoken so to her husband, felt like a stain on her whole life. Hard words between those who have loved remain hideous in memory, like seeing greatness and beauty sunk into vice and rags.

The comparison of past and present pressed on her until it turned into bodily wretchedness. She felt benumbed to everything except inward throbbing and needed some hard contact as if to keep herself from dissolving. She drew her hands tight along the harsh knotted cord at her waist. She rose and seized the rough lid of the chest: was there anything more to go in? No. She shut it, pressing her palm on the carving as if it were a rough plank to hold her up, and locked it.

Then she remembered the last details of her equipment as a Pinzochera. The large leather purse—the scarsella—must hang from her rope-girdle, with small coin in it. Her florins and small jewels, gifts from her godfather and cousin Brigida, were safely fastened within her mantle. On the other side must hang the rosary.

As she hung the rosary at her waist, it did not occur to her that more than garments might be required for her disguise—that her air, her carriage, her very eyes were as unlike as possible those of a sister trained to lowered lids and lips that moved in silent iteration. Her inexperience kept her from picturing distant details; it also fed her proud courage by shutting out foreboding of insult or danger. She knew that unhappy wives sometimes fled to friends or to a cloister; both were impossible to her. She had devised a lot of her own: to go to Venice, to the most learned woman in the world, Cassandra Fedele, and ask how an instructed woman might support herself in lonely life.

Practical difficulties did not daunt her; nor did the darkness at the end. Her life, she believed, could never be happy again, but it must not—could not—be ignoble. And with a pathetic mixture of childish romance and woman’s trial, her father’s philosophy, which had little to do with this decisive deed, still coloured her imagination of the future. So far as she could conceive her solitary loveless life, she saw it animated by proud stoic heroism and by an indistinct yet strong purpose of labour—labour that might make her wise enough to write something that would rescue her father’s name from oblivion. She was, after all, only a young girl, poor Romola, who had found herself at the end of her joys.

There were still things to do. There was a small key in a casket on the table—but now she saw her taper was dying and she had forgotten to provide another light. In a few moments the room was in total darkness. Feeling her way to the nearest chair, she sat down to wait for morning.

The thought of that key had summoned memories which, through the past week, had returned with the sharpened vividness remembered words gain when we learn a new meaning for them. Since the shock of revelation that had seemed to divide her forever from Tito, her last interview with Dino had never been absent from her mind for many hours. It solicited her the more because, while the images pressed with almost the force of sensation, they stirred thoughts within her that resisted.

Inwardly she heard again and again the dying prophetic voice: “The man whose face was a blank loosed thy hand and departed; and as he went, I could see his face, and it was the face of the great Tempter… And thou, Romola, didst wring thy hands and seek for water, and there was none… and the plain was bare and stony again, and thou wast alone in the midst of it. And then it seemed that the night fell, and I saw no more.”

She saw again the wasted face, the straining gaze at the crucifix, the awe that had compelled her to kneel, the last broken words and then the unbroken silence. The scene had been like a sudden opening into a world separate from all her lifelong knowledge. It came back now not as tale but as presence—sound remembered so vividly she could almost hear the thin breath stop.

Yet her mind roused itself to resist impressions that, from being mere phantoms, seemed to grow solid even in daylight. As a strong body struggles against fumes more violently when they begin to stifle, a strong soul struggles against phantasies more urgently when they threaten to govern in place of thought.

What had Dino’s vision to do with her real sorrows? The fitting of certain words was chance; the rest was vague—nay, those words themselves were vague, determined by nothing but Dino’s memories and beliefs. He believed pagan learning fatal; he believed celibacy holier than marriage; he remembered their home and the objects in the library; out of such threads, his vision had been woven. What warrant could she have for believing and acting on it? None. True as the foreboding had proved, she could still see with unshaken conviction that to have renounced Tito in obedience to a warning like that would have been meagre-hearted folly. Her trust had been delusive, but she would choose again to have acted on it rather than become a creature led by phantoms and broken whispers, in a world where there was the large music of reasonable speech and the warm grasp of living hands.

And yet those memories persisted, linking themselves with her present lot, offering her a narrow glimpse into lives she had never understood—the lives of men and women led by inward voices and images. She heard herself think, in the darkness, as if speaking to another self:

“If they were only a little stronger in me, I should lose the sense of what that vision really was, and take it for prophetic light. I might in time get to be a seer of visions myself, like the Suora Maddalena, and Camilla Rucellai, and the rest.”

She shuddered. All her instruction, all the main influences of her life had fortified her scorn of that sickly superstition—men and women with eyes too weak for daylight, sitting in dark swamps and trying to read destiny by the chance flame of wandering vapours.

Yet she was conscious of something deeper than mere coincidence of words. Something in her was moved by the idea of Dino’s experience and by the fellowship it implied—a supreme fellowship with suffering. If there were much more of such experience in the world, she felt she would like to understand it; would like to know what thoughts could make men sink in ecstasy before painted agonies of martyrdom. There seemed to be something there beyond madness. Around her, all springs felt dried; she wondered what other waters existed where men drank and found strength in the desert.

And then, in the darkness, the memory returned of those moments in the Duomo when she had sobbed with a mysterious mingling of rapture and pain while Fra Girolamo offered himself as willing sacrifice for the people—moments that came back like a brief taste of some far-off fountain. But again she shrank from the allure of impressions that would draw her into the sphere of visions and narrow fears—those fears that had compelled Dino to outrage natural affection.

She sat waiting for the morning, in her coarse serge, with the rope at her waist and the rosary hanging at her side, while outside the city’s bells died slowly into distance and the winter night settled over Florence like ash over a fire.

Romola was wakened by a light tapping—timid as a moth’s wing—at her chamber-door. The cold, unseasoned light of early morning lay flat in the room, turning every surface to a pale truth. Maso had come for the travelling-wallet.

When she opened, the old man started as if a draught had struck him. He had been used to the graceful outline crowned with her shining hair; now there were only the thick folds of a grey mantle and, beneath the dark cowl, a face blanched and shadowed, as if night had not quite released it.

“It is well, Maso,” she said, forcing steadiness into her voice, as one might hold a knife firm while the hand trembles. “Here is the wallet—quite ready. You will go on quietly, and I shall not be far behind you. When you get out of the gates you may go more slowly, for I shall perhaps join you before you get to Trespiano.”

She closed the door on him gently, as though even a latch might make too loud a sound in a house still asleep. Then her fingers sought the key she had taken from the casket as the last act of the night.

It was the original key of the little painted tabernacle. Tito had forgotten to drown it in the Arno. Such small things lodge themselves where the eye does not think to look—caught in a corner of the embroidered scarsella he had worn with his purple tunic. Long after their marriage Romola had found it there; she had put it by, not using it, but keeping a quiet, inward satisfaction that the means of opening was within reach.

The cabinet on which the tabernacle stood had been moved close to a window; the wan morning made the painted forms just discernible to her, who knew them by heart: triumphant Bacchus with his clusters and vine-clad spear, clasping crowned Ariadne; Loves showering roses; a wreathed vessel; dolphins with cunning eyes; and the rippled sea, all circled by a border of flowers like a bower promised by some gentler world.

She looked at those familiar images and felt a new bitterness, sharper because of the chill. The pictures were not a tomb where sorrow might lie quiet; they were a screen that had lied. Foolish Ariadne—gazing up as if that bright face with hyacinthine curls, tendril-like among the vines, held the deep secret of her life.

“Ariadne is wonderfully transformed,” Romola thought. “She would look strange among the vines and roses now.”

She took up the mirror and looked once more at herself. The morning light made the sight so strange—so like the outline of a figure already withdrawn from its former name—that she set the mirror down again, shrinking, almost as strongly as she had shrunk from the joyous Ariadne.

For the cowl around her face brought back a dread that had haunted her since childhood: the dread of being drawn, at last, into fellowship with what she had always despised—into the company of howling fanatics and weeping nuns. She had wrapped herself in their outward sign, and felt it like a garment that did not belong to her skin.

Hastily—too hastily to allow herself a second thought—she thrust the key into the tabernacle. It turned. She opened it and took out the crucifix without looking; her fingers trembled as they found the little ring. She passed a cord through it, hung it round her neck, and hid it within the bosom of her mantle as one hides a spark under ashes.

“For Dino’s sake,” she said inwardly. That name, like an old dialect word spoken in the dark, carried meanings no dominant speech could translate.

Still, there were letters to be written—letters Maso was to carry back from Bologna. She wrote them briefly, as if too many words would only make a louder echo.

The first was to Tito:

“Tito, my love for you is dead; and therefore, so far as I was yours, I too am dead. Do not try to put in force any laws for the sake of fetching me back: that would bring you no happiness. The Romola you married can never return. I need explain nothing to you after the words I uttered to you the last time we spoke long together. If you supposed them to be words of transient anger, you will know now that they were the sign of an irreversible change.

“I think you will fulfil my wish that my bridal chest should be sent to my godfather, who gave it me. It contains my wedding-clothes and the portraits and other relics of my father and mother.”

She folded the ring inside that letter—as if sealing a vow turned to ash—and wrote Tito’s name outside.

The next letter was to Bernardo del Nero:

“Dearest Godfather,—If I could have been any good to your life by staying I would not have gone away to a distance. But now I am gone. Do not ask the reason; and if you love my father, try to prevent any one from seeking me. I could not bear my life at Florence. I cannot bear to tell any one why. Help to cover my lot in silence. I have asked that my bridal chest should be sent to you: when you open it, you will know the reason. Please to give all the things that were my mother’s to my cousin Brigida, and ask her to forgive me for not saying any words of parting to her.

“Farewell, my second father. The best thing I have in life is still to remember your goodness and be grateful to you.

“Romola.”

Romola placed the letters, along with the crucifix, within the bosom of her mantle. The paper lay against her as bread might lie against a traveller’s ribs—thin, necessary, carrying the last taste of home. Now everything was done. She was ready to depart.

No one stirred in the house. She went down the stairs almost as quietly as a grey phantom and out into the silent street. Her heart beat violently, yet there was a strange enjoyment in the firmness of her tread on the broad flags—in the swiftness of movement, like a chained resolution at last released.

Anxiety to carry through the act, and dread of hindrance, kept sorrow at bay. When she reached the Ponte Rubaconte, she felt less that Santa Croce was near than that the yellow seam of morning, splitting the grey, was widening; and unless she hastened, she must meet faces—voices—questions. She was keenly aware, too, of the city’s waking sounds beginning to thicken: a shutter lifted, a distant hinge complaining, the first hollow roll of a cart somewhere far off. Florence, even before it spoke, prepared to be loud.

Her simplest road led on to the Borgo Pinti and then along by the walls to the Porta San Gallo. That path took her by the Piazza di Santa Croce. She walked through it steadily, rapidly, not trusting herself to look towards the church. It was not devotion that pulled at her, but the fear of being seen: the thought that eyes might turn on her with curiosity and recognition, and that indifferent minds might begin to speculate on her private sorrows. The very idea felt like a physical torture. She felt degraded even by that act of her husband from which she suffered helplessly—degraded because the shame was public the moment it became known, and Florence was a city where talk moved like wind through streets.

But no windows opened to watch the tall grey sister with the firm step and the proud carriage of the cowled head. Her way lay aside from the early traffic; and when she reached the Porta San Gallo it was easy to pass, for a dispute was going forward about the toll on panniers of eggs and other market-produce just entering. The argument rose and fell—voices sharp, then muffled—like the cluck and scold of a waking farmyard. It made a veil of sound behind which she slipped unnoticed.

Out. Once past the houses of the Borgo she would be beyond Florence’s last fringe; the sky would widen above her, and she would have entered on her new life: loneliness and endurance, but freedom. She had been strong enough to snap the bonds she had accepted in blind faith. Whatever befell, she would no more feel the breath of soft hated lips warm upon her cheek; no longer feel the breath of an odious mind stifling her own.

The bare wintry morning and chill air were welcome in their severity. Leafless trees and sombre hills did not wear the masks of beauty and joy—the gods she had forsaken for ever. Yet presently the light burst forth with sudden strength, flinging shadows across the road, as if the sun would chase away all greyness by force.

In such moments light is felt like a divine presence—not as a thought, but as something that stirs the deepest, inarticulate sensibilities. It awakens the shadows instantaneously, and with them a kind of awe. So the great momentousness of her act became more conscious as she walked in the impalpable golden glory—and saw, stretched before her, the long shadow of herself that could not be escaped.

Hitherto she had met no one but an occasional contadino with mules; and the many level turnings had prevented her from seeing that Maso was not far ahead. But when she had passed Pietra and began to rise, she lifted the hanging roof of her cowl and looked eagerly forward.

She let it drop again at once.

She had seen, not Maso, but two monks approaching within a few yards. The edge of the cowl had made a pent-house on her brow; for the last minutes she had been looking only at the brightness on the path and her own tall shrouded shadow like a dread spectre. Now she wished she had not looked up.

Her disguise made her especially dislike encountering monks. They might expect pious passwords, some accustomed phrase, some dialect of devotion she did not know how to speak; and she walked on with a careful appearance of unconsciousness until the black skirts passed by her. Their footsteps went down-hill and faded quickly; but the meeting had set her heart beating in a new, uneasy way. There was shame in this studied concealment, and it grew sharper under actual glances when she was striving to seem unaware.

Seeing a great flat stone against a cypress that rose from a projecting green bank, she yielded to the desire—born of the slight shock—to sit and rest. She turned her back on Florence, not meaning to look that way until the monks were quite out of sight. When she was seated she raised the edge of her cowl again and discerned Maso and the mules at a distance where it was not hopeless to overtake them; the old man would likely linger, expecting her.

Meanwhile she might pause a little.

She was free and alone.

Tito’s journey to Rome—so neatly timed that it loosened, without a show of violence, the knots that held Romola in Florence—was decided as such things often are, not with a trumpet-blast of statecraft, but over a supper-table the evening before.

He went towards that supper in the temper of a man who expects his pleasures to come garnished with advantage. There would be meats chosen with care, wines that had slept long in cool darkness, and company whose names, spoken aloud, made a sort of music in the mouth. The place itself promised a graceful kind of ease: the Selva, the Orto de’ Rucellai—the Rucellai gardens—where laurels and ilex made corridors of deep green, and torches turned their polished leaves to hammered metal.

Bernardo Rucellai, the master of that ground, was Florentine to the marrow: wealthy, learned, practised in public life, and careful that even his pleasures should wear the look of antiquity. His very name carried an old commerce in it, as if one could smell the sea on the rocks where the little lichen clung—_orcella_, _roccella_—drinking in light through its pale stems until, by a secret handling, it gave it back in a purple-red stain. A Levant trader had brought that dye, _oricello_, to Florence long before Bernardo’s time; and from that gained colour—so grateful to the human eye—the family had taken its softly altered Tuscan name. Bernardo stood out upon that purple background with added splendours: alliances with the Medici, embassies, the gonfalonier’s dignity, a palace, a church façade faced in black and white marble, rare trees planted and tended, antiquities gathered as other men gather spices, and a Latin so pure it might have been strained like clear broth through linen. His garden had become a kind of second academy since Lorenzo’s death: a place where grave men met under clipped greenery, tasting old words and old histories as if they were preserved fruits.

The invitation had reached Tito through Lorenzo Tornabuoni with a weight that made it feel less like an entertainment than a summons. Florence was hungry with public questions; and Tito, who had learned to detect the flavour of politics even beneath sweet sauces, felt sure that party purposes would be advanced by the same hands that served stewed fish and poured old Greek wine. Bernardo was not only influential; he was one of the chosen Twenty who for three weeks had held the city’s reins. That knowledge warmed Tito’s spirits as much as any spiced draught could have done. Without it, he might have found room for uneasy conjecture as to whether the distinguished were to be also dull; for he had supped in the Rucellai gardens before, and remembered evenings where a man was expected not merely to assent to an entire scheme of the universe—which would have cost Tito no effort—but to swallow its exposition from first origin to last ripeness, course after course, without so much as a crust of relief.

The night was dark; only at intervals, when Tito crossed the small circle of light cast by a lamp before an image of the Virgin, did his figure take shape enough for recognition: tall, graceful, his mantle folded with that ease which made his very movements seem composed. And at each such pool of light, a watcher might have seen another figure keeping pace behind him: thickset, elderly, in a serge tunic and a felt hat—moving with a dogged persistence that was not the common drift of passers-by.

When Tito halted at the gate of the Rucellai gardens, the follower halted too.

The _sportello_, the smaller door within the great gate, was already held open by a servant distracted by some question and slow to close and chain it again after the last arrival. Tito slipped in quickly, gave his name, and passed along the path between evergreen bushes that shone as if they had been oiled and laid over metal.

The other man entered as well.

“Your name?” the servant demanded, turning at last.

“Baldassarre Calvo,” came the answer without a stumble.

“You are not a guest. The guests have all passed.”

“I belong to Tito Melema, who has just gone in. I am to wait in the gardens.”

The servant hesitated. “I had orders to admit only guests. Are you a servant of Messer Tito?”

“No, friend, I am not a servant; I am a scholar.”

There are men who, if you say “I am a buffalo” with quiet conviction, will step aside and let the creature go by. The porter gave way. Baldassarre entered, and heard the door shut and chained behind him—an iron sound that seemed to set a seal on what he had come to do—as he vanished among the glossy, torchlit leaves.

Those short, ready answers marked a great change in Baldassarre since the last time he had stood face to face with Tito, when rage had driven him to the dagger and the dagger had snapped in two like dry twig. The change had come with suddenness, as if some inward knot had been cut.

When Tito’s shadow had passed before the hovel as he went homeward, Baldassarre had been sitting in that exhausted tremor which follows a great outburst—the body helpless as after fever, yet the mind sometimes curiously clear, as if the passion had burned away a smoke that usually lay between a man and his memories. He had felt unable to rise. His limbs were numb; a chill was on him; his hands shook. But around him there was no longer the habitual dimness and slipping phantoms. Images stood firm. His past lay open and continuous, a long road that had seemed to lead only to a taste of bitterness at the end.

For a while he was too absorbed even to note the miracle: he simply lived those years again. Then the clearness travelled, as light runs along a wall, and came to rest on what had just happened. He knew where he was. He remembered Monna Lisa, and Tessa—and with them, the meaning that had been hidden from him like a word heard but never understood.

So—_he_ was the husband. The husband whose wife had another wife in the Via de’ Bardi.

Something in him urged flight: to gather up the broken dagger, to go, to leave no trace behind; for in that poor remnant of self-respect it seemed that hiding his feebleness was the nearest thing to power. He leaned and took up the fragments. Then his eye went to the book lying open at his side.

It was a fine, large manuscript—Pausanias, oddly bound, a volume that in other years he had known as one knows the feel of a well-used knife in the hand. Moonlight lay on the page. He could make out the big letters at the head: ΜΕΣΣΕΝΙΚΑ. ΚΒ′.

An hour or two earlier, those characters had been nothing to him but black marks—like weather-stains on a wall. Now they were signs again: not dead ink, but the old magic that summons whole worlds.

With that moonbeam on the page, Messenia rose before him: its struggle against Spartan oppression, the long bitterness of the conquered. He snatched up the book. The light was too thin to read by; but he did not need to read. He knew the chapter. He read inwardly.

He saw Aristocrates the traitor, stoned by the whole people—stone after stone cast by hands that had suffered—cast out unburied, and a pillar set up with verses telling how Time brings justice home to the unjust. The words rose in him and set off innumerable vibrations, as when a single struck string wakes others hidden in the instrument. He forgot his age. He could have shouted aloud. The light had come back—mother of knowledge and joy!

In that exultation his limbs found strength. With broken dagger and book, he went out under the broad moonlight. The air was sharp and frosty; he felt no cold, only a glow, as if inward fire had taken the place of warmth. He walked the open spaces of that high ground, pausing where the city lay spread beneath him: domes and towers sleeping darkly under their sleeping guardians, the mountains; the river’s pale gleam; the valley trailing away toward peaks of snow. What had been a weary maze was now something he could command. He felt, in that rare moment of clearness, the strange mental empire common to us all at times, but to him doubled by contrast with long days when memory had been only the ache of something lost.

His mind flashed through Florence as through a familiar house: streets, houses, men’s names, their alliances and grudges, the secret ways by which influence moved. He was once more a man who knew cities, who had travelled, who had been trained by wide experience to see with an instructed vision. And the keen delight of it was the delight of language itself—the sensation of having names again, as if he had recovered taste and smell after illness. Names were not mere tokens; they were full of places, of voices, of remembered accents—Greek and Tuscan, each with its own grain and savour that could not be exchanged without loss. He ran through that wealth like an heir let suddenly into his inheritance.

Yet even while the mind exulted, one End presided within him—a dark deity shut in the innermost chamber. It only seemed forgotten while its sacrifice was being prepared.

When the first triumph had spent itself, his thoughts gathered and fastened on Tito.

That fair, slippery viper should not escape him now. Thanks to this struggling justice, the heart that had never quivered with tenderness had its selfish fibres—sensitive only for itself—that could be reached by pain’s sharp point. The soul that bowed to no right bowed to the great lord of mortals, Pain. Baldassarre felt he could search out every secret of Tito’s life now. He knew some already, and the broken dagger—what looked like frustration—had been the beginning of achievement.

Perhaps that sudden rage had shaken loose the obstruction that had stifled his soul. Twice before his memory had returned in patches when danger had whipped him into action: once when he had defended himself against an enraged dog; once when waves had overtaken him and he had scrambled up a rock to save himself. But what if, as then, the light were to die again, and the dreary blank return? Even as he feared it, the fear seemed to begin a weakening. He thought, with a kind of alarm, that his excited vigil on the hill was burning up his strength, and that he might sink the faster for it. He searched anxiously for shelter, for some corner where he could lie down out of the wind. At last he nestled against a heap of warm garden straw—straw that held, as straw does, a faint sour-sweet breath of last summer’s stalks and the animals that had fed on them—and so fell asleep.

When he opened his eyes it was daylight.

For the first moments he was bewildered, as if he were two men and did not know which one had awakened: the dim creature of sensibility without knowledge, living among shadows like the sad heir of fallen greatness—or the man of recovered power. Surely the last; for the night returned to him at once: the recognition of Pausanias, the crowding resurgence of facts and names, the wide prospect on the hill that had given him a waking like that of some Maenad, amazed at morning on a mountain-top.

He took up the book again. He read—and remembered without reading. A name was enough: with it rose deeds, places, faces; the chain of association held firm. A deed recalled a name, and the mind linked them as deftly as a cook binds a sauce back to smoothness after it has threatened to break—patient heat, the right motion, the secret proportion. The fibres were active still. The self he had recovered had not fled.

But what he found there, in those remembered histories, was not comfort. There were tales of inexpiable crimes; and there were tales, too, of guilt that seemed to prosper. Sanctuaries existed for swift-footed miscreants; baseness had armour; the weapons of justice sometimes snapped against it, as his dagger had snapped. What then? If baseness triumphed everywhere else—if it could heap up the goods of the world and even hold the keys of hell—it could never triumph over the hatred it had itself awakened. It could invent no torture greater than the torture of submitting to its smile. In Baldassarre there burned an emotion that asked for no motive, feared no consequence, needed no nourishment beyond itself—a fire that consumed all other desire.

Now, in the clear morning, gladness came back only as the hope of vengeance. From that day until the evening when he entered the Rucellai gardens, he had been ceaseless in inquiry—cautious, patient, watchful—learning Tito’s position and circumstances, contriving almost daily to follow his movements. He did not wish to raise alarm. He wanted a moment chosen like a cut made where the nerve lies exposed: when Tito was at the summit of confident ease, surrounded by men whose favour he depended on, in the very air of approval.

He did not seek payment, nor the public recognition of himself for his own sake. His whole soul bent toward one thing: to find the sharpest edge of disgrace and shame by which a selfish smiler could be pierced; to send through Tito’s marrow the most sudden shock of dread. He could lie hard; he could live scantily. He spent most of what money he had left to buy another poniard. Hunger and thirst came to him like they come to the poor every day; he fed them when he must, without pleasure, on coarse bread and whatever thin wine he could procure. The only exquisite thing he desired was an exquisite vengeance.

He avoided, too, those who might carry word to Tito. He never entered Nello’s shop, though he saw Tito go there; he turned aside to avoid meeting Piero di Cosimo. The very possibility of frustration sharpened his eagerness; and with it ran another trembling urgency: the fear that his memory might slip away again. Whether from that fear’s agitation or from some other cause, he had twice felt a mental dizziness, a wavering, as if the inward sense were beginning to lose the distinct forms of things. Once he had tried to enter the Palazzo Vecchio and reach a council-chamber where Tito was, and had failed.

But this evening—this evening, as he followed Tito into the torchlit green of Bernardo Rucellai’s garden and heard the chain fall behind him—he felt that the occasion had come at last.

On stepping into the pavilion, Tito’s eyes travelled with their quick, practised ease over the gathered faces, and what he read there confirmed what he had already guessed on the path through the gardens: this was no mere supper thrown for pleasure, but a supper meant to do the old Florentine work of binding men together—politics kneaded into bread, sealed with wine, and made easier to swallow by laughter.

The Rucellai were among the few in Florence who still understood the ceremony of a great table. In a city that prided itself on sober living, there were households where abundance was treated almost as a public language—where the ordering of courses and the choice of spices spoke as plainly as any speech in the Palazzo. Here, splendour had the decent excuse of tradition. And if the talk would not rise to the high altitudes that once belonged to these gardens, no one minded the bust of Plato looking on: marble could be made to bless anything, from philosophy to stewed fish, and the frescoed Virtues on the walls could endure a little good eating without blushing.

That same Plato had watched, in other seasons, a different sort of feast. After Lorenzo’s death the gatherings of the Platonic Academy had been transplanted here; and on the thirteenth of November—said to be Plato’s own day—the scholars would come, their moderation carefully displayed, their admiration less so. Under laurel branches, the old marble brow had looked down on Mirandola’s youth and Mirandola’s later humility; on Marsilio Ficino’s patient mind made almost soft by too single a diet of thought; on Poliziano, whose Latin had blood in it; and earlier still on Alberti, large and vigorous as an oak among reeds—artist and inventor, poet and engineer at once. Their names were the loud ones; behind them were the quieter labours, like furrows made by hands long dead—work that fed later generations without being thanked.

Bernardo Rucellai himself would have held a place among such men even without this pavilion and this table. Not yet old—four-and-forty—and already wearing that air of guarded dignity which makes an introduction feel like a privilege. He had the reputation of an amazingly pure Latinity, and the shrewdness not to be trapped into displaying it for any curious foreigner. To-night he greeted Tito with a favour more marked than usual, and placed him between Lorenzo Tornabuoni and Giannozzo Pucci—young men of the Medicean side, polished, watchful, and hungry for their chance.

Before any serious word could be risked, the household’s ritual softened the company into a single breathing creature. The great brass bowl went round, warm water scented with herbs—rosemary and something sharper that lifted like citrus when it met the skin. Men held out pale hands heavy with rings; droplets slid from knuckles into the basin and were caught again by the servant’s cloth. Wax-lights made the damp fingers gleam. The air carried the clean, faintly starchy fragrance of fresh white damask newly come from France, and underneath it the more persuasive smell of the kitchen—fat turned sweet in heat, wine simmered down, pepper waking as if it had a voice.

The first remarks were as light as the first mouthfuls: gossip and jokes served as a prelude, like little salted things that invited thirst.

“What would Dante’s old Florentine say,” some one asked, “if you brought him back under his leathern belt and bone clasp and set him down before silver forks?”

That notion ran round, brightening each man into an ancestor for a moment. It was agreed, with a comfortable air of wisdom, that posterity would always look indecent to the dead.

Meanwhile the forks—newly fashionable, their silver tines flashing—toyed with those small dishes that are meant to awaken appetite without satisfying it: morsels of liver cooked to the precise point where resistance ceases and the richness spreads, warm and yielding, across the tongue. The brass service had enamelled silver centres; men admired the workmanship between bites. Naturally the talk found its way to the confetti dish: Antonio Pollajuolo’s masterpiece, and Pollajuolo himself seduced, as they said with half envy, by patronising Popes from Florence to a Rome more glittering than any Florentine family could provide.

“Ah, I remember,” said Niccolò Ridolfi, a middle-aged man with that negligent ease which is in truth the most long-trained form of command. “I remember our Antonio in a fury about his chiselling and enamelling. He took to painting out of spite—‘The artist who puts his work into gold and silver,’ said he, ‘puts his brains into the melting-pot.’”

“And his foreboding may prove true enough,” said Giannozzo Pucci. “If this pretty war with Pisa goes on, and the revolt spreads, it is not only our silver dishes that will go. Antonio’s silver saints round the altar of San Giovanni may vanish some day from the eyes of the faithful—to be worshipped more devoutly as coin.”

“The Frate is preparing us for that already,” Tornabuoni said, with a laugh that tried to sound careless. “He tells the people God will not have silver crucifixes and starving stomachs—says the church is best adorned with the gems of holiness and the fine gold of brotherly love.”

“A very useful doctrine for war-finance,” Bernardo Rucellai observed dryly, “as many a condottiere has found. But politics come after the confetti, Lorenzo—when we can drink wine enough to wash them down. They are too solid to be taken with roast and boiled.”

“Yes, indeed,” Ridolfi answered. “Luigi Pulci would have said this delicate boiled kid must be eaten with an impartial mind. I remember a day at Careggi—Luigi rattling as usual—maintaining that nothing perverted the palate like opinion. ‘Opinion,’ said he, ‘corrupts the saliva—that’s why men took to pepper. Scepticism is the only philosophy that doesn’t bring a taste in the mouth.’ ‘Nay,’ says poor Lorenzo de’ Medici, ‘you must be out there, Luigi. Here is this untainted sceptic, Matteo Franco, who wants hotter sauce than any of us.’ ‘Because he has a strong opinion of himself,’ Luigi flashes out—‘which is the original egg of all opinion.’ He a sceptic? He believes in the immortality of his own verses. Poor Luigi—his mind was sharpest steel; it could touch nothing without cutting.”

“And yet gentle-hearted,” said Pucci. “His talk seemed to me only soap-bubbles—yet he went into dithyrambs about eating and drinking, and was as temperate as a butterfly.”

Course followed course with the assured gravity of wealth. After roast and boiled came capon and game, and then the crowning caprice: a peacock cooked, they said, after Apicius’s receipt for partridges—roasted with the feathers on, and then arranged so that it might look, at a distance, like a living bird at rest, its glossy colours saved for the eye while the flesh within had been sacrificed to fashion. A confidential servant—the official carver—approached it almost as a priest approaches an altar, and with respectful skill turned the classical, insipid creature to expose the plucked breast, from which he dispensed the delicate slices to each of the honourable company.

Hardly any one dared refuse. To decline would have sounded like a criticism of the host, of tradition, of rank itself. Tito quoted Horace with airy grace, then broke his slice into harmless fragments and scattered them over his plate as if he were feeding a bird. Bernardo Rucellai made a learned remark about the ancient price of peacocks’ eggs, and did not pretend to eat. Ridolfi held a mouthful balanced on his fork while he told, as if it were the most natural thing in the world, a favourite story of Pulci’s about a man of Siena who wished to give a splendid entertainment at a moderate cost, so bought a wild goose, cut off its beak and webbed feet, and boiled it in its feathers to pass it for a pea-hen.

Very little peacock went down any throat; but that did not matter. The company had the satisfaction of knowing the peacock had been served; the dish had done its social work. To sit where such foolish expense could be offered without apology was to feel oneself, for an hour, inside the circle of the city’s richest men—inside the language of privilege. And at such a time, when Fra Girolamo’s sermons were teaching Florence to suspect luxury as a sin against the hungry, even silence about the peacock’s toughness had its politics.

Beyond the pavilion’s warm breath of candle-smoke, wine, and spiced fat, the gardens lay in chill obscurity. In that darkness a solitary man moved in widening and narrowing circuits like something driven by a string pulled tight.

Baldassarre paused among the trees and stared in at the windows. Each window was a bright picture cut out against the gloom: rings flashing, cups lifted, heads thrown back in laughter. He could hear the interlacing voices, that peculiar music of a table where men speak at once and understand one another through habit as much as through words. He saw Tito’s gestures—careless, graceful, as if his whole body were fluent in persuasion—and heard Tito’s voice rise and fall, now distinct, now mingling into the merry confusion.

Baldassarre’s mind was strung to a pitch that made the sounds inside feel like blows. He was preparing himself for the moment when he could force an entrance—when he could step from this cold into that light and make the light serve his vengeance. And the sight of Tito’s easy gaiety gave him a savage satisfaction: the victim was fattening himself, laughing, warming his blood, making his nerves more tender for torture.

But the men among the branching tapers could know nothing of the pale fierce face outside. Light can be a curtain as well as darkness.

Within, as the dishes grew heavier and the wine more liberal, the talk, like a stream, deepened and turned from glitter to current. The sense of citizenship pressed on every mind just then; even indifferent men felt the city’s pulse. What Fra Girolamo was saying and prompting lay under all conversation, like a bass note you cannot ignore. Before the stewed fish was removed and while the favourite sweets still waited, his name rose, despite Bernardo Rucellai’s earlier prohibition, to the surface again. Politics slipped in as easily as sauce.

At first, while servants were still within earshot, it was only gossip: what had been done in the Palazzo on the first day of voting for the Great Council; how hot-tempered and domineering Francesco Valori was, as if austere virtue gave him a right to command; how any one who heard Soderini’s speeches and also listened to the Frate’s sermons could tell they were kneaded in the same trough.

“My opinion is,” Ridolfi said, “the Frate has a longer head for public matters than Soderini, or any Piagnone among them. Depend upon it, Soderini is his mouthpiece more than he is Soderini’s.”

“No, Niccolò,” said Bernardo Rucellai. “There I differ. The Frate has an acute mind; he sees quickly what serves his ends. But Pagolantonio Soderini has long experience—has studied the Venetian Council. He is not likely to be much indebted to a monk for ideas. No: Soderini loads the cannon—Fra Girolamo brings the powder and lights the match. He is master of the people, and the people are getting master of us. Ecco!”

When the room was at last clear of servants and only wine moved from hand to hand, Lorenzo Tornabuoni leaned forward, and the loosened restraint of privacy made his voice warmer.

“Whether Soderini is indebted or not,” he said, “we are indebted to the Frate for the general amnesty that has gone along with this scheme of the Council. We might have done without fear of God and reform of morals being passed by majority of black beans; but the excellent proposition that our Medicean heads should be allowed to remain comfortably on our shoulders—and that we should not be obliged to hand over our property in fines—has my warm approval. And you may rely upon it, Fra Girolamo is as firm as rock on that point of promoting peace. I have had an interview with him.”

A murmur ran along the farther end of the table. Men leaned, listening. Bernardo Rucellai only nodded, as if he had expected it and wished Tornabuoni to continue.

“Yes,” Tornabuoni went on, “I was favoured with an interview in the Frate’s own cell—not a common favour. I believe even Francesco Valori seldom sees him in private. But I think he saw me the more willingly because I was not a ready-made follower; I had to be converted. And for my part, I see clearly enough the only safe policy for us Mediceans is to throw our strength into the scale of the Frate’s party. We are not strong enough to make head on our own behalf; and if the Frate and the popular party were upset, every one here knows perfectly well what other party would be uppermost just now—Nerli, Alberti, Pazzi, the rest—Arrabbiati, as somebody christened them the other day—who, instead of giving us amnesty, would fly at our throats like mad dogs, and not be satisfied till they had banished half of us.”

Assent broke out—short, emphatic sounds, the clink of a cup set down.

“A wise dissimulation,” Tornabuoni continued, “is the only course for moderate rational men in times of violent party feeling. I need hardly tell this company what my real attachments are. I am not the only man here tied personally to the banished family. But apart from that, I agree with older friends—who allow me to speak before them—that the only lasting peaceful state for Florence is the predominance of some single family interest. The Frate’s theory—that we are to have a popular government where every man strives only for the general good, knows no party names—may do for some island of Cristoforo Colombo’s finding, but will never do for our fine old quarrelsome Florence. A change must come. With patience and caution we may determine the change in our favour. Meanwhile, the best thing is to keep the Frate’s flag flying, for if any other were hoisted now it would be a black flag for us.”

“It’s true,” Ridolfi said curtly. “What you say is true, Lorenzo. For my part, I am too old for any one to believe I’ve changed my feathers. And there are certain of us—old Bernardo del Nero for one—whom you would never persuade to borrow another man’s shield. But we can lie still like sleepy old dogs; barking would be no use. As for this psalm-singing party who vote for nothing but the glory of God, and talk as if vice could be swept out with a besom by the Magnificent Eight, their day will not be long. After all the talk of scholars, there are but two sorts of government: one where men show their teeth, and one where they show their tongues and lick the feet of the strongest. They’ll get their Great Council finally voted to-morrow—that’s certain—and think they’ve found a new plan. But as sure as there’s human skin under every lucco in the Council, the new plan will end like every other—in snarling or in licking. That’s my view as a plain man. Not that I think it becoming in men of family, with others depending on them, to go hunting reasons in the air like doctors of law. I say frankly, as head of my family, I shall be true to my old alliances; and I’ve never yet seen a chalk-mark on political reasons to tell me which are true and which false. Bernardo Rucellai is a man of reasons, I know; I’ve no objection to anyone spinning fine reasons for me—so long as they don’t interfere with my actions as a man who has faith to keep.”

“If that is an appeal to me, Niccolò,” Bernardo Rucellai answered with a formal dignity almost comic beside Ridolfi’s blunt ease, “I may say that while my wishes are partly determined by long-standing relations, I cannot enter into positive schemes with persons whose actions I cannot control. I myself might be content with a restoration of the old order—only with modifications, important modifications. And on one point I concur with Lorenzo Tornabuoni: our friends should throw the weight of their interest into the scale of the popular party. For myself, I condescend to no dissimulation; nor do I at present see the party or scheme that commands my full assent. In all there is crudity, confusion; and of all the twenty men who are my colleagues in the present crisis there is not one with whom I do not find myself in wide disagreement.”

Ridolfi shrugged, leaving that to stand. Wine warmed the room into competing voices; several men wanted the lead at once, and as usual the company broke into little knots, pairs and trios, the way a loaf breaks along its natural seams.

This was precisely what Lorenzo Tornabuoni and Giannozzo Pucci had foreseen. They were among the first to turn away from the broad public talk and draw Tito into a closer, quieter conversation—pushing their seats back, turning their backs half to the table as if to create, by posture alone, a private chamber within the larger one.

“In truth, Melema,” Tornabuoni said, crossing one hose-clad leg over the other and caressing his ankle in an idle, self-possessed way, “I know no man in Florence who can serve our party better than you. You see what most of our friends are—men who can no more hide their prejudices than a dog can hide the tone of his bark; or else men with ties so notorious they must always be suspected. Giannozzo and I, I flatter myself, can overcome that suspicion—we have that power of concealment and finesse without which a cultivated man is at a disadvantage compared with a wild bull or a savage. But except yourself, I know no one on whom we could rely for necessary discretion.”

“Yes,” Pucci added, laying his hand with friendly possession on Tito’s shoulder, “you can help us better than if you were Ulysses himself. For I am convinced Ulysses often made himself disagreeable. To manage men one must have a sharp mind in a velvet sheath. And there is not a soul in Florence who could undertake a business like this journey to Rome with the same safety you can. Your scholarship is always a pretext for such journeys; and better than scholarship is your talent. Niccolò Machiavelli might have done for us if he had been on our side—hardly so well. He is too much bitten with notions; he hasn’t your power of fascination. All the worse for him. He has lost a chance, and you have got it.”

Tornabuoni lowered his voice as if he were sprinkling spice into a dish that must not taste too strongly of itself.

“You have only to play your game well, Melema, and the future belongs to you. The Medici will keep a foot in Rome as well as Florence; the time may not be far when they can make a finer career for adherents than in old days. Why should you not take orders some day? There is a cardinal’s hat at the end of that road, and you would not be the first Greek to wear it.”

Tito laughed—lightly, almost musically. His intelligence measured the exaggeration; yet the flattery had a pleasant savour, like a rich sauce tasted at the tip of the tongue.

“My joints are not so stiff yet,” he said, “that I can’t be induced to run without so high a prize. The income of an abbey or two held in commendam—without the trouble of getting my head shaved—would satisfy me at present.”

“I was not joking,” said Tornabuoni, with grave suavity. “A scholar is always the better for taking orders. But we’ll speak of that another time. One object now is that you should win the confidence of the men who hang about San Marco. That is what Giannozzo and I shall do; but you can carry it farther, because you are less observed. In that way you can know their doings thoroughly, and make a broader screen for your agency on our side. Nothing can be done before you start for Rome—this business between Piero de’ Medici and the French nobles must be effected at once. I mean when you come back, of course; I need say no more. You could make yourself the pet votary of San Marco if you liked; but you are wise enough to know effective dissimulation is never immoderate.”

“If it were not that adhesion to the popular side is necessary to your safety as our agent,” Pucci said, more fraternal, less patron-like than Tornabuoni, “I could have wished your skill employed in another way, for which it is even better fitted. But now we must find some other man among us to get into the confidence of our sworn enemies, the Arrabbiati. We need to know their movements more than those of the Frate’s party, who are strong enough to play above-board. Still—it would have been difficult for you, with your known relations to the Medici a little while back, and your wife’s sort of kinship with Bernardo del Nero. We must find a man with no distinguished connections, who has not yet taken any side.”

Tito, almost without thinking, pushed his hair backward—his habitual gesture when he felt the pressure of a plan forming under words. He looked straight at Pucci; a barely perceptible smile rested on his lip, as if he were tasting something sharp and promising.

“No need to look out for any one else,” he said promptly. “I can manage the whole business with perfect ease. I will engage to make myself the special confidant of that thick-headed Dolfo Spini, and know his projects before he knows them himself.”

The confidence was unusual in Tito; but his blood was lifted. A new path opened before him, and along it hung prizes higher than any he had dared to name in his own mind. Hitherto he had thought of success as favour bestowed—something one received with bows and gratitude. Now it flashed upon him as power—power possible even to a man without ancestral roots, without a party name, without beliefs that could bind him. Each group that imagined him a tool might become dependent on him; each would feed him with secrets as a kitchen feeds a favoured guest with morsels before the feast. His foreignness, his indifference to the inherited dialects of feeling and prejudice around him—things that once made him cautious—turned suddenly into advantages. In the rich mingled sound of the supper—cups clinking, voices thickening, the hush that fell and rose like wind through trees—he felt newly awake to his own adroitness, as if he had found at last the right instrument and discovered his fingers fit it.

And whatever motives might once have checked him—whatever tenderness of conscience, whatever recoil from layered falsehood—had been, by slow degrees, strangled in him by the successive falsities of his life.

When Romola lowered herself on the cold stone beneath the cypress, the place seemed to conspire in her favor, offering a kind of solitude that had the taste of clean water after a long fever. The road dipped away as if the earth itself had scooped out a hollow to hold her secrecy; beyond it the mountains sat dark and still, their outlines sharp as a knife-edge against the paling sky. The morning was spare and honest: no clatter of carts, no market cries, only a thin thread of birdsong and the soft sifting of wind through needles and leaf—sound not as tumult but as shelter, a natural hush that let her hear her own breath, and the faint pulse of fear beneath it.

Florence was behind her, along with the accustomed walls and rules and faces. Tito—already riding toward Siena—was behind her too, each hour widening the distance in the opposite direction. For the first time in all her life she felt herself alone in the presence of earth and sky, with no human will interposed to lay down a law for her.

Then, close—so close that the consonants seemed to touch the skin at her ear—a voice said:

“You are Romola de’ Bardi, the wife of Tito Melema.”

The sound struck like a hand laid suddenly on the shoulder: not violent, but arresting with a force that made the blood move.
