She knew that voice; she had heard it before, and it had always entered her like a vibration through bone. Because she knew it, she did not turn her head or lift her eyes. She sat very still, shaken by awe and yet inwardly angry with herself for being shaken at all. A monk in a black skirt dared to come between her and the open air—dared to push his words into the one quiet she had claimed. That was all. And yet it felt as if something men name Destiny had come down from its carved throne and taken fleshly hold of her.

“You are fleeing from Florence in disguise,” the voice continued. “I have a command from God to stop you. You are not permitted to flee.”

The imperative tone made her resentment flare hotter, like oil catching in a pan. She would not turn; she would not grant him the reward of seeing her face. Motionless, she said, “What right have you to speak to me, or to hinder me?”

“The right of a messenger. You have put on a religious garb, and you have no religious purpose. You have sought the garb as a disguise. But you were not suffered to pass me without being discerned. It was declared to me who you were: it is declared to me that you are seeking to escape from the lot God has laid upon you. You wish your true name and your true place in life to be hidden, that you may choose for yourself a new name and a new place, and have no rule but your own will. And I have a command to call you back. My daughter, you must return to your place.”

Each sentence tightened her like a cord. She felt herself most determined not to yield any sign, precisely because something within her had already begun to tremble, and she dreaded that tremor more than his intrusion. Her voice sharpened with irritation. “I will not return. I acknowledge no right of priests and monks to interfere with my actions. You have no power over me.”

“I know—I know you have been brought up in scorn of obedience. But it is not the poor monk who claims to interfere with you: it is the truth that commands you. And you cannot escape it. Either you must obey it, and it will lead you; or you must disobey it, and it will hang on you with the weight of a chain which you will drag for ever. But you will obey it, my daughter. Your old servant will return to you with the mules; my companion is gone to fetch him; and you will go back to Florence.”

At that, anger surged into her eyes. She sprang up and faced him.

It was Fra Girolamo—Savonarola—standing near enough that the air between them seemed a narrow passage full of his presence. She had known it already without looking; yet now the certainty came with the shock of seeing him. She was nearly as tall as he was; their faces were almost level, and her defiant words rose ready—then fell back unspoken. For she met his calm glance, and her anger, which had felt so justified a moment before, sank as if it had become suddenly irrelevant.

There was nothing theatrical in his face, nothing crafted for admiration. It was not beautiful; it was strong-featured, pared down by a will that had disciplined flesh as one disciplines a kitchen fire—kept low, kept true, allowed no wasteful blaze. The power of his gaze was not in any glitter or mastery; it was in the plain fact that it held concern for her with no taste of possession. It was as if he looked on her not as prey for rebuke, nor as a symbol to be used, but as a fellow creature in danger—one more human life bound into the common loaf of suffering. Romola had never met a glance where simple fellowship was felt like a bond; and that bond, once felt, made it hard to insist he had no authority even to speak.

She stood silent. He spoke again.

“You assert your freedom proudly, my daughter. But who is so base as the debtor that thinks himself free?”

The word debtor stung. Her face changed as if a pale light had flashed across it.

“And you are flying from your debts: the debt of a Florentine woman; the debt of a wife. You are turning your back on the lot that has been appointed for you—you are going to choose another. But can man or woman choose duties? No more than they can choose their birthplace or their father and mother. My daughter, you are fleeing from the presence of God into the wilderness.”

As her anger melted, something else rose—an uneasy presentiment that submission might contain a strength she had never tried. If this man could show her a law that was not mere constraint but truth—if he could name what she had not been able to name—then perhaps. Yet it seemed impossible that he could know what compelled her. Still, she could not simply refuse him now; reverence had edged its way into her resistance. Without forethought, she gave him a title she had never spoken to him before.

“My father,” she said, “you cannot know the reasons which compel me to go. None can know them but myself. None can judge for me. I have been driven by great sorrow. I am resolved to go.”

“I know enough, my daughter: my mind has been so far illuminated concerning you, that I know enough. You are not happy in your married life; but I am not a confessor, and I seek to know nothing that should be reserved for the seal of confession. I have a divine warrant to stop you, which does not depend on such knowledge. You were warned by a message from heaven, delivered in my presence—you were warned before marriage, when you might still have lawfully chosen to be free from the marriage-bond. But you chose the bond; and in wilfully breaking it—I speak to you as a pagan, if the holy mystery of matrimony is not sacred to you—you are breaking a pledge. Of what wrongs will you complain, my daughter, when you yourself are committing one of the greatest wrongs a woman and a citizen can be guilty of—withdrawing in secrecy and disguise from a pledge which you have given in the face of God and your fellow-men? Of what wrongs will you complain, when you yourself are breaking the simplest law that lies at the foundation of the trust which binds man to man—faithfulness to the spoken word? This, then, is the wisdom you have gained by scorning the mysteries of the Church?—not to see the bare duty of integrity, where the Church would have taught you to see, not integrity only, but religion.”

The blood rushed to Romola’s cheeks; she shrank as if he had struck her. The thought that her own act—secret flight, borrowed habit—could stand in any kinship to Tito’s falseness turned her faint with disgust. “I would not have put on a disguise,” she began; but the words broke. Her throat tightened and would not let her pass.

“And to break that pledge you fly from Florence,” Savonarola continued, “Florence, where there are the only men and women in the world to whom you owe the debt of a fellow-citizen.”

“I should never have quitted Florence,” Romola said, her voice trembling like a string drawn too tight, “as long as there was any hope of my fulfilling a duty to my father there.”

“And do you own no tie but that of a child to her father in the flesh?” His tone did not soften; it deepened, as if taking in a wider space. “Your life has been spent in blindness, my daughter. You have lived with those who sit on a hill aloof, and look down on the life of their fellow-men. I know their vain discourse. It is of what has been in the times which they fill with their own fancied wisdom, while they scorn God’s work in the present. And doubtless you were taught how there were pagan women who felt what it was to live for the Republic; yet you have never felt that you, a Florentine woman, should live for Florence. If your own people are wearing a yoke, will you slip from under it, instead of struggling with them to lighten it? There is hunger and misery in our streets, yet you say, ‘I care not; I have my own sorrows; I will go away, if peradventure I can ease them.’ The servants of God are struggling after a law of justice, peace, and charity, that the hundred thousand citizens among whom you were born may be governed righteously; but you think no more of this than if you were a bird, that may spread its wings and fly whither it will in search of food to its liking. And yet you have scorned the teaching of the Church, my daughter. As if you, a wilful wanderer, following your own blind choice, were not below the humblest Florentine woman who stretches forth her hands with her own people, and craves a blessing for them; and feels a close sisterhood with the neighbour who kneels beside her and is not of her own blood; and thinks of the mighty purpose that God has for Florence; and waits and endures because the promised work is great, and she feels herself little.”

Romola lifted her head, driven by the need to vindicate herself from the picture his words painted—a woman slipping away for ease, to find some sweeter table elsewhere. “I was not going away to ease and self-indulgence,” she said. “I was going away to hardship. I expect no joy: it is gone from my life.”

“You are seeking your own will, my daughter. You are seeking some good other than the law you are bound to obey. But how will you find good? It is not a thing of choice: it is a river that flows from the foot of the Invisible Throne, and flows by the path of obedience. I say again, man cannot choose his duties. You may choose to forsake your duties, and choose not to have the sorrow they bring. But you will go forth; and what will you find, my daughter? Sorrow without duty—bitter herbs, and no bread with them.”

Bitter herbs. The phrase was plain, homely, and it landed in her body with the force of a remembered taste: greens pulled too young and boiled too long, the mouth puckering with astringency, the belly left empty for lack of real food. In that single image he made her imagined exile seem thin—an austere bowl set before her with no sustaining loaf beside it.

“But if you knew,” she said, and her hands clasped tightly as though to keep her from flying apart, “if you knew what it was to me—how impossible it seemed to me to bear it.”

“My daughter,” he said, and his hand lifted, pointing—not at her face, but at the cord around her neck, “you carry something within your mantle; draw it forth, and look at it.”

She started; yet the impulse that ruled her now was to do what he commanded. Her self-doubt had been seized by a will stronger than her own. She drew out the crucifix and held it, trembling.

“There,” Savonarola said, still indicating it, “is the image of a Supreme Offering, made by Supreme Love, because the need of man was great.”

He paused. Romola’s fingers shook around the small, hard shape; the wood felt colder than the morning air. A sudden gulf opened between her present and her past self—between the woman who now clutched the crucifix as if it could anchor her, and the girl who had first taken it from this very man’s hands. What a long road lay between those moments—paved with words, silences, betrayals, duties fulfilled and duties avoided. And if life had held so many secrets since then, what else still waited, unimagined?

When his voice sounded again, she pressed the crucifix against her mantle with a quick, involuntary movement, as one might press warm bread to the chest to keep its heat, and she looked at him with more submission than before.

“Conform your life to that image, my daughter; make your sorrow an offering: and when the fire of Divine charity burns within you, and you behold the need of your fellow-men by the light of that flame, you will not call your offering great. You have carried yourself proudly, as one who held herself not of common blood or of common thoughts; but you have been as one unborn to the true life of man. What! you say your love for your father no longer tells you to stay in Florence? Then, since that tie is snapped, you are without a law, without religion: you are no better than a beast of the field when she is robbed of her young. If the yearning of a fleshly love is gone, you are without love, without obligation. See, then, my daughter, how you are below the life of the believer who worships that image of the Supreme Offering, and feels the glow of a common life with the lost multitude for whom that offering was made, and beholds the history of the world as the history of a great redemption in which he is himself a fellow-worker, in his own place and among his own people! If you held that faith, my beloved daughter, you would not be a wanderer flying from suffering, and blindly seeking the good of a freedom which is lawlessness. You would feel that Florence was the home of your soul as well as your birthplace, because you would see the work that was given you to do there. If you forsake your place, who will fill it? You ought to be in your place now, helping in the great work by which God will purify Florence, and raise it to be the guide of the nations. What! the earth is full of iniquity—full of groans—the light is still struggling with a mighty darkness, and you say, ‘I cannot bear my bonds; I will burst them asunder; I will go where no man claims me’? My daughter, every bond of your life is a debt: the right lies in the payment of that debt; it can lie nowhere else. In vain will you wander over the earth; you will be wandering for ever away from the right.”

Inside her, forces grappled: the immense personal influence of the Frate—his emotion and belief like a bell that set the air trembling—and her own dawning sense that his words named a law higher than any she had obeyed before. Yet resistance still clung, like dough that will not at once take the yeast. One thought rose sharp and desperate.

“How, then, could Dino be right?” she said. “He broke ties. He forsook his place.”

“That was a special vocation. He was constrained to depart, else he could not have attained the higher life. It would have been stifled within him.”

“And I too,” Romola said, lifting her hands to her brow, her voice pulled out as if she were being dragged toward torture. “Father, you may be wrong.”

“Ask your conscience, my daughter. You have no vocation such as your brother had. You are a wife. You seek to break your ties in self-will and anger, not because the higher life calls upon you to renounce them. The higher life begins for us, my daughter, when we renounce our own will to bow before a Divine law. That seems hard to you. It is the portal of wisdom, and freedom, and blessedness. And the symbol of it hangs before you. That wisdom is the religion of the Cross. And you stand aloof from it: you are a pagan; you have been taught to say, ‘I am as the wise men who lived before the time when the Jew of Nazareth was crucified.’ And that is your wisdom! To be as the dead whose eyes are closed, and whose ear is deaf to the work of God that has been since their time. What has your dead wisdom done for you, my daughter? It has left you without a heart for the neighbours among whom you dwell, without care for the great work by which Florence is to be regenerated and the world made holy; it has left you without a share in the Divine life which quenches the sense of suffering Self in the ardours of an ever-growing love. And now, when the sword has pierced your soul, you say, ‘I will go away; I cannot bear my sorrow.’ And you think nothing of the sorrow and the wrong that are within the walls of the city where you dwell: you would leave your place empty, when it ought to be filled with your pity and your labour. If there is wickedness in the streets, your steps should shine with the light of purity; if there is a cry of anguish, you, my daughter, because you know the meaning of the cry, should be there to still it. My beloved daughter, sorrow has come to teach you a new worship: the sign of it hangs before you.”

His words did not float away into abstraction; they rooted themselves in the world she knew—streets with hunger in them, voices crying out, a city that was not merely stone but breath and sound, the shared noise of many lives. She had left that living chorus behind for this clean silence, thinking it freedom. Now, in the stillness under the cypress, his voice itself became like the city’s summons—an alarm-bell set against the temptation to vanish. It made the hush feel less like sanctuary and more like a dangerous emptiness, a place where a person might lose the language of her own people and begin to speak only to herself.

Romola felt—before she could admit it—that she would obey and go back. Something in him had interpreted that very revulsion from ease, that new fellowship with suffering which had already begun to stir within her like a slow, inevitable rising of leaven. His arresting voice had altered the conditions of her life; it seemed impossible to go on as if she had not heard it. Yet she shrank as one who sees the path she must take and sees, too, that it runs across hot lava.

And the instinctive shrinking from return to her husband woke doubts again, like a bitter taste returning after one has swallowed.

She turned her eyes away from Fra Girolamo and stood for a minute with her hands clasped before her, unmoving, like a statue set up by some forgotten roadside vow. At last she spoke, as if the words were wrung from her, still staring at the ground.

“My husband… he is not… my love is gone!”

“My daughter, there is the bond of a higher love. Marriage is not carnal only, made for selfish delight. See what that thought leads you to! It leads you to wander away in a false garb from all the obligations of your place and name. That would not have been, if you had learned that it is a sacramental vow, from which none but God can release you. My daughter, your life is not as a grain of sand, to be blown by the winds; it is a thing of flesh and blood, that dies if it be sundered. Your husband is not a malefactor?”

Romola started, the word jolting her. “Heaven forbid! No; I accuse him of nothing.”

“I did not suppose he was a malefactor. I meant, that if he were a malefactor, your place would be in the prison beside him. My daughter, if the cross comes to you as a wife, you must carry it as a wife. You may say, ‘I will forsake my husband,’ but you cannot cease to be a wife.”

“Yet if—oh, how could I bear—” She had begun to utter what she tried at once to drive back into silence, as if speaking it would make it real beyond endurance.

“Make your marriage-sorrows an offering too, my daughter: an offering to the great work by which sin and sorrow are being made to cease. The end is sure, and is already beginning. Here in Florence it is beginning, and the eyes of faith behold it. And it may be our blessedness to die for it: to die daily by the crucifixion of our selfish will—to die at last by laying our bodies on the altar. My daughter, you are a child of Florence; fulfil the duties of that great inheritance. Live for Florence—for your own people, whom God is preparing to bless the earth. Bear the anguish and the smart. The iron is sharp—I know, I know—it rends the tender flesh. The draught is bitterness on the lips. But there is rapture in the cup—there is the vision which makes all life below it dross for ever. Come, my daughter, come back to your place!”

As he spoke with growing intensity—his arms folded as they had been from the first, yet his face lit as if an inward flame fed it—Romola felt herself enclosed by the heat of his faith. Doubts that had chilled her melted away as frost melts when the sun finally finds it. She was subdued by the sense of something unspeakably great calling her—calling her not into private escape but into the common life she had tried to step out of, the city’s harsh music and hunger and prayers.

In a voice that was like a low, prayerful cry, she said, “Father, I will be guided. Teach me! I will go back.”

Almost without knowing she was doing it, she sank on her knees. Savonarola stretched out his hands over her; but whatever he felt could no longer pass through the channel of speech, and he was silent.

“Rise, my daughter,” Fra Girolamo said at last, and his voice—spare as bread in a year of scarcity—seemed to draw a straight line through the hush of the hill. “Your servant waits not far off with the mules. It is time that I go onward to Florence.”

Romola rose from her knees. The stone had chilled them through the serge; the cold had crept, thread by thread, up her bones. Yet that very chill, accepted without flinching, had been to her like a consecration. Kneeling there, she had made her yielding into an act, and the act had bruised her will so thoroughly that even the smallest motion—whether to speak, whether to beckon—felt as if it must be ordered for her, lest she fall back into the old self-command that had led her to revolt.

She lifted the edge of her cowl. On the hill’s rim, ten yards away, Maso and another Dominican stood with their backs turned, as if the world behind them were a temptation they had agreed not to taste. Below, Florence lay muffled in wintry air: a city whose sounds rose even here, faint as a distant psalm—cart wheels softened by damp earth, a bell that seemed to ring through wool, the far cry of a vendor made thin by cold. Romola looked from them back to Savonarola without speaking. The summons to Maso, she felt, must come from him and not from her—like the blessing before a meal, without which even honest hunger feels unlawful.

“I will go and call them,” he said, answering the appeal in her eyes. “And I will recommend you, my daughter, to the brother who is with me. You desire to put yourself under guidance, and to learn that wisdom which has been hitherto as foolishness to you. A chief gate of that wisdom is the sacrament of confession. You will need a confessor; and I desire to put you under the care of Fra Salvestro, one of the brethren of San Marco, in whom I most confide.”

“I would rather have no guidance but yours, father,” Romola said. The words came quickly, like breath drawn when a door is suddenly opened on a draught: she wanted the warmth she had just felt near him to continue, as one wants the hand that has steadied a knife to remain upon the wrist until the cut is finished.

“My daughter, I do not act as a confessor. The vocation I have withdraws me from offices that would force me into frequent contact with the laity, and interfere with my special duties.”

“Then shall I not be able to speak to you in private? if I waver, if—” The sentence broke. A sharp fear rose in her—fear not of punishment, but of losing the one influence that had held her like a strong spice whose scent cannot be forgotten once it has entered the cloth.

“My daughter, if your soul has need of the word in private from my lips, you will let me know it through Fra Salvestro, and I will see you in the sacristy or in the choir of San Marco. And I will not cease to watch over you. I will instruct my brother concerning you, that he may guide you into that path of labour for the suffering and the hungry to which you are called as a daughter of Florence in these times of hard need. I desire to behold you among the feebler and more ignorant sisters as the apple-tree among the trees of the forest, so that your fairness and all natural gifts may be but as a lamp through which the Divine light shines the more purely. I will go now and call your servant.”

He turned away; his robe moved with the dry, disciplined sound of wool brushed by winter air. Romola heard his steps go—measured, unseduced by haste—and the small ecology of the hill came forward again: the whisper of bare twigs, the thin scratch of grit under a sandal, the breath of a mule somewhere below shifting its load and letting out a low, patient sound like a sigh held long.

When Maso had been sent a little way in advance, Fra Salvestro came forward, and Savonarola led Romola towards him. All along, her mind had been braced to obey what was hard rather than what was easy; to resist Savonarola’s counsel now would be to snatch back independence at the very moment she was living by its renunciation, as if a fasting person should suddenly demand delicacies in the name of freedom. Still, as she came nearer, she felt the old inward shrinking from a guide who was a stranger—unknown hands at the kneading-trough of her conscience.

She bowed reverently before looking at him; but when she raised her head and saw him fully, reluctance changed into a quick, uneasy doubt that fluttered at her heart.

There are men whose mere presence is a shelter—a hearth you trust because the smoke draws clean and the sound of the fire is steady. And there are others to whom one must bring trust ready-made, like food carried in a cloth to a house where nothing is set out. That difference struck Romola at once, as Savonarola’s stern, kindled countenance gave place to Fra Salvestro Maruffi.

It was not that Fra Salvestro was repulsive. His face was handsomer than Fra Girolamo’s, his person a little taller; his manner had practiced smoothness, as of one long accustomed to the confessional whispers of noble houses, where sins are told with a careful tongue. He had been accepted as director by many among the chief in Florence, and experience had given him the phrases of exhortation as a cook has the common receipts—how much salt of warning, how much oil of comfort, when to add the name of God as if it were saffron that must not be wasted.

But his features had the uncertain look of a mind that could not pour itself wholly into one great passion or belief. The muscles of his face seemed always ready to relax out of lofty meaning, as if prose insisted on coming when poetry was demanded, not because he lied, but because he could not be possessed. The expression was like diluted wine—still wine, yet unable to warm. To an ardent nature, such shallowness is more chilling than open harshness.

Fra Salvestro, too, had that peculiar liability to visions, born—so men said—of a constitution inclined to somnambulism. Savonarola believed in the supernatural character of these visitations, while Fra Salvestro had once resisted such an interpretation and even rebuked Savonarola’s prophetic preaching. In a world thick with marvels and credulities, that contrast was no measure of greatness: the greater spirit was the one that could use belief as a flame and not as a fog.

As Fra Salvestro began to address her—offering encouragement, urging her to patience and obedience—Romola felt a faint chill steal back over her. After her first angry resistance to Savonarola had melted, she had forgotten the old dread of being drawn into sour, monkish fanaticism. But now the fear returned, not as a command, only as a weather-change: like grey cloud closing over sunrise, making the road ahead look longer, more level, more without promise.

And perhaps of all sombre roads, the one most trying is that by which we go back after having trodden it with a strong resolution. It is easy to rush forward into the unknown; it is harder to turn again toward the familiar threshold, carrying in one’s hands the newly accepted burden.

When they re-entered the city gates, light snow began to fall. It did not come down with any loud insistence—no storm with a roaring voice—but softly, in innumerable small touches. The flakes made the air seem quieter than before; they damped the far city clamour, as if Florence were wrapped in linen. Romola, the grey sister, walked hastily homeward from the Piazza di San Marco; her steps made dark marks on the thin whitening of the stones, each footprint a brief stain, as if decision itself left traces that could not be hidden.

She trod the bridge again. Beneath, the river’s sound had changed with the cold—less garrulous, more secret, as water is when it runs under a skin of ice. She turned in at the large door in the Via de’ Bardi; the familiar hinges gave their accustomed complaint, and the house received her with its own enclosed silence—a domestic silence that held stored scents: old wood, faded herbs hung long ago, the faint remnant of lamp-oil. Her cowl, laden and damp, clung about her face; the wet wool had that raw sheep-smell that winter brings out, and it made her human, bodily, unromantic in the very hour when her spirit had tried to be pure flame.

She went up to her room. She threw off the serge. She destroyed the parting letters—paper that had been meant to travel, now fed to secrecy with quick hands. She replaced all her precious trifles, as one lays back small household relics in their right places—each object a syllable of memory in a language only she could speak. She unbound her hair. She put on her usual black dress.

Instead of taking a long, exciting journey, she was to sit down again in her accustomed place. The same walls; the same window; the same narrow portion of Florence framed in stone. The snow thickened against the panes, a white, soundless persistence; and she was alone.

She felt the dreariness—keenly, as the mouth feels plain bread after spiced meats. Yet her courage was high, like that of a seeker who has struck new signs of gold in a stream-bed and will endure cold fingers and numb feet for the promise of a gleam. She was going to thread life by a fresh clue. She had thrown all the energy of her will into renunciation.

The empty tabernacle remained locked, and she placed Dino’s crucifix outside it—wood and carved pain set where the eye must meet it, as if to say that what she had shut away within herself would now be watched from without. Nothing broke the outward monotony of her solitary home until night came like a white ghost at the windows—paler than the snow, because darkness itself seemed diluted by the falling flakes.

Yet of all her days, this was to Romola the most memorable Christmas-eve: the year 1494, when the city’s bells rang through muffled air and hunger crouched in many doorways, and she sat in silence learning how large a life can be when it is reduced to one room, one conscience, and the sound of the world kept at a distance by snow.

It was the thirtieth of October, 1496. Morning lay clear over Florence, the air rinsed by an honest autumn wind that came down from the hills and through the narrow veins of street and loggia with a sound like a steady breathing. In other seasons the city would have listened for that wind—how it worried the plane leaves along the Arno, how it made the hanging shop-signs creak and the shutters clap like impatient hands. But now Florence listened past the roofs, past the bells, past the hawkers’ cracked cries, to the sea she could not see.

The sea had spoken in gales. It had flung back from the Leghorn coast the ships from Marseilles—ships that should have come heavy with corn and with soldiery. And Florence needed both with the same gnawing urgency: bread first, then men to defend the right to eat it. Hunger had a face in the streets—cheeks sharpened, lips greyed, eyes too bright—and where hunger went, pestilence hovered with its noiseless footfall, as if the very air were learning a new, poisonous music.

All Italy seemed tuned against Florence. The French king—hailed once as a new Charlemagne, sweeping into Italy with anticipatory triumph and taking Naples as easily as a man might lift a lid—had gone away again fifteen months before; and there were fears that grief for a new-born son lost had slackened what languid intention remained in him to return and set wrongs right. Against him a league had been formed—a Holy League, with Pope Borgia at its head—to “drive out the barbarians” still holding Naples. It sounded like piety, but it looked, to any clear sight, like wolves agreeing to chase off other wolves and then quarrel over the carcass. And Florence was not counted as fellow-hunter so much as meat.

Florence alone among the chief Italian states had refused to join that League, clinging still to the French alliance. The refusal had its price. Pisa, still fighting like a creature that will not be penned, was encouraged by strong forces from Venice and Milan; and the German Emperor Maximilian himself had come to help the Pisans with such troops as he had, attempting to seize Leghorn while Venetian and Genoese ships invested the coast. If Leghorn fell—if that single mouth to the sea were gagged—how were succours to reach Florence, hedged in by the Pope’s bitter ill-will and the jealous teeth of lesser states?

The government had shown a stubborn heart in this need, meeting loss and defeat with renewed effort: raising money, raising soldiers, and never forgetting the old Italian weapon of the conciliatory embassy. And, breaking with precedent, it had resolved not to shut out the starving country folk and the mendicants turned away from other gates—people who came flocking to Florence as birds come from a land of snow. The party of Savonarola held the strongest place in that government; and these acts—open gates, strained charity, endurance under isolation—were not spared criticism. The disaffected were many, and their judgments were ready: Florence ought to join the League, they said, and not draw down hostility by clinging to a foreign ally. Florence ought to feed her own citizens first, and not invite famine and pestilence within the walls by harbouring alien hunger.

Each day the want sharpened; each day the murmurs rose with it, like an undertone thickening beneath a chant. And for a month and more Fra Girolamo had been silent in the pulpit, obedient to a mandate from Rome. Silence, in a starving city, is not peace: it is the hush before outbreak. When the news came that the ships from Marseilles had been driven back and no corn was coming, the need for a voice that could pour patience into suffering became too urgent to resist. In defiance of Rome the Signoria asked Savonarola to preach; and two days before this morning he had mounted the pulpit again in the Duomo and told the people only to wait, to stand fast, and divine help would surely come. He had pledged his own body to that promise: let them strip the frock from him, he said, if Florence persevered in piety and citizenship and God did not rescue her.

But on this thirtieth there were no signs of rescue. The streets had their old sounds—carts creaking, sandals scuffing, the water murmuring under bridge-arches—yet beneath them ran the thin, perpetual note of emptiness: the hollow cough, the quarrel that began too quickly, the child’s cry that ended too soon.

Perhaps—so men whispered, with the same earnestness they put into measuring out the last handful of meal—perhaps if the precious Tabernacle of the Madonna dell’ Impruneta were brought into Florence and carried in solemn procession to the Duomo, the Mother rich in sorrows and therefore in mercy would plead for the suffering city. For a century and a half there were records: drought broken, floods stilled, pestilence scattered, famine turned away, wars averted, after the Florentines had fetched that hidden image within their walls. The high house of Buondelmonti, patrons of the church at L’Impruneta, guarded the veiled treasure with bare sword; wealth had been poured into chantings, chapels, ever-burning lights; and lands had been added until men quarrelled for the honour of serving her. The Florentines believed in her graciousness with the easy certainty with which they believed in bread when there was bread; and a proverb ran that Florence had a Madonna who would do what they pleased. When had they needed her pity more than now?

Already, the evening before, the tabernacle containing the miraculous image had been brought with high escort from L’Impruneta—six miles beyond the gate of San Piero that looks towards Rome—and had been deposited in the church of San Gaggio outside the gate, to be fetched thence by all the fraternities, trades, and authorities of Florence in ordered devotion. But the Pitying Mother had not yet crossed the threshold of the walls, and the morning rose on unchanged misery.

Not only the hospitals were full; courtyards of private houses had become refuges and infirmaries; still the want lay unsheltered. Early, as usual, members of the fraternities who made it their duty to bury the unfriended dead went searching and bearing away the bodies that had sunk by the wayside, the bier’s poles creaking to a rhythm the city had learned too well. As usual, too, women moved through the streets with the plain, swift step of accustomed mercy—women whose forms and bearing spoke of good birth even under homely cloth. They carried broth-pots that must be made to stretch, baskets of softened bread, little flasks of thin wine; their very garments were quiet, as if they would not add a harsh note to suffering.

One such figure was easily known as Romola de’ Bardi.

She wore the simplest black serge, and over her head a plain black drapery that hid all her hair save the bands of gold that rippled apart upon her brow. She was advancing from the Ponte Vecchio towards the Por’ Santa Maria—straight from the bridge into the narrow line of street—when she found her way checked by the pausing of a bier. The brethren of San Jacopo del Popolo, who went searching for unburied dead, had stopped; the men at the head stooped to examine something; and a cluster of idle workmen, their features sharpened by hunger, pressed in, all talking at once, their voices clattering against one another like tin pans.

“He’s dead, I tell you! Messer Domeneddio has loved him well enough to take him.”

“Ah, and it would be well for us all if we could have our legs stretched out and go with our heads two or three bracci foremost! It’s ill standing upright with hunger to prop you.”

“Well, well, he’s an old fellow. Death has got a poor bargain. Life’s had the best of him.”

“And no Florentine, ten to one! A beggar turned out of Siena. San Giovanni defend us! They’ve no need of soldiers to fight us. They send us an army of starving men.”

“No, no! This man is one of the prisoners turned out of the Stinche. I know by the grey patch where the prison badge was.”

“Keep quiet! Lend a hand! Don’t you see the brethren are going to lift him on the bier?”

“It’s likely he’s alive enough if he could only look it. The soul may be inside him if it had only a drop of vernaccia to warm it.”

“In truth, I think he is not dead,” said one of the brethren, when they had lifted him upon the bier. “He has perhaps only sunk down for want of food.”

“Let me try to give him some wine,” said Romola, coming forward.

At her belt she carried a small flask, and from long practice in the service of the sick she had learnt neatness where clumsiness can kill. She loosened the flask, and leaning over the prostrate body, she slipped a small ivory implement between the clenched teeth, as gently as one coaxes open a shell to save what is within. Then she let fall a few drops of wine—sharp, thin, with the scent of pressed grape-skin and cask-wood. The old man’s throat moved; the stimulus was answered: he swallowed.

She poured more, not in a flooding mercy but with the measure that respects a failing body: drop, pause, drop, listening as a cook listens to the first quiet simmer after a boil—watchful for the smallest sign that life is returning. Presently the head moved a little towards her; the eyelids lifted; and the eyes opened full upon her with the vague, wavering look of consciousness coming back as a lamp comes back when the wick is raised.

Then recognition—complete and involuntary—passed over Romola like a cold hand.

Those wild dark eyes in the sallow, deep-lined face, the white beard grown long again, were like an unmistakable signature to a remembered handwriting. Two summers had not blotted that image: the escaped prisoner she had seen in the Duomo on the day Tito first wore armour; the same terror-grasping figure in the strange sketch she had once seen in Piero’s studio. A wretched tremor took her—palpitation, faintness, as if the street beneath her had shifted. Here, perhaps, lay at last the knowledge she had been shut out from: some secret more bitter than all bitterness she had already swallowed.

For an instant she had the impulse to dart away as from a sight of horror. And then—stronger, more imperious—came the need to remain close beside this old man whom her heart, with a divination that was keener than any argument, told her had been injured by her husband.

Even in that conflict she did not cease her ministry. She still bent towards him, her right hand ready to administer more wine; her left passed under his neck to support him. Her fingers trembled, but the habit of soothing helpfulness guided them even when thought was shaken.

Baldassarre was looking at her for the first time. In the weeks before her flight and his arrest, Romola’s close seclusion in trouble had denied him the chance he had sought of seeing the wife who lived in the Via de’ Bardi; and now the descriptions he had heard of a fair, golden-haired woman fell away like foam. Hunger and exhaustion made his mind dim, but his gaze clung to her as a man clings to a sound in the dark.

“Will it not be well to carry him to the steps of San Stefano?” said Romola. “We shall cease then to stop up the street, and you can go on your way with your bier.”

They had only to move some thirty yards. By the time they reached the steps Baldassarre could make an effort to help himself down, and they propped him against the church doorway, his back to stone that held the morning’s chill. The charitable brethren lifted their poles again and passed on with their bier, the creak of wood and leather fading into the city’s restless murmur. But the circle of watchers did not fade: those who had nothing to do and much to say had increased, and now that it was certain the old man lived, the feeling grew less friendly. Respect for Romola kept voices lower, but could not sweeten them.

“Ah, they gave him his morsel every day in the Stinche—that’s why he can’t do so well without it. You and I, Cecco, know better what it is to go to bed fasting.”

“Gnaffè! that’s why the Magnificent Eight have turned out some of the prisoners, that they may shelter honest people instead. But if every thief is to be brought to life with good wine and wheaten bread, we Ciompi had better go and fill ourselves in Arno while the water’s plenty.”

Romola sat on the step beside Baldassarre. From her basket came the mild, clean smell of soft bread—bread no longer warm from the oven, but tender, meant for mouths without strength: a crumb that would not scrape the throat raw. She spoke to him quietly, as one speaks to the fevered, shaping her words so they might be taken in.

“Can you eat a little bread now? Perhaps by-and-by you will be able, if I leave it with you. I must go on, because I have promised to be at the hospital. But I will come back if you will wait here, and then I will take you to some shelter. Do you understand? Will you wait? I will come back.”

He looked dreamily, and his lips repeated only the last—like an echo caught in a vault.

“Come back.”

She opened her basket and put a piece of the soft bread into his hand, closing his fingers on it as if to teach them their duty.

“Do you keep your bread for those that can’t swallow, madonna?” said a rough-looking fellow in a red night-cap, elbowing his way nearer. The men pressed in, a hungry closeness that had its own smell—old sweat, sour wine, wool-dust, and the faint rancour that rises when bellies are empty.

“If anybody isn’t hungry,” said another, “I say, let him alone. He’s better off than people who’ve got craving stomachs and no breakfast.”

“Yes, indeed; if a man’s a mind to die, it’s a time to encourage him, instead of making him come back to life against his will. Dead men want no trencher.”

“Oh, you don’t understand the Frate’s charity,” said a young man in an excellent cloth tunic, his face unpinched by want. “The Frate has been preaching to the birds, like Saint Anthony, and he’s been telling the hawks they were made to feed the sparrows, as every good Florentine citizen was made to feed six starving beggar-men from Arezzo or Bologna. Madonna, there, is a pious Piagnone: she’s not going to throw away her good bread on honest citizens who’ve got all the Frate’s prophecies to swallow.”

“Come, madonna,” said the man in the red cap, “the old thief doesn’t eat the bread, you see: you’d better try us. We fast so much, we’re half saints already.”

The circle narrowed until there was hardly air between Romola and the coarse bodies that hemmed her. She had taken from her basket a small horn-cup; she crumbled the bread into it and moistened it with wine, not drowning it but making a sop—soft as mercy, easy for a failing throat. Through all the ugly talk she had seemed not to heed; her attention was on the old man’s mouth, the way his jaw slackened, the swallow that came too slowly.

But now she rose.

She looked round at the faces before her, and the men nearest drew back a little—instinctively, as if their nearness were a fault belonging to those behind them. Romola held out the basket of bread to the man in the night-cap. There was no reproach in her gaze, only a directness that made the words heavier than anger.

“Hunger is hard to bear, I know, and you have the power to take this bread if you will. It was saved for sick women and children. You are strong men; but if you do not choose to suffer because you are strong, you have the power to take everything from the weak. You can take the bread from this basket; but I shall watch by this old man; I shall resist your taking the bread from him.”

For a few moments there was perfect silence. The street seemed to hold its breath; even the small autumn wind sounded louder as it slid along the stone and set a shutter tapping somewhere like a nervous finger. Romola’s own face, pale and a little pinched by fasting, with the deepened eye-socket of one who has denied herself without complaint, had all the more force for its simplicity. Her hazel eyes were large and steady, and the men felt the weight of being seen—named, as it were, in the old language of conscience that hunger cannot quite kill.

The man in the night-cap looked foolish; he backed, thrusting his elbow into his neighbour’s ribs with an air of rebuke, as if he had been the one most offended by the crowd’s rudeness. The backing became general, each man eager to imply he had been pushed forward against his will; and the young man in the fine tunic had slipped away.

At that moment the armed servitors of the Signoria, beginning to patrol the line of streets through which the day’s procession would pass, came up to scatter the group that blocked the narrow way. A threatening mace made the retreat quicker. The man called Cecco sprang up the church steps out of reach and, turning, spoke to Romola with a rough respect.

“Madonna, if you want to go on your errands, I’ll take care of the old man.”

Cecco was wild-looking: a ragged tunic, shaggy and variegated with cloth-dust and clinging fragments of wool, fell away from bare bony arms and a long sinewy neck. His square jaw was shaded by bristly black beard; his bridgeless nose and low forehead made his face seem crushed down for packing; and a narrow strip of red rag tied over his ears appeared to assist the compression. Yet his voice held a note not wholly hardened.

Romola hesitated, looking at him—measuring with her eyes what she could not know.

“Don’t distrust me, madonna,” Cecco said at once, understanding her glance. “I am not so pretty as you, but I’ve got an old mother who eats my porridge for me. What! there’s a heart inside me, and I’ve bought a candle for the most Holy Virgin before now. Besides, see there, the old fellow is eating his sop. He’s hale enough: he’ll be on his legs as well as the best of us by-and-by.”

“Thank you for offering to take care of him, friend,” Romola said, with a touch of penitence for her doubt.

Then she leaned towards Baldassarre, her hand hovering a moment as if she would steady his shoulder with a promise.

“Pray wait for me till I come again.”

He assented with a slight movement of head and hand, and Romola went on, turning her steps towards the hospital of San Matteo in the Piazza di San Marco, where other hungers and other faint voices were waiting for what little comfort hands could make out of scarcity.

Romola, on her way back from the hospital, chose the longer road, letting her steps draw a wide curve toward the river as if the Arno’s damp breath might cool the fever of her thoughts. The streets had begun to smell of late-autumn smoke and sour wine lees, and from open doors came the faint, homely scents of boiled cabbage and yesterday’s bread warming on a tile—poor comfort, yet comfort still. She meant to reach the Ponte Vecchio and hasten to San Stefano in search of Baldassarre. She shrank from learning more—each new fact about him seemed like another thorn pressed into the flesh of duty—yet to leave him unlooked-for felt like abandoning a claim that had fastened itself near her heart.

But when she came to the meeting of the roads, where the Por’ Santa Maria would open at her right and the bridge lie to her left, the current of the crowd caught her and turned her. A hush fell as if a hand had been laid upon the city’s mouth; then, as one body, people dropped to their knees. Romola sank with them, her skirts gathering dust, her palms pressed together before she had time to decide.

The Cross was passing—the great Cross of the Duomo, borne high and steady like a mast in a windless sea.

When it had gone by and she rose, the change from kneeling to standing made her aware of her fatigue as sharply as a cramp. Walking had kept her mind occupied; standing left her to feel her own weight, her limbs, the slight trembling that came after long strain. Beside her, a shopkeeper—one of the hose-vendors whose face she had seen again and again beneath the Duomo vaulting—leaned toward her with the familiar, almost familial confidence Florence now gave her.

“Madonna Romola, you will be weary of standing. Gian Fantoni will be glad to give you a seat in his house. Here—his door is close. Let me open it. What! He loves God and the Frate as we do. His house is yours.”

It was a strange thing: the house in the Via de’ Bardi had become less “home” to her than this ringed body of streets, towers, and bells, where at every turning she met a look that asked help or offered fellowship. She let herself be guided through the open door on her right-hand. Up a narrow stair that smelled of wool and warm oil, she was led to an upper window. There a stout woman, with three children pressed close to her skirts, all in the plain garb of the Piagnoni, made space with reverence, as if Romola were not merely a woman but an emblem of the city’s own penitence. Bright lengths of drapery hung below the sill—cloth for hose, cloth for cloaks—like strips of captured sunset.

From that corner she could see the procession moving in solemn slowness over the Ponte Vecchio, and beyond it the river flowing out toward Santa Trinita. The air held a trembling of sound, but not the expected chanting. No wail rose, no hymn braided itself through the streets. There was only the measured tramp of feet, and the faint sweep of woollen garments brushing against one another—an austere music, as if Florence had decided that even her sorrow must be economical, saving breath as she saved flour.

The first footsteps that passed within her sight were young: a long train of Florentine youth, fresh faces beardless as peeled almonds, bearing high among them the white image of the youthful Jesus. A golden glory shone above his head; he stood by the tall cross where thorns and nails lay ready. Their shoulders moved in time like men carrying heavy sacks of grain—silent labor in a season when every household knew the precise weight of want.

After those came the Companies of Discipline, mysterious as a masked night. Each wore a garb that hid the entire head and face save for the eyes. Everyone knew these shrouded forms were citizens—men who on other days counted coin, weighed wool, argued contracts, drew up laws—yet here no one could be singled out as son or husband or father. Their individuality had been laid down like a tool at the door. They walked as symbols of a shared vow. Each company bore its color and badge, but all were swathed in the same obliterating cloth, leaving only the gaze, the bare fact of human sight, and the wordless fellowship of moving together.

Compared with these blanked figures, the monks seemed almost startlingly personal, even under tonsure and frock—faces with their own histories written in the mouth and brow. First flowed the white of reformed Benedictines; then the far longer stream of the Frati Minori, Franciscans all in grey, knotted cord at their waists, some with wooden _zoccoli_ beneath bare feet, the clack of those soles a thin percussion against the stones. There were many of them in Florence—zealous lovers of mankind, and, in that age, often haters of the Dominicans. After the grey came the black of the Augustinians of San Spirito, with more cultivated human faces above it—men who had inherited Boccaccio’s library and been, when learning was rarer, the most learned company in Florence. Then the white over dark of the Carmelites; and again the unmixed black of the Servites, that Florentine order founded by seven merchants who had forsaken gain for the Divine Mother.

Now the crowd’s breath seemed to tighten. Hearts beat faster, in hatred or in love, for over the bridge came a stream of black mantles over white scapularies. Everyone knew: the Dominicans.

Those of Fiesole passed first—black parted by white, one after another, tonsured head after tonsured head. Their mantles were coarse, many threadbare, some almost ragged; the Prior of San Marco had drawn the fraternities under his rule into strict poverty and harder discipline. Still expectation held, suspended like a pot over a low flame. Then at last, among the line of black and white, one mantle—only a little more worn than the rest—seemed singled out by a force that was not cloth and stitch. Above it was a tonsured head that might not have struck a stranger as remarkable, had it not already been fixed on bronze medals, with the sword of God on the reverse; had it not been seen ringed by an armed guard on the way to the Duomo; had it not been transfigured by the inward fire of the orator when it turned upon a multitude.

Savonarola.

No one dared break the stillness with a cry that would rise above the solemn tramp and the hush of garment-sweep; yet his ear, and every ear near him, caught a mingled sound—slow hissing that longed to become curses, and low murmurs that longed to become blessings. Perhaps he heard the balance tilt toward hatred. Two or three of his disciples near the front dropped to their knees as if divinity itself were passing. The movement ran like a subtle shock along the street-sides: some remained rigid, but most bent the knee and bowed the head.

Hatred, too, found its gesture. As Savonarola went up the Por’ Santa Maria, Romola saw, from an upper window, a man spit down upon him.

The procession did not end with him. More monks followed—the Frati Umiliati from Ognissanti, with their old glorious tradition of being among the earliest workers in the wool-trade; then Vallombrosans and other Benedictine varieties, reminding any instructed eye by niceties of form and color that in earlier ages of abuse, reformers had risen and marked a change of spirit by a change of garb. At last the shaven crowns ceased, and there came the train of secular priests.

Then, in long array, followed the twenty-one incorporated Arts of Florence, banners floating above them in proud declaration that each had its distinct function—from the bakers of bread to the judges and notaries. The word “bread” was not an abstraction in those days; it was the remembered weight of loaves, the sting of flour dust, the smell of starter kept alive like a child through lean weeks, the sound of crust cracking under a knife that had become careful and thin. Even from Romola’s window, the city’s hunger seemed to sit behind every banner like an uninvited guest.

After the Arts came the secondary officers of State, from lesser to greater, until the line of secularities was broken by the Canons of the Duomo. They carried a sacred relic: the very head of San Zenobio, enclosed in silver—the immortal bishop whose virtues were held to have saved Florence perhaps a thousand years before. Here was the nucleus of the procession. Behind the relic came the archbishop in a gorgeous cope, canopy held above him; and after him the hidden Image.

Hidden first by rich curtains of brocade enclosing an outer painted tabernacle, and within that by a more ancient tabernacle that had not been opened in the memory of living men, nor in the memory of their fathers. In that inner shrine was the image of the Pitying Mother, found long ago in the soil of L’Impruneta—found, they said, with a cry as the spade struck it. It was a story told as naturally as any household tale: a spade, a stone, a voice from earth. Myth and labor, miracle and digging, braided into one.

In former times the unseen Image had scarcely ever been carried to the Duomo without rich gifts borne before it—veils and curtains and mantles offered by emulous men and communities. People loved to recite such lists: gold, silk, jewels, the sumptuous vocabulary of devotion. And the richest tale of all was that of the poor abbess and her nuns who had no money for materials, and so—so the story went—wove a mantle of gold brocade with their prayers, embroidered and adorned it with prayers, and saw it presented in the great Piazza by two beautiful youths who spread white wings and vanished into the blue.

But today there were no gifts before the tabernacle. No donations were to be given except to the poor. That had been Fra Girolamo’s counsel: not gifts to invisible powers, but help to visible need. Altars had been raised before churches at various points, and there the oblations for the poor were laid down. Not even a torch was carried. The hidden Mother, surely, cared less for torches and brocade than for the wail of hungry people.

Florence was at extremity. She had exhausted her own strength, spent her own cunning, and could only wait for something beyond her reach—something that, in every age, has been called divine. The Frate in the torn mantle had said help would certainly come. Many faint hearts clung more to his word than to any virtue of the unseen Image. Yet there were fierce hearts, too, who held secret rejoicing that his word might be proved false. Even in prayer, power struggles moved like rats beneath a pantry floor—quick, unseen, always hungry.

Slowly the tabernacle advanced; knees bent; the air thickened with silence. The priests and chaplains from L’Impruneta stirred no party passion in the onlookers. The procession was about to close with the Priors and the Gonfaloniere. That long train of companies and symbols—silent music that stirred the mind as a chorus stirs it—was passing out of sight, and now only a faint yearning hope wrestled with habitual despondency.

Romola’s heart had been swelling—half foreboding, half with the enthusiasm of fellowship that the last two years had made habitual to her, like the very consciousness of clothing to a vain woman. She gave a deep sigh, as if released from a long inward strain, and remained on her knees from sheer languor.

Then, sudden as a knife-flash between shutters, something bright-colored darted into view on the distant bridge.

In the same instant Romola sprang up, stretched her arms, and leaned from the window. The black drapery fell from her head; the gold of her hair caught the light; her face flushed as if an inner lamp had flared. A shout burst forth at once. The last troops of the procession paused. Faces swung as one toward the distant bridge.

The bridge was already behind the newcomer: a horseman drove at full gallop along the Lung’ Arno. His bay horse ran so hard the foam streaked its sides white; his cap flew loose by his red _becchetto_; and in his hand he waved an olive-branch.

A messenger—good tidings. The olive-branch spoke before any mouth could.

But the people would not wait for the message to arrive in orderly fashion. They surged to meet him, seized his rein, pressed in, jostling and trampling. Romola, peering down through the bright cloth and the crush of bodies, recognized the rider.

It was Tito—her husband—sent a few days earlier to Pisa on a private embassy.

The recognition did not brighten her eyes anew. Her first impulse of expectation had already spent itself; what ruled her now was the need to know whether the news meant bread—real bread, ground grain, ovens lit again—relief that could be portioned into meals.

“Good news!” voices cried up at him, hoarse with hope. “Best news!” “News to be paid with hose!”—_novelle da calze_—men shouted, as if the old jest about rewarding a messenger could conjure a full granary.

“Good news,” Tito returned vaguely, smiling into their faces as they tugged his horse forward, until he gained the spot at the meeting of the roads where the Gonfaloniere and Priors awaited him. There he checked the horse, bowed low, and spoke with clear ceremony:

“Magnificent Signori! I have to deliver to you the joyful news that the galleys from France, laden with corn and men, have arrived safely in the port of Leghorn, by favour of a strong wind, which kept the enemy’s fleet at a distance.”

The words seemed to quiver through the stones and up the walls, vibrating along the streets like sound in a vaulted church. A shout tore the air, rolled along the river, broke and rose again—one wave after another. The joy ran down the line of the procession toward the Duomo; and from farther off came answering cries, fainter but obedient, like the intermediate plash across a great lake when the whole water has taken one impulse.

For minutes there was no more speaking. The Signoria themselves lifted their caps and stood bare-headed, as if before something that had come from beyond their own contrivance—from that region people named “divine” when they could not bear to call it mere chance.

At last, when the signal was given for the procession’s end to move forward again, Tito added, smiling still, his tone graceful as if laying a garnish on the truth:

“I ought to say, that any hose to be bestowed by the Magnificent Signoria in reward of these tidings are due, not to me, but to another man who had ridden hard to bring them, and would have been here in my place if his horse had not broken down just before he reached Signa. Meo di Sasso will doubtless be here in an hour or two, and may all the more justly claim the glory of the messenger, because he has had the chief labour and has lost the chief delight.”

It was well phrased—the necessary statement offered as generosity. After a word of reply from the _Proposto_, the dignified extremity of the procession moved on. Tito turned his horse’s head to follow it. Already the great bell of the Palazzo Vecchio began to swing, giving the people’s joy a larger voice—metallic, insistent, filling the air with a sound that would seep into courtyards and kitchens, into rooms where women measured the last handful of meal and listened with a fear that had become habitual.

Now that his attention was no longer held by urgent ceremony, one might have expected him to look up and recognize Romola at the window. But he seemed occupied with his cap, which, as the eager crowd led his horse, he managed to seize and set straight, while his right hand remained encumbered with the olive-branch. He wore a becoming air of weariness after exertion.

Romola made no sign. She did not lean farther out, did not call, did not lift a hand to catch his glance. She drew her black drapery over her head again and sat perfectly still.

Yet she felt almost sure Tito had seen her. He had that power of seeing everything—of letting nothing escape him—without seeming to see it at all.

The crowd had hardly rolled away toward the Piazza before Romola came down into the street and hastened to the steps of San Stefano. Cecco, drawn like the rest by that tide of bodies and bells, was gone; but Baldassarre stood where she had left him, alone against the church-door, the horn-cup in his hand as if it were the last vessel in the world that belonged to him.

Something in him had changed as if a shutter had been flung back. The vacant, half-wandering look of a mind that had returned only by fragments was gone; in its place there burned a fixed fierceness—no wild ranting, but the glare of a creature that has watched its prey pass safely beyond bars, and bites the iron with its eyes. When Romola came near and spoke, that look struck on her as though she were the very object of it. She started; then the thought came quickly—he had seen Tito.

And with that thought, against her will, there rose a thin, shamefaced hope—hope like the taste of water when one has been too long in dust: perhaps this old man was the guilty one; perhaps the dread, the secrecy, the inward recoil she had felt in her husband had not had this misery for its root. If she could bring Tito face to face with him—if she could know, and so either be set free from suspicion or be made sure of her fear.

“If you will come with me,” she said, steadying her voice as one steadies a bowl filled too near the brim, “I can give you shelter and food until you are quite rested and strong. Will you come?”

“Yes,” Baldassarre answered, and then, as if his words were for himself alone, he repeated with a hungry mutter, “I shall be glad to get my strength. I want to get my strength.”

“Come,” she said, inviting him to walk at her side; and she chose the way by the Arno toward the Ponte Rubaconte, where the air was wider, and fewer faces pressed near. Under the arch of the city’s glad sound, the river ran with a steady, indifferent swash against stone; and above it the bells pealed, rich and exultant, as if the very bronze had been fed and warmed.

“I think you are not a Florentine,” Romola said at last, trying to lead him by a small, safe thread. The bridge beneath them was thronged with the after-murmur of the procession, but here and there a pause opened, and the river’s voice crept in.

He looked round at her without speaking. Suspicion sat on him like a rough cloak; his bodily weakness made the fog in his mind thicker, not thinner, and he guarded his thought as a miser guards his last coin. But Romola’s gaze was not that of a questioner who would seize and use; it was the gaze of one who has carried burdens and learned reverence for pain. Slowly, as if against his will, he answered—

“No. I am no Florentine; I am a lonely man.”

She saw his reluctance, and dared not press him, lest he should turn away and be lost. Yet her mind would not be still. If he had been the wrong-doer, why this dread and secrecy? Why that hatred which had looked through him like a knife-blade? They went on in silence until they reached the entrance into the Via de’ Bardi. There Baldassarre turned on her with a sudden movement, as if some shock had passed through his nerves—some remembered turn of stone, some scent of a familiar lane, some old echo of footsteps.

A few moments after, Romola paused at the half-open door of the court and turned toward him. Before she could speak, he broke out—

“Ah! you are his wife.”

“Whose wife?” Romola said. The words were like the quick fall of a shutter; her heart leaped, and stood listening.

But it was impossible for Baldassarre, in that instant, to recall a name. The very force with which Tito’s image pressed on him seemed to drive out all speech that could label it. He made no answer; only looked at her with a strange fixedness, as if he would pin her to the wall with his eyes and read what he needed there.

Romola opened the door wide and showed him the court. Straw lay thick over the stones, and on it four or five sick people were stretched—bodies made small by hunger, faces sharpened, hands lying like broken twigs. Among them little children crawled or sat, tiny pale creatures biting straws and gurgling with the innocent industry of starving mouths, as if the straw itself could be turned to sweetness by persistence. The air was the mingled breath of sickness, damp straw, and scant living—yet threaded now with the far promise carried by sound: bells, bells, bells, beating the news into every alley.

“If you will come in,” Romola said, her voice trembling as if she feared to disturb that frail heap of lives, “I will find you a comfortable place, and bring you some more food.”

“No, I will not come in,” Baldassarre said. Yet he did not go. He stood arrested, weighted by impressions his mind was too confused to master—like a man in a dream who sees a door and cannot remember whether it opens toward safety or toward fire.

“Can I do nothing for you?” Romola said. “Let me give you some money that you may buy food. It will be more plentiful soon.”

She drew her scarsella, and held out her palm with several grossi—more than she would have offered to any other man in the same want; for his misery clung to her with a particular dread, and she tried to ease it as one eases a pain by pressing hard elsewhere.

He looked at the coins a little while; then he said, with the abruptness of a decision long prepared—

“Yes, I will take them.”

She poured them into his hand. He closed his fingers tightly over them as if to keep not merely the silver, but the power inside it.

“Tell me,” Romola began, almost as if she pleaded. “What shall you—”

But Baldassarre had already turned away. He walked toward the bridge again, and when he had passed it he went straight up the Via del Fosso, as if led by scent rather than sight. There was Niccolò Caparra’s shop, crowded with the bright and dark bodies of weapons—steel catching light, hilts worn smooth by hands, blades sleeping in rows as loaves sleep in a baker’s window, each with its own promise of use.

Niccolò himself was that moment in procession with the armourers of Florence; only an apprentice was in the shop—a lad whose eyes were on trade rather than on faces. Baldassarre’s hunger altered: it was not bread his gaze devoured first. His eyes chose what they wanted with the swift certainty of a starving man choosing a crust. The apprentice, less observant and less scrupulous than his master, took three grossi for a sharp hunting-knife without hesitation.

It was small enough to hide; small enough to seem almost harmless—yet its edge was keen as a confession. Baldassarre thrust it within the breast of his tunic and walked on feeling stronger, as if the blade were a bone returned to him. That sharpness might give deadliness to the thrust of an aged arm: at least it was a companion; it was a power in league with him, even if it failed. It would break against armour—but was armour always there? In those long months while vengeance had lain in prison, baseness might have grown forgetful and secure. The knife had been bought with the traitor’s own money. That was just.

Before he had taken the coins, he had known what he would do with them—buy a weapon. Yes, and if possible buy food too: food to nourish the arm that would grasp the weapon; food to nourish the body which was the temple of vengeance. When he had had enough bread, he should be able to think and act—to think first how he could hide himself, lest Tito should have him dragged away again.

With that need of hiding in his mind, he turned into the narrowest streets, where stone leaned toward stone, and the city’s great rejoicing became a muffled throb. He bought meat and bread, and sat down under the first loggia to eat. The bread was coarse, but to him it was substance, it was fuel for hatred; the meat, salt and dark, sat heavy on the tongue like an oath. Above, the bells swung into louder and louder peals of joy; the sound seized on him and made his body vibrate along with the air, yet to him it was not gladness but the voice of that strong world which was against him, ringing its triumph and leaving him outside it.

Romola watched him until he disappeared round the turning into the Piazza de’ Mozzi—half feeling that his departure was a relief, half reproaching herself for not pressing him harder, for not forcing the truth, for not learning whether there was in his lot any guiltless misery which she was not helpless to relieve. Yet what could she have done if the truth had proved to be a painful secret about her husband, added to the anxieties already weighing on her? Surely a wife might be permitted to desire ignorance of a husband’s wrong-doing—since she alone must not protest and warn men against him. But that thought caught in too many fine fibres of feeling to be followed now; she was weary, and weariness makes even a righteous tangle feel like a net over the face.

It was a time to rejoice. Help had come to Florence. She turned into the court to tell the good news to her patients on their straw beds. She closed the door behind her lest the bells should drown her voice; then she threw back the black drapery from her head so the women might see her better, and stood among them as if she were the messenger of something they could taste.

“Corn is coming,” she said. “The bells are ringing because they have brought the news.”

They all raised themselves to listen, each movement a slow expenditure. The children trotted or crawled toward her and tugged her black skirts, impatient at being so far from her face, as if her features were a warm loaf they needed near them. She yielded, weary as she was, and sat down on the straw. The little pale things peeped into her basket with the grave curiosity of hunger, pulled her hair down through their fingers, and the feeble voices around her murmured—

“The Holy Virgin be praised!”

“It was the procession!”

“The Mother of God has had pity on us!”

The words were old words—handed down like a household recipe whose measures are never written, only remembered by the tongue. In them, gratitude took the shape of names that had survived the ruin of many other names; for the poor, praise must often speak in the dominant lexicon that power has taught them, even when their own private sense of mercy has no exact translation.

At last Romola rose from the heap of straw, too tired to try and smile any longer.

“I will come by-and-by,” she said, turning toward the stone steps, “to bring you your dinner.”

“Bless you, madonna! bless you!” came the faint chorus, in much the same tone in which a few minutes before they had praised and thanked the unseen Madonna.

Romola cared a great deal for that music. Not the bells—those were too loud, too proud, too easily made to serve whatever master held the city’s rope. But the thin human sound in the court, the breaths shaping blessing, the children’s gurgles and small coughs, the rustle of straw as bodies shifted: that was a gentler sound-world, one that did not bruise the ear, one that asked rather than commanded. She had no innate taste for tending the sick and clothing the ragged, as some women have, to whom the details are welcome for their own sake like kneading dough or sorting herbs. Her early training had kept her aloof from such labours; without the inspiration of her deepest feeling, they would have been irksome, like work done in a foreign dialect that never lies easy on the tongue.

But they had become the one unshaken resting-place of her mind—the one narrow pathway where the light fell clear. If the gulf between herself and Tito, which only gathered a more perceptible wideness from her attempts to bridge it by submission, brought doubt whether the bond she laboured to be true to might itself be false—if she came away from her confessor, Fra Salvestro, or from contact with Savonarola’s disciples, with a sickening sense of their narrowness, and an almost impetuous reaction toward her old contempt for what she had once called superstition—she recovered firm footing here, among straw and fever and the plain needs that have no rhetoric.

Whatever else made her doubt, the help she gave to her fellow-citizens made her sure that Fra Girolamo had been right to call her back. According to his unforgotten words, her place had not been empty; it had been filled with her love and her labour. Florence had had need of her; and the more her own sorrow pressed upon her, the more gladness—stern, quiet gladness—she felt in the memories stretching through two long years: hours and moments when she had lightened the burden of life to others, giving not only alms but attention, not only bread but the recognition that their pain had a name in her mind.

All the ardour of her nature, which could no longer spend itself in a daughter’s tenderness or a wife’s trust, had transformed itself into an enthusiasm of sympathy with the general life. She had ceased to think her own lot could be happy—had ceased to think of happiness at all. The end of her days seemed to be the diminishing of sorrow, as one thins a broth so that many may have a portion, even if none be richly fed.

Her zeal was continually stirred to fresh vigour by Savonarola’s influence. In spite of the wearisome visions and allegories from which she recoiled when they came as stale repetitions from lips that did not burn with them, her strong affinity for his passionate sympathy and the splendour of his aims had lost none of its power. His indignation against abuses and oppression—those daily stories of Church and States—had kindled the ready fire in her also. His care for liberty and purity of government in Florence, and his constant reference of that immediate struggle to a wider regeneration, created in her a new consciousness: the great drama of human existence was not a distant pageant, but a living action in which her life had a part.

Through her daily contact with the less fortunate—through these courts where the voice was low and the air smelled of damp straw and thin broth—that consciousness grew firmer than a vague sentiment. It became a more definite motive of self-denying practice. She thought little of dogmas, and shrank from fixing her mind closely on the Frate’s prophecies of scourge and swift renewal. But she had submitted her mind to his and entered into communion with the Church because there she found an immediate satisfaction for moral needs that all her former culture had left hungry. Savonarola’s voice had given her a reason for living apart from personal enjoyment and personal affection; yet it was a reason that seemed to need feeding with forces beyond her own, and her use of the Church’s offices was like a watching and waiting—listening, as one listens in the dark for a returning step, if by any means fresh strength might come.

The pressing problem for Romola then was not controversy but endurance: to keep alive that flame of unselfish emotion by which a life of sadness might still be a life of active love. Her trust in Savonarola’s nature as greater than her own made a large part of the strength she had found, and that trust was not easily shaken. It is not force of intellect that causes ready repulsion from the aberrations and eccentricities of greatness—any more than it is sharp vision that makes the eye explore the warts on a face bright with human meaning; it is simply the negation of high sensibility.

Romola was so deeply moved by the grand energies in him that she listened patiently even when the words were strange to her inward speech—patiently, because in his living voice there was an earnestness that carried meanings no written phrase could translate. No soul is desolate while there remains a human being toward whom it can feel trust and reverence. Romola’s trust in Savonarola was like a rope stretched securely along a difficult path, making her step elastic while she grasped it.
