If it were suddenly removed, no firmness of ground could keep her from staggering—or perhaps from falling.

After the day’s loud rejoicings—after that olive-branch which chance had put into his hand and the people had pressed to their lips as if it were a consecrated herb—Tito Melema found the rest of his errands of a colder, studied sort. He halted at the Palazzo Vecchio and waited beneath its stone gaze for the return of the Ten, who held the threads of war and foreign speech; and when they came, he delivered, with a smooth fulness, what he had gathered in Pisa—those half-opened doors, those measured answers, the scent of fear and bargaining that hangs in the corridors where men decide whether cities shall be eaten like bread or spared.

He spoke as one who sets dishes in order: first the clean facts, then the seasonings—names, times, plausible intentions. Bernardo del Nero, sitting among the Ten, felt admiration forced from him as one may swallow a draught too bitter for choice but too wholesome to refuse. He would have spat it out if he could. The old dislike that had once lain dormant had risen again, sharper since the selling of Bardo’s library; and though Romola had said nothing—her silence like a locked chest that forbade prying—Bernardo’s long-used eyes read other signs. A woman’s face can keep counsel, yet it cannot hide the wasting that comes when the daily bread is made of grief. He had seen Romola move through Florence not with a girl’s step but with a pale steadfastness, and he had heard where her feet were going: to Fra Girolamo’s sermons, to the Piagnoni, to those places where the very air seems thin with fasting.

“In truth,” he said to himself, “if they are unhappy and childless, they must needs seize on some madness or some overstrained holiness. And my poor Romola—Latin and Greek have not made her less woman; they have only given her a larger pain to feel with. This Greek husband—so useful, so smooth-handled—may cut the fingers that use him. Yet—solco torto, sacco dritto—crooked furrows do fill sacks.”

With that old Florentine belief that politics must take its agents as the market takes its eels—slippery, dubious, still fit for supper—he held his peace. For Romola’s sake there were things he would not name; and beyond those he had nothing to allege except what everyone in Florence alleged and forgot: that Tito was a Greek, and that he smiled.

When his formal duty was done and the Ten dismissed him, Tito felt the day’s official labour fall from him as a cloak. He was tired, dust-dried from riding; sweat and road-grit clung to him, and his mouth tasted of leather and stale wine. Yet he did not go home. There were certain things in his scarsella—and certain thoughts in his mind—that he longed to be rid of; but the unburdening must seem accidental, never hunted after.

He walked away from the Palace with the saunter of one who has nowhere to be. The procession had ended, yet the bells still shook the air. Florence was like a kitchen after a feast where the pots are emptied but the steam and clatter linger; the streets were full of restless bodies seeking another course to the meal of joy. Since the new discipline had declared Christ the special King of the Florentines and would have all pleasures taste of piety, there was still, in many young throats shouting “Viva Gesù!”, a hunger for rougher seasoning—for stones flung in honest exuberance, for the old street-fury that made gratitude audible.

Tito could not pass without being known. Hands caught at his sleeve; mouths, hot with wine and shouting, asked questions that breathed on him like a crowd in a bakehouse. He escaped by giving them a better quarry: he told them Meo di Sasso, the true messenger from Leghorn, must be nearing the Porta San Frediano. Meo, he said, would tell more than Tito knew. So he slipped away, turning their attention as one turns boiling milk from spilling by lifting the pot at the right moment.

At the Piazza del Duomo he let his long eyes wander over the space with the look of pure idleness, though he was searching as carefully as a buyer in the market who must find a particular fish before it spoils. The day’s gathering at the Duomo had left more loungers and talkers than common about the Baptistery rails and around Nello’s shop. Tito’s glance found what he wanted—so precisely that he made his face more indifferent than ever.

A group leaned there in expensive ease. Tito seemed to notice the tallest only by chance as he half passed, turning his head with a slight greeting and tossing the end of his becchetto over his shoulder.

The man thus greeted was one who wore his claims like embroidery. He had on a tunic rich with stitched ornament and an ostentation of linen after the newest French mode; a sword and poniard hung at his belt, fine as jewellery but meant for flesh. His hat carried a red plume—a defiant flare against the new Florentine gravity, which under the Piagnoni had grown severe as Lent. His youth made his breadth—the wide face, the heavy waist—seem less the promise of strength than the stamp of coarseness; and his eyes had that rude desecrating stare which is like a bad smell in a narrow room.

He and his companions—young men too, armed and costly dressed—were laughing with a loudness that was itself a protest, as if laughter could beat down suspicion by mere noise. For there were reasons why Messer Dolfo Spini, leader of the Compagnacci—the Evil Companions—might need to prove he was not mortified. Dolfo, heir of the great house by the loggia over Santa Trinita bridge, had drawn together the dissolute youth of the old aristocratic party, enemies to Medici, enemies to the popular government, and bitterest enemies of Savonarola. They had made themselves sworn champions of extravagant suppers and the pleasant sins of the flesh, as if a well-roasted capon and a flagon of strong wine were holy relics to be defended against reformers who threatened to make the world chaste and temperate until life should taste like water without salt.

Up to this very morning Dolfo had been crying that Florence was given up to famine and ruin through her obedience to the Frate, and that salvation lay only in joining the League and driving Fra Girolamo out—sending him to Rome where, he said, he had long since been summoned by the Pope. It was not likely such a man felt pure joy now that succour had come as if to justify Savonarola’s prediction; and indeed, as Tito joined the group by Nello’s door, the laughter that broke out again rang hollow.

For at the centre of the group, leaning against the door-post, stood a close-shaven, keen-eyed young man who listened to men as others taste sauces, discerning the hidden bitterness at once. Niccolò Macchiavelli had already learned the small secrets of egoism as one learns the notes of a street: by walking it daily.

“Messer Dolfo’s head,” he was saying, “is more pumpkin than I thought. I measure men’s dulness by the devices they trust in for deceiving others. The dullest beast is he who grins and says he does not mind, just after he has had his shins kicked.” He let the circle widen as Tito came near, and his smile sharpened like a knife laid flat on the palm. “If I were a trifle duller, I should pretend to be fond of this Melema, who has got a secretaryship that would exactly suit me—as if Latin ill-paid could love better Latin that is better paid! Melema, you are a pestiferously clever fellow, in my way, and I am sorry to hear you have had another piece of good-luck to-day.”

“Questionable luck, Niccolò,” Tito answered, touching his shoulder with friendly ease. “I have got nothing by it yet but being laid hold of and breathed upon by wool-beaters, when I am as soiled and battered with riding as a tabellario from Bologna.”

At the sound of Tito’s voice, Nello the barber came forward, nimble as one who lives by keeping his hands clean while all Florence brings him its dust.

“Ah, you want a touch of my art, Messer Oratore,” he cried. “Your chin has yesterday’s crop upon it. Come, come—consign yourself to the priest of all the Muses. Sandro—quick with the lather!”

“In truth, Nello, that is what I most desire at this moment,” Tito said, seating himself. “That was why I turned hither instead of going home at once when I had done my business at the Palazzo.”

The shop smelled of warm soap and sharpened steel, of damp cloth and the faint sweetness of some herb-water that Nello used to finish a gentleman’s hair—the scent of rosemary and something citrine, like peel bruised under the thumb. Outside, the bells still shook the air; inside, the shears made a smaller music, the rasp of strop on blade a steady whisper. In that mingled sound—public thunder and domestic scraping—Florence seemed to breathe.

“Yes, indeed,” said Nello, spreading the lather with the practised stroke of one who knows how to soften what is rough. “It is not fitting that you should present yourself to Madonna Romola with a rusty chin and a tangled zazzera. Nothing that is not dainty ought to approach the Florentine lily; though I see her going about like a sunbeam among the rags that line our corners—if indeed she is not more like a moonbeam now, for I thought yesterday, when I met her, she looked as pale and worn as that fainting Madonna of Fra Giovanni’s. You must see to it, my bel erudito: she keeps too many fasts and vigils in your absence.”

Tito’s shoulders lifted in a melancholy shrug under the barber’s hands. “It is too true, Nello. She has been depriving herself of half her proper food every day during this famine. But what can I do? Her mind has been set all aflame. A husband’s influence is powerless against the Frate’s.”

“As every other influence is likely to be, that of the Holy Father included,” said Domenico Cennini, who had followed Tito in and now stood among the door-group that crowded nearer, drawn as much by politics as by the pleasant sight of a man being made handsome. “I don’t know whether you have gathered anything at Pisa about how the wind sits at Rome, Melema?”

“Secrets of the council-chamber, Messer Domenico,” Tito returned with a smile, opening his palms as if to show they held nothing. “An envoy must be as dumb as a father confessor.”

“Certainly, certainly. I ask no breach of that rule. But my belief is: if his Holiness drives Fra Girolamo to extremity, the Frate will move heaven and earth to get a General Council of the Church—ay, and would get it too; and I, for one, should not be sorry, though I am no Piagnone.”

“With leave of your greater experience, Messer Domenico,” Macchiavelli said, his thumbs hooked into his belt, his tone enjoying its own clearness as a cook enjoys a knife that cuts true, “I must differ from you—not in your wish to see a General Council that might reform the Church, but in your belief that the Frate will checkmate his Holiness. The Frate’s game is impossible.

“If he had contented himself with preaching against Rome’s vices and prophesying, in some undefined way, that Italy would be scourged, Pope Alexander would have let him spend his breath thus as long as he could find hearers. Such spiritual blasts knock down no walls. But the Frate wants to be more than a trumpet: he wants to be a lever—and what is more, he is a lever. He would spread the doctrine of Christ by maintaining a popular government in Florence; and the Pope, as I know on the best authority, has private views to the contrary.”

“Then Florence will stand by the Frate,” Cennini broke in, heat rising in him like quick-fermenting dough. “I might prefer he would let his prophesying alone, but if our freedom to choose our own government is attacked—I am an obedient son of the Church, yet I would vote for resisting Pope Alexander the Sixth, as our forefathers resisted Pope Gregory the Eleventh.”

“But pardon me,” Macchiavelli said, unruffled, letting the argument unfold in his hands like a well-laid map. “Have you correctly seized the Frate’s position? How is it he has become a lever worth attacking by so acute a man as his Holiness? Because he has got the ear of the people: because he gives them threats and promises they believe come straight from God—not only about hell, purgatory, paradise, but about Pisa and our Great Council. Let events go against him so as to shake that faith, and the cause of his power will be the cause of his fall.

“He is piling three sorts of hatred upon his head: the hatred of average mankind against anyone who would lay a strict yoke of virtue on them; the hatred of stronger powers in Italy who want to farm Florence for their own profit; and the hatred of the people, to whom he has ventured to promise good in this world instead of confining his promises to the next. If a prophet is to keep power, he must be a prophet like Mahomet, with an army at his back—so that when faith faints it may be frightened into life again.”

“Rather sum up the three sorts in one,” said Francesco Cei, impetuous, his poet’s blood quick to boil, “and say he has won the hatred of all men who have sense and honesty by inventing hypocritical lies. His place is among the false prophets in the Inferno, who walk with their heads turned hind-foremost.”

“You are too angry, my Francesco,” Macchiavelli said, smiling as one who has heard many pots boil over. “You poets are apt to cut the clouds in your wrath. I am no votary of the Frate’s, and would not lay down my little finger for his veracity. But veracity is a plant of paradise; the seeds have never flourished beyond the walls. You, yourself, tell poetical lies only—partly compelled by fervour, partly to please your audience—and you object to lies in prose. The Frate differs from you only as to the boundary of poetry. When he gets into the pulpit of the Duomo, he has fervour within and an audience without. Ecco!”

“You are somewhat lax there, Niccolò,” said Cennini gravely. “I believe in the Frate’s integrity, though I do not believe in his prophecies; and as long as integrity is not disproved, we have a popular party strong enough to protect him and resist foreign interference.”

“A party that seems strong enough,” Macchiavelli returned, with a shrug and an almost imperceptible glance towards Tito, who meanwhile abandoned himself to Nello’s combing and scenting with a pleasure that was nearly voluptuous—each tooth of the comb drawing through hair like a rake through fine flour. “But how many Mediceans are there among you? How many who will not be turned by a private grudge?”

“As to the Mediceans,” said Cennini, “I believe there is very little genuine feeling left for them. Who would risk much for Piero de’ Medici? A few old staunch friends, perhaps, like Bernardo del Nero. But even some most connected with the family are hearty friends of the popular government and would exert themselves for the Frate. I was talking with Giannozzo Pucci only a little while ago, and I am convinced there is nothing he would set his face against more than against any attempt to alter the new order of things.”

“You are right there, Messer Domenico,” Tito said, laughing, the meaning in his eyes like spice one tastes after swallowing. He rose from the chair as Nello wiped away the last foam with a cloth warm from hot water. “And I fancy the tender passion came in aid of hard theory. I am persuaded jealousy lay at the bottom of Giannozzo’s alienation from Piero de’ Medici; else so amiable a creature would never feel the bitterness he sometimes lets escape him in that quarter. He was in the procession with you, I suppose?”

“No,” Cennini answered. “He is at his villa—went there three days ago.”

Tito adjusted his cap, glanced down at his splashed hose as if the words were no more than street dust on his ears. In truth, he had gained what he sought. In his scarsella lay a crushed gold ring, engaged to be delivered to Giannozzo Pucci—a sign rather than a gift, like a seal that calls a man back to town. Tito had received it from an envoy of Piero de’ Medici, whom he had ridden out of his way to meet at Certaldo on the Siena road. Since Pucci was out of Florence, the ring must go by Fra Michele, a Carthusian lay-brother in Medicean service; and the sight of that gold circle would draw Pucci home to hear the unspoken part of Tito’s mission.

“Behold him!” Nello cried, flourishing his comb as if it were a sceptre and pointing it at Tito. “The handsomest scholar in the world or in the wolds—del mondo o di maremma—now he has passed through my hands! A trifle thinner in the face, though, than when he came first in his bloom to Florence—eh? And, I vow, there are lines faintly hinting themselves about your mouth, Messer Oratore! Ah, mind is an enemy to beauty. I myself was thought beautiful by women once—when I was in swaddling-bands. But now—oimè! I carry my unwritten poems in cipher on my face!”

The company laughed. Nello held up the hand-mirror and looked at himself with tragic vanity; the shop rang with voices, with the clink of metal, with the far-off bell-surge that poured through the open door like a river of sound. Tito, smiling with them, made his farewell sign and went out into the Piazza’s brightness.

“I am of our old Piero di Cosimo’s mind,” Francesco Cei said when the door had closed. “I do not half like Melema. That trick of smiling grows stronger—no wonder he has lines about the mouth.”

“He is too successful,” Macchiavelli answered lightly. “I am sure something is wrong with him, else he would not have that secretaryship.”

“He is an able man,” Cennini said, judicial as one weighing grain. “My brother and I have found him useful with our Greek sheets, and he gives satisfaction to the Ten. I like to see a young man work his way upward by merit. The secretary Scala, who befriended him from the first, thinks highly of him still, I know.”

“Doubtless,” said a notary in the background. “He writes Scala’s official letters for him—or corrects them—and gets well paid for it.”

“I wish Messer Bartolommeo would pay me to doctor his gouty Latin,” Macchiavelli said, with a shrug. “Did he tell you about the pay, Ser Ceccone, or was it Melema himself?” He made his face innocently ironic, as if asking whether a sauce had been salted by the cook or by the diner.

“Melema? no indeed,” Ser Ceccone replied. “He is as close as a nut. He never brags. That is why he is employed everywhere. They say he is getting rich by doing all sorts of underhand work.”

“It is a little too bad,” Macchiavelli murmured, “and so many able notaries out of employment!”

“Well,” Cei persisted, “I thought it was a nasty story a year or two ago about the man who said Melema had stolen jewels. It got hushed up somehow; but I remember Piero di Cosimo said he believed there was something in it, for he saw Melema’s face when the man laid hold of him, and never saw a visage so ‘painted with fear,’ as our sour old Dante says.”

Nello’s easy humour turned sharp as a razor edge. “Come, spit no more of that venom, Francesco, else I shall deem it my public duty to cut your hair awry next time I get you under my scissors. That story was a lie. Bernardo Rucellai and the Magnificent Eight knew all about it. The man was a dangerous madman, and was properly kept from mischief in prison. As for our Piero di Cosimo, his wits chase the wind of Mongibello: he has such extravagant fancy he would take a lizard for a crocodile. No—let that tale lie. It has been dead and buried too long—our noses object to it.”

“It is true,” Macchiavelli said, with the calm of one who prefers law to gossip. “You forget the danger of the precedent, Francesco. The next mad beggarman may accuse you of stealing his verses—or me, God help me! of stealing his coppers.” He turned his head towards the Piazza. “Ah! Dolfo Spini has carried his red feather out. That captain of swaggerers would like the Republic to lose Pisa, merely for the chance of seeing the people tear the frock off the Frate’s back. With your pardon, Francesco—I know he is a friend of yours—there are few things I should like better than to see him play Capo d’Oca, who went to the tournament blowing his trumpets and came back with them in a bag.”

The evening had come down early and sullen, with a thin rain that seemed less to fall than to breathe upon the stones. Romola was returning from San Matteo after vespers, Maso plodding at her side with the lantern held low so the wavering light ran along the wet walls and picked out the glisten of puddles like spilled oil. In the muffled streets, sound carried strangely: the soft slap of their steps, the lantern’s faint clink, a shutter banging once and then settling into a steady complaint, as if even the wood were uneasy under the weather.

Near San Marco she met Tito as he was coming out from the monastery. He had been in and out of the Via de’ Bardi all day without quite meeting her—so it had been for a long while now: two lives moving in the same house like parallel channels, kept from cutting into each other by careful banks. He proposed at once to see her home and, with the same easy command that made obedience look like courtesy, sent Maso away because the old man’s short steps “wearied” him.

It was the sort of attention Tito paid only when the street itself seemed to demand it. Between husband and wife there was no open quarrel, no storm that cleared the air. They had passed beyond the stage where remonstrance is still an attempt at agreement. They spoke of public matters and of household matters with the guarded precision of people reading from different copies of the same text. If Tito wished a supper in the old library—now made into a banqueting-room with pleasant hangings and polished boards—Romola assented and saw that the bread was warmed, the wine drawn, the knives set straight. If she needed money for her charities, it was found, as if by accident, among the accounts. In return she helped him with transcriptions and digests, laying out his notes with the careful hand of one bred among manuscripts and meanings.

And yet, throughout the day, he would avoid meeting her eyes, as if a glance were a kind of oath; he would pretend to suppose she was absent rather than seek her in her own room, and would jest—lightly, like someone tapping a thin crust to see if it would break—that she preferred solitude to his society. Once, after her return from that flight she had renounced, she had tried, timidly, to go back toward frankness. But Romola could not come to peace except by open speech—by laying the wound bare and asking what could heal it. Tito could only be brought back to her by a tenderness in her that would have required oblivion. He wanted the old fondness without the old truth. She could be gentle, submissive, exact in all duties; she could keep down the involuntary recoil. But she could not counterfeit warmth, any more than yesterday’s bread can be made new by polishing its crust.

She knew it, and he knew it. That knowledge made her, to him, a danger—one more reason to keep her outside of secrets. In politics he had sought to persuade her that the Medici cause was hopeless and that, both in theory and prudence, he served the popular government in which she now had a fervent stake. But impressions, subtle as odours caught in a passageway, made her uneasy about his relations with San Marco. She was torn between dreading to see what would confirm her suspicion and a restless impulse to watch, lest harm should be done that she might have stopped.

As they walked, Tito said, with that agreeable smoothness which could make even exertion sound like a compliment, “My business is not ended yet. I will conduct you to our door, Romola, and then I must fulfil another commission. It may take me an hour before I can return and rest—which I greatly need.”

He began to speak of Pisa, of things seen and people met, as if the mind could be fed on travellers’ anecdotes the way a household is fed on soups and stews: by small additions, by patient simmering, by a cook’s knack of making yesterday serve for to-day. Romola listened without answers, hearing beneath his words the faint percussion of rain and the distant mutter of a city settling into night.

They were nearing a loggia where a lamp burned before a painted Madonna. The light, caught in the damp, made a pale halo in the air; the smell there was of wet plaster and lamp-oil, and in the sheltered hollow of the arcade someone had lately stood with a cloak that still held the scent of smoke and wine. The street had been quiet, but now the sound of many footsteps swelled toward them, with voices blurred together as if the street itself had taken a mouthful of talk and was chewing it.

“We shall not reach home without a soaking,” Tito said quickly, and with a slight startled movement hurried Romola up into the loggia. “Let us shelter a moment.”

“It is only a drizzling rain,” Romola said, surprised. “Why should we wait?”

“No,” he answered. “I feel it thickening.”

But it was not the rain he had felt. With the habitual wakefulness of a mind trained to danger and advantage, he had caught, in the lamp’s glimmer, a red feather and the glitter of a sword-hilt among the approaching group—marks of a man he least wished to meet here, with Romola at his side.

He had already had one interview that day with Dolfo Spini, and the “commission” he spoke of was a second meeting with him—a sequel to Tito’s visit at San Marco. For Tito had long been shaping a plan with the delicacy of a falsifier trimming vellum to fit a stolen seal. He had been the bearer of letters to Savonarola—letters forged with consummate care; and one, by a stratagem bold enough to delight a cynical mind, bore the very name and seal of the Cardinal of Naples, that Cardinal who in Rome had exerted himself most for the Frate.

Those letters declared that the Cardinal, travelling from Pisa, was unwilling for strong reasons to enter Florence, yet eager at this juncture to take counsel with Savonarola. He would pause at San Casciano that very day—ten miles from the city—and at dawn would ride out in the plain garb of a priest and meet Savonarola, as if by chance, five miles along the Florence road, two hours after sunrise.

The plot that opened with those letters was simple enough in its cruelty. Dolfo Spini and a band of Compagnacci were to lie in ambush at a lonely spot beyond the gates. They were to seize Savonarola, along with the Dominican who must accompany him, and deliver both to a small detachment of Milanese horse waiting near San Casciano, to carry them into Roman territory. In Florence the Frate’s friends already thought it necessary he should be guarded when he preached; beyond the walls he would be on a road where even an honest cry can be swallowed by hedges and wet air.

There was always the chance Savonarola would suspect a trap. He had for some time avoided risking himself outside the city. On that, Tito’s scheme depended: giving him too little time to weigh and doubt, letting the Frate’s hunger—his eager longing to knit together forces within and without the Church toward a General Council, and his hope of immediate service from a powerful cardinal—overrun his caution.

Tito had insisted on putting the letters into Savonarola’s hand alone and, with art that could make inference sound like innocence, had admitted that he could guess their purport: a rendezvous outside the gates. He urged the Frate to ask the Signoria for an armed guard and offered—privately—to carry the request. Savonarola replied briefly that it was impossible: privacy and a guard could not go together. His eye flashed; Tito read the flash as resolve.

Whether Savonarola went or stayed, Tito believed himself secure. If the Frate fell, there were diamonds in question, and papal favour. If he did not, Tito’s adroitness would have strengthened him with Savonarola and with Spini; and any confidence wrung from either made him more valuable still to Medicean interests. He had the cold assurance of a man who tastes all dishes and is loyal to none, finding every flavour hollow except the one that feeds his own advantage.

Only Spini was an awkward companion. His cunning delighted in plots, but his mind lacked the tight-lidded control secrecy needs. He drank, and when wine loosened him he could become affectionate and loud—one of those Florentine “Beoni” whose laughter seems at first harmless until it begins to spill names and hints like overfilled cups. Though he and Tito had agreed to greet each other in public with coolness, there was always the risk that, in a sudden encounter, Spini would blurt and clasp and call him comrade before witnesses.

Now Tito’s hope was that Spini had not recognized him. The lamp had thrown Tito’s face into sudden light and shadow like a coin turned in the hand; and Tito, with his marked grace and foreign-bright features, was as easy to know as a captain with a red feather. Romola, in her dark shroud, had not been noticed; she stood behind Tito’s shoulder, tucked into the corner of the loggia where the air smelt of damp stone.

The hope lasted only a breath.

“Ha! my carrier-pigeon!” grated Spini’s harsh voice—meant for an undertone and all the more ugly for it. His hand came down on Tito’s shoulder with the familiarity of a blow. “Why did you run into hiding? You didn’t know comrades were coming. It’s well I caught you—it saves time. What of the chase to-morrow morning? Will the bald-headed game rise? Are the falcons ready?”

Tito felt his lips blanch. If rage had been native to him, it would have flamed now against this bull-faced accomplice—too clumsy to lead, too noisy to serve. But his excitement was the quick calculation of danger: how to stop Spini without making Romola’s suspicion blaze into certainty. To hush him outright might sharpen her watchfulness into action; to repel him angrily might make the wine-heavy Compagnaccio savage. Tito chose a third path—proof that Romola still held one power over him: the power of dread.

He pressed her hand, a small pressure meant as warning or command, and said, in a tone of hearty comradeship, “Yes, Dolfo, you may prepare in all security. But take no trumpets with you.”

“Don’t be afraid,” Spini answered, piqued. “No need to play Ser Saccente with me. I know where the devil keeps his tail as well as you. What—did he swallow the bait whole? The prophetic nose didn’t scent the hook?”

He lowered his voice a little, with the blundering air of a man who thinks secrecy consists in bending his head rather than in keeping his tongue still. Tito thought, with a cold inward disgust, He will never be satisfied till he has emptied the bag.

Aloud Tito said, “Swallowed all as easily as you swallow a cup of Trebbiano. Ha! I see torches—there must be a dead body coming. They say the pestilence spreads.”

The smell of torches—pitch and resin—was indeed beginning to taint the damp air, and their light flickered on the wet street like fire playing over fish-scales.

“Santiddio! I hate the sight of biers,” Spini muttered, and moved off in haste. “Good-night.”

The torches were real, but they did not escort a corpse. They went before a church dignitary returning homeward; Tito had used the hint of death and plague as one might throw an unpleasant spice into a pot to make a guest push it away.

When Spini had gone, Tito turned to Romola and spoke quietly, as if he were smoothing a wrinkled cloth. “Do not be alarmed by anything that _bestia_ has said. We can go on now—the rain has not increased.”

But Romola was already trembling with a resolute indignation that made her breath short. Tito’s unconcern only hardened her distrust; she felt every easy tone as a hand pressing her down.

“I will not go on,” she said. “I will not move nearer home until I have some security against this treachery being done.”

“Wait, at least, until these torches have passed,” Tito answered, perfectly self-possessed; and beneath that self-possession a new dislike rose—cold, hard, unimpassioned—at the thought that his wife might thwart him, not with tears but with will.

The torches came by with the Vicario dell’Arcivescovo. Tito did reverence; Romola saw only forms and light, heard the soft murmur of those who accompanied him. The city’s soundscape pressed close: footsteps on wet stone, the hiss of rain on flame, the distant call of a watchman, all making a net in which her thoughts struggled.

If, to prevent this betrayal she believed in with the force of long foreboding, she had needed at that instant to seize Tito and fling herself and him into a ravine, she felt she could have done it. Union with him? The discipline of two years, the daily self-quelling, seemed wiped away. In its place there was only a terrible clearness: they were divided.

They were nearly in darkness again. Only the Madonna’s lamp behind them gave a thin outline to Tito’s profile and left Romola’s face half-hidden under her veil.

“Tell me the truth, Tito,” she said, low and shaken. “This time tell me the truth. It will be safer for you.”

“Why should I desire to tell you anything else, my angry saint?” Tito replied, and a slight contempt ran under the words like bitter lees under clear wine. “Since the truth is precisely that which should make you rejoice—that my knowledge of a plot of Spini’s enables me to secure the Frate from falling victim to it.”

“What is the plot?”

“That I decline to tell,” he said. “It is enough that the Frate’s safety will be secured.”

“It is a plot to draw him beyond the gates, that Spini may murder him.”

“There has been no intention of murder,” Tito said smoothly. “It is a plot to compel him to obey the Pope’s summons to Rome. But as I serve the popular government, and believe the Frate’s presence here is necessary to maintain it at present, I choose to prevent his departure. You may sleep to-night with an easy mind.”

Romola was silent a moment. In the silence she heard the drip from the loggia’s edge and the far-off thrum of tavern voices—men warmed by wine and talk, careless of what their noise did to the night. Then she said, with anguish that made the words heavy, “Tito, it is of no use. I have no belief in you.”

He shrugged; even in dimness she saw the gesture: palms spread, as if to show empty hands. The cold anger of a man who does not burn but hardens was setting within him.

“If the Frate leaves the city—if any harm comes to him,” Romola said after a pause, her voice changing into a steadier iron, “I will declare what I have heard to the Signoria, and you will be disgraced. What if I am your wife?” The words came faster, as if once spoken they must be driven home. “I will be disgraced with you. If we are united, I am that part of you that will save you from crime. Others shall not be betrayed.”

“I am quite aware of what you would be likely to do, _anima mia_,” Tito answered in the coolest liquidity of his tone. “Therefore, if you have a small amount of reasoning at your disposal just now, consider that if you believe me in nothing else, you may believe me when I say I will take care of myself—and not put it in your power to ruin me.”

“Then you assure me the Frate is warned—he will not go beyond the gates?”

“He shall not go beyond the gates.”

Even then distrust did not loosen its grip. It sat in her mind like an unclean smell that clings after the pot is scoured.

“I will go back to San Marco now and find out,” Romola said, making a movement as if to turn.

“You shall not!” Tito whispered bitterly, seizing both her wrists with the full force of his grip. “I am master of you. You shall not set yourself in opposition to me.”

Footsteps were approaching. Tito had heard them; that was why he kept his voice low. Romola, mastered, did not struggle—partly because her pride recoiled from such a contest in the street, partly because she too heard the coming voices and felt the eyes that might turn upon them. The grasp on her wrists—this blunt assertion of his physical predominance—sent through her not a vulgar fury but a shuddering horror, as if she had been forced to touch something she could not wash from her skin.

They moved out from the loggia and walked on under the small, steady rain. For a while neither spoke. The first rush of alarm and indignation began to ebb in Romola, leaving behind a heavier mixture: habits of self-questioning, memories of impulse subdued, that proud reserve which discipline had never changed. In her earlier vehemence, open opposition to the husband from whom her soul revolted had seemed almost a temptation because it was so simple. Now she felt again the old check—the sense of boundaries, of consequences, of a dignity that would not stoop even to save itself.

She began to cling, as a starving person clings to the hope of a crust, to the probabilities that might spare her from a desperate course. Tito would not risk betrayal by her; now that she knew of the plot, whatever his first purpose, he must reckon with the fact. She needed only to keep over him the certainty that if he deceived her her lips would not remain closed. And it was possible—yes, she must hold to that possibility until it was shattered—that Tito had never meant to aid in betraying the Frate.

Tito, too, was busy within himself. He walked as if his feet had learned the streets by heart while his mind ran its own errands. He did not speak again until they were near home, where the familiar stones and the doorway’s shadow seemed to promise safety simply because they were known.

“Well, Romola,” he said then, “have you had time to recover calmness? If so, you can supply your want of belief in me by a little rational inference. You can see, I presume, that if I had intended to further Spini’s plot, I should now be aware that having a fair Piagnone for my wife—who knows the secret—would be a serious obstacle.”

He chose the tone easiest to him now: not pleading, which he guessed would fail, but cool reasoning, as if arranging accounts on a table.

“Yes, Tito,” she said in a low voice, “I think you believe that I would guard the Republic from further treachery. You are right. If the Frate is betrayed, I will denounce you.”

She paused, and the effort to soften came like swallowing something dry. “But it was not so. I have perhaps spoken too hastily—you never meant it. Only…why will you seem to be that man’s comrade?”

“Such relations are inevitable to practical men, Romola,” he replied, pleased to see her struggling back toward control. “You fair creatures live in the clouds. Pray go to rest with an easy heart.”

He opened the door for her, and the house received them with its familiar quiet—quiet that, like a well-managed kitchen, can hide the heat and the sharp tools that make its order possible.

Tito’s contrivances—those neatly tied knots by which he loved to draw other men into the shape of his own advantage—had been fretted loose by accidents as light as wind-sown seed. It was seldom he chose to pace the evening streets with Romola; yet on this one night, when her company was the one inconvenience he could not afford, she had walked beside him. Florence was a board where a clever player set his pieces with dry fingers—and then some breath, some child’s cry, some door opening at the wrong moment, sent the whole array trembling.

It was not that the failure of Dolfo Spini’s violence troubled him in itself. What stung was the necessity of fitting his next move to two different watchers without letting either see the seam. A warning must go to the Frate; an explanation must pacify Spini; and both must be so timed that no one should say Tito’s hands had been in the dough from the first.

If he went straight to San Marco before the monks slept, his warning would press too close upon the delivery of the forged letters—close enough to make even the dull suspicious. If he ran at once to Spini, he must give the true reason for the warning, since he could not yet pretend that he had only just discovered Savonarola’s change of purpose; and Spini’s mind, like a dog’s, did not weigh motives—only scents. It would smell at once that Tito had turned, that he had thwarted, that he had betrayed the betrayers. Yet if he waited until morning to speak to Savonarola, the chance to soften Spini beforehand would be gone; the Compagnacci would come back balked and raging, and their rage, once awake, did not know how to lie down again.

That risk, however, was the one Tito chose. He trusted to his own voice, to the oily patience that could stroke anger into a semblance of calm; he told himself he could always soothe Spini by making the failure look like nothing more than the Frate’s over-caution. Still, he was annoyed—annoyed enough that, had he been forced to smile, the effort would have shown.

He resolved he would not meet Romola again that night. He did not go home.

Romola watched until dawn without loosening her dress. The sound of the rain thickened, then deepened—drops multiplying into a steady drumming that filled the house as if the very walls had learned a dark chant. She found herself listening as one listens to a hearth-fire when the world outside grows dangerous: the rain made a roof of noise, a broad, sheltering roar that seemed to hold men back from running their errands of cruelty. Under that broad percussion her thoughts went on working, sharper and sharper, like a knife that will not be laid down.

It was not only doubt of Tito that possessed her now, but doubt of herself—doubt that bit deeper because it had her own voice. What lie might he not have told? What design might he not be carrying, still unguessed? Everyone who trusted him, she felt, stood in peril; and it was childish to lull herself with any hope to the contrary. Yet was she, out of pride—out of the shrinking delicacy that called itself duty—refusing to warn men because the warning would shame her as a wife?

“If he is a malefactor, my place is in prison by his side.” That claim she could meet without trembling. But could she, because she was a wife, let him become a malefactor—let him do the injuries that would make the prison his due—when perhaps a word of hers might prevent it?

Prayer would not come. The posture of the soul that waits, open-handed, expecting—she could not reach it. Her mind moved too feverishly, turning and turning like a mill that cannot stop because the stream is swollen. As the night wore on, her imagination, quickened into disease, made schemes within schemes: ways in which Tito might still evade, still strike, still leave her warnings too late. And then, toward daybreak, the rain slackened. The hard battering on the tiles became a thinner patter, then only a drip. A breeze rose, swept the last clouds away, and the morning fell clear on roofs and towers as if nothing in the world had been threatened.

That calm made her unrest unbearable. Noise had been a veil; now the city’s waking sounds came cleanly through it—the first carts creaking, the first shutters thrown back, the voices beginning their day as if safety were a habit. She wrapped her mantle about her and ran up to the loggia, as if the breadth of the landscape might answer her, as if beyond the line of roofs there might be some visible token—some moving speck—telling her whether Savonarola walked toward safety or toward a snare. But the roofs hid the streets; and the streets were precisely where peril travelled.

If she went to her godfather, might she not stir him—without betraying Tito by name—into measures that would keep Fra Girolamo within the gates? But that might already be too late. Bitterly she remembered how she had failed to wring from Tito any detail that could guide her, any hour, any message, any name; and the time was slipping. It was already long past seven.

She must go to San Marco. There was nothing else.

She hurried down the stairs, went out into the street without pausing to look in on the sick folk she had made part of her daily duty, and walked swiftly along the Via de’ Bardi toward the Ponte Vecchio. She would cut through the heart of Florence—not only because it was the straightest road, but because the great Piazza offered one desperate chance: she might meet Tito. Some last remnant of longing—half hope, half the old hunger to be spared—clung to the thought that he might satisfy her that the Frate was safe, and she could turn back without exposing her own terrible knowledge.

Before the Palazzo Vecchio she looked eagerly into the pillared court; then her eyes swept the Piazza. But the well-known figure—once painted in her heart by young love, and now branded there by gnawing pain—was nowhere.

She pressed on to the Piazza del Duomo. The square was already alive: worshippers mounting and descending the marble steps; men halted in knots of talk; market-people shifting their burdens, the smell of damp wicker and wet cloth rising from baskets, and the faint sourness of yesterday’s greens. Somewhere a vendor’s cry rang out and was answered; the morning’s soundscape gathered itself like a net—voices, footsteps, the rumble of wheels—each note distinct in the clean air after rain.

Between moving figures Romola caught sight of Tito.

He had been at San Marco; now he had turned into Nello’s shop, and stood there as if the morning were made for his ease. He leaned against the door-post, talking with the air of a man who had slept well. His cap was in his hand; he shook back his freshly-combed hair with that small flourish which always suggested that even his gestures had been practised before a mirror.

The sight struck Romola like the sudden taste of something bitter in the middle of bread. After her night of watching—after the drum of rain and the inner tumult—his smoothness, his untroubled manner among the ordinary commerce of the day, convulsed her with indignation. And it heightened her dread: hardness like that could do anything.

She recognised Cronaca and two other frequenters of San Marco standing near him. A thought flashed, clear and cold: I will force him to speak before them. Let his words be bound by their hearing.

Her step, light with haste and resolution, brought her close before Tito could move away. Cronaca, turning, said simply, “Here comes Madonna Romola.”

A slight shock went through Tito as if a hand had touched the back of his neck. For an instant his skill deserted him, and then he gathered it again, needing all his self-command to hold his face in a look that should be no more than surprise.

Romola was haggard from her sleeplessness; but in her eyes there was now something that was not merely anxiety—a flash as if a blade had caught the morning light. She did not waste breath.

“Is the Frate gone beyond the gates?”

“No,” Tito said. The word came out steadily enough; yet he felt helpless before her in a way he had seldom felt before any human being.

“And you are certain that he is not going?” she insisted, as if she meant to nail the certainty down with the witness of the men beside him.

“I am certain that he is not going.”

“That is enough,” Romola said.

She turned at once and went up the steps, seeking refuge in the Duomo—some shadowed space where she might gather herself, where the vast hush might take her beating heart and make it quiet again, away from this bright, noisy square and the intolerable composure of the man who had made her night a torment.

Tito watched her retreating figure with a feeling that came nearer hatred than anything he had known. The men around him were not only true followers of the Frate. There was Ser Ceccone too—the notary—who, like Tito himself, served the Mediceans in secret. Ser Francesco di Ser Barone—called by those who knew him only by the shorter name that clung to him like dirt, Ser Ceccone—was no scholar, no handsome man, no favourite of fortune, and generosity was as foreign to him as music to a stone. He was a traitor without charm.

And for that very reason, he was not fond of Tito Melema.

Late afternoon had thickened the air in the Via de’ Bardi until even the street seemed to breathe more slowly. The day’s brightness had sunk into that Florentine dusk which does not so much fall as steep itself—like saffron threads left too long in warm broth—turning edges and corners to blur, and making the lamps that were being lit below sound louder than they looked: flint on steel, the short flare, the tiny hungry hiss.

Romola sat in her narrow room opposite the cabinet, copying documents as she had done so often that the scratch of her pen had become a kind of household clock. The ink smelled faintly metallic; the parchment held a dry animal tang. Beside her was the small economy of any studious room—sand for drying, wax, twine—and the whole place carried the subdued hush of a convent cell, broken only by the low cough of the Arno in the distance and the occasional cry of a vendor turning a corner. That voice, that dialect sung out over stones and water, always pierced her with a strange tenderness; it was Florence speaking itself into being, syllable by syllable, as if memory depended on sound.

She was about to desist, because the light had grown too dim for accurate strokes, when Tito entered.

He came straight to that room as if he had aimed at it. He did not pause to call, nor did he lay aside cap and mantle. He leaned an elbow on the cabinet and stood directly before her, close enough that the chill damp of the street clung to him—wet wool, leather, and rain that had been in contact with old walls. His silence pressed on her like a weight set down without ceremony.

All day Romola had held fast to the assurance that the Frate was safe. With that certainty came reaction: penitence for the distrust and indignation that had driven her, in the morning, to speak publicly to her husband of what he wished to keep private. She told herself she had likely been wrong. It was easy—too easy—to imagine that the scheming duplicity of parties, which even her godfather had spoken of as inseparable from Florentine tactics, might account for Tito’s connection with Spini without proving that Tito meant to further a plot. She had been rehearsing words of atonement, tasting them in her mind like bread one offers after bitterness, hoping they might break the two years’ silence between them.

That silence had been complete. Tito did not even know she had once fled and come back again. They had never approached an avowal of that past which, in its young love and in the shock that shattered love, lay shut away like a banquet-room after death has broken the feast: tables still set in memory, but the air spoiled.

Romola lifted her eyes with the submissive look born of self-reproach; but something in Tito’s face arrested her speech. The blandness she remembered had drawn itself tight. There was a hidden tension in him, as when a man’s arm appears calm but the muscles under the skin are working at some silent violence.

For some moments they only looked at each other. Romola heard, with a kind of cruel distinctness, the house’s small sounds: a servant moving far below, the soft knock of a pot-lid, and then—thin and fragrant through the corridor—the ghost of supper beginning: oil warming in a pan, garlic bruised, the first sharp sweetness of onion meeting heat. Domestic routine went on, faithful as the bells; and yet in this room the air felt as if it had been cleared for judgment.

Tito, too, felt a crisis had come.

“Romola,” he began, in that cool liquid tone which made her shiver, “it is time that we should understand each other.”

“That is what I most desire, Tito,” she said, faintly.

Her face, pale and sweet with all its anger gone and only the timidity of self-doubt remaining, gave a marked predominance to his dark strength.

“You took a step this morning,” Tito continued, “which you must now yourself perceive to have been useless—which exposed you to remark and may involve me in serious practical difficulties.”

“I acknowledge that I was too hasty,” Romola said. “I am sorry for any injustice I may have done you.”

She spoke more firmly, as if the very act of confession ought to soften him. She watched for it the way one watches the surface of wine for a change of light—an answering sign.

None came.

“I wish you once for all to understand,” he said, without any change of voice, “that such collisions are incompatible with our position as husband and wife. I wish you to reflect on the mode in which you were led to that step, that the process may not be repeated.”

“That depends chiefly on you, Tito,” Romola answered, taking fire in spite of herself.

It was not what she had meant to say. But speech between two souls long divided does not follow the path one has laid out; it trips, it jolts, it strikes sparks from flint.

“You would say, I suppose,” Tito replied, “that nothing is to occur in future which can excite your unreasonable suspicions. You were frank enough to say last night that you have no belief in me. I am not surprised at any exaggerated conclusion you may draw from slight premises, but I wish to point out to you what is likely to be the fruit of your making such exaggerated conclusions a ground for interfering in affairs of which you are ignorant. Your attention is thoroughly awake to what I am saying?”

“Yes,” Romola said, flushing—resentment rising in her throat at this cold superiority that treated her mind as if it were a child’s hand snatching at knives.

“Well, then,” he went on, “it may possibly not be very long before some other chance words or incidents set your imagination at work devising crimes for me, and you may perhaps rush to the Palazzo Vecchio to alarm the Signoria and set the city in an uproar. Shall I tell you what may be the result? Not simply the disgrace of your husband, to which you look forward with so much courage, but the arrest and ruin of many among the chief men in Florence, including Messer Bernardo del Nero.”

The name struck her like a slap. The flush died; her lips went pale, which was unusual with her—she was not made for fear. But Tito’s words had brought up consequences with the terrible clearness of a map unrolled: corridors of power, doors broken, men dragged, families left to hunger, the city’s great machine of rumor and punishment grinding on. Florence could be tender as a mother at table and cruel as a butcher in the square; it depended on who spoke first and in what language—who set the lexicon of guilt.

Tito saw his success and pressed it.

“You would perhaps flatter yourself,” he said, “that you were performing a heroic deed of deliverance. You might as well try to turn locks with fine words as apply such notions to the politics of Florence. The question now is, not whether you can have any belief in me, but whether, now you have been warned, you will dare to rush, like a blind man with a torch in his hand, amongst intricate affairs of which you know nothing.”

Romola felt as if her mind were held in a vice. She could almost hear the vice tightening—not in imagination only, but in the actual soundscape of the city outside: the steady hammering somewhere down the street, iron against iron; a cart’s wheel complaining; a boy’s voice rehearsing an oath he did not understand. A whole world trained to noise that drowned the delicate distinctions by which a conscience tries to live.

“I am too rash,” she said. “I will try not to be rash.”

“Remember,” Tito said, with unsparing insistence, “that your act of distrust towards me this morning might, for aught you knew, have had more fatal effects than that sacrifice of your husband which you have learned to contemplate without flinching.”

“Tito, it is not so,” Romola burst out, pleading, rising and going nearer, driven to speak by something desperate. “It is false that I would willingly sacrifice you. It has been the greatest effort of my life to cling to you. I went away in my anger two years ago, and I came back again because I was more bound to you than to anything else on earth. But it is useless. You shut me out from your mind. You affect to think of me as a being too unreasonable to share in the knowledge of your affairs. You will be open with me about nothing.”

She bent towards him with dilated eyes and laid her hand on his arm—an appeal made with the whole body, as if warmth and touch could translate what words had failed to carry. Her fingers met the texture of his sleeve, dampened at the edge, and beneath it the firm pressure of his forearm. In another life, that contact would have drawn tenderness like the scent drawn out of crushed herbs.

But Tito’s face did not soften. Romola’s touch and glance no longer stirred any fiber of tenderness in him. The good-humored, tolerant Tito who was gentle toward the world felt himself becoming strangely hard toward the wife whose presence had once been his strongest influence. He was not a man made for hatred—hardly even for impatience; yet there was in him a masculine effectiveness of intellect and purpose, an edge that could work its way quietly. Romola’s energy thwarted his. And no man, unless exceptionally feeble, endures being thwarted by his wife. Marriage, for most, must become either sympathy or conquest.

No emotion darted across his face at her first mention of having gone away. Only his lips set a little harder, and he smiled slightly, not with mirth but with the thinness of decision.

“My Romola,” he said, “when certain conditions are ascertained, we must make up our minds to them. No amount of wishing will fill the Arno, as your people say, or turn a plum into an orange. I have not observed even that prayers have much efficacy that way. You are so constituted as to have certain strong impressions inaccessible to reason. I cannot share those impressions, and you have withdrawn all trust from me in consequence. You have changed towards me; it has followed that I have changed towards you. It is useless to take any retrospect. We have simply to adapt ourselves to altered conditions.”

His tone made the words feel like a physician’s pronouncement over a body: nothing to be done but accommodate to loss.

“Tito, it would not be useless for us to speak openly,” Romola said, exasperation rising from the effort of pushing living feeling against a lifeless resistance. “It was the sense of deception in you that changed me, and that has kept us apart. And it is not true that I changed first. You changed towards me the night you first wore that chain-armour. You had some secret from me—it was about that old man—and I saw him again yesterday. Tito”—her voice tightened with entreaty—“if you would once tell me everything, let it be what it may—I would not mind pain—that there might be no wall between us! Is it not possible that we could begin a new life?”

This time a flash crossed Tito’s face. He stood perfectly still, but the flash seemed to whiten him, as if a sudden cold had touched his blood. For a moment the whole room felt sharpened: the pen on the table, the grit of the drying sand between fingers, the faint smell of warmed oil drifting up from below as if supper were insisting on itself, indifferent to sin.

He did not answer her plea. After a pause, he said quietly, “Your impetuosity about trifles, Romola, has a freezing influence that would cool the baths of Nero.”

The phrase cut. Romola shrank, then drew herself up into her usual self-sustained posture, as if she must recover dignity the way one steadies a dish one has almost dropped.

Tito went on, his paleness governed now by will. “If by ‘that old man’ you mean the mad Jacopo di Nola who attempted my life and made a strange accusation against me—of which I told you nothing because it would have alarmed you to no purpose—he, poor wretch, has died in prison. I saw his name in the list of dead.”

“I know nothing about his accusation,” Romola said. “But I know he is the man whom I saw with the rope round his neck in the Duomo—the man whose portrait Piero di Cosimo painted, grasping your arm as he saw him grasp it the day the French entered, the day you first wore the armour.”

“And where is he now, pray?” Tito asked, still pale, but holding himself.

“He was lying lifeless in the street from starvation,” Romola said. The words brought back the sensation as if it were present: the stench of unwashed flesh and cold stone, the hollow sound of breath that was hardly sound at all, the way hunger makes even the air smell empty. “I revived him with bread and wine. I brought him to our door, but he refused to come in. Then I gave him some money, and he went away without telling me anything. But he had found out that I was your wife. Who is he?”

“A man,” Tito said, “half mad, half imbecile, who was once my father’s servant in Greece, and who has a rancorous hatred towards me because I got him dismissed for theft. Now you have the whole mystery—and the further satisfaction of knowing that I am again in danger of assassination. The fact of my wearing the armour, about which you seem to have thought so much, must have led you to infer that I was in danger from this man. Was that the reason you chose to cultivate his acquaintance and invite him into the house?”

Romola was mute. To speak was like rushing with bare breast against a shield; the shield did not even ring, it merely stopped you.

Tito moved from his leaning posture, slowly took off cap and mantle, and pushed back his hair. The gesture had the composure of someone who believes the matter is ended. Romola stood upright, looking at him as she might at an oncoming deadly force to be met only with silent endurance.

“We need not refer to these matters again, Romola,” he said, in the same tone with which he had first entered—precise, cool, and final. “It is enough if you will remember that the next time your generous ardour leads you to interfere in political affairs, you are likely, not to save any one from danger, but to be raising scaffolds and setting houses on fire. You are not yet a sufficiently ardent Piagnone to believe that Messer Bernardo del Nero is the prince of darkness, and Messer Francesco Valori the archangel Michael. I think I need demand no promise from you?”

“I have understood you too well, Tito,” she said.

“It is enough,” he answered, and left the room.

The door’s closing sounded louder than it should have—wood meeting wood, latch catching—like a sentence sealed. The quiet that followed was not peace but absence, as after a choir stops and the ear keeps listening for the missing harmony. From below came the ordinary music of the household: the clink of earthenware, the soft pour of liquid, the low exchange of servants in Florentine speech—words thick with local turns that could never be carried whole into any other tongue. Romola felt the cruelty of it: in the kitchen, things were still translatable—salt, oil, bread; in her marriage, nothing was.

She turned and sank into her seat, despair changing her limbs to heaviness.

“O God, I have tried—I cannot help it. We shall always be divided.”

The words passed silently through her mind. Then, as if startled by a sudden vision that forced itself into voice, she said aloud, “Unless—unless misery should come and join us!”

Tito, too, carried away a new thought when he had closed the door behind him. His project of leaving Florence—as soon as his life there had become a high enough stepping-stone to a life elsewhere, perhaps at Rome or Milan—now for the first time had attached itself to a desire to be free from Romola, to leave her behind. She had ceased to belong to the desirable furniture of his life. There was no possibility of an easy relation between them without genuineness on his part, and genuineness implied confession; confession meant a change of purpose. Tito had as little bent that way as a leopard has to lap milk when its teeth are grown.

From all relations that were not easy and agreeable, he shrank: why cling to them? And Romola had made his relations difficult with others besides herself. There had been a troublesome interview with Dolfo Spini, who had returned in a rage after an ineffectual soaking with rain and long waiting in ambush. That morning’s scene at Nello’s door, once carried into Spini’s ear, might sprout into something more unmanageable than suspicion—rumor, accusation, a vocabulary not of truth but of advantage.

Yet Tito believed, at least, that he had mastered Romola by a terror that appealed to the strongest forces of her nature. He had alarmed her affection and conscience with shadowy consequences; he had arrested her intellect by hanging before it the idea of hopeless complexity, as if moral judgment were a child’s game unsuited to the labyrinth of Florence.

Still, he was not at ease. The world was not yet quite cushioned with velvet; and even if it had been, he could not have abandoned himself to softness with thorough enjoyment.

For before he went out again that evening, he put on his coat of chain-armour.

The wintry days went over Romola as white-laden ships glide past a solitary watcher on the shore—each alike in its muffled pace, each freighted with some unseen change. After Tito’s half-spoken warning, dread had spoiled her curiosity; she began to choose ignorance as one chooses a darker room when the light shows too plainly what one fears to see. The German Emperor had withdrawn again; the sharpest peril to Florence seemed eased; yet the city’s hunger and cold did not withdraw with him. Distress still sat in doorways and under arches, and Romola’s hands were still needed—measuring out help, carrying messages, soothing the sick, arranging bread and broth with the quiet exactness of one who knows that nourishment is not an idea but a warmth and a smell and a strength returning to the limbs. In such tasks her mind found refuge from suspicion.

She dared not rejoice that the relief which had come at the last moment—relief that many declared a sign of Heaven’s favour on the Frate’s party—was making that party triumphant. Francesco Valori, fiery chief of the Piagnoni, had been chosen Gonfaloniere at the year’s beginning and was pushing, within his two months, to do as much as his ardour called “liberal” and his enemies called “tyrannical.” For a little while it looked like strength for the defenders of freedom and a shield for Savonarola; yet Romola had grown quick to every omen that darkened her foreboding. The present, whatever its brightness, felt to her like a pot set on embers: within it, mixed seeds of change were warming toward a boil that might scald.

By Carnival time—mid-February, when the air can smell at once of damp stone and the first faint promise of spring—her presentiment took shape. The Mediceans had ceased to be patient; they were openly labouring to secure Bernardo del Nero as the next Gonfaloniere.

On the last day of Carnival, between ten and eleven in the morning, Romola went out as she had promised, towards the Corso degli Albizzi to fetch her cousin Brigida. Both were to start early from the Via de’ Bardi and take their places at a window Tito had reserved in the Piazza della Signoria, where a spectacle was expected so strange, so new, that even Florentine eyes—long accustomed to pageant—burned to see it. The Piagnoni were shaping Carnival in their own image. Dolfo Spini and his companions had fought for the dear old masques, the rough tricks, the songs salted with indecency; but such things were not to live in a city where Christ had been proclaimed king.

Romola set out with the languor that comes upon anyone facing a long day of sight-seeing not from eagerness but from love—when one submits to noise and press and waiting because some child, or some friend with a child’s delight, longs for it. An epoch in Carnival it might be; it stirred no enthusiasm in her. She did not know it was an epoch in her own life too—when another destiny would no longer lie hidden, but would begin to be visibly twisted with hers.

She chose to pass through the great Piazza first, to take her own survey of what was preparing there while she was still alone. Entering from the south, she stopped short. Something monstrous and many-coloured rose before her—a pyramid, or rather a fir-tree made vast: sixty feet high, its “branches” widened into shelves, each tier spreading broader until the base ran to an eighty-yard circumference. The Piazza swarmed. Slender youths in white garments, olive wreaths on their heads, moved to and fro like pale flames tamed into human shapes, carrying baskets filled with bright objects. Men older and heavier—some in monastic frocks, some in the loose tunics and dark-red caps of artists—helped, judged, adjusted, then walked away to view the whole at a distance. On the marble steps of Orgagna’s Loggia stood a knot of watchers who held themselves aloof with discontent and scorn; among them Romola recognized Piero di Cosimo, his rough head set like a weathered stone.

She drew nearer. The tiers were crowded with things arranged as if for a market—only this market was for the fire. Tapestries and brocades with shameless figures; pictures and sculptures condemned as temptations; gaming-boards and tables; playing-cards with the very blocks for printing them; dice and the tools of gambling. Music-books of a worldly kind; instruments—lutes with smooth bellies, drums, cymbals, trumpets—whose very shapes seemed to promise riot and ringing excess. Masks and masquerade garments from old Carnivals. Fine copies of Ovid, Boccaccio, Petrarch, Pulci—books denounced as vain or impure. And among them the small, intimate paraphernalia that cling most obstinately to household life: rouge-pots; coils of false hair; mirrors that catch and flatter; perfumes; powders; veils so thin they were less concealment than invitation. At the summit stood an unflattering effigy of a Venetian merchant—perhaps a creature of rumour more than history—said to have offered a great sum for these marketable abominations; and above him, uglier still, the symbolic figure of old debauched Carnival itself, lifted up as if only to have farther to fall.

Within the pyramid, hidden behind the tiers of “vanities,” lay dry fuel and gunpowder. At evening, on this last day, it was to be lit. Trumpets would sound; the pile would blaze; the grim old Carnival would tumble down into the flames amid songs of reform.

Such a crowning act could scarcely have been brought about without the peculiar organisation Savonarola had begun two years before. Florence’s boyhood and youth were no longer left to their own genial impulse toward street mischief and crude dissoluteness. Under the training of Fra Domenico—Savonarola’s lieutenant—lads and striplings, the city’s hope, were to keep pure words on their lips, to burn with zeal for an Unseen Good that should shame the slackness of their elders, and to know pleasures only of an angelic sort—chanting divine praises, walking in white robes.

It was for them that seats had been raised high against the walls of the Duomo. It was to them Savonarola appealed as the future glory of a city chosen for God’s work. Those fresh-cheeked troops were the chief agents in this regenerated merriment, a sacred parody of the old. Had there been bonfires in former Carnivals? There would be a bonfire now—consuming impurity. Had there been symbolic processions? There would be processions now—but the symbols would be white robes and red crosses and olive wreaths: emblems of peace and innocent gladness; and banners and images held aloft would tell the triumphs of goodness. Had there been dancing in rings under the open sky to choruses of loose song? There would be dancing in rings now—monks and laity clasped in fraternal joy—and the music would be hymns. Even the street collections were to be greater than ever: not for gross and superfluous suppers, but for the hungry and needy. And besides alms, there was the collecting of the Anathema—the objects to be laid on the great bonfire.

Troops of young inquisitors went from house to house on this business, knocking at doors with an excitement that was half piety, half triumph. After the more obvious vanities were surrendered, perhaps the Madonna of a household still kept certain little reddened balls from the Levant—meant to coax a bloom onto a sallow cheek, and with it a false innocence. Let her bring them down, then, and drop them into the basket of doom. Or perhaps she had ringlets and coils of “dead hair.” Let her carry them to the street-door, not on her head but in her hands, and publicly renounce the Anathema that hid respectable age beneath a ghastly mockery of youth. In return she would hear young voices pronounce a blessing on her and her house.

The beardless inquisitors did their work willingly. To coerce by shame—or by that spiritual pelting which stings worse than stones—into surrendering things it will vex one to lose, is a form of “piety” readily learned by boyhood; and if some obstinate man grew furious and threatened whip or cudgel, that too had the spice of danger.

Savonarola himself felt—plainly enough—how difficult it is for noble yearning to see the right means, and how easily the mind, impatient for great ends, leans toward supernatural constraint as the only sure hope. The Florentine youth had foul tongues and evil habits. At first it seemed unmingled blessing that they now shouted “Viva Gesù!” Yet he was forced at last to warn from the pulpit: there was too much shouting; sacred words, repeated as if they were pebbles tossed for sport, would be brought into contempt. Let there be no more of that cry until the next Festa.

Still, the long stream of white-robed youth that went at dawn to the Duomo to receive the communion from Savonarola’s hands had been a sight of beauty; and doubtless many of those young souls stored memories of awe and hope that might one day save them from sinking into a vulgar sense of their work as men and citizens. There is no conscious obedience that does not mark an advance beyond lawlessness. These boys would become the men who fought greatly and endured greatly in the last struggle of their Republic.

Now, in the hours between early communion and dinner-time, they made their final rounds for alms and vanities. That was why Romola had seen the slim white figures moving about the base of the enormous pyramid, their steps soft on stone, their voices rising and falling like the calls of swallows—an aural net spread over the Piazza. In Florence the sound of a thing was never merely sound: it was governance. A chant could soothe a street; a trumpet could turn it into a weapon; and Romola, moving through that tide of voices, felt how the city’s spirit was being tuned—how certain words, shouted and repeated, could become the only permitted language, making other modes of feeling seem like sins because they had no sanctioned name.

“What think you of this folly, Madonna Romola?” said a brusque voice close to her ear.

She turned. Piero di Cosimo had come up beside her, his face set in its habitual grimness.

“Your Piagnoni will make l’inferno a pleasant prospect to us, if they carry things their own way on earth. It’s enough to fetch a cudgel over the mountains to see painters—Lorenzo di Credi, and young Baccio there—helping to burn colour out of life in this fashion.”

“My good Piero,” Romola said, looking up and smiling, “even you must be glad to see some of these things burnt. Look at the gewgaws and wigs and rouge-pots. I have heard you speak against them as angrily as Fra Girolamo himself.”

“What then?” Piero snapped, turning on her as if her mildness were an insult. “I never said a woman should make a black patch of herself against the background. Va! Madonna Antigone—it’s a shame for a woman with your hair and shoulders to run into such nonsense. Leave it to women who are not worth painting. What! the most holy Virgin herself has always been dressed well; that’s doctrine of the Church. Talk of heresy, indeed! And I should like to know what the excellent Messer Bardo would have said to the burning of the divine poets by these Frati, who are no better an imitation of men than if they were onions with the bulbs uppermost. Look—Petrarch sticking up beside a rouge-pot! Do the idiots pretend that the heavenly Laura was a painted harridan? And Boccaccio, now—do you mean to say, Madonna Romola—you who are fit to be a model for a wise Saint Catherine of Egypt—do you mean to say you have never read the stories of the immortal Messer Giovanni?”

“It is true I have read them, Piero,” Romola answered. “Some of them many times, when I was a little girl. I used to take the book down when my father was asleep, so that I could read to myself.”

“Ebbene?” Piero said, fierce as if he were challenging her to confess to pleasure.

“There are things in them I do not want ever to forget,” Romola said; and for a moment the Piazza’s mingled smells—damp wool, cold stone, the faint resin of stacked wood—seemed to sharpen into one clear memory, as if recollection too had an odour. “But you must confess, Piero, a great many of those stories are only about low deceit for the lowest ends. Men do not need books to make them think lightly of vice, as if life were a vulgar joke. And I cannot blame Fra Girolamo for teaching that we owe our time to something better.”

“Yes, yes—it’s very well to say so now you’ve read them,” Piero retorted bitterly. He turned on his heel and strode away, his steps loud on the stone, like a protest that would not be absorbed into the hymn-sounds.

Romola too moved on, smiling at Piero’s innuendo with a tenderness for his anger—because she knew her father would have felt something like it. For herself she felt no inward collision with the strict, sombre view of pleasure that tried to repress poetry while it repressed vice. Sorrow and joy each have their narrowness. A religious ardour like Savonarola’s—an ardour that in the end may bless mankind by thrusting the soul toward sympathy with pain, indignation against wrong, and the subduing of sensual desire—will always draw upon itself the reproach of negation.

Romola’s own life had given her an affinity with sadness that made her unjust toward merriment. That subtle refinement we call Taste was subdued in her by the need for a deeper motive—just as the palate’s niceties vanish before urgent hunger. Moving habitually among the city’s suffering, and carrying in her heart a woman’s heaviest disappointment, she found no dissonance in the severity that allied itself with self-renouncing strength. And yet, as she passed under the mingled murmur of the Piazza—hymns and admonitions, footfalls, the rustle of baskets, the thin calls of boys—she felt, without putting it into words, how much power lay in what was named and what was forbidden to be named; how a city could be ruled not only by laws and swords, but by the very sounds it allowed to live in its streets.

That morning the city seemed to hold its breath between winter and Lent. February’s sun lay pale as watered wine on the roofs, and the breeze that moved along the streets carried with it a mingled smell of damp stone, olive-wood smoke, and the faint, teasing sweetness that always attended holidays—fried dough, sugared almonds, spilled must warming in the light. Over it all ran the Florence of sound: shutters knocked open, a vendor’s call ricocheting down a lane, the shuffle of many shoes beginning their slow drift toward the Piazza. Even before the spectacle arrived, the day had its own music—less a trumpet than a constant, human murmur.

Into that murmur came Tessa.

She was easy to know, not in black like so many women now, but in her old honest colours—red, green, and white—moving with the quick, hopeful step of someone who still believed that going out could be simple. She no longer lived on the hill of San Giorgio. After what had happened there with Baldassarre, Tito—Naldo, as she called him—had chosen a different house for her, still quiet, still airy, set by wide garden grounds north of the Porta Santa Croce.
