The air there had birds in it, and the softer acoustics of leaves and open space: less of the clang that rose from the river traffic, less of the harsh shouting that scraped at the nerves like a blunt knife.

She had not come to see the Carnival without asking. The evening before, Tito had been with her, and she had waited, as she had learned to do, for the right moment—when his face had smoothed itself into that radiant ease he could still summon in her rooms. He sat in the straight-backed carved chair he had bought for his own comfort when he visited, one arm about sturdy Lillo, the other laid lightly on Tessa’s shoulder while she steadied little Ninna on her uncertain legs.

Tessa could not read letters, but she had learned to read his brow and mouth as if they were a page—where weariness lodged, where amusement woke, where impatience flickered. And in those visits, he was nearer than anywhere else to the bright, gentle-humoured youth who had once woken under the Loggia de’ Cerchi, when deceit had not yet asked him for hostages. He felt it too, though he would not have named it: here, with Tessa, he needed no guile. Her ignorance and innocence formed a shelter that asked nothing of him but the sound of his name in small voices.

“Babbo,” they called, and the word was sweet in his ears for the brief time he allowed it to be true.

When he thought of leaving Florence, he never thought of leaving Tessa and the children behind. Fondness—real, green-leaf fondness—clung to them: round cheeks, wide eyes, the warm weight of a child leaning into his knee. Somewhere in him, kindness still had a spring, and Tessa kept it from freezing. Romola—poor Romola—by the very effort of her sacrifice, chilled him into a hard dislike he had once thought impossible, and that dislike hardened him further. Tessa did the opposite without intending: she asked for so little, and gave so much soft ordinary life in return.

“Ninna is very good without me now,” Tessa began, letting the child sit down with a thump on the floor. “I can leave her with Monna Lisa any time, and if she is in the cradle and cries, Lillo is as sensible as can be—he goes and thumps Monna Lisa.”

Lillo, taking this as praise and command, sprang down from Tito’s knee and marched across the room to Monna Lisa, who sat spinning with her head slowly shaking—as if her deafness had become a habit of refusal. Lillo’s small fist landed against her arm in a solid little blow of summons.

“A wonderful boy!” Tito said, laughing.

“Isn’t he?” Tessa leaned closer, her desire rising and catching in her throat until she made it small and neat. “And I might go and see the Carnival to-morrow, just for an hour or two—mightn’t I?”

“Oh, you wicked pigeon,” he said, pinching her cheek. “Those are your longings, are they? What have you to do with carnivals now you are an old woman with two children?”

“But old women like to see things,” she answered, her lower lip beginning to hang. “Monna Lisa said she should like to go, only she’s so deaf she can’t hear what is behind her, and she thinks we couldn’t take care of both the children.”

His face sobered. “No, indeed, Tessa. You must not think of taking the children into the crowded streets, else I shall be angry.”

“I have never been into the Piazza without leave,” she pleaded, frightened by his tone. “Not since Holy Saturday. And I think Nofri is dead, for you know the poor madre died. And I shall never forget the Carnival I saw once; it was so pretty—all roses and a king and queen under them—and singing. I liked it better than the San Giovanni.”

“But there’s nothing like that now,” he said. “They are going to make a bonfire in the Piazza—that’s all. And I cannot let you go out by yourself in the evening.”

“Oh no, no! I don’t want to go in the evening. Only by daylight, to see the procession. There will be a procession—is it not true?”

“Yes, after a sort,” he said, dryly. “As lively as a flight of cranes. You must not expect roses and glittering kings and queens. Still, any string of people called a procession will please your blue eyes. They have raised a thing in the Piazza de’ Signori for the bonfire—you may like to see it. But come home early, and look like a grave little old woman; and if you see any men with feathers and swords, keep out of their way. They are very fierce, and like to cut old women’s heads off.”

“Santa Madonna!” Tessa cried, then caught his laughter and half-laughed too, though fear always rose quickly in her. “But I will keep away. Only—” she leaned in and whispered at his ear, warm breath and secrecy—“if I might take Lillo with me! He is very sensible.”

“But who will thump Monna Lisa then, if she doesn’t hear?” Tito said, keeping his face serious with effort. “No, Tessa. You could not take care of Lillo in a crowd, and he’s too heavy for you to carry.”

“It is true,” she admitted, saddened. “And he likes to run away. I forgot that. Then I will go alone. But now look at Ninna—you have not looked at her enough.”

Ninna was at that tumbling age when a child seems made of good dough and gravity, a fair solid that keeps finding its base—falling, righting itself, falling again, always landing on life. Tessa snatched her up and displayed the new teeth with pride, the damp sweetness of baby breath rising as she laughed. While Tito gave due attention, she whispered again, “And shall I buy some confetti for the children?”

He drew small coins from his scarsella and poured them into her palm.

“That will buy no end,” Tessa said, delight in her voice like a spoon striking a pot. “I shall not mind going without Lillo so much, if I bring him something.”

So in the morning she set out toward the great Piazza where the bonfire would be. She wore only her green woollen dress: the breeze did not bite, and she would not put on a mantle that would hide the new necklace and the new silver-mounted clasp at her belt—the only ornaments Tito had ever given her. She did not think of her figure; no one had ever told her it was pretty. But she did think of those bright pieces of metal and stone against her throat and waist, sure they would command respect, sure that any rich contadina would envy them. She adjusted her white hood so the necklace showed at the front, and took her small basket—empty now, soon to be filled with coloured sweets and crisp delights for Lillo and Ninna.

As she walked, the city’s holiday sound thickened: people lingered in knots; voices were looser, laughter more frequent. Country folk in their best garments drifted toward the centre like flocks, and the streets answered them with echo and clatter. Tessa smelled frying oil from some doorway where cakes were being turned, and the faint spicy note of hot wine. Her thoughts were mostly of purchases—what would be most pleasing to Lillo’s hungry hands, what would make Ninna’s eyes widen.

She did not think of anyone watching her.

But she had been watched the moment she descended from her upper storey. Now, as she tripped cheerily under the February sun, someone kept her in sight: a man bent beneath a package of yarn.

Baldassarre had taken to such burdens as a means of earning his scant bread—and keeping the sacred fire of vengeance alive. Often he had come out of his way to pass this house, the house Tito had once led him to at evening. Often he had waited, uncertain, fearful, hoping for proof that this was indeed the place where one of Tito’s wives lived. His long imprisonment had sharpened suspicion into a trembling instinct; he believed in a diabolic fortune that shielded Tito, and he dared not pursue him except in a crowd or in darkness. If Tito’s eyes fell on him, he felt—no, he knew—he would again be seized, mocked, dragged away, robbed even of his knife, cast helpless into a cell.

So his fierce purpose had become stealthy, serpent-like, waiting for a single dart of the fang. He could not hear again the voice that had once thundered promise of vengeance in the Duomo; he had returned there many times, but that voice seemed stifled now by cunning, by strong-armed wickedness, by the new fearful piety that burned old joys like straw. Justice was weak and unfriended. Baldassarre’s mind, enfeebled and yet obstinate, had carried one heavy question for months: did Tito still wear the armour? For a long time his fainting hope would have been content with one successful stab on this side of the grave. But he would never risk his precious knife again. When at last he knew the sharp steel was useless, and that he had no hope but in some new device, the knowledge settled on him like lead.

A dim vision returned again and again: win one of the two wives to aid him. The wife who had lived on the hill was gone; if he could find her again, perhaps he could seize a thread and work toward clarity. This morning, at last, he had succeeded. He watched the green-and-white figure, bent under his yarn, and tried with feeble eyes to interpret her life from lines and colours as one reads a faded painting.

Tessa passed through long streets with little sign of Carnival beyond the holiday loitering. She began to feel disappointed—no roses, no kings and queens—only the usual shouting that on any day filled Florence like a rough river. Then she saw a man with a pedlar’s basket, apparently selling nothing but little red crosses.

A little red cross would be pretty above her bed; it would also keep off harm, and might make Ninna stronger. She crossed the street to ask the price, counting her coins in her mind, already grieving if she must take from the confetti.

But as she drew near, the pedlar turned, and she recognised Bratti Ferravecchi—an old acquaintance from the Mercato. Habit told her to avoid old acquaintances: Tito had commanded it. She turned away quickly, but Bratti’s eye was trained like a hawk’s at corners, and her movement did not escape him. A tap on her arm arrested her—the tap of a red cross.

“Young woman,” Bratti said, “you come from some castello a good way off, else you’d never think of walking about this blessed Carnival without a red cross in your hand. Santa Madonna! Four white quattrini is a small price to pay for your soul—prices rise in purgatory, let me tell you.”

“Oh, I should like one,” Tessa said hastily, “but I couldn’t spare four white quattrini.”

Bratti had first regarded her only as a customer, but now her voice lit recognition in him. “By the head of San Giovanni, it must be the little Tessa—looking as fresh as a ripe apple! What! you’ve done none the worse, then, for running away from father Nofri? You were in the right of it. He goes on crutches now, and a crabbed fellow with crutches is dangerous; he can reach across the house and beat a woman as he sits.”

“I’m married,” Tessa said, demurely, remembering Tito’s injunction to look grave. “And my husband takes great care of me.”

“Ah! then you’ve fallen on your feet. Nofri said you were good-for-nothing vermin; but what then? An ass may bray a good while before he shakes the stars down. I always said you did well to run away, and it isn’t often Bratti’s in the wrong. Well, and so you’ve got a husband and plenty of money? Then you’ll never think much of giving four white quattrini for a red cross. I get no profit; but what with the famine and the new religion, all other merchandise is gone down. You live in the country where the chestnuts are plenty, eh? You’ve never wanted for polenta, I can see.”

“No, I’ve never wanted anything,” Tessa answered, guarded.

“Then you can afford to buy a cross. I got a Padre to bless them, and you get blessing and all for four quattrini. It isn’t for the profit; I hardly get a danaro by the whole lot. But they’re holy wares, and it’s getting harder and harder work to see your way to Paradise. The very Carnival is like Holy Week. The least you can do to keep the Devil from getting the upper hand is to buy a cross. God guard you! think what the Devil’s tooth is! You’ve seen him biting the man in San Giovanni, I should hope?”

Tessa felt teased and frightened; Bratti’s words scraped at her like a rough wool. “Oh, Bratti,” she said with a troubled face, “I want to buy a great many confetti. I’ve got little Lillo and Ninna at home. Nice coloured sweet things cost a great deal. They will not like the cross so well—though I know it would be good to have it.”

“Come, then,” Bratti said, with the air of a man laying up merits by imagining extortion and then renouncing it, “since you’re an old acquaintance, you shall have it for two quattrini. It’s making you a present of the cross, to say nothing of the blessing.”

Tessa reached out her two quattrini with trembling hesitation. Bratti stopped her abruptly.

“Stop a bit! Where do you live?”

“Oh, a long way off,” she answered almost by reflex, her mind on the coins. “Beyond San Ambrogio, in the Via Piccola, at the top of the house where the wood is stacked below.”

“Very good,” Bratti said, patronising. “Then I’ll let you have the cross on trust, and call for the money. So you live inside the gates? Well, well, I shall be passing.”

“No, no!” Tessa cried, frightened at the thought of Tito’s anger if Bratti came to her door. “I can spare the money. Take it now.”

But Bratti set his jaw. “No. I’m not a hard-hearted pedlar. I’ll call and see if you’ve got any rags, and you shall make a bargain. See—here’s the cross. And there’s Pippo’s shop not far behind you. Go and fill your basket, and I must go and get mine empty. Addio, piccina.”

He moved away before she could refuse. Tessa stood with the red cross in her hand, and a fluttering in her chest like a bird trapped behind ribs. She had let him know too much. There were more dangers in coming out than in staying at home. She hurried into Pippo’s shop, resolved to turn her money into confetti quickly before any other accident could find her.

In Pippo’s, the air was dense with sugar and spice, with the floury breath of almond paste, with the sharp clean scent of anise. Jars stood like little treasure chests: bright comfits, twisted sugared seeds, tiny cakes glazed to a hard shine that would crack between teeth. Tessa chose by colour as much as by cost, thinking of Lillo’s greedy delight and Ninna’s solemn, open-mouthed wonder. The basket grew heavier; the paper parcels made a crisp music as they shifted, and that sound soothed her—the domestic sound of provision, the promise of mouths made happy.

When she came out into the Via de’ Libraj, her face had returned to its childlike content. And now, at last, she thought she saw a procession: white robes, a banner. Her heart began to beat faster, expectation rising like yeast.

She drew aside; the street was narrow, and the closeness forced her to look closely. The banner was beautiful: the Holy Mother with the Babe. Since having her own babies, Tessa’s love for that pictured mother had grown deeper, more intimate, as if the painted Madonna might understand the weight of a child’s head against the shoulder and the ache that comes with tenderness. The white-robed figures wore green wreaths, and each carried a little red cross. Tessa felt a small proud satisfaction that she too held a red cross in her hand.

But something was new: some of the white figures carried baskets between them. What were baskets for? Tessa had only time to wonder before the band wheeled aside and came straight toward her.

The movement startled her. She trembled with a sense of something holy turned suddenly watchful, like a saint in a picture leaning out of the frame. She saw close to her a round, boyish face, lower than her own, and heard a treble voice say, “Sister, you carry the Anathema about you. Yield it up to the blessed Gesù, and He will adorn you with the gems of His grace.”

She understood nothing. Her mind leapt first to her basket of sweets—were these alarming angels going to take them? She looked down, almost in panic.

“No, sister,” said a taller youth, pointing not at the basket but at her throat and waist. “It is those vanities that are the Anathema. Take off that necklace and unclasp that belt, that they may be burned in the holy Bonfire of Vanities, and save you from burning.”

“It is the truth, my sister,” said one taller still—the archangel of the band. “Listen to these voices speaking the divine message. You already carry a red cross. Let that be your only adornment. Yield up your necklace and belt, and you shall obtain grace.”

A great coldness washed through Tessa. She dared not say no, but she could not give up what she loved—those few bright things that were hers, bought for her by the man she trusted, the man who called her “pigeon” and brought coins for confetti. Her lips quivered; tears rushed into her eyes. The street blurred. She felt only confused terror and misery.

Then a gentle hand touched her arm, and a voice—soft, steady, like cool water over a burn—said, “Do not be afraid; no one shall harm you.”

Tessa looked up. Before her stood a lady in black, with a young face and hazel eyes that held love as if it were a kind of light. Tessa had never seen anyone like her. Under other circumstances she might have been struck dumb with awe, but in that moment awe was swallowed by relief: protection had a face.

The tears fell faster, loosening the knot in her throat. She clutched at her necklace as if it might be snatched away by holiness itself and sobbed, “I can’t give them to be burnt. My husband—he bought them for me—and they are so pretty—and Ninna—oh, I wish I’d never come!”

“Do not ask her for them,” the lady said to the white-robed boys, her tone mild yet carrying authority like a bell carrying over a crowd. “It answers no good end for people to give up such things against their will. That is not what Fra Girolamo approves. He would have such things given up freely.”

The name—Fra Girolamo—moved through the street like a shadow. The boys did not resist. Their train shifted and hurried on, as if drawn by a new prey of ribbons and bright metal further down the way.

Tessa stood trembling, her necklace still warm under her fingers. “Oh, I will go back to the house,” she said, shaken. “I will go nowhere else. But if I should meet them again, and you not be there?” Her voice asked everything of this strange lady, as a child asks bread.

“Stay a little,” the lady said. “Come with me under this doorway, and we will hide the necklace and clasp, and then you will be in no danger.”

She led Tessa beneath an archway where the street’s noise softened, the echoes falling away into quiet. Even the city sounded different there: the holiday clatter dulled to a distant wash, as if thick cloth had been hung between Tessa and fear.

“Now,” said the lady, “can we find room for your necklace and belt in your basket? Ah—your basket is full of crisp things that will break. Let us be careful, and lay the heavy necklace under them.”

Her hands moved with a housekeeper’s gentleness, lifting the light parcels so they did not crack, shifting them so the sugared shells would not crush. The simple domestic care—how she respected the fragile sweetness—felt to Tessa like stepping from nightmare onto firm ground. The lady unfastened the necklace and unclasped the belt while Tessa did nothing but look up into that bending face.

“They are sweets for Lillo and Ninna,” Tessa said, watching her basket as if it were the cradle of all she loved.

“Those are your children?” The lady smiled.

“Yes. And I would rather go home to them than see any more of the Carnival. I shall never like bonfires again.”

“You have not far to go to the Piazza de’ Signori,” the lady said gently, “and there you would see the pile for the great bonfire.”

“No, oh no!” Tessa answered quickly. “I will go back.”

“You live at some castello, doubtless,” the lady said, not waiting for correction. “Towards which gate do you go?”

“Towards Por’ Santa Croce.”

“Come then.” She took Tessa by the hand and led her to a corner opposite, where the street opened into a straighter way. The sounds shifted there: less crowd, more footfall, a dog barking somewhere behind a wall. “If you go down there, you will soon be in a straight road. And I must leave you now, because someone else expects me. You will not be frightened. Your pretty things are safe now. Addio.”

“Addio, Madonna,” Tessa whispered, not knowing what else she should say to such a person.

And in an instant the lady was gone, her tall dark figure gliding away and vanishing round the stonework as if she belonged to another current of the city—one that moved with purpose, not with holiday drift.

Tessa turned to catch one last glimpse and saw only emptiness where the gentle authority had been. Then she began walking home in wonder, longing for Monna Lisa’s familiar deafness, for the kitchen smells of simple cooking, for the soft, everyday noises of children—those small, truthful sounds that could heal the mind better than any procession.

All the while, Baldassarre had kept her in sight—until the moment she parted from the lady in black.

Then he went away with his bundle of yarn, his feet carrying him as if pulled by thought.

He had seen the two wives together. The sight brought vividness to the dim shapes in his mind, as if colour had been laid freshly on a faded fresco. His imagining always needed the senses to stiffen it into certainty.

The tall wife—the noble, rightful one—she had blood in her that could kindle to resentment. She would understand scholarship, he thought, and understand too how learning might be locked away by the wreck of a body like treasure buried by an earthquake. She could believe him. Better: she would be inclined to believe him if he proved that her husband was unfaithful. Women cared about that. They would take vengeance for that.

If she loved him, then injury would flame in her—a second will, a second strength added to his own. He lingered on the thought with keen longing, not seeing—unable to see—how pain might recoil upon innocence. Both wives had been kind to him; their acts, bound up with the image of their faces, had not vanished from his memory. Yet the idea of their suffering did not rise as a restraint. Pain, to him, seemed the order of the world for all except the hard and base.

If any were innocent, if any were noble—where could the utmost gladness lie for them? Where it lay for him: in unconquerable hatred and triumphant vengeance.

But he must be cautious. He must watch the noble wife in the Via de’ Bardi and learn more of her. Even now frustration was possible. There was no power left to him but patience.

When Romola had said that someone else was waiting for her, she meant her cousin Brigida; yet she had not guessed how urgently that good woman needed shelter—not from rain or cold, but from the sharp, clean wind of righteousness that had begun to sweep Florence, stripping the city of its bright excess as one strips rosemary from a twig for the pot.

They were walking back toward the Piazza together, and from a distance they had already seen the white-robed youths collect and halt before Tessa. Romola, drawing nearer, caught the contadina’s frightened face, the poor girl’s helplessness set out plainly as bread on a bare board. “Wait for me a moment, cousin,” Romola said, turning.

Monna Brigida’s hand tightened on Romola’s sleeve, then fell away as if scorched. “Ah—I will not go on,” she answered hastily. “Come for me to Boni’s shop. I shall go back there.”

There were reasons for this sudden retreat, as palpable to Brigida as the feel of a corset-lace pulled too tight. She knew what she carried on her person—those little vanities that were like sweetmeats for the eyes and bitter in the conscience: rouge rubbed into the cheeks, false braids heavy as ripened grapes, pearl embroidery that caught the light and returned it with a cold, delighted glitter. And now, with the Piagnoni abroad, she had begun to fear—truly fear—that paint and purchased hair and ornament did not merely change the face: they endangered the soul.

It was as if the city’s very air had been seasoned with a new herb—sharp, medicinal, hard to disguise. What used to taste harmless had acquired an after-flavor of reproach. Even the familiar pleasures of dressing—pins, ribbons, the pleasing tug of braids made to sit properly—had turned uncertain, as if someone had swapped the sugar for salt. And there was Romola herself, young, grave, beautiful, moving through the world with a steadiness that made Brigida’s own life—once so full of mirrors and small triumphs—feel suddenly frivolous, even culpable.

A widow of five-and-fifty whose contentment has long been kneaded from what she thinks of her own appearance, and what she believes others think of it, does not easily learn to feed on penitence. Brigida’s mornings at her toilet had become skirmishes. If the soul prospered better without these trappings, was it worth the trouble to put on rouge and braids at all?

Yet when she lifted the hand-mirror and saw the sallow skin, the baggy cheeks, the crow’s-feet that no simpering could smooth away—when she parted the grey hair and tried to let it lie in the plain Piagnone fashion, meekly framing her face—courage curdled. Monna Berta would certainly laugh and call her an old hag; and as Monna Berta was only fifty-two, her cruelty had the edge of that small superiority. Every woman who was not of the Piagnoni would shrug. The men would address her like their grandmother. Whereas a woman of five-and-fifty was not so very old—she only required a little making up, a little arranging, like yesterday’s stew warmed and improved with a pinch of spice.

So the rouge went on again, the braids were pinned, the embroidered berretta settled in its pride. The mirror returned the accustomed effect, and Brigida breathed easier, as if she had found the familiar savor again. And her neck—if she covered it, people might suppose it too old to show; but with necklaces lying upon it, it looked better than Monna Berta’s. Even this day, preparing for the Piagnone Carnival, she had fought that battle, and the mixture of fear and longing that had set her hands trembling now drove her backward, toward the safety of Boni’s shop, rather than forward into the streets where collectors of the Anathema might seize on her when Romola was not beside her.

But Brigida was not quick enough.

The white-robed boys in the rear of the troop that had turned toward Tessa had already seen her before she changed direction. Perhaps it even made their surrender of Tessa easier—there was a larger, richer target now, bearing on her head and cheeks the dangerous weight of forbidden finery. Several of the youths were very young, trained early to a zeal that had the fervor of a flame and the heedlessness of a flame too, consuming whatever lay nearest.

A small fellow of ten—olive wreath above cherubic cheeks, wide brown eyes that looked as if they truly expected heaven and hell to lean close at any moment—was the first to reach Brigida and plant himself across her way. His face held an odd mixture: awe at existence, longing to be good, and beneath it the restless itch to command and meddle.

Brigida felt anger rise like pepper in the throat. Her eyes searched for an open door, a threshold to slip across; but there was none near, and flight now would only sharpen pursuit. It was not the cherubic child who spoke first, however, but a youth of fifteen carrying one handle of a broad basket.

“Venerable mother!” he began, with the practiced voice of someone reciting a formula that had been applauded. “The blessed Jesus commands you to give up the Anathema which you carry upon you. That cap embroidered with pearls, those jewels that fasten up your false hair—let them be given up and sold for the poor; and cast the hair itself away from you, as a lie that is only fit for burning. Doubtless, too, you have other jewels under your silk mantle.”

Another youth, holding the other handle, chimed in quickly, his tongue full of Fra Girolamo’s turns of speech. “Yes, lady, they are too heavy for you: heavier than a millstone, and weighting you for perdition. Will you adorn yourself with the hunger of the poor, and be proud to carry God’s curse upon your head?”

Then the child spoke in a sweet soprano that made the words more terrible, as when a clear flute plays a lament over a funeral procession. “In truth you are old, buona madre. You look very ugly with the red on your cheeks and that black glistening hair, and those fine things. It is only Satan who can like to see you. Your Angel is sorry. He wants you to rub away the red.”

He snatched a soft silk scarf from the basket and held it out—like a napkin offered at table, except it was meant to wipe away not sauce but identity. Brigida’s anger and mortification sank fast into a deeper alarm. Monna Berta and the gay world were not there to witness and rescue her pride. Instead she was ringed by young monitors in white robes with wreaths and red crosses—faces bright with a candor that had no mercy in it, like light on a bare plate that shows every stain.

Her Franciscan confessor, Fra Cristoforo of Santa Croce, was not at hand to stiffen her distrust of Dominican severity. She felt herself helplessly taken, shaken by the vague sense that a supreme warning had come—come with feet and voices, come in a rush of white sleeves and basket-handles. No other course suggested itself. She took the scarf and rubbed her cheeks, trembling, obedient as a child made to wash.

“It is well, madonna,” said the second youth. “It is a holy beginning. And when you have taken those vanities from your head, the dew of heavenly grace will descend on it.”

The mischief in the troop—always mingled with sincerity—grew stronger. The cherubic boy put his hand to one of the jewelled pins fastening the braids to the berretta and drew it out. The heavy black plait fell down over Brigida’s face like a curtain dropped without warning; it dragged her head-gear forward. Shamed into haste, she lifted both hands, undid the remaining fastenings, and flung into the basket of doom her beloved crimson-velvet berretta with its unsurpassed embroidery of seed-pearls.

There she stood unrouged: grey hair pushed back from a face where certain deep lines of age had triumphed over fullness. It was as if a rich pastry had been scraped bare to show the honest, darker crumb beneath.

But the berretta was not left quietly in the basket. With impish zeal the youngsters lifted it up and displayed it pitilessly, false hair dangling like a caught fish.

“See, venerable mother,” said the taller youth, “what ugly lies you have delivered yourself from! And now you look like the blessed Saint Anna, the mother of the Holy Virgin.”

In Brigida’s mind, thoughts tumbled—going into a convent at once, never showing herself in the world again, shutting the door on every mirror. There was nothing possible, she told herself, but to take care of her soul. Of course people were laughing; she did not need to turn her head to taste that bitterness. Perhaps it would be better, truly, to be forced to think more of Paradise.

But when the thought came—sharp as vinegar—that the dear accustomed world was no longer hers to choose, hard tears gathered, those scant tears that only moisten elderly eyes. Through the blur she saw a large rough hand holding a red cross thrust suddenly before her over the boys’ shoulders, and heard a strong guttural voice that cut across the chanting zeal like a hawker’s cry across church music:

“Only four quattrini, madonna, blessing and all! Buy it. You’ll find a comfort in it now your wig’s gone. Deh! what are we sinners doing all our lives? Making soup in a basket, and getting nothing but the scum for our stomachs. Better buy a blessing, madonna! Only four quattrini; the profit is not so much as the smell of a danaro, and it goes to the poor.”

In dim-eyed confusion Brigida was already fumbling toward her embroidered scarsella hidden beneath her silk mantle, ready for yet another submission, when the group opened—parted as if a stronger current had entered—and a figure appeared that felt to Brigida like an angel loosening prison-bolts.

“Romola, look at me!” she cried, piteously, thrusting out both hands.

The white troop began to move away, with a faint sense, perhaps, that their zeal about head-gear had been excessive enough to excuse them from pressing her further for offerings. Romola, smitten with pity, could hardly keep from smiling at the sudden apparition of her cousin in a genuine, unadorned guise so unlike every remembered image. She took the black drapery from her own head and threw it over Brigida’s, covering the grey hair like a cloth drawn over a cooling loaf.

“There,” Romola said, softly, as if quieting a frightened animal. “No one will remark you now. We will turn down the Via del Palagio and go straight to our house.”

They hastened away. Brigida clung to Romola’s hand tightly, as if touch were proof that she had not been abandoned to the street and its judgments. The soundscape around them—boys’ voices fading, laughter pricking, footsteps scraping stone—seemed to Brigida like a hostile chorus, while Romola’s steady pace and low words made a small refuge of rhythm.

“Ah, my Romola, my dear child!” Brigida sobbed, the short fat woman taking quick little steps to keep up with the tall young figure beside her. “What an old scarecrow I am! I must be good—I mean to be good!”

“Yes, yes; buy a cross!” the guttural voice pursued, as persistent as a fly that has scented sweet must. The rough hand thrust itself forward again with the red cross: for Bratti would not be abashed by Romola’s presence into abandoning a likely customer, and he had followed their retreat as quietly as a man carrying a tray follows the hunger in a crowd. “Only four quattrini, blessing and all—and if there was any profit, it would all go to the poor.”

Brigida would have had to pause even in a less submissive mood. She lifted one hand, deprecating, to stop Romola’s remonstrance; with the other she reached out a grosso—worth many white quattrini—and said pleadingly, “Take it, good man, and begone.”

“You’re in the right, madonna,” Bratti said, snatching the coin with the quickness of trade and pushing the cross into her hand. “I’ll not offer you change, for I might as well rob you of a mass. What! we must all be scorched a little, but you’ll come off the easier; better fall from the window than the roof. A good Easter and a good year to you!”

When he turned away at last, Brigida’s voice broke with a kind of comic despair that was half sincerity, half the habit of appealing to an audience. “Well, Romola, if I’m to be a Piagnone it’s no matter how I look!”

“Dear cousin,” Romola answered, smiling at her with an affection that made the words warm instead of sharp, “you don’t know how much better you look than you ever did before. I see now how good-natured your face is, like yourself. That red and finery seemed to thrust themselves forward and hide expression. Ask our Piero or any other painter if he would not rather paint your portrait now than before. I think all lines of the human face have something either touching or grand, unless they seem to come from low passions. How fine old men are, like my godfather! Why should not old women look grand and simple?”

“Yes—when one gets to be sixty, my Romola,” Brigida said, relapsing a little into her old calculations, as if counting years like measures of flour. “But I’m only fifty-five, and Monna Berta, and everybody—” She checked herself, breath catching; then, as if the day’s stripping had left her with only the essential, she added, “But it’s no use: I will be good, like you. Your mother—if she’d been alive—would have been as old as I am; we were cousins together. One must either die or get old. But it doesn’t matter about being old, if one’s a Piagnone.”

The happenings of that Carnival day seemed, at first, to leave Romola nothing to carry in her hands but the same plain burden she had taken up before: cousin Brigida’s wavering endurance of age, her peevish shame at grey hairs, her frightened pride that needed steadying as one steadies a pot on the fire when it threatens to boil over. Yet those bright follies of Carnival had opened upon a Lent that held Romola as if the city itself had become a great kitchen at dawn, all hearths lit, all vessels set to simmer, and every hour demanding watchfulness lest something unseen should scorch, sour, or spill.

Bernardo del Nero was Gonfaloniere. The Medicean party had strained hard and gained that triumph; and with it Romola’s inward foreboding thickened, like a broth darkening when the lid is lifted and one sees how much has reduced away. She felt some scheme in the air—prepared quietly, as men salt meat before a journey, meaning it for a season of scarcity—something that might ripen into success or into betrayal while her godfather held the staff of office.

Each morning, when the first weak light crept into her room, it seemed not merely daybreak but that fear returning—touching her temples, sitting on her chest, making even the familiar sounds in the house—wood shifting, a distant footstep—seem like furtive signals. She carried it with her through the streets on her way to the early sermon; yet in the Duomo, as men forget the dread of death when steel rings against steel, she forgot the chill, because there was a larger tumult to enter.

Savonarola was preaching—his last course of Lenten sermons he would ever be allowed to end in that vast, echoing place. He knew excommunication hung close, and he had come to the point of defying it. His words, sharp as a knife that will not spare sinew because the butcher is tender-hearted, laid bare the Church’s condition; he called things by their names, refusing those polite seasonings that disguise rancidness. He proclaimed renovation with a confidence that mounted, phrase by phrase, as if he were piling faggots and setting fire to them beneath the old, damp timbers of corruption.

Of his own destiny he spoke as one who sees two roads open and cannot tell, at each step, which his foot is taking. At times he seemed to behold himself as part of the coming revolt, his voice blown through Christendom like a trumpet that makes old walls tremble; he spoke of the Church as a dead body that might yet quiver into new life, as Lazarus quivered when the Divine voice pierced the sealed darkness. Then, with a sudden turn—as if a draught had entered and made the flame waver—he spoke as if there were nothing before him but persecution and martyrdom: this life a vigil; dawn, only after death.

For any mind not utterly dull, such a position had its own dreadful impressiveness, even for those—like Macchiavelli—ready to interpret the Frate’s fervour by a key that allowed no loftiness. To Romola, whose kindred ardour made her believe in the genuine greatness of Savonarola’s purpose, the crisis stirred her like something that belonged to her own lot. It sank into her as an exalting memory, and the heat of it went with her into her daily labours.

Those labours asked for more than patience; they asked for courage, the kind that is used up and must be renewed as bread is, day by day. Famine had not yet loosened its grip from Florence. Distress, long continued, grows heavier not because it is worse each hour, but because it is always there: the same hollow cheeks, the same hands tremoring over an empty bowl, the same dull eyes waiting for what cannot be promised. Disease spread among the crowded lanes; the Plague was expected, spoken of as men speak of a storm they smell in the air. Romola went among the sick and hungry and murmuring. The sour odour of close rooms, of damp straw, of unwashed bodies, clung to her clothes; the thin gruel she stirred in poor households had a smell of burnt grain and too much water; yet she took pains all the same—rinsing a pot, scraping what remained at the bottom into a child’s mouth, coaxing a fevered woman to sip warmed wine with herbs when she could procure them. And when her limbs were weary and her pity felt like a mere handful thrown into a sea, it seemed good to be inspired by something besides pity—to believe in a heroism struggling toward sublime ends, toward which her small acts might tend, as dew tends toward an unseen harvest.

Yet that mighty music which rolled through the Duomo did not keep its harmonies unbroken. Since the first days of glowing hope—when the Frate, seeing the near triumph of good in the reform of the Republic and the coming of the French deliverer, had preached peace and charity and the oblivion of political differences—conditions had changed. Intrigue had been too stubborn for oblivion; the French deliverer, turning his back on what men had named his mission, seemed to have wrought harm by disappointing faith. Hostility, petty and grand, attacked Savonarola with new weapons and new determination.

So contention and self-vindication sounded more and more in his sermons. The popular demand pressed him not only for insistence and detail about visions and private revelations, but for a tone of defiant confidence against objectors. He who had denounced the thirst for miracles and declared them unrelated to true faith, had come to say that at the right moment the Divine power would attest the truth of his prophetic preaching by a miracle. And as the vision of triumphant good receded behind the felt predominance of evil, his threats of coming vengeance against vicious tyrants and corrupt priests gained impetus—no longer purely from indignant zeal, but with a sting that could only come from personal exasperation.

In a great public orator who gives himself up to the moment, the conflict of selfish and unselfish emotion—hidden in most men’s secret chambers—stands out terribly clear: the language of inner voices is written, as it were, in letters of fire where all may read. If the jar of exasperation pained Romola, there was another hearer in that crowd for whom those harsh notes were the only thrilling ones, as deep bass vibrations are the only thing that pierces certain deafness.

Baldassarre had learned that the wonderful Frate was preaching again. As often as he could, he came to drink in the threats of a voice that sounded to him like justice made audible. He came the more because he had seen Romola come; he was waiting and watching for the hour when not only outward chance but his own shifting mind would make it possible to seek speech with her.

Twice Romola had caught sight of his face in the Duomo—once when its dark glance fixed itself upon hers. She wished not to see it again, and yet she looked for it, as men look for a portent’s return. But whatever revelation might lie in that old man belonged, she told herself, to the past; and her anxiety was drawn almost wholly into the present.

The stirring Lent passed. April—the second and last month of her godfather’s authority—drew near its close, and nothing had happened to fulfil her foreboding. In the public mind too there had been fears; rumours had travelled from Rome of menacing activity on the part of Piero de’ Medici; but in a few days Bernardo would be out of power, and suspicion might prove only smoke. Romola tried to gather courage from the review of her own futile tremblings, as one tastes a sauce and thinks, Perhaps it was only my palate that was wrong, not the pot.

Then, on the twenty-seventh, as she went on her usual errands of mercy in the afternoon, a messenger met her from Camilla Rucellai—chief among the feminine seers of Florence—praying her to come at once on matters of the highest moment.

Romola shrank. There was in her an unconquerable repulsion from the shrill volubility of those illuminated women, whose excitability seemed to her like froth rising where there should be clear substance. And she had, just now, a special reluctance toward Camilla, for a report had reached her that the woman had announced revelations hostile to Bernardo del Nero. Romola’s first impulse was to send back a refusal. The message might concern public affairs; and she felt, with something like bodily nausea, the wish to shut her ears against knowledge that might only heap weight upon her already strained mind.

But it had become her habit—painful, drilled into her by sorrow and responsibility—to reject the first prompting and obey outward claims. Cowardice and selfishness, she reproved herself; was she to let her presentiments make her refuse a call? So she complied, and went straight to Camilla.

She found the nervous grey-haired woman in a chamber contrived to resemble a convent cell. The bareness was a kind of stage-bareness, as if someone had swept away ordinary living not for cleanliness but for effect. Camilla’s thin fingers clutched Romola as she sat; and the eager voice, beginning in a loud whisper, made Romola feel a physical shrinking, as if a sharp smell had rushed into her nostrils—too much of some pungent herb bruised under a careless hand.

Camilla had a vision to relate. It had been revealed to her by Romola’s Angel—so she said—that Romola knew certain secrets about her godfather, Bernardo del Nero, which, if disclosed, might save the Republic from peril. As Camilla narrated, her voice rose in pitch and volume, leaping upward like a kettle whose lid begins to chatter. She ended by exhorting Romola to obey her Angel’s command and separate herself from the enemy of God.

Romola’s impetuosity belonged to a massive nature; unless deeply stirred, her manner was calm, held-in. She had a constitutional disgust for the shallow excitability of women like Camilla, whose faculties seemed wrought into fantasies until there was no steady remainder for thought or true emotion. Before Camilla had finished, Romola started up and tried to wrench her arm free. Camilla’s grip tightened.

It was useless. The prophetess held on like a crab; and Romola’s resistance, instead of sobering her, drove her into wilder assertion. She burst into shriller statements of other visions meant to corroborate the first. Christ Himself had appeared to her, she said, and ordered her to send His command to certain citizens in office: they were to throw Bernardo del Nero from the window of the Palazzo Vecchio. Fra Girolamo knew of it—and this time, Camilla declared, he had not dared to say the vision lacked Divine authority.

“And since then,” Camilla cried, her excited treble straining upward as her eyes strained too, “the Blessed Infant has come to me and laid a wafer of sweetness on my tongue, in token of his pleasure that I had done his will.”

“Let me go!” Romola’s voice came deep with anger, like something forced up from under stone. “God grant you are mad! else you are detestably wicked!”

Her effort was too strong now even for Camilla. Romola wrenched her arm free and rushed out. She did not pause until she had hurried far along the street and found herself near the church of the Badia.

To pass behind the curtain under the old stone arch was to step into a hush that shut out the street’s jostling. The city’s sounds—barrows rattling on stones, voices bargaining, a hammer striking—fell away, and what remained was the faint, living acoustics of sanctuary: a footfall softened, a breath, the distant murmur that might have been prayer or only the building’s own ancient settling. It was as if the very air had been strained clean, leaving a quiet that could nourish the mind the way clear water nourishes a tired palate.

She went in and sank on the altar-step before Filippino Lippi’s serene Virgin appearing to Saint Bernard, hoping the inward tumult would subside in that place where every object suggested peace persisting in the midst of turmoil.

The sharpest pressure on her was Camilla’s claim that Savonarola had countenanced such wicked folly. Romola did not believe for a moment that he had sanctioned the throwing of Bernardo del Nero from a window as a Divine command; she felt sure there was falsehood or mistake. Savonarola had grown more severe against malcontents; yet strict law and order were fundamental in his political teaching.

Still—since he knew the possibly fatal effects of visions like Camilla’s, since he distrusted such spirit-seeing women and kept away from them as much as possible—why, with his readiness to denounce wrong from the pulpit, did he not publicly denounce these pretended revelations that cast darkness, not light, across the idea of a Supreme Will?

Why?

The answer came with painful clearness, as when one tastes bitterness and knows at once it has entered the whole dish. He was fettered inwardly by the consciousness that such revelations were not, at their base, distinctly separable from his own visions. He was fettered outwardly by the consequence he foresaw: a cry raised even among his own party that he wished to suppress all Divine inspiration of which he was not the vessel—he, or his confidential supplementary seer, Fra Salvestro.

Kneeling with her face buried against the stone of the altar-step, Romola endured one of those sickening moments when the enthusiasm that had come to her as the only energy making life seem worth living appeared bound up, inevitably, with vain dreams and wilful shutting of eyes. She thought, with a sudden pull of longing, of her godfather’s strong worldly sense, his dignified prudence, his untheoretic virtues—virtues like well-leavened bread, not dazzling but sustaining. Was he to be treated as an Agag because he believed a more restricted government better than the Great Council, and because he would not pretend to forget old ties to the banished family?

But with that thought rose again her presentiment of some plot to restore the Medici; and again she felt the popular party was half justified in its fierce suspicion. Again she felt the sacredness of keeping Florence’s government pure, of keeping out a vicious rule. There, the Frate was right; he had carried her understanding irrevocably with him.

Yet at this moment the assent of her understanding came alone, unwillingly. Her heart recoiled from a right allied to so much narrowness—a right that seemed to entail a hard, systematic judging of men by assents and denials that lay like thin labels upon the surface of manhood. Her affection and respect clung with new tenacity to her godfather; and with him clung the memories of her father—memories allied to the refusal to divide men into sheep and goats by some easy political or religious mark, as one sorts grain by a sieve that cannot measure nourishment.

After all that can be said about the widening power of ideas, it remains true they would not act so strongly if they were not taken into a solvent of feeling. The great world-struggle of developing thought is foreshadowed again and again in the struggle of the affections, seeking justification for love and hope. If Romola’s intellect had been less able to discern complexity, the early loving associations of her life would have forbidden her to accept implicitly Savonarola’s denunciatory exclusiveness. She had felt simply that his mind offered deeper, more efficacious truth than any other; and the breathing-room she found in his large view of human duty had made her patient toward what she could not absorb—so long as its practical effect did not strike against any strong force within her.

Now a sudden insurrection of feeling had brought the collision. Her indignation, once roused by Camilla’s visions, could not stop there; it ran like flame along kindred facts in Savonarola’s teaching. For the moment she felt what was true in the scornful sarcasms flung against him more keenly than what was false. It was an illumination that made all life look ghastly.

Where were the beings to whom she could cling—work with—endure with—believing she was working for the right? On the side whence moral energy came lay a fanaticism from which she shrank with newly startled repulsion. On the side to which she was drawn by affection and memory lay the presentiment of secret plotting—something her judgment told her would not unfairly be called crime.

And surmounting every other thought was the dread inspired by Tito’s hints: lest that presentiment should become knowledge in such a way that she would be torn by irreconcilable claims.

Calmness would not come even here. The serene faces in the picture—the saint writing in rocky solitude, visited by celestial peace—did not bring peace to her. That rocky solitude was too far away; Romola was pressed in the hard crush of human difficulty, where the loud world intruded even into prayer.

She rose, thinking to hasten back to her sick people in the courtyard—thinking that by some immediate beneficent act, as by giving a thirsty mouth a cup held steady, she might revive in herself that sense of life’s worth which at this instant was unfed by any wider faith.

But when she turned, she found herself face to face with a man standing only two yards off.

It was Baldassarre.

“I would speak with you,” Baldassarre said, when Romola’s eyes at last met his without shrinking.

It was plain he had followed her out of Santa Maria del Fiore and waited, like a shadow that dared not cross the light. The air around them held the day’s last heat—stone warmed through, incense long since thinned—yet his voice had the dry rasp of someone who had breathed too much dust.

“Yes,” Romola answered, with the same meek steadiness with which she might have taken on a hard penance. She felt, in the very muscles of her throat, that she was about to swallow something bitter and must not gag.

“But you would go where no one can hear us?” she added.

“Where he will not come upon us,” Baldassarre murmured, darting a glance behind him as if the very paving-stones carried messages. “Out—in the air—away from the streets.”

“I sometimes go to San Miniato at this hour,” Romola said. “If you will, I will go now. Follow me. It is far; but there we may be solitary.”

He nodded—quickly, hungrily—and she set out at once, choosing the long climb rather than any alley where voices echoed and men’s shoulders brushed too close. To many a woman it would have seemed a peril to lead so wild-looking a stranger toward loneliness; but Romola’s life had lately taught her that danger did not always announce itself with a knife or a shout. Sometimes it came sweetened, served up like sugared almonds at a wedding feast, and only later did the mouth learn it had been fed on poison.

They went upward through the changing sound of Florence: the bright clatter of hoof and cart-wheels thinning behind them, the cries of vendors sinking to a distant chatter, until there was more wind than voice, more leaf than laughter. Cicadas had begun their thin, relentless sawing in the scrub; now and then a bell-note travelled from a lower church and died in the open air like steam off hot bread.

When the afternoon was far advanced and the sun already stooped low in the west, Romola paused on rough ground in the shadow of tall cypress-trunks. The earth here was stony and pale, as if flour had been sifted over it; between stones, a few tough herbs clung on—wild fennel and thyme bruised underfoot, giving off sharp scents that pricked at the nostrils and made the mouth water with the remembered bite of country food.

She looked around for Baldassarre. He was not far behind; but when he reached her he dropped heavily onto an edge of rock and hard soil, as though the hill had taken payment from his bones. The thickset frame that once had fought and endured—the frame that had first shown itself to her with a rope round it in the Duomo—had lost its sturdy vigor. Under the tremor of exertion his eyes seemed vaguer, as if the mind behind them were groping for its own name.

“The hill is steep,” Romola said, sitting near him with compassionate gentleness. “And I fear you have been weakened by want.”

He turned his head and fixed his eyes on her. A long silence followed, not stubborn but helpless: the pause of a man who feels words on the edge of him the way one feels hunger—certain, gnawing, and yet unable to seize a morsel. Romola held herself still, almost holding her breath, as if any impatience in her would make the fragile thing he was trying to bring forth crumble back into dark.

He looked like no more than a common-bred, neglected old man. Yet Romola’s days had been spent near such figures now—near the poor, the sick, the down-trodden—and she had learned to see tragedy lodged in coarse hands and broken nails, to recognize that the great disasters of the world often ended in very small, domestic miseries: empty bowls, thin blankets, the ache of walking too far on too little bread.

Gradually his glance gathered itself, as flame gathers from a wick. At last, with abrupt emphasis, he said, “Ah! you would have been my daughter!”

The color rushed into Romola’s face and fled as swiftly, leaving her lips pale and parted. She sat like a marble image that had heard a verdict.

In that one word—daughter—the whole story leapt into shape inside her, as if someone had thrown a lamp into a closed room. Tito’s smiling evasions, his easy turns of phrase, his practiced tenderness: her mind seized them and held them up to a merciless new light. There could be no check, in the first instant, to the belief that sprang from her knowledge of his nature.

Her face, betraying so much, stirred Baldassarre like wine. For the first time his words had struck where they meant to strike. He leaned toward her, eagerness hardening his voice, and laid his rough hand on her arm.

“You are a woman of proud blood—is it not true?” he said. “You go to hear the preacher; you hate baseness—baseness that smiles and triumphs. You hate your husband?”

“Oh God! were you really his father?” Romola whispered. She was too filled with the images crowding upon her—the boy in Greek curls, the man with gentle eyes—to take note even of the hatred Baldassarre tried to stir. “Or was it as he said? Did you take him when he was little?”

“Ah, you believe me—you know what he is!” Baldassarre cried, exulting. His grip tightened, as if the contact itself fed his strength. “You will help me?”

“Yes,” Romola said—meaning pity, meaning human help, meaning any healing one might give to a ruined soul.

She laid her palm gently on the hand bruising her arm. The skin beneath her touch was hard and cracked, like bark; it reminded her of hands that had dug and lifted and gone hungry. Tears rose in her eyes as she looked at him.

“Oh, it is piteous!” she said. “Tell me—you were a great scholar; you taught him. How is it?”

She broke off, a chill darting through her. Tito had called this man mad. And where, in this broken creature, were the signs of refinement, of past learning? Yet she did not snatch away her hand. She had learned that revulsion can wound worse than a blow. She sat perfectly still, and listened more cautiously.

“It is gone!—it is all gone!” Baldassarre said. “And they would not believe me, because he lied, and said I was mad; and they had me dragged to prison. And I am old—my mind will not come back. And the world is against me.”

His eyes sank as if a wave of despondency passed over him, leaving him cold. Then he looked up again, and the fire returned.

“But you are not against me,” he said. “He made you love him, and he has been false to you; and you hate him. Yes—he made me love him. He was beautiful and gentle, and I was a lonely man. I took him when they were beating him. He slept in my bosom when he was little, and I watched him as he grew, and gave him all my knowledge, and everything that was mine I meant to be his. I had many things; money, and books, and gems. He had my gems—he sold them; and he left me in slavery. He never came to seek me; and when I came back poor and in misery, he denied me. He said I was a madman.”

“He told us his father was dead—was drowned,” Romola said faintly, as if saying it could change it. “Surely he must have believed it then. Oh—he could not have been so base then!”

A vision rose, keen as the smell of new-baked bread that brings back a whole morning: those first days of her marriage, when Tito’s presence seemed a gentle nourishment, and she had swallowed his words as easily as milk. The yearning regret within that memory loosened, for a moment, the rigid horror. Tears broke free; with one great sob they rushed down her face.

“Ah, you are young, and the tears come easily,” Baldassarre said, with an impatient edge. “But tears are no good. They only put out the fire within—and it is the fire that works. Tears will hinder us. Listen to me.”

Romola started slightly. Again the thought flickered—madness. If this were madness, it might be dangerous; if it were truth, it was more dangerous still. Yet she did not dare to show doubt. Better to keep his confidence, to gather facts, to find firm ground beneath her feet in a world that had become slippery.

“Tell me,” she said, keeping her voice as gentle as she could, “how did you lose your memory—your scholarship?”

“I was ill,” Baldassarre answered. “I can’t tell how long—it was a blank. I remember nothing. Only at last I was sitting in the sun among the stones, and everything else was darkness. And slowly, and by degrees, I felt something besides that: a longing for something—I did not know what—that never came. And when I was in the ship on the waters I began to know what I longed for. It was for the Boy to come back—it was to find all my thoughts again, for I was locked away outside them all. And I am outside now. I feel nothing but a wall and darkness.”

As he spoke, his voice went dreamy, and he fell silent, resting his head between his hands. The wind moved through the cypress like a long exhalation. Below, Florence was only a dim spread of roofs and towers, and its human noises were swallowed; up here, sound belonged to leaf, insect, and the far cry of a bird.

Romola’s doubts sank again under the weight of pity. She had watched her own father’s daily pain—how Bardo missed Dino and the future he had laid up for him like carefully stored grain. Loss, she knew, could hollow out the mind, leaving it echoing.

“It all came back once,” Baldassarre said suddenly, raising his head. “I was master of everything. I saw all the world again, and my gems, and my books. I thought I had him in my power, and I went to expose him where—where the lights were and the trees; and he lied again, and said I was mad, and they dragged me away to prison… Wickedness is strong; and he wears armour.”

The fierceness flared. He seized her arm again.

“But you will help me? He has been false to you too. He has another wife, and she has children. He makes her believe he is her husband, and she is a foolish, helpless thing. I will show you where she lives.”

The first shock that shot through Romola turned to visible anger. The indignity to her as a woman rose, instinctive and burning; it was as if her very name had been taken from her and given to another mouth to speak. Baldassarre felt that heat and mistook it for the thirst he wanted.

“You hate him,” he urged. “Is it not true? There is no love between you; I know that. I know women can hate; and you have proud blood. You hate falseness, and you can love revenge.”

Romola sat as if bound, not feeling his bruising grasp. Her thoughts clashed and would not settle: shame, pity for the other woman, horror at Tito, a dim dread of the violence in the man beside her. Even the very words Baldassarre used—wife, rightful, justice—seemed to carry invisible weights. In Florence, words were weapons as much as knives; the wrong word, in the wrong mouth, could strip a person of place and protection. And Romola, who had grown up among scholars, felt with sick clarity how little any phrase could translate the whole truth of what she had lived. The heart’s experience had no clean Latin for it, no Greek that would preserve its exact flavor; it was like trying to keep the scent of crushed thyme in a closed fist.

“You shall contrive it,” Baldassarre said at last, bending toward her in an eager whisper. “I have learned by heart that you are his rightful wife. You are a noble woman. You go to hear the preacher of vengeance; you will help justice. But you will think for me. My mind goes—everything goes sometimes—all but the fire. The fire is God: it is justice: it will not die. You believe that—is it not true? If they will not hang him for robbing me, you will take away his armour—you will make him go without it, and I will stab him. I have a knife, and my arm is still strong enough.”

He thrust his hand beneath his tunic and drew out a hidden knife. In the dimming light the blade caught a cold gleam. He ran his thumb along the edge absentmindedly, as if the sharpness were a thing he must taste to keep his purpose alive.

It seemed to Romola that each hour brought a new hardness, a new test. Her mind was too quick and sound to waste soft, scolding words on a man in this state; she knew they would be like pouring water into cracked earth. She chose not to answer his last speech. Better to turn him aside, gain time, let his heat cool, and—meanwhile—learn what she could.

She spoke, her voice trembling despite her effort at steadiness. “You say she is foolish and helpless—that other wife—and believes him to be her real husband. Perhaps he is. Perhaps he married her before he married me.”

“I cannot tell,” Baldassarre said, pausing, his fingers still on the knife-edge. Bewilderment crossed his face as if a door in his mind had slammed. “I can remember no more. I only know where she lives. You shall see her. I will take you; but not now,” he added hurriedly. “He may be there. The night is coming on.”

Romola started with sudden awareness. The sun had set; the hills were darkening. The wind had cooled, and the cypress shadows lay long and thick. Far off, Florence’s murmurs were almost gone; in their place were the closer sounds—the rasp of insects, the faint crackle of dry leaves—so that even her own breath seemed loud in her ears. The world up here felt watchful, like a kitchen at night when the fire has gone down and every tiny settling of the house can be heard.

“It is true,” she said, rising. “But you will come and take me—when?”

“In the morning,” Baldassarre replied, as if her question meant only impatience for vengeance. “Come to me where you came to me to-day—in the church. I will be there at ten; and if you are not there, I will go again towards mid-day. Can you remember?”

“Mid-day,” Romola repeated, fastening the word as one ties a knot.

“Mid-day,” Baldassarre echoed—then, as if the number slipped from him and only the broader mark remained, he said again, “Only mid-day. The same place, and mid-day.”

He rose too, catching her arm once more with his left hand while he held the knife in his right.

“And after that,” he said, his whisper thick with desire, “we will have our revenge. He shall feel the sharp edge of justice. The world is against me, but you will help me.”

“I would help you in other ways,” Romola said, making a first timid attempt to pierce the illusion. “I fear you are in want; you have to labour and get little. I should like to bring you comforts, and make you feel again that there is someone who cares for you.”

“Talk no more about that,” Baldassarre said fiercely. “I will have nothing else. Help me to wring one drop of vengeance on this side of the grave. I have nothing but my knife. It is sharp; but there is a moment after the thrust when men see the face of death—and it shall be my face that he will see.”

He let go and sank back into a sitting posture, as if the blaze in him had spent itself on those words. Romola stood, feeling a helplessness like hunger: a need that could not be satisfied by any food she knew how to provide. She must defer every intention till the morrow—till she could think, seek counsel, find some way to guard the living without yielding to the deadliness he called justice.

“Mid-day, then,” she said distinctly, putting firmness into the syllables.

“Yes,” Baldassarre answered, exhaustion falling over him like a cloak. “Go; I will rest here.”

She hurried away down the slope, her steps careful on the loose stones, the scent of bruised herbs rising with each footfall. At the last point from which he would likely still be visible, she turned. He sat where she had left him, hunched in the gathering dark—cypress behind him, knife hidden again, the air around him full of the small relentless sounds of the hillside.

Romola had gone out with one intent in her like a broth that, left too long over the coals, will not be held back from boiling. All the afternoon it had thickened and risen—no longer a chosen resolve but a necessity, as bodily as thirst. She did not wait for Maso’s slow, careful step, nor measure which streets were safest. She crossed the bridge where the Arno lay black as steeped olives, the last red of day dying behind it, and the wind in the arches made a hollow music that seemed to hurry her feet.

The city had the evening’s usual smells—damp stone, lamp-oil, stale wine from shutters newly barred—but they came to her as if through cloth. Sound was clearer than scent: the scrape of sandals, the mutter of men in doorways, the sudden far clang of a bell that made her heart jump, as if every note were a hand laid on her shoulder. She took the most direct way to the Old Palace. She might meet Tito there. It did not matter. She could not weigh chances; she must empty her heart, as one must lift the lid from a pot before it bursts.

She scarcely knew what she passed—the pillared court, the wide stairs—only that she asked an usher for the Gonfaloniere, gave her name, and begged for a private room. She was left among frescoed figures whose painted lips held their silence, while newly-lit tapers began to smell of warm tallow, a homely, kitchen-like odour in that public grandeur.

The door opened. Bernardo del Nero entered, his white head still carried erect above his silk lucco.

“Romola, my child—what is this?” His voice held the startled tenderness of one who has heard a dish crash in the next room.

She had uncovered her head. She went toward him without speaking. He laid a hand on her shoulder and held her a little away, as if to see whether fever had changed her. Her face was drawn with fatigue and long inward struggle; her hair had loosened and fallen; but her eyes had a bright, strained life, as if mind had for the moment conquered body.

“What has he done?” Bernardo said abruptly. “Tell me everything, child; throw away pride. I am your father.”

“It is not about myself—nothing about myself,” Romola answered, too quickly, as if the words tasted bitter. “Dearest godfather, it is about you. I have heard things—some I cannot tell you. But you are in danger in the palace; you are in danger everywhere. There are fanatical men who would harm you, and—and there are traitors. Trust nobody. If you trust, you will be betrayed.”

Bernardo smiled, the way an old man smiles at a young housewife warning him that knives are sharp. “Have you worked yourself into this agitation, my poor child,” he said, and his hand rose to her head, patting it gently, “to tell such old truth as that to an old man like me?”

“Oh no, no! They are not old truths that I mean,” Romola cried. Her hands clasped hard together, as if that pressure could keep back what must not be spoken. “They are fresh things that I know, but cannot tell. Dearest godfather, you know I am not foolish. I would not come to you without reason. Is it too late to warn you against any one—every one who seems to be working on your side? Is it too late to say, ‘Go to your villa and keep away in the country when these three more days of office are over?’ Oh God! perhaps it is too late! and if any harm comes to you, it will be as if I had done it!”

The last words burst from her as steam breaks through a crust. The confession startled her into silence; it was as if she had spilled something that could never be gathered up again.

“I mean,” she added, faltering, “I know nothing positive. I only know what fills me with fears.”

“Poor child!” Bernardo said. He looked at her a moment with a quiet, discerning gaze, weighing her as he might weigh the truth of a report. Then his tone softened into counsel.

“Go, Romola—go home and rest. These fears may be only big ugly shadows of something very little and harmless. Even traitors must see their interest in betraying; the rats will run where they smell the cheese, and there is no knowing yet which way the scent will come.”

He paused, his eyes turning away, his mind withdrawing into that inward chamber where old men keep their settled decisions. With a slow shrug he added, “As for warnings, they are of no use to me, child. I enter into no plots, but I never forsake my colours. If I march abreast with obstinate men, who will rush on guns and pikes, I must share the consequences. Let us say no more about that. I have not many years left at the bottom of my sack for them to rob me of. Go, child; go home and rest.”

His hand rested again on her head, not as on a petitioner but as on a daughter. Romola could not help clinging to his arm and pressing her brow against his shoulder. That touch was like the last crust of bread left from a happier loaf—plain, necessary, and suddenly precious. All her young filial life, even in its troubles, rose before her as something clean and sweet compared with the hateful confusion into which her days had fallen.

“Is silence best, my Romola?” the old man asked.

“Yes, now; but I cannot tell whether it always will be,” she answered, lifting her head with a look that begged for permission and pardon at once.

“Well, you have a father’s ear while I am above ground,” he said; then he lifted the black drapery and folded it round her head with his own hands, as if to shield her from night air, adding, “and a father’s home; remember that.”

He opened the door. “There—hasten away. You are like a black ghost; you will be safe enough.”

That night, when Romola fell asleep, she sank into a deep sleep, the kind that comes when suffering has spent itself to the edge and the body claims its due. Habit was rigid in her, yet she slept far beyond sunrise, as if she must hoard strength for more pain.

She woke to the sound of guns.

The booming came through the walls in slow shocks, and with each report the air seemed to tremble like a tightened drum-skin. Beneath the cannon there was the constant under-sound of Florence waking wrong—doors slammed not with morning leisure but with haste; feet ran; voices gathered into a hoarse chorus that rose and fell, as when a market quarrel begins at one stall and spreads, except that now it was the whole city that was the market.

Maso was at her door, full of frightened diligence, and his words tumbled out with those circumstantial additions old men make when they cannot bear to know less than others.

“Madonna—Piero de’ Medici, with thirteen hundred men, is before the gate that looks toward Rome. A countryman came in and alarmed the Signoria before it was light—else, they say, the city would have been taken sleeping in its bed like a babe.”

Tito was not in the house; he had been summoned to the Palazzo long ago.

Romola sent Maso out again to gather what news he could, while she went up to the loggia again and again, trying to read the far-off movements as if they were letters she must decipher to save a life. The morning carried a sharpness in the air; the smell of smoke was thin but persistent, like scorched herbs. Yet sound was what ruled her: every volley, every shout, every sudden burst of laughter that seemed out of place, like a cracked note in sacred singing.

Maso returned. The great Piazza, he said, was full of armed men; many chief citizens suspected as friends of the Medici had been summoned to the palace and kept there. Some people did not care whether Piero entered or not; some even said the Signoria had invited him. But whatever bargains men whispered over their tables, the city was giving him an ugly welcome. Soldiers from Pisa were coming against him.

Those hours afterward did not lodge in Romola’s memory as cleanly as ordinary days. They were a churn of dread and recollection, and only a few things stood out as fixed: she knew she had walked, despite alarms in the streets, to the Badia at the appointed time; she knew she had waited there in vain.

And one scene, when she came out of the church and stood a little on the steps while the doors were being closed for the afternoon interval, came back to her afterward as if it had been a wakeful vision.

The streets were full, and not only with men bearing pikes. Faces and tones had changed: a lift at the corner of the mouth, a quickness of eye, an easing in shoulders that had been braced. The guns fired again—but the sound, which had shaken her awake like a sentence, now provoked laughter, as if the city were tasting danger and finding it not so bitter as expected.

She soon learned why.

Piero de’ Medici and his horsemen had turned their backs on Florence and were galloping as fast as they could along the Siena road.

A substantial shop-keeping Piagnone, still holding his pike as if it were part of his arm, told her with a grim, everyday certainty, as one tells of a loaf sold out too dear. “It is true,” he ended, bitterness tightening his emphasis. “Piero is gone, but there are those left behind who were in the secret of his coming—we all know that; and if the new Signoria does its duty we shall soon know who they are.”

The words struck through Romola like a sharp spasm. Yet the evil they foretold was not the nearest thing. When she entered her home again, what pressed on her most was the fear that she had lost sight—perhaps for a long while—of Baldassarre.

The days stretched themselves out, longer in light, shorter in mercy; and yet they brought neither what Romola most yearned for nor what she most feared. No sign came from Baldassarre. No sudden unmasking of the whispered conspiracy broke through, even though the Government kept its eyes and ears sharpened as if the city were a kitchen full of cats and stolen meat. Waiting became a daily task—like tending a pot that must not boil over, though you can never quite lift the lid without scalding yourself.

But the season did not leave her empty-handed. It brought other presences—close, urgent, and bodily—that pressed themselves upon her as insistently as heat in narrow streets. It brought the Plague spreading from door to door, and it brought Rome’s sentence against Savonarola. These two things—death in the alleys and a curse pronounced beneath painted vaults—stayed her from drifting farther into that cold, proud distance she had begun to feel toward the Frate. They drew her back, fastened her again to the man who had once turned her eyes from the treasures of the mind to the duties of the hand, and who now seemed to stand almost alone against men who wanted virtue silenced because it made their pleasures look like rot.

For Romola could not go day after day into rooms that stank of fever and stale linen—could not lift a cup to cracked lips, or wipe away the sour sweat that gathered at temples, or coax the swallowing of a thin broth whose few grains of salt were like a promise—without remembering who had first made her believe that such acts were not mere pity but a kind of righteousness. Even the simplest preparation had become sacred to her, because the Plague turned cooking itself into a measure of conscience: to choose what was nourishing and possible in a city where fear had emptied markets; to steep herbs carefully, to skim the scum, to keep the spoon and the cup clean when every touch might carry death; to set a slice of bread near a dying child and hear the faint, grateful sound of chewing as though it were a small hymn.
