In those houses the world was reduced to smells—vinegar, sweat, old straw, the metallic taint of blood—and to sounds: the rasping breath that seemed to scrape the throat from within, the wet cough, the thin crying that could no longer rise to a wail, the soft scuffling of feet that tried not to wake the sick. And Romola, who had never learned to pray as other Florentines did, began to measure the soul by these very things: whether one could still hear suffering without turning away, whether one could still bear the stink and not let disgust harden into cruelty.

So too she could not see the silencing of a man whose difference from the great mass of the clergy lay less in doctrine than in an iron resolve to make the Christian life something more than a costume worn on feast-days—could not see him struck at, not for heresy but for earnestness—without feeling herself drawn, stubbornly, to his side.

Far into the hot days of June, the Excommunication—already some weeks arrived from Rome—was solemnly published in the Duomo. Romola went, not because she needed to be convinced, but because she wanted the resistance it stirred in her to grow steadier, like a fire fed on hard wood. She wanted that sympathy with Savonarola—one of the few sources left of her strength—to be warmed into endurance.

The scene in the great church was a remembered place made strange, as if a familiar dish had been served with the seasonings taken away and the bread left stale. It was not the Duomo she had known on those mornings when citizen faces filled the vast space under the light, rising young above old, a living amphitheatre of hope encircling the worn memories of age. It was not that mighty voice that once had made every word seem to ring on the stones and pass into the blood. Instead, there were bare walls at evening, made more sombre by the glimmer of tapers. There was the black and grey flock of monks and secular clergy, heads bent, faces unexpectant, as if they had come to watch a task done, not to listen for truth. There was the occasional tinkling of little bells in the pauses of a voice that read monotonously—each phrase falling with the dull, measured certainty of a pestle grinding something already ground. The words had been hanging in churches long enough; now they were spoken aloud as if speech itself could make them heavier.

Romola listened, and what struck her, almost as sharply as the sentence, was the soundscape of it all: the bells’ small, cold chime; the reader’s droning cadence that made the Latin less like living speech than like a rope being laid out, length by length; the hush that did not feel like reverence so much as a withholding of breath; and then, at last, the extinction of the tapers—darkness brought on deliberately—and the slow, shuffling tread of monkish feet departing in dim silence. Silence, in that moment, was not peace. It was the hush of a household after a quarrel when no one dares to set a pot on the fire lest the clink betray them.

Her ardour for the Frate was doubled as she saw, here and there, the gleeful triumph in hard, coarse faces—the sort of look that rejoices when a strict voice is gagged because it has named what others want left unnamed. And she saw too the fear-stricken confusion in faces she knew for his friends: men and women who had clung to him strongly, now trembling as if the very air had become unsafe to breathe.

For the question—where obedience must end and resistance begin—was never simple. It was made almost unbearable by the belief, rooted in most pious Florentine hearts, that the Church was not a human bargain struck among parties and kept alive by money and influence, but a living organism, instinct with divine power to bless and to curse. That belief was not, for them, an opinion they had chosen; it was an inalienable impression, like the concavity of the sky—something you never argue with because it is simply there. And when Savonarola, in his written arguments, dared to say that the Excommunication was unjust, and therefore not valid, the timid trembled the more: it was as if he had flung a stone at an image that might bleed and then call down invisible vengeance. Against that mystic immeasurable power there seemed no weapon and no defence—only submission, like lying still when fever shakes you.

But Romola—whose early mind had not been nourished on those traditional Christian associations, because her father had lived apart, turning to the old learning as to a private vineyard—felt her relation to the Church only through Savonarola. His moral force had been the only authority she had bowed to. In his excommunication she saw less the thunder of heaven than the menace of hostile vice. On one side stood a man who—whatever his errors—had given his life to public virtue and spiritual purity; and on the other she saw the assault of alarmed selfishness, headed by a lustful, greedy, lying, murderous old man, Rodrigo Borgia, now raised to the pinnacle of infamy as Pope Alexander the Sixth.

The fine shades that soften such antitheses rarely appear except to neutrals—those who can afford to notice folly in martyrs and prudence in the men who burn them. Romola could not afford that kind of clarity. She needed a strength that neutrality never gives. And in this sentence from Rome, which simplified and ennobled Savonarola’s resistant position by showing how wide the struggle was, she felt—as one feels, in a crowded sickroom, when an experienced hand arrives and sets to work without flinching—a sort of rescue from the threatening isolation of criticism and doubt.

For the Frate was now drawn out of that smaller and more personal antagonism against Florentine enemies into which he so often fell in the unchecked excitement of the pulpit. He stood, instead, as a man appealing to the Christian world against the vicious use of ecclesiastical power. Standard-bearer, yes—leaping into the breach. Life is never so clear, never so temptingly simple, as when one watches a generous act that risks everything. The heart beats faster at the sight, and one almost believes that to choose the higher path will not break us.

By a new current of such enthusiasm, Romola was carried through the difficult summer days.

Yet she kept her other burden shut within her. She had ventured on no word to Tito that could betray her late interview with Baldassarre, or the revelation Baldassarre had flung at her like a handful of bitter herbs. What would such speech win? No admission of truth. More likely a cool smile, a light sarcasm about her compassion for an assassin. Baldassarre—shattered, wandering—was evidently helpless. The danger was not that he would strike Tito, but that Tito, finding his traces, might pursue some new scheme for ridding himself of the injured man who haunted him like a sound you cannot locate: a footstep at night, always just beyond the door.

Romola felt she could do nothing decisive until she saw Baldassarre again and learned the full truth about that “other wife”—learned whether she was the wife to whom Tito had first been bound. The thought of that other wife, with all it implied, was a wound that cut into her hereditary pride with a sharpness that surprised her, as if some ancient family taste—salt and iron—had been suddenly forced upon her tongue. It mingled with the earliest memories of her illusory love, and it began to eat away what lingering tenderness still clung to the old image of her husband. Because she could not doubt the rest of Baldassarre’s revelation, she shrank from Tito with a horror that might have broken into passionate words in spite of herself—if he had not been more than usually absent from home.

Like many of the wealthier citizens in that time of pestilence, he spent the intervals of business chiefly in the country. The agreeable Melema was welcome at many villas; and since Romola had refused to leave the city, he had no need to provide a country residence of his own. His absence left the house quieter—but not peaceful. A quiet house can be like a pantry with the door shut: the very stillness makes you think of what is stored inside, what might be spoiling unseen.

At last, in the later days of July, when the public troubles that had absorbed her activity and much of her thought began to ease, Romola found herself less defended against her private misery. The Plague had almost disappeared. The position of Savonarola looked more hopeful under a favourable magistracy, who were writing urgent vindicatory letters to Rome, entreating the withdrawal of the Excommunication. Romola’s healthy, vigorous frame began to pay its debt: after continuous excitement and over-exertion there came the inevitable languor—heaviness in the limbs, a thirst that no water quite met, a weariness like bread that has been twice baked and left too long in heat. But her mind would not let her remain at home without some peremptory occupation, except during the sultry hours when the very air seemed to press down like a hand.

In the cool of morning and evening she walked out constantly, changing her direction as much as she could, with a vague hope that if Baldassarre still lived she might meet him. She listened as she walked—not only with her eyes. In one street she would hear the return of ordinary life: a knife tapping a board, a woman beating dust from cloth, a vendor calling figs or beans in a voice that carried like a bell across a little piazza. In another, the city still held remnants of sickness: a muffled sob behind shutters, a cough that seemed to bruise the air, the creak of a cart that had lately borne the dead and now carried only firewood. Florence’s sounds—so easily made harsh by fear, so easily softened by habit—entered her like food, nourishing or nauseating, and each change in them altered the weight of her thoughts.

Perhaps, she told herself, some illness had brought on a new paralysis of memory; perhaps he had forgotten where she lived—forgotten even that she existed. That was the most sanguine explanation she could find, like seasoning a bitter dish because one cannot bear it plain.

The explanation she felt most probable was simpler, and colder.

That Baldassarre had died of the Plague.

The day had hardly begun its full blaze, yet the heat already lay on Romola’s shoulders like a woollen mantle. Coming from San Marco, she kept close to the wall where the stones still held a night-coolness; even so, the sun pressed into every open street, and the air tasted of dust warmed into a faint bitterness. At Santa Croce she turned in among the intersecting lanes, where the light fell in long blades between high houses.

Borgo la Croce was strangely still. No hammer rang, no cart rattled, no vendors cried their wares. Only her own steps answered her, a measured tapping on the pavement that made the quiet seem deeper. As she neared a bend she saw, a little way before her, a child—no more than three years old—running with the uncertain, rolling haste of a young creature loosed from watchful hands. He wore only a white shirt that reached to his knees; his bare legs were already filmed with street-dust. He stopped, looked about, and for an instant she saw only his back: square and sturdy, with a cloud of reddish-brown curls like sun-touched chestnut husk.

Then he turned. Dark eyes brimmed and spilled. His lower lip thrust forward, trembling; fat brown fists clutched his shirt as if it were the only thing that could keep him from falling out of the world. Romola’s tall black figure cast a shadow on him, and the shadow, more than her, broke his last thread of courage: he drew breath and let out a sobbing cry that seemed too large for so small a throat.

Romola uncovered her head at once, as if to show she brought no menace, and went down on the hot stones beside him. She gathered him with both arms and laid her cheek to his, speaking in the soft, coaxing cadence that rises in women before they have time to think. The sobs swelled louder, then—like a sudden shower that ends in a moment—ceased. His face unknotted, and he stared at her open-mouthed, as if he had never seen a human face so near.

“You have lost yourself, little one,” she murmured, kissing his damp cheek. “Never mind. We will find the house again. Perhaps mamma will meet us.”

It seemed plain he had slipped away when a mother’s eyes were elsewhere; and Romola expected the pursuing footsteps, the frantic call, any moment. None came.

“Oh, what a heavy, heavy boy!” she said, trying to lift him. He was dense as a small sack of grain. “I cannot carry you. Come then—you must toddle by my side.”

He did not speak. One fist still clung to his shirt with stubborn tenacity; the other placed itself in her hand with a grave consent, as if their bargain were settled.

“You have a mamma?” Romola asked, looking down at him with a yearning she did not name.

He gave no answer. This was no chirping little bird of a child, but a square-shouldered tiny man, serious in his distress and serious in his silence.

Yet he knew his way. At the turning by San Ambrogio he dragged her towards the front with a determined pull, head thrust forward like a small ox in harness.

“Ah—that is the way home?” Romola said, letting the corner of her mouth soften into a smile.

He only tugged harder: go faster.

Another turning earned the same decisive judgement, and then the street opened into a quieter reach where garden ground lay beyond the walls and the air smelled faintly of damp earth and leaves. At the end stood a house, and before it the boy halted, drawing her toward a flight of worn stone steps. He would not let go her hand, and she would not leave him until she was sure she put him into familiar arms.

They mounted into dimness—the sudden withdrawal from sun into shadow made the air feel cooler, almost wet on the skin. At the landing, light spilled from an open doorway. They passed a small lobby and came to another open door. Romola paused on the threshold. No one had heard her.

At the far end of the room, opposite the light, sat Tessa on a low chair with one hand resting on the cradle’s edge. Her head hung a little to one side; she slept fast, the sleep of someone worn with rocking and watchfulness. Near the window, her back to the door, Monna Lisa worked at a bowl—pulling apart leaves, stripping away limp outer edges, rinsing the crisp hearts, as if preparing salad were a prayer said with fingers. Her deafness made the room doubly still: the soft scrape of leaf against earthenware, the faint drip of water, were all the sound.

There was barely time for Romola’s eyes to take in the scene before the boy snatched his hand free and ran to Tessa’s side. He did not shake her, only leaned his head against her arm and turned those solemn eyes back toward Romola, as if to judge what would come next.

The pressure woke Tessa. She blinked, bewildered; then her gaze found the figure at the doorway. In an instant she started up, blushed so deeply it seemed to climb into her hairline, and began to tremble—neither advancing nor speaking, held between fear and gratitude.

“Ah—we have seen each other before,” Romola said, smiling as she came forward. “I am glad it was your little boy. He was crying in the street; I suppose he had run away. We walked together a little way, and then he knew where he was and brought me here. But you had not missed him? That is well—else you would have been frightened.”

At the thought of how near loss had been, Tessa’s colour fled. With a half sob she seized Lillo’s arm and hurried to Monna Lisa, speaking loudly into the old woman’s ear.

“Oh, Lisa, you are wicked! Why will you stand with your back to the door? Lillo ran away ever so far into the street.”

“Holy Mother!” Monna Lisa said, in her meek, thick tone, letting the spoon drop from her hands. “Where were you, then? I thought you were there, and had your eye on him.”

“But you know I go to sleep when I am rocking,” Tessa answered with pettish helplessness—the plaint of one who is blamed for being what she is.

“Well, well,” Monna Lisa said, recovering the spoon, “we must keep the outer door shut, or else tie him up; for he’ll be as cunning as Satan before long, and that’s the holy truth. But how came he back, then?”

The question brought Tessa back to Romola, and she turned, blushing and timid again. Monna Lisa’s eyes followed, and the old woman made a low reverence.

“Doubtless the most noble lady brought him back,” she said; and then, stepping nearer, she added with domestic frankness, “It’s my shame for him to have been found with only his shirt on; but he kicked and wouldn’t have his other clothes this morning, and the mother—poor thing—will never hear of his being beaten. But what’s an old woman to do without a stick when the lad’s legs get so strong? Let your nobleness look at his legs.”

Lillo, aware that his legs were under discussion, pulled his shirt up higher and looked down at their olive roundness with a solemn curiosity. Romola laughed—the sound broke the tightness in Tessa’s throat—and she bent to give him a caressing shake and a kiss.

That easy laughter loosened something in Tessa too. When Naldo had been told of the Carnival adventure, and she had asked who the heavenly lady was who came when she was wanted and vanished again—whether it could be the Madonna herself—he had answered, “Not exactly, my Tessa; only one of the saints,” and would say no more. So Romola had remained, in Tessa’s mingled scraps of memory and church-pictures, like a figure from painted walls. Now the figure laughed at a child’s legs, and touched him as women touch children, and the awe softened into trust. Tessa’s fears tended more toward ugly things and harsh voices than toward anything good.

“Ninna’s in the cradle,” she said. “She’s pretty too.”

Romola went to the cradle. The infant lay with a damp curl on her forehead, her little mouth puckering in sleep; and as Romola leaned in, the baby stirred and opened blue eyes, startled into life by a new shadow.

“Ah—she is waking: she has opened her blue eyes,” Romola said. “You must take her up, and I will sit down in this chair—may I?—and nurse Lillo. Come, Lillo!”

She sat in Tito’s chair. The fact struck her only as she lowered herself: the familiar weight of possession about it, the sense of a man’s usual place. She held out her arms. Lillo hesitated, then pointed at her with small fingers, half puzzled, half indignant.

“That’s Babbo’s chair,” he said, as if the chair itself were a rule.

“But Babbo is not here, and I shall go soon. Come—let me nurse you as he does,” Romola answered.

As she lifted him she wondered, sharply and for the first time, what sort of Babbo he might be—what sort of man had a wife dressed like a contadina and yet carrying about her a daintiness that suggested ease, a little softness of body and of hand that belonged to plenty and to idleness rather than to field-work. Lillo, discovering the lap to be as comfortable as any throne, settled into it and began to explore Romola’s dress and fingers, searching for ornaments beyond her rosary with the serious greed of a child who knows there are hidden treasures in the world.

Tessa, occupied with coaxing Ninna past her waking peevishness, now sat down again on her low chair near Romola’s knee, arranging the baby’s tiny person as if setting out a dish to be admired—tilting the little head, smoothing the shift, jealous that the strange lady’s eyes, like Naldo’s, seemed to return always to the boy.

“Lillo was going to be angry with me, because I sat in Babbo’s chair,” Romola said, bending to kiss Ninna’s little foot, warm and milk-scented. “Will he come soon and want it?”

“Ah, no!” Tessa said. “You can sit in it a long while. I shall be sorry when you go. When you first came to take care of me at the Carnival, I thought it was wonderful; you came and went away again so fast. And Naldo said, perhaps you were a saint, and that made me tremble a little—though the saints are very good, I know; and you were good to me, and now you have taken care of Lillo. Perhaps you will always come and take care of me. That was how Naldo did, a long while ago; he came and took care of me when I was frightened, one San Giovanni. I couldn’t think where he came from—he was so beautiful and good. And so are you.”

“Naldo is your husband,” Romola said. It was not a question; it was the quiet fitting together of what she saw. “His eyes are like Lillo’s.”

“Ah! you know him!” Tessa paused, wonder widening her. “Perhaps you know Nofri and Peretola, and our house on the hill, and everything. Yes—like Lillo’s; but not his hair. His hair is dark and long—ah! if you know it—ecco!”

She slipped her hand to a thin red silk cord at her neck and drew from her bosom the tiny old parchment breve, the horn of red coral, and, with them, a long dark curl tied carefully at one end. She held the curl toward Romola, keeping it out of Ninna’s grasping hand.

“It is a fresh one. I cut it lately. See how bright it is!” She laid it against the white of Romola’s fingers so that its darkness seemed to drink the light. “They get dim, and then he lets me cut another when his hair is grown; and I put it with the breve, because sometimes he is away a long while, and then I think it helps to take care of me.”

A shiver went through Romola as if the curl were not hair but a cord pulled across her nerves. At Tessa’s first words of a husband who came she knew not whence, a possibility had risen—one of those faint, terrible shapes that leap up instantly in a mind that has been searching. Now, seeing the curl laid on her hand, it seemed for an instant a mocking likeness of the lock she herself had cut to wind with one of her own, years ago. But she held herself still. She wanted truth, and she wanted it without striking pain into this simple, trusting creature—this woman with the child’s mind lodged inside her.

“It is a beautiful curl,” Romola said, mastering the impulse to draw her hand away. “Lillo’s curls will be like it, perhaps, for his cheek too is dark. And you never know where your husband goes to when he leaves you?”

“No,” Tessa said, tucking away her treasures beyond the children’s reach. “But I know Messer San Michele takes care of him, for he gave him a beautiful coat, all made of little chains; and if he puts that on, nobody can kill him. And perhaps, if—”

She hesitated; the old dreamlike awe began to rise again, now that talk had led her into deeper water. “If you were a saint, you would take care of him too, because you have taken care of me and Lillo.”

Romola’s certainty came like a blow that made the blood rush. A flush sprang up, quick and hot; but she had bent her cheek against Lillo’s head so that the child’s curls hid the tremor of her mouth. The feeling inside that flush was strange—something like exultation at the thought that the wife’s burden might be lifted from her shoulders at last; that this ignorant little being might be Tito’s lawful wife. Exultation—shameful word for a proud woman; yet it rose, because it promised a way out of a duty that had become an insoluble knot.

And yet Tessa’s appeal, so artless, so full of the need to be guarded, pierced her. Romola lifted her head and spoke with a steadiness that sounded like authority even to herself.

“I will always take care of you, if I see you need me. But that beautiful coat—your husband did not wear it when you were first married? Perhaps he used not to be so long away from you then?”

“Ah, yes! he was. Much—much longer. So long, I thought he would never come back. I used to cry. Oh me! I was beaten then—a long, long while ago at Peretola, where we had the goats and mules.”

“And how long had you been married before your husband had that chain-coat?” Romola said.

Her heart began to beat so fast it seemed each pulse must betray her. She watched Tessa’s hands as if they were counting out her fate.

Tessa looked up, meditative, and began to count on her fingers.

“The chestnuts were ripe when we were married,” she said, marking thumb and fingers as she spoke; “and then again they were ripe at Peretola before he came back, and then again, after that, on the hill. And soon the soldiers came, and we heard the trumpets, and then Naldo had the coat.”

Romola drew in her breath. “You had been married more than two years. In which church were you married?”

Tessa gave a small start. The directness of Romola’s question made her feel, dimly, that she was being led where Naldo had once forbidden her to go. She looked up with hesitating doubt.

“Naldo said I was never to tell about that,” she whispered. “Do you think he would not be angry if I told you?”

“It is right that you should tell me,” Romola said, mild and firm. “Tell me everything.”

If Naldo’s command had been fresh, her obedience might have held; but the years had blurred it into something like a shadow on the mind. And the very strangeness of speaking what she had never spoken before made her voice sink as if she were confessing.

“It was not in a church—it was at the Natività, when there was a fair, and all the people went overnight to see the Madonna in the Nunziata, and my mother was ill and couldn’t go, and I took the bunch of cocoons for her; and then he came to me in the church and I heard him say, ‘Tessa!’ I knew him because he had taken care of me at the San Giovanni; and then we went into the piazza where the fair was, and I had some berlingozzi, for I was hungry and he was very good to me; and at the end of the piazza there was a holy father, and an altar like what they have at the processions outside the churches. So he married us, and then Naldo took me back into the church and left me; and I went home, and my mother died, and Nofri began to beat me more, and Naldo never came back. And I used to cry, and once at the Carnival I saw him and followed him, and he was angry, and said he would come some time, I must wait. So I went and waited; but, oh! it was a long while before he came; but he would have come if he could, for he was good; and then he took me away, because I cried and said I could not bear to stay with Nofri. And, oh! I was so glad, and since then I have been always happy, for I don’t mind about the goats and mules, because I have Lillo and Ninna now; and Naldo is never angry, only I think he doesn’t love Ninna so well as Lillo, and she is pretty.”

As she spoke, the room seemed to fill with more than words: the remembered sounds of fair and church—the muffled chant, the shuffle of feet, the sudden flare of trumpets in her story—rose and fell like distant echoes, until the present quiet returned with the soft rustle of salad leaves and the baby’s small, fretful sigh.

Tessa forgot her earlier caution and fell to showering Ninna with kisses, devouring her as if love were food and the child were sweet bread. Romola sat in silence, eyes turned inward and seeing nothing of the cradle, nothing of the salad bowl, nothing even of the child on her lap. The tale had not brought the simple release she had felt for an instant in her pulse. The marriage had been no lawful knot, no clear external law that could untie hers. The difficulty remained—only changed in shape.

Lillo felt the change at once. He had given no caress back to her, yet he demanded them as his due; and when her arm slackened he tugged her head toward him with both brown arms.

“Play with me again!” he said.

Romola started as if wakened. She clasped him anew, pressing him to her, and looked from him to Tessa. Tessa had paused in her kissing and was again gazing up at Romola with that placid, worshipping delight, as if Romola’s face itself were a protection.

Something in Romola’s expression altered—slowly, like a lamp turned and trimmed so that it gives a warmer light. Her mouth softened; her eyes lost their hard inward stare and took in the room, the two children, the poor domestic order. Presently she drew her scissors from her scarsella. The three pair of wide eyes—Lillo’s, Tessa’s, even Ninna’s newly opened blue glance—followed the gleam of metal with the intentness of kittens.

Romola lifted one of her long wavy locks and cut it off cleanly. The severed hair fell heavy into her hand like a relinquished tie.

“I must go away from you now,” she said, “but I will leave this lock of hair, that it may remind you of me; because if you are ever in trouble you can think that perhaps God will send me to take care of you again. I cannot tell you where to find me; but if I ever know that you want me, I will come to you. Addio.”

She set Lillo down quickly, as if staying another moment might undo her steadiness, and held out her hand. Tessa kissed it, awe and sorrow mingled in her breath. Romola’s mind pressed on her like the heat outside; she needed solitude as one needs water. But she did not forget the least among them: she turned aside to lay her hand on Monna Lisa’s shoulder and make a friendly farewell sign.

Before the old woman had finished her deep reverence, Romola had gone.

Tessa and Monna Lisa moved toward each other by the same impulse. The two children clung to their mother’s skirts, as if they, too, felt that something invisible had passed through the room.

“Do you think she was a saint?” Tessa asked in Lisa’s ear, showing the lock.

Monna Lisa rejected the notion with a backward flick of her fingers; then, stroking the rippled gold as if weighing it, she said—

“She’s a great and noble lady. I saw such in my youth.”

Romola went home and sat alone through the sultry hours, while the city’s sounds thickened and thinned outside—distant bells, far-off calls, the flutter of pigeons like a soft brushing in the air. In that slow, breathing soundscape, each noise seemed to measure her solitude. By evening she held the heavy certainty that her lot was unchanged.

She was flung back on the conflict between an outward law—sacred, far-reaching, binding the household to the city as the city was bound to God—and the inward facts that had grown more peremptory day by day. Savonarola’s teaching had entered her like a stern music: return to the place appointed; do not cast off bonds because they gall; do not make private ease the judge over public duty. The holiness attached to close relations, and most of all to the closest, was the outward shape of a deeper human good; and to abandon inherited or chosen ties lightly, because they had ceased to please, was to tear up virtue by the roots. What else had Tito’s crime toward Baldassarre been—if not abandonment driven to its last horror of falsity and ingratitude?

And yet—what was she to do with a bond that had become nothing but the stifling predominance of a nature she despised? She had striven, long, to make union possible; each attempt only sharpened the impossibility. The marriage had turned into degrading servitude, and her soul recoiled as from a tainted dish set on her table day after day—food that one is commanded to eat, and that sickens one even while one strives to be grateful.

Law was sacred. Yes. But rebellion might be sacred too.

The thought flashed on her with a dreadful clarity: her problem was the same in kind as Savonarola’s—where obedience ends and where rebellion begins; where the soul must act on its own warrant without appeal to any tribunal, even against a law not unarmed with divine lightnings—lightnings that may fall if the warrant is false.

Before the sun went down she had taken her resolve. She would ask counsel neither of her godfather nor of Savonarola until she had made one determined effort to speak freely with Tito and obtain his consent that she should live apart from him. She did not desire to leave him clandestinely again; she did not desire to forsake Florence. She would tell him that if ever he felt a real need of her, she would come back. Could more faithfulness be demanded?

A shudder ran through her at the image of his refusal clothed in a sneer—at his suggestion that the only scandal-proof escape was a convent. He knew how her mind revolted from that narrow rule, not only from personal repugnance, but because her father’s dearest memories forbade it: the cloister was linked with his deepest griefs and bitterest dislike, like a word in a hated tongue that cannot be sweetened by pious use.

Tito had announced he would come home this evening. She would wait and speak at once; during the day his ear was hard to catch. If he so much as scented personal words, he slipped away with an ease that looked unpremeditated, leaving her speaking into emptiness.

She sent for Maso to say she would wait for his master. The old man looked at her and lingered—hesitation and wondering anxiety written in the lines of his face—but when she asked no question he turned away slowly. Why ask? Perhaps Maso only knew, or guessed, what she already knew.

Tito came late. Romola had been pacing up and down the long room that had once been the library. The windows stood open; night had not cooled the air, only thickened it. She wore a loose white linen robe instead of her usual black—something washed and plain, that let the skin breathe. The slight coolness after her long hours of heat and motionless thought made her more wakeful, not less; and when at last she took up the lamp and went to open the door herself, her eyes must have startled him—bright with sleeplessness and with pain turned into resolve, so unlike her usual quiescent self-restraint before him.

But it seemed this was what he expected.

“Ah! it is you, Romola. Maso is gone to bed,” he said gravely, quietly, stepping in and closing the door for her with a deliberate hand. Then he turned and looked at her more fully than he was wont, as if measuring the change in her.

“You have heard it all, I see.”

Tito had not spoken idly when he let fall, with that lightness which was always half a screen and half a lure, that he was safe.

For three months—months in which he had watched Florence like a cook watching a pot whose boil cannot be hurried, only managed—he had been laying by his stores. He had salted and sealed his provisions of influence at Rome and at Milan, passing on hints, names, and private currents of intention against the Frate and the popular party, and receiving in return the kind of promises that are never written, only tasted in the air like distant smoke. At the same time, he had seasoned his manner for the Piagnoni, cultivating their good will with a deft hand, showing them, by fine touches and careful omissions, that his political convictions were wholly on their side—yet never troubling them with any show of religious ardour. He knew how a kitchen changes when zeal enters it: some men begin to burn what should be browned, others refuse to touch a knife at all. Tito offered them no fervours to distrust; he gave them plausibility, service, and a civil tongue.

And all the while he had not withdrawn from the Mediceans—had, indeed, made himself more necessary to them, more used, more trusted. The triple game did not tire him. It had become a kind of daily craft: like kneading, which is repetition with small variations, and the hands learn the truth of the dough before the mind names it. Besides, the Mediceans themselves admitted duplicity as a principle—so long as it ran outward. To outwit an opponent was fair stratagem; to outwit a friend seemed to them a baseness they had no temptation towards. They did not measure Tito by any standard that could have warned them. He had none of their hereditary bonds, no old alliances, no ancestral resentments that made their own mutual honour, such as it was, intelligible to them. The very absence that made him convenient as an instrument also made him unsafe as a companion; but convenience has a loud voice in councils where men listen for advantage.

Among the Roman and Milanese friends of the aristocratic party—the Arrabbiati, Savonarola’s bitterest enemies—the habit of underhand correspondence and espionage had become almost a trade. In such a trade, the best service was the deepest hypocrisy, and the heaviest pay went to him who could most perfectly keep a face. To suspect an agent because he played his part well would have been, in their own logic, absurdity.

On the other side, the Piagnoni, with the directness that belongs to energetic conviction, were the readier to credit Tito with sincerity in his adhesion because he did not counterfeit their devotions. His very coolness had the air of honesty, as if he were a man who cared for the public good but not for cant. It is one of the oldest powers in the world: to let others supply, from their own hunger, the meaning of your silence.

Under these conditions the three months had been flattering. The result Tito cared for most was not a triumph for Florence but a position for himself—at Rome or at Milan. He had grown more determined, as days went on, that when the favourable moment came he would quit Florence for one of those great capitals where rewards were richer, life less scrupulously observed, and talent and learning had a wider market, like grain carried downriver to a city that eats magnificently and asks fewer questions of the farmer. At present, Milan weighed heavier than Rome. If, within the year, he could render certain services to Duke Ludovico Sforza, a place at the Milanese court offered itself—glittering, spacious, and, to Tito’s imagination, cleaner than this narrow Florentine street-life where every step struck against someone’s memory.

He had foreseen that the Medicean conspirators might be discovered; what he could not foresee was the particular accident by which their secrecy would be torn. Lamberto dell’Antella arrested with a tell-tale letter on his person and rancour in his heart—there was no calculating for that. In the wide net that followed, Tito could not wholly escape implication. He had never expected to escape it if the discovery grew broad. But his mind ran quickly along the necessary course, choosing the surest path with the fewest thorns.

It is pleasant to keep a whole skin; but skin is sensitive to weather, and even safety can feel like damp. By nightfall—before he went home—he had secured the three things he most cared to carry out of the storm. He was to be freed from all proceedings against him for complicity with the Mediceans. He was to retain his secretaryship another year unless he resigned it sooner. And the price by which he bought these guarantees—the most bitter ingredient in his bargain—was to be kept as a State secret.

Most men would have thought that price heavy. Tito himself would rather not have paid it. But he had long trained himself to swallow what was necessary without showing distaste.

His first step had been to win Francesco Valori. Valori was not only one of the Ten under whom Tito held his secretaryship, but one of the special council appointed to investigate the evidence. He stood at the head of the Piagnoni—capable of fine qualities without any softening of his partisanship, arrogant enough to alienate friends, and capable of bitter personal animosities. One of the bitterest of these, well-known to those who listened for such notes, was directed against Bernardo del Nero.

Tito obtained a brief private interview with him, and before he spoke he exacted a pledge of secrecy. Then, with that ease which made confession look like candour rather than necessity, he avowed his own agency for the Mediceans. He was frank about his motives—frank as a man is frank who knows that the right kind of frankness is only another arrangement of concealment. He declared he had always believed the Medicean efforts futile, and that he sincerely preferred the maintenance of the popular government. He affected to confide, as if it were an intimate secret between allies, his personal dislike of Bernardo del Nero. Having thus set out the board and chosen the dishes, he came to his main offering.

There was, he said, another Medicean plot: one meant to secure Florence for Piero de’ Medici, to be carried into execution in the middle of this very August. If the government would grant him certain conditions, he could, by a journey to Siena and into Romagna—where Piero was again trying to gather forces—obtain documentary evidence to lay before the council. But for this to succeed, his character as a Medicean agent must remain unshaken in Medicean eyes. The fact that he was also a source of information to the authorities must be wrapped in profound secrecy. Still, some odour might escape—like a strong spice that clings to the fingers no matter how often they are rinsed. And before he incurred the consequences of acting against men who trusted him, he must be assured of immunity from prosecution as a Medicean and of retention of office for a year.

To Valori, these propositions did not sound as they sound to any reader who thinks of treachery as a single, clear taste. Valori’s mind was not intensely bent on estimating Tito’s conduct; it was intensely bent on procuring an extreme sentence against the five prisoners already taken. There would be immense efforts to save them. It was desirable—on public grounds, Valori would have said—that evidence should be as strong as possible, to alarm all well-affected men at the dangers of clemency.

Legal proceedings in that time had their own coarse kitchen of truth. Evidence was one of those desirable things that were often got only by foul means. To seize a few men and torture them into confessing everybody’s guilt was a step that passed for justice; and it was not always easy to see the next step, unless some traitor turned up, ready to carry the dish farther into the hall. Lamberto dell’Antella had already been tortured to help his willingness to tell more than he knew. Even so, additional and stronger facts were wanted—especially against Bernardo del Nero, who so far seemed only to have refrained from betraying the plot after failing to discourage it. The welfare of Florence demanded, Valori believed, that Bernardo’s guilt should be put in the strongest light. Perhaps Valori did not fully know how much his zeal was mixed—how hatred, like a pungent herb, can make itself seem like the flavour of righteousness.

He decided that Tito’s proposal should be accepted. He laid it before his colleagues without disclosing Tito’s name, and persuaded them.

Late in the day Tito was admitted to the special council. He produced among them a deep sensation by revealing this further plot to restore Piero—one prepared, he said, for the middle of August itself. Documentary proof would do more than anything to make the right course clear. Tito received a commission to start for Siena by break of day; and, besides that, he carried away from the council-chamber the written guarantee of his immunity and his retention of office.

Among the twenty Florentines who bent their grave eyes on him as he stood there—graceful, composed, speaking of startling things with easy periphrasis, and with that air of unaffected admission of motives short of the highest which is often the most calculated affectation—there were several who, even in their preoccupation, revised their estimate of him. They concluded, without speech, that this ingenious Greek was to be used for public needs rather than private intimacy. Unprincipled men were useful. They enabled those with more scruples to keep their hands tolerably clean in a world where dirty work was always waiting, like a pile of fish that must be gutted if anyone is to eat.

Indeed, unless a man held the Frate’s extravagant belief that purity and loftiness could be pursued on earth as more than words, it was not clear to respectable Florentine brains how life could be conducted in any department without instruments it would not be unbecoming to kick or spit upon at the moment of paying wages. Some of these very men were soon to need unscrupulousness as decided as Tito’s for a memorable transaction; but, as their poet Pulci had said, it is one thing to enjoy the fruits of treachery and another to love the traitor.

Florence had always had a harsh ear. The same society could raise a gibbet for a murderer and a gibbet for a martyr; could hiss a dastardly act and hiss, with equal strength, a generous truth spoken aloud. In that mingled sound—censure and applause thrown like stones in a narrow street—there was not hopeless confusion, but struggling order; yet the sound itself mattered. A city lives inside its noises as much as inside its walls: the clatter of hooves on stone, the rasp of shutters, the cries of sellers, the sudden hush that means danger, the hiss that means judgement. Those who despised Savonarola called his words mere breath; yet breath moves crowds. And when judgement turns to public sound, it becomes a kind of weather no man can entirely escape.

Tito, at least, did not escape it inwardly. He was not unaware that he had sunk a little in the estimation of the men who accepted his services. He had the self-contemplation that accompanies a habit of acting on well-considered reasons, whatever their quality; and if he could have chosen, he would have declined to see himself disapproved by men of the world. He had never meant to be disapproved. He had meant always to conduct himself so ably that, even when he departed from other men’s standards, they should not perceive it. With Romola, that concealment had become impossible; and it was that impossibility which had raised the barrier between them.

He shrank from condemnatory judgements as from a climate that would not suit his lungs. Yet events were not so plastic to cleverness as he wished. Things had inconveniently turned.

In truth he bore no rancour against Messer Bernardo del Nero. He even liked Lorenzo Tornabuoni and Giannozzo Pucci. He had served them ably; had their party won, he would have deserved a high reward. But was he to renounce all agreeable fruits because their party had failed? His promise to furnish additional proof against them would, he believed, make little difference to their fate. He was convinced they would escape extreme consequences. But if he had not offered it, his own fortunes—so carefully built—would have been ruined at the foundation.

And what motive could any man really have, except his own interest?

Florentines whose passions were tied up in their precarious political schemes might have no self-interest separable from family pride and old attachments and hatreds. A simpleton might swallow whole some old philosophy, take the indigestion for a divine afflux or an inward monitor, and call his self-conceit virtue. Fanatics who believed in Scourge and Renovation might see their interest in a palm-branch and a white robe hereafter. But a man of clear intellect—so Tito argued to himself—did not let his course be determined by such questionable fumes.

Had not Pontanus, poet and philosopher of unrivalled Latinity, made a splendid oration at Naples to welcome the French king who had come to dethrone Pontanus’s own royal friend and patron? And yet Pontanus held up his head and prospered. Men did not truly care for these matters, unless their personal spleen was touched. Weakness alone was despised. Power of any sort carried its immunity. A man could scarcely mount high without incurring unpleasant necessities that laid him open to enmity—and perhaps to a little hissing when enmity wanted a pretext.

It was that faint prognostic of hissing—gathered from small indications among the council—that made this day feel like an epoch to Tito and drove him to such inward pleading. Not that he had taken a deeper step in wrong-doing; he could not feel any tie to the Mediceans stronger than the tie to his father. But his conduct to his father had been hidden by successful lying: this act did not admit of total concealment. In its very nature it was a revelation, and revelation brings sound with it—the whisper first, then the hiss.

Well. A little patience, and in another year—perhaps in half a year—he might turn his back on these eager Florentines with their futile quarrels and sinking fortunes. His brilliant success here had carried ugly flaws: he had fallen in love with the wrong woman, and Baldassarre had returned under circumstances no mind could measure. But as Tito galloped with loose rein towards Siena, the night air flowing past him with the smell of dust and sweat and crushed herbs from the roadside, he saw a future in which those mistakes would no longer hunt him. He had money already safe out of Florence. He was eight-and-twenty, in the fresh ripeness of strength; he knew his skill had been tried and found serviceable. Could he not strip himself of the past as of rehearsal clothing, throw the old bundle away, and robe himself at last for the real scene?

It did not enter into his meditations that, on issuing from the council-chamber and descending the stairs, he had brushed against a man whose face he had not paused to recognize in the lamplight.

The man was Ser Ceccone—also willing to serve the State by giving information against unsuccessful employers.

Tito came back from Siena, and almost at once was gone again on some other errand, vanishing out of Florence as readily as a man steps from a bright loggia into a shadowed street. He did not return until the seventeenth of August.

Nearly a fortnight had slipped by since the arrests, and the five accused men were still behind stone and iron, still without sentence, still held in that feverish uncertainty which can gnaw a family more cruelly than a judgment. For Romola, those days had narrowed into one continual watching—like a cook who cannot leave the hearth because the pot’s fate depends on the moment the boil turns. Everything else—her household, the city’s quarrels, even her own weariness—had become a far-off murmur beside the one question: would her godfather live?

Sometimes the chances seemed to rise in the prisoners’ favor simply because time was passing. Delay meant more hands could be set to work, more doors tried, more voices softened. And delay was the easiest virtue for magistrates who feared hatred whichever way they leaned. One party cried that the Republic was in danger, that mercy would be a trumpet-call to enemies. Another knew well that to condemn five citizens of eminent name to death and confiscation would plant rancor like bitter seed in every allied house, and that those who cast the fatal votes would have to harvest that bitterness for years.

The judgment properly belonged to the Eight who ruled criminal justice, and the sentence depended on a majority of six votes—the infamous six beans, those small pale counters by which Florence measured life and death as if with pulses shaken into a bowl. But the Eight shrank, as men will shrink when they feel the weight of the axe-handle in their own palms. They sought to share responsibility with the Signoria. The Signoria, in turn, shrugged away the burden and proposed an appeal to the Great Council; for a law urged through nearly three years before—one of the proud, often-quoted ornaments of the new popular government—gave any citizen condemned by the six beans the right to appeal.

Yet even that hope became a contest. The friends of the accused resisted an appeal at this stage, chiefly because they wanted delay, and strict legality demanded that sentence come before appeal. Their resistance prevailed. A middle course was taken: the matter was referred on the seventeenth to a large mixed assembly—higher magistracies, the Senate of Eighty, and certain chosen citizens—so that judgment might be diffused like responsibility in a watered stew.

That day, with anxiety tightened by the thought that before evening her godfather’s fate might be fixed beyond recall, Romola had gained leave to see him a second time, but only under watch and with witnesses. She returned afterward to the Via de’ Bardi with her cousin Brigida, still ignorant of what the council had done. Brigida, restless and practical, went out again to wait near sources of sure news, at the house of a friend connected with the magistracies, promising to bring back authentic tidings the moment they could be had.

Left alone, Romola sank on the first seat in the bright saloon as if her body had been set down there by other hands. The room glimmered with costly order, with the polished surfaces and carved edges that declared comfort; yet her mind took no hold of any of it. She sat with her back toward the door, her head pressed into her hands. Outside, Florence spoke in its accustomed chorus—footsteps striking stone, a distant cart’s wooden complaint, the thin call of a street-seller, the fluttering hush of pigeons—and under it, like a continual undertone, the Arno’s dull breathing. Each sound came as a reminder that the city kept living, kept bargaining and gossiping and cooking its soups, while men’s lives were measured out by councils.

It seemed long since Brigida had gone. Romola expected her return. But when the door opened, the step that entered was not Brigida’s.

Since that night of parting from Tito, Romola had had no outward proof that could be held up like a written charge to warrant her belief that he had bought his safety by betrayal. On the contrary, she had heard enough to know that the Mediceans still trusted him and believed him busy with errands in Romagna, cloaking their work as government service. The obscurity surrounding the evidence had allowed everyone to suppose that Tito had slipped free of implication.

But her suspicion would not be washed away by any public opinion. The image of his conduct toward Baldassarre had stained every thought of him. It was as if she had once seen him at some dreadful work—blood on the hands—and afterward every ordinary gesture carried a remembered redness. At the sound of his step on the stone floor, a chill passed through her like a draught through an unlatched shutter. She could not turn. She could not rise. Greeting was impossible.

He did not speak at first. After an instant’s pause he took a seat on the opposite side of the table, facing her. Then she lifted her eyes.

He met her look without impatience and said coolly, as if they were speaking of business to be set in order: “This meeting corresponds with our parting, Romola. But I understand it is a moment of terrible suspense. I am come—if you will listen—to bring you the relief of hope.”

She started, shifting her posture, and looked at him with distrust that did not yet harden into refusal.

“It will not be unwelcome to you to hear,” he went on, “even though it is I who tell it, that the council is prorogued till the twenty-first. The Eight have been frightened at last into passing a sentence of condemnation; but the demand has now been made on behalf of the condemned for the appeal to the Great Council.”

The doubt fell away from her face. Her voice came quickly: “And when is it to be made?”

“It has not yet been granted; but it may be granted. The Special Council is to meet again on the twenty-first to deliberate whether the appeal shall be allowed or not. In the meantime there is an interval of three days—three days in which chances may occur in favor of the prisoners—in which interest may be used on their behalf.”

Romola sprang up. Color rose in her cheeks like a sudden flame under the skin, as if her blood had caught the word “interval” and ran with it. Her hands trembled. In that moment she forgot even Tito. Three days were like three fresh loaves set before the starving: not deliverance, but something to hold the soul from fainting.

“Possibly,” Tito said, rising also, “your own intention anticipates what I was going to say. You are thinking of the Frate.”

“I am,” Romola said, turning her startled gaze on him. “Has he done anything? Is there anything to tell me?”

“Only this. Messer Francesco Valori’s bitterness and violence chiefly determined the course of things to-day. Half the men who gave their opinion against the prisoners were frightened into it. But there are numerous friends of Fra Girolamo both in the Special Council and out of it who are strongly opposed to a sentence of death—Piero Guicciardini, for example, one member of the Signoria who resisted stoutly; and Giovan Battista Ridolfi, Piagnone as he is, will not lightly forgive the death of his brother Niccolò.”

“But how can the appeal be denied,” Romola said, indignation sharpening her voice, “when it is the law—when it was one of the chief glories of the popular government to have passed the law?”

“They call this an exceptional case. Of course there are ingenious arguments.” Tito’s tone was lightly ironic. “But there is much more loud bluster about the danger of the Republic. Still—no opposition could prevent the prorogation. And a certain powerful influence, rightly applied during these three days, might determine wavering courage in favor of granting the appeal, and might even check Valori’s headlong enmity.”

He paused, watching the effect of each phrase as a man might watch a sauce thicken, cautious not to let it curdle. “It happens to have come to my knowledge that the Frate has so far interfered as to send a message to Valori in favor of Lorenzo Tornabuoni. I know you can sometimes have access to the Frate. It might at all events be worth while to use your privilege now.”

“It is true,” Romola said, as if speaking to herself rather than to him. “I cannot believe the Frate would approve denying the appeal.”

“I heard it said by more than one person in the court of the Palazzo,” Tito continued, “that it would be to the everlasting discredit of Fra Girolamo if he allowed a government almost entirely made up of his party to deny the appeal without entering his protest—when he has been boasting in his books and sermons that it was he who got the law passed. But between ourselves”—his voice softened into a familiarity that stung—“with all respect for your Frate’s ability, my Romola, he has got into the practice of preaching that form of human sacrifice called killing tyrants and wicked malcontents, which some of his followers are likely to think inconsistent with lenity in the present case.”

“I know, I know,” Romola said, pain tightening her mouth. “But he is driven into those excesses of speech. It used to be different.” Her words came with a weary tenderness, as if she were defending some old, half-forgotten household song in a dialect few now understood. “I will ask for an interview. I cannot rest without it. I trust in the greatness of his heart.”

Her eyes were bent toward the floor, her mind already moving away from the room, away from Tito, toward San Marco and its echoing cloisters. She scarcely felt that the voice she heard belonged to her husband.

“Better lose no time, then,” Tito said, with unmixed suavity, turning his cap between his fingers as if ready to take his leave. “And now, Romola, you will perhaps be able to see, in spite of prejudice, that my wishes go with yours in this matter. You will not regard the misfortune of my safety as an offence.”

The words struck her like a sudden harsh note in an otherwise tolerable harmony—an ugly clang that made all the surrounding sounds jar. Full consciousness of him returned, not as domestic familiarity but as something intrusive.

She looked at him without speaking.

“At least,” he added, and his tone hardened slightly, “you will endeavor to base our intercourse on some other reasonings than that because an evil deed is possible, I have done it. Am I alone to be beyond the pale of your extensive charity?”

The feeling driven back from her lips a fortnight earlier surged up with gathered force, as if every day of silence had fed it. She spoke with a decision that told him she no longer weighed consequences.

“It is too late, Tito. There is no killing the suspicion that deceit has once begotten. And now I know everything. I know who that old man was: he was your father, to whom you owe everything—to whom you owe more than if you had been his own child. Beside that, it is a small thing that you broke my trust and my father’s. As long as you deny the truth about that old man, there is a horror rising between us: the law that should make us one can never be obeyed. I too am a human being. I have a soul of my own that abhors your actions. Our union is a pretence—as if a perpetual lie could be a sacred marriage.”

Tito did not answer at once. When he did, the caution in his voice was no longer lazy; it was sharpened by alarm, calculated like a merchant’s figures.

“And you mean to carry out that independence by quitting me, I presume?”

“I desire to quit you,” Romola said, impetuously.

“And supposing I do not submit to part with what the law gives me some security for retaining?” Tito’s words came more quickly now, as if he wished to leave no pause in which her resolve could find breath. “You will then, of course, proclaim your reasons in the ear of all Florence. You will bring forward your mad assassin—who is doubtless ready to obey your call—and you will tell the world that you believe his testimony because he is so rational as to desire to assassinate me.”

His voice grew colder with each sentence, like water poured over fire. “You will first inform the Signoria that I am a Medicean conspirator, and then you will inform the Mediceans that I have betrayed them; and in both cases you will offer the excellent proof that you believe me capable in general of everything bad. It will certainly be a striking position for a wife to adopt. And if, on such evidence, you succeed in holding me up to infamy, you will have surpassed all the heroines of the Greek drama.”

He paused, enjoying the weight of his own mastery. Romola stood mute.

“I believe you have no other grievance against me,” he went on, “except that I have failed in fulfilling some lofty indefinite conditions on which you gave me your wifely affection—so that by withdrawing it you have gradually reduced me to the careful supply of your wants as a fair Piagnone of high condition and liberal charities. I think your success in gibbeting me is not certain. But doubtless you would begin by winning the ear of Messer Bernardo del Nero?”

“Why do I speak of anything?” Romola cried at last, as anguish broke through like a sob that cannot be stifled. She sank back into her chair. “It is hateful in me to be thinking of myself.”

She did not notice when Tito left the room, nor how long the air held his presence after the door had closed. The sounds of the house came back—some far clink, a footfall, the faint rustle of fabric—and outside, the city’s unceasing breath, like a great creature that never sleeps.

When the door opened again, Monna Brigida entered; and in that instant Romola sprang up as if roused by a bell.

“Cousin,” she said, “we must go to San Marco directly. I must see my confessor, Fra Salvestro.”

Morning had only just settled into its early brightness when Romola set out again for San Marco. The light lay fresh on the baked stones, pale gold in the joints of the pavement, while from open doorways came the day’s first domestic breath—wood-smoke that still clung to last night’s hearth, wet laundry hanging in shaded courts, the faint sour-sweet of fermenting must from a vintner’s back room. The city was waking as a body wakes: with a stretch, a groan, a sharpening of appetite.

She had obtained, through Fra Salvestro the evening before, a promise of an interview with Fra Girolamo in the chapter-house. Savonarola’s life was fenced about with such rigid care—he would not give calumny even a pretext—that private interviews were rare, and when they occurred they were arranged so that they could not be mistaken for secret plotting. The hour chosen was one when other visitors were likely to be in the outer cloisters, the convent’s quiet crossed by ordinary footsteps, the harmless murmur of lay voices.

Romola chose her way through the heart of Florence, not because it was the shortest, but because she wanted—she needed—to taste the air of the city, to feel what temper was rising, as a cook reads the moment when a pot begins to turn: first a faint change of scent, then a quickening, then the boil that will not be denied. She listened to Florence as to a kitchen before a feast: the clatter of shutters, the ring of a hammer in a smithy, the scrape of a chair dragged out into a loggia where men would sit and argue. Everywhere there were knots of talkers. Trade was languid, and when hands are idle, tongues labor harder.

Every loggia, every convenient corner of the piazza, every shop-front that made a rendezvous for gossips was astir with the excitement of gratuitous debate. The three days’ interval before the conspirators’ fate would be sealed was being spent like coin: both sides meant to spend it to the last farthing, to purchase the popular mood.

Handbills were already in circulation. Some offered, in black capitals large enough to be read by a man striding past, the alternative of justice upon the conspirators or ruin to the Republic; others, in equally emphatic print, urged observance of the law and the granting of the Appeal. Around those jutting islets of heavy type there lay lakes of smaller characters: arguments, reasons, insinuations, names. In that time—so proud of the new triumph of printing—there was a belief that no reasoning was so widely convincing as question-begging phrases in large letters. Romola, who had been trained among books and knew how often the truth hid where the eye was least tempted to look, cared far more for what was set down in the small print. She hurried, yet her gaze kept straying, anxiously searching for a loose sheet she could secure before it was pasted up high or ripped down by an officer’s hand.

For a long way she saw none except those clutched by eager readers, or plastered on walls from which, in places, sbirri were already tearing them down, the paper coming away with a dry rasp and leaving wet paste like a bruised mark on the plaster. At last, slipping behind San Giovanni with a quickened pace—she wanted to avoid the many acquaintances who frequented the piazza—she saw Bratti with a stock of handbills, exchanging them for small coin as briskly as a fruit-seller counts figs.

Bratti was no stranger to her. Florence’s humble lives were not unknown to Romola; she had learned, with her father, that the city’s mind was not only in council chambers and libraries, but at the bread-stalls, the oil-sellers, the corners where boys bawled news. Turning to him, she said, “Have you two sorts of handbills, Bratti? Let me have them quickly.”

“Two sorts,” Bratti replied, separating the wet sheets with a slowness that scraped her nerves. The paper still held the press’s damp coldness and a sharp smell of ink, like crushed walnuts mixed with iron. “There’s ‘Law,’ and there’s ‘Justice.’”

“Which sort do you sell most of?”

“‘Justice’—‘Justice’ goes the quickest,—so I raised the price, and made it two danari.” He held up the sheet as if it were a cut of meat and he was the butcher. “But then I bethought me the ‘Law’ was good ware too, and had as good a right to be charged for as ‘Justice;’ for people set no store by cheap things, and if I sold the ‘Law’ at one danaro, I should be doing it a wrong. And I’m a fair trader. ‘Law,’ or ‘Justice,’ it’s all one to me; they’re good wares. I got ’em both for nothing, and I sell ’em at a fair profit. But you’ll want more than one of a sort?”

“No, no: here’s a white quattrino for the two,” Romola said, folding the bills quickly, as if to keep their poison from spilling into the air, and hurrying away. The thin paper crackled between her fingers, and the ink smudged faintly on her glove like soot.

Soon she was in the outer cloisters of San Marco. The noise of the city fell back as if someone had shut a door on it; here the sound was of sandals on stone, of a low cough, of voices softened by arches. Fra Salvestro was awaiting her under the cloister, but did not notice her light step at first; he was chatting, according to his habit, with lay visitors. Under a government friendly to the Frate, the timidity about frequenting San Marco—which had followed the first shock of the Excommunication—had been gradually giving way. There were always faces now: earnest, curious, calculating.

In one of the visitors Romola recognized a well-known satellite of Francesco Valori, Andrea Cambini, whose hands never rested when he spoke, as if he must knead the air to make his meaning rise. Fra Salvestro listened with that air of trivial curiosity which tells that the listener cares very much about news and very little about its quality. Romola had always found this trait repulsive; now it was exasperating. The disjointed words reaching her ear made it plain Cambini was expounding something about the conspirators’ fate. The talk had the harsh relish of scandal, like cheap garlic rubbed on stale bread: it stings, it fills the mouth, it leaves no nourishment.

Romola chose not to approach the group. As soon as she saw that she had caught Fra Salvestro’s attention, she turned towards the door of the chapter-house. Fra Salvestro made a sign of approval and disappeared within the inner cloister. A lay Brother stood ready and opened the door for her; it swung on its hinges with a heavy sigh and shut behind her with a dull finality.

The chapter-house received her as it always did: cool air holding the faint odor of old plaster, candle-wax, and stone that had drunk prayers for generations. The frescoed figures on the walls looked down with their perpetual sorrow, those painted faces fixed in a grief that time could not soften. Once, long ago, those mournful saints had seemed to mourn with her when she came here with the wound of Dino’s death raw in her. The place could not help dragging back some of that memory; but the present pressed so strongly that the recollection was less a clear picture than a recurrence of pressure and chill, as if the same yearning had come again to be met by the same marble refusal.

She would not let the remembrance grow. She opened the handbills at once, thinking she might read in the interval before Fra Girolamo appeared. The paper that urged observance of the law was set forth with arguments in smaller type: the right of appeal, the danger of precedent, the dignity of a Republic that does not strike in haste. Romola’s eyes moved quickly, devouring line after line, while her ears kept their own vigil for the door.

By the time she reached the end, the door was opening. She doubled up the sheets and stood expectant. When Savonarola entered, she knelt by custom, as those did who saw him in private; but at his benedictory greeting she rose and stood facing him from a few yards’ distance.

It had been an unusually long while since she had seen him. His seclusion since the Excommunication had made his presence rarer, and the late months had visibly deepened in his face the marks of overtaxed mental labor and bodily severity: the skin drawn tighter over the bones, the eyes set as if they had stared too long into firelight. Yet Romola was less conscious of these changes than of something harder to name. Was it that the expression of serene elevation and pure human fellowship which had once moved her was now less present? Or was it that the new division between them—born of her feeling about her godfather—roused slumbering sources of alienation and clouded her own sight? Perhaps both currents ran together. So often our relations are decided by such coincident streams: the inexcusable word seldom comes until affection has already been worn thin by the strain of repeated excuses.

Savonarola’s glance at her had a hardness, the hardness of a mind preoccupied with itself. He divined why she had sought him: it would be about the conspirators. On that subject he had already had to quell inner voices that might grow loud again if Romola’s pleading encouraged them. Seated in his cell correcting sheets of his Triumph of the Cross, it had been easier to rest on a resolution of neutrality.

“It is a question of moment, doubtless, on which you wished to see me, my daughter,” he began. The tone was gentle, but its gentleness had the feel of control, not of spontaneous softness. “I know you are not wont to lay stress on small matters.”

“Father, you know what it is before I tell you,” Romola said. Once she began, everything else fell away as if a table had been swept clear for one dish only. “You know what I am caring for—it is for the life of the old man I love best in the world. The thought of him has gone together with the thought of my father as long as I remember the daylight. That is my warrant for coming to you, even if my coming should have been needless. Perhaps it is: perhaps you have already determined that your power over the hearts of men shall be used to prevent them from denying to Florentines a right which you yourself helped to earn for them.”

“I meddle not with the functions of the State, my daughter,” Fra Girolamo said. The words came with a firmness that was less anger than resistance. He was strongly disinclined to reopen outwardly a debate he had already fought inwardly. “I have preached and laboured that Florence should have a good government, for a good government is needful to the perfecting of the Christian life; but I keep away my hands from particular affairs which it is the office of experienced citizens to administer.”

“Surely, father—” Romola broke off. The first word had burst out almost impetuously, but she checked herself, stung by the sudden sense that she was remonstrating with the man who had once been her guide, her pillar. In rebelling she bruised her own reverence.

Savonarola was too quick not to see the conflict arresting her. He was too noble at this moment to take refuge in that calm evasiveness into which he was often hurried in public by the pressure of a crowd. “Say what is in your heart; speak on, my daughter,” he said. He stood with his arms laid one upon the other, looking at her with quiet expectation.

“I was going to say, father, that this matter is surely of higher moment than many about which I have heard you preach and exhort fervidly.” Her voice gathered again. “If it belonged to you to urge that men condemned for offences against the State should have the right to appeal to the Great Council—if you count it a glory to have won that right for them—can it less belong to you to declare yourself against the right being denied to almost the first men who need it? Surely that touches the Christian life more closely than whether you knew beforehand that the Dauphin would die, or whether Pisa will be conquered.”

A subtle movement passed over Savonarola’s lips, like a subdued sign of pain. Then he answered, “My daughter, I speak as it is given me to speak—I am not master of the times when I may become the vehicle of knowledge beyond the common lights of men. In this case I have no illumination beyond what wisdom may give to those who are charged with the safety of the State. As to the law of Appeal against the Six Votes, I laboured to have it passed in order that no Florentine should be subject to loss of life and goods through the private hatred of a few who might happen to be in power; but these five men, who have desired to overthrow a free government and restore a corrupt tyrant, have been condemned with the assent of a large assembly of their fellow-citizens. They refused at first to have their cause brought before the Great Council. They have lost the right to the appeal.”

“How can they have lost it?” Romola said. Her breath came faster; her cheeks warmed as if she stood too close to a brazier. “It is the right to appeal against condemnation, and they have never been condemned till now; and—forgive me, father—it is private hatred that would deny them the appeal; it is the violence of the few that frightens others; else why was the assembly divided again directly after it had seemed to agree? And if anything weighs against the observance of the law, let this weigh for it—that you used to preach more earnestly than all else that there should be no place given to hatred and bloodshed because of these party strifes, so that private ill-will should not find its opportunities in public acts. Father, you know there is private hatred concerned here: will it not dishonour you not to have interposed on the side of mercy, when there are many who hold that it is also the side of law and justice?”

“My daughter,” Fra Girolamo said, and now emotion showed more plainly, as heat shows through the thin skin of a fruit, “there is a mercy which is weakness, and even treason against the common good. The safety of Florence—which means even more than the welfare of Florentines—now demands severity, as it once demanded mercy. It is not only for a past plot that these men are condemned, but also for a plot which has not yet been executed; and the devices that were leading to its execution are not put an end to: the tyrant is still gathering his forces in Romagna, and the enemies of Florence, who sit in the highest places of Italy, are ready to hurl any stone that will crush her.”

“What plot?” Romola said. The question leapt out of her as if her mind had struck against something sharp. She reddened and trembled, alarmed surprise shaking her.

“You carry papers in your hand, I see,” Savonarola said, pointing to the folded handbills. “One of them will, perhaps, tell you that the government has had new information.”

Romola opened the second handbill hastily. The small print swam for a moment, then steadied. It proclaimed that the government now had positive evidence of a second plot, to be carried out in this August time. The words were meant to harden hearts; they lay on the page like salt thrown on raw flesh.

To Romola it read like a confirmation of something more intimate and more vile—that Tito, always slipping between nets, had won his safety by foul means. His recent pretence of wishing the Frate to exert himself on behalf of the condemned now turned rancid in her mind, as if she had tasted honey and found it smeared over rot. She crushed the paper in her hand, the crisp sheet wrinkling into a hard knot.

“Father,” she said, and a new passion broke through, “what safety can there be for Florence when the worst man can always escape?” Then, as memory flashed from the thought of her husband, she went on more bitterly: “And have not you yourself encouraged this deception which corrupts the life of Florence, by wanting more favour to be shown to Lorenzo Tornabuoni, who has worn two faces, and flattered you with a show of affection, when my godfather has always been honest? Ask all Florence who of those five men has the truest heart, and there will not be many who will name any other name than Bernardo del Nero. You did interpose with Francesco Valori for the sake of one prisoner: you have not then been neutral; and you know your word will be powerful.”

“I do not desire the death of Bernardo,” Savonarola said, colouring deeply. The redness rose like a sudden tide.

“It would be enough if he were sent out of the city,” he added, as if offering a compromise to his own conscience.

“Then why do you not speak to save an old man of seventy-five from dying a death of ignominy—to give him at least the fair chances of the law?” Romola burst out. Her impetuosity swept away prudence; she forgot everything but the sting of what seemed to her injustice. “It is not that you feel bound to be neutral; else why did you speak for Lorenzo Tornabuoni? You spoke for him because he is more friendly to San Marco; my godfather feigns no friendship. It is not, then, as a Medicean that my godfather is to die; it is as a man you have no love for!”

When she paused, cheeks glowing, lips quivering, there was dead silence. The chapter-house seemed to hold its breath.
