In that stillness, Romola heard her own words echoing back inside her, and in the echo they clashed painfully with the memories that clung to Savonarola’s presence: the voice that had once sounded like clear water, the hand she had thought strong and clean. The silence expanded with compunction and with a sudden self-doubt that hurt like an over-tight band. Had she committed sacrilege in her passion?

Yet she could retract nothing. Her whole being clung to her plea, and she could not make her mind submit to Savonarola’s refusal. All the more she needed, in this very rebellion, to satisfy the reverence that still lived in her like a native dialect she could not wholly forget.

She moved suddenly towards him. “Forgive me, father; it is pain to me to have spoken those words—yet I cannot help speaking. I am little and feeble compared with you; you brought me light and strength. But I submitted because I felt the proffered strength—because I saw the light. Now I cannot see it. Father, you yourself declare there comes a moment when the soul must have no guide but the voice within it, to tell whether the consecrated thing has sacred virtue. And therefore I must speak.”

Savonarola had a susceptibility to opposition that was hardly separable from a power-loving and powerful nature—accustomed to seek great ends that cast a reflected grandeur on the means. His sermons could burn with that red flame. If he had been meaner, he would have shown irritation at Romola’s freedom, so unlike the deference he usually received. But now those feelings were swallowed up in the harder struggle that made half the tragedy of his life: a mind hungry for purity and simplicity, yet caught in a tangle of demands, false ideas, and outward conditions that made simplicity impossible.

He listened, alive to every suggestion in her words, and rapidly surveyed again—as he had done before—the courses open to him and their likely results. But it was a question where arguments could seem decisive only in proportion as they were charged with feeling, and she had given him no new impulse that could shift his bias. He looked at her and said, “You have full pardon for your frankness, my daughter. You speak, I know, out of the fulness of your family affections. But these affections must give way to the needs of the Republic. If those men who have a close acquaintance with the affairs of the State believe, as I understand they do, that the public safety requires the extreme punishment of the law to fall on the five conspirators, I cannot control their opinion, seeing that I stand aloof from such affairs.”

“Then you desire that they should die? You desire that the Appeal should be denied them?” Romola said. Again she felt repelled, as if he had held out a cup and then withdrawn it with an explanation that tasted like excuse.

“I have said that I do not desire their death.”

“Then,” Romola said, and indignation rose again like a second fermentation, “you can be indifferent that Florentines should inflict death which you do not desire, when you might have protested against it—when you might have helped to hinder it, by urging the observance of a law which you held it good to get passed. Father, you used not to stand aloof: you used not to shrink from protesting. Do not say you cannot protest where the lives of men are concerned; say rather you desire their death. Say rather you hold it good for Florence that there shall be more blood and more hatred. Will the death of five Mediceans put an end to parties in Florence? Will the death of a noble old man like Bernardo del Nero save a city that holds such men as Dolfo Spini?”

“My daughter, it is enough.” Savonarola’s voice had the hard edge of a knife laid down on a board. “The cause of freedom, which is the cause of God’s kingdom upon earth, is often most injured by the enemies who carry within them the power of certain human virtues. The wickedest man is often not the most insurmountable obstacle to the triumph of good.”

“Then why do you say again that you do not desire my godfather’s death?” Romola said. Anger and despair mingled until she could not separate them. “Rather, you hold it the more needful he should die because he is the better man. I cannot unravel your thoughts, father; I cannot hear the real voice of your judgment and conscience.”

A moment’s pause—thick, strained. Then Savonarola spoke with keener emotion than before. “Be thankful, my daughter, if your own soul has been spared perplexity; and judge not those to whom a harder lot has been given. You see one ground of action in this matter. I see many. I have to choose that which will further the work intrusted to me. The end I seek is one to which minor respects must be sacrificed. The death of five men—were they less guilty than these—is a light matter weighed against the withstanding of the vicious tyrannies which stifle the life of Italy, and foster the corruption of the Church; a light matter weighed against the furthering of God’s kingdom upon earth, the end for which I live and am willing myself to die.”

Under other circumstances, Romola might have been touched by the appeal at the beginning of his speech. But she was now utterly opposed to him. What he called perplexity seemed to her sophistry and doubleness; the more he spoke of sacrificing “minor respects,” the more she felt the bitter taste of a language that makes killing sound like prudence, as if words themselves were being used to salt and preserve cruelty. His phrases seemed to belong to a lexicon of power—grand, dominant, certain—under which the untranslatable tremor of one old man’s life, one family’s love, could be flattened and made negligible.

She answered almost with bitterness. “Do you, then, know so well what will further the coming of God’s kingdom, father, that you will dare to despise the plea of mercy—of justice—of faithfulness to your own teaching? Has the French king, then, brought renovation to Italy? Take care, father, lest your enemies have some reason when they say that in your visions of what will further God’s kingdom you see only what will strengthen your own party.”

“And that is true!” Savonarola said, and his eyes flashed. In that instant Romola’s voice seemed to him the voice of his enemies. “The cause of my party is the cause of God’s kingdom.”

“I do not believe it!” Romola said. Her whole frame shook with passionate repugnance, as if her very senses rejected the sound of it. “God’s kingdom is something wider—else, let me stand outside it with the beings that I love.”

The two faces were lit, each by an opposite certainty, each by an opposite emotion. Further words were impossible. Romola drew her veil over her head with a haste that was almost a gesture of self-defense, and she went out in silence, leaving behind her the cool air, the mourning frescoes, and the sound of her own footfall—brief, sharp, and then swallowed by the convent’s stone.

Three nights after, when the moon should have been climbing above the roofs that hemmed in the great square before the Old Palace, it found no pavement to silver and no orderly alternation of light and shadow to lay down like a patterned cloth. The stones were hidden as if the city had poured its own living substance over them: only heads, shoulders, hands lifted and clenched, the glimmer of eyes and steel, the heaving of breath in a mass that struggled and swayed, filled the piazza to its edges. Florence, that could on other nights be heard in separate threads—the quick patter of feet, a lute’s thin trembling, the soft scamper of late lovers along a wall—was now one single harsh instrument. A roar made of shouts and curses, of trampling soles and bodies thrust aside, of the accidental clank of arms, rose and fell; and across that tumult, nothing came clean except, now and then, a sudden shriek like a bird pierced, or the heavy drop of a bell’s toll that seemed to strike the air itself into dull pieces.

Almost all who could call themselves the public were awake. Those not already wedged within the piazza were pushing to enter it, finding the very act of standing still impossible, because the crowd had become a kind of tide. Within the palace, in the council-chamber, all the chief magistracies were still gathered: the Eighty, and the selected citizens who had argued through the long daylight and the torchlit hours whether the prisoners should have the Appeal, or whether the sentence must be carried out at once to forestall the perilous chances of waiting. Their debate had not been mere debate; it had been quarrel and menace, loud enough that the harshness of it leaked through walls and corridors to the multitude outside, so that the square’s roar was answered by another roar from within, like two seas meeting.

Only in the last hour had the question been decided. Four of the Signoria had stood obstinately for the Appeal even when the argument ceased to be law and became threat—houses to be sacked, families to be turned into targets for the crowd’s rage. And then Francesco Valori—brief, furious, as men are when their anger is a weapon they mean to use at once—had made his party’s meaning plain by declaring that if the Signoria would not defend the liberties of Florence by executing those five perfidious citizens, there would be others ready to take the cause in hand, to the peril of all who opposed it. The Florentine Cato triumphed. When the beans were counted again, the four white that had stood for mercy did not appear; all nine were black—fatal, unanimous. They decided the death of the five without delay, and they decided also, though no one spoke it aloud and it would ripen more slowly, the death of Francesco Valori.

Now the judicial Eight had gone to the Bargello to prepare the execution; and the five condemned men were being led barefoot and in irons through the midst of the council. Their friends had contrived it, with that desperate hope which clings to the visible. Would not Florentines be moved by seeing such ignominy hung on two venerable men like Bernardo del Nero and Niccolò Ridolfi—men whose bias had been taken long before the new order made Mediceanism retrograde? Would not hearts soften at the sight of two brilliant, popular young men like Tornabuoni and Pucci, whose places would be left like empty chairs at every gathering of chief citizens? It was useless. The pity that stirred now was the kind that does not rescue: it only ripens late into revenge.

While that bitter procession passed upstairs, Romola stood below in the palace court, her back against one of the massive pillars, as if she needed the old stone’s steadiness. She was waiting for the moment when her godfather would appear on his way to death. By the use of strong interest she had won permission to visit him in the evening and remain with him until the council’s result should be determined. And now she waited with his confessor, meaning to follow the guard that would lead him to the Bargello. Her heart was bent on clinging to the childless old man to the last instant, as her father would have clung; and she had overborne every remonstrance.

Giovan Battista Ridolfi, a disciple of Savonarola, was beside her. He was going in bitterness to see the death of his elder brother Niccolò, yet he had promised Romola should be guarded, as if in that service he could keep hold of some shred of decency amid the city’s frenzy. Tito, too, was in the palace, but Romola had not seen him. Since the evening of the seventeenth they had avoided each other. Tito knew only by inference, from the report of the Frate’s neutrality, that her pleading had failed.

He was now among official personages—Florentine and foreign—who had waited out the long council. He wore, except when addressed, the subdued gravity of a man in painful conflict between public duty and private feeling. And when someone alluded to his wife, in connection with the condemned, he implied that her mind was violently excited; that the mere fact of his continuing to hold office under a government concerned in her godfather’s condemnation roused in her a diseased hostility; and that for her sake it was best he should not approach her.

“Ah, the old Bardi blood!” said Cennini, shrugging. “I shall not be surprised if this business shakes her loose from the Frate, as well as some others I could name.”

“It is excusable in a woman,” said a young French envoy—smiling, and bowing to Tito—“to think her affections must overrule the good of the State, and that nobody is to be beheaded who is anybody’s cousin; but such a view is not to be encouraged in the male population. It seems to me your Florentine polity is much weakened by it.”

“That is true,” said Niccolò Macchiavelli. “But where personal ties are strong, the hostilities they raise must be taken due account of. Many of these half-way severities are mere hot-headed blundering. The only safe blows to be inflicted on men and parties are the blows that are too heavy to be avenged.”

“Niccolò,” said Cennini, “there is a clever wickedness in thy talk sometimes that makes me mistrust thy pleasant young face as if it were a mask of Satan.”

“Not at all, my good Domenico,” Macchiavelli answered, smiling, laying his hand on the elder’s shoulder. “Satan was a blunderer, an introducer of novità, who made a stupendous failure. If he had succeeded, we should all have been worshipping him, and his portrait would have been more flattered.”

“Well, well,” said Cennini, “I say not thy doctrine is not too clever for Satan: I only say it is wicked enough for him.”

“I tell you,” said Macchiavelli, “my doctrine is the doctrine of all men who seek an end a little farther off than their own noses. Ask our Frate, our prophet, how his universal renovation is to be brought about: he will tell you, first, by getting a free and pure government; and since it appears that this cannot be done by making all Florentines love each other, it must be done by cutting off every head that happens to be obstinately in the way. Only if a man incurs odium by sanctioning a severity that is not thorough enough to be final, he commits a blunder. And something like that blunder, I suspect, the Frate has committed. It was an occasion on which he might have won some lustre by exerting himself to maintain the Appeal; instead of that, he has lost lustre, and has gained no strength.”

Before any reply could rise, the expected announcement came: the prisoners were about to leave the council-chamber. The majority hurried toward the door, eager to secure place behind the guard—intent, with passions hot or curiosity cold, on seeing the execution at the Bargello. Tito was among those who remained behind. He had a native repugnance to sights of death and pain, and five days earlier, when execution had seemed possible, he had hoped for exile as the utmost. His safety demanded no more.

But now he felt a grim ease in the thought that Bernardo del Nero’s head off his shoulders would be a guarantee. Romola’s new knowledge, her new attitude since his return, had planted in him a dread of what she could do—how a single act of hers might make him an object of suspicion and odium, bringing frustration under unpleasant circumstances. Her belief in Baldassarre had plainly fixed her wavering feelings against further submission; and if her godfather lived, she would win him to share her belief without much trouble. Romola was more than ever an unmanageable fact in his destiny. But with Bernardo dead, the difficulties she would face in setting herself against her husband would likely be too great for her shrinking pride. So he had breathed easier when he learned the Eight had gone to order the instant erection of the scaffold.

Four other men—his intimates and confederates—were to die beside Bernardo. But a man’s safety is a god that makes grim demands. Tito felt them grim; and yet, even pursuing what he found agreeable, life forced him into desiring what was disagreeable. He had known that paradox before. Now, as through the open doorway came the shuffle of many feet and the clank of metal on the stairs, he could still answer the French envoy’s questions without showing more than sad resignation to State necessity.

Those sounds fell on Romola as if her hearing had been sharpened until each noise had a blade. In that courtyard the echoes did not blur; they came back hard from stone—the ring of iron, the scrape of a sandal sole, the low murmur that swelled and broke like water thrown against a quay. She needed no arm. She shed no tears. It was as if her whole being were strung past the point where grief and joy are separate things: intensity without softness, like a flame that has burned away smoke.

Since her godfather’s fate had been decided, the struggle within her had given way to an inward union with him. She was asserting for him, as if the words were a shelter she could set up against the world, that though he suffered as a traitor he did not deserve the name. He was the victim of a collision between two fidelities. It was not given him to die for the noblest cause, and yet he died because of his nobleness: he might have been meaner and found it easier to avoid this guilt. In her, sympathy for the individual lot rose up against the formulas by which parties judged actions. She would tread the way with her second father to the scaffold and defy ignominy by knowing it was undeserved.

The way was fenced by three hundred armed men, placed there by Valori’s orders—another contradiction in the night’s contradictions: alarm proclaimed at once that the people would tear the conspirators limb from limb, and alarm also that some might try to rescue them in the midst of a hostile crowd. The press of bodies along the passage breathed heat and stale wine and the sharpness of torches. And always the sound—sound that was almost a physical weight—rolled over them, as if Florence’s own throat were hoarse with its need.

When they reached the court of the Bargello, Romola was allowed to approach Bernardo with his confessor for a moment of farewell. Even in that agitated throng, many eyes turned to them, as the aged man, forgetting his irons, lifted his bound hands toward the golden head bent down to him—then checked himself, as if the very gesture must be obedient now, and leaned to kiss her. She took the fettered hands when they dropped again and kissed them as if they were sacred things.

“My poor Romola,” Bernardo said low, “I have only to die, but thou hast to live—and I shall not be there to help thee.”

“Yes,” Romola answered, hurried, as if the words must be spoken before time could snatch them away. “You will help me—always—because I shall remember you.”

They took her away and led her up the steps to the loggia that ran round the grand old court. There she stood under a dark arch, choosing her place as one chooses a vow. She meant to look until the moment her godfather laid his head on the block. Bernardo was to suffer first. Battista Ridolfi, close beside her, had promised that once she had seen the last look of the man who, alone in all the world, had shared her pitying love for her father, he would lead her out through a door behind them.

And still, behind the iron of her resolve, a possibility worked like a seed that refuses to die: that rescue might yet come, some hand might thrust itself between justice and blood, something would keep that scaffold unstained. Time dragged and snapped. There was constant movement below—torches wavering in their rings, light jerking across carved stone faces that looked down with their old, indifferent mouths; then the same light striking a pale cheek tightened with rage, or a mouth bitten white with held-back sobs—near kin of the condemned who would soon receive the dead and carry them home. The crowd pressed denser about the black scaffold until the court seemed a trough filled to the brim with humanity.

Romola’s face, against the darkness of the arch, looked like marble—still, colorless, a thing carved to endure. The sound in the court was not one sound but many, knotted together: muttered prayers, a sharp laugh that came and was strangled, the thick breathing of men pressed chest to back, and the heavy waves of noise rushing in through the entrance from the piazza beyond. It was as if she stood in a storm-tossed sea and cared nothing for the storm, caring only to hold out a signal until the eyes that sought it could seek it no more.

Suddenly the tumult sank. The very tapers seemed to tremble themselves into quiet. On the scaffold the executioner was ready. Bernardo del Nero appeared, ascending with a slow, firm step.

Romola did not move. No cry escaped her—not even a stifled sound. She stood more firmly, as if her steadiness could lend him steadiness. She saw him pause, the white head kept erect, and she heard his voice distinctly, carrying across that brief hush:

“It is but a short space of life that my fellow-citizens have taken from me.”

As he spoke, his gaze moved slowly round. She felt—felt as one feels a hand laid on the heart—that his eyes rested on her. Her arms stretched out toward him, but whether in the air or only within her, she did not know. Then she saw no more.

After what seemed a long while, a voice said, “My daughter, all is peace now. I can conduct you to your house.”

She uncovered her head and found Bernardo’s confessor beside her, and they were no longer in the open loggia but in a room where grave men talked in subdued tones, as if words themselves must now tread carefully.

“I am ready,” Romola said, starting up. “Let us lose no time.”

All clinging, she thought, was ended. All strength now must be gathered for one purpose: to escape from a grasp under which she shuddered.

On the eighth day from that night which had broken and remade her, Romola stood where the land ended and the Mediterranean began—just above what was then the small fishing village of Viareggio. The sea had the slow, summer breathing of a creature asleep: a hush that rose and fell, and in its hush the shore answered with a soft, repeated sound, as if the pebbles were being taught one syllable and could never learn another. After Florence, that unceasing clatter of wheels and voices and iron in the blood, the plain music of water was like a hand laid on a fevered brow.

Again she had fled. Again the grey religious dress was on her—rough cloth that rasped the wrists when she moved, a smell of stale wool warmed by her body. This time she wore it with an indifference that was more desolate than any disguise. What did a badge matter, or a name? She could not find, beneath the name she had been given, any single duty that held fast and did not crumble the moment she touched it.

Duty—men spoke it as if it were a loaf that could be cut and shared, as if its substance were the same for every mouth. But what force made duty holy, what kneaded it and baked it into something one could live on, if not love believing in some good beyond the self? The bonds of affection that had once drawn her toward endurance seemed snapped, and their broken ends only whipped her when she tried to move. Even in marriage—the bond she had been taught to imagine mystic, indissoluble by its own nature—she no longer saw a sacred union, no longer even the plain obligation of a chosen pledge. Had she not proved that the thing pledged to was impossible? Freedom pressed on her with an overmastering impulse, yet it offered only the exchange of one calamity for another. There is no compensation for the woman who feels the chief relation of her life has been only a mistake: she has lost her crown. Some deepest secret of blessedness has brushed her ear, half-whispered, and then withdrawn for ever, leaving not wisdom but a hungry ache.

What had supported her through that supreme sorrow had slipped away too. The sense of a great end—some purpose that could lift the commonest act, as bread is lifted by heat into something airy and fit to sustain—was eclipsed now. She saw instead a confusion of human things, as if all effort were only fingers tugging at a net of tangled threads; all fellowship, whether of resistance or advocacy, only unfairness and exclusiveness in a different dress.

And what, then, was the man she had reverenced as the very type of heroism—not the heroism of hard endurance, but of willing self-offering love? What was the cause he struggled for? Romola had lost her trust in Savonarola. That fervour of admiration which had once made her overlook his aberrations and see only the grand sweep of his course was gone. Now that her tenderness for her godfather had set her in antagonism to the Frate, she saw, with a painful, magnifying lucidity, every harsh inconsistency in his teaching. In the bitterness of disappointment she told herself that his striving for the renovation of Church and world was a striving after a name—no more nourishing than the title of a book. A name which, in practice, came to mean measures to strengthen his own place in Florence; even questionable words and deeds, undertaken to keep his influence from suffering through his own errors.

That political reform which had once given her a new appetite for life seemed to dwindle, in this new light, into narrow devices for Florence’s safety—contemptibly at odds with alternating professions of blind trust in Divine care. It was inevitable that she should judge him unfairly where an individual’s suffering was concerned: she looked with the eyes of personal tenderness, and he with the eyes of theoretic conviction. When he declared that his party’s cause was the cause of God’s kingdom, she heard only the ring of egoism. Perhaps such words are rarely spoken without that meaner ring; yet they are the very formula of all energetic belief. And if energetic belief, pursuing a grand and distant end, is always in danger of turning into demon-worship—letting son and daughter pass through fire with a readiness that scarcely looks like sacrifice—so too the nearest fellow-feeling has its peril. It can grow timid and sceptical toward the larger aims without which life cannot rise into religion.

So Romola was being blinded by her tears. Whoever has known what it is to lose faith in a fellow-man whom one has profoundly loved and revered will not lightly suppose the shock leaves faith in Invisible Goodness untouched. When high human trust sinks, the dignity of life sinks too; we cease to believe in our own better self, since that self is part of a common nature now degraded in our thought. The finer impulses are dulled, as delicate herbs lose their scent if bruised too long under rough hands.

She felt even the springs of her once active pity drying, leaving only a barren, egoistic complaining. Had not she suffered too? Few had cared for her, while she had cared for many. She had done enough; she had strained toward the impossible, and was weary of this stifling, crowded life. She longed for repose in mere sensation—the old girlish dream from sultry afternoons, when she had fancied herself floating, naïad-like, in waters that asked nothing and judged nothing.

The clear waves seemed to invite her, cool as a well in summer. She wished she could lie down to sleep on them and pass from sleep into death. But she could not directly seek death: the fulness of young life in her forbade the clear, deliberate act. She could only wish that death would come to her, as storms come.

Where she had paused, the shore curved inward into a deep bend. A small boat with a sail was moored there, rocking with a patience that seemed almost human. She stood looking at it, and—like a remembered taste that turns suddenly into craving—her mind slipped back to a story she had once loved in Boccaccio. In those days, when her father fell asleep and she slid from her stool to sit on the floor with the forbidden sweetness of the Decamerone, she had read of fair Gostanza, who, lovelorn and despairing, desired to live no longer, yet had not the courage to strike at her young life. She had put herself into a boat, pushed off to sea, wrapped her mantle over her head, hoping to be wrecked—hoping fear would be made helpless, unable to flee from death.

It had been only a thought then, a story held at arm’s length like a tale of salt and wind. But now, as Romola paced and paused again, she saw another boat gliding black against the red-gold water—one man in it, rowing toward the bend where the smaller boat waited. When she walked on a little and watched, she saw him land, pull his boat ashore, and begin to unload his catch and gear.

Perhaps he owned the small boat too. He would be gone soon; the chance would be gone with him—the chance, at least, of possessing that frail means of drifting away. She had not yet admitted to herself that she meant to use it, but the eagerness that rose in her disclosed how a half-unconscious thought had ripened into desire.

“Is that little boat yours also?” she said.

The fisherman looked up, startled by the tall grey figure that had come upon him in the evening solitude. He made a reverence, taking her for a holy Sister wandering in some mysterious errand. His hands smelled of seaweed and fish; his clothes held the day’s brine. Yes, it was his boat: an old one, hardly seaworthy, yet worth mending to any man who would buy it. By the blessing of San Antonio—whose chapel stood in the village yonder—his fishing had prospered; he had now a better boat, which had once been Gianni’s, before Gianni died. But he had not sold the old one.

Romola asked the price. While he was still busy with his unloading—nets folded, damp ropes coiled like sleeping snakes—she thrust the money into a little satchel on the ground, where the remnant of his dinner lay: bread with a hard crust softened at the broken edge by oil, perhaps a pinch of salt that clung to everything in that place as if the air itself were seasoned.

Then she watched him furl the sail, and asked, with a steadiness that made her seem merely curious, how he would set it if he wanted to go out to sea. The fisherman answered, pointing and demonstrating with the practical exactness of a man who knows wind the way a baker knows heat. She listened, storing the small instructions as if they were nothing more than household knowledge—how to fasten, how to loosen, how to let the cloth take the breeze without tearing itself to pieces.

After that she paced up and down and waited, counting not minutes but changes in light and sound. Her imagination of herself gliding away in that boat on darkening water grew more urgent, as the thought of a cool brook in sultriness becomes thirst that hurts. To be freed from choice when every motive was bruised; to commit herself, sleeping, to destiny which would either bring death, or else bring her to new necessities that might rouse a new life—this beckoned her the more because the soft evening air made her long to rest in still solitude instead of returning to the village’s heat and noise.

At last the slow fisherman gathered up his movables and walked away, his footsteps a brief rasp on the sand. Soon the gold shrank and darkened in sea and sky. No living thing was in sight; no sound but the lulling monotony of waves that kept time without music. There was no tide in this sea to bear her outward if she waited for an ebb; but Romola felt the breeze from the land rising a little, and it seemed like a hand pushing.

She got into the boat. The wood was worn smooth where hands had gripped it; it smelled of tar and old wet, of long days when hunger and hope had been measured by nets. She unfurled the sail, fastened it as she had been shown in that first brief lesson. The cloth caught the light breeze—she saw it fill, saw the boat answer—and that was all she cared for.

Then she loosed the boat from its moorings and urged it with an oar, pushing until the shore was no longer near enough to accuse her with its nearness. Farther out: until the sea was dark even toward the west, and the stars disclosed themselves like a palpitating life over the wide heavens.

At last she rested. She threw back her cowl, and took off the kerchief beneath it that confined her hair. She doubled cowl and kerchief under her head for a pillow against one of the boat’s ribs. The fair head was still very young and could bear a hard pillow.

So she lay, the soft night air breathing on her while she glided on water that felt, by its very sound, like a vast cradle. She was alone now. She had freed herself from all claims; she had freed herself even from that burden of choice which presses heavier when claims have loosened their guiding hold.

Had she found the dream of her girlhood—repose in mere sensation? No. Memories clung to her like broken wings, heavy, useless, impossible to lift. Memories of human sympathy—sympathy that, even when it wounds, leaves a thirst that the Great Mother has no milk to still. In the wide spaces of sea and sky, Romola felt orphaned. The far-off writing of the heavens sent her no message of love. The stars were bright, indifferent, and in their clean light she felt herself looked at without being seen.

A great sob rose in her, salt as the air, and she wished that she might be gliding into death.

She drew the cowl over her head again, choosing darkness rather than that starlight which seemed to her like the hard light of eyes. Presently she felt as if she were in the grave, and yet not resting there: as if her hands were touching the hands of beloved dead beside her, and she was trying to wake them.

About ten o’clock on the morning of the twenty-seventh of February, Florence began to flow as if the stones themselves had been tipped toward one point, and the people—tailors with their shears still in their pockets, bakers with flour ghosting their sleeves, women who had left dough to rise beneath damp linen, boys smelling of smoke and orange peel—were carried in a steady current to San Marco.

It was the last morning of Carnival. Everyone knew a second Bonfire of Vanities was being built before the Old Palace—another hungry pyre to lick up masks and mirrors, ribands and books, the bright trifles that had made the streets sing only yesterday. Yet at this hour the city’s appetite had turned from flame to voice. The Piazza of San Marco was choked, not with dancing, but with bodies pressed close as wheat in a granary, all the more compact for the quiet that held them. The only motion was the swelling pressure of latecomers at every opening, and the stubborn resistance of those already wedged in front, braced shoulder to shoulder as if against a flood.

A semicircular barrier had been set before the church. Within it the Dominican brethren of San Marco were gathering, black mantles folding and unfolding like ravens’ wings as they took their places. The temporary wooden pulpit—fresh boards, resin-scented where the sun warmed them—stood above the church door, empty still, like a baking peel held out waiting for bread.

It was to be climbed by the man whom the Pope’s command had driven from the pulpit of the Duomo; the man whom the other clergy were forbidden to consort with, whom Florentines were forbidden to hear under threat of excommunication—and whom, despite all that, they still came to listen to in his own church, and from whose hands they still, on this very morning, would accept the Communion.

He had said aloud what many had only muttered in kitchens and botteghe, between the scrape of a knife on a board and the thud of a pestle: that a wicked Pope bought into office by bribery was no Christ’s vicar; that curses from such a mouth were broken swords, hilts without blades; that commands contrary to the Christian life must be disobeyed—nay, could not lawfully be obeyed.

But words, however sharp, were not enough when they began to cut into bread.

So long as believing in the Frate promised no visible calamity—so long as it felt like an amulet pinned inside the doublet, a special safety in a dangerous world—Florence asked for no sign. His preaching had been music to which the people marched willingly, in step with their own wishes. Now belief meant immediate blows: merchants hearing their contracts fray; bankers imagining foreign coin refusing their touch; artisans fearing the shutters would come down; the city’s stance among the Italian States trembling; an interdict hanging over Florence like a lid over a pot, suffocating not only trade but marriage, burial, baptism—every domestic rite by which memory was kept warm.

And so, like hunger rising in a house where the larder is failing, one demand had begun to swell in the public throat: What miracle showest thou?

It had come to Savonarola’s ear slowly at first, then faster and faster, until it could be heard even beneath psalmody. Outwardly he answered with assurance: the miracle would come in its fitting time. Inwardly, faith stirred and wavered as all living things do. Yet his speech did not waver. Those who must speak for crowds often speak on yesterday’s faith, hoping it will return tomorrow; and if the crowd’s belly is empty, it cannot be told to wait on a philosopher’s hunger.

The pulpit had been built for this—wood and nails in answer to impatience for a supernatural guarantee.

While the brethren filed in, the crowd’s faces were not yet fixed on the pulpit. They watched the monks instead—picking out familiar cheekbones and family resemblances, remembering whose son had once hawked figs at a corner, whose brother had stitched doublets in the Mercato Vecchio, whose cousin kept a little vineyard beyond the city walls. In Florence, even holiness had kinship lines; even Latin was carried on Tuscan breath.

Then the number of monks was complete. Books fluttered open. The chant began, a thin, persistent wail that threaded itself through the piazza like the keening of wind between cypresses. It was not the chant alone that made the great mass of bodies settle into stillness; it was expectation—felt, shared, and passed along like a quiet signal. People began to say under their breath, “Fra Girolamo must be coming now.”

Silence spread as if a pale solemn light had been set over the upturned faces, and all at once eyes were trained on the empty pulpit.

The next instant, it was not empty.

A figure, covered head to foot in black cowl and mantle, had entered and was kneeling, bent low, face turned away. The monks’ chant went on, and to the eager multitude the time seemed to stretch—like waiting for water to boil when thirst makes every second audible. Yet no one broke the hush. The Frate’s audiences with Heaven still carried electric awe for this mixed crowd; even those who had come with stones in their mind felt their arms slacken, as if the air itself had thickened around their wrists.

At last there was a faint vibration among the multitude—each giving his neighbor an aspen-like touch—as when watchers of the sky see what they hoped for disclose itself without sound. The Frate had risen. He turned toward them and pushed back his cowl a little.

The chant ceased, and for those nearest it was as if the sound that had been filling their ears had abruptly merged into something else: the force of Savonarola’s glance sweeping the piazza in silence.

He stretched out his hands.

They were hands of exquisite delicacy, so refined they seemed less made to grasp than to feel—hands that carried their own kind of speech, as if the part of his soul masked by that strong passionate face had found another language. His face, for all its vigor, was written over now with deeper lines around mouth and brow than forty-four years of ordinary living would carve: lines etched by fasts, by vigils, by the repeated heat and cooling of his own emotion.

At the first outstretched gesture, some in the front ranks dropped to their knees, and here and there a devout disciple farther back followed, as if pulled downward by the gravity of belief. But the greater number stood, stiffly erect. Some resisted the impulse to kneel before an excommunicated man—what if judgment fell on them in that very act? Others held themselves up with scorn and hatred of the ambitious deceiver staging another comedy—yet even they felt an unwilling impotence, like a man caught under the tide of a fashion he despises but cannot stop.

Then the voice came: clear, low at first, laying the Latin on the air as one lays salt on meat, with a steadiness meant to preserve. “Misereatur vestri—”

More knees touched stone.

As the words rose higher and yet clearer, the count of erect heads dwindled. And when he cried, “Benedicat vos omnipotens Deus—” it burst forth in a masculine trumpet-note, as if the blessing itself had to protest its right to be spoken under the clutch of a demon trying to stifle it. It rang to the extremities of the piazza. Under it every head bowed, as wheat bends when the wind passes.

After the blessing he fell to his knees again and hid his face, spent for a moment. Such jets of feeling were necessary to him. He had told the people long ago, “Without preaching I cannot live.” Yet it was a life that shattered him, as fire shatters the earthen pot that holds it too long.

After a few minutes some rose, stiff-legged, rubbing numb hands; but many stayed kneeling, and all watched him with an intentness that made the piazza seem a single creature holding its breath.

Savonarola took up a crystal vessel containing the consecrated Host. The sunlight, struggling through greyness, struck it now and then with pale glints, like a knife flashing above a board. He was about to speak.

“You remember, my children,” he said, “three days ago I besought you—when I should hold this Sacrament in my hand in the face of you all—to pray fervently to the Most High that if this work of mine does not come from Him, He will send a fire and consume me, that I may vanish into the eternal darkness away from His light which I have hidden with my falsity. Again I beseech you to make that prayer, and to make it now.”

A breathless moment followed. Perhaps no one truly prayed; perhaps some tried, in devout obedience, as one tries to chew when the mouth is dry with fear. Most consciousness was seized by the sense that Savonarola was praying—his voice not loud, but distinctly audible in the wide stillness.

“Lord, if I have not wrought in sincerity of soul, if my word cometh not from Thee, strike me in this moment with Thy thunder, and let the fires of Thy wrath enclose me.”

He stopped. He stood motionless with the Mystery in his hand, eyes lifted, the whole of him quivering as if his flesh were a string drawn too tight. No one moved. No one spoke. Even the piazza seemed to listen, and in that listening every small sound—cloth settling on a shoulder, a distant hoof on stone, the faint crackle of a brazier somewhere behind shutters—took on the weight of omen. The city’s own acoustic life, usually so braided with calling vendors, clattering carts, and the cheerful metallic din of work, was reduced to a thin thread. In that thread people heard their fate.

Sunlight, for the last quarter of an hour only piercing the grey in fitful streaks across the convent wall, made some spectators start timidly, as if Heaven were testing its match. Then the light widened. With a gentle quickness, like a smile, brightness poured itself directly onto the crystal vase—set it burning white—and spread over Savonarola’s face with mild glorification, as if the day had chosen him.

An instantaneous shout surged through the piazza: “Behold the answer!”

The warm radiance thrilled through Savonarola’s frame, and so did the shout. In that pulse he tasted untroubled triumph—his last. For a moment the future opened in him like a door: a grander scene to come, an audience representing all Christendom, where he would be sealed again as messenger of supreme righteousness, charged full with Divine strength.

But the strain was more than his body could bear. While the shout still rang, he turned away and disappeared within the church.

When he was gone, the sunlight seemed to lose its singled-out intention. It spread impartially over all things clean and unclean, saint and skeptic, velvet and patched wool. And with the crowd’s movement—knees unbending, feet shuffling, people pushing back toward the openings—voices rose into a confusion in which strong discords and varying scales of laughter told plainly that, in the kneeling and silence, hostility and scorn had only submitted unwillingly to a momentary spell.

From an upper loggia in one of the houses opposite the church, Tito had watched the whole scene with attentive eyes, safe above the press, as if in a theater-box where one could hear the roar below without being touched by it.

“It seems to me the plaudits are giving way to criticism,” he said, turning slightly toward the man beside him. “Nevertheless it was a striking moment, eh, Messer Pietro? Fra Girolamo is a man to make one understand there was a time when the monk’s frock was a symbol of power over men’s minds rather than over the keys of women’s cupboards.”

“Assuredly,” said Pietro Cennini. “And until I have seen proof that Fra Girolamo has much less faith in God’s judgments than the common run of men, instead of having considerably more, I shall not believe he would brave Heaven in this way if his soul were laden with a conscious lie.”

A month after that Carnival, on a morning near the end of March, Tito came down the marble steps of the Old Palace with the measured ease of a man whose errand was heavy but whose face must never confess it. The air had the thin, rinsed cleanness of early spring; night’s damp still clung in the joints of the stones, and the city, waking, was a choir of small noises—the slap of sandals on flagging, the creak of shutters, the cough of a mule in some courtyard, and, above all, the bells, whose bronze throats kept calling and calling, as if sound alone could hold Florence together.

He was bound for San Marco; yet he chose not the straight way, but a circuit by Santa Croce, where the people would be streaming out after the early sermon. It was a roundabout road, but it offered what he wanted: a crowd, already warmed by argument, and the thick hum of many voices that could be steered, as one steers a pot by turning the flame and letting the simmer do the work.

Savonarola’s voice had been silenced now—even in San Marco. The Signoria, hostile and harried, had obeyed a new papal letter, threatening Florence with an interdict if that “wretched worm” and “monstrous idol” were not forbidden to preach and sent to Rome to ask pardon. And when a man cannot be heard, the next best thing, for those who hunger for heat, is to hear him assaulted. In Santa Croce the Franciscan appointed for the Quaresimal sermons had offered to clinch his arguments by walking through fire with Fra Girolamo. Had not the Dominican prophesied that his doctrine would be proved by miracle at the fitting time? Here, then—said Santa Croce—was the fitting time. Let him walk into flame; if he came out unhurt, Heaven had set its seal; if he burned, his falsity would smoke in every nostril.

Savonarola, according to his habit, had taken no notice of these pulpit blows. But the challenger was Fra Francesco di Puglia—the very Franciscan who, at Prato the year before, had flung a similar gauntlet at Fra Domenico, the Prophet’s ardent follower, only to be called away while the heat was still only in words. Honest Fra Domenico, preaching Lenten sermons to the women in the Via del Cocomero, heard of this and, as a man leaps to snatch a knife from a child, took up the challenge himself. The people, who loved a short road to certainty, began to thicken with interest. But Savonarola, keenly alive to the dangers in the discussion itself, commanded Fra Domenico to withdraw and secede. The Franciscan professed himself content: he had not challenged any subaltern; he had challenged Fra Girolamo.

Since then the daily frenzy had slackened—until this morning.

When Tito entered the Piazza di Santa Croce, he found, as he had expected, a broad pour of people from the great church doors. The piazza received them like a basin takes a spill: they did not scatter at once, but eddied toward a particular spot near the entrance of the Franciscan monastery. There, fastened up by order of the Signoria, hung a large placard, its official hand bold enough to be read at a distance. Tito drifted with the current, threading the press with a careless leisure that deceived anyone who did not know the kind of patience a schemer cultivates: the patience of a cook watching a sauce that must not be hurried, though the whole feast depends on it.

Curiosity, however, was balked. The manuscript was chiefly in Latin—black letters with the air of authority, yet dumb to most of the mouths around it. Men who could shout a phrase of Scripture caught from a sermon, and who could spell their own names in a jumble of consonants, stood now with the irritating sensation that their neighbour might know more than they did. In the crowd the soundscape shifted: less laughter, more snappish questioning, the scrape of boots as men jostled for a better angle, the quick, impatient sucking of breath through teeth. Ignorance has its own noise.

“It’s the Frate’s doctrines that he’s to prove by being burned,” declared Goro, that large public character, wheezing his way to the forefront as if he were born for it. “The Signoria has taken it in hand, and the writing is to let us know. It’s what the Padre has been telling us about in his sermon.”

“Nay, Goro,” said a sleek shopkeeper, pitying him as one pities a man who salts his stew twice, “thou hast got thy legs into twisted hose there. The Frate has to prove his doctrines by not being burned. He is to walk through the fire, and come out on the other side sound and whole.”

“Yes, yes,” put in a young sculptor, white-streaked cap and tunic worn jauntily like a badge of work and youth. “But Fra Girolamo objects to walking through the fire. Being sound and whole already, he sees no reason to walk through the fire to come out in just the same condition. He leaves such odds and ends to Fra Domenico.”

“Then I say he flinches like a coward,” cried Goro. “Suffocation! that was what he did at the Carnival. He had us all in the Piazza to see the lightning strike him, and nothing came of it.”

“Stop that bleating,” said a tall shoemaker who had stepped in to catch part of the sermon, bunches of slippers slung over his shoulders like garlands of leather. Even his voice seemed tanned, toughened by work. “You are about as wise as a calf with water on its brain. The Frate will flinch from nothing. He’ll say nothing beforehand, perhaps, but when the moment comes he’ll walk through the fire without asking any grey-frock to keep him company. But I would give a shoestring to know what this Latin all is.”

“There’s so much of it,” muttered the shopkeeper, peering up as if the letters might yield by force. “Else I’m pretty good at guessing. Is there no scholar to be seen?”

Heads turned. In that turning, eyes caught on Tito approaching from behind.

“Here is one,” said the young sculptor, smiling and lifting his cap.

“It is the secretary of the Ten,” said the shopkeeper, and he too doffed—an uncommon respect from Florentines, who do not bend easily except to the very highest. But Tito’s splendour and grace exacted it as naturally as fine cloth asks to be touched. His black mantle, fastened with a gold fibula, lay on him like a regal garment; his ordinary black velvet cap seemed by some trick of bearing an exceptional head-dress. The hardening about his cheeks and mouth—the chief change since his coming to Florence—read, to a superficial glance, as added manliness.

He raised his cap at once.

“Thanks, my friend,” he said. “I merely wished, as you did, to see what is at the foot of this placard—ah, it is as I expected. I had been informed that the government permits any one who will to subscribe his name as a candidate to enter the fire—which is a liberality worthy of the magnificent Signoria—reserving, of course, the right to make a selection.”

He let the pause fall, tasting it, then went on with that cool, liquid mildness that compelled attention.

“And doubtless many believers will be eager to subscribe. For what is it to enter the fire to one whose faith is firm? A man is afraid of fire because he believes it will burn him; but if he believes the contrary—” He lifted his shoulders and left the sentence to complete itself in their minds. “For which reason I have never been one to disbelieve the Frate when he has said that he would enter the fire to prove his doctrine. For in his place, if you believed the fire would not burn you, which of you, my friends, would not enter it as readily as you would walk along the dry bed of the Mugnone?”

As he looked from face to face, something changed in several men—an eagerness that became suddenly cautious, like a dog invited to sniff something pungent and not sure whether it will please or sting. Once burning becomes practical, theories acquire a smell.

“Then, Messer Segretario,” said the young sculptor, “it seems to me Fra Francesco is the greater hero, for he offers to enter the fire for the truth, though he is sure the fire will burn him.”

“I do not deny it,” Tito answered, blandly. “But if it turns out that Fra Francesco is mistaken, he will have been burned for the wrong side, and the Church has never reckoned such victims martyrs. We must suspend our judgment until the trial has really taken place.”

“It is true,” said the shopkeeper, with subdued impatience. “But will you favour us by interpreting the Latin?”

“Assuredly.” Tito smiled, as if the request were a compliment he could not refuse. “It does but express the conclusions—the doctrines—which the Frate specially teaches, and which the trial by fire is to prove true or false. They are doubtless familiar to you. First, that Florence—”

“Let us have the Latin bit by bit, and then tell us what it means,” said the shoemaker. “Then we’ll know if you give the right meaning.”

“Yes, yes; that’s fair,” wheezed Goro.

“Willingly,” said Tito, as if he were beginning a recipe in a kitchen where all had opinions and few could read. “You will then judge if I give the right meaning. _Ecclesia Dei indiget renovatione_; that is, the Church of God needs purifying, or regenerating.”

“It is true,” came several voices at once, as if the words, though foreign, were seasoned with a familiar bitterness.

“That means, the priests ought to lead better lives,” said the shoemaker. “There needs no miracle to prove that. That’s what the Frate has always been saying.”

“_Flagellabitur_,” Tito went on, his finger moving as if he were slicing the text into portions. “That is, it will be scourged. _Renovabitur_: it will be purified. _Florentia quoque post flagellam renovabitur et prosperabitur_: Florence also, after the scourging, shall be purified and shall prosper.”

“That means we are to get Pisa again,” said the shopkeeper, swiftly translating prophecy into commerce.

“And get the wool from England as we used to do, I should hope,” said an elderly man in an old-fashioned berretta, who had been silent until now. “There’s been scourging enough with the sinking of the trade.”

At that moment a tall personage with a red feather issued from the convent door and threw Tito an indifferent glance. The crowd, with more timidity than respect, shrank to make a lane: Dolfo Spini. Tito tossed his becchetto carelessly over his left shoulder and turned back to his reading, as if a captain of the Compagnacci were no more than a gust of wind.

“_Infideles convertentur ad Christum_,” he continued. “That is, the infidels shall be converted to Christ.”

“Those are the Turks and the Moors,” said the shopkeeper, dispassionately. “Well, I’ve nothing to say against that.”

“_Haec autem omnia erunt temporibus nostris_: and all these things shall happen in our times.”

“Why, what use would they be else?” said Goro, pleased to find himself able to clap at something.

“_Excommunicato nuper lata contra Reverendum Patrem nostrum Fratrem Hieronymum nulla est_: the excommunication lately pronounced against our reverend father, Fra Girolamo, is null. _Non observantes eam non peccant_: those who disregard it are not committing a sin.”

“I shall know better what to say to that when we have had the Trial by Fire,” the shopkeeper answered, with the air of a man who will not buy a cheese until he has cut it.

“Which doubtless will clear up everything,” said Tito, and in his voice the phrase could be taken as reverence or ridicule, as the hearer pleased. “That is all the Latin—all the conclusions that are to be proved true or false by the trial. The rest you can perceive is simply a proclamation of the Signoria in good Tuscan, calling on such as are eager to walk through the fire, to come to the Palazzo and subscribe their names. Can I serve you further? If not—”

He raised his cap and bent slightly. The movement was so easy it looked not like strategy but like nature. Then he slipped away, quickening his pace once the piazza noises fell behind him. The bells of Santa Croce were still pulsing, but now there were quieter sounds in the side streets: a woman shaking a cloth from an upper window, the soft clink of a pail chain, the whisper of broom on stone—domestic rhythms that made public miracles seem, for an instant, like theatre set against the daily cooking of lives.

After two or three turnings he paused before a door in a quiet street and gave a light, peculiar knock. It was opened by a young woman. He chucked her under the chin as he asked if the Padrone was within, and then, without further ceremony, passed through another door standing ajar.

He entered a handsome but untidy room where Dolfo Spini sat playing with a fine stag-hound. The creature alternately snuffed at a basket of pups and licked Spini’s hands with that affectionate disregard of her master’s morals which some men find among the most agreeable attributes of her sex. Spini merely looked up as Tito came in, but continued his play, out of that obstinate persistence in an irrelevant action by which slow-witted sensual people thwart their own purposes.

Tito waited, patient as a man who knows that time, like dough, can be made to rise by warmth and left alone.

“A handsome _bracca_ that,” he said quietly, standing with his thumbs in his belt. Presently he added, in that mild tone that nevertheless drew the ear as surely as a knife draws the eye, “When you have finished such caresses as cannot possibly be deferred, my Dolfo, we will talk of business, if you please. My time—which I could wish to be eternity at your service—is not entirely my own this morning.”

“Down, Mischief, down!” Spini snarled suddenly, shoving the dog aside. “Malediction!” He rose and came close, laying a heavy hand on Tito’s shoulder. “I hope your sharp wits see all the ins and outs of this business, my fine necromancer, for it seems to me no clearer than the bottom of a sack.”

“What is your difficulty, my cavalier?”

“These accursed Frati Minori at Santa Croce. They are drawing back now. Fra Francesco himself seems afraid of sticking to his challenge. He talks of the Prophet using magic to get up a false miracle—thinks he himself might be dragged into the fire and burned, and the Prophet might come out whole by magic, and the Church be none the better. And then, after all our talking, there’s not so much as a blessed lay brother who will offer himself to pair with that pious sheep Fra Domenico.”

“It is the peculiar stupidity of the tonsured skull,” said Tito, “that prevents them from seeing how little consequence it is whether they are burned or not. Have you sworn well to them that they shall be in no danger of entering the fire?”

“No,” said Spini, blinking, “because one of them will be obliged to go in with Fra Domenico, who thinks it a thousand years till the fagots are ready.”

“Not at all.” Tito’s voice was gentle, but it laid out the steps as if he were setting a board and placing each dish exactly where it must stand. “Fra Domenico himself is not likely to go in. I have told you before—only your powerful mind is not to be impressed without more repetition than suffices for the vulgar—I have told you that now you have got the Signoria to take up this affair and prevent it from being hushed up by Fra Girolamo, nothing is necessary but that on a given day the fuel should be prepared in the Piazza, and the people got together with the expectation of seeing something prodigious. If, after that, the Prophet quits the Piazza without any appearance of a miracle on his side, he is ruined with the people. They will be ready to pelt him out of the city. The Signoria will find it easy to banish him from the territory, and his Holiness may do as he likes with him. Therefore, my Alcibiades, swear to the Franciscans that their grey-frocks shall not come within singeing distance of the fire.”

Spini rubbed the back of his head with one hand and tapped his sword against his leg with the other, as if the clang might drive sense through bone.

“But,” he said at last, “unless we fall on him in the Piazza when the people are in a rage, and make an end of him and his lies then and there, Valori and the Salviati and the Albizzi will take up arms and raise a fight for him. I know that was talked of when there was the hubbub on Ascension Sunday. And the people may turn round again: there may be a story raised of the French king coming again, or some other cursed chance in the hypocrite’s favour. The city will never be safe till he’s out of it.”

“He will be out of it before long,” said Tito, “without your giving yourself any further trouble than this little comedy of the Trial by Fire. The wine and the sun will make vinegar without any shouting to help them, as your Florentine sages would say. You will have the satisfaction of delivering your city from an incubus by an able stratagem, instead of risking blunders with sword-thrusts.”

“But suppose he did get magic and the devil to help him, and walk through the fire after all?” Spini’s mouth twisted into a grimace meant to disguise a certain shyness, as if he were reluctant to let superstition be heard in daylight. “How do you know there’s nothing in those things? Plenty of scholars believe in them, and this Frate is bad enough for anything.”

“Oh, of course there are such things,” said Tito, with a shrug, as if granting the point cost him nothing. “But I have particular reasons for knowing that the Frate is not on such terms with the devil as can give him any confidence in this affair. The only magic he relies on is his own ability.”

“Ability!” Spini scoffed. “Do you call it ability to be setting Florence at loggerheads with the Pope and all the powers of Italy—all to keep beckoning at the French king who never comes? You may call him able, but I call him a hypocrite who wants to be master of everybody and get himself made Pope.”

“You judge with your usual penetration, my captain,” said Tito, and the compliment slid in like oil, making the hard thought shine. “But our opinions do not clash. The Frate, wanting to be master, and to carry out his projects against the Pope, requires the lever of a foreign power, and requires Florence as a fulcrum. I used to think him a narrow-minded bigot, but now I think him a shrewd ambitious man who knows what he is aiming at, and directs his aim as skilfully as you direct a ball when you are playing at _maglio_.”

“Yes, yes,” said Spini, mollified, even pleased. “I can aim a ball.”

“It is true,” Tito returned, with bland gravity. “And I should not have troubled you with my trivial remark on the Frate’s ability, but that you may see how this will heighten the credit of your success against him at Rome and at Milan, which is sure to serve you in good stead when the city comes to change its policy.”

“Well, thou art a good little demon, and shalt have good pay,” Spini said, patronisingly; and it seemed only natural to him that Tito should smile with gratification as he began—

“Of course, any advantage to me depends entirely on your—”

“We shall have our supper at my palace to-night,” Spini broke in, with a significant nod and an affectionate pat on Tito’s shoulder, “and I shall expound the new scheme to them all.”

“Pardon, my magnificent patron,” said Tito. “The scheme has been the same from the first—it has never varied except in your memory. Are you sure you have fast hold of it now?”

Spini rehearsed it, slowly, with the air of a man repeating a charm.

“One thing more,” he said, as Tito turned to go. “There is that sharp-nosed notary, Ser Ceccone. He has been handy of late. Tell me—you who can see a man wink when you’re behind him—do you think I may go on making use of him?”

Tito dared not say No. He knew Spini too well to trust him with advice when Spini’s vanity and self-interest were not already engaged in concealing the adviser.

“Doubtless,” he answered promptly. “I have nothing to say against Ceccone.”

Yet the mention pricked him—an abrupt, passing twinge, like a fishbone caught in a mouthful that was meant to be smoothly enjoyed. Tito’s nature was keenly alive to circumstances that might be turned against him; his memory kept a pantry of such possibilities, always stocked, always ready for sudden hunger. He did not forget that October morning more than a year ago when Romola had appeared at the door of Nello’s shop and compelled him, under her direct gaze, to declare his certainty that Fra Girolamo was not going outside the gates. Ser Ceccone had witnessed that scene. And Tito had long felt, without knowing why, that the notary disliked him.

Lately, since a turn in affairs, that dislike had become more dangerous. After being implicated in Medicean plots and finding it advisable to retire into the country, Ser Ceccone had reappeared in the city, attached himself to the Arrabbiati, and cultivated Dolfo Spini’s patronage. Spini, among intimates, loved confidential narratives of his own doings; and if the notary’s power of combination were sharpened by enmity, he might gather knowledge that could be used against Tito with unpleasant effect.

It would be pitiable—to be balked in well-conducted schemes by an insignificant notary; to be lamed by the sting of an insect offended unawares. “But,” Tito told himself, as he went his way again into the streets where the day’s noises had risen—hammer on metal, vendor’s cry, the shuffle of many feet—“the man’s dislike can be nothing deeper than the ill-humour of a dinnerless dog. I shall conquer it if I can make him prosperous.” And he had been glad of the opportunity that had presented itself to provide the notary with a temporary post as an extra _cancelliere_ under the Ten, believing that with this sop and the expectation of more, the waspish cur must be cured of biting.

But perfect scheming demands omniscience. The envy that fed Ser Ceccone’s spite had been sharpened into hatred by causes Tito did not know.

That evening when Tito, returning from his critical audience with the Special Council, had brushed past Ser Ceccone on the stairs, the notary—newly returned from Pistoja and just learning of the conspirators’ arrest—had been on an errand that bore a humble resemblance to Tito’s. He too, without giving up a show of popular zeal, had put himself into the Medicean lottery. He too had been privy to the unexecuted plot, willing to tell what he knew—only he knew much less to tell. He too would have gone on treacherous errands, but a more eligible agent had forestalled him.

His propositions were received coldly. The council, he was told, already possessed what was needed; and since he had been thus busy in sedition, it would be well for him to retire out of the way of mischief, otherwise the government might be obliged to take note of him. Ser Ceccone wanted no evidence to attribute his failure to Tito; his spite was bitterer because the nature of the case compelled him to silence.

Nor was that the whole of his grudge. On issuing from his hiding-place and attaching himself to the Arrabbiati, he had earned some pay as a spy reporting Florentine affairs to the Milanese court. But the pay had been small, despite his pains to write full letters; and lately he had been told that his news was seldom more than a late and imperfect edition of what was known already. Ser Ceccone had no positive knowledge that Tito had an underhand connection with the Arrabbiati and the Court of Milan—but he had a suspicion, and he chewed it with as strong a savour as if it were certainty, rolling it in his mind the way a man rolls a harsh herb on his tongue, not for pleasure but because the bitterness itself feels like power.

Tito’s coming to San Marco had been asked for and agreed to; no sudden knock in the night, no furtive entry as if he carried contraband. Fra Niccolò, the Prior’s secretary, met him and led him upward by the narrow spiral stair whose worn stone held the chill of centuries and the faint smell of damp wool and extinguished lamp-wick. Above, the long passages stretched, quiet as a cloistered stomach between meals: doors shut, cells emptied by the hour of relaxation, the house breathing in a hush broken only by sandals scuffing and a distant cough that fell and was swallowed.

Here and there Fra Angelico’s frescoes flashed on the whitewashed walls—Madonna and Child, crowns and lilies—so tender and sudden that they seemed like color seen after fasting, a sweetness on the tongue of the eye. But most of what the narrow windows admitted fell on bare things: a hard pallet, a crucifix, a shelf, a jug—objects plain as black bread and as necessary.

At the end of one corridor, beyond an antechamber where the Prior often wrote and received, a door stood half-open. The long blade of daylight from a high window cut across the floor and struck the back of a kneeling figure in the white Dominican tunic and scapulary. He might have been any friar, bending to confess trivial rebellions—an unchaste thought while chanting, a mean spark of pleasure at another man’s blotched illumination—any soul busy with the ordinary ladder of prayer and obedience.

But under that white cloth beat a consciousness that would have startled the most seasoned confessor. The man kneeling was Savonarola; and though Latin prayer moved on his lips, he was not praying. He had thrown himself down as one puts a hand to water when heat and dust burn—seeking calm by the accustomed act—yet the mind would not drink. While his palms pressed his face and his mouth shaped, “Cor mundum crea in me,” his inward ear was full of other sounds: the taunts of enemies, the coarse laughter of those who made a snare out of piety, the thunder of a Piazza waiting to be fed with spectacle.

Worse than his enemies were his friends. That morning he had felt anew how his own followers, as greedily as the Arrabbiati, urged the Trial by Fire. They wanted, and almost expected, that he—he himself—should at last take the challenge and draw down the long-promised miracle like rain on a thirsty harvest. Had he not said God would declare Himself at the fitting time? To plain Florentines hungry to settle party quarrels, no time could be more fitting than now. Fra Domenico’s ardor to walk through flame was a bright omen to them, a whiff of incense before the miracle; but Savonarola knew—felt like a knife at the roots of his tongue—that their secret longing for his own entry into the fire was not quieted by any reasons he gave for refusing.

And yet he could not satisfy them. He could not even fully satisfy himself.

He had not lied when he spoke of divine attestation; he could believe in a miracle that lay at a distance, veiled by the strong reasons his mind could marshal for its coming; he could believe more easily still in inward miracles—in prophetic heat, in sudden illuminations that struck his thought with a certainty like a bell-note. But this particular miracle—the passage of a human body through fire unhurt—pressed its details against his imagination until belief buckled. It was one thing to assent in doctrine; it was another to picture the stacked faggots, the heat shivering the air, the hair singeing, the flesh blistering. His nature was a fierce mixture: a sensibility that could flood an idea with ecstasy, and—alternating with it—a practical judgment sharpened to the hard edges of outward fact. Here the practical side was roused to cruelty by his physical quickness of nerve: he knew pain too well to let the mind treat it as a mere word.

Practical belief is not the same as professed opinion. A man may accept in theory that iron should not burn him and still draw back from it; the nerves argue faster than syllogisms. And with Savonarola, when the Trial by Fire was made immediate, he could not believe—could not bring himself, even for a moment, to believe—that any man would walk through those flames untouched. More bitter still: he could not believe that even if he resolved to offer himself, he would not shrink at the last step, when the heat struck the face like a door flung open into an oven.

But Florence did not love fine distinctions. It has always seemed to the common run of men a proof of vigor to find moral knots easy, and to judge conduct by blunt alternatives. What would seem plainer than that a man who spoke of a miracle, yet drew back from the test proposed, had spoken without belief? Were not Fra Domenico and Fra Mariano, and scores of Piagnoni, eager to enter the fire? If their courage was greater, was it not because their faith was greater?

Savonarola could not have explained himself even to friends who loved him, even if he had been able to set his own heart’s motions into clear speech. Naked feelings hasten to dress themselves in ready-made propositions. To tell the truth about what passes within, sincerity is not enough; one needs an understanding as merciless as a knife and as patient as a cook who keeps tasting until the seasoning is exact.

His lips moved; his ears no longer heard the Latin. Within him, arguments rose and arranged themselves as if for a tribunal.

“To appeal to Heaven by rashly taking a challenge set as a snare by ignoble foes would be to tempt God, and the appeal would not be answered. Let the Pope’s legate come; let the ambassadors of all the great powers come and pledge that a General Council, reform, the cleansing of the Church—let all this hang on the miracle, and I will enter the flames, trusting God will not withhold His seal from a work so vast. Until then I must not leap from the chariot because every loud braggart calls. Fra Domenico’s zeal may be a sign of vocation, a pledge that the miracle—”

But when he forced his mind close to the threatened scene in the Piazza, the imagination would not look on it from a safe distance. It felt it. The thought of fire ran along his nerves into his fingertips, and belief recoiled like skin from heat. The miracle could not be. No—the trial itself must be hindered; he was warranted in doing all he could to stop it.

And yet: the preparations might go on, the wood might be piled, the people might gather, the solemnities might be performed. He could no longer resist without bringing dishonor on himself—yes, and therefore, as he told himself with that swift sliding from “me” to “the cause of God,” dishonor on the work he led. But the Franciscan would not truly mean to enter; while he hung back there would be means to prevent Fra Domenico’s entrance. Or, if the worst came, Fra Domenico could carry the consecrated Host, the Mystery, in his hand; and with that, perhaps, the natural effects of fire might be stayed. Or—more likely—this demand would be refused, and refusal might be the final obstacle.

But such intentions could not be spoken aloud. Outwardly he must seem frank, waiting, trusting, as if his inward world matched his public posture. That cleft between reality and seeming was not the Christian simplicity he had hungered for in youth and preached as the fruit of divine life. Yet who, when cheeks burn and shouts ring, remembers the morning’s cool yearnings and knows he has not belied them?

“O God,” his mind cried, though his lips were now silent, “it is for the people—because they are blind—because their faith hangs on me. If I cast myself in ashes, who will lift the standard? Have I not been led by a way I knew not to the work that lies before me?”

The conflict did not end; it only shifted its weight. In place of the immediate dread, there rose again the intoxication of vast results—Europe listening, thrones moved, corruption judged. In that glow the sharpness of present danger blurred, and he remained kneeling, still as a statue, while within him the future sounded like distant trumpets.

Then the knock came—measured, expected.

Savonarola drew his mantle about him as was his custom when he received visitors, and stepped out from the inner cell. Whatever tempest had been beating inside, his face met the world with the command of one who is used to making others feel his will through speech. He looked at Tito with a self-possession that might have come from settled resolution rather than from wrestling.

Tito did not kneel. He made only a deep, perfectly calculated reverence—deference without abasement—which Savonarola received without blessing or sacerdotal phrase. He motioned Tito to sit, and spoke at once.

“Your business is something of weight, my son, that could not be conveyed through others?”

“Assuredly, father—else I should not have presumed to ask it. I will not waste your time with a proem. Messer Domenico Mazzinghi let fall a remark from which I gathered you might wish to use the next special courier the Ten send to France. I entreat you to pardon my officiousness; but Messer Domenico is away at his villa, and a courier carrying important letters is to depart for Lyons at daybreak to-morrow.”

Savonarola’s face, trained to obedience like a disciplined troop, did not alter in any gross way. Men of force learn to hold their features as they hold their tongue. But his eyes—under strong inward stimulus—betrayed him: they widened, brightened, took on a flash no will could wholly suppress. He looked steadily at Tito and did not answer at once, as if weighing whether this information served a purpose.

Tito’s glance was one of those that never seems to observe and misses little. He had expected that very dilation and light, having noted it before. The moment he saw it, he bent his attention to a small thing: he adjusted the gold fibula at his mantle as if it had slipped—an air of patient waiting, the modesty of a man who had no desire to pierce the Prior’s mind.

In truth Savonarola had expected this intimation from Domenico Mazzinghi, a disciple among the Ten whom he had already used to send a private letter to the Florentine ambassador in France—preparing the way for a letter to the French king, now lying ready in the desk near at hand. It called on the king to aid in summoning a General Council to reform the Church and begin by deposing Pope Alexander—no rightful Pope, but a vicious unbeliever, raised by corruption and ruling by simony. Tito did not know the contents; yet his subtle talent for construction, guided by hints and hopes, had led him to guess enough to set his desire on intercepting what was to go.

“It is true, my son,” Savonarola said at last, with guarded quiet. “I have letters I would gladly send by safe conveyance under cover to our ambassador. Our community has affairs in France—you know—we are responsible, among other things, for a debt to that singularly wise Frenchman, Signor Philippe de Comines, for the Medici library we purchased.
