But I think Messer Domenico may return before evening, and I shall have more time to prepare if I wait to deposit the letters in his hands.”

“Assuredly, reverend father,” Tito replied, smooth as poured oil, “that might be better on all grounds except one: if anything should hinder Messer Domenico’s return, the despatch of the letters would require either my coming to San Marco again at a late hour, or your sending them by Fra Niccolò. And I know you wish to guard against false inferences that might be drawn from too frequent communication between yourself and any officer of the government.”

He threw the difficulty out gently, like a man laying a cloth on a table to see if it would lie flat. And he felt that the more reluctance the Frate showed, the more likely his conjecture was right.

Savonarola did not answer. His mouth kept its firmness; but a faint color rose under the skin, the suppressed excitement mounting. This, then, would be the critical moment—the moment of letting that letter pass out of his hands.

“It is most probable Messer Domenico will return in time,” Tito said, as if the matter were settled. He rose. “With your permission, father, I will take my leave. I would not trespass on your time now that my errand is done. But as I may not be favored with another interview, I venture to confide to you—what is not yet known to others except to the magnificent Ten—that I contemplate resigning my secretaryship and leaving Florence shortly. Am I presuming too much on your interest in what relates chiefly to myself?”

“Speak on, my son,” Savonarola said. “I desire to know your prospects.”

“I find I have mistaken my vocation in forsaking pure letters, for which I was trained. The politics of Florence are worthy to occupy the greatest mind—to occupy yours—when a man can execute his own ideas. But when, like me, he can only be the instrument of changing schemes, he needs the minor attachments of a born Florentine. Also, my wife’s unhappy alienation from a Florentine residence since the painful events of August naturally influences me. I wish to join her.”

Savonarola inclined his head with approval; the domestic note, the mention of a wife estranged and sorrowing, touched his pastoral habit.

“I intend, then, soon to leave Florence, visit the chief courts of Europe, and widen my acquaintance with men of letters in the universities. I shall go first to Hungary, where scholars are welcome; and I shall probably start in a week or ten days. I have not concealed from you, father, that I am no religious enthusiast; I have not my wife’s ardor. But religious enthusiasm is not necessary, as I conceive, in order to appreciate the grandeur and justice of your views concerning the government of nations and the Church. If you condescend to entrust me with any commission that will further the relations you wish to establish, I shall feel honored. May I now take my leave?”

“Stay, my son,” said Savonarola. “When you depart I will send a letter to your wife, whose spiritual welfare I would fain be assured of—for she left me in anger. And as for the letters to France—such as I have ready—”

He rose and turned to the desk as he spoke. He drew out a letter addressed in his own minute, exquisite hand—handwriting that, like the delicate marginalia in his Bibles, seemed made for patient truth rather than for haste. He slipped it within a larger sheet and sealed it.

“Pardon me, father,” Tito said quickly, before the Frate could offer it, “unless it were your decided wish, I would rather not incur the responsibility of carrying the letter away. Messer Domenico Mazzinghi will doubtless return; or if not, Fra Niccolò can bring it to me at the second hour of the evening, when I shall place the other despatches in the courier’s hands.”

“At present, my son,” Savonarola answered, waving aside the point, “I wish you to address this packet to our ambassador in your own hand, which is preferable to my secretary’s.”

Tito sat again and wrote the address. While he wrote, Savonarola stood with folded arms; the color in his face rose higher, and at last his lip quivered—an involuntary betrayal, as if the sealed paper in his presence were still alive and resisting separation.

Tito rose, the packet in hand, and was moving away when Savonarola spoke abruptly, decision cutting through the hesitation that had made his silence heavy.

“Take it, my son. There is no use in waiting. It does not please me that Fra Niccolò should have needless errands to the Palazzo.”

As Tito received the letter, Savonarola remained standing in a suppressed excitement that seemed to forbid further words. Passionate natures like his cast a subtle influence—when they are absent-minded with inward strain, the very air grows still, as if sound itself were held back. Tito made a deep reverence and went out, the letter hidden under his mantle.

The packet was duly delivered to the courier, and so carried out of Florence. But before that happened, another messenger—quietly hired by Tito—had already borne information in cipher, sent by relays to the armed agents of Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan, who watched the borders for this very purpose: to intercept such despatches as they could seize when they crossed into Milanese reach.

Little more than a week had passed, and yet the Piazza della Signoria, which had lately smoked with the sweet, choking incense of vanities, now prepared a stranger feast for the eyes and—so men joked with their empty bellies—for the nose. It was the seventh of April. By mid-day the great square was packed as if Florence meant to press its whole weight upon one moment and force Heaven to answer.

From early morning the city had been crawling up its own stone skin. Men wedged themselves where no human body was meant to rest: perched on iron rods that bit into the thighs, clung to slender pillars with arms and legs locked like vines, sat astride the rough shoulders of carved saints above doorways, found a palm’s breadth of seat on an architrave and held by iron rings and staples hammered into old masonry. They had come to see a Miracle, and scraped flesh or numbed feet seemed a cheap price. Most lives are spent hearing of wonders and believing them in the dim way one believes in a distant storm. To-day Florence would watch a wonder blaze in the open, as plainly as a cook watches his oil take heat. At the very least—so the crowd reasoned with that crude logic that makes spectacle into proof—they would see half a miracle: if the monk did not walk whole out of the flames, they would see him step in, and infer he burned somewhere between.

There were reasons to trust that something would be done. Before their very eyes lay the long platform, eight feet broad and twenty yards long, set slantwise across the Piazza like a serving-board for a terrible banquet. On it was piled a grove of fuel: thick boughs of dry oak laid as a foundation—seasoned wood that would catch greedily—then crackling thorns, and above them tow and rags soaked with oil, the sort used for fine flaming in Florentine illuminations, but here prepared to lick living flesh. Even at a distance, one could smell the promise in it: the resinous dryness of oak, the sharp, green-bitter tang of thorn, the rancid slick of old oil on cloth. It began at the corner of the marble terrace before the Old Palace, close to Marzocco, the stone lion, whose worn face frowned down the length of that oblique pyre as if already offended by the smoke it expected.

And there were men enough to prove the city meant business. Five hundred hired soldiers of the Signoria stood before the palace; five hundred Compagnacci, under Dolfo Spini, were massed far off on the opposite side; and three hundred armed citizens of another temper, led by Marco Salviati—Savonarola’s friend—kept station in front of Orgagna’s Loggia. Under that Loggia the Franciscans and Dominicans would stand, each with his champion, like two kitchens sworn to prove whose bread had God’s blessing.

High dignities were involved, money spent, labour measured out; the platform itself declared, with its carpentered straightness and its heaped tinder, that no one intended an anticlimax. If the monks burned, that too would be “God speaking,” and many were ready to hear Him say—plainly, like a verdict shouted over a market stall—that Fra Girolamo was no prophet. Mid-day was close, and half the Loggia already had its occupants: on the side towards the Palace, grey mantles filled the space—Franciscans who had entered and taken their places in silence. The other half, boarded off, held only a small altar, bare as a clean board waiting for bread.

Then from the farther side of the Piazza rose chanting—two hundred voices swelling into one heavy wave. The sound rolled along the stone façades and up to the roofs where men crouched, and it changed the air as surely as a drum changes marching feet. Many were satisfied, if not with the chant itself, at least with what it meant: the Dominicans were coming.

“Let God arise, and let His enemies be scattered.” The prayer, shouted and repeated, struck some ears—those who were not already intoxicated by party—as something less like humble petition than like a cook’s loud boasting over a dish not yet tasted. At the head of the procession walked Fra Domenico, his simple mind lifted into a sincere exaltation, his intention honest and terrible: to enter the flames for the glory of God and of Fra Girolamo. He wore a flame-coloured velvet cope that caught every eye the way a bright pepper catches the tongue. Cross in hand, he advanced as if he had already felt the heat and found it sweet.

Behind him came Savonarola, not in splendour but in the white vestment of a priest, carrying in both hands a vessel that held the consecrated Host. He too chanted loudly. He too looked firm; and under the pressing gaze of a whole Piazza—anxiety here, curiosity there, malice everywhere like grit between teeth—there was a hard brightening in his face, an energy that answered scrutiny as flint answers steel.

For we are made so, almost all of us, that the false seeming we dread in solitude—the part we have rehearsed with inward shrinking because necessity drives us—will take hold of our muscles and our voice, and when expectant eyes and ears are upon us it feels, for that hour, like the easiest thing in the world. And the stimulus upon Savonarola that day cannot be weighed by ordinary experience. Perhaps no man has ruled the hearts of others without a need to dominate; and that need grows more imperious when life has so tangled Self with a purpose not selfish that they are hard to separate even in conscience. So on that day, the doubleness that tempts every public career—priest, orator, statesman—stood more sharply in Savonarola’s own sense as an acted part than ever before. He was not struggling against the prospect of martyrdom; he was struggling against the prospect of ruin. Therefore he looked and moved as if confidence filled him, while foreboding lay on his heart with the dead weight of lead.

That heaviness was not only for the probable issue of the trial. Another event, already past, had set a different mind into sunny satisfaction—a mind looking down at the worn prophet from a window of the Old Palace. Two evenings earlier word had come that the Florentine courier of the Ten had been arrested and robbed of his despatches. Savonarola’s letter, so rashly trusted to travelling hands, was already with the Duke of Milan, and would soon be in the Pope’s—adding fuel to rage and a new colour of justification to extreme measures.

Tito Melema felt no malignity in his satisfaction. It was the mild, cool self-gratulation of a man who has won a game requiring hypotheses and finesse, not the hot triumph that shakes the blood. This bundle of desire and contrivance called human nature, moulded into a plain-faced Frate Predicatore with his high nose and heavy under lip, was not a pathetic object to a brilliant scholar who congratulated himself on understanding everything. Still, Tito admitted to himself, Fra Girolamo was immensely clever: he mingled absurd superstition—or fabrication—with notions about government that were not babble, and he could keep secrets. Tito bore him no more spite than he bore Saint Dominic. Indeed, Fra Girolamo’s existence had been useful—one rung in a ladder from which Tito meant presently to leap to a smooth footing far more to his taste. Everything was now arranged for that leap: let one more sun rise and set, and he hoped to be gone from Florence. He had been industrious enough to feel himself at leisure to enjoy to-day’s comedy—a comedy that thick-headed Dolfo Spini could never have staged without him.

The chanting did not cease; it grew into a deafening roar as the Piagnoni throughout the Piazza took it up, lifting their little red crosses like the badge of a guild. Sound became the day’s weather: it pressed on the skull, it filled the chest, it made men shout who had not meant to open their mouths. The good Fra Domenico in flame-colour knelt at the altar where the Sacrament had been set, waiting his summons. On the Franciscan side there was no chant, no bright colour—only grey and silence, a quiet so tense it seemed like the moment in a kitchen when hands pause because the sauce is about to turn.

Yet the silence hid its own fear. Pale Franciscan faces looked uneasily over the boarding toward that flame-coloured cope. It had an evil look; it might be enchanted. A monk might walk out of fire untouched and still be the devil’s trick. The crowd’s hunger for certainty was like hunger for bread: it made them imagine smell and taste before anything was served.

Now there was passing to and fro between the Loggia and the marble terrace of the Palazzo. The roar slackened as attention sharpened. From far vantage points it was hard to see whether the pyre had been kindled; in the distance, even fire can look like sunlight on oiled cloth. But the new movement did not begin the miracle; it delayed it. Dignified Florentines appointed as moderators went in and out of the Palace; debate thickened with the Franciscans.

At last it seemed Fra Domenico was being fetched toward the Palace. His flame-coloured cope disappeared within. Then another Dominican was taken away. And still the Loggia looked as it had: Fra Girolamo in white, standing in the same place; the fuel waiting, the air chilled by clouds gathering as if Heaven itself were drawing a lid over the day.

When Fra Domenico came out again, he was changed. He had exchanged all his clothes with another brother, and two Franciscans guarded him on either flank—as if enchantment were a scent that might cling to velvet and travel—lest, coming near Savonarola, he should be bewitched anew. From far off, perched men shifted, their cramped limbs briefly forgotten.

“Ah,” the spectators reasoned, “Fra Domenico will not enter. It is Fra Girolamo who will offer himself after all. We shall see him move, and if he comes out, we shall have a fine view.”

But Savonarola did not move toward the platform. He moved only as men move when they speak: the small gestures that match syllables. His voice—bold, firm, with an edge of ironic remonstrance, like Elijah addressing the priests of Baal—demanded an end to these petty delays. Yet speech is the most irritating argument to those out of hearing, pinched by hunger and cold. They had been standing since dawn; their mouths were dry; their ears were full of other men’s breath and murmured impatience. What need for words? If the miracle did not begin, whose fault could it be but Fra Girolamo’s—he who had been forward enough with challenge when no fuel lay in sight?

Still more movement, more slow and invisible dispute. The afternoon seemed to slip faster because the light changed: clouds gathered, dulling the colours of stone and cloth, and sending a chill through bodies already weary. The crowd began to feel the platform less as a promise than as an insult—like a table set lavishly and then withheld.

Now the objection was the crucifix. Fra Domenico wished to carry it into the fire, and the Franciscans would not allow such profanation. After some resistance Savonarola yielded—another concession he could show like a coin to those who counted such things. But immediately he placed in Fra Domenico’s hands the vessel holding the consecrated Host. In the back of his mind hovered the possibility that the sacred presence might, in extremity, avert fire’s ordinary appetite; but he counted more on a different outcome than on any physical marvel. Taking up the Host, he said quietly, as if this had been understood from the first:

“Since they are not willing that you should enter with the crucifix, my brother, enter simply with the Sacrament.”

A new horror ran through the Franciscans, audible even without words—the quickened shuffling, the intake of many breaths. Savonarola’s firmness only hardened.

It was impious presumption, the Franciscans insisted, to carry the Sacrament into the fire. If it were burned, scandal would spread among the weak and ignorant like sourness through milk.

“Not at all,” came the answer: even if it were burned, only the Accidents would be consumed; the Substance would remain.

Here was a question that could be argued until sunset and still spring back elastic as before. And because it was a preliminary question, no one could settle it simply by proceeding to the trial. All that was needed to paralyse the day was that both sides remain firm: Franciscans refusing to permit the Host in the fire, and Fra Domenico refusing to enter without it.

Meanwhile the clouds lowered; the air grew colder. The chanting, tiresome as it had been, was missed when it ceased and gave way to argument that could not be heard. In its place rose a confused talk from all parts of the Piazza, the loosening sound of expectation unravelling. It suggested, more irritatingly than any single shout, that nothing decisive would come—that the whole day would spoil like a dish neglected between hearth and table.

Then, here and there, sharp cries dropped into the murmur like stones into water, and other voices answered, until scorn rose by degrees.

“Light the fire and drive them in!”

“Let us have a smell of roast—we want our dinner!”

“Come, Prophet—shall anything happen before twenty-four hours are over?”

“Yes, yes—what’s your last vision?”

“Oh, he’s got a dozen in his inside; they’re the small change for a miracle!”

“Ola, Frate! Never mind wasting the fuel!”

The same going and coming between Loggia and Palace continued, slow and unintelligible to the multitude, like insects touching antennae and retreating with no apparent result. But the crowd did not need to hear words to invent meaning. Fra Girolamo was constantly speaking: therefore he was the hindrance. Everybody was appealing to him: therefore he was hanging back.

Soon individual shouts drowned into an uproar—not only voices, but clashing metal and trampling feet. The irritated suggestions of the people stirred old impulses in Dolfo Spini and his Compagnacci. Here, they thought, was a chance to end Florentine difficulties by taking the arch-hypocrite himself. Their armed men surged toward the Loggia, thrusting the crowd aside or driving them against the hired soldiers before the Palace.

At that movement all else paused—monks and magistrates alike—in a palpitating watch. The Loggia, however, was well guarded by Salviati’s band, and the Signoria’s soldiers helped beat back the rush. The trampling and shouting rolled backward again toward the Tetto de’ Pisani.

And then the heavens darkened as if in answer—not with fire, but with water. The scattered drops that had been felt like cold fingers became a sheet of rain, thickening rapidly, drumming on helmets, on bare heads, on the wooden platform, soaking the tow and rags, running in streams off the boards. It struck stone and cloth with a loud, unrelenting hiss; it flattened banners and mantles; it turned dust to paste underfoot. The whole Piazza smelled suddenly of wet wood and damp wool, of oil being denied its flame, of human breath trapped under rain-cooled air. Men who had fancied the savour of roasting now swallowed rainwater and bile. Disgust and rage, having no outlet, were driven inward to ferment in the damp darkness.

Everybody knew then the Trial by Fire would not happen. The Signoria could be glad of the rain; it was an excuse no one could dispute, better than any pretext, for ordering both parties home. It was the issue Savonarola had expected and, in one sense, desired; yet “glad” was a poor word for what entered him as that rain fell. The demand that he enter the fire ended; but with the same irresistible certainty with which cold wet took possession of his body, he knew his enemies’ design was fulfilled and his honour not saved. He would have to make his way back to San Marco through an enraged crowd. Hearts that once would have defended him with their lives would turn away or turn upon him.

When the rain slackened and ceased, he asked the Signoria for a guard, and it was granted. Had he said he was willing to die for the work of his life? He had not lied. But to die in dishonour—held up to scorn as a hypocrite, a false prophet—that, in his inward sense, was not martyrdom.

“O God! that is not martyrdom,” his soul cried within him. “It is the blotting out of a life that has been a protest against wrong. Let me die because of the worth that is in me, not because of my weakness.”

Light broke through the clouds as he left the Loggia with the Sacrament in his hand, guarded as he went, walking as he had come. But there was no glory in that light—no smile. It was only the patient, impartial light that shines on, justifying or condemning by revealing, slowly, the ripening history of all things. No blessing met his ears, no tone of pity—only taunts and threats, voices made hoarse by wet and disappointment. He knew it for a foretaste of bitterness; yet under moral attack his courage rose. He showed no sign of dismay.

From the window of the Old Palace, Tito watched him descend the steps.

“Well parried, Frate!” Tito said, as Savonarola passed beneath. “But I fear your career at Florence is ended. What say you, my Niccolò?”

“It is a pity his falsehoods were not all of a wise sort,” said Macchiavelli, with a melancholy shrug. “With the times so much on his side as they are about Church affairs, he might have done something great.”

Palm Sunday had come again—Olive Sunday, as the Valdarno folk called it when the trees outside the walls were already silvering with new leaf and the presses were being scrubbed in readiness for another year’s oil. The rain of yesterday had washed the stones clean, so that Florence woke under a sky that looked freshly unsealed, and the morning light lay on roof-tiles and river like a thin, clear broth poured over everything, drawing out every savor.

In San Marco the air itself seemed changed—cool with the mingled breath of people and incense, and threaded by the smallest sounds: the rustle of olive boughs, the faint creak of benches, the soft coughs that rose and died as if each throat remembered it stood in a holy place. Above that domestic hush of a crowd settling itself, Savonarola’s voice fell from the pulpit with the plain steadiness of one who had already tasted what was to come. There was no thunder in him now, but a grave sincerity, like bread broken without ornament. He told them he was ready to die. The visions that had carried him like a wind over the city’s rooftops had narrowed until he saw only his own end, and he named it as calmly as a man naming the hour of a meal.

When he lifted his hands in benediction, faces rose to him—women with their eyes wet and steady, men with the look of laborers listening for the bell that releases them, children whose attention wavered and then returned as if tugged back by the sound of his cadence. He looked once, took the sight into himself, and then descended. There was in the way he turned from them a finality like the last extinguishing of a hearth at night: the warmth remains in the stones, but you know no more flame will be laid there by that hand.

Before the sun had set, Florence was not a church but a furnace.

All day the city had worn its quiet like a thin crust over embers. When evening came, what had smouldered broke open again into open fury—fury not left to chance, but fed and guided, with the sly help that comes when officials look away at the needed moment. It began at the Duomo. Certain Compagnacci, eager as men who have sniffed blood, pushed to hinder the sermon the Piagnoni had gathered to hear. Words went hot; shoulders knocked; then steel showed. And as soon as the affray was born, the cry rose with it—one cry swallowing all others: “To San Marco! Fire to San Marco!”

The sound ran like a knife along the streets. Long before daylight had died, church and convent were under siege, surrounded by an ever-swelling multitude whose anger had the rhythm of waves—surging, falling back, and surging again, louder.

Inside, the convent had not been left to bare hands. The brethren, long aware of the hostility thickening beyond their walls, had arms ready. Some fought in their long white tunics with a vigor that made them seem less friars than old crusaders risen in their own cloth; the serge did not hide the muscle beneath it. Savonarola commanded them, pleaded with them, but the instinct to defend one’s shelter is older than obedience, and stronger when doors are about to give way.

Laymen too had stayed—men who had chosen not to flee when safety lay outside. They fought with a bitterness of loyalty. There was firing from the high altar, close by the great crucifix—as if the very place where bread and wine were lifted could also spit flame. From the convent roof stones and hot embers poured down: gritty, burning hail, with the sharp smell of scorched wood and singed cloth rising each time it struck. In the cloisters, where prayer had so often paced in circles, swords rang at close quarters. The stone arcades caught and threw back the clamor until it was hard to tell where any sound began; Florence’s own acoustic life had turned on itself, the sacred spaces made into echoing chambers for hate.

The attack lasted into deep night, though the assailants were many. The Government’s demonstrations had all gone against the convent. Early in the struggle guards were sent—yet not to scatter the crowd or quiet the street’s roar, but to command those within to lay down their arms, to order laymen to depart, and to require Savonarola himself to quit Florentine territory within twelve hours.

Had he stepped out then, he could scarcely have escaped being torn apart. He was willing to go; it was his friends who hindered him, for willingness is not always wisdom when a mob is the judge. Even for laymen of high name it was perilous to slip away by the garden wall. Yet some did. Among them was Francesco Valori, grey-haired and resolute, who hoped to raise help from without—still believing, as men do, that rescue can be summoned like servants with a bell if only one rings hard enough.

By deep night the struggle could not have endured much longer. The Compagnacci, maddened and still increasing, might soon have carried their swords into the library where Savonarola prayed with those brethren who had not taken arms, or who had laid them down at his command. Then, like a second gust of wind coming to push a wavering flame into one chosen direction, a new body of guards arrived. They bore a commission from the Signoria to demand the persons of Fra Girolamo and his two coadjutors, Fra Domenico and Fra Salvestro.

Lantern-light wavered across stone and faces. When the convent door opened and the Frate appeared between guards who offered him no safety but the hardness of a prison, a roar went up—triumphant hate, thick as smoke. The crowd surged into the narrow street, each man striving to be first in the stream, to stand nearest the captive prophet, to earn the luxury of insult, and if possible to land a blow. Armed Compagnacci slid among the guards, not hindered from doing so. They pressed close enough to spit, to strike, to kick.

Savonarola felt hands on him—dragging, shoving; he felt the lanterns lifted deliberately to throw their light on him, so that deriding faces might drink in the sight. He heard the coarse words that are always ready in a city, like garbage kept in a corner and flung out when the chance comes. He felt spittle and blows. And with it came, strangely, a sense that the worst bitterness had already passed. If men judged him guilty and were set on his blood, then only death waited. There is a kind of ease in knowing the menu will not change.

Yet the bitterest drop cannot be pressed upon the lips from without. The lowest depth is not martyrdom, but the moment when, in silence, one covers one’s head and feels: I am not worthy to be a martyr; the Truth will prosper, but not by me. That thought—untranslatable into the shouted language around him, which had only names for triumph and disgrace—lay inside him like a stone.

He disappeared under the doorway of the Old Palace, and the crowd’s brief imperfect triumph was like a taste that makes a beast crave more. If the prophet was taken, were there not the houses of his friends to be sacked?

Already half the armed multitude, too far back to share much in the siege, had been busy at a more profitable work: attacking rich houses—not with random hunger for plunder, but with a discriminating knowledge of whose doors should be broken. It showed guidance. The rabble with clubs and staves were officered by sword-girt Compagnacci. The riot wore a mask, but the hand beneath it was practiced.

And was there not—next criminal after the Frate—the ambitious Francesco Valori, suspected of wishing, with the Frate’s help, to make himself Doge or Gonfaloniere for life? The grey-haired man who eight months before had lifted arm and voice in fierce demand for justice on five fellow-citizens had escaped from San Marco only to meet what others called justice now. He saw his house surrounded by an angry greedy throng; he saw his wife shot dead with an arrow; and he himself, on his way to answer a summons to the Palazzo, was murdered by the swords of men named Ridolfi and Tornabuoni. Thus the Masque of the Furies—called Riot—played on through night into early morning, turning Florence’s streets into a stage where each new shriek was a cue.

The chief director did not show himself. He had reasons for keeping his red feather out of sight while work was done before dawn. He issued orders from a private retreat—one house, one room, in a quiet street between Santa Croce and San Marco: the same place where Tito had once paid a secret visit to Dolfo Spini.

There Spini, captain of the Compagnacci, sat through the memorable night receiving visitors who came and went and came again—some in the guise of armed youths with heated eyes, others obscurely dressed and apparently unarmed. The room smelled of tallow and wine. On the table stood abundant drink, with cups set ready as if for a feast; and though Spini watched himself against being made stupid by excess, he took enough from time to time to sharpen the excitement that the continual news fed in him. The tapers had burned down into low shapeless masses, their wicks drowning in grease; and through holes in the shutters the outer light began to mark itself—a sombre grey, like the first skim of dawn on cold broth.

Among the obscure visitors Ser Ceccone came often. As the hours drew towards morning twilight he stayed, a constant companion beside Francesco Cei, who lay in rather careless hiding within Florence, expecting his banishment to be revoked as soon as the Frate’s fall was secure. While messages arrived and were muttered over, Spini sprang from his seat and began to walk up and down, his face flushed with anger at some talk that had passed between his two unmilitary companions. At last he burst out, the words spitting like oil on a hot pan.

“The devil spit him! He shall pay for it, though. Ha, ha! The claws shall be down on him when he little thinks of them. So he was to be the great man after all! He’s been pretending to chuck everything towards my cap, as if I were a blind beggarman, and all the while he’s been winking and filling his own scarsella. I should like to hang skins about him and set my hounds on him! And he’s got that fine ruby of mine—I was fool enough to give him yesterday. Malediction! And he was laughing at me in his sleeve two years ago, and spoiling the best plan that ever was laid. I was a fool for trusting myself with a rascal who had long-twisted contrivances that nobody could see to the end of but himself.”

“A Greek, too, who dropped into Florence with gems packed about him,” said Francesco Cei, with a slight smile of amusement at Spini’s fuming. “You did not choose your confidant very wisely, my Dolfo.”

“He’s a cursed deal cleverer than you, Francesco—and handsomer too,” Spini snapped, turning on him with the general desire to worry whatever came within reach.

“I humbly conceive,” Ser Ceccone began, smoothing his hands as if they were parchment he wished to keep uncreased, “that Messer Francesco’s poetic genius will outweigh—”

“Yes, yes, rub your hands! I hate that notary’s trick of yours,” Spini broke in, for this roughness was a part of his patronage. Then he jerked his head as footsteps sounded. “But there comes Taddeo, or somebody. Now’s the time. What news, eh?”

Two Compagnacci entered with the look of men who have run through smoke and shouting, their faces hot and their breath still carrying the outside din as if it clung in their throats.

“Bad,” said one. “The people have made up their minds they were going to have the sacking of Soderini’s house, and now they have been balked. We shall have them turning on us if we don’t take care. I suspect there are some Mediceans buzzing about among them, and we may see them attacking your palace over the bridge before long, unless we can find a bait for them another way.”

“I have it!” Spini said, the words coming quick as a knife drawn. He seized Taddeo by the belt and pulled him aside, speaking low and rapid, giving directions with the precision of a man portioning meat on a board—this for here, that for there, quick work, no waste. Meanwhile the other man continued to tell Cei how the Signoria had interfered about Soderini’s house.

“Ecco!” Spini exclaimed at last, giving Taddeo a slight push toward the door. “Go—and make quick work.”

In the hour when the sky is neither night nor day, when the Arno seems to exhale its own cold breath and the stones of Florence hold a damp that seeps through soles, a man went out alone on the Oltrarno bank. He kept within the walls, yet chose a place no household watched—a reach of river where granaries and warehouses turned their backs like sullen beasts, leaving a sloping verge of long grass and rushes to drink the overflow of gutters. The gutters were his companions. They carried, now and then, the small mercies of a city that wastes as it feeds: a heel of bread that had fallen from a porter’s basket, carrot tops trimmed away in haste, apple-parings flung from some morning’s peeling, all sent down in thin bright ribbons of water that gurgled with a sound like a secret being told.

Baldassarre had learned those sounds as another man learns the crackle of a hearth. They were his kitchen now—those runlets, those rank stems, that sour smell of wet earth and grain-dust from the storehouses. He sat among the grass and bent over the swift channelled flow beside him, not praying—he had long since worn through that cloth—but watching with the same intentness a cook gives to a simmering pot when there is little fuel and one must not waste a bubble.

He had once been given a large piece of bread by that friendly current, and more than once a raw carrot, and parings still sweet at the rind. It was worth waiting where no eye could mock him. It might spare him for a day the worst hunger of all: the hunger that makes a man sit on a church-step beyond Porta San Frediano and beg without words, offering his very silence as alms-receipt.

He hated that. Not because his belly did not plead—his belly had become an animal he carried like any other burden—but because in him there lived, beneath all feebleness, one stubborn appetite that was not for food. He desired to live for the taste of vengeance, for the moment when the traitor’s name would be spoken true and not twisted by fine tongues. It was no longer hope, not even a plan: only that fixed possibility that can occupy a mind the way a forgotten dialect occupies an old man’s mouth—ready at any moment to leap forth whole, though no one around will understand it. Like a woman who watches a headland for a ship every dawn when all her neighbours have long agreed the ship went down, Baldassarre waited for something dim and formless, a sign without a shape, that made his heart pulse hard as if some hand had shaken him awake.

Since the monks of San Miniato had nursed him in their hospital until he could stand; since he had watched in vain for the Wife who was to help him and had begun to believe she lay among the pestilence-dead that filled the city like a stench in cloth; since his knife was gone and his body too broken for work and his mind too clouded for contrivance—since then he had moved like a man half translated into another language, his old speech still in him, but the city answering in sounds that did not fit. Yet he came, again and again, into the chill grey, and listened to the runlets, and watched the river that had a faint promise in it.

On the other side of Florence, far from that quiet reach, the morning was being kneaded into uproar.

The Compagnacci—those bands of armed men whom the Signoria, embarrassed if not secretly willing, let swagger and strike—had divided like a torrent meeting stones, parting into two violent streams. One pressed toward the Ponte Rubaconte, the larger surged for the Ponte Vecchio. In both, a word passed mouth to mouth—brief as a cook’s command in a hot kitchen, yet changing all hands at once—and almost every man knew his errand: to go into the Via de’ Bardi and sack a house there. If a man asked for reasons in such a crowd, he might as well ask why fire runs along dry straw. The armed leaders knew more; a brief order flies, and the meeting was set before a certain house toward the eastern end, where the master would likely be pulled from his morning sleep.

But that master had not slept.

Tito Melema’s desire to quit Florence had grown sharp with yesterday’s events: investigations would follow; appeals might be made; delay was a net, and in every mesh he felt danger. Falsehood had served him well and fattened like a hog at a rich trough, but it had nourished its twin beside it—Fear. He no longer wore armour; he no longer watched every shadow for Baldassarre. Yet from the corpse of that old fear something had risen: a habit, undying, that made his skin tighten at a footfall and his mind measure exits as naturally as it measured advantage.

He would not be safe, he told himself, until the fierce turbid air of Florence lay behind him. And now he was ready. Maso was to deliver the house to a new tenant. Horses and mules waited at San Gallo. Tessa and the children had been lodged for the night in the Borgo outside the gate—wrapped and placed like precious provisions to be carried out early before heat or thieves could spoil the journey—and would be dressed and ready to mount when he joined them.

He went down the stone steps into the courtyard and through the great doorway. In that cold light he was not the same Tito who had first entered that house with youth’s ease and had made, as he now named it, the mistake of falling in love with Romola. That life was cast off like a worn garment. He would leave it in Florence’s hands and go on with new silk on his shoulders.

He turned toward the Piazza dei Mozzi, intending the Ponte Rubaconte. Then sounds reached him—first distant, like the deep stir of a market before the stalls are set, then nearer: a tramp, a clatter of iron, voices thick with drink and anger. The noises of men are like the noises of mills: once they begin, they grind. He wheeled and walked quickly the other way.

Was the mob coming into Oltrarno? It was vexation as well as fear: he would have preferred the quieter road. He must go by the Ponte Vecchio. Unpleasant sensations tightened his throat; he drew his mantle close and hastened, the damp air smelling of river and closed-up houses.

No one saw him in the twilight. Yet before he had reached the end of the Via de’ Bardi, the same sounds fell on his ear again, louder and nearer. Had he been deceived before? No—this was the roll of a crowd. Coming over the Ponte Vecchio.

Again he turned—fear outrunning reflection—and found, too late, that the mob was also entering the street from the opposite end. He would not go back into his house. After all, they would not be hunting him—so he tried to tell himself. But he had valuables on him, and a mob is like a pot that has boiled over: it scalds whatever is nearest. Necessity did the work of courage. He went on toward the bridge.

The rush and trampling and confused voices grew so loud ahead that he ceased to hear what might be behind. He reached the end of the street. The crowd pouring from the bridge met him at the turning and closed round him. He had not time even to wonder at a sudden shout before he felt himself seized—not first by unarmed hands, but by men with weapons. His cap was knocked off; he was thrust violently forward among the rabble along the narrow passage of the bridge, where shops and woodwork narrowed the way and sound rebounded as if inside a barrel.

Then the words came distinct, flung like stones: “Piagnone! Medicean! Piagnone! Throw him over the bridge!”

His mantle was torn off him with such force that the pulls would have throttled him if the fibula had not given way. Fingers clawed at his scarsella, but the crowd’s own pressing and dragging foiled the snatch; it still hung at his side. Shouting and yelling—half without motive, mere relish of insult as of rancid wine—rang in his ears, spreading even to those who had not yet seen him and only knew there was a man to curse.

His horror fixed itself on one point: to reach the open arches at the centre. If they struck him down before then, he would be trampled and finished in the crush. There was one hope, black as the river itself—that they might throw him over before they had beaten the strength out of him. His whole soul narrowed to that hope and its reverse.

Yes—the arches. He saw the widening above the parapet, and in that moment, bloodless and with eyes stretched wide by terror, the mind that had lived on quick invention found one last resource. He fumbled at the clasp of his belt, mastered it with desperate speed, and flung belt and scarsella forward toward a yard of clear space against the parapet, crying out in a ringing voice that cut through the din like a knife through crust—

“There are diamonds! there is gold!”

In the instant, hands relaxed. Greed is a quicker hunger than hate. Men surged toward the thrown prize. Tito flung himself onto the parapet with a leap born of panic and strength, and the next moment he plunged—plunged with a great plash into the dark Arno far below.

It was his chance, and it was a good one. His life had once before been saved by fine swimming; as he came up after his long dive and the river closed cold around his skin, he tasted deliverance as sharply as if it were wine after thirst. He struck out with all the vigour still in his limbs. The current helped him, tugging him onward as if the river itself had taken sides.

If only he could pass beyond the Ponte alla Carrara, he might land where few watched, and even yet reach San Gallo. Life, he told himself, was still before him—another table laid, another city to feed on and be fed by.

On the bridge the mob shouted and bellowed, peering over, but they could not see far along the dark stream: they saw no more than a ripple and a vanishing blackness. They believed him drowned, as men often believe what pleases them.

Yet from another angle a face could be seen moving with the current—pale olive made white above the water, a face with a square forehead, long low arch of brows, and lustrous agate-like eyes that would not easily be forgotten. Onward it went with inflated quivering nostrils, the blue veins distended on the temples, hair floating like weed, sleeves heavy with water.

One bridge was passed—the Santa Trinita. Should he risk landing now rather than trust his strength? He fancied he heard cries pursuing him; terror pressed hardest from the side of men. Better the indefinite risk of mud and darkness than the certain hands of a crowd. He swam on, panting, straining. He had not slept; his muscles were not as fresh as his confidence pretended.

The next bridge—the last—was passed. He knew it, but in the tumult of blood in his ears he felt only vaguely that safety was possible, that he might land. But where? The current had its way with him. Exhaustion brought that dreamy slipping of mind that comes before unconsciousness, when sounds become muffled as if heard through cloth.

Now, at last, eyes discerned him—aged eyes trained by hunger to see chances at a distance.

Baldassarre had lifted his head from the runlet that brought him nothing. He had seen a pale object coming along the broader stream, and the sight struck him with that same start a cook has when a long-expected delivery appears at the kitchen door. Could this be fortune for him? He stared until the object gathered form; then he leaned forward, the blankness breaking, as if a lamp had been lit behind his eyes. Yet he did not move. He watched—motionless—because something was being brought to him.

The river cast a man’s body violently onto the grass two yards from him, as a wave casts a drowned branch. In the same instant Baldassarre sprang like a panther despite his years, clutching the velvet tunic, falling forward on the body, and flashing a look into the face.

Dead—was he dead? The eyes were rigid. The mouth slack. The skin cold with the river’s touch. For one beat of his heart despair iced him: if death had already taken this prey, what was vengeance now but an empty word?

But no—Justice had brought him. Men could look dead and yet have life creep back, as embers glow again when stirred. Baldassarre did not feel feeble then. His hands knew their work. He thrust his large fingers into the neck of the tunic and held them there, kneeling beside the body, watching the face with a fierce hope that trembled.

Rigid still. The half-fallen lids locked the eyes against him. Could it be that he was dead? There was no measure of time; it stretched and twisted like a bad dream. At last—surely—the eyelids quivered. The eyes were no longer stone. A vibrating light returned; they opened wide.

“Ah, yes! You see me—you know me!”

Tito knew him. But in that instant he did not know whether life or death had washed him into his injured father’s grasp. Perhaps death meant this chill gloom forever, with the hideous past leaning over him and no waking.

Baldassarre’s only dread was that those young limbs would escape. He pressed his knuckles against the round throat and knelt upon the chest with all the force his aged frame could summon. Let death come now, he thought—let it come while I hold him.

Again he watched the face. When the eyes grew rigid again, he dared not trust the seeming death. He would not loose his hold until a witness came. Justice, he believed, would send someone—an ear to hear, a tongue to speak what happened in plain words the city could not smooth into lies. Then he, Baldassarre, would say, “I killed this traitor to whom I was once a father.” They might believe him now; and he would be content with the struggle of justice on earth. Then he would desire to die with his hold on the body, and follow the traitor to hell, clutching still.

So he knelt, knuckles hard at the throat, hand hooked in the tunic, not trusting the stillness, holding fast with the obstinacy of a man who has had his true name taken from him and will not surrender the last syllable. The river beside them ran on with its ceaseless voice: slapping, whispering, sucking at the reeds—indifferent music, older than Florence, yet in that hour it seemed like a chorus under the act of a tragedy.

Light strengthened. His limbs gave way. He could kneel no longer, and he sank to sit upon the body, still clutching at the tunic’s neck as if it were the only rope left to him in a world of slipping ground.

Hours passed. No witness came. No eyes from the distant embankment detected two human bodies among tall grass by the riverside. Florence was busy with greater affairs and the preparation of a deeper tragedy. Not long after those two lay there, Savonarola was being tortured, crying out in his agony, “I will confess!” The city’s soundscape was filled with other cries—iron on stone, orders barked, moans stifled behind walls—so that this quiet reach of the Arno, with its whispering reeds and gurgling runlets, might have been another world.

It was not until the sun leaned westward that a waggon drawn by a mild grey ox came to the grassy margin. The man who led it bent to gather the round stones heaped there ready for carrying away; and as he straightened, something in the grass startled him—two bodies, one old and one young, locked together. The aged man had fallen forward, his dead clutch still fastening the other’s garment. It was not possible to separate them. Better to lift them as they were into the waggon and carry them into the great Piazza, so notice might be given to the Eight.

As the waggon entered the frequented streets, a crowd gathered and thickened around it, escorting the strange burden with that same appetite for spectacle that draws men to a cookshop window when the scent of roasting begins. People craned, jostled, listened for names. For a long while no one knew the bodies: the old face had fallen forward, half hiding the younger.

Then recognition spread like a spice thrown into warm wine.

“I know that old man,” Piero di Cosimo testified. “I painted his likeness once. He is the prisoner who clutched Melema on the steps of the Duomo.”

“He is perhaps the same old man who appeared at supper in my gardens,” said Bernardo Rucellai, one of the Eight. “I had forgotten him. I thought he had died in prison. But there is no knowing the truth now.”

And indeed, who shall put his finger on the work of justice and say, “It is there”? The city could name bodies and yet fail to name the meaning. Justice, like the Kingdom of God, is not outside us as a finished fact; it is within us as a great yearning—felt in the throat like hunger, heard in the ear like a remembered tongue, clung to with hands that will not let go even when the life has gone out of them.

Romola’s passage from dream to waking was like a slow ferrying—first down into a thick, unbroken sleep, then up again through busy, tangled visions, until she seemed to stretch her arms beneath the vault of the Bargello, where the taper-flames flared and flared, growing so fierce that darkness itself was burnt away. When her lids lifted, it was not fire that filled her eyes, but morning.

Her boat lay motionless in a small creek, as if the sea, too, had chosen to rest there. To her right spread the Mediterranean—sapphire, speckless, a sheet of blue so clean it might have been newly washed and laid out to dry beneath the sun. To her left, the land drew inward into one of those sheltered curves repeated all along that coast like a refrain: a bowl of green set in mountain folds, with slopes softened by tree-shadow, leaning up toward rock. Here and there a pale path winked between leaf and bough, climbing toward a huddle of buildings that seemed to have scrambled up the hillside simply to lift its belfry for the village below to look at, as one lifts a loaf high to see if it has browned evenly.

The sun had only begun its work. Its rays struck the westward horn of the crescent and gilded it, while the rest lay under a dew-cooled veil. The air held stillness as if it were a kept chamber. No oar dipped; no goat-bell answered; even the water had curved itself into quiet.

Warmth fell on Romola’s limbs with the gentleness of a hand laid on a fevered brow. She lay without moving, scarcely watching, only receiving—light through the lashes, salt-bright air through the nostrils, the faint rhythm of her own breathing in the hush. There are wakings in youth when bare existence is a draught of Lethe: sensation so subtle, so indefinite, that it is bliss without recollection and without craving. For a little while it seemed as if the agitated past had slid away as utterly as the Bargello’s darkness had been blotted out; as if the long afternoons of girlhood, when time itself had been wide and drowsy, had come back.

Then the thought returned, clear and edged: she was in the boat that had carried her through the night.

It had not borne her to death. It had rocked her, like a cradle, into another morning. And, despite the despair with which she had let herself drift, she felt the simple gladness of being alive under familiar sunlight instead of in an unknown dark.

Could she not remain? Here no sound from Florence would reach her. Yet even as she tried to hold fast the peace, shapes rose behind the golden haze of her mind—domes and towers, walls cut by a river, hills enclosing what she had fled. She sat up, willing herself to resist the rush of thought that began to count distances, to ask how far the current had carried her. Why should she mind? This nook looked sheltered; there would be villagers—plain people—who would not harm her. For a little while, at least, she might rest and resolve nothing. Bread and milk: the notion came like a domestic promise. She would buy it, and then lie down again in green quiet, letting life pause.

She turned her face back toward the crescent valley, as if by looking she could drink in that same first draught of stillness. She had scarcely held herself in that contemplative posture a few minutes when a sound cleft the calm.

A cry—thin at first, then steady, then piercing, drawn out without mercy. Not the shout of a man or the bark of a dog, but the continuous wail of a small child in distress, rising and rising until it seemed to press against Romola’s breast. It was all the more intolerable because it broke upon such peace; as if a knife had struck into fresh bread.

She started, setting a foot on the boat’s side, ready to spring to shore—then paused, listening, thinking, The mother must be near; it will cease. It did not. It went on, urgent and helpless, pulling her as a hand pulls at a sleeve. She leapt onto the beach and walked rapidly, not even certain at first which way she went, only following the line of the sound.

It seemed to come from a rough tangle of garden-growth to her right, where a half-ruined hovel sagged like a toothless mouth in the green. She climbed over a low broken stone fence and crossed patches of weedy crops and corn left standing—ripe, heavy-headed, neglected. The cry sharpened. Her pace quickened. Yet even in haste she felt the air change as she left the sea behind: the salt cleanliness thinned, and a heaviness met her, as if the green luxuriance hid a foulness underneath, the way sweet fruit can conceal rot.

The doorway yawned. The child’s cry darted through her like pain. She stepped within—and the dimness inside struck her with a shock of awe and horror.

On straw scattered over the floor lay three bodies: a tall man, a girl of about eight, and a young woman. The woman’s long black hair was being clutched and pulled by the living child who screamed beside her, as if the child thought to wake her by force.

Romola’s past among death and sickness made her swift. She lifted the little creature at once—olive-dark, light as hunger, hot with panic—and drew it to her bosom, rocking it, murmuring without knowing what words she used. Even while she soothed, her eyes went back to the bodies, searching for any sign of breath, of warmth that might answer her touch. The strongly marked type in their faces, the foreignness of their clothes, made her think they were Spanish or Portuguese Jews—one of those families driven out by the Inquisition, cast like refuse from port to port, preyed on by greed at sea and by superstition on land.

But the young woman’s body, though slack and still, had not the same wasted look as the man and the child. Doubt rose: could she be alive? Romola knelt and lifted the yellow woollen drapery that lay across the bosom to lay her hand to the heart—then stopped, chilled.

Purple spots.

The pestilence: the old, familiar mark she had learned to read as plainly as a cook reads scorch on the crust of a cake. It changed everything. If the villagers knew, they would not hurry to her aid; they might shrink from her as from fire. Yet the child needed milk; it needed a woman’s arms; it needed life.

She would find someone. She had money. She could buy goat’s milk, if nothing more. She rose with the child pressed to her, and began to make her way toward the village.

Across the cultivated ground she saw signs that were wrong in their quietness: patches of corn left too long, stalks over-heavy with grain no sickle had touched; golden apples and dark figs fallen and rotting where they lay, sweetening the air with the thick, sick scent of wasted harvest. There were grassy spaces, but no cow, no sheep, no goat moving through them. The silence began to feel less like peace and more like a held breath.

She hurried toward the densest cluster of houses, where there should be the clatter of morning—doors, voices, the scrape of pails, the thin music of daily labor. To quiet the child she stooped as she went, snatched up two figs, and bit off little pieces of the sweet, granular pulp, pressing them against the hungry mouth. The baby’s sobs took rhythm with the chewing; its cry fell to whimpers.

Between two lines of dwellings she entered the village street. It was already late enough for smoke to have risen, for voices to have crossed and called from one threshold to another. But there was no one. Doors stood open on emptiness, as if the houses had exhaled their inhabitants in the night and had not drawn them back.

The oppressive taint in the air thickened—heat mixed with sourness, with something like breath that had turned foul. An open doorway showed only a bare room. Another doorway: and there, in the dull light, a man lay dead with his garments on, his head fallen across a spade handle, an earthenware cruse still in his hand as if thirst had struck him down in the act of reaching. It was death caught mid-gesture, domestic and brutal.

Horror took possession of Romola. A village of unburied dead? She tried to listen for any faint stir, any cough or groan; but when she stopped feeding the child, it cried again, and the cry filled her ears, drowning any other sound.

At last she saw movement: a figure crawling slowly out of a house, then sinking down to sit against the wall. Romola hastened. The figure was a young woman, face flushed and drawn with fever, eyes bright with pain; she too clutched a pitcher.

As Romola approached, the woman did not start. The need in her was too consuming for surprise.

“Water—get me water!” she moaned.

Romola stooped, took the pitcher, and spoke close to her ear with the gentleness one uses to a child or a delirious mind. “You shall have water. Can you point me to the well?”

A trembling hand lifted toward the farther end of the street. Romola set off, as fast as she could manage with pitcher and child. The baby, lulled by fig pulp, quieted; its mouth worked, sticky with sweetness. With the cry stilled, Romola could hear again—the deadness of the village, the faint hiss of her own breath, the dull thud of her steps on packed earth.

The well lay beyond the street’s end. As she neared it, her gaze lifted instinctively to the opposite slope below the church, searching for anything living. High up, on a patch of grass between trees, she saw it—life in simple forms: a cow and two goats, small figures of sustenance against the green. She began tracing in her mind the path that would take her there once she had done her errand. Milk. She could already imagine the warm smell of it, the comfort of its heaviness on the tongue, the way it would quiet the hollow ache in her own belly and the sharper hunger in the child.

So intent was she on that line of ascent that she did not notice how close she had come to the well, nor that someone approaching from the other side had stopped short, eyes fixed on her.

At that moment, in that place, Romola’s figure might have seemed unearthly even to a less frightened mind: the long grey garment falling in straight lines that made her movement look like gliding; her hair rolling back, its left side caught by sun so that it shone; her face lifted, intent; and on her arm the little olive baby looking out with jet-black eyes, solemn as a tiny judge. A boy of fifteen, an acolyte accustomed to swinging a censer before painted Madonnas, stared as if a fresco had stepped out of plaster.

She has a pitcher—to fetch water for the sick. It is the Holy Mother, come for those with the pestilence.

Terror turned his limbs. He flung down his vessel and fled, black-and-white figure darting away up toward the slope Romola had been watching.

Romola saw him only in passing, and the sight might have puzzled her, but the parched sufferer behind her was urgent in her mind. She drew water quickly, half-filled the pitcher, and hastened back. In the sick woman’s house she found a small cup and noticed, with brief, practical surprise, salt meat and meal laid by—no sign here of famine, only of sudden plague.

She set the baby down on the floor for a moment. The child squatted unsteadily, eyes following her hands. Romola lifted water to the fevered woman, who drank greedily, throat working, then let her head fall back, eyes closing as if relief itself were a narcotic.

When she opened her eyes again, her gaze clung to Romola’s face. “Who are you?” she asked, voice thin.

“I came over the sea,” Romola said. “I came this morning. Are all the people dead in these houses?”

“I think they are all ill now—those that are not dead.” Her words dragged as if each one cost effort. “My father and my sister lie dead upstairs. There is no one to bury them. Soon I shall die.”

“Not so, I hope,” Romola said, though she did not give false comfort lightly. “I am come to take care of you. I am used to the pestilence; I am not afraid. But there must be some left who are not ill. I saw a youth running toward the mountain.”

“I cannot tell,” the woman whispered. “When the pestilence came, many went away—drove off the cows and goats. Give me more water.”

Romola gave it, and as the woman drank, Romola’s thoughts arranged themselves with the quick logic of necessity. If she followed the boy’s flight, she might find those who had escaped infection: the able-bodied, the frightened, the ones who still had strength to act. She must secure help for the child first—someone to feed it, to hold it when Romola went back among the sick and the dead. Then she could return, moving from house to house as she had moved in Florence, doing what hands and courage could do when medicine failed.

She promised the sick woman she would come back, lifted the dark bantling again, and set off toward the slope.

No burden of choice weighed her now. The longing for death, so heavy the night before, had fallen away as if it had been a cloak she had slipped off on waking. Her body was weary, hungry, thirsty, but her mind had a single direction: to find milk, then hands, then help.

The ascent wound. With the child on her arm, the path seemed longer than it looked from below. Heat pressed down; the earth smelled baked; the leaves held a faint bitterness where sun had warmed their oils. She began to feel faint, the hollow in her stomach sharpening. When the path made a double turning, she paused, thinking she might wait nearer the cow—someone would come to milk her—rather than climb all the way to the church before she had taken any rest.

She raised her eyes, measuring the steepness. Between boughs, no more than five yards off, she saw a broad, round face watching her—still as if carved—beneath it the black skirt of a priest’s garment, and a hand grasping a bucket.

Romola stood quietly, letting him see she did not rush. She had witnessed how dread mastered people in plague-time: it made them hide like animals and strike like animals. She lifted her voice with gentle pleading.

“I came over the sea. I am hungry, and so is the child. Will you not give us some milk?”

She had guessed part of the truth—this was the parish priest, this was the keeper of the cow—but she had not guessed what her words meant inside his frightened mind.

Only a short time before, the boy—Jacopo—had burst upon the priest with a tale: he had seen the Holy Mother with the Babe, fetching water for the sick. She was tall as cypresses. There was light about her head. She looked up toward the church. The old pievano had not wholly believed: he had lived more than fifty years without seeing the Madonna step down into his valley. He had suspected the boy’s eyes had turned some ordinary marvel into a miracle. Yet fear had pricked him. Before daring to come down and milk, he had mumbled many Aves, and his conscience—never entirely quiet—had tormented him. He trembled at the pestilence; he trembled too at the thought that Mercy itself might demand more from him than prayers.

So when he suddenly saw Romola at the parted way, her refined accent and her pleading tone did not reassure him. They sounded, in his panic, preternatural. He did not quite believe she was holy; but he feared she might be—and he feared equally that if there was a miracle, it would not be arranged for his comfort. He dared not run; he dared not advance.

“Come down,” Romola said after a pause, her voice steady, carrying authority without harshness. “Do not fear. Fear rather to deny food to the hungry when they ask you.”

A moment later the boughs parted and the priest stepped into view: thickset, broad-faced, harmless-looking, his black frock worn and soiled, bucket in hand. He kept a timid distance as he went in silence toward the tethered cow.

Romola followed, watching him. He seated himself and began to milk, hands nervous at first, the stream striking the pail with that soft, insistent sound which is itself a kind of comfort—like rain heard from inside. He poured milk into a brass cup he carried and handed it to her.

Romola lifted the cup to the child’s mouth. The baby drank eagerly, lips pursed, then loosened, sucking with a greed that was almost furious. Milk ran in a thin line at the corner; the child smacked, then sucked its own milky lips as if astonished by the richness. Romola drank too; the warm sweetness spread through her, easing the faintness and the dryness in her throat.

The priest watched from his low stool. He recognized, now that he was closer, that the baby was Hebrew—its dark skin and hair, the cast of its features. He recognized, too, that Romola was no vaporous apparition but a substantial woman. Yet the strangeness remained: why was she here, alone, with a plague-child in her arms? It felt, to his frightened mind, as if the world had shifted under his feet. He had a presentiment that his life—so long circled by small duties and large fears—was about to be altered.

Romola smiled down at the baby’s satisfied mouth and held out the cup again. “Give us more, good father.”

He obeyed more readily, though dread still lived in him like a lodged thorn.

When the second cup had been drained, Romola looked down at him and spoke with mild decision, as one speaks when bread must be kneaded and there is no time for hesitation.

“Now tell me, father, how this pestilence came—and why you let your people die without the sacraments, and lie unburied. For I have come over the sea to help those who are left alive. And you, too, will help them now.”

He told the tale, his words stumbling where shame and fear caught them. While he spoke, Jacopo—who had fled—crept back, peeping and edging forward behind bushes until he stood watching, wide-eyed.

Three families of Jews, twenty souls, had been put ashore weeks ago; some were already ill with the pestilence. The villagers, the priest said, had refused shelter to the miscreants, giving them only a distant hovel and heaps of straw. When the strangers died, some of the people had thrown the bodies into the sea. Then a great storm had come, and the sea—angry, implacable—had brought the bodies back again, casting them up as if refusing to be made an accomplice. Terror seized the village. A grave was dug and the bodies buried. But then the pestilence struck the Christians. Most fled over the mountain, driving away their few cattle and carrying provisions. The priest had not fled: he had stayed and prayed, and he had persuaded Jacopo to remain with him. Yet he confessed that mortal terror had mastered him; he had not dared to go down among the sick.

“You will fear no longer,” Romola said, her tone warming with encouraging command. “You will come down with me. We will see who is living. We will look for the dead and bury them. I have walked for months where the pestilence was, and see—I am strong.”

Then she turned her face toward the peeping boy and motioned. “Jacopo will come too.”

Jacopo came out slowly, as if something unseen drew him.

“Come, Jacopo,” Romola said again, smiling, letting kindness soften the order. “You will carry the child for me. See—your arms are strong, and I am tired.”

To Jacopo it was dreadful: to hold the plague-child, to go down into the valley of sickness. To the priest it was dreadful too. Yet both felt themselves under an influence stronger than dread—not the confusion of miracle now, but the sharper conviction that this woman was sent, and that to refuse her would be to refuse God’s command spoken in a human tongue.

“Now we will carry down the milk,” Romola said, “and see if any one wants it.”

So they went together down the slope—the priest with his bucket, the boy with the child held at arm’s length at first and then closer as the little one settled, Romola walking between them, her gaze already measuring doors, windows, thresholds—places where life might still be found. In the valley that morning, those who had given themselves up to despair saw help arrive, not with trumpets but with a cup of milk and hands willing to lift a head, wash a face, carry water, and speak without fear.

There were scarcely more than a score alive in all that nook between mountain and sea. But all were comforted; most were saved. The dead, who had lain with open doors around them as if the village had forgotten its own names, were gathered and buried. The air, which had seemed loaded with corruption, learned again the humbler smells of life: damp earth turned for graves, then for planting; smoke rising from cookfires; milk warming in pots; bread baking until its crust sent out that particular scent that makes even grief take one breath of solace.

Days lengthened into weeks; weeks into months. The men dug and sowed again. The women began once more to go to the well with their great vases on their heads, and their steps made the street audible in a way Romola came to love—the soft pad of sandals, the clink of pottery, the low calls from one doorway to another, as if sound itself were proof of survival. The valley’s acoustic emptiness, so terrible in those first hours, filled again with small human noises and the answering bleat of goats, the occasional lowing of cattle, the bell from the church up the slope cutting the air in measured strokes that marked time not as doom but as return.

The Hebrew baby grew sturdier. It ceased to be only a foundling in her arms and became a child with habits—wanting what it saw, crawling toward any basket that smelled of eggs or honey, smearing its hands in whatever sweetness it could reach. In time it was baptized in the mountain church, and named Benedetto, and the little dark creature—once nothing but hunger and a cry—became a tottering, tumbling Christian child, as much a part of the villagers’ future as any olive shoot newly planted.

But by then Romola herself began to pay the cost. The strain that purpose had kept at bay returned as fatigue and languor, settling into her bones. She took as a dwelling one of the abandoned houses standing a little apart from the village street. There, on a thick heap of clean straw—soft and fragrant, a bed for those who had never demanded down—she lay still through most of the daylight hours. A widow, made solitary by the pestilence, tended her and the little Benedetto, bringing water, washing cloths, setting by her hand whatever food the others had brought.

Each day the Padre, Jacopo, and the small flock of survivors came to the cottage to see the blessed Lady. They brought offerings of their best—honey that smelled of thyme and wild blossoms; fresh cakes still warm, their crusts browned and faintly crackling; eggs with shells cool as smooth stones; polenta, golden and steaming, cut with a string and laid on a board. The gifts were as much gratitude as sustenance. The sound of their steps outside, the murmured greetings, the rustle of baskets, became part of the cottage’s life.

It was a sight none of them forgot, a sight they repeated when they were old—how the sweet, sainted lady with the fair face and golden hair and brown eyes that seemed to carry blessing lay weary after labors that had saved them; how the queer little black Benedetto crawled on the straw by her side and wanted everything that was brought; how she always gave him a bit of what she took—letting him taste the honey, breaking off a corner of cake, wetting his lips with milk—and told them that if they loved her, they must be good to Benedetto.

In later years the valley told legends about the blessed Lady who had come over the sea. The tales grew as tales do: light gathered around her head; her step was said to have made the sick air sweeter; the sea itself was said to have carried her like a servant bearing a queen. Yet through all the embroidery, anyone who listened closely could hear the plain thread underneath: that once, in a time of terror, a woman had come and done beautiful, loving deeds there—feeding, tending, burying, commanding frightened men into courage—so that those ready to perish were rescued, and a child who had nothing but a cry was given a name that the village could speak.

In the deep, hushed hours of winter—when the valley lay cupped in cold and Romola lay still, mending as one mends after fever—her mind travelled backward and forward with a new steadiness, as if some hand had pressed a fresh seal into softening wax and left its mark clear.

She remembered, with a sort of shame that burned without heat, how she had once felt herself loose from every tie: unmoored, purposeless, sinking into a peevish solitude where even sorrow became a private luxury. There had been a moment when she had let the thought rock her like a lullaby—Life gives me nothing; I am tired; I want to die—and she had carried that inward sob down into sleep.

But the instant after waking in the boat—after that cry had reached her across the water like a bell heard through fog—she had not stopped to argue herself back into endurance. She had simply lived. She had moved as hunger moves a hand toward bread: urgently, without reasoning, answering need because it called. She had not told herself, as she used to do in Florence, that it was good to live in order to lighten sorrow; she had been drawn into the work as naturally as a cook is drawn to a fire when a pot boils over—no speeches, no maxims, only quick hands and attention.

It was a new baptism for her, not of ceremony but of necessity. In Florence, everything simple between human creature and human creature had been knotted for her into special bindings—marriage, the State, discipleship—till affection and duty had become a tangle where one could scarcely breathe. When those bindings had disappointed her trust, the recoil had stunned her sympathy, as if a loud clang had left her ears ringing and made every softer sound seem distant.

Here, among these people whose lives turned on seed and sickness, on the keeping of goats and the curing of a child’s cough, she had found again the plain scale of suffering: it could be measured by a hand laid on a brow, by water warmed, by barley broth stirred until it thickened, by a clean cloth torn and folded. And in the quiet where the only harshness was the wind in the bare branches or the far crack of wood in the frost, she said to herself:

“It was baseness in me to desire death. If everything else is doubtful, this suffering that I can help is certain. If the glory of the cross is an illusion, the sorrow is only the truer. While the strength is in my arm, I will stretch it out to the fainting; while the light visits my eyes, they shall seek the forsaken.”

Then, as soon as the valley’s need no longer pressed upon her from morning to night—when the fevers eased, and the children’s cries grew fewer, and there were hours unfilled with sudden calls—her heart, released from the people nearest at hand, rushed back into its older channels. Florence returned upon her with the insistence of appetite. Familiar faces, familiar lanes, familiar voices—those sounds she had once thought she could escape—came back as if they were the only language her inward self entirely understood. No new kindness, no new gratitude, could feed her as those memories fed her; the living fibre of her feeling took its nourishment from what it had long known.

Complete severance from one’s accustomed life makes a rare space for looking inward, and in that space Romola judged herself as she had never done before. Compunction—born in natures that feel others’ possible pain as keenly as their own actual pain—began to stir and gather force. She questioned the justice of her conclusions, the rightness of her deeds. Had she been rash? arrogant? always impatient that others were not as good as they should be, while she herself had failed to be faithful to what she had once recognised as the best?

Her flight rose before her as something cowardly—self-care disguised as renunciation. Savonarola had once taken her back on grounds that now seemed truer and deeper than those which had driven her out the second time. How could she feel the needs of strangers and not feel, above all, the needs of those nearest by bond and history?

But self-reproach met its own recoil. The memory of her life with Tito—of the conditions that made any real union impossible, while their outward union forced on her a whole daily discipline of false duty, a concealment and a sanctioning of what her whole mind revolted from—told her again that flight had been her only resource. There are minds so dull in sensibility that they never doubt; but all others must suffer this recurring conflict, where life’s many-twisted conditions have forbidden the fulfilment of a bond. For, strictly, there is no replacing of relations: the new does not cancel the old. The breach remains a wound; and until the scar is hard, conscience keeps turning back to look at it with troubled eyes.
