Romola shrank with dread from any renewed closeness to Tito, and yet she could not be at ease in ignorance of his fate. The thought would rise unbidden, as persistent as the smell of smoke in hair after one has been near a fire: What if he were in misery? what if he needed her? There was still, within her, a thin thread of pain that testified to Fra Girolamo’s words—that she could not cease to be a wife. Could anything utterly cease for her that had once mingled with the current of her heart’s blood?

Florence returned like hunger; her feelings could not wander forever after the possible and the vague. To have divided herself from all that for ever—was that truly strength? Or was it the pride of one who says, “This world is not good enough for me,” when in truth she had simply been bruised and frightened? If she had been higher, would she so easily have lost trust?

Even her indignant grief for her godfather no longer held sole possession of her. Her sense of debt to Savonarola recovered its predominance. Nothing that had come, or might yet come, could undo the fact that there had been a great inspiration in him—something that had wakened new life in her, as leaven wakes sluggish dough. Who else, in all her experience, could claim from her the same gratitude? His errors—might they not bring calamity? The possibility made her restless, as if some harsh, jarring note had entered the valley’s quiet and she could not find its source.

She could not rest. Perhaps it was the return of strength with the first budding leaves—the sap rising, the air softened, the mornings less iron-cold—that made her active again. Perhaps it was simply longing, keen as thirst, to draw nearer to Florence. She did not picture herself daring to enter the city; but to be near enough to learn what was happening there urged itself with a force that pushed every other purpose aside.

So one morning in March, when the light had a gentler colour and the earth-smell was no longer shut away under hard frost, the people of the valley gathered to see the blessed Lady depart. Jacopo had fetched a mule for her and was to go with her over the mountains. The Padre, too, was to accompany her as far as the nearest town, that he might aid her in learning the safest road by which she could reach Pistoja. The little store of trinkets and money she had carried with her and never touched in this valley was abundant for her needs.

If she had been less drawn away by that inward pull, it would have been a harder moment when she walked along the village street for the last time. The place had its own domestic music now: the soft cluck of hens near doorways, the creak of a pail at the well, the low talk of men whose tongues kept to the valley’s old turns of speech—phrases that did not travel well beyond these slopes, meanings packed in sounds that would be thinned and altered in the city. Romola listened as one listens before leaving a country where the very names of herbs and tools are different—where memory lives in syllables as much as in faces.

Near the well the Padre and Jacopo waited with the mule. She had scarcely reached them before the wailing began. The people knelt and kissed her hands; they clung to her skirts and pressed their lips on the grey folds, crying out between sobs:

“Ah, why will you go, when the good season is beginning and the crops will be plentiful? Why will you go?”

“Do not be sorry,” Romola said, and her voice—so often constrained in Florence—came now with the plain tenderness these people understood. “You are well now, and I shall remember you. I must go and see if my own people want me.”

“Ah, yes—if they have the pestilence!”

“Look at us again, Madonna!”

“Yes, yes,” others cried quickly, as if promising could bind her back. “We will be good to the little Benedetto!”

At last she mounted the mule. But when Benedetto saw her lifted into this new height, turned away from him, he sent up a vigorous screaming—sharp, indignant, the sound of a small creature robbed. It gave all the people an excuse to surge after her, insisting that he must ride too, perched on the mule’s neck as far as the foot of the slope. Someone thrust him up; his little hands gripped, his cries broke into sobs, and Romola steadied him against her with the instinctive care she had practised in these months, as if a child were as natural a burden as a loaf is a natural comfort.

The parting had to come; even the valley’s love could not make the road shorter. When they reached the place where the path began to rise, Benedetto was taken down, and the people’s hands, which had held him and her and the mule’s coarse mane, fell away one by one. Romola turned again and again as she went upward. Each time she looked back she saw them lingering like a little flock, their figures small against the greening, waiting to catch the last waving of her hand, as if that motion could carry a blessing farther than words, beyond the reach of dialect, into whatever strange and louder world lay on the other side of the mountains.

On the fourteenth day of April Romola passed again beneath the gates of Florence, and the very air that met her seemed thickened with breath and rumor, as if the city had been boiling a bitter broth through the night and could not help sending up its steam. She had meant to halt longer at Pistoja; but no one report there would keep faith with the next—Savonarola had walked through fire; Savonarola had failed; Savonarola had fled; Savonarola had been taken. Rest was impossible while the story shifted under her feet like loose stones.

At Prato, when she was already feeling herself drawn, step by step, toward the city she dreaded, she met an Augustinian monk of San Spirito—the very man who had once taken her godfather’s confessions. His cowl was dusted as if he had been pushed in a crowd; his voice carried the hoarseness of a throat that had shouted or wept. He told her what had happened in Florence, not as a tale brought from afar, but as something still ringing in his ears.

Savonarola had been arrested. And Tito—Tito was dead.

The monk had stood in the living stream that followed the waggon into the Piazza, that slow heaving tide of bodies and breath, curses and prayers. What Florence “generally knew,” he gave her: Tito had escaped an assaulting mob by leaping into the Arno, but had been murdered on the bank by an old man who had long borne him enmity.

Romola heard as one hears the clack of a mill-wheel one has lived beside all one’s life—mechanical, inevitable, dreadful in its continuance. Yet she understood the catastrophe as no other listener in Florence could understand it; for to them Tito’s death was a public rumor with a shape like any other; to her it was the last act of a long deceit whose taste still lay on her tongue, sharp as spoiled oil.

Of Fra Girolamo, the monk spoke with that unfavorable bias usual among the Black Brethren toward the brother who showed white beneath his black: Savonarola, he said, had confessed himself a deceiver of the people. Even before the words were fully spent Romola felt the lash of them—confession wrested by torture, truth and untruth kneaded together like dough under brutal hands until nothing could be distinguished but submission.

She paused no longer. That evening she was within Florence, in Monna Brigida’s house, seated under a storm of exclamations—joy and wailing mingled, narrative pouring over her like water from a tipped jar. Brigida had backslidden in Romola’s absence into false hair, and at the first sight of her had dragged it off as if it scorched her head.

“I’ll not mind being grey,” she cried, shaking her own thin locks. “Not if my dear child will stay with me.”

Romola, under her long widow’s veil, sat in an agitated silence. Brigida’s gossip—this neighbor said that, that one swore the other—fell on her dulled sense as rain falls on stone. The two great facts she had come to Florence to meet—Tito’s death and Fra Girolamo’s confession of duplicity under coercion—pressed on her like a weight laid across her ribs; they left her hardly any power for lesser matters. All the mind she could command, under that awe-stricken grief, gathered itself to two purposes that would not be put aside: to try and see Savonarola, and to learn what had become of Tessa and the children.

“Tell me, cousin,” she said abruptly, cutting across Brigida’s plans for their living together as one might cut a thread, “has anything been seen or said since Tito’s death of a young woman with two little children?”

Monna Brigida started, rounded her eyes, and lifted both hands. “Cristo! no. What—was he so bad as that, my poor child? Ah, then, that was why you went away and left me word only that you went of your own free will. Well, well; if I’d known that, I shouldn’t have thought you so strange and flighty. For I did say to myself—though I didn’t tell anybody else—‘What was she to go away from her husband for, leaving him to mischief, only because they cut poor Bernardo’s head off? She’s got her father’s temper,’ I said, ‘that’s what it is.’ Well, well; never scold me, child: Bardo was fierce, you can’t deny it. But if you had only told me the truth, that there was a young hussey and children, I should have understood it all.”

Romola’s fingers tightened under her veil as if they had found a rough edge. “Has anything been seen or said of her?” she urged.

“No; and the less the better,” Brigida answered, lowering her voice as if the walls were full of ears. “They say enough of ill about him without that. But since that was the reason you went—”

“No, dear cousin,” Romola broke in, her earnestness sounding like the clear ring of a knife on stone, “pray do not talk so. I wish above all things to find that young woman and her children, and to take care of them. They are quite helpless. Say nothing against it; that is the thing I shall do first of all.”

Brigida drew back, baffled; her mouth puckered in a discomfited shrug. “Well,” she muttered, “if that’s being a Piagnone, I’ve been taking peas for paternosters. Why, Fra Girolamo said as good as that widows ought not to marry again. Step in at the door and it’s a sin and a shame, it seems; but come down the chimney and you’re welcome. Two children—Santiddio!”

“Cousin, the poor thing has done no conscious wrong,” Romola said, and her voice softened, as if she were crumbling bread into a bowl to make it easy to swallow. “She is ignorant of everything. I will tell you—but not now.”

Early the next morning Romola went beyond San Ambrogio to the house where she had once found Tessa. The street had its usual life—women bargaining over greens that still held a night’s damp, a boy carrying warm flat loaves in a cloth that let out their faint sour-sweet steam, the chatter of vendors striking and falling like sparrows’ calls. But to Romola every sound seemed set too loud, too close; Florence’s noise pressed on her like an argument that would not allow silence for thought.

At the house she sought, she found only emptiness. Tessa was gone.

Romola’s mind leapt at once to the likeliest thread: Tito had sent her away beforehand to some place where he meant to join her; he would not willingly have torn himself from those children. The conjecture cut her with an extra pain, because it carried with it an image she could not drive away—Tessa, that childish creature, waiting by some roadside, waiting and waiting, hungry, bewildered, with the children tugging at her and no understanding why the promised arms did not come.

Those living near could tell her nothing, except that old deaf Lisa had gone away a week ago with her goods, and no one knew where Tessa had gone. Romola found no further active search open to her. She had no starting-point for inquiry, and not only her innate reserve but a nobler sensitiveness made her shrink from parading Tessa’s relation to Tito, and her own purpose, before the eyes of Florence—shrinking from an ostentation of generosity that would be another kind of cruelty.

Days passed in anxious inaction, as if time itself had become a hard loaf she could not break. Even when her thoughts were driven toward other necessities, her heart would begin to throb if she caught sight of a pair of round brown legs beneath a short skirt, or a short woman in contadina dress. She never told herself that it was heroism, or exalted charity, to seek these beings. She needed something she was bound specially to care for. She yearned—almost with a physical hunger—to clasp the children and make them love her. That at least would be some sweet result, for others as well as herself, out of her long sorrow.

There was property of Tito’s to which she could lay claim; but she distrusted the cleanness of that money, as one distrusts water drawn from a tainted well. She had determined to make it all over to the State, except so much as equaled the price of her father’s library. That would be enough for the modest support of Tessa and the children.

Monna Brigida, however, pushed all plans into the background with clamorous insistence: Romola must live with her and never forsake her till Brigida had seen herself safe in Paradise—else why had she been persuaded to turn Piagnone?—and if Romola wanted to rear other people’s children, then Brigida must rear them too.

“Only,” Brigida would add, with a meaningful lift of brow, “they must be found first.”

Romola felt the full force of that little sting. Yet strong feeling, unsatisfied, breeds its own superstition—of hope or despair. Romola’s was the superstition of hope: somehow she was to find that mother and the children.

At last, as if Providence had tired of her pacing in place, a new direction for inquiry offered itself. She learned that Tito had provided horses and mules to await him at San Gallo; therefore he meant to leave Florence by the gate of San Gallo. She determined—without much confidence, but with the stubbornness of one who will at least touch every door-handle—to question the gatekeepers whether any one answering to Tessa’s description, with two little children, had passed out before the morning of the ninth of April.

She walked along the Via San Gallo, watchful under her long veil lest she miss any sign. In the city’s soundscape she could pick out the particular textures: the iron-shod hooves striking cobble, the watery slap where a cartwheel found mud, the shrill thinness of a child’s cry ricocheting off stone, the deeper human murmur that was Florence’s perpetual hearth-fire. To Romola, worn by grief, the city’s roar felt like a violence; it was not the honest noise of field and wind, where each sound had room to die, but a crowded clamor that flattened every note into the same harsh coin. Even art here was cried in the street like cheap fruit.

In that very street she descried Bratti, chaffering with a customer—Bratti, the roaming man who knew the ways of small bargains and smaller secrets. She thought he might aid her; she would not mind speaking of Tessa to him.

But as she put aside her veil and crossed toward him, she saw something hanging from the corner of his basket, and her heart sprang up with a hope so sudden it seemed to lift her by the throat.

“Bratti, my friend,” she said, so abruptly that her words struck like a hand on a table, “where did you get that necklace?”

“Your servant, madonna,” Bratti replied, looking at her with his usual deliberate coolness, as if surprise were a luxury he never bought. “It’s a necklace worth money, but I shall get little by it, for my heart’s too tender for a trader’s. I have promised to keep it in pledge.”

“Pray tell me where you got it,” Romola said; and now her voice trembled in spite of her effort. “From a little woman named Tessa—is it not true?”

“Ah! if you know her,” said Bratti, “and would redeem it of me at a small profit, and give it her again, you’d be doing a charity. For she cried at parting with it—you’d have thought she was running into a brook. It’s a small profit I’ll charge you. You shall have it for a florin, for I don’t like to be hard-hearted.”

“Where is she?” Romola demanded, already drawing out the coin, already unclasping the beads from his basket with hands that could scarcely obey her.

“Outside the gate there,” Bratti said, nodding toward San Gallo, “at the other end of the Borgo, at old Sibilla Manetti’s. Anybody will tell you which is the house.”

Romola went as if her feet had learned a new swiftness. She blessed—without knowing why she blessed it—the Carnival incident that had burned the look of this necklace into her memory: each bead a small dark seed of recognition, each one now a breadcrumb leading her out of bewilderment.

Soon she stood at the house. The poor widow who opened to her talked at once, with that needful eagerness of poverty to explain itself: the young woman and the children were in the inner room—had been promised fetching-away a fortnight ago and more—had no money, only their clothes, to pay for food and lodging. But since madonna knew them—

Romola waited for no more. She opened the door.

Tessa sat on the low bed. Her crying had passed into tearless sobs; her face had the look of something bruised and left too long in the air. She stared with sad blank eyes at the two children playing in the corner—Lillo with his skirt pulled over his head, roaring at Ninna to frighten her, then peeping out again to see whether his thunder had struck. Ninna, smaller and solemn, half-laughed, half-wondered, as if even play had become uncertain without a grown hand to steady it.

The door was behind Tessa; she did not turn when it opened, thinking it only the old woman. Expectation was no longer alive in her—like a fire gone down to ash.

Romola had thrown aside her veil. She paused a moment, holding the necklace where it could catch the light. Then she spoke, and the sound of her voice—pure, firm, the same voice that used to cheer her father in his darkened study—fell into that poor room like a clear note in a muddied stream.

“Tessa!”

Tessa started to her feet and wheeled round. Her eyes, wide and incredulous, fastened on Romola as if on an apparition that might vanish if she blinked.

“See,” Romola said, and with a tenderness that was also an authority she clasped the beads again on Tessa’s neck, fastening them as one fastens a child’s cloak against cold. “God has sent me to you again.”

The poor thing gave a cry that broke into sobbing, and clung to the arms that had fastened the necklace, clung as if those arms were the only solid thing left in the world. She could not speak.

The children, startled by the cry, toddled from their corner and caught at their mother’s skirts. They looked up at Romola with wide eyes—two small faces in which the same blood that had wronged Romola now pleaded without words. Romola felt their gaze like a touch on her skin, and the hunger in her—hunger for some duty that would not mock her—answered.

That day they all went home to Monna Brigida’s, in the Borgo degli Albizzi.

On the way, by gentle degrees, Romola made known to Tessa that Naldo could never come to her again—not because he had grown cruel, but because he was dead. The words had to be given as one gives a child bitter medicine: slowly, with pauses, with the hand ready to soothe the choke that follows.

Tessa’s grief was bewilderment more than rebellion; she clutched at the children as if to count them and be certain they were still there, as if the world were a basket from which things slipped unseen.

“But be comforted, my Tessa,” Romola said, drawing her nearer. “I am come to take care of you always. And we have got Lillo and Ninna.”

Monna Brigida’s mouth twitched in the struggle between awe of Romola and the desire to speak too soon. “Let be, for the present,” she thought. “But it seems to me a thousand years till I tell this little contadina—who seems not to know how many fingers she’s got on her hand—who Romola is. And I will tell her some day, else she’ll never know her place. It’s all very well for Romola; nobody will call their souls their own when she’s by. But if I’m to have this puss-faced minx living in my house she must be humble to me.”

Yet even Brigida’s resentment softened when supper came. The children’s small mouths, opening trustfully for sweetmeats, touched that old domestic place in her where grief and pride and piety all ended at the table. She wanted to give them too many sweets, and Romola had to check her, as one checks a cook’s over-generous hand with sugar when children’s bellies are at stake.

At the last, as Brigida was going to bed, she confessed in a lower, reluctant tenderness, “It would be a shame not to take care of such cherubs. But you must give up to me a little, Romola, about their eating, and those things. For you have never had a baby, and I had twins—only they died as soon as they were born.”

When Romola brought Tessa home with the children, April had already thinned toward its end; the evenings were longer, and the city’s many tongues seemed to take advantage of the extra light to wag the more. Yet it was not the noisy happiness of little feet in her rooms that made Romola’s heart beat quicker, nor the small domestic tasks she set herself—measuring out bread, warming milk, making sure the beans were well rinsed of grit, that the rosemary and bay did not scorch in the pot. It was another hunger that had been growing in her, sharpened by every rumor and every contradiction—a hunger to know the truth of Fra Girolamo, and to taste in it, if she could, something that was not corrupted.

That hunger had been driven to its keenest edge by a printed thing that had begun to pass from hand to hand like a piece of contraband spice—Fra Girolamo’s Trial, or, as everyone called it with a grim sort of relish, his Confession: the words said to have been drawn from him by the sixteen Florentine citizens commissioned to question him. The Signoria had ordered it put forth, and then, as if the city’s ear had proved too quick for their liking, as if the sound of those pages crackling in a thousand rooms had turned into a roar of suspicion, they had tried to call it back with severe measures. But paper has its own cunning. Copies were “mislaid.” A second edition—careful to proclaim that it was not by order of the Signoria—soon slipped into eager hands as quietly as a loaf passed at night to a starving neighbor.

Romola, who had begun to despair of ever speaking with the Frate, read the printed evidence again and again. She read it the way a careful cook will taste a broth in which too many hands have dipped—again and again, searching for what is native to the thing itself and what is foreign, what is the true savor of the ingredients and what is the taint of the vessel. She could not be content with the sharp assertions traded in the streets and under the loggie—one man swearing the Frate had been proved a liar, another swearing the paper was pure forgery, each voice louder than the last, as if volume could replace knowledge. The city’s soundscape itself seemed diseased: the clatter of hooves on stone, the vendors’ cries, the shrill quarrels that rose and broke like waves—noise piled on noise until thought was choked as surely as a flame under wet ash. Florence had always been full of sound; now the sounds pressed like a fever.

Among the more devout followers of Savonarola, his reported want of constancy under torture, and his retraction of prophetic claims, had produced a consternation so deep it could not be pushed aside at once. Yet even in their grief there came, soon enough, a counter-taste—suspicion that would grow into a certainty for them—that any reported words which stood in inexplicable contradiction to their faith had not come from the prophet’s lips at all, but from the falsifying pen of Ser Ceccone, that notary of evil repute who had made the digest of the examination. They spoke of that name as if it were a bitter herb bruised into an otherwise wholesome dish.

And indeed there were facts that threw immediate discredit on the printed document, even for those who were not ready to swear to outright falsification. Was not the list of sixteen examiners half made up of the prophet’s bitterest enemies? Was not the notorious Dolfo Spini one of the new Eight, prematurely elected, as if to load the dice against a man whose ruin had been determined? It was a murder with slow formalities, everyone could see it: a knife hidden under velvet, a cord drawn out with legal phrases. In the Old Palace, beneath the echoing corridors and the murmur of officials’ feet, the Signoria had resolved to drive a bargain with the Pope and with the Duke of Milan by extinguishing the man who was a molestation alike to vicious citizens and to greedy foreign tyrants, as well as to a corrupt clergy. The Frate had been doomed beforehand. The only question now pretended to exist was whether the Republic, in return for permission to lay a tax on ecclesiastical property, should deliver him alive into the hands of the Pope, or whether the Pope should further concede what Florentine dignity demanded—the privilege of hanging and burning its own prophet on its own piazza.

Under such circumstances, who could give full credit to this so-called confession? If the Frate had denied his prophetic gift, was it not plausible that the denial had been wrenched from him by the agony of torture—agony that, in his sensitive frame, must quickly produce raving? What if these wicked examiners declared he had only had the torture of the rope and pulley thrice, and only on one day, and that his confessions had been made when he was under no bodily coercion—was that to be believed? Many said no; and the “many” were made more certain by the measure of their pain. He had been tortured more, they insisted; he had been tortured in proportion to the distress his confessions had created in the hearts of those who loved him. It was a strange arithmetic, but grief counts that way.

Other friends of Savonarola—less ardent partisans—did not doubt the substantial genuineness of the confession, however much the notary might have colored it with transpositions and additions. Yet they argued, with indignation that was calmer only because it had steadier roots, that even so there was nothing warranting death, not even grave punishment. If this examination were the only evidence against him, then he would die not for any crime, but because he had made himself inconvenient—to the Pope; to the rapacious Italian States that wanted to dismember their Tuscan neighbor; to unworthy citizens hungry to gratify private ambition against the common weal. Not a shadow of political crime had been proved. Not one stain had been detected on his private conduct. His fellow-monks, including one who had once been his secretary and was cultivated enough to criticize his rule as Prior, bore witness—even after the shock of his retraction—to an unimpeachable purity and consistency of life that had commanded their unsuspecting veneration.

Even the Pope had been unable to raise a charge of heresy against Fra Girolamo except on the ground of disobedience to a mandate and disregard of the sentence of excommunication. It was difficult to justify that breach of discipline by argument; but there was a moral uprising in grave minds against the Court of Rome which tended to confound the tidy distinction between the Church and churchmen, and so to lighten the scandal of disobedience. Men of ordinary morality and public spirit felt that the triumph of the Frate’s enemies was the triumph of gross license. Keen Florentines like Soderini and Piero Guicciardini may well have smiled angrily at a severity which dispensed with law in order to hang and burn a man in whom the seductions of a public career had warped the strictness of his veracity; may well have remarked that if the Frate had mixed a deeper fraud with a zeal and ability less inconvenient to high personages, the fraud would have been regarded as a useful oil for ecclesiastical and political wheels.

Nevertheless, such shrewd men were forced to admit that however poor a figure the Florentine government made in its clumsy pretense of judicial warrant for what had been predetermined as policy, the measures of the Pope against Savonarola were measures of self-defense. Not to try to rid himself of a man who wanted to stir the Powers of Europe to summon a General Council and depose him would have been adding ineptitude to iniquity. There was no denying that toward Alexander the Sixth Savonarola was a rebel—and, much more, a dangerous rebel. Florence had heard him say, and had understood, that he would not obey the devil. It was inevitably a life-and-death struggle between the Frate and the Pope; but it was less inevitable that Florence should make itself the Pope’s executioner.

Romola’s ears were filled all day with these suggestions: faith, still ardent under its wounds, and worldly discernment, measuring human nature by what it called possibility. She could be satisfied with neither. In the pauses of her household—when she had sent Tessa with a basket to fetch greens, when she herself had listened to the small bubbling of the pot as the beans softened, when she had broken stale bread into a bowl and let it drink broth until it turned again to tenderness—she brought her mind back to the printed document with a steady, painful attention. She had observed things through the years of her discipleship—things recorded half consciously, like smells that lodge in cloth—that whispered a presentiment Savonarola’s retraction was not merely a spasm to escape torture. But against that whisper rose the cry of her own soul for some explanation that would still let her believe the main striving of his life had been pure and grand.

She remembered, too, her recent season of selfish discontent—the blighting wind that had come with the loss of her trust, drying her inward world until good seemed tasteless. The recollection produced in her that strange reaction known to those who have been down into despair: a kind of faith springing up from the depths, not because it is easy, but because without it life becomes unendurable. It was impossible, she told herself now, that the negative, disbelieving thoughts which had made her soul so arid could be founded in the truth of things. Impossible that it had not been a living spirit, and no hollow pretense, that once breathed in the Frate’s words and kindled new life in her. Whatever falsehood there had been in him had been a fall, not a purpose: an entanglement that tightened gradually, in which he struggled, not a contrivance nourished by success.

Looking at the printed confessions, she saw sentences that bore the stamp of bungling fabrication—heavy emphasis, crude repetition in self-accusation, such as none but the lowest hypocrites use when speaking to other men. And precisely because those sentences struck so harshly against the rest—against the man she had known, and against the general tone of what was printed—she was strengthened in the impression that the remainder represented, in the main, what had really fallen from his lips. Hardly a word was dishonorable to him except what turned on his prophetic annunciations. He was unvarying in his statement of the ends he had pursued for Florence, for the Church, for the world; and apart from the mixture of falsity in the claim to special inspiration by which he had sought to lay hold of men’s minds, there was no admission of unworthy means. Even in this confession, even with the notary’s malign phrases left standing like grit under the teeth, Fra Girolamo shone as a man who had sought his own glory indeed, but sought it by laboring for the highest end—the moral welfare of men—not by vague exhortations, but by striving to turn beliefs into energies that would work through all the details of life.

One passage fixed itself in her memory as a taste does—sharp, lasting, impossible to rinse away:

“Everything that I have done, I have done with the design of being for ever famous in the present and in future ages; and that I might win credit in Florence; and that nothing of great import should be done without my sanction. And when I had thus established my position in Florence, I had it in my mind to do great things in Italy and beyond Italy, by means of those chief personages with whom I had contracted friendship and consulted on high matters, such as this of the General Council. And in proportion as my first efforts succeeded, I should have adopted further measures. Above all, when the General Council had once been brought about, I intended to rouse the princes of Christendom, and especially those beyond the borders of Italy, to subdue the infidels. It was not much in my thoughts to get myself made a Cardinal or Pope, for when I should have achieved the work I had in view, I should, without being Pope, have been the first man in the world in the authority I should have possessed, and the reverence that would have been paid me. If I had been made Pope, I would not have refused the office: but it seemed to me that to be the head of that work was a greater thing than to be Pope, because a man without virtue may be Pope; but such a work as I contemplated demanded a man of excellent virtues.”

That blending of ambition with belief in the supremacy of goodness was no new tone to Romola. She had been used to hear it ring through the Duomo—the same metal struck, the same resonance. It was Savonarola’s habit to conceive great things and to feel himself the man to do them. Iniquity should be brought low; justice, purity, love should triumph; and they should triumph by his voice, his work, his blood. In moments of ecstatic contemplation, doubtless, the sense of self melted into the sense of the Unspeakable, and there lay the elements of genuine self-abasement. But in the presence of fellow-men whom he must move, pre-eminence seemed a condition of life itself.

Perhaps, Romola thought, even when the confession described a doubleness conscious and deliberate, it implied no more than that wavering of belief about one’s own impressions and motives to which any human being not made stupid by inflexible self-confidence must be liable under a marked change of outward conditions. In the Frate’s tumultuous life, what room there was for altered self-judgment when, instead of eyes that venerated and knees that knelt, instead of a great work visibly on its way to fulfillment and stamping its agent as chosen, there came hooting and spitting and curses; then the hard faces of enemies sitting as judges; then the horrible torture; and with the torture, the irrepressible cry: It is true, what you would have me say—let me go—do not torture me again—yes, yes, I am guilty. O God! Thy stroke has reached me!

As Romola thought of the anguish that must have followed—whether, in the subsequent solitude of the prison, conscience retracted or confirmed the self-taxing words—that anguish seemed to press upon her own heart and draw out slow, bitter tears. Every vulgar, self-ignorant person in Florence was pronouncing glibly on the man’s demerits, while he was knowing a depth of sorrow that can be known only by the soul that has loved and sought the most perfect thing and beholds itself fallen.

She had not then seen—what she would see later—the evidence of the Frate’s state of mind after he had thus laid his mouth in the dust. As the days went by, the reports of new unpublished examinations—reports that had drawn the city’s curiosity as the smell of roasting draws a crowd—ceased. Savonarola was left alone in his prison, and for a while they allowed him pen and ink, that he might use his bruised and strained right arm to write. He wrote. But what he wrote was no vindication, no protest, no clever argument to shake his enemies’ hold. It was a continued colloquy with the divine purity to which he sought complete reunion; an outpouring of self-abasement; a long cry for inward renovation. No lingering echoes of the old vehement self-assertion—Look at my work, for it is good, and those who set their faces against it are children of the devil. Instead, the voice of Sadness told him: God placed thee in the midst of the people even as if thou hadst been one of the excellent. In this way thou hast taught others and hast failed to learn thyself. Thou hast cured others, and thou thyself hast been still diseased. Thy heart was lifted up at the beauty of thy own deeds, and through this thou hast lost thy wisdom and art become, and shalt be to all eternity, nothing. After so many benefits with which God has honored thee, thou art fallen into the depths of the sea; and after so many gifts bestowed on thee, thou, by thy pride and vainglory, hast scandalised all the world.

And when Hope spoke and argued that divine love had not forsaken him, it said nothing now of a great work to be done, nothing of Florence saved and nations moved. It only said: Thou art not forsaken—else why is thy heart bowed in penitence? That too is a gift.

There is no worthy evidence that from the time of his imprisonment to the supreme moment Savonarola thought or spoke of himself as a martyr. Martyrdom had been for him a passion dividing the dream of the future with the triumph of beholding his work achieved. And now, in place of both, had come a resignation which he called by no glorifying name. But therefore he may the more fitly be called a martyr by his fellow-men to all time. For power rose against him not because of his sins but because of his greatness—not because he sought to deceive the world, but because he sought to make it noble. And through that greatness he endured a double agony: not only reviling, torture, and the death-throe, but the agony of sinking from the vision of glorious achievement into that deep shadow where he could only say, I count as nothing; darkness encompasses me; yet the light I saw was the true light.

Romola could not drive from her mind the sentence that had gone from mouth to mouth through Florence, repeating itself like the refrain of a street-song no one dared to sing aloud in full: “Pray for me, for God has withdrawn from me the spirit of prophecy.”

It was not the words alone that shook her, but the sound of them as they were carried—broken by corners, thinned by distance, thickened by crowds—through the city’s lanes and under its arches. Florence had a way, in those days, of making every judgment a kind of chorus. Even when a man whispered, the stones seemed to take it up and give it back, altered. Those syllables, once spoken within the walls of San Marco, had become something else on the Piazza: half pity, half triumph, and always, always noise.

And with the noise came new reports, piteous enough to make certainty feel like cruelty. On the nineteenth of May, under a sunshine that made the Arno look harmless and the city’s washed walls seem newly forgiven, the two Papal Commissaries rode in to finish the trial. They entered to acclamations—acclamations not for justice, nor even for peace, but for a scapegoat.

Now the cry ran, “It is the Frate’s deception that has brought on all our misfortunes; let him be burned, and all things will be right, and our evils will cease.” Romola heard it as one hears an ugly tune hammered out by boys on a door: the rhythm of it was simple enough to catch anyone, and all the more dangerous for that.

The next day there was fresh torture—fresh, as if pain were a loaf that could be cut again and again from the same scant dough. Savonarola’s shattered, sensitive frame was brought to meet the implements; and at the first sight of them he fell in convulsed agitation to his knees. In brief, passionate words he retracted his confession—declared he had spoken falsely when he denied his prophetic gift, and that if he suffered, he would suffer for the truth.

“The things that I have spoken, I had them from God.”

It did not save him. The torture was laid on still; and under it he was asked why he had uttered those retracting words. Men were not demons in those days—Romola clung to that thought, the way one clings to the memory of a familiar domestic sound when the city outside is howling—but the law of the chamber held that only concessions of guilt counted as reasons for release.

And the answer came, dreadful in its human doubleness: “I said it that I might seem good; tear me no more, I will tell you the truth.”

There were Florentine assessors there; words did not stay inside the chamber. These two retractions—one from confession, one from retraction—ran out into the streets like spilled oil, impossible to gather back. They entered Romola’s mind and made everything slide. Doubt, which she had tried to hold at the edge of her life, came and sat down at the hearth.

But another thought—sharp as a blade and just as cold—flashed through her. There would be a moment when he could speak without hope of escape; when dread of pain would no longer bargain with dread of falsehood; when they had brought him into the presence of death. When he was lifted above the people and looked on them for the last time, they could not hinder him from a final, decisive word.

I will be there.

Three days later, on the twenty-third of May, 1498, the Piazza was prepared again. A long narrow platform stretched across it from the Palazzo Vecchio towards the Tetta de’ Pisani. But there was no grove of fuel as before—no cunningly arranged thicket to pretend at some old rite. Instead, there was one great heap of fuel set on the circular area at the platform’s end: wood stacked as if it were winter provision for a poor quarter, except that this was provision for a different kind of hunger.

Above it rose a gibbet with three halters. It had two arms, and in spite of care to avoid resemblance—one arm sawn short—it still looked enough like a cross to make some beholders uneasy, as if the city had tried to disguise a sacrilege and failed.

On the marble terrace of the Palazzo stood three tribunals: one by the door for the Bishop, who would perform the degradation of Fra Girolamo and the two brethren chosen to suffer as his followers and accomplices; another for the Papal Commissaries, to pronounce them heretics and schismatics and deliver them to the secular arm; and a third near Marzocco, close to where the platform began, for the Gonfaloniere and the Eight, who were to pronounce sentence of death.

Again the Piazza was thronged with expectant faces; again there was to be a great fire kindled. In the mass pressed around the gibbet the expectation had the hard glitter of hatred, or the stony stare of curiosity that finds its entertainment in barbarity. Yet there were still those—Piagnoni, insulted, grieving, enduring—who kept a last thin thread of hope, that God would interpose with some sign, even now, to declare His servant.

And there were more, trembling as Romola trembled, who looked forward to that final moment not for a miracle of flame or storm, but for a sentence: “O people, I was innocent of deceit.”

Romola stood at a window on the north side of the Piazza, far from the marble terrace and its formal cruelty. Near her, also looking on with painful uncertainty, was a young Florentine of two-and-twenty, Jacopo Nardi—one of those rare men whose love of a great figure is not stronger than their desire to tell the truth about him.

He watched Romola’s struggle between shuddering horror and the yearning to witness what might happen at the last, and said to her with respectful gentleness, “Madonna, there is no need for you to look at these cruel things. I will tell you when he comes out of the Palazzo. Trust to me; I know what you would see.”

Romola covered her face. But sound is a tyrant even when eyes are shut. The hootings rose and fell like a dirty tide; the crowd’s voices rubbed against one another—coarse laughter, splintered curses, the sharp, nasal mockery that turns human suffering into a jest. In the midst of it she heard other things too: the hollow tremor of the platform under many feet; a bell in the distance that kept its own slow truth; the faint clatter of metal that might have been a soldier’s harness, or might have been the implements waiting.

At last Jacopo touched her arm. “He comes.”

She looked.

Savonarola was led out in his Dominican garb. Even at that distance she could see how the robe hung on him, as if cloth itself had become heavy with the months of prison and strain. He was brought before the Bishop, and the ceremony began: stripped of the black mantle, the white scapulary, the long white tunic—piece by piece, like a household taking away a table’s linen after a feast has been declared sinful. There is something in degradation, apart from hatred, that the baser part of any multitude understands and enjoys: it is the satire of it, the sudden transformation of a man into “only a man,” as if that were humiliation enough.

When he stood in the close woollen under-tunic, telling of no sacred office and no rank, there rose another hoot of triumph. He had been degraded, cut off from the Church Militant; and to eyes eager for simple pictures, that was proof.

The three degraded brethren passed on to the tribunal of the Papal Commissaries. “Schismatic,” “heretic”—the words rang out with a kind of official neatness, as if naming could finish the work and leave the speakers clean. Then they were led past the third tribunal—that of Florentine officials to pronounce the sentence; and even from her window, Romola could discern among them Dolfo Spini, odious in his grave black lucco, one of the Eight. His very stillness seemed like a sneer.

Then the three figures, in their close white raiment, began to tread along the platform amidst yells and grating tones of insult.

“Cover your eyes, Madonna,” Jacopo murmured. “Fra Girolamo will be the last.”

Romola did not keep them covered long. The compulsion to see was like thirst: it returned as soon as one tried to deny it.

Savonarola had mounted the steps. He was not far off now. She could see him look round upon the multitude.

For one instant the air seemed to pull itself taut, as when a cook pauses with the knife above the herb-bundle, listening for a child’s footfall—waiting for the one sound that will change what comes next. It was the instant of expectation, when even hatred wants its victim to play his part well.

But in that same moment, expectation died. Romola saw what he was seeing: torches waving to kindle the fuel beneath his dead body, their flames restless and hungry; faces glaring with a yet worse light than the torches gave. She heard what he was hearing: gross jests flung up at him like refuse, taunts and curses that tasted of sour wine and stale garlic in the breath that carried them.

The moment was past. Whatever word she had dreamed of—whatever final clear note that might cut through all this noise—was swallowed. She covered her face again; and though the Piazza still roared, and the city still strained to be heard, she knew only this: Savonarola’s voice had passed into eternal silence.

* * *

On the evening of the twenty-second of May, 1509, five persons whose lives had crossed and recrossed in ways none of them could have foreseen were seated in a handsome upper room opening onto a loggia. From its right-hand corner one could look along the Borgo Pinti and over the city gate towards Fiesole and the solemn heights beyond—those hills that kept their own old language of wind and bird-call when cities forgot.

At one end of the room an archway opened into a narrow inner recess where light fell from above on a small altar covered with fair white linen. Over it hung a picture, discernible at the distance of the seated party only as the small full-length portrait of a Dominican Brother. Branches and wreaths of flowers shaded it from the overhead light; the fresh tapers below it were unlit, waiting. Yet the decoration was not complete. Part of the floor was strewn with green boughs and a confusion of flowers—some still cool with evening, some already breathing out sweetness as they warmed.

Among them sat a delicate blue-eyed girl of thirteen, tossing her long light-brown hair out of her eyes as she chose blossoms for the wreaths she was weaving, or looked up at her mother’s work and told her how to do it with an air of gentle authority—like one correcting the pinch of salt in a sauce, not out of pride but out of instinctive rightness.

For Tessa was not clever at weaving flowers, nor had her fingers grown more adroit with time—only much fatter. She went slowly, turning her head this way and that, asking Ninna’s opinion with sincere deference. Tessa never ceased to be astonished at the wisdom of her children. She still wore her contadina gown—only broader now; and the silver pin was in her rough curly brown hair. Around her neck lay the memorable necklace: a red cord under it, ending mysteriously in her bosom. Her rounded face had an even more perfect look of childish content than it had borne in youth: everybody was so good, she thought. Even Monna Brigida never found fault now; she did little else than sleep—which, to Tessa’s mind, was an amiable practice and one she herself enjoyed.

Monna Brigida was asleep at that moment in a straight-backed arm-chair a couple of yards away. Her hair, parting backward under her black hood, had that soft whiteness that is like nothing else—simply the lovely whiteness of aged hair. Her chin had sunk on her bosom; her hands rested on the chair’s elbow. She had not been weaving or helping; she had been looking on, as usual, and as usual had fallen asleep.

The other two figures were seated farther off, at the wide doorway opening onto the loggia. Lillo sat on the ground with his back against the angle of the doorpost, long legs stretched out, a large book open on his knee. Now and then he made a dash at an inquisitive fly with a livelier interest than he gave to the finely printed copy of Petrarch held open at one place, as if he were learning something by heart.

Romola sat nearly opposite him, but her eyes were fixed absently on the distant mountains. Life’s eager strain had left its marks: the finely moulded cheek had sunk a little; the golden crown of hair was less massive. Yet there was a placidity in her face that had never belonged to it in youth, as if the worst sorrows—known once, while life was new—had burned away a certain fever of expectation and left only a steadier warmth.

At first she was not aware that Lillo had stopped looking at his book and was watching her with a slightly impatient air—wanting to talk, but unsure whether she would accept the interruption. But persevering looks make themselves felt. Romola turned from the mountains and met his dark gaze; her smile grew brighter as she looked at him, as if he had called her back by sound alone.

He shuffled closer, still keeping the book on his lap, until he could lodge his chin on her knee.

“What is it, Lillo?” she said, pulling his hair back from his brow.

He was a handsome lad, but his features were turning more massive and less regular than his father’s: the Tuscan peasant blood showed itself, like the darker grain in a loaf made from mixed flours.

“Mamma—Romola, what am I to be?” he asked, well content that there was now a prospect of talk until it would be too late to con “Spirto gentil” any longer.

“What should you like to be, Lillo? You might be a scholar. My father was a scholar, you know, and taught me a great deal. That is why I can teach you.”

“Yes,” Lillo said, hesitating. “But he is old and blind in the picture. Did he get a great deal of glory?”

“Not much, Lillo. The world was not always kind to him. He saw meaner men put into higher places because they could flatter and say what was false. And then his dear son thought it right to leave him and become a monk; after that my father, blind and lonely, felt unable to do the things that would have made his learning of greater use to men—so that he might still have lived in his works after he was in his grave.”

“I should not like that sort of life,” Lillo said promptly. “I should like to be something that would make me a great man, and very happy besides—something that would not hinder me from having a good deal of pleasure.”

“That is not easy, my Lillo,” Romola said. “It is only a poor sort of happiness that comes from caring very much about our own narrow pleasures. The highest happiness—the kind that can go with being a great man—comes from wide thoughts and much feeling for the rest of the world as well as ourselves. And often it brings so much pain with it that we can only tell it from pain by this: that we would choose it before everything else, because our souls see it is good.”

Her voice had that quiet rhythm which, in a house, can steady even restless children: not the rhythm of a sermon shouted at a crowd, but of counsel given while hands are busy and flowers are being sorted. Outside, through the open doorway, Florence had its usual evening sounds—distant footsteps, a cart rumbling where stones were uneven, a calling voice softened by distance. In the loggia the air carried the scent of bruised greenery and blossom; every movement among the strewn boughs released another small cloud of sweetness.

“There are so many things wrong and difficult in the world,” Romola went on, “that no man can be great—he can hardly keep himself from wickedness—unless he gives up thinking much about pleasure or rewards, and gets strength to endure what is hard and painful. My father had the greatness that belongs to integrity; he chose poverty and obscurity rather than falsehood. And there was Fra Girolamo—you know why I keep to-morrow sacred: he had the greatness that belongs to a life spent in struggling against powerful wrong, and trying to raise men to the highest deeds they are capable of.”

Lillo’s eyes were fixed on her now, no longer wandering to the fly.

“So, my Lillo,” she said, “if you mean to act nobly and seek to know the best things God has put within reach of men, you must learn to fix your mind on that end, and not on what will happen to you because of it. Remember, if you were to choose something lower and make it the rule of your life to seek your own pleasure and escape what is disagreeable—calamity might come just the same. And it would be calamity falling on a base mind. That is the one form of sorrow that has no balm in it, and that may well make a man say, ‘It would have been better for me if I had never been born.’”

She paused, as if the words had brought a taste into her mouth that she did not wish to deepen. Her hands took Lillo’s cheeks between them; his young eyes met hers, intent and a little troubled.

“I will tell you something, Lillo,” she said.

He waited, still as a child listening to an old tale—half craving its horror, half afraid of it.

“There was a man,” Romola said, and her voice grew unsteady, “to whom I was very near, so that I could see a great deal of his life. He made almost every one fond of him: he was young, clever, beautiful, and his manners were gentle and kind. I believe, when I first knew him, he never thought of anything cruel or base. But because he tried to slip away from everything unpleasant, and cared for nothing so much as his own safety—he came at last to commit some of the basest deeds. He denied his father and left him to misery; he betrayed every trust that was reposed in him, that he might keep himself safe and get rich and prosperous. Yet calamity overtook him.”

Again she paused. The room was full of small domestic sounds—the dry whisper of petals as Ninna chose them, the faint scrape of Tessa’s clumsy fingers among stems, the soft breathing of Monna Brigida asleep. These were sounds that kept memory from becoming only a story: they insisted on the present.

Lillo looked up at Romola with awed wonder, as if he had been shown, in a single sentence, how a familiar dialect can be turned against itself—how words like “safety,” “prosperity,” “pleasure” can hide a cruelty that does not name itself.

“Another time, my Lillo,” Romola said, drawing back from what she might have confessed further. “I will tell you another time. See—there are our old Piero di Cosimo and Nello coming up the Borgo Pinti, bringing us their flowers. Let us go and wave our hands to them, that they may know we see them.”

They rose and stood at the corner of the loggia, looking down the street. The evening air brought with it the city’s layered murmur, softened now: a vendor’s last call, a shutter closing, the distant splash of water poured into a basin. Under it all, like a remembered refrain, Florence carried the older sounds of human life at rest—so different from the roar Romola had heard on the day of fire.

“How queer old Piero is!” Lillo said, as the two figures approached, burdened with their flowers, the greenery bobbing with each step. “He abuses you for dressing the altar and thinking so much of Fra Girolamo, and yet he brings you the flowers.”

“Never mind,” Romola said quietly. “There are many good people who did not love Fra Girolamo. Perhaps I should never have learned to love him if he had not helped me when I was in great need.”

And as she waved, the gesture seemed to bind together what Florence so often tore apart: the public cry and the private grief, the remembered voice and the last silence, the wreaths being woven by a child’s sure hands and the unlit tapers waiting beneath a painted Dominican’s calm gaze.
